en: Dharma is the foundation of the entire world;
this is the Prajñāpāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Granthamālā Mīmāṃsākoṣa.
Fourth Part: (Ja–Na) Editor:
Brahmabhūta: Kevalānandasarasvatī;
Phālguna, bright fortnight, 7th day, Monday; Śaka year 1877. Publisher’s Note.

The authors of this Mīmāṃsā-koṣa, my venerable teachers Kevalānandasvāmī, departed for the state of Brahman, leaving behind this impermanent world, even before completing its printing and publication. Nevertheless, out of being overcome by compassion, they personally brought the composition of the Koṣa to completion; it was only through their grace that the printing and publication were to be finalized.
This fourth volume, whose printing was commenced in their very presence, is being published today on this auspicious anniversary of their first year.
We desire to print and publish whatever other volumes remain in due order every year.
The compilation, printing, and publication of these works could only be accomplished through the financial assistance of the provincial states, the Union of India, and the public, and not otherwise.

The venerable teachers have, out of compassion for their students and by their own power, spontaneously accomplished this task until the very last breath. Those who desire the advancement of knowledge must discharge this debt. We hope that the provincial states, the Indian Union, and those who cherish learning will provide financial and other assistance in the repayment of this obligation.
We joyfully announce that this compilation was completed by Śrī Raṅganātha Śāstrin, who is foremost in the task of accomplishing our work and devoted to the service of his guru’s feet.

Regarding the number of sections (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth: in this fourth part, there are 143 Bhāṣya sections, 37 Saṃkarṣa sections, 173 Kevalānandīya sections, 16 Tautātitā sections, 279 Nyāyas, and 3,840 Laghusiddhāntas.
Now, beginning from the first part, there are 599 *bhāṣya* sections, 184 *saṃkarṣa* sections, 456 *Kevalānandīya* sections, 36 *Tautātitā* sections, 905 *nyāyas*, and 13,163 *laghusiddhāntas*.
[This was written] on the 7th day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna by Lakṣmaṇa Śāstrī Jośī, Tarkatīrtha, Director of the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala, Chief Editor of the Dharmakośa.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the sprinkling with clarified butter (*ājyavyāghāraṇa*) occurs only at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). Having prescribed, "He sprinkles the Viṣṇus," the rule concludes with the injunction, "At the third [pressing] with clarified butter. Thus, the sprinkling is enjoined specifically for the third pressing.

In that context, the word "at the third" (*tṛtīye*) merely restates what is already established, while the injunction serves to prescribe only the accessory (*guṇa*) characterized by clarified butter.
Because a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) would result from restricting both [the time and the ritual] to two specific times;
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.17 states that in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the drawing of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup occurs only at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
A woman who has conceived between [the first and second pressings] should [participate] because of the statement regarding the third pressing.
The Commentary: Now, this is considered.
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Regarding it, it is heard in scripture: "He who takes up the Ṣoḍaśī [cup] bestows power and vigor upon himself.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should it be taken up at each pressing (savana), or only at the third pressing?
What is established? That it occurs at each pressing (*savana*). Why? Because it is heard in scripture that one "takes up the *ṣoḍaśin* at every pressing.
And when an action is defined by verbal testimony, verbal testimony is our authority.
"Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśī cup is drawn at each pressing.
This being the position reached, we reply:
its drawing should take place at the third pressing.
Why? Because of a scriptural statement.
For there is indeed such a statement: "At the third pressing, he draws the Ṣoḍaśin from the Āgrayaṇa."
Our word is the authority;
therefore, it should be drawn at the third pressing.
As for what was said—that the *ṣoḍaśī* cup is to be drawn at every pressing—[that is not so].
This is equal to the taking of the draughts at the third pressing. How so? "It is to be taken at the morning pressing;
the morning pressing is indeed splendor."
The thunderbolt is fashioned from brilliance alone;
it is to be drawn at the midday pressing.
Indeed, the midday pressing is vigor.
He fashions the thunderbolt from vital energy alone.
It is to be drawn at the third pressing;
for the third pressing is indeed cattle.
He fashions the thunderbolt from the very cattle;
for if he were to take it at the morning pressing, the thunderbolt would be left over at the later pressings.
"If it were at the midday pressing, one would strike the thunderbolt in the middle;
it is to be drawn at the third pressing.
Thus he draws it at all pressings, for it has not been brought down during the earlier pressings."

Śālikanātha: What, then, is the reason for this intermediate inquiry? (Anticipating and refuting the reason stated by the Prābhākara: In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the root section (*mūlādhikaraṇa*), the *ukthya* will be declared to be an indicator of time (*kālopalakṣaṇa*). Once that is settled, it would be impossible to suspect the drawing of [the cups] during the two preceding pressings (*savana*), because those two lack the *ukthya*.
Therefore, if you say that it was considered in the middle [of the work], that is incorrect.
Even so, the deliberation regarding what ought to be done should follow the completion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), not in its midst.
Furthermore, based on such statements as "it is to be drawn at the morning pressing" (*prātaḥsavane grahītavyaḥ*), the drawing of this [cup] during all three pressings is suspected;
and no obstacle to the authority of that scriptural statement is possible.

Therefore, although it is not possible [to perform the Ukthya] at a time subsequent to the two earlier pressings because of the absence of the Ukthya in them, nevertheless, it must be accepted on the strength of the scriptural injunction. As for the mention of the time, it will be intended to refer to the taking of the draughts in the third pressing. (He refutes the opponent's view: It is indeed found that the Ukthya exists even in the two earlier pressings (i.e., the existence of the Kratu-Ukthya in the two earlier pressings).

(He states the purpose for the intermediate reflection according to his own view: Therefore, the author of the Sūtras follows diverse paths; one must simply say that even amidst one reflection, he has introduced another reflection due to a relevant occasion (*prasaṅga*). [As in the verse: "In the pressings, either at the third, or by the mention of 'three,' it would be in all three."
Two [options] are censured; let the third injunction alone be accepted therein.

Bhaṭṭa: This section (adhikaraṇa), although placed by the author of the Sūtras within the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) of the preceding section for the sake of ease of exposition, is now treated separately.

In considering whether the appearance of the Ṣoḍaśin cup should be taken as a rule in all three pressings (savana), or only optionally in the third pressing alone, it is beyond dispute that, according to the statement of another school, "He draws [the cup] at each pressing," which is not subordinate to anything else, it must indeed be drawn in all three pressings.

And therefore, by virtue of being part of the same syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that [text], [it is understood that] "he is to be drawn at the morning pressing" (*prātaḥsavane grāhyaḥ*); for the morning pressing is indeed splendor (*tejas*), [and thus it serves] for the attainment of splendor. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, at the third pressing, within the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)... [in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*].

Thus he fashions the thunderbolt. It is to be drawn at the midday pressing; the midday pressing is indeed brilliance, so it is from brilliance itself that he fashions the thunderbolt. It is to be drawn at the third pressing; the third pressing is indeed cattle, so it is for the sake of cattle that he fashions the thunderbolt.

If he were to draw it at the morning pressing, it would be left over for the subsequent pressings; if he were to draw it at the midday pressing, he would strike the thunderbolt in the middle. Therefore, it is to be drawn at the third pressing.

Furthermore, although there is a statement in another school (*śālā*) saying, "Therefore, [the *saṃgrahaṇī*] is to be performed at all *savanas*; it was not brought [as such] at the morning *savana*," it is nevertheless prescribed for the three *savanas* alone.

This is because the gerundive suffix (*kṛtyapratyaya*) in the word "to be taken" (*grāhyaḥ*) is heard everywhere; otherwise, as in the case of "one should praise with a *sāman*," this rule would lack authority. Moreover, since no term of the *Mīmāṃsā* (critical analysis) is heard here—as in the case of the *Tryambaka* passage—it is untenable to assume that this is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).

In accordance with the principle of generic characteristics (*jātilakṣaṇanyāya*), for the sake of achieving syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the preceding injunction, one should assume the injunction as it is stated; however, the alternative assumption of an injunction pertaining specifically to the third extraction (*tārtīyasavanika*) need not be suspected, because its attainment of syntactic unity with other recensional branches (*śālāntara*) is no different [from the former], and because it would necessitate further hypothetical construction (*kalpāpādaka*).

This being the case, since it is determined that the passage—preceded by a censure of the morning pressing (*pūrvasavana*)—is intended solely for the injunction of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) alone, the restriction of the previous injunction is also understood to be subordinate to it, in order to achieve syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*) according to the maxim of the *jatila-yavāgū* (the wild rice gruel). There is no harm even if there is no syntactic unity with another recension (*śālā*), because the option (*vikalpa*) arises as its result and is therefore not a defect.
In this specific recension, the injunction pertains only to the third pressing; furthermore, by including all three pressings, there is an abundance of results.
Nor is there an absence of the *ukthya* following the first two pressings (*savana*), because the *ukthya* status exists in all three pressings.
Maṇḍana states: "That [Ṣoḍaśin] is certainly to be drawn at the third pressing.
That is the Ṣoḍaśin.
Śaṅkara: "And that [occurs] at the third pressing. 10. Oṃ: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, at the third pressing, there is a double spreading of the sacrificial seats (dvirviṣṇya-viharaṇa).

There are three ways of arranging the *dhiṣṇya* hearths according to the distinction of the *savana*s (pressings). With reference to these, there are injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*) such as: "At the morning pressing they arrange [the hearths] with fuel-sticks; at the third [pressing], with *śalākā* sticks.
Since there is no injunction of a subordinate quality for a fourth [pressing], there is no fourth arrangement.
This being the case, the accomplishment of the fourth *viharaṇa* (spreading apart) follows from the injunction: "One should perform the *jyotiṣṭoma* for the *adhiṣṇya* fires.

Nor should it be argued that, as in the case following the command (*praiṣa*) "Perform the *jyotiṣṭoma* for the fires," the *jyotiṣṭoma* consists merely in the kindling by removing the ashes of the fires already spread apart during the third pressing;
for that is untenable, since the *adhiṣṇya* fires, unlike the great fires (*mahāgni*), do not undergo the ritual vigil (*jāgaraṇa*).
For this very reason, the statement "so many indeed are the bodies of Agni," and so forth, which mentions the number thirty-three for each, is consistent;
for in the absence of the fourth *viharaṇa*, there would result either an excess or a deficiency.
And that [calculation] is as follows:
There are twenty-eight [hearths] due to the fourfold establishment of the six *dhiṣṇya* hearths and the *mārjālīya*.
There are three each for the *śāmitra* and the *aupayājya* hearths due to the distinction between the animals. There are four *nirmanthya* hearths.

The Āgnīdhrīya fire together with the Mahāgnis makes five; this is the formal determination (saṃkalpa). 3|1|16. Oṃ: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana), the invocation of the deities for the Soma-oblation and the subsequent oblations need not be performed again.
Because there is no exclusion of the wife until the conclusion of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Vi. 12.2.14. In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the term *vahiṣpavamāna*—as in "the *vahiṣpavamāna* consists of thirty [verses]"—is a name (*nāmadheya*), not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Bhā.
4.1.2.3. Oṃ. In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the number one hundred and twelve is assigned [to the cows] as if they were protectors included within the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The Section on the Sacrificial Fee (Dakṣiṇā).
In the proximity of an injunction regarding substances, the number [mentioned] should pertain to those [substances], because it is a subordinate attribute (*guṇa*).

Bhāṣya: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [enjoined by the text]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. In that context, this is recited: "A cow, a horse, a mule, a donkey, goats, sheep, rice, barley, sesame, and beans; its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of one hundred and twelve."

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the number twelve hundred here refer to twelve hundred substances such as cows and so forth, or to a single substance? If it refers to a single substance, is there no restriction regarding which one it may be, or is it specifically beans (*māṣas*)? Or rather, is the number to be fulfilled by all [substances] combined, or by those of a single class?

When [the rule applies] to a single species, is it a restriction for any animal whatsoever, or specifically for cattle? When it is for cattle, is it a restriction for any particular cattle, or for cows? These will be the possible positions.

What, then, is the prima facie position? When substances are being enjoined, in the proximity of which substances? Of cows and the like. In what context are they being enjoined? In connection with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). A number is recited: "Its sacrificial fee consists of one hundred and twelve."
There would be a number for each one of those [animals], such as cows and so forth.
Why? Because the number is prescribed as a subordinate factor (guṇa), while the cows and so forth are the primary factors (pradhāna).
How so? The connection is not made in this way: "There should be one hundred and twelve."
How, then, is it? [The answer is: "One hundred and twelve for him.
In this way, the mention of "for him" (tasya) becomes meaningful;
otherwise, it would either be redundant or a mere restatement.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, even the singular number included within the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) would be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to the context of the primary rite. Furthermore,
when an accessory (*guṇa*) is enjoined in proximity to the principal acts, it is differentiated for each principal act.
And there is a purpose for this enumeration:
the substances, such as cows and so forth, are to be made to correspond in number to that [enumeration].
In that regard, no distinction is perceived.
Should all of this be performed, or not?
If the substance were not to possess this number, then the scriptural injunction regarding it would be contradicted.
Therefore, each individual substance is to be consecrated with this [formula].
*Dupā*: This topic (*adhikaraṇa*) has arisen by way of the discussion on the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
(Therefore, there is a contextual connection.
Alternatively, once the archetype (*prakṛti*) has been determined, there follows the consideration of the sacrificial fee in the modified rite (*vikṛti*).

(An investigation into the manner of the displacement of the sacrificial fee) A Sūtra exists [introducing an example]: Now, are the cows and other items subsidiary to the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) of this sentence, "It has one hundred and ninety *stotrīyā* verses"?

How so? Having stated, "It has one hundred and ninety *stotrīyā* verses," he says: "Of those, the one hundred and eighty [verses] are thirty-six *virāj*s; there are six seasons; thus the *virāj*s are established in the seasons" [6 x 6 = 36]. In this way, the *stotrīyā* verses are praised as being *virāj*s.

Then, from the [Taittirīya] section, it says: "Now, as for those ten [remaining stotriyas]: this is indeed the Virāj that is centered in the self (ātman-pratiṣṭhāpanī). These ten stotriyas are praised by means of the ten items beginning with the cow.
Therefore, because of this [explanatory passage], this [passage from the Chāndogya] is not an example.
What then is the example? One should look for such a statement in the Ādhvaryava [portion].
Or it may be considered a *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical argument).
Alternatively, this is merely an illustrative example from the *Chāndogya*:

"Its [sacrifice] consists of twelve hundred. If, in this sentence, the word "its" (*tasya*) were a qualifier of the specific sacrifice (*ṛtu*), it would fail to provide a justification for a specific course of action.

Although the cows and other items have been mentioned as *arthavādas* (explanatory passages), nevertheless, as they recur [in the mind], they alone are connected with the word *tasya* ("of that"). [The meaning is: "The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for that substance is one hundred and twelve.
The number belongs to that very thing indicated by the word *tat*.
However, it must be considered: of what does this reference by the word *tat* refer?
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): [The number] is connected with each individual cow and so forth.
Why? Because all cows and the rest are referred to by the word "that" (*tat*), and by means of the genitive case, the number is enjoined as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) belonging to them alone.
[Objection: But if there is a connection with many cows and the rest, would it not follow that the plural form "of them" (*teṣām*) should be used?

It is said: here, the cows and other items are the primary factors with respect to the number (and are thus denoted by that word); and the number of the item being denoted is not intended to be significant, just as in the case of a "house.
Alternatively, this is a connection based on the *tantra* principle: "that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); its [amount] is one hundred and twelve."

Even so (although there is an injunction regarding cows and other items with respect to the sacrificial fee, nevertheless), the number is subordinate to the substances because of the similarity of the word ending in the genitive case;
due to this equality, the qualities belong to each one individually because of their connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
Commentary: The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position.
"That each of them [should have] twelve hundred"—this is not so; it might apply to some one individual. Why? Because the qualities are equal.
For even the cows and so forth are connected with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), as is the number.
It is not the number that is enjoined for the cows and so forth;
rather, it is the sacrificial fee that is enjoined as qualified by the number, not the cows and so forth.

Why? Because if the number were not connected with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), then the number would be rendered meaningless by its connection with cows and other items whose quantity is otherwise unrestricted.
Furthermore, since the word "that" (*tat*) would be in grammatical apposition with the things numbered, the plural form would have to be used;
thus, in reference to the cows and so forth, the expression "one hundred and twelve" (*dvādaśaśatam*) would not appear in the singular.
Therefore, when this number is applied to any single substance that serves as the means of purchase, the purchase of that very substance is accomplished.
Consequently, the number belongs to one [substance], not to each individual one.
In this way, the hearing of the singular number will be consistent with its form.
Objection: Since it is a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the mention of that word is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Response:
Even if the mention is not intended to be significant, the number that is restated (*anūdyate*) must be expressed by that very mention.

Just as when it is stated by way of a defining characteristic that "one belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste must not be killed," the designation does not occur in the dual number, such as "two Brāhmaṇas must not be killed.
He says: "When referring to a genus (jāti), the plural number is used for a single entity."
The singular number is used for many, but the dual number is never used for one or for many.
Therefore, here there is an indication either by means of a plural-ending term or by means of a singular-ending term for many. To this it is replied:
This very same principle applies when a genus is denoted;
however, the genus is not conveyed by that word.
Rather, it denotes only the individual present [in proximity].
Therefore, it must be the number of some single [thing].
[Objection: But surely the number is subordinate to the substances.
Why? Because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

For instance, if the *tiṣṭhan* (standing) were enjoined with respect to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) within the Jyotiṣṭoma— since it is uttered only once and yet would have to apply to that [fee] within the Jyotiṣṭoma— then both the number (expressed by the genitive case) and the standing would have to be enjoined with respect to that [fee], resulting in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Furthermore, even if one were to accept a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) and enjoin the number with reference to that [gift] by means of the word *tat* (i.e., *tad-uddeśena*), even so, the number would not be an integral part (*anaṅga*) of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because it is not enjoined with respect to it—as stated in the rule: "In that case, there is the fault of a single sentence" (*tatraikam avamājo ’jñam*, 4.1.5.11). How so? Even in the case of a simultaneous connection (*tantra-sambandha*), the cows and other items are themselves qualified by the number (but the number is not qualified by the sacrificial fee). In that regard, the faults such as syntactical split have already been mentioned [in the discussion on] "there is one" (*tatraikam*); those same faults would apply here as well.
Therefore, the triad consisting of the cows and so forth, the number, and that word (*tacchabda*) is enjoined with respect to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Since that word refers to the substance, the rule "when denoting a genus" (*jātyākhyāyām*) does not apply here either.
Or rather, it would apply only in its proximity, for the connection is established through syntactical unity (*vākya*).
Commentary: This is a sūtra following the preceding word.
When [the gift] included within the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma... in the Jyotiṣṭoma included within the sacrificial fee.
If one is encouraged by twelve hundred measures of rice, would that [rice] constitute his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)?
We say: no;
for a sacrificial fee is that which causes capability (*dakṣa-karaṇī*).
Skill is power.
That which brings about destruction is not skillful;
therefore, that which brings about destruction is not a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*).
The state of being satiated is the subject of the statement’s excess.
He says: even for those who know the *vrīhi* grains, [the merit] amounts to twelve hundred, and it produces whatever measure of strength there may be.
To this it is replied: this so-called "strength" is relative;
for that very same person is stronger with respect to one [person], yet weaker with respect to another.

In this context, "āśitambhava" means the absence of weakness; for one who possesses strength becomes so through being nourished (*āśita*). Thus, from the point of being nourished onwards, it is the production of strength.
Therefore, that substance which is *āśitambhava* is *bhūti* (prosperity), and that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
When it is established that more than that [is required] for the purpose of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it occurs by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement.

In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) known as the *ṛtapeya*, by the authority of the scriptural statement, even the offering of a small amount of milk is prescribed in place of the sacrificial fee; this is the *somacamas* (Soma-cup).
That [cup] is established through its dependence on its substrate.

All animals, however, have the Jyotiṣṭoma as their primary [archetype], according to the division of directions [in the ritual manuals]. At the Jyotiṣṭoma, during the Dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice, it is said: "With the fringe of the *daśāpavitra*, he cleanses the cup (*graha*)."
In that case, the cleansing must be performed for all the cups (*graha*), not for just one;
the singular number in the word "cup" (*graham*) is not intended to be restrictive.

(Sūtras 3.1.13–15). Regarding the division of directions in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, after the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation sacrifice], the *Ārambhaṇīyā-iṣṭi* [commencement sacrifice] should be performed first.
Because it begins with the commencement [of the sacrifice].

10.1.2. Oṃ. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the accomplishment of consecration (*dīkṣā*) is achieved through the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice; it is not by means of the staff and other items alone. Therefore, the performance of the duties of the consecrated (*dīkṣita-dharma*) takes place at the conclusion of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*.
One becomes initiated (*dīkṣita*) through the announcement by another, because of the connection with all the elements of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Commentary: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard: "One being initiated should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.
Likewise: "He initiates him with a staff; he initiates him with a girdle; he initiates him with a black antelope skin," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does one become initiated by all [the rites], or is one initiated by those that are desired? What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is by all.
Why? Because of the connection with initiation.

There is a connection with initiation (*dīkṣā*); "he initiates him with a staff" means "he performs initiation for him. If it were accepted that [the staff] itself is the initiated one, how could one perform its initiation with a staff?
Therefore, by that which is desired [as the agent], it is not the initiated one.
Furthermore, we do not observe the word "initiated" (dīkṣita) being applied to this [act]. However, the word "initiated" is used in reference to the formal announcement (āvedana).
Therefore, one would not be considered initiated merely by that much.
Furthermore, when conjunction is possible, an alternative is not logical;
there would be a contradiction in one case,
whereby the injunction regarding the performance would be sublated.

Therefore, even though the remaining [passage] expresses a connection with initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) within the injunction of performance; thus, one should become initiated at the time of the announcement. As stated in the *Ṭup-ṭīkā*: "He initiates with a staff" means "he effects initiation by means of a staff" (due to the use of the instrumental case), so the staff is for the purpose of initiation.
The offering to Agni-Viṣṇu (*āgnāvaiṣṇava*) is also for the purpose of initiation, because of its syntactic connection with the word "being initiated" (*dīkṣiyamāṇa*).
Therefore, he is initiated at the very end.
For if he were initiated by means of the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu, then it would not be stated that "he initiates him with a staff.
Therefore, he is not initiated here [at the beginning], but rather at the very end.
Nor is there an option regarding [the staff and other implements]. Why? Because that which is called "initiation" is not observed [to consist in them].
In this regard, one becomes initiated by as much as is prescribed as the means [of initiation], and not by a mere portion thereof.

He says: From the indication by means of the instrumental case, it is understood that the status of being the instrument of initiation belongs to each [element] independently of the others, just as rice grains (independently of barley) possess the status of being the instrument for making the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

If it is argued that because they provide a visible benefit, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them—that is not so; for like the rice, the sacrificial cake can be produced through their combination (*samuccaya*) as well.
(Therefore, the provision of a visible benefit is not the cause for an option.)
What then? The instrumental case-ending, however, indicates that the items such as the *puroḍāśa* are independent causes (*kāraṇa*) by virtue of being the material cause (*prakṛti*).
That [instrumental indication] would be sublated if there were a combination [of means]; therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
Likewise here as well (since the staff and other items are each indicated by the instrumental case-ending, there should be an option).
It is said: (this is an unequal comparison).
Here, as the material cause (*prakṛti-dravya*) of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), one material cause is required.
Its restriction is established by the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇa-vibhakti*) [in the word] "with rice" (*vrīhibhiḥ*), [meaning] "only with rice" or "wherever [rice is available]."

However, the fact that the staff and other implements serve that purpose (*tādarthya*) is not yet understood; [therefore], by means of the instrumental case ending (*daṇḍena dīkṣayati*), an *apūrva* is produced.
And since that purposefulness has an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) object, it is performed by all [the implements].
(Nevertheless, how is there a combination? To this he says: In this case, they will all be subsumed (*upasaṃhriṣyante*)—that is, combined—by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).
Or rather, they are intended; for they have that as their purpose, due to their connection with the specific purpose of the oblation.
The Commentary states: Or rather, he should be consecrated (dīkṣita);
for that [initiation] has that as its purpose—the purpose of consecration.

How so? That [initiation] belongs to one who is being initiated (*dīkṣiyamāṇa*). If he becomes initiated at a time subsequent to that [act], then it is understood from that statement that "he is initiated" only then.
Once the ritual act that is the cause of initiation has been completed, why would he not be considered initiated?
For in the sentence, the word "dīkṣitaḥ" (initiated) indicates that [the action] is independent.
As for the connection with initiation expressed by "he initiates with a staff" (*daṇḍena dīkṣayati*), how could that [staff] exist within the state of being initiated?
It is understood rather that he brings about initiation by means of the staff.

As for the claim that the word *dīkṣita* does not occur immediately thereafter, it is not that the word is not employed; rather, the reason is the absence of its referent. Even though the referent exists, the word is not employed because there is no occasion for it at that point.
Furthermore, it is understood from the scriptural statement, "One being consecrated should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu," that he is consecrated by another [rite].

As for the fact that the word *dīkṣita* occurs at the time of the formal announcement (*āvedana*), even though this is accepted as belonging to the consecrated person, it is not a primary constituent part (*avigraha*).
And the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*) is also not a primary constituent part.

For it is understood that initiation is the single cause [of the state], since it brings about one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*). In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the *Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* sacrifice; the *Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* in the Jyotiṣṭoma [is established]—the *Dīkṣita* is indeed a consecration (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, a *saṃskāra* is produced by action (*kriyā*),
and staffs and the like do not possess the nature of action. Now, it might be argued that staffs and so forth serve as *saṃskāras* because they accomplish an action.

He states the reply: Since no action such as "offering" (*samarpaṇa*) is heard [in the text], it is not known what action they perform while employing the sacrificial implements (*saṃskārārtha*) for the sake of purification.
Therefore, because they consist of mere substances (due to the lack of knowledge regarding their form as actions), there would be no determination of the sentence-meaning at all.
Furthermore, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is prescribed as a means for one who "is about to be initiated" (*dīkṣiṣyamāṇaḥ*), that is, one who desires to obtain initiation; it is not otherwise.
Just as the *agnihotra* is for [attaining] heaven;

(the author states the meaning of the sūtra, "and the designation is likewise"): if this very rite is performed as the initiation (*dīkṣā*), then its designation as "*dīkṣaṇīyā*" is appropriate (and not otherwise).
Therefore, due to the connection with an independent statement and the designation, it is the *dīkṣaṇīyā* alone that produces the state of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*).

(He shows the connection of the definition of reflection by summarizing the meaning of the Sūtra: "Or they are accepted"—namely, that the Agnihotra and other rites are not [merely] things to be performed; such is the connection characterized by sequence.
And the designation is likewise.
The Bhāṣya says: From this too we see that it is for the purpose of the *īḍā* and *dīkṣaṇīyā* offerings, and that activity is desired.)
Why? Because the principle that "the designation is likewise" has been taught as a logical rule.
How so? A designation such as *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiatory rite) functions to indicate its purpose, just like the terms *sthānīya* (hospitality) or *bhojanīya* (meal).
Therefore, we see that this [rite] is for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣaṇīyā*), and its performance is desired.
Śā— "The initiation (*dīkṣā*) is enjoined by an independent sentence;
the staff and so forth—which are of the nature of non-action (the reading is *daṇḍādi tu akriyārūpam* rather than *daṇḍādikriyārūpam*)—are mentioned as its indicators (*vyañjana*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)."

Soma: [Objection] Just as one does not become an *āyit* merely by piling [the fire-altar], so too one does not become *dīkṣita* (initiated) merely by [the act of] *ihi*. This is the connection [of the objection].

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: Because of the connection with initiation (*dīkṣā*) through all [acts] beginning with the *iṣṭivat*, one becomes *dīkṣita* after the announcement (*āvedana*), that is, immediately following the announcement.
Regarding the rule *enapā dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.31), one must assume the statement "the ablative case is also seen" (*pañcamy api dṛśyate*) and thereby justify the usage *pareṇa āvedanāt*.
Thus it is stated in the *Tantraratna*.
As for the purpose: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the duties of one initiated are to be undertaken by initiation alone;
according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the duties of one initiated are to be undertaken upon the completion of the staff and other [initiation rites].

The doubt is as follows: "Is initiation [accomplished] by means of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice and so forth, or rather by the fire [alone]? [This doubt extends up to the words] "or rather by the *iṣṭi* alone.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated as: "[It is accomplished] by the fire."
The application of the *saṃskāra* (consecration) is indeed for the sake of the *iṣṭi* (sacrifice), because the staff (*daṇḍa*) and other items are intended for that purpose.

The Bhaṭṭa [school] states: "One who is being initiated offers an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu" (*āgnāvaiṣṇavam ekādaśakapālam nirvapati dīkṣiyamāṇaḥ*). From this, it is understood that the present-tense suffix (*laṭ*) is prescribed in the sense of an action performed for the sake of another action.

Furthermore, through such statements as "He initiates him with a staff," "He initiates him with a girdle," and "He initiates him with a black antelope skin," where the instrumental case is used, it is established that the staff and other items serve the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that the staff (*daṇḍa*) and other such items have as their effect merely the removal of attachment (*anabhiṣakta*), because they are heard of in the context of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Moreover, since there are numerous instances of the term *dīkṣayati*, it would follow that those [other meanings] would have to be figurative (*lakṣaṇā*), which lacks authority. Furthermore, this initiation—which consists of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and takes the form of a fitness conducive to non-attachment—is inferred from its being "moistened" (*abhisyandita*); for the staff and other items are subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Nor is it of the nature of remembrance (*smaraṇa*), because its connection [to the act of remembering] has not been previously established.

Or, let it be granted that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* itself produces the state of initiation (*dīkṣā*); even so, the duties of the initiated (*dīkṣita*), such as restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), do not commence at the conclusion of that rite. This is because the injunction for undertaking those restraints and observances occurs only after the announcement (*āvedana*), the command (*preṣaṇa*), and the giving of the staff (*daṇḍa*) and other items—specifically following the formula: "You are initiated; speak the speech of the initiated; speak only the truth, do not speak falsehood. Otherwise, the act of announcement would result in having a merely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.
For this very reason, Pārthasārathi’s statement that the undertaking of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) constitutes initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself is untenable;
for in the *āvedana* and *preṣa* formulas, the undertaking of restraints and observances is mentioned at a time subsequent to the connection with initiation.
Thus, the initiation itself [is established] in the Jyotiṣṭoma, as is the desire for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering], and the duration of initiation in the Jyotiṣṭoma.

This is the occasion [for discussion]. Furthermore, since the staff (*daṇḍa*) and other implements possess an established form, it is not possible for them to serve the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*) without the knowledge that they are to be accomplished through action.

Nor should it be argued that their status as being defined by that [action] is merely a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), based on the fact that they serve the purpose of the instigating activity first understood from the verbal root—as in such expressions as "he causes [him] to act by means of speech alone."

If that were the case—meaning if one were to accept that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice has [the *dīkṣā*] as its direct purpose—it would result in the undesirable consequence of it having an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.

Therefore, for that reason, it is more appropriate to accept that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* has either the *dīkṣā* itself or the state of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*) as its purpose; this state of being initiated is what serves the function of producing the knowledge of the two restraints (*yama-niyama*) which constitute the fruit of the *dīkṣā*. This is just as the mantra "agan" is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice by virtue of manifesting the fruit of the sacrifice.
For this very reason, since the understanding of a mediated relationship is possible through the relationship-bearer itself, there is no need for even indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And its status as a producer of knowledge is by way of being a reminder (*smāraka*).

Even though the relationship [between the staff and the Brāhmaṇa] is not understood through another means of knowledge (*māna*), its status as a reminder is established simply because it would otherwise be unintelligible (*anupapatti*) according to the method of injunction (*vidhi-naya*).

Furthermore, since the specific injunctions for each case enjoin actions such as "carrying" or "wearing around the neck" for the staff and so forth, there is no possibility of these things being reminders when they are not connected to an action.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are one thousand eight hundred and twelve [cows] (1,812);
thus, the wording of the mantra, "May Tutha distribute you, O Viśvedevas," does not become merely optional.

However, where there is only a single substance as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), such as "a cow is the sacrificial fee" and so forth, there the gift must indeed be given undivided, as there is no other way.
"But when there is a difference in substance, one must divide [the gift] accordingly.
And because there is a reciprocal service, as in the world.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, there is giving for the sake of a reciprocal service; it is not merely for the sake of merit."
Furthermore, for the purpose of purchase (*parikraya*), one must conclude a transaction with a servant;
if, however, it were addressed to an assembly (*pariṣad*) and the price were divided among them, it would not be a sale with the owner.
In that case, it would simply be termed a "purchase" (*parikraya*).

Just as in the world, when something is given from among wood, oxen, and so forth, those who bring the wood are bargained for along with their owner; and from them, the owner distributes and assigns [the goods], saying, "This one is yours, this one is yours. In the same way, it should be understood here as well.
Therefore, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to these [priests].
Furthermore, it also shows a distribution.
The Commentary states: Moreover, it shows a distribution, since they recite a mantra that expresses such a distribution.
"May Viśvedas distribute it among you all.
Having spread out the black antelope skin, he gives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"He gives facing toward them; thus he gratifies the ancestors who are turned toward him."
He gives to the Brahman; he gives to those who have spread [the grass]; he gives to the Prasṛta.
He gives to the Hotṛ;
he gives to the Neṣṭṛ.
"He gives to the Adhvaryus seated at the Havirdhāna shed;
he gives to the Udgātṛs;
he gives according to his faith to those who have reached their verses (prāptarkas) seated within the Sadas."
Thus, the observation of the division is logically established.
Therefore, it should be given to the priests.
Śābarabhāṣya: "It is settled that this gift is for the purpose of hiring the officiating priests" (10.2.22–28).
Therefore, because they are predominant, they are not intended to be expressed exhaustively.

Therefore, the gift of each [item] such as the *pradhāna* (the principal) and so forth is given individually. Soma—[this is] the connection because of the consideration of a specific point in the preceding [section]. As for the meaning of the *sūtra*: in that regard, the gift of cows and other items should be by way of division, because the divisions of the principal items to be given to the priests are distinct; for without distributing them, it would be impossible for each respective priest to take possession of each respective item.

In this context (*mūla*), since the primary act of giving performed for the sake of the assembly cannot be accomplished without the recipient being capable of utilizing the gift as a priest (*ṛtvij*), the individual giving was established to ensure its fulfillment. However, the Prābhākaras have stated that because there is no acquisition of merit through benefiting others, and because the status of another is not attained [by the recipient], the giving to the assembly is merely a formal renunciation (*tyāga*), and not a primary act of giving.

Regarding the gift of a cow (*godāna*) when it is prescribed by one's own will, is there a restriction even for *Animiṣa*? Is there non-division or division [of the merit]? The first case [non-division] follows from the non-statement of a restrictive rule.
Non-division occurs when there is abundance; however, "abundance" is not intended here.
In the case of division, the signs of the respective ownership established by the owners are observed.
In the mantra, "May Tutha, the All-Knowing, distribute you," there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for distribution.
(The meaning of the mantra is: "O cows, may the deity named Tutha distribute you.
Bhaṭṭa: Regarding this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) being given to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there arises the deliberation as to whether it should be given after being divided or not.

In the injunction, "He gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests," since the plurality of the priests is intended to be significant by virtue of being the recipients of the gift, the fee must be given to them collectively as an undivided whole. Nor does the giving of an undivided whole entail the impossibility of the gift's purpose being fulfilled, nor does it result in the gift becoming a mere synonym for a single unit; for in cases such as "The cow is the sacrificial fee," where there is a single indivisible substance, the term is understood to refer to a composite whole. Since such an understanding is possible here as well, that [purpose] is thereby achieved. Therefore, just as in those cases, even though individual ownership arises through the division performed by those [priests], there is no defect.

In reality, however, since the priests (*ṛtvij*) here are the intended objects (*uddeśya*), neither their plurality nor their collective nature is intended to be significant. Consequently, as in the case of the injunction "He performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) with clarified butter mixed with curds," it is understood—by the principle that qualities apply to each individual principal—that the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is connected to each priest individually; thus, there is no occasion for a division [of the fee]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: here, the priests are not understood through the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of being merely the agents of the action. Since the dative case (*caturthī*) denotes the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*), there is no grounds for resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to interpret it otherwise. Therefore, the entire fee must be divided among them.

Therefore, just as in the case of "he gives a cow to one who knows the Veda," where the act of giving—qualified by both [the recipient and the object]—has heaven as its purpose, so too here, because the act of giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) qualified by both [the priest and the fee] is understood to have the purpose of bringing the priests, and because the plurality and concomitance residing in the priests are enjoined, the sacrificial fee applies to each [priest] individually as a whole.

For this very reason, in both cases, since the substance such as the cow possesses two objects (dvikarmaka), there is only the indication of instrumentality (karaṇatva) as in the case of the *saktu* offering.

Furthermore, because in another scriptural passage regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is like the *jauhavī* oblation and so forth, and because the single *upanayana* is enjoined for the sake of the priests as a whole—just as the *prayāja* offerings and others are directed toward the deities—the connection is with each part individually; thus, there is no repetition of the entire sacrificial fee for each individual priest.
Therefore, the giving of the sacrificial fee occurs everywhere only for the priests taken collectively.
For this very reason, even in the case of the *anvāhārya* rice and other such items, they are given without being divided.

For instance, just as in the case of "the cow is the sacrificial fee" (*dhenurdakṣiṇā*) and so forth, there is indivisibility by one [person] at other times, such a thing does not exist regarding the twelve-hundred-fold sacrificial fee (*dvādaśaśatadakṣiṇā*) in the *Anvāhārya* and other parts of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

In this regard, where the logic of a collective [gift] is not set forth in the division of the *anvāhārya* (the supplementary fee), and since the plural number is used everywhere, the gift is prescribed as being for the collective group; nevertheless, because there exists evidence—both from the force of the mantra-text, "May Viśvedevas distribute you," and from the authority of such scriptural statements as "He gives to the *agnīdh*, to the *hotṛ*, to the *udgātṛ*"—the distribution must indeed take place.
Maṇḍana states: "The distribution of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is certainly [required]."
Śaṅkara says: "The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be distributed.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the distribution of the twelve-hundred-fold fee must be made in accordance with the designations 'those who receive a third,' 'those who receive a quarter,' and so forth."
"It should be equal, because it is not so heard.
Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is recited: "A cow, a horse, a mule...
In this context, the meaning is that these should be given after being divided [equally].

Now, regarding this *śāṇḍyaka*: is the division equal, or is there inequality caused by the ritual action (*karman*), or is it caused by the scriptural statement (*śabda*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? The division should be equal, because no specific distinction is heard.
Where no distinction is heard, there the division ought to be equal.
How so? It follows that everything must be given to one [person] if there is nothing to be given to another.
In that case, as long as another is not deprived when something is given to one, so much should not be given to that one;
rather, it should be given without distinction.
Thus it is for each individual.
Therefore, because of the hearing of this specific rule, it should be given equally.
[The sūtra] "It should be equal, because there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" has been established; and as a relevant digression, the matter of partition is also sufficient.
"Or rather, due to the inequality of karma.
Commentary: The word "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position.
It would not be equal.
The inequality would indeed be caused by karma.
To him who performs much karma, much death is allotted.
Therefore, the inequality is in accordance with karma.

They would be unequal in terms of purchase; there is an unequal recourse in the scriptural injunction regarding the rule; and because of the purchase, it is applicable to the ritual action, as is seen from the specific observation regarding prosperity.
Commentary: This is not a disparity caused by the ritual action itself.
What then? It is the nature of being a benefactor.
That assistance is made known by direct scriptural statement (śruti).
Therefore, there is a disparity created by the scripture;
consequently, they would be unequal in the matter of hiring (parikraya).
For their designations are irregular:
some are called *arthins*, some *tṛtīyins*, and some *pādins*.
Those for whose sake [the offerings are made] are the *arthins*.
And how does it come about that they have a share in the object?
If the object is given to them.

Thus, in the scriptural injunction regarding the rules for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*), they are designated as "those who receive a third part" (*tṛtīyinaḥ*) and "those who receive a quarter part" (*pādinaḥ*).
Or rather, due to the performance [of rituals], it is not possible for there to be inequality caused by the performance of actions.
What, then, is this distinction that is observed? It is in the case of spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
"Prosperity" refers to the fruit of prosperity.
We speak of the fruit of success as lasting twelve days:
"The Adhvaryu initiates the patron (yajamāna), then he initiates the Brāhmaṇa, then the Udgātṛ, and then the Hotṛ."

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated him, initiates those who are entitled to the second rank: the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin for the Brahman, the Prastotṛ for the Udgātṛ, and the Maitrāvaruṇa for the Hotṛ.

Then the Neṣṭṛ, having initiated him, initiates those who are entitled to the third rank: the Agnīdh for the Brahman, the Pratihartṛ for the Udgātṛ, and the Acchāvāka for the Hotṛ. Then the Neṣṭṛ, having initiated him, initiates those who are entitled to the fourth rank: the Potṛ for the Brahman, the Subrahmaṇya for the Udgātṛ, and the Āgnīdhra for the Hotṛ.
Then, after that, he initiates those who have not yet been initiated, or a student sent by his teacher.

Thus, the mention of "those seeking wealth," "those entitled to a third part," and "those entitled to a quarter" is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

If, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), these portions were assigned to them according to their respective designations, then the observation [of these shares] in the twelve-day sacrifice becomes logically consistent.

Therefore, because of the designation by means of the object and so forth, there ought to be a disparity caused by the scriptural designation (*samākhyā*). Soma: Since the distribution was established in the preceding section, this [section] is considered as the means of carrying that out; such is the connection (*saṅgati*). Vi: "Is that distribution equal or not? Because no specific distinction is heard, it is equal."
There might be inequality according to the effort [expended], but let it not be so, because of the designation [of the Veda].
Bhaṭṭa: Even partition (*vibhāga*) is a regulator that is exactly the same everywhere;
it occurs according to the correspondence with effort and so forth.

However, in the case of the *soma* sacrifice, for the purpose of determining the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣā-krama-vibhāga*) in the sacrificial session (*satra*), by the force of the scriptural name (*samākhyā*) heard in the sentence, "Those who desire [the fruit], those who receive a third [share], those who receive a quarter [share],"...
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the continuous stream-offering (dhārāgraha).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are only two [such offerings] in the first two [pressings], because the rule for their distribution is prescribed therein.
But when the *aśā* and other items have been combined, the distribution should be made by those [officiants] according to their desire, equally, or in proportion to their labor;
the same applies to the *anvāhārya* and so forth.

Furthermore, the explanation of the distribution through these two sections is for the purpose of its utility in the distribution of the portions of the teacher (*ācārya*) and others that will be described later.
Maṇḍana: "One should perform the division in accordance with the designation.
Śaṅkara: "That division is accepted as such.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are the *dhārāgraha* [libations]."
"He takes [the cups] by pouring.
These cups are those beginning with the Aindravāyava. (Vi.
10.5.17). In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the distribution of the *dhiṣṇya* hearths begins from the Āgnīdhrīya.

The distribution (*viharaṇa*) of the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, which is enjoined by the passage beginning with "They distribute [the fires] at the *savana* for the *agnīdh*" and so forth, should take place on the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), because even those [hearths] are subordinate to that [altar] and serve the purpose of the oblation (*homa*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because of the restrictive injunction, "The *agnīdh* distributes the *dhiṣṇyas*," it is established that the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth also possesses the character of the *āhavanīya* fire, and thus its connection with the oblation is logically justified.
From that very [source] follows the performance (*viharaṇa*).

[In the case of] the *saṃkalpa* (12.15), regarding the mantra for crossing a river in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: "O Goddess, protect me... Since there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), other auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are not required.
And those things which are not desired do not form a single syntactical unit.
Therefore, it is understood that they are not applicable.
But if this is so, does the [new] rule ending with *śaṃkhviḍā* not sublate any additional meaning from the two preceding ones?
It is said: this is not a fault;
for there is no separate sentence for that whose unity of meaning one wishes to maintain.
The purpose of this statement is that the conclusion should be by means of the subsequent [verses]. Therefore, the ritual procedure should conclude with the subsequent ones. [Dūṣaṇa says:
The ritual procedure ending with the *śaṃyu* formula is enjoined.
And that [act], being enjoined as one whose auxiliary benefit is already established (*klṛptopakārā*), satisfies the requirement of the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice, just like the *ājyabhāga* offerings.

And when it is deposited in that [sacrifice], two ends of the conch-shell are mentioned without distinction. In that case, if the first end of the conch-shell were to be grasped, those ritual acts which are understood to be performed prior to the two subsequent conch-shells would be sublated.
But when the subsequent [alternative] is adopted, nothing is sublated; rather, the meaning of the word is fully accomplished.
[This applies] to the wife in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, in the Prāyaṇīya and other rites. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, in the Prāyaṇīya and other rites...

In considering whether there is also a state of being counted as a whole, excluding the *anuyāja* offerings, it is argued that [the sacrifice] is undertaken again. However, here "undertaking again" does not have that meaning;
rather, that which was for the sake of the *soma* sacrifice accomplishes the purpose elsewhere through *prasaṅga* (incidental application).
One should accomplish it, provided that its purpose for the sake of desire is known;
however, that [purpose] is made known right here,
whereas for those pertaining to this world, it is understood from the archetype (prakṛti).
Therefore, the example of "speaking the truth" (*satyavādin*) is [applicable].
However, the purpose of being for the sake of Soma has been explained in the third chapter regarding the specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Regarding the deliberation as to whether the original vow (*vrata-upāyana*) should be performed or not—having concluded that it should be performed—it follows that even for the sake of Soma, since the vow is already established by that very same commitment (*saṃkalpa*) to speak the truth, practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and so forth, which remains unreleased until the completion [of the sacrifice], its requirements are fulfilled through incidental application (*prasaṅga*); thus, the vow need not be undertaken again.

Soma: It is stated that although the *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) need not be performed because it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), the *vratopāyana* (the undertaking of the vow) must be performed because it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). Viśvarūpa: Does the *vratopāyana* exist [in the *iṣṭi* sacrifice] or not? It exists there by virtue of the *codaka* (the rule of extension). However, because there would be a contradiction if one who has already undertaken the vow were not to relinquish it, it does not exist there again. Bhaṭṭa: In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves, the taking of the vow is prescribed by means of the mantra "O Agni, Lord of Vows" (*agne vratapate*).
A *vrata* (vow) consists of a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) such as speaking the truth, practicing celibacy, and so forth.

Indeed, speaking the truth is enjoined in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "He, for his part, should speak only the truth. By the inclusion of the word "he" (*sa*), this is established as a duty of the person who has performed the *kṛta* rite.
For this very reason, the injunction "one should not speak untruth" constitutes a distinct connection (*saṃyogāntara*), because it pertains to the pure duty of the *kṛta* stage.
The suspicion that the other [text] might be redundant because it is not proximate is set aside by the fact that it belongs to a different recension (*śākhā*).

The same should be understood regarding the injunction for celibacy (*brahmacarya*): "That student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should not eat meat. Since the prohibition of sexual intercourse and meat belongs to another recension, there is no contradiction.

This very vow (*vrata*) should also not be performed during the *somāgneyīṣṭi* and similar rites; for after the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the requirement is fulfilled by the undertaking of the *dīkṣā-vrata* made for the sake of the *soma* sacrifice, which remains unreleased until the end. Nor can it be argued how there could be "incidental fulfillment" (*prasaṅga*) between the performance of the present-world vow and the *soma*-related vow, since they produce distinct types of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); for even when two distinct types of acts are maintained through a single performance (*tantra*), it is logically possible for them to produce distinct types of unseen merit.

For this very reason, although the observance of the rule of speaking the truth and so forth is a prerequisite, since its purpose is accomplished by that very resolution (*saṃkalpa*) made for the sake of the *Soma* sacrifice, no separate resolution need be made. This is because a resolution already made once would be rendered useless by making it again, and because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra "I shall perform the vow" (*vrataṃ cariṣyāmi*) would be inappropriate during the period when one is currently engaged in the vow.

Nor can it be argued that even when a lifelong resolution to speak the truth has been made for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*), a new resolution is nevertheless made for rites such as the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and that the same should apply here.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the fruit-cup (phalacamas), it must be stated that even though the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) has been made for the sake of Soma in the form of the Bṛhatī [verse] within the Jyotiṣṭoma, the performance of that same resolve again with respect to its subsidiaries and so forth is not intended. This is because there is no obstacle to performing again for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) a resolve that was previously made for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); and furthermore, there is no obstacle to the general resolve for common vows such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), even when there is a specific rule such as "speaking the truth."

In the present case, however, because a general resolve has already been made, performing [the vow] again for the sake of the *iṣṭi* and other rites would be contradictory; this is the distinction. Nor should it be argued that even so, since the vow intended for the Soma sacrifice—by way of purifying the agent—is common to both the subsidiaries and the primary rite, it serves the purpose of the *iṣṭi* and others as well, and thus the *iṣṭi*-related vow would simply be sublated by the directly taught (*aupadeśika*) resolve for the vow [of the Soma sacrifice], rather than being a case of *prasaṅga* (extended application). This is because, although the vow is indeed common to both the subsidiary and the primary through its function of purifying the agent, the *iṣṭi*-related vow is not sublated by the resolve for the vow of the Soma sacrifice. Rather, due to the specific connection with the Soma sacrifice, the *iṣṭi*-related vow is merely set aside (*bādha*), while the requirement for the Soma sacrifice is fulfilled through *prasaṅga*. This is because the Soma sacrifice possesses a greater force of application (*balavattara-prayoga*) due to its specific connection, whereas the *iṣṭi* lacks such a specific connection. Furthermore, the resolve for the vow is not merely a mental act; rather, it is a physical action consisting of the undertaking of the vow, which is performed at the time of the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Therefore, when the Soma sacrifice is performed, the vow undertaken at that time does not apply to the *iṣṭi*, and thus there is no need for a separate performance of the vow for the *iṣṭi*. Consequently, the *iṣṭi*-related vow is sublated by the resolve for the vow of the Soma sacrifice. Thus, it is established that there is *prasaṅga*. Alternatively, one might argue: "Even if the vow is common to both the subsidiary and the primary, the *iṣṭi*-related vow is sublated by the resolve for the vow of the Soma sacrifice, and therefore there is no *prasaṅga*. To this we reply: No. Even though the vow is common to both the subsidiary and the primary, the *iṣṭi*-related vow is not sublated by the resolve for the vow of the Soma sacrifice. Rather, because the Soma sacrifice has a stronger force of application due to its specific connection, and because the *iṣṭi* lacks such a specific connection, the *iṣṭi*-related vow is merely set aside, and the requirement for the Soma sacrifice is fulfilled through *prasaṅga*. Moreover, the resolve for the vow is not a mere mental act; it is a physical action consisting of the undertaking of the vow, performed at the time of the initiation. Therefore, when the Soma sacrifice is performed, the vow undertaken at that time does not apply to the *iṣṭi*, and thus there is no need for a separate performance of the vow for the *iṣṭi*. Hence, the *iṣṭi*-related vow is sublated by the resolve for the vow of the Soma sacrifice, and it is established that there is *prasaṅga*. Furthermore, the following objection might be raised: "In the case of the *prayāja* and other rites, since they are performed within the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, they do not require a separate performance for the *sānnāyya-yāga*; thus, there is *prasaṅga*. However, in the case of the *vrata*, since it is not performed within the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, it would require a separate performance for the *sānnāyya-yāga*, and thus there can be no *prasaṅga*. To this we reply: No. Even if the *vrata* is not performed within the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, it is nevertheless connected to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* through the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore, just as the *prayāja* and others do not require a separate performance for the *sānnāyya-yāga* because they are performed within the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, so too the *vrata* does not require a separate performance for the *sānnāyya-yāga* because it is connected to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* through the agent. Consequently, there is *prasaṅga*. Alternatively, one might argue: "Even if the *vrata* is connected to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* through the agent, since it is not performed within the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, it would require a separate performance for the *sānnāyya-yāga*, and thus there can be no *prasaṅga*. To this we reply: No. Even if the *vrata* is not performed within the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, it is nevertheless connected to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* through the agent. Therefore, just as the *prayāja* and others do not require a separate performance for the *sānnāyya-yāga* because they are performed within the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, so too the *vrata* does not require a separate performance for the *sānnāyya-yāga* because it is connected to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* through the agent. Because of the statement, "The *dīkṣās* belong to the Soma," the nature of the vow (*vrata*) consists in the undertaking of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). Since the *dīkṣā* serves only the purpose of the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*), it does not apply in common to the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*).
Therefore, it is indeed proper that there is no extension (*prasaṅga*) [of the *dīkṣā*] to the *prāyaṇīyā* and other such rites.

However, in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, since the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the vow intended for the Soma occurs after the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, an extension is untenable; thus, the undertaking and the release of the sacrificial vow (*aiṣṭikavrata*) are appropriate.

Bodhāyana and others do not accept that for him [the sacrificer] even from that [point]. Maṇḍana states: "The *iṣṭi*s are parts of the Soma sacrifice; there is no further vow (*vrata*) after that. Śaṃkara says: "Likewise, there is no undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*)."
12. The Fruit-Cup in the Jyotiṣṭoma (for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya). The Topic of the Fruit-Cup (phalacamasādhikaraṇa).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is a chant called the Bahiṣpavamāna during the morning pressing (Vi. 1.4.3).
Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma, when there is an interruption (apaccheda)—meaning a disruption or desisting—from the Bahiṣpavamāna (starting with the udgātṛ), there is an expiation (prāyaścitta).
Apaccheda means a cessation or withdrawal.

Bhāṣya 6.1.17–21 (Sūtras 49–56): Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is stated: "One should perform the Bārhadvira as the Brahmasāman for a Brāhmaṇa, the Pārthurasa for a Rājanya, and the Rāyovājīya for a Vaiśya. In this context, the Abhīvarta serves as the Brahmasāman for the obligatory (nitya) performance;
the others, however, are contingent (naimittika).
(The *brahmadhāma* is the *sāman* for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s recitation.
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the singing of the *raurava* and *audhājasa* *sāmans* occurs upon a *bārhatatṛca* produced by the rearrangement of *bṛhatī* and *paṅkti* verses;
however, it is [also] in the *pragātha* form.
9|2|6|25 Section 2.

Commentary: Or rather, it is as follows. There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [enjoined by the text]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. In that context, it is said: "The morning Pavamāna stotra of the middle day has three meters (tri-chandas) and five Sāmans; two [Sāmans], the Gāyatra and the Āmahīyava, occur on a triplet (tṛca) of Gāyatrī verses; the Raurava and Audhājaya occur on a triplet of Bṛhatī verses; and the Auśana occurs on other Triṣṭubh verses."
Regarding these two *sāmans*, the *raurava* and the *yaudhājaya*: their former [verse] is a *bṛhatī*: "Being purified with his stream, O Soma, clothing himself in waters, he flows;
he sits upon the seat of the navel of Truth, the golden god.
The latter is the method of analysis: "Milking the heavenly milk, he has occupied the dear, victorious breath in the midst."
"Having taken leave of his wife, the wise one, supported by the *tṛca*, proceeds.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the chanting be performed in the *sāman*s after bringing in two other *bṛhatī* verses, or should the chanting be performed in the form of *bṛhatī*s by first arranging those two—the previous *bṛhatī* and the subsequent *vicārapaddhati*—into a *tṛca* sequence? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That two other *bṛhatī*s should be brought in.
Why? Because in this way, the application of the Ṛks will become meaningful.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"But it is a Prāgāthika."
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.

The meaning is that the *sāman* singing should be performed using the *prāgāthika* verses, and there is no need for the introduction of the two original *bṛhatī* verses. It should be performed using those very same [verses] which constitute the original context.
For they thus remember: "The *pragātha* consists of two *vāhanta*s.
If the two *bṛhatī*s were brought in [as constituent parts], there would be no *pragātha*;
in that case, the traditional rule (*smṛti*) would be contradicted.
Therefore, the singing should be performed according to the original meters.
And in its own [meter].
The Commentary states: "And thus, in its own Vedic meter, the singing will take place according to the original form."
There is neither the abandonment of what is under discussion nor the introduction of what is not;
therefore, for this reason as well, there is no arrival of other *bṛhatī*s.
And [this applies] to the *pragātha* as well.
Commentary: In this way, the term *pragātha* will be logically justified;
for it denotes excellence in singing (*gāna*), and that excellence occurs when [the verse] is taken up by feet (*pāda*).
Therefore, for this reason also, other Bṛhatīs are not the material cause.
[This is known] from the observation of an indicative mark and from the fact of their being distinct.
The Commentary states: "And by means of distinction, it shows an indicative mark."
"What is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for your position? He replies: "The midday pressing (*mādhyandinaṃ savanam*) occurs during the *bahiṣpavamāna*.

How is this an indicative mark? If the singing (*gāna*) is performed in the *bṛhatī* meter at the *prasthāna*, then they will recite all the verses (*ṛc*) that are traditionally handed down (*samāmnātāḥ*) for the entire pressing.
Otherwise, there would be an excess of the two *bṛhatī* verses specifically prescribed for their own respective chants.
This is now specified: in the *agāyatrāmīya* chant, there are two triplets (*tṛca*) consisting of *gāyatrī* verses; these amount to six *gāyatrīs*.
In the *rauravaudhājaya* chant, there are [two triplets] consisting of *bṛhatī* verses; these also amount to six *bṛhatīs*. In the *auśana* chant, there is another [set] in *triṣṭubh* verses.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, those [verses] which are Bṛhatīs are also three Triṣṭubhs.
Now, when the Saptadaśa-stoma is performed with either the Bṛhat or the Rathantara as the Hotṛ’s Pṛṣṭha-laud, there are five Bṛhatīs.
And there are twelve quarters. How so? For this is the *triṣṭubh* therein: "He makes the *hiṃ* call with five [verses]: three times with three, once with one;
he makes the *hiṃ* call with five: once with one, three times with three, once with one."
"For he performs [the *saptamī*] with one, with three, and with three.
In that context, [the sequence is]: first with three *bṛhatī*s, then with one *kakubh*, again with one *kakubh*;
thereafter again with one *bṛhatī*, with three *kakubh*s, and with one *kakubh*.
Thus, there are four *bṛhatī*s and six *kakubh*s; then again one *bṛhatī*, then three *kakubh*s, and then again three *kakubh*s. In this way, there are five *bṛhatī*s and twelve *kakubh*s.
Together with those *bṛhatī*s, there are eleven *bṛhatī*s.

Then, from the six *gāyatrī*s—four *gāyatrī*s [remaining] together with twelve *kakubh*s—there are twelve *bṛhatī*s; thus, there are twenty-three. Then, in the *vāmadevya*, there are seventeen *gāyatrī*s; together with the two remaining *pāvamānī* *gāyatrī*s, there are nineteen *gāyatrī*s.
Then, from the *naubhasa* and *kāleya*, there are seventeen *bṛhatīs* on one side and seventeen on the other, making thirty in total.
Together with the twenty-three *bṛhatīs* previously calculated, there are fifty-seven *bṛhatīs*.
As for those nineteen *gāyatrīs*, together with their fifty-seven *gāyatrī* feet, they become fifty-seven *bṛhatīs* and fifty-seven *triṣṭubhs*.
It is established that there are six *triṣṭubh* verses together with the *pāvamānī* *triṣṭubhs*.

Now, regarding the origin of the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans], the introduction of two *kakubh* verses is performed; consequently, those [verses] which are chanted at the *savana* do not amount to six *triṣṭubhs*.
As for those two *kakubh* verses which are introduced at the two *savanas* where they were not previously chanted, their performance occurs ten times.
By that, the number sixty is completed.

Those *ṛc*s which are prescribed for the *savana* in the *Sāman* [text] are what are referred to here by the word *savana*; the term *savana* is not used here in the sense of the ritual performance (*karman*).
For in that context, there are many *triṣṭubh* verses across the three *savanas*.
"The midday pressing consists of six *triṣṭubh*s.

Therefore, regarding that which is the preceding *bṛhatī* and the subsequent *viṣṭārapaṅkti*, one should first perform the *gāyana* [chanting] there. Dupa says: "The midday pressing consists of six *triṣṭubh*s"—this view is appropriate for the first [case], not for the bringing in of two *triṣṭubh*s.
"The word *savana* does not [apply] here to the ritual action" (the Bhāṣya statement "there is no application of the word *savana* to the ritual action," however, is found further on;

it is cited here for the sake of logic). If the word *savana* were to apply to the ritual action (that is, to the *ṛc*s that constitute parts of the ritual), then—since the word *savana* denotes the three pressings (*savana*) of the sacrifice—it would apply only to the Jyotiṣṭoma as a whole, and could not be specified by the term "midday" (*mādhyaṃdina*).
In that case, this application [of the rule] would not occur: "The midday pressing consists of six *triṣṭubh*s" (because there is a plurality of *triṣṭubh* verses).

If the word *savana* does not denote the ritual action itself, but rather refers by indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the *ṛc*-verses that are constituent parts of the pressing, then the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *triṣṭubh* and the word *savana* is established.

And if the word *savana* were to apply [to the midday pressing] through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *triṣṭubh*—that is, by virtue of the proximity of the word "six *triṣṭubhs*" in the statement "the midday pressing"—then there would be many *triṣṭubhs* for the Ācārya, the Hotṛ, and the Udgātṛ at the midday pressing; and if that were the case, the usage "the midday pressing consists of six *triṣṭubhs*" would not be possible.
(Therefore, this statement refers to those verses which are recited in the Sāmaveda within the context of the midday pressing.)

Furthermore, regarding the statement "The midday pressing consists of six *triṣṭubh* verses," the term *savana* (pressing) refers only to those *ṛc*s that are heard within the ritual context and end with the word *ām* [or are otherwise defined as such]. If, however, *triṣṭubh* verses were to be brought in from elsewhere, they would have to be imported from the *Dāśatayī* collection; in that case, one would have to establish a contextual connection (*prakaraṇa-sambandha*) for those two [the *triṣṭubh* verses and the *savana*], yet there is no evidence for this.
Furthermore, by the force of the term *pragātha*, an expansion (*prathana*) must necessarily be performed.

And if that [expansion] were to be brought about by taking [verses] from the *utpattiṣṭubh* and *bṛhatī*, the statement "six *triṣṭubhs*" would be inconsistent, as would the mention of the *pragātha*.
Soma—there are five stotras in the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*): one for the *pavamāna-stoma* and four *pṛṣṭhas*.
In that [rite], the Pavamāna [laud] has the fifteen-fold stoma, and the Pṛṣṭha [lauds] have the seventeen-fold stoma;
