thus, there are eighty-two stotriya verses.
Among these, some are explicitly recited, some are obtained through recitation, and some are obtained through repetition.

In that context, there are twelve *kakubh* verses, each consisting of twenty-eight syllables; twenty-three *gāyatrī* verses, each consisting of twenty-four syllables; forty-five *bṛhatī* verses, each consisting of thirty-six syllables; and three *triṣṭubh* verses, each consisting of forty-four syllables.
Therein, when those twelve *kakubh* verses are combined with twelve *gāyatrī* verses, they result in twelve *triṣṭubh* verses.
Thus, eight three-footed *gāyatrī* verses have passed away.
There remain fifteen *gāyatrīs*, which have forty-five *pādas*.
In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, that many *bṛhatīs*— forty-five *bṛhatīs*— are combined with those same number of *pādas*, resulting in forty-five *triṣṭubhs*.
And since three [verses] are traditionally recited, sixty *triṣṭubh* verses are thus completed.
Regarding the *vi-* [section]: "In the *yaudhājaya* and the *raurava*, there is the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*;
then the *anavam*, as before five [verses], and thirty-six are called the *mahiman*."
"In the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, there are three hymns: first, 'uccā te jātam,' which contains three Gāyatrīs;
second, 'punānaḥ soma,' which is in the form of a Pragātha;
therein, the first verse is a Bṛhatī and the second is a Viṣṭārapaṅkti."
"pra tu drava parikōṣām" is the third [sūkta], in which there are three triṣṭubhs.

In the Pṛṣṭha-stomas, "abhi tvā śūra" is the first sūkta in the form of a pragātha; therein, the former [verse] is a bṛhatī and the latter is a paṅkti (specifically a satobṛhatī). "kayā naścitra" is the second.
In that context, there are three *gāyatrī* verses;
the third is in the form of a *pragātha*, namely "taṃ vo dasmam ṛtīṣaham," wherein the *bṛhatī* serves as the *stotrabṛhatī*;
and the fourth belongs to the *pragātha* beginning with "tarobhir no vidad vasu."
In this pressing (savana), there are seven hymns (sūktas).
Within them, nine Sāmans are to be sung.
In the first hymn, the two Sāmans Gāyatra and Āmīvatya are to be chanted.
In the second [stotra], the Raurava and Yājña;
in the third, the Auśana;
in the fourth, the Rathantara.
In the fifth [day] is the Vāmadevya;
in the sixth, the Naudhasa;
in the seventh, the Kāleya.
Bhaṭṭa: Or rather, it is thus.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, regarding the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, it is heard in scripture: "The Mādhyandina-pavamāna has three meters; it is an insertion (āvāpa) consisting of five Sāmans.

And there are explanatory passages for that purpose: "The Gāyatra and Mahīdvatya belong to the Gāyatrī meter; the Raurava and Audhājaya belong to the [next] triplet (tuca); the Auśana belongs to the Triṣṭubh."
In that regard, for the Raurava and Audhājaya [sāmans], the first [verse] is a Bṛhatī and the second is a Viṣṭārapaṅkti, as they are recited in the Saṃhitā.
However, here, because the two verses beginning with "vā ī" are specifically prescribed as a *tṛca* (a triplet), the latter two are indeed established as being in the Bṛhatī meter.
This being the case, there is no application of the Raurava and Audhājaya [sāmans] to the verse beginning with "vā ī"; for such a [Bṛhatī] *yoni* (source-verse) is already obtained.
Nor is it an injunction regarding the substrate of the *tuc* [verse], precisely because that is already established.
Nor is it an injunction regarding the substrate of the *āīta*, because the specific [element] is different.
For this very reason, there is no injunction of the two *sāmans* by means of a qualified location.

In that context, the injunction regarding the *bṛhatī* meter would apply only by way of reference to the *tṛca* (triplet). However, that too is impossible in either case—whether by way of delimitation through the delimitor (*avacchedakāvacchedena*) or by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*).

If it were accepted by way of delimitation through the delimitor, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the definition [of a *pragātha*] being lost due to the absence of its recitation in that [specific *tṛca*], as indicated by the technical name *pragātha-saraṇa*.
Therefore, in accordance with that, it must be accepted precisely by way of coreferentiality.

And thus, since that [expansion] is already established in reality, these sentences should be understood as restatements (*anuvāda*) intended to explain the meaning of the preceding sentence. Indeed, it is not reasonable for any learned person to claim that these [sentences] serve to obtain the *sāman* in the subsequent verses, for that is already obtained by the phrase "yadyonyām" itself. In every respect, the expansion is established here as well.

Nor does the statement "vā īte" possess the status of a valid authority for the *prayoga* (application) solely on the basis of its being a *yoni-bṛhatī*, since that is established by the very fact of its being a *saraṇa* (a specific type of verse) belonging to the *tucā-varga*. Furthermore, it should be noted that although the qualification of that which is renowned as a *bṛhatī* is possible through the delimitation of its defining characteristics (*avacchedaka*), such a course was not adopted because it would entail the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication).

In this regard, having recited the first *bṛhatī* consisting of thirty-six syllables, by repeating the other [three] quarters twice, one *bṛhatī* is formed with the first half of the subsequent forty-syllable *viṣṭārapaṅkti*, and another is formed with the second half by repeating the other quarters twice; such is the nature of the first [verse] to be understood.
Here, in all cases, because the difference is slight, even if there is a deficiency of a few syllables, there is no violation of the essential form of that meter.

As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—(the long syntactical connection being "ity uktam")—"The midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinaṃ savanam*) consists of six *triṣṭubh*s"—this indicative mark (*liṅga*) also applies to the first [verse] of this [hymn]. For instance, at the midday pressing there are five stotras: the Mādhyandina Pavamāna has the fifteen-fold hymn-form (*pañcadaśastoma*); the four *pṛṣṭha* stotras have the seventeen-fold hymn-form (*saptadaśa*). Among those, in the Pavamāna, there are six *gāyatrīs* in the Gāyatra and Ābhīśava Sāmans; six *bṛhatīs* in the Raurava and Audhājaya Sāmans; and three *triṣṭubhs* in the Auśana Sāman.

On the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ, there are five *bṛhatīs* and twelve *kakups*; this is because, according to the traditional recitation (*āmnāna*) regarding the method of chanting (*viṣṭuti*), the commencement begins with a *tṛca*.

On the *pṛṣṭha* of the Maitrāvaruṇa, there are seventeen *gāyatrīs*. Above the *svāhākṛt-pṛṣṭha* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, there are seventeen *bṛhatīs* each; this is likewise due to the repetition of the *tryṛca*. Thus, there are forty-five principal *bṛhatīs*. Among the six *gāyatrīs* consisting of twenty-four syllables and three feet, there are twelve [syllables] added by way of the feet of four *gāyatrīs*, each consisting of twelve syllables.
The previously mentioned twenty-eight *kakubh* verses consist of twelve *bṛhatīs* each comprising thirty-six syllables.

Thus, there are fifty-seven *bṛhatīs*. These, together with the two remaining *gāyatrīs* from among the six *gāyatrīs*, amount to seventeen *gāyatrīs*. When combined one foot at a time with the fifty-seven *bṛhatīs*, they become fifty-seven *triṣṭubhs* consisting of forty-four syllables each.
[This occurs] in the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice regarding the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* chants.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are thirty-six [verses] consisting of these three Triṣṭubhs of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans].
This indicative mark (liṅga) is applicable only to the first [performance].
Otherwise, if one were to bring together other *bṛhatī*s for the five [verses] and other *kakubh*s for the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ, the number six would be untenable.
For here, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as heard in the text—"the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) with thirty-six"—would not be possible, as it would be contradicted.

Therefore, by accepting a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word "midday pressing" itself—the understanding being that those verses collected in the midday pressing which are recited in the Sāmaveda are [meant by] "outside"—the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for bringing them from the *daśatayī* collections becomes untenable.

This [interpretation] was stated; however, since it is simpler to define the *stotrīyās* of the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*) themselves when a definition is required—and because it is logically consistent that even those brought from elsewhere possess that same nature—it was disregarded.
Maṇḍana says: "The *bṛhatī* is not [defined] by the subsequent [verse] being recited.
Śaṅkara says: "[It applies] also to the *yoṣit*, *jaya*, and *muleṣu*."
It should be sung as a *pragātha*.
9. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, when the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [sāmans] have been accomplished through the spreading of their own respective final verses, the singing is like that of two *kakubh* verses.
The Prāgāthika section, however, has the following commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "The *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] is the *Bṛhat*," and "The *pṛṣṭha* is the *Rathantara*.
The source (*yoni*) of the *Rathantara* is the *Bṛhatī* verse: "abhi tvā śūra nonumo 'dugdhā iva dhenavaḥ" (We cry out to you, O Hero, like unmilked cows).
O Indra, you are the ruler of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, and the ruler of all that stands still.
(Thus) the subsequent line [states]: "There is no hiring of priests in the Jyotiṣṭoma."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it would have to be assumed that the Maitrāvaruṇa and others are mentioned;
in such an assumption, the word would be rendered meaningless.
Therefore, the substance consecrated by the purchase of the *yājyā* must be employed here;
otherwise, there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*).
Consequently, whether such a substance exists or not, the purchase of the *yājyā* must be performed.

Now, as for what was said regarding "as in common worldly practice": in the world, action is characterized by its purpose, not by the word. One acts according to the purpose, not according to the word. In the Veda, however, the purpose is understood solely through the word; therefore, it must be performed exactly as [prescribed] by that word.
Therefore, it must be performed even when [the specific cause] is absent.

*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: On account of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is employed for the sake of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) and is caused by that; this is the subsequent position (*uttara-pakṣa*). *Soma*: Here too, because there is no contradiction between the general scriptural statement and the particulars, it has the particulars as its scope; thus, there is a connection due to direct perception (*pratyakṣatvāt*).

The rule is this: only a substance that has been purified (*mārjita*) accomplishes the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), and nothing else. As it is said: "Whether the purchase of the *yājyā* (offering verse) is absent or even present, the former [purified substance] should be used for the sake of the *apūrva*, even if one possesses other substances."
"In the absence of purchase" refers to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*;

[this is] the section concerning the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, when there is the option of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), the quality of having the *śukra* cup first is prescribed; and when there is the state of being accompanied by verses (*jagatsāhatva*), the quality of having the *āgrayaṇa* cup first is prescribed.
In that regard, when there is a displacement [of the order], it should be understood that the *āgrayaṇa* comes first (i.e., the *āgrayaṇa-agra* rule applies).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the duties pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna-dharma*) serve the primary sacrifice alone by virtue of the factor of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva-aṃśa*), but they do not serve both the subsidiaries and the primary by virtue of the factor of being the agent (*kartṛtva-aṃśa*).
PMS 3.1.26, p. 1077: An exclusion (parisaṃkhyā) of the mantras pertaining to the sacrificer in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

Regarding those modifications of the Darśapūrṇamāsa that occur within the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is no extension (atideśa) of the *yājamāna* mantras. This is because, when the *yājamāna* mantra "He who has become glory, he has arrived" (*yaśo babhūva sa ā babhūva*) is enjoined again, the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of all other [mantras] is established by the performance of the *yājamāna* [mantra] at the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the Siddhāntin replies]: Even though it is enjoined again as a mantra for the consecration of the Soma (*sutasakṣānumantraṇa*), it does not constitute an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), because—just like the two *ājyabhāga* offerings—it serves the purpose of providing a benefit already established in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Thus, [it is concluded in] Saṃkarṣa.

The Commentary states: Since the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*) brings about simultaneity (*sahatva*), there is *anusamaya* (sequential performance) according to the individual items.
The inquiry is whether the act of eating (*bhakṣaṇa*) exists [simultaneously], or whether eating exists elsewhere [only] in the sense of mere priority (*prāthamyamātra*).

What is established? By the principle that "if [something] is not enjoined by another," since it is possible for this to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) in some way, a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) is untenable; furthermore, because the "firstness" is not otherwise established, it is impossible to enjoin the act of eating as a restatement of that [firstness]. Thus the statement is expressed as: "He who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call is the first. Now, one might object: since it is not established, the eating itself cannot be restated either. [Response: Because it is established by the name (*samākhyā*), it is understood as a restatement.
For indeed, that [vaṣaṭkartṛ] has a right to consume from the cups by virtue of his designation; thus, he can be referred to [by the text].
And among those [cup-holders], whoever performs the vaṣaṭ at a particular time, he is the first to consume at that time.
In this regard, it might be argued that since there is no priority among these other cups, a restatement (anuvāda) is not possible.
This is not a fault.
For it is not necessarily the case that only that which is applicable everywhere must be restated; rather, all restatements depend upon what is applicable according to the circumstances.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Vaiśvadeva [cup] exists in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.
When the primary oblations have indeed been performed (Bhāṣya 3.7.7,
9), the Vaiśvadeva cups are drawn in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
therein, all the deities are worshipped.
Within that [sacrifice], there are also eight deities.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, in the Vaisarjana and other oblations, only clarified butter (ājya) is used, not Soma.

Since the Soma-related *darvihomas* prescribed by such injunctions as "He offers the *vaisarjana* oblations" require a substance, it might be argued that the Soma under discussion is restricted [as the substance] because it is present and serves as the primary offering material (*vahyardha*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because the Soma substance is employed in only a few specific functions while it is absent in others—such as the *āhavanīya* fire—and because clarified butter (*ājya*) is designated by the term "oblation" (*havis*) in the *kośa* and other sources, it is the one that applies when no specific substance is prescribed; furthermore, according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "Clarified butter is the oblation when no [specific] direction is given," those oblations should indeed be performed with clarified butter.

For this very reason, in the statement "he mixes the *pālīvat* with clarified butter (*ājya*) by heating it over the *dhiṣṇya* hearths," the reference to the clarified butter as something already established is logically consistent. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the mantra "perform the vow" (*vrataṃ kuruṣva*) is connected to the injunction for performing the vow consisting of drinking milk, and not to the release of speech (*vāg-vimoka*).
"He performs the vow; he releases his speech"—thus the recitation of the *praiṣa* (direction) is prescribed at the time of releasing speech.
This is enjoined as occurring at that specific time. (Vi.
3.2.4). In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the carrying forward of the fire to the Āgnīdhra shed is performed from the Śālāmukhīya fire itself.

Since the Āgnīdhra fire and others must necessarily be treated as *āhavanīya* fires by virtue of being the locus for oblations within the sacrificial essence, it follows that the deities of the Uttaravedi must be brought forth [to those fires].
This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the conclusion is that the deities are brought forth from the *Śālāmukhīya* fire itself.
For the Śruti text, "The priests go forward with Agni at their head, or with Soma at their head," prescribes movement toward the east (prāñcaḥ) by means of the term "prāñcaḥ."

Regarding the injunction, "Recite for the two [fires] being led forth to the Āgnīdhrīya and the [Āhavanīya]," the leading forth of the fire situated within the Śālāmukhīya—just as the *sola-tā* plant is moved from there—is performed in accordance with the conjunction understood from the *dvandva* compound in the leading forth of the fire and the leading forth of Soma-rāja. Precisely because its source (*apādāna*) is the Gārhapatya, the Āgnīdhrīya is merely a portion of the Āhavanīya; therefore, it does not serve as the locus for the oblation (*homa*).

Even after the carrying forward of the fire to the northern altar (*auttaravedika*), until the carrying forward of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire, the portion belonging to the *āhavanīya* exists here; therefore, it is spoken of as having the *āhavanīya* as its source (*apādāna*).
As for the Smṛti statement, "This [fire] from now on," the Bhāṣya explains that it refers to the period subsequent to the carrying forward of the *āgnīdhrīya*.
(Saṃkarṣa 3.2.14)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is stated: “One who practices sorcery should draw the cups beginning with the Śukra; one against whom sorcery is practiced should draw the cups beginning with the Manthin. Here, the Śukra and other cups do not possess the status of being drawn from the stream (*dhārāgraha*).
Thus, there is indeed a displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the Śukra and the others.
And that reduction is like seizing the tip of a stream, not its entirety;
as with the reduction of the taking, there is also a reduction of the settling,
yet even when there is a reduction of the settling, there is no reduction of the offering.
10|5|22. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, when the Bṛhat-sāman is used, there is the precedence of the Śukra cup: "If the Bṛhat-sāman is used, one should draw the cups beginning with the Śukra.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, sixteen performers (priests) are to be chosen; the Soma sacrifice should thus have that many performers.
Bhāṣya 3.7.21–24: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Ṣoḍaśin cup is to be taken only at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana).
The Ṣoḍaśin mentioned in the Jyotiṣṭoma is inserted only into the Agniṣṭoma form, not into the modified (vikṛti) sacrifices.
Vi. 10.5.9: In the Jyotiṣṭoma when it is performed with the Ṣoḍaśin-stotra, there is the performance of the subsequent oblations (pratihomas), beginning from the morning Agnihotra.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the injunction regarding the "seeing" (saṃdarśana) is heard; it applies to the modified sacrifices (vikṛti), not to the archetype (prakṛti).
Vārttika 3.3.11–24: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the commendatory statement (arthavāda): "He indeed would be [the sacrificer]."

By the passage beginning with, “He for whom this hearth (dhiṣṇya) is prescribed meditates upon it,” and ending with, “Indeed, they drag the sacrificer away when they carry the animal-cooking fire from the Āhavanīya; therefore, one should either use that very [fire] or produce one's own fire, so that the sacrificer may possess his own [sacrificial] fire,” the fire for cooking the animal sacrifice is determined.
In that context, by the phrase “it should be that very [fire],” the Āhavanīya itself is meant;
for, since it was introduced in the statement, “The Āhavanīya is indeed the sacrificer,” it alone remains present in the mind.

This being the case, it is the *prājahita* fire itself that is denoted by that term, because of its capacity for conceptualization (*vikalpika*) belonging to the same category as the *nirmanthya* fire;

for in all instances, a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is necessary for both sides of a dichotomy. Furthermore, the *prājahita* is similar to the worldly *nirmanthya* fire insofar as it is produced by churning.

The meaning is that [the fire] must either be one churned according to the Vedic method or one churned by an extraordinary (alaukika) method. Furthermore, since the dragging of the sacrificer during the carrying of the Āhavanīya fire is censured, it follows as a necessity that the fire being prescribed for the sacrificer’s own attainment must be distinct from the ordinary Āhavanīya;
for a comparison between one thing and another is only possible when they are different.
Therefore, this statement refers specifically to the *prājahita* fire. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there is the speaking of truth and so forth; in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, [there is the offering] of Soma.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, because the observances such as truthful speech have ceased [for the sacrificer], the vow pertaining to the Darśa sacrifice is accomplished by incidental application (prasaṅga). Vi.

11.1.12. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, during the measuring of the Sadas and other rites, the desire for the Dhṛṣṭi and so forth belongs to the sacrificer (yājamāna), not to the officiating priest (ārtvijya). This is the section concerning the [specific] ritual manuals (kāṇḍādhikaraṇa).
Likewise, regarding the section on desire (Kāmādhikaraṇa) [2.8.6]:
in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the worship of the Sadas pavilion must be performed with the verse addressed to Indra (aindrī ṛc), and not with any verse from the Daśatayī.
This follows the principle of the Āgneyī [verse].
3|1|8: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the taking of the Sataṃpada cup and other such acts are not the motivators for the purchase and bringing of the Soma;
this is the principle of the "anointing of the axle" (akṣāmyañjana-nyāya).
4|1|10: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, even the gift of one's entire property (*sarvasva-dakṣiṇā*) must be given when the [standard] twelve-hundred [cows] are absent.
6|7|9: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the after-offerings (anuyājas) are subsidiary elements of the Savanīya animal sacrifice.
Regarding them, there is a displacement [of the time] according to the rule: "They perform the after-offerings before the Āgnimāruta [offering].

4|3|15: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, because the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) of the Savanīya animal sacrifices fall within the procedure (tantra) of the Savanīya animal sacrifice, the animal is the governing element (tantrī), and the sacrificial cakes are incidental (prasaṅgī).

Therefore, after the *āgnimāruta* section, the five after-offerings (*anuyāja*s) performed in the form of the limbs of the animal sacrifice also accomplish the purpose of the after-offerings for the morning-sacrifice cakes (*prātaḥsavanika-puroḍāśa*) by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the after-offerings for the *savanīya* cakes are accomplished by incidental application through the fivefold ritual procedure (*pāṅkta-tantra*). This is the principle of the *savanīya* and others (*savanīyādi-nyāya*).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, because the Savanīya sacrificial cakes belonging to the three pressings (*savana*) are performed at different times, there is a repetition of the *haviskṛt* invocation mantra associated with them.

Vi. 11.1.21: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the Savanīya sacrificial cakes, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the offerings of the flour-residue (*piṣṭalepa*) and the *phalīkaraṇa* husks along with the after-offerings (*anuyāja*).

5|1|15. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the duties pertaining to the cups (grahadharmas), such as placing them on the altar and wiping them, must be performed even when they depend on the pressing (savana). This is the section concerning the duties of the cups (vi.
3|6|9). In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Sutyā day occurs on a festival day (parvan); therefore, the Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi must be performed prior to that, on a non-festival day (aparvan).
The Principle of the Conflict between the Primary and the Accessory (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*).

Bhāṣya 12.1.9.29: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the mantra used for the *subrahmaṇyā* invocation—beginning with “O Indra, come! O you who possess bay horses, come! O son of Medhātithi, O you whose horse is Vṛṣaṇaśva! O Gauravaskandin! O paramour of Ahalyā!”—is dedicated to Indra.
However, in the modified form (*vikṛti*) known as the Agniṣṭut, the *subrahmaṇyā* becomes dedicated to Agni.
Therefore, in that case, a modification (*ūha*) must be made by saying "come first," because [the deity] is present there;
however, in cases such as "O Harivan, this is for Medhātithi's ram," no modification is made, because the purpose is praise (*stuti*), even though the deity is not present.
The ritualists (*yājñika*), however, perform the modification as follows: "Come first, O Rohitāśva, Bṛhadbhāna, Dhūmaketu, Jātavedas, in the place of movement."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the sprinkling of the Dhiṣṇya hearths is performed with Soma using the *pariplu* ladle.

In the case of the injunction “He offers with the *sūrya* [ladle],” although the *prakṛta* (contextually relevant) *sarpa* [ladle] might be obtained as the instrument for sprinkling the *dhiṣṇya* fires—since it is also contextually present—it is established that the *pariplu* [ladle] alone serves as the instrument for the sprinkling. This is because the *pariplu* is presented in the Vedic text as the instrument for taking [the liquid]: “Sitting in the afternoon, having taken [the liquid] from the *droṇakalaśa* with the *pariplu*, he sprinkles the *dhiṣṇyas*. Otherwise, the act of taking [the liquid] with the *pariplu* would result in serving a merely invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.

*Saṃkarṣa* 3.2.19: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, regarding the injunction “One should sacrifice with Soma” (*somena yajeta*), the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is the enjoiner of a new, previously unknown ritual action (*apūrva-karma*).

It is not, however, a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of the collection of actions such as “He draws [the cup] for Indra and Vāyu” (*aindravāyavaṃ gṛhṇāti*) or “He draws [the cup] for Mitra and Varuṇa” (*maitrāvaruṇaṃ gṛhṇāti*).

Bhāṣya 2.1.6.17–20: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, in the passages “One should sacrifice with Soma,” “He offers the oblation” (*dakṣiṇāṃ juhoti*), and “He gives gold to the Ātreya,” there is a distinction of the new ritual action (*apūrva-bheda*) with each word.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the measuring and the lowering of the Soma must be performed with a cloth.
Regarding the measuring and the bringing down [of the Soma], these belong to the archetype of the Soma sacrifice because of a specific scriptural statement.
The Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the measuring and the bringing down are prescribed.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the measuring be done by whatever means and the bringing down by whatever means, or should the measuring be done on cloth and the bringing down by means of cloth?
What is the prima facie view? That there is no restriction as to where the measuring takes place, nor any restriction as to the means by which the bringing down occurs.
For in this way, under such lack of restriction, there will be simplicity and precedence in performance.
This being the prima facie view, we reply:
The measurement is to be performed on the cloth, and the removal [of the grain] must be done with the cloth.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement.
This is the scriptural statement:
"He measures with a cloth and performs the removal with a cloth"—
by the force of this statement, there must be a restriction.
Or rather, there is no doubt at all in this matter.
From the statement, it follows that the measurement is performed on the cloth and the removal [of the Soma] is done with the cloth.
This being the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), it is stated as a subject for further discussion in order to consider a specific point.
And regarding that which is stated as a subject for further discussion, there is no need for the presentation of the prima facie and final positions (*pūrvottarapakṣau*) therein.
Soma: Because this is a sūtra concerning the attainment [of the Soma], there is no separate connection.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the consumption of Soma. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the consumption of Soma:
"The bringing down [of the Soma] and the measuring are also [performed] on the Kaṭha-vasas cloth."
There might be some height [of the Soma], due to the absence [of cloth], or there might be equality with the cloth because of the scriptural statement.

Bhāṭṭa—(It should be understood that the three topical sections located in the Bhāṣya at 20, 21, and 23 have been unified here. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, based on the scriptural statements, "He measures the Soma on a cloth" and "He brings down [the Soma] with a cloth," the measuring and bringing down of the Soma are accomplished by means of a cloth. And during the *ahargaṇa* (multi-day sacrifice), for the purpose of bringing down the Soma every day, there should be a different cloth each day.
For as much Soma as is sufficient for one day, having been placed in the *havirdhāna* cart, that much must be drawn down with a cloth each day.
The remainder must likewise be kept in the cart, covered by a cloth.

Consequently, in this case, another cloth must be produced from the beginning until the last day; however, on the last day, it is to be done with a human-sized piece [of cloth], according to the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Nor should it be said that even before the *uttama* [verse], one must perform the *upāvaharaṇa* by taking up only a single distinct mouth from the *mānava* [cup] and using that very same one;
for the *upāvaharaṇa* is prescribed to be performed with the *grāvastut* [cup] which has been spread out (*āstṛta*).

And since that cup is connected to the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa (4.2.6), it is regularly employed as the reciter of the *grāvastotrīya* verses and the *anuṣṭubh* meters, and thus lacks the status of being a separate vessel (*havyabhāva*).
Furthermore, the intermediate measurements should not be taken only at the time of measurement.

For, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), because of convenience, the carrying down (*upanayanam*) of the sacrificial post was performed at the time of sprinkling with the very same garment used for measurement at the time of purchase; however, that is not the actual scriptural meaning. Therefore, since there is no evidence for taking them at the time of measurement, they are to be taken only at the time of carrying down.
Thus, even though the singularity of the *vajra* is implied by the sense, it is set aside, and this constitutes a connection to the chapter.
Maṇḍana: "In the removal of pride, [there is] clothing.
Śaṅkara: "By that clothing, pride is removed.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, when the Soma is unavailable, pūtīka plants, ādāra plants, or phālguna plants serve as substitutes.
In that context, there is no optionality between *soma* and substances such as *pūtīka*;
rather, there is a daily requirement for substances such as *pūtīka*.
(Vi. 6.3.13). In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the purchase of *soma* is performed with ten substances, including goats and gold.

12.4.13: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the Soma substance which is obtained optionally through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) is a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*).
4.2.9: In the Soma-purchase section of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the dual number in the phrase "he yokes two oxen" (*anaḍvāhau yunakti*) is indeed intended to be significant.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the consumption of Soma must be preceded by permission, and this applies only to those who share a single vessel, because they are associated with that same vessel. Commentary: This is doubted: should anyone at all be asked for permission, or only one who shares the same vessel?
Since there is no specification mentioned, it follows that anyone at all [may do so]. To this, it is replied:
that authorization, indeed, should be for those who share a single vessel.
Why? Because in this context, "requesting permission" (*anujñāpana*) constitutes the act of eating.

And this is the form of requesting permission: when one person desires to do what ought to be done by another, he says, "Please grant me leave," or when one wishes to engage in activities such as eating together, he seeks to win over the other's mind.
This, however, is not possible at all if they are using separate vessels.

For in that case, one person should not perform what is to be done by another, nor should one desire to do so; or, because of eating together, one might bring the substance for the other. However, when the Soma is in a single vessel and the consecration is to be performed jointly, an equal division follows as a matter of logic.
If it were drunk there without being divided, it might happen that one person would drink what was intended to be drunk by another.

In that regard, a request for permission is possible as follows: "Half [of the drink] should be drunk by you and half by me; perhaps I might drink more or less than that, so you should grant me your permission.
Or: "While drinking from the same vessel with you, it is right for me to act in a way that pleases your mind.
Thus, a request for permission is possible.
Therefore, this should take place in a single vessel—
or rather, if this were prescribed as something not already established, then it would have to be requested from somewhere or other;
however, this is simply brought from the ordinary world.
His acquisition [of food] in whatever kind of place it may be is not prohibited.

However, when there is an equal distribution among those who share the same vessel, according to the principle that "it should be equal because it is so heard in scripture," one who does not eat meat [or forbidden food] should perform the act after obtaining permission.

Even though there is no transgression by means of the *soma* juice and no absence of the eight defects resulting from it, since the arising of resentment is possible through direct eating together, [permission must be sought].
Therefore, this is the occasion for permission;
thus, [the rule applies] to those who share a single vessel.
As for Soma—since it concerns the performance of the archetype sacrifice (prakṛti), there is a logical connection (saṃgati).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: that performance should indeed be with a single vessel (*ekapātra*), because the purpose is concentrated therein. As it is said: "Is there an offering for all [the priests], or should it be for those who share a single vessel?"

The first [alternative] would follow from the eight reasons, while the last would follow from the addition of ten. Bhāṭṭa: This permission should be accepted by one who has the capacity to consume [the portion] in a single vessel, precisely because it achieves a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha), and because it serves to prevent quarrels caused by the occasion of unequal portions and so forth.
Since that [quarrel] could be prevented even by other means, this [permission] is a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi).
However, if permission were required for anyone other than these, there would be the defect of it being an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction) whose purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
For this very reason, where there is only one eater in a single vessel, there is no taking of permission at all;
likewise, even for the last eater, there is no taking of permission due to the absence of any purpose.
The ritualists, however, practice as follows:
Maṇḍana says, "But one who uses the same vessel must be asked for permission";
Śaṅkara says, "And when there is a single vessel, there is the state of being offered."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the consumption of Soma, the sequence of mantras for requesting permission and granting it follows the sense of the matter;
therein, the response follows from the sense itself.
The Commentary states: this is understood from the words "tadupahūta upahavya" as that by which one should cause [the other] to give permission.

Now, there is a doubt regarding the response: is it a worldly response, or is it this very [Vedic] one? What is the prima facie view? This Vedic response has been enjoined for the purpose of answering a question; however, even this worldly response ought to be possible as a reply.
This being the case, we reply:
in this matter, the answer is precisely this.
But surely, it is [the Upahavya] because of the indicative mark of the question?
It is said: that which was previously capable of being the response, namely "You are invited," shall perform the function of the response.
He says: this assumption is the reverse.
For normally, there should first be a question, and then a reply.
It is said in response:
by implication, the task of providing a reply will occur first.
For meaning is indeed stronger in due order.
Or—the reading in the Sūtra is "vadanam" (speaking). It is taken as a compound; or it is a common worldly usage where both the question and the answer occur in a single instance.
This being the prima facie position, it is replied:
setting aside the order of recitation by means of the order of meaning, the formula "upahūtaḥ" (you are invited) should be employed in the granting of permission.
Since the permission is stated by means of the Soma-mantra, there is a connection [of this topic] due to the consideration of the restrictive application of that mantra.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: regarding the phrase "upahūta upahavyasa," the response should be made with the word "upahūtaḥ" (invoked), according to the sense and the force of the context. (Mīmāṃsākośa 230)
Vi— "The two [mantras] 'upahavya' and 'upahūta' should apply to the two acts of requesting permission and granting permission; or rather, they are divided at the beginning.
Because there is no division [of the mantra itself], it applies to the whole, not by virtue of its indicative mark (liṅga)."
In the case of the [mantra] "upahavya," there is knowledge of permission; for the others, it is otherwise. Another [author] has stated in the previous section that it is external.
Maṇḍana says: "The response partakes of the preceding mantra."
Śaṅkara: "There should be a division of that mantra.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, at the consumption of the Soma, both the oblation (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*) are the joint causes [for the recitation].
And because of the oblation and the pressing."
Commentary: There is another reason for the sequence of the oblation (*homa*) and the drinking (*amiṣava*).
How so? [The text says]: "Having offered the *iṣu* arrows in the Āhavanīya fire while at the *Havirdhāna* shed, they go back day by day and consume the portions (*bhakṣa*) in the *Sadas*.
This does not prescribe a sequence of location—that the consumption occurs after the oblation has been completed.
Because eating has not [otherwise] been established;
and because two sequences would have to be enjoined, the sentence "having pressed [the juice] and having offered" would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*);
furthermore, because the sequence is already established by the very nature of the purpose.
For no one is entitled to a presentation [of a portion] when a purpose has not been established.

Nor are the *homābhiṣava* (the offering and the pressing) enjoined by the mere absence of eating; for the pressing is for the sake of the offering, and the offering is for the sake of the fruit [of the sacrifice].
Therefore, eating is prescribed for those who perform the offering and the pressing.
"Those who dry [the Soma] and those who offer oblations shall consume it.
Or rather: Is the consumption [of Soma] caused by these two factors alone? No, it is said;
there is another consumption following from the offering and the pressing.

How so? For it is stated thus: "Having offered the oblations in the Āhavanīya fire with the *prāvabhiḥ* verses while in the *havirdhāna* shed, they go back day by day and consume the portions (*bhakṣas*) in the *sadas*.
In that case, the offering (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*) are already established as possessing their respective qualities and are not being enjoined [anew].

If it is argued that this scriptural statement is for the purpose of prescribing the sequence—just like the sentence regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), such as "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the sacrificer, initiates the Brahman," and so forth—that is not the case here.
Because this sequence is established by the very nature of the facts:
for it is not possible to press that which has already been offered, nor is there Soma left of that which has already been consumed.
As they proceed from the location of the Āhavanīya fire toward the *sadas* (this word is in the accusative case), they reach it every single day.

Furthermore, for the sake of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and the subsequent consumption—which are necessary for the Hotṛ and others in the sacrificial hall (*sadas*)—the Soma juices must be brought into the hall (the meaning being "into the *sadas*").
And the *upahavya* cup must be offered by the Adhvaryu.
Therefore, the phrase "in the hall" (*sadasi*) is restated [as a reference].
Regarding the consumption of Soma in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice (1834): in the Jyotiṣṭoma, that which is obtained through mere consumption is enjoined as the occasion for the Soma-consumption.

In this context, the purpose of including the words "having offered" (*hutvā*) and "having pressed" (*abhiṣuṣya*) is so that the act of consumption may be established as having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*) as those preceding actions.
For it is not possible that the drinking is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the oblation and the pressing, both of which have already had their purposes ascertained;
and since the drinking is already understood to be a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the Soma, there is no hearing of a connection with anything else as its subordinate part.
Therefore, by implication, the oblation and the pressing are known to be the conditions (*nimitta*).

Therefore, even one who performs the *abhiṣava* (pressing) and the *homa* (offering) should consume the *soma*. [The opponent asks: "Are only those who possess the name, the word, and the sixfold act the deities of consumption? Or are the presser and the offerer as well? In that regard, let the first view stand according to the direction of the argument: having pressed the *soma* in the *havirdhāna* shed and offered it, one should consume it in the *sadas*."
Thus, because he possesses learning, he may eat just as others do.
(The word "cause" [hetu] must necessarily be stated, as in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "for the sake of establishing the cause.

Bhaṭṭa: This is another occasion for the consumption [of the soma]: "Having pressed [the soma] with stones in the two Havirdhāna sheds, and having offered it in the Āhavanīya fire, they consume the portions facing west beyond the Sadas.

Here, because all the subordinate elements such as the Havirdhāna sheds are already established by injunctions and are thus obtained through the sense of the text, only that which is not yet obtained—the act of consuming itself performed by those who perform the offering, the pressing, and the consuming—is to be enjoined.

Although consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) is already established for the performers of the offering (*homa*), the pressing (*abhiṣava*), and the consumption itself in the *hariyojana* and other rites, nevertheless, because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bhaṅga*) if it were merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already known, it must be treated as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

Furthermore, this [consumption] is not simply that which was previously enjoined, because in all such cases there is another performer specifically enjoined by the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).

Therefore, a distinct act of consumption, having the same agent as the offering and the pressing, is indeed enjoined; or else, following the principle of the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, there is merely a difference in the performance (*prayoga-bheda*) of the sixfold-consecrated consumption (*ṣaṭkāra-bhakṣa*) itself, in accordance with the subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of the agent.

Nor is it [the case that the injunction applies] at the time of production, because of its being a regulator; for it is the "firstness" (*prāthamya*), which is connected to production, that serves as the regulator in the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance sentence.
However, it should be understood that if "firstness" were connected to the performance (*prayoga*), then it would indeed be a separate ritual act.

And here, since the status of being performed by the same agent who performs the pressing and the eating is already established for the oblation (*homa*) simply by virtue of the designation (*samākhyā*) "Adhvaryu," and because the primary [act] is already established, it is the eating alone for which the status of being performed by the same agent who performs the pressing and the eating is enjoined, [thereby] precluding the status of being performed by different agents for the oblation and the eating.
Since the *homa* (offering) and *abhiṣava* (pressing) have their results already established, they serve as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the *vaṣaṭkāra*, just like the deity.
It will be stated in the sixth [book] (6.4.7) that these two together constitute the occasion.

Therefore, whoever performs the repetition of the *homa* and *abhiṣava*—whether he be the Adhvaryu, the Prati-praśāstṛ, or anyone else—at whichever cup (*graha*) or goblet (*camasa*) it occurs, he shall consume [the soma] there.
Maṇḍana: "And one who performs the oblation and the consecration should consume [it]. Śaṅkara: "The oblation and the consecration..."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the remnants of the Soma— those substances such as the Adhvaryu and others who are produced for the purpose of performing the ritual acts—
are not heard of [in the scripture] as being for sale in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Therefore, [the *dakṣiṇā*] does not belong to any one of the officiating priests (*adhvaryu*, etc.).
Viśvarūpa says: "Among these, there is either one who sells the Soma, or none at all, because of the absence of formal selection (*varaṇa*).
There is one [priest], for there is no partial performance of the rite; the sale is performed by him alone."
Bhaṭṭa: But the seller of Soma is indeed someone else.
For the act of appointment (*varaṇa*) and so forth is performed to secure persons for the performance of the constituent parts of that [sacrifice] which have already been enjoined.

However, since selling is not enjoined, even though it is necessary because the prescribed purchase cannot otherwise be accomplished, it is nonetheless not a constituent part (*anaṅga*), because the purchase can be achieved by subsisting on sales performed by persons who engage in them out of natural inclination (*rāga*) while accepting the fault [of selling], and because it is not [logically] entailed (*anākṣepāt*).
Therefore, since those who have been chosen for that [sacrifice] do not apply there, he is indeed someone else.
Maṇḍana: "The seller is other than those [who are eligible] by nature.
Śaṅkara: "He is censured for selling Soma."
Oṃ. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, because there is an injunction for the consumption of the remnants of the Soma, the consumption of Soma exists.
"Because there is no statement [to that effect], the eating [of the Soma] is not established.
Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, they recite the Soma portions. Regarding these...
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is distress regarding the oblation and the pressing.
How so? It is not connected in this way: "having pressed, then having offered, then one should consume."
By this [text], no sequence is established such that "one should press and offer," nor that "those who press and offer shall consume.
The sentence would be split [if interpreted otherwise]: "having pressed they shall consume" and "having offered they shall consume.

Therefore, there is no mutual connection between the offering and the pressing; thus, the consumption may be connected with one [act] as well as with the other, namely, "having pressed they shall consume" and "having offered they shall consume."
Therefore, eating occurs by means of one or the other cause.

*dup—* (In the third book [3.5.12–32], it was established that the sentence beginning with "When [the soma] has been pressed by the stones in the *havirdhāna* shed" (*havirdhāne grāvabhirabhipyute*) prescribes a consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) performed by the same agent as the pressing (*abhiṣava*) and the offering (*homa*); here, that very point is recalled as an introductory premise. Even though there is the denotation of various constituent elements (*padārtha*)—(that is to say, although many constituent elements such as the offering, the pressing, their sequence, and the procedure are indeed mentioned)—the sequence between the offering and the pressing is not prescribed (the meaning is that neither the offering, nor the pressing, nor their sequence is being prescribed), for the matter is ambiguous.
Alternatively, it is doubtful whether the general rule applies to that particular instance or to another;
thus, that general injunction would not apply to the particular injunction. What is the reason? Because an option between them is improper.
How is an option (vikalpa) unjustified? To this it is replied:

if the status of having the *varmā* as the locus is heard [prescribed] for these oblations (*homa*), then by one who resorts to an option on the grounds that "it does not exist in one alternative," a dependence upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be postulated. On the other hand, if the status of having the *varmā* as the locus is not heard for these [oblations], then it exists in one alternative; thus, there is no dependence upon a means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, the non-mention of the *varman* would be unintended even though it is heard [in the text].

To this it is replied: "The existence [of the *varman*] occurs by implication (*arthāt*) in one alternative; and that implication is the cessation of the *homa* and the attainment of the *āhavanīya* fire. This is not so.
If merely the cessation of the *homa* were to be performed, then that would be accomplished by means of the *āhavanīya* fire as well, by implication.
But here, the status of being the locus for the armor is also enjoined. That [status] would not be subsumed if the Āhavanīya fire were employed [as the locus];
and if it were not subsumed, the injunction regarding the performance would be contradicted.
To this it is replied:
although the status of the armor as the locus is also enjoined in the oblation, because it is subordinate, it makes the oblation perfect.
Therefore, even if it is not included there, there is no fault.
It will become consistent through another legal case;
therefore, it is merely an option.
To this, it is said: "No."
In this context, the connection with the *varma* and other oblations (*homa*) is prescribed;
and that [connection] is the primary element, not the oblation itself.
If that were not brought into application, the rite would not be performed according to the scriptural injunction.
To this it is replied:
even when a relationship is being enjoined, a substance is enjoined; one is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the other is the means (*sādhana*).
That which is the goal to be accomplished is the primary element (*pradhāna*).
And that is the oblation; therefore, there is an option.
Furthermore, even when the connection is being heard, the oblation must necessarily be adopted.
And as for the *homa*, it follows that the *āhavanīya* fire must indeed be used.
That is not so,
because the *āhavanīya* is not prescribed [for this purpose].

How is there a lack of knowledge? Because it does not apply to the specific cases. How is there no application? Because when the altar (*varman*) is the locus, it is impossible for [the fire] to be known as having the *āhavanīya* fire as its locus, both with respect to the cognition and the performance [of the rite].
If the altar is also known as the locus, then it is neither possible to know nor to perform [the rite] as having the *āhavanīya* fire as its locus.
He said:
"It should be done in such a way as is possible; thus there will be no contradiction of the rule. Therefore, the Āhavanīya fire will take precedence over the Varmā and other [fires]."
It is said:
this would indeed be so if the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire could not be established without subverting the *varman* and other [prohibitions].
For it can be accomplished in two ways: either by subverting the *varman* and so forth, or by avoiding them.
In that case, the suffix *varman* is elided for the sake of negation;

we shall effect this elision, and thus the designation of the *āhavanīya* fire comes into being. Even if it is impossible to perform [the action], why should it not be considered as having been accomplished?
"What is impossible shall not be done.
He said: "This which is called the general injunction (sāmānya-pratyaya) attaches its effect to all particulars.
If this is so, then by that [injunction], the Āhavanīya fire is prescribed for the oblations of the Darśa and other rites, as well as for others."
In that regard, the notion of the *āhavanīya* fire associated with the *varmādi-homa* cannot be set aside.
Therefore, it follows that [the general rule] should remain, setting aside the *varmādi-homa*.
To this, it is replied:
This is not so;
for a word denoting a universal does not denote particulars.
And if it were to denote them, it would not be possible [to apply the term] to a cow that has just been born, because there would have been no prior perception [of it].
And because it has been previously observed in the case of a generality, [the application] is possible;
therefore, words do not denote particulars. Consequently, in the oblation of *varma* and so forth, there is the cognition of the *āhavanīya* fire.
Or, even when saluting, one does not salute in the primary sense;
how then? By way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
And secondary indication is sublated by direct denotation (śruti).
Therefore, since the *varma* and other [mantras] are obtained through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) for the *varmādi-homa*, it is impossible to enjoin the *āhavanīya* fire [as their locus].
To this, he replies:
"But could it not be the reverse? Once the *āhavanīya* is obtained, it would be impossible to have the cognition of the *varmādi* [mantras as its locus]."

It might be so; however, in this specific case, the cognition of the *varma* (armor) and other items is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), whereas the cognition of the *āhavanīya* fire is based on secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
It has been stated that a cognition based on direct scriptural statement is more authoritative.
But is it not the case that even regarding the general [fire], the cognition of the *āhavanīya* is based on direct scriptural statement?
It is said:
the cognition of the *varman* and other [mantras] is also based on direct scriptural statement (*śrauta*) regarding the general category.
For that [cognition] is enjoined in relation to a specific *homa*, and it does not qualify this [category] as being anything other than *homa*.

Therefore, excluding the *varma* and other such oblations, the *āhavanīya* fire shall be employed in all other oblations. [Durga: (The discussion regarding the particle *na* is concluded. Now, based on the principle of the general being set aside by the particular (*prāptabādha*), the sublation of the general by the particular is considered. But surely, because the two ritual acts serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there can be neither an option (*vikalpa*) nor a relationship of sublation and sublated; rather, there must be a combination (*samuccaya*) since there is no contradiction. Therefore, this is not a topic that needs to be commenced.

How so? [Is it because it has an unseen purpose? The answer is: the sacrifice does not imply a substratum (*ādhāra*), because it is accomplished even without a substratum. And if it were to imply a substratum, then the *āhavanīya* fire would be restricted [as the sole locus].

Just as in the case of "the cake on eight potsherds is for Agni," where some material substance inherent to the eight potsherds is implied, and therein rice (*vrīhi*) is restricted [as that substance].
In this case, however, the substratum is enjoined by the force of the statement itself (and is not merely implied and restricted;
therefore, it serves an invisible purpose).

Therefore, just as the *prayāja* offerings (which assist by means of an invisible effect) are not treated as optional alternatives to the *upahoma* offerings, nor is there a relationship of sublation between them,
so it is here as well [regarding the substance and the deity]. And thus it has been stated (6.3.15–20) that there is no substitute for the deity, the material, or the ritual action.
(For indeed, a substitute would exist only in the case of such a requirement.
Therefore, since the section on substitutes (6.4.13–17) has already established that combination alone is appropriate, why is this topic (adhikaraṇa) commenced? It is said: True.

Just as there is an implication of a substance by the statement "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni," the Āhavanīya fire is not similarly implied by the sacrifice; nevertheless, it is not connected [to the sacrifice] unless there is a need for it.

For instance, the phrase "in the Āhavanīya fire" is expectant, and it is rendered free of expectancy by the word "he offers"; likewise, "he offers" is also expectant and is rendered free of expectancy by the mention of the Āhavanīya fire.

For if there were no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) here, then there would be no connection at all [in the injunction] "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire" (because the fire is expected as a substratum). Therefore, that *āhavanīya* fire, being enjoined, benefits the oblation through its visible function alone, by serving as the substratum for the offering of the substance.

(He objects, considering that the purpose is visible [dṛṣṭārthatā], on the grounds that since the two substances to be brought in are already seen, they serve as the substratum, and because that [substratum] is already seen, there can be no combination: "In this way, when the measure of the *varmā* and so forth is established, sublation (*bādha*) and option (*vikalpa*) would occur; however, a substitute (*pratinidhi*) would apply because of its visible purpose, just like other substances.
It is replied: This is appropriate in the case of other substances.

In that regard, by the injunction "There is an eight-potherd cake for Agni," the sacrifice is enjoined as the means to the fruit. When the rice grains are no longer available once the ritual has commenced, the injunction of the sacrifice still requires a substance (in order to accomplish it). And since such a requirement exists, the use of a substitute is appropriate.
But when the Āhavanīya fire is absent at the commencement of the rite, then the injunction for the sacrifice does not imply the Āhavanīya (since the sacrifice is possible even without it).
Therefore, there can be no substitute for the Āhavanīya.

[Objection: By this same logic (that there is no substitute because it is not implied by the injunction for the sacrifice), would it not follow that a substitute for the deity is possible (since the deity is implied by the sacrifice)?
Regarding this, some explain:
a substitute is used on account of similarity.
If the word for the primary deity is not remembered, then its similarity cannot be known; therefore, because it is impossible [otherwise], a substitute is employed.
Now, it is traditionally taught that when the primary substance is available, that alone should be used (and not a substitute).

[The author] refutes this view: If one proceeds in this manner, then when the rice has been lost while the ritual has already commenced, the sacrifice must necessarily be completed by the force of the scriptural injunction; yet, since no rice remains and it is impossible to obtain it, one cannot provide a substitute of similar quality. In such a situation, the sacrifice should simply not be performed.
Nor should one argue that such a situation never occurs.
[This was said] perhaps due to a confusion of the mind (*cittabhrama*).

Therefore, [the claim that] "because of the absence of similarity, there is no substitute for a deity"—this is incorrect. Consequently, others [of the same class] must also be mentioned as being fit to serve as substitutes for the deity.
And that has been described in the eighth [chapter], in the section on the *adhikaraṇa* (6.3.15).

(He concludes the present topic: Therefore, because it serves an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatvāt*), the *āhavanīya* fire is not implied by the injunction for the sacrifice; thus, this is not contradicted by the section on substitutes (*pratinidhi*).

Furthermore, the *āhavanīya* fire, independent of the footprint, attains the status of a locus through the locative case, and the footprint likewise is independent of the *āhavanīya*; (for this reason also, there is no combination).

Just as the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇa-vibhakti*) in "with rice" (*vrīhibhiḥ*) conveys rice that is independent of barley, as it does in "with barley" (*yavaiḥ*); so too, one who were to perform a combination (*samuccaya*) would not fail to produce the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—for indeed, the cake can be produced even with mixed grains—but he would contradict the meaning conveyed by the sentence (namely, its form of independence). Therefore, in that case, there is an option (*vikalpa*) based solely on the word itself, not from the nature of the thing.

In the same way here as well, because [the two fires] are independent [of one another], the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed accomplished even by the two combined; however, there is no contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If there were a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the two substrates (*padārtha*), then either the fire-altar (*pada*) would be placed upon the Āhavanīya fire, or the Āhavanīya fire would be placed upon the altar.
When the Āhavanīya fire is placed upon the altar and thus becomes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the oblation (*homa*), then the altar could no longer be the locus.
The same should be stated regarding the word (the locus of the oblation). Therefore, neither in reality nor by means of the word is a conjunction between the object and the substrate possible.
However, an example is raised:
"When one offers," and "One offers on the path"—here, the hearing of the root *juhoti* (to offer) is common to both the [term] *āhavanīya* and the word *padam*.
Thus, here too it is simply the general case of *homa*, and elsewhere it is that same [general case].
Therefore, because of this relationship of general and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-bhāva*), the relationship of sublation and non-sublation (*bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva*) is not tenable.
However, [the other case] is as stated in the *Mīmāṃsākośa* 231.
In the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites, [the application occurs] by way of the path and the day;
an illustrative example for the Jyotiṣṭoma and others must be sought.
That is explained as follows:

"He offers the *patnīsaṃyāja* oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire. Here, the word *patnīsaṃyāja* denotes a specific [type of] sacrifice (*yāga*). In the case of "When he offers in the *āhavanīya*," only the general [category] is heard [and not the specific].
Therefore, the relationship of sublation and sublated is established here, as in the example: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya.

(He first demonstrates the principle in the illustration: In that case, by the word "Brāhmaṇa," the genus (*jāti*) of the Brāhmaṇas—characterized by the exclusion of other castes—is indicated; whereas in the case of Kauṇḍinya, it is the individual (*vyakti*) itself that is characterized by the exclusion of other castes.
Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya, no universal (sāmānya) exists [in this case],

such as "cowness" (golam), which is excluded from horses and the like and follows after individuals such as the brindled cow (śāvaleyādi). [The argument] is by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmyeṇa), because it is not so here.
To the question "How so?", he says: That [circularity] is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, no such entity exists in Kauṇḍinya—an intermediate generality (*avāntara-sāmānya*)—which, having been grasped through direct perception, would cause a word to function.
Therefore, by the word "Kauṇḍinya," only a particular (*viśeṣa*) is expressed.

Furthermore, this statement regarding the word-meaning [is made] with respect to the sentence-meaning [in the example]: "The lineage is the offspring of Kuṇḍina. If the sentence-meaning were indeed the denotation of the word, then [this word] would not convey a universal (sāmānya). (This is because the sentence-meaning is of a specific nature; for a genus (*jāti*) cannot be the offspring of Kuṇḍina. Therefore, it is only a particular (*viśeṣa*) that is expressed by this word.
And in that case, the function [the denoted meaning] follows immediately [for a word, since the denoted meaning is indeed immediately contiguous].

In the other case [the general rule], the application of the function is general; the specific [meaning] must later be delimited by the definition [of the term] along with its auxiliaries such as context and so forth.
Therefore, there is remoteness in that case, whereas here there is proximity.

(The author applies the principle by way of an illustration: By this same principle, the Āhavanīya fire is set aside by the Gārhapatya fire [which is specifically prescribed] in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

This very example is applicable here as well; in this case too, there exists the relationship of sublation and that which is sublated between these two, precisely through the terms "general" and "particular.
For the Āhavanīya fire, having been produced by the injunctions beginning with "the sacrificer," stands in need of a purpose.
In the case of the *anārambhya-adhikaraṇa*, the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇabhāva*) is prescribed for oblations (*homāḥ*) in a general sense.
Here, however, an oblation qualified by a specific spot (*pada*) is mentioned.
In that context, the *āhavanīya* fire cannot be prescribed, because the oblation is already established by the spot.

The *āhavanīya* fire, being enjoined by its originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), is prescribed in accordance with those oblations (*homa*) that have been understood [from that injunction]. In that regard, it is appropriate to enjoin the *āhavanīya* for pure (i.e., baseless) oblations, because of its suitability; however, it does not apply to those [oblations] which are produced already possessing a substratum (*sādhikaraṇa*), because of its unsuitability.

Therefore, even in this case, there is sublation of this very [general rule]; thus, the scripture concerning the *āhavanīya* fire pertains to a different scope. As it is said: "Since the general [rule] is also obtained through direct perception, just like the particular, there is no sublation by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, nor is there sublation as in the case of extended application (*atideśa*). (Because the *pada* and *āhavanīya* fires are equal, an option [*vikalpa*] alone is appropriate.)
This being the position reached, we reply:
"The application [of the rule] occurs by virtue of the general instruction and the definition of the specific;
having heard [the rule] regarding the specific, it is therefore more powerful."

In the *patnīsaṃyāja* and other rites, having heard of the *gārhapatya* and other fires as being obtained through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), one sets aside the *āhavanīya* fire which is obtained more slowly through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); this is "sublation" (*bādha*). Soma [says]: The meaning of the sūtra is this: that scriptural rule which is general should be at a distance from—that is, far removed from—a specific rule; the sense is that a general rule does not operate within the scope of a specific one.
For the general rule is delayed by its state of uncertainty as to how far its scope extends toward the specific, and because an option (*vikalpa*) is improper.

Vi: "The Āhavanīya fire, being subject to option, is set aside by the footstep and other [rites], because the general rule is overridden by the specific one due to the equality of what is stated directly. Since there is no sublation by that which is stated through indicative mark (liṅga), it remains optional."
Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would occur for the sake of a specific meaning; therefore, it is sublated by the primary sense.

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains: even though the general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*) is already established, the particular rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*) prescribing the *pada* and so forth possesses greater force than the *taddhita* suffix, the *āhavanīya* fire, and the like.

Furthermore, since the purpose of the *homa* (oblation) is established through mere implication (*ākṣepa*) even without an explicit statement of purpose, and since the *padāhavanīya* fire also serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it is produced as a substratum precisely by virtue of its being expressed in the locative case; therefore, because both [the general rule and the specific rule] independently establish the *homa* as having that substratum, and because this would otherwise be untenable, a conflict necessarily arises, whereby the sublation of the general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra`) regarding that subject is logically justified.

The general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*)—namely, the injunction regarding the *juhū* ladle—because it expresses the generality of *homa*, prescribes the *āhavanīya* fire for every instance of *homa* by means of a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the individual [ladle]. However, as soon as that general rule is observed through its possible connection and would apply to all instances of *homa* by first indicating the specific individuals whose relationship is already known, the *pada-homa* (foot-offering) becomes satisfied by the very fact that it has been prescribed for a *homa* of a different class; thus, the *pada-homa* does not take the *āhavanīya* fire.

And although even a homa of a different class is indeed indicated by the root *juhoti*, there is also indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the specific difference (*vaijātya*) that serves as the delimitor of what is to be indicated; for the root *juhoti* denotes the general category of *homa* which pervades [all instances], just as the word "path" applies to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth, milk...
Thus, there is greater weight [to the latter]. Nevertheless, because it is enjoined by a direct injunction (*vidhi*), it possesses superior force due to its immediate presentation;
for here, a *homa* of a different class, qualified by specific words, is indeed what is being enjoined.
And for this reason, the *pada* possesses greater force due to its being "taught at the time of origination" (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).

Even if the oblation were obtained through another sentence, nevertheless, because the injunction regarding the *pada* is established by the contextual sentence (*prākaraṇika-vākya*) as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [oblation], it possesses greater force due to its contextuality and so forth, as well as its lack of other occasion (*niravakāśatva*).
Consequently, the *āhavanīya* fire—being taught generally—is "taught after the origination" (*utpanna-śiṣṭa*) and is not taught outside of a specific context (*anārabhya-vihita*).
And because it has room for application (*sāvakāśa*), it is weak;
therefore, in reality, that scripture concerns only matters other than the *padahoma*.
This [contrary] notion is merely an illusion produced by not seeing the relevant passage, for it is said that when that passage is seen, the former is sublated.
It should be understood that in this way, by means of a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*), even a general prohibition (*sāmānyaniṣedha*) is set aside, just as a general injunction is.

For this very reason, the prohibition "one should not kill" does not apply to enjoined killing, because it finds its scope only in cases other than those enjoined. Now, one might object: there is no evidence for restricting the scope of a prohibition; for although it is understood from the prohibition that all killing whatsoever is a means to evil, there is no sublation [of that understanding] when it is understood through an injunction that enjoined killing is everywhere a means to benefit.
For it is not contradictory for something to be the object of an injunction even when its status as a means to an undesirable end is understood;
because such undesirability [is neutralized] by the absence of intense aversion, and activity toward heaven and the like is possible through mere desire alone.

For this very reason, even in the case of worldly violence, activity is indeed observed when there is an absence of intense aversion to such undesirability, provided there is an intensity of desire for the immediate result.

For in all cases of positive injunction, regarding its object such as a sacrifice, one merely infers that it is a means to that which— in reality— is the object of intense passion, namely heaven and the like. And by means of prohibition, regarding its own object such as violence, one merely infers that it is a means to that which— in reality— is the object of intense aversion, namely sin and the like.
The intensity of passion and hatred, however, occurs occasionally due to the force of karma from previous births; in such cases, there is no operation of injunctions or prohibitions.

Furthermore, regarding their respective functions—namely, being the means to sin and being the means to heaven—there is no contradiction whatsoever, just as there is none between [their] not being the means to immediate pleasure or pain.

Therefore, since there is no contradiction between the animal sacrifice (*daikṣa*) and other such acts of killing being the means to assist the ritual (*ṛtūpakāra*), even though they are designated by the term "sin" (*pratyavāya*), the prohibition does not have a scope restricted to those [acts] alone.

Even in those cases where there is a scriptural injunction regarding the sin incurred by non-performance at a site of perpetual sacrifice (*nityapuṇyayāga*), there is no contradiction whatsoever, because activity is rendered possible through the following supposition: that while the sin is slight upon performance, it is much greater upon non-performance.
For this very reason, it is said: "A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; of this there is no doubt.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa."
Thus, in the *Manusmṛti* (2.87), even the praise of recitation (*japa*) and other such acts becomes appropriate.
For one who is "friendly" (*maitraḥ*) is free from violence and the like.
If it is argued that for this very reason, this alone is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the followers of Sāṅkhya;

This is indeed the general purport of the questions regarding the dwelling of Jaimini: "By dharma one dispels evil"; "In the dharma known as *pravṛtti*, the highest fruit is the attainment of heaven";
"For from dharma there can arise no evil that leads to hell";
and "O dear one, no doer of good ever goes to a miserable state."
Dharma, when practiced again and again, increases one’s reputation;
praised by the elders, a person thereafter takes no delight in evil. For those whose sins have been shaken off by Dharma, their heart's desires are fulfilled.

"The unrighteous and the sinful fall into calamity"— from such passages in the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas, which are characterized by an unrestricted perspective, it is understood that *dharmaness* (the quality of being dharma) is pervaded by the non-production of sin, while *adharmaness* (the quality of being adharma) is pervaded by the production of sin.
For this very reason, some maintain that according to the rule, whatever action is subject to injunction or prohibition, that too must be denotable by the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

Therefore, just as in the case of an injunction there is an inference that [the action] has desire as its means (*icchādhanatva*), so too there is an inference that it produces demerit (*pāpajanakatva*). Consequently, the prohibition, being in contradiction with that [inference], pertains only to a domain other than that [injunction]. While postulating the production of demerit, it results in having a scope distinct from that [injunction]; thus, even here, the sublation (*bādha*) consisting of the restriction of the general prohibition by a specific [provision] is established.
It has been stated that the general injunction is not restricted by the specific prohibition, but rather there is an option (*vikalpa*); however, this is not the case when the situation is reversed.

For this very reason, Vyāsa’s Sūtra states: "If it be argued that [the world] is impure, we say no, because of the Word" (Brahma-sūtra 3.1.25). Maṇḍana says: "Even in the case of a burnt offering, the armor is not sublated. Śaṅkara says: "The sublation of the general is due to the particular."

10. In the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, after the *paśupuroḍāśa* of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, one offers the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) of the Devasū. Regarding these eight oblations, their requirements are fulfilled through *prasaṅga* (extension/application) by means of the characteristics of the *puroḍāśa*, and there is no performance of specific duties (*svadharma*) for these oblations themselves.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and similar observances are obligatory (*nitya*).
Likewise, this is the case regarding the designations of food, drink, clothing, and oblations.
The Commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard [in scripture]: "Milk is the fast-food for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel for a Rājanya, and meat for a Vaiśya.
Similarly, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is a directive: "Place the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass."
