In the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, when there is a displacement (*utkarṣa*), [the text says]: "He takes up the *sruva* and the *sruks*; he girds the wife with the words, 'Rise up from this, rise up with clarified butter (*ājyena*)'.
Likewise, it is heard in the *Vājapeya*: "The garment is made of *darbha* grass."

In the animal sacrifice, there is the *saṃśata-homa* with the formula: "If the animal has made a sound, or has struck its breast, or has stepped [wrongly], may Agni deliver me from that sin, from that distress.
Likewise, there is the statement: "He who hates us and whom we hate.
These are the illustrative statements.
Regarding these, there is doubt: should one who has no other food fast by subsisting on milk, gruel, or meat, or even when such food is available?
Likewise, should one who does not respond to the meaning of a command when it is issued be commanded again, or even while he is responding?
Similarly, should one who has no garment made of thread put on one made of *darbha* grass, or even when such a garment is available?
Likewise, if one's sacrificial animal should bleat or strike its chest with its foot, he should offer an oblation with this mantra; and so too would anyone else.
Likewise, for one who hates someone and is hated by that person in return, this very mantra [is prescribed] in the section concerning the *Jyotiṣmatī* sacrifice.

The sequence for the placement of the accents: First, since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice belongs to the Yajurveda, it would obtain the sixfold quality (*ṣāḍguṇya*) by extension; however, that is set aside by the rule: "By the first [quality] before the *sviṣṭakṛt*, by the middle [quality] at the *iḍā*, and by the remainder in the third place.
Even that is further set aside by the rule: "With whatever degree of voice one desires."

Although both [the terms *yatkiñcit* and *yāvatyā*] are equally based on scriptural statement and equally possess a specific scope—since the word *yatkiñcit*, by its very individual form, denotes all things without exception—nevertheless, because *yatkiñcit* has a limited scope (*sāvakāśatva*), it is proper that it should be set aside by the accentuation of the words *yāvatyā* and so forth.

Consequently, since words such as *dīkṣaṇīyā* denote only the primary sacrifices, the accentuation "as much as" (*yāvatyā*) applies only to those; however, in the case of the *agniṣṭomas*, there occurs only the sixfold quality (*ṣāḍguṇya*) brought about by the word *yatkiñcit*.

Regarding the accent in the phrase "uccaiḥ pravayaṇe," it is due to the third-case ending; thus, in the section concerning the Jyotiṣmatī sacrifice, the suffix *ṇamul* denotes the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) whose instrument is the *pravargya*.

Like the case of the *ṇamul* suffix and others, the application of the *takrakauṇḍinya* maxim involves the postulation of an intermediate [result]; for this [action], which produces a different form of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) in relation to the *agnihotra*, there is indeed the status of being an auxiliary that assists by direct contact (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).
The distinction is that the *medana-homa* serves as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), because its visible form—namely, the production of a *kapāla* (potsherd)—is sublated.

For this very reason, since there is no purpose for its production, the statement "when the *agnihotra* has not been offered" is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the fact that [the *kapāla*] remains unobtained even after the *agnihotra* has been offered. However, the specific distinction regarding the *medana-homa* is that it is performed with a mantra prior to the removal (*udvāsana*), even though the function of the *kapāla* has already been accomplished.

In every respect, even though the fire has been consecrated (*praṇīta*), since it serves the purpose of the *agnihotra*, and because both the occasion (*nimitta*) and the consecration (*saṃskāra*) exist, the *iṣṭi* must indeed be performed for that purpose.

Nor is there any inequality in this case regarding the beginning of the ten-day period (*daśāha*) due to the absence of the act of drawing out the fire (*udgharaṇa*); for there is no absence of the occasion (*nimitta*) because there is no destruction of the fire already drawn out (*udghṛta*). This is because "the state of being drawn out" (*udghṛtatva*) is not intended as a qualification of the fire, just as [the state of] being fit for the oblation (*havirbhavyatva*) is not.

This being the prima facie view, it is held that here "having been set aside" (*udghṛtatva*) is not a qualifying attribute of the subject (*uddeśyaviśe�ṣaṇa*). Rather, the occasion for the rite is the destruction of the substance as qualified by the state of having been set aside for use in a performance yet to be performed; this follows the logic of the *takrakauṇḍinya* rule.

This is illustrated by the section on the carpenter (*takṣādhikaraṇa*), where, according to the principle of specific individuals and locations, the gift to Kauṇḍinya is prescribed by means of the scripturally stated gift to the carpenter.
In that context, by the word "brāhmaṇa," the generic class (jāti) of Brāhmaṇas is set aside due to contradiction (*virodha*). (Ṭupṭīkā 10.8.11, p. 2077).
[The word] denotes the caste (*varṇa*), while in the case of Kauṇḍinya, it refers specifically to the individual (*vyakti*).
And the logic of the "curd-Kauṇḍinya" case does not apply here.
[Objection: But surely, even in the view that maintains the universal (*ākṛti*), there exists a commonality that is a distinct entity.
[The author replies: And it is not the case that, in the instance of Kauṇḍinya, the performance or non-performance of an action resides only in the individual (*vyakti*).

Since it is possible for the word’s meaning [to be a universal], there exists an intermediate universal (*avāntara-sāmānya*) which the cognition grasps; why then should the word be subjected to further investigation?
Even if this distinction does not exist, the word nevertheless functions.
Therefore, by the word "Kauṇḍinya," only a particular (*viśeṣa*) is expressed.
In the case of humans composing the meaning of the Vedas—as in "I am mixing curd," and so forth—the result occurs; furthermore, in the case of the sentence-meaning, it does not convey a generality.
Therefore, it will exist in common worldly usage.

In the view that [the word] denotes an individual, there would be an option; for only a specific [individual] is expressed by the word. And in that case, the operation applies only to the immediate [successor], as in the case of curds and buttermilk for Kauṇḍinya, because of the weakness of the general statement; whereas in the other case, it applies generally.
The distinction is to be determined by context and other such factors;
however, in the other case, it is exactly the reverse.
Pāṇini 2.1.133, p. 307; therefore, in that case there is remoteness (*viprakarṣa*), whereas here there is proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*).
By this principle, it is the *takrakauṇḍinya-nyāya* (the maxim of the curd for Kauṇḍinya).

It is not logical that within a single scripture, the *gārhapatya* fire—qualified by a specific injunction—should be present (*prati sannāda*) in relation to certain [rites] such as the *patnīsaṃyāja*, yet non-existent (*asattva*) in relation to others.
It is sublated.

*Ṭupṭīkā* 10.8.16, pp. 2072–73. Therefore, in cases such as "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas; let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya," the principle of the "buttermilk for Kauṇḍinya" (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*) applies.

Indeed, various practices are observed for every individual Brāhmaṇa because there is no single, universal scripture. Therefore, if it is argued that based on the observation of those times, certain rules are restricted by their general nature—

such as saying that the offering of curd, buttermilk, and so forth does not apply to Kauṇḍinya— then it would follow that they would likewise not apply to his mother and others, nor to other Brāhmaṇas who are not Kauṇḍinyas.
For the operation of a universal occurs specifically [through its particulars].
Now, if that [universal] exists in them, then it must also exist in Kauṇḍinya.
Certainly; by establishing [this], they consider the word "brāhmaṇa" to be a universal.

Now, as for the claim that "it does not exist with respect to this [person], but it exists with respect to others," Ratnākaraśānti says: even that is merely our desire to deceive regarding a single object.
Furthermore, no difference in cognition is found here, by which there might be no contradiction due to the simultaneous grasping and non-grasping [of the same thing].
Nor is a difference in the treatises (śāstra) understood from being grasped at once, such that one could assert "the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another."

Furthermore, under the view that the individual is the referent, [the rule] might sometimes not apply because the individual was not previously perceived; however, under the view that the class-form (*ākṛti*) is the referent, since the object is one and the same, the single grammatical rule (*śāstra*) operates simultaneously.

Therefore, seeing that there is no other recourse for the subsequent rule, and just as in the case of a mirage, one concludes that the cognition of the general form was an error, thinking: "This error of mine arose previously through the conceptualization of this object.

Consequently, even though the cognition of Kauṇḍinya arises at the time of the arrival of Māṭhara and others, having determined it to be an error, one considers its purpose—the subordinate element—to be sublated due to the absence of its result.

This is the section concerning the carpenter (*takṣan*), namely the recollection of the carpenter.
The science of carpentry (*takṣaśāstra*). There is no rule that mundane work such as house construction, once begun, must necessarily be completed.
In the world, actions are not like those in the Veda; therefore, there is knowledge of the Supreme Person (*adhipuruṣajñāna*) beyond them.
Commentary: Someone has begun building a house, or [constructing] a cart or a chariot;
his desire has been fulfilled, or he has obtained the fruit [of his labor].
In this regard, there is a doubt: must it necessarily be completed by him, or may it be abandoned according to his wish?
What is established? In the world, actions of this kind, once commenced, must be brought to completion.
Just as with Vedic rites, so too must these be completed by necessity. Why? Because from that [completion] arises knowledge of the Supreme Person.
Therefore, that knowledge must belong to the carpenter.
Why? Because of the sacred scripture (śāstra).
For the scripture concerning carpentry is indeed revealed in the Veda (āmnāyate).
In this case as well, the activity of deities is accepted, such that "these deities are in the eastern direction" and "those others are in the other directions.
Just as there is censure by the learned when a ritual act performed according to scripture is commenced but not completed, so too should it be here.
[The section on the carpenter (Takṣādhikaraṇa): 1851. Hewing is a consecratory rite for the sacrificial post (yūpa).
And regarding their transgression, there is a scriptural text;
the Commentary states: "In the event of a transgression by those common people, a penance-ordinance is handed down by those carpenters:
'If the *āra* is broken, an ox dedicated to Indra must be sacrificed.'"
And it is said, "One should feed milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to a Brāhmaṇa.
If this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) were for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it would not be derived from the scripture.
However, if it is for the purpose of avoiding a contingency (*prasaṅga-parihārārtha*), then it is understood that it is indeed already established [by the scripture].

But their acquisition is not based on scripture; scripture would not be the originator [of the act], therefore it must be understood through the purpose (artha). Or rather, scripture is meaningful only when [the act] has already been acquired.
Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
We say that their acquisition is not based on scripture.
From this tradition (smṛti), a scripture (śāstra) is inferred by you;
there is no tradition without a scripture, nor is a treatise composed by experts possible without a tradition.

Therefore it is said: in this case, there is a traditional recollection (*smṛti*) that "this work, such as building a house, becomes beautiful"; yet from this action, no unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) arises. Furthermore, that beauty can be known even without the scripture.
And having known [the object], one acts accordingly.
Therefore, the scripture must be formulated for that memory;
if it were not obtained through the scripture, then the scripture would be rendered purposeless—thus it is formulated as being meaningful.
Therefore, this is stated in the scripture (*śāstra*).
And regarding what is stated in the scripture, when something is partially performed and then abandoned, the learned (*śiṣṭa*) accept it entirely, as do the deities (*devatā*).
However, even here the deities have not been formally accepted [as recipients], such that one might think, "In this direction this deity will be sacrificed to, and in that direction that one."
It is said:
the learned remember the mantras for the person and the deities, but not for the house;
therefore, there is no fault.
Śā—(The established conclusion, however: "For in the case of houses and other things intended for visible purposes, the acquisition [of the result] occurs even without scripture;
therefore, scripture need not be postulated, since the deity is indeed for the sake of the human agent.
Consequently, there is no rule regarding completion.
Soma—In the preceding section, there was a connection due to the refutation [of the opponent's view].
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: in the world, actions such as building houses and the like are completed just as in the case of the Vedas;
they "pertain to man" (adhipuruṣa), and thus the knowledge of these worldly actions is derived from that very same scripture. This is the reason.
Whether it is mundane—whether it can be completed or not—it depends on the application of scriptural rules (*śāstrakalpanā*).
As for the first [type], there is no rule that it must be completed, because it is merely a household task and lacks the application of scriptural rules.
Therefore, there is no necessity that it must necessarily be brought to completion.

Bhaṭṭa: But as for worldly activities such as household chores and the like, since they are not based on the scriptures (*aśāstrīya*), and because there is no reproach from the learned (*śiṣṭa*) when they fall outside the scope of the scriptures, there is no need for expiation due to the absence of a motivating cause (*prayojaka*). Nor can it be argued that these too are scriptural (*śāstrīya*) because they are rooted in the *śilpa-śruti* (scriptures on arts and crafts); for, being subject to worldly interests such as wealth and pleasure, they are merely worldly in nature and lack a foundation in the [Vedic] *śruti*.

Regarding those rites based on the construction of a house, which are occasional (*naimittika*) and intended for human goals—such as the propitiatory rite for the site (*vāstuśānti*) and so forth, as well as [the rule] "If the *indrakīla* pillar is broken, a barren cow must be offered, and a Brāhmaṇa must be fed milk-rice (*pāyasa*)" and the like—their status as being grounded in scripture (*śāstrīyatva*) is fully established.
Maṇḍana states: "There is no restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding worldly matters when they are combined. Śaṅkara states: "There is indeed no restrictive rule regarding the worldly."
There is no mantra for gifts given to carpenters, washermen, and the like;
however, there is a mantra for giving to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Which [mantra]?

Regarding the *Takṣaśāstra* (6.2.4.16–18): The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the carpentry science (*takṣaśāstra*) is also inferred from the Veda by means of the carpenter’s work, the commencement of a rite necessitates its completion.

However, because the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā*), which has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), serves the purpose of building a house with a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), it is for the benefit of the person depending on that [house]; thus, even though the house-building work is conjoined with the worship of the site, the deity does not serve as the substratum (*āśraya*) for the house-work itself.

Since the injunction for expiation, "If the *āra* at the front of the house is broken, [one should perform] the *indravāhabandhya*," is also solely for the benefit of the person (*puruṣārtha*), it follows that even in this case, the act of building a house has no scriptural basis (*śāstrīyatva*). This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

It has been stated that there is no fixed rule that whatever degree of distance exists must necessarily be completed [by the ritual], because there is no observed defect [in failing to do so]. (Vi.
6.2.4) This is because of the traditional authority of the carpenter (takṣan-smṛti).

for that beauty which exists can be known even without the scripture, and it is capable of being understood [through direct perception].
Therefore, that Smṛti must be considered as having its source in Śāstra. (Bhāṣya 6.2.4.18). In the Takṣa-Smṛti, worldly activities such as the construction of chariots and houses are taught.

That Smṛti is not rooted in the Veda, because the means for achieving visible purposes—such as functional efficacy and aesthetic beauty—are established through positive and negative concomitance alone.
But the carpenter’s memory is rooted in the equanimity of a person skilled in reasoning (uhāpoha);
and there is no rule that the work described by that memory must necessarily be completed.
The act of carving is a subordinate action (guṇakarma) to be performed upon the sacrificial post (yūpa). [Vi. 2.1.4] Carving is a property of the sacrificial post.

and if that were the case, it would result in an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) expressed by another word.
And since that [negation] is of the nature of aversion (*dveṣa*), it has precisely the meaning of a primary injunction (*pradhāna*).
To this it is replied: we do not say that the rule (*niyama*) is verbal in nature or that its form consists in the exclusion of others.
What then? It is simply the communication of the status of being a means to a transcendental result (*apūrvasādhanatā*), even though that [status] is already established by worldly usage.
And because that [act] has cessation as its fruit, it is called a "restrictive rule" (*niyama*).

In this context, what is intended by the threshing's status as a means to the *apūrva*—that which is to be made known by the injunction—is its direct production of the *apūrva*, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, or is it the production of husk-removal for the sake of the *apūrva*? It cannot be the former, because the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) does not accept that.
Nor can it be the production of husk-removal for the sake of the *apūrva*, because even so, that is already established through worldly experience.
Now,
these [topics] are divided into two parts; this is the section concerning the division into two for the sake of the meaning.

In those rites such as *āghāra* (sprinkling) and *āvahana* (invoking), by which one desires to produce, refine, or transform a substance such as clarified butter (*abhiśrīta*) and the like, the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the action is understood;
for that action has the substance as its primary object, being intended for the purpose of preparing the substance.
For in that case, the substance is primary by virtue of being the object to be prepared.
That is to say, verbal forms such as *ādadhīta* ("one should install") and *avahanti* ("one threshes"), which denote such qualities and actions, are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).

A substance is employed [for the sake of these], just as by the act of installation (*ādhāna*) fires are produced, by the act of choosing (*varaṇa*) priests are consecrated (*saṃskriyante*), and by threshing (*avaghāta*) or grinding (*peṣaṇa*) rice-grains (*vrīhi*) or husked rice (*taṇḍula*) are transformed; these are subordinate because the purification of a substance that serves a purpose is what is desired.
Who? [The agent].
According to the principle that "those two are of two kinds," the substance is intended to be prepared by means of placing [the fuel] upon the fire;
the visible refinement (*saṃskāra*) belongs to the fire itself, as in such passages as "having taken [the fuel], he places it [on the fire]" (*āghārād āhṛtya avadadhāti*).
Since the acceptability of the primary substance (*prakṛtadravya*) has already been refuted in the rule "those [materials] are of two kinds" (*tāni dvaidham*), [this point is established].
Bhāṭṭa 4.1.11.

By this, it is indicated that the principle—"since it is improper to assume an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) when it is possible [otherwise]"—serves to refute the doubt that even though the rule *tāni dvaidham* prescribes the splitting [of the wood], it must necessarily have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*) because of its application at times when no ritual action is being performed. Thus, the word *athaivaṃ* [in the commentary] suggests this [understanding of the] knowledge.
Section on the Twofold Nature of Actions (Ke. Tānidvaidhādhikaraṇa): Some actions are primary (pradhāna), while others are subordinate (guṇa).
Their characteristics are now stated.
These [verbs] are twofold, being either subordinate or principal.
The Commentary states: It has been understood that these are denoters of the object of *bhāvanā*.
Furthermore, words expressing *bhāva* (action) are of many kinds: those such as *yajati*, *juhoti*, and *dadāti*; and those such as *dogdhi*, *pinaṣṭi*, and *vilāpayati*.
Regarding these, there is a doubt: do all of them enjoin primary acts (*pradhānakarman*), or are some of them preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarman*)?
Since they denote the meaning of the root, it follows specifically that all are expressive of primary acts; to this we reply:
they must be divided into two classes.
They are of two kinds: some denote principal acts (*pradhānakarman*), and some denote preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarman*).
Even so, all of them are meaningful; and since they are meaningful, it is not possible to assume that [the principal act] is absent from any of them.
Therefore, not all of them denote principal acts.

Or rather, since it would follow everywhere that the distinction of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) conforms to the distinctions of the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), this section on the discrimination between the subordinate (*guṇa*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) is commenced as an exception to that.

As for the purpose therein: according to the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), even when rice is used in place of *caru*, the rice grains are to be employed for the sake of threshing and so forth; whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), they are not to be produced [as a primary end].

Furthermore, those things by which a substance is acquired— such as fire being obtained or produced by kindling (*āghāna*), or priests being consecrated by selection (*varaṇa*), or rice by threshing (*avahanana*), or rice-grains (or flour) by grinding (*peṣaṇa*)— are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), because they are desired for the sake of preparing a substance that serves a purpose. When, however, both [the primary and subordinate acts] are performed equally whether for a visible purpose or not, then what is the point of this inquiry?
This is explained as follows:

Even though the *caru* (rice-pap) is preferred, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the threshing—which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*)—must be performed using *vrīhi* rice as the means.
Why? Because "the substance prescribed for the primary act does not sublate the substance of its subsidiary."
Just as in the case of the *prayāja* and *yajyā*, by that [reasoning] there would be the sublation of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*).
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, they are set aside.
Why? Because "the substance that serves the primary purpose is connected with the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) as well;
therefore, it is to be purified by all [the rites], such as threshing (*hanti*) and so forth."
And Priyajña.

"But surely, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the threshing is dependent on the rice-grains employed by the primary sacrifice, it lacks a motive force (*aprayojakatva*) in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*); therefore, when rice-grains are not obtained through the primary sacrifice in a *caru* offering made of *priyaṅgu* seeds, the threshing would not apply.
This is not so.
For the connection with the rice-grains is equal, whether derived from scripture or from the sacrifice itself.
And since it is equal to the sacrifice for the sake of strength (vājinejyā) and so forth, it is not without a purpose.

In the case of the two injunctions, "One should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhiryajeta*) and "One threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), which are equal in their status as scriptural commands, there is no specific reason to distinguish that one is the motivator (*prayojikā*) and the other is not.
Nor is the threshing an incidental byproduct (*anuniṣpādita*) like the whey-offering (*vājina*).

Nor is it—as in the case of the six acts (or the seventh step of the *ekāhayani* sacrifice)—a state of having its requirements satisfied through dependence on another, such as being dependent on the *prakṛti* (the model sacrifice) or the *hāyanī* cow.
Nor is it like the case of the "upper half" and so forth of a single substance;
nor is it a ritual action whose purpose is the expression of meaning, as in the phrase "by the cooking of the sacrificial cake.
Therefore, threshing is also a motivator (*prayojaka*).

Furthermore, under this view, rice grains intended for sacrifice (*yāga*) need not necessarily be threshed, since there is no difference in the accomplishment of the ritual action even with respect to worldly grains.
Nor is there any means of proof (*pramāṇa*) here for taking the grains mentioned in the context (*prakṛta*), because the context (*prakaraṇa*) does not serve as a differentiator.
Nor can a distinction be made on the basis of the specific qualification (*adhikāra*).
This is because of the maxim: "There can be no qualification among equals.

(The meaning is that since there is no further expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*), there is no authority for grasping the subject matter under discussion, as the possibility of postulating a distinction is rejected in the sūtra of the ninth section.

On the other hand, in the view that they are *saṃskāras* (purificatory acts), because they would otherwise be purposeless (*ānarthakya*) with respect to worldly [acts]—[note: in Ānandāśrama’s edition it is printed as *ānarthakye na*, but we consider it to be a third-case ending]—and because they do not have a visible effect, their application to the subject at hand will occur only with difficulty, by way of being specific means for the *apūrva* (transcendental result). Furthermore, even if they were to provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), there is no purposelessness whatsoever for the threshing when the sacrifice itself is being accomplished by worldly means; therefore, since this is based on direct Vedic statement (*śrautatvāt*), it is proper to accept only the *vrīhi* grain.

(He himself states other purposes: At that time, the threshing is merely for the sake of the *dharma* (ritual merit), and like the threshing of all-herb (*sarvauṣadha*) materials, it should be performed only once, not until the rice-grains are fully produced.
Furthermore, the state of being rice-grain might be achieved for the principal grains even by means of splitting and so forth.

And because there is no distinction in its context (*prakaraṇa*), it becomes equal to the *sānnāyya*, the *upāṃśuyāja*, and others; thus, it is to be employed even in those [other] contexts—these and others are the purposes.
(Three purposes have been stated;
by the word "etcetera" [in the sūtra], there are two further purposes: even in the case of barley, threshing applies only to rice, and it applies to all three [grains]—thus [there are] two purposes.
[Sutramālā, p. 626].)

It is established that [the ritual] should be performed according to the distinctions of the verbal roots (ākhyāta) and according to the distinctions of the preceding [sections]. An exception to this is now being made.
Its connection is indeed with the section concerning the *soma* sacrifice (*somābhiṣava*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: those verbal roots (*ākhyāta*) are of two kinds—those that express a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*) and those that express a principal action (*pradhānakarman*).
Regarding this, [the question arises]: "Is the *apūrva* produced by threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth a means (*upāya*), or not?
Or is it the very same [apūrva] produced by [the root] *yajati* (to sacrifice) and so forth? This is the division of the sentence.
But in the case of the *haṭṭa* and the *tupavimoka*, there is no new transcendental result (*apūrva*) because they depend on the substance;
thus, their dissimilarity to the *yajati* and other such acts is established by the singular mention of the restrictive *apūrva*.

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains that in the earlier Veda, in passages such as "One threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the instrumentality of threshing toward the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) of the result is beyond dispute.
In that context, the result is not the rice-grains themselves, because they are not produced [by the action].

Nor is it the state of being husked (*vaituṣya*), because its status as something produced by [threshing] is already established in common worldly experience and thus cannot be the object of an injunction.

Nor can there be a restrictive rule (*niyama*) intended to produce the result of threshing even when [the grain] is already obtained through other means, such as by breaking it with a blade, because that too would be futile.

Nor does it follow from this that [threshing] has no purpose at all; for since an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) must necessarily be postulated, it is postulated precisely from the scripturally enjoined threshing itself.
Therefore, threshing is indeed for the sake of an unseen merit.

Furthermore, that unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) does not reside in the rice grains themselves, because the self is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to that which is delimited by the essence [of the self].

Therefore, as before, the threshing is performed upon the rice grains themselves; thus, because it arises from a specific kind of rice, it is enjoined as a subsidiary act (*upakāraka*) for the sake of the unseen merit.
This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since an invisible result is improper when a visible one is possible, the removal of the husk is indeed the fruit of the threshing.

Nor is the injunction redundant because the act is already established by its very nature, for another means such as splitting [the grain] would otherwise result in an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); rather, it is the restriction (*niyama*) itself—based on threshing—that is enjoined for the sake of the unseen merit. Thus, all [the arguments] are resolved. 1860. All this is the sense.
The restriction based on threshing is indeed what is enjoined for the purpose of the unseen merit.
For this very reason, in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, since there is an absence of threshing (*avaghāta*), that [threshing] is omitted.

In reality, however, it is the scripturally enjoined threshing itself that is to be prescribed for the purpose of producing the state of being free from husks (*vitṛṣībhāva*) by way of implication (*ākṣepa*).
Consequently, because it is established through implication, the result is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) characterized by the exclusion of alternatives such as splitting (*dalana*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since the state of being dehusked (*vaituṣya*) can also be produced by means of a splitting (*dalana*), the injunction [of threshing] would otherwise be rendered purposeless. Moreover, the assumption of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the rice grains arising from threshing itself must be considered unavoidable.

And regarding that unseen potency, only its status as something produced (*janyatva*) is postulated on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), not its status as a motivator (*prayojakatva*), because such a potency is postulated only in respect to the visible result of dehusking itself.
Therefore, in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, since there is an absence of husking (*vaituṣya*), that [act] is omitted;

for, by the postulation of another implied injunction, the expression of the two results is accomplished by one or indeed by the second [act] alone, and thus there is no plurality of objects of reference (*uddeśyatā*).

Furthermore, since the respective unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is understood—by the means of knowledge grasping the substratum of the second and subsequent acts—to reside specifically in the *vrīhi* grains and so forth, their status as the locus of equality (*samatva-adhikaraṇatā*) is established precisely in that capacity, and not in their capacity as the self (*ātmatva*).

And therefore, since threshing is enjoined for the purpose of producing an unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*) by way of the disintegration of rice-grains that serve as the means to the *apūrva*, its status as a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*) is established.

The practical consequence (*prayojana*) is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), another variety of rice would have to be procured for threshing and so forth in relation to the rice intended for the sacrifice; however, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), this is not the case.
Maṇḍana says: "Indeed, threshing is merely a preparatory act."
Śaṅkara says: "The two-fold division has been stated as desired by us:
(1) that which expresses the primary action (*pradhānakarma*), and (2) that which expresses the secondary action (*guṇakarma*)."

6. (The two-fold nature of the definition of *ākhyāta* [verbs] by means of the fifth and sixth [sections]). In the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, it is established that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the producer of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), and that substances and the like are for the sake of that [verbal meaning]. The section beginning with "tadapavāda" is the *tānidvaidhādhikaraṇa*.

In the *tānidvaidhādhikaraṇa* (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.4–7), it is stated that a subordinate action (*guṇakarma*) is one that provides a visible benefit, while a primary action (*pradhānakarma*) is one that provides an invisible benefit.

Even though they are prompted by the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), the threshing of grain (*avaghāta*) and the like, as well as the mantras, do not serve the purpose of the *apūrva* through an invisible medium (*adṛṣṭa*)—unlike the *pratyāja* and other such rites—as has been refuted in the section concerning the twofold nature of mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*) and elsewhere. Rather, they function through visible means such as the rice grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth.
(Soma.
9.1.1) All these are prompted by their respective purposes, because they possess their own specific time.

In the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* and the *Kutūhala*, the sūtra "amathya svakālatvāt" is treated as a separate [sūtra] and established as a distinct topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the logic of the "intermediate embryo. Having set aside the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is accepted solely as being for the purpose of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). The authors of the *Vārttika* have also stated: "This very final conclusion, whose prima facie argument is inferred and established by the logic set forth in the sūtra of the other topical section, is expressed here through a division of the sūtra's wording."
However, having stated "by the division of the sūtra" (*sūtrabhedena*), it was actually said "by the division of the sūtra-sentence" (*sūtravākyabhedena*).
Therefore, the Vārttikakāra does not consider the sūtra to be different from that of the Bhaṭṭa or Ku-bhaṭṭa.
Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya, after stating "it has been understood that this cannot be refuted in any way," he accepted the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of that very sūtra-sentence.
It is indeed appropriate that nothing is stated regarding fire in the subsequent sūtra, and one should follow that accordingly.
However, the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika do not consider the statement "because [the action] has its own time, it cannot be postponed" (amathya svakālatvāt) to be a separate sūtra.
Ke.
Regarding those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) mentioned in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* as being "the master plus nineteen," they should all be for the sake of all [the ritual acts].
In the sacrificial rites, whoever desires to perform a particular task and is capable of doing so should perform it;
there is no fixed restriction (*vyavasthā*) in that regard.
Why? Because of being hired; that is, because he has been engaged in the sacrificial acts through payment.
This is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
Here, the established conclusion (siddhānta) will appear in the subsequent sūtra: "Because of his connection with that [payment], [the fruit belongs] to the action."

In this context, following the logic of the "interior womb" (*antarāgarbhaṇī*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the domain of fire: "Because they are restricted to their own time. Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) set forth is as follows: "The *āhavanīya* and other fires are not for all purposes; rather, they are only for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

If one were to admit that they also serve the sake of the ectype (*vikṛti*), then since the ectype is [already] obtained through the extended injunction (*codaka*) because it is modeled after the archetype, there would be the fault of tautology (*dviruktatva*)."
This being the case, it is replied:
all matters are not to be disregarded; rather, they serve the purpose of all rites consisting of the preparation of the natural state.
Why? Because of their own specific time: the seasons such as spring, the lunar mansions such as Kṛttikā, and so forth, constitute the proper time for the fires.
Those for whom the time for their establishment (ādhāna) has been prescribed as their own specific time are "of fixed time" (svakāla), meaning they are not subject to displacement.
For their establishment is nowhere prescribed with reference to the time of a sacrifice.
Because they have their own specific time, they are "not subject to displacement" (amathya) and are for the sake of all [rites]; this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
The determination of action would arise from conjunction with that [self], because conjunction possesses purposefulness.
This is the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), whereas the preceding sūtra presented the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Because of that connection—that is, because of the connection of specific actions with specific persons such as the Adhvaryu and Hotṛ priests, and because such a connection is known through titles (*samākhyā*) and other means—there is indeed a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) and not a lack of restriction.
Thus, because the connection—the connection between the action and the person—is purposeful, and because the result is thereby accomplished, there is indeed a fixed rule.
For if there were a connection with the *adhvaryu*, it would be fruitless;
one should teach him that which is designated as the *ādhvaryava* [section], because of the suffix *aṇ*.

The *adhvaryava* ritual action must be performed by the *adhvaryu* alone, and not by the *hotṛ* nor the *udgātṛ*. The ritual action designated as *hautra*, such as the recitation of the *śastra* and so forth, must be performed by the *hotṛ* alone, and not by the *adhvaryu* nor the *udgātṛ*. The ritual action consisting of the singing of the *stotra*, which belongs to the *audgātra*, must be performed by the *udgātṛ* alone, and not by the *adhvaryu* nor the *hotṛ*; such is the established rule.
On this point, Sudhā states: Because of the connection with the ritual action by those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there should be a fixed assignment according to their designations (*samākhyā*).

Since a fixed assignment is possible, and because the designation known as *hautra*—which consists of the connection with the *hautra* priest—is capable of establishing a fixed order required by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*) through its application to the meaning of the scripture that would otherwise result in an option (*vikalpa*) when such a fixed order exists, it is logical for it to function like a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the absence of any contradiction. This is because the application [of the designation] possesses purposefulness.
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The phrase "one should teach him" (*tam adhyāpayīta*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fact that the initiated boy (*upanīta*) is the agent, as established by proximity.

When, however, there is no intention to express the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) in the two sentences concerning initiation and teaching, it is an injunction for the act of initiating and teaching (*upagamanādhyāpana-vidhi*). (Maṇi, p. 4)
According to the principle that "in whatever manner one worships it, that very thing one becomes," from superior worship, a superior result indeed arises for the sake of liberation.
This is the *Śvetāśvatara-bhāṣya*.
There is also the principle: "Because of being produced and destroyed by that, even the composite [body] is likewise."

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even though the action (kriyā) rests upon the substrate (āmāśrita), because it is momentary and perishes immediately upon arising, it cannot initiate the *apūrva* according to the principle that 'an effect arises from that which has arisen'. [Sūtra-bhāṣya, p.
"Indeed, by that food is prepared"—this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) for the injunction "He offers with the sun" (Vi.

1.2.3). Regarding the statement, "Therefore, one *sāman* is performed upon a *ṛc* triplet as a hymn," one might object: "Is not a threefold prescription also seen following a *ṛc* based on its name (*samākhyā*)?"
No;
for even there, it is accepted that the injunction belongs to the name itself.
Therefore, the statement "one should give at that time" and "one should not give at that time" is a prohibition in the form of a permission (*abhyanujñā*).
(The meaning is: it should be given in times of prosperity, but it should not be given in times of poverty.
Bāla. pṛ. 33: "Therefore, the Veda should be studied"—this is enjoined as an independent injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*).

Or [it may be taken] from the Āgrayaṇa vessel. Regarding the question— whether the Ṣoḍaśī cup should be drawn directly from the Āgrayaṇa vessel after the Ukthya, or from the Āgrayaṇa vessel itself— the discussion begins with the established conclusion (siddhānta).
The drawing of that cup named *ṣoḍaśin* should be performed from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel, because of the scriptural statement: "He draws the *ṣoḍaśin* from the *āgrayaṇa*.
The word "because of the scriptural statement" (*vacanāt*) is drawn forward—that is, extracted—from the subsequent sūtra.
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the Ukthya:
the drawing of the Ṣoḍaśin cup must be performed from the Āgrayaṇa vessel and from the Ukthya vessel.
This is because of the scriptural statements: "He draws the Ṣoḍaśin from the Āgrayaṇa" and "He draws the Ṣoḍaśin from the Ukthya."
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). [The opponent argues:
"In the absence of repetition, the word *parāc* (away/forth) is used because of its meaning.
But in that case, should not the *ṣoḍaśī* cup be drawn separately by means of repetition from both the *āgrayaṇa* vessel and the *ukthya* vessel?"
Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "He who draws the *ṣoḍaśin* cup while facing away.
The word *parāk* occurs in the sense of non-repetition (*anabhyāsa*).

Since the word *parāk* has that as its meaning—namely, being for the sake of that—it is understood from the statement "He recites the *sāmidhenī* verses facing away" that this refers to non-repetition.
Thus, because of the word *parāc* (away) and the vessel (*pātra*), a separate drawing [of the Soma] by repetition is not tenable.
Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśī* cup should be drawn only once from the two vessels, namely the *ukthya* and the *āgrayaṇa*.
This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Because of the statement regarding the non-interruption of the *ukthya*.
For this reason as well, the *ṣoḍaśī* cup is to be drawn from both the *ukthya* and the *āgrayaṇa*:
"They indeed interrupt the *ukthya* when they lead forward the *ukthyas* and the *ṣoḍaśī* from there. Thus, it shows that the *ukthya* serves as the ablative source for the vessel.
Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśī* cup should be drawn from both the *ukthya* and the *āgrayaṇa*;
or rather, it should be drawn from the *āgrayaṇa* alone, because the word *parāk* denotes a location, as in the case of the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*).
The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view.
The *ṣoḍaśī* draught is to be drawn from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel itself,
not from the *ukthya* vessel. This is because, in the passage "When he draws the *ṣoḍaśī* while facing away," the word *parāk* denotes direction (space), which implies a specific time.
When it is stated that "the Ṣoḍaśī should be taken immediately after the Ukthya," the Ukthya does not possess the status of an ablative (*apādāna*).

Therefore, it means simply that the Ṣoḍaśī is to be taken from the Āgrayaṇa vessel immediately after the Ukthya. This is like the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*); for instance, in the rule "he establishes them again after having gone away" (*parāṅgamyādhadhāt punaradadhāti*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) denotes a connection of time, not an ablative relation. Thus—
Because it belongs to the Āgrayaṇa, as in the case of "his cow," so here too;
therefore, the conclusion is that the Ṣoḍaśin cup is to be taken from the Āgrayaṇa alone.
The separation [of the *ṣoḍaśin*] is due to the commonality of the *stoma*.

As for what was stated by the proponent—that because of the statement of separation, "For they indeed cut off this *uktha*, when they lead forth the *ukthas* and the *ṣoḍaśin* from that," the *uktha* functions as the point of departure (*apādāna*)—that is not so;
the mention of separation is said on account of the commonality of the *stoma*.
That which is called the *uktha* cup is characterized by the twenty-one-fold hymn (*ekaviṃśa-stoma*), and the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is likewise so characterized.
Thus, due to the commonality of the twenty-one-fold hymn, a metaphorical identification of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with the *uktha* division is made.
The "division of the *uktha*" (*ukthaviccheda*) refers to the fact that during the performance, they bring forth three *uktha* cups, and immediately thereafter they bring forth the *ṣoḍaśin*.

Furthermore, in the phrase "then they lead forth" (*tataḥ praṇayanti*), the ablative case does not denote an *apādāna* (point of departure), but rather a connection with time; thus, it means that immediately after the *ukthya-praṇayana*, they lead forth the *ṣoḍaśin*.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the drawing of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel alone, and not from the *ukthya* as well.
Ke.
Its specification is by means of the designation (*samākhyāna*) of the instruction (*upadeśa*).

In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was stated that there is a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) because, through the designation of the master’s residence (*svāmisadana*) and so forth, one knows the connection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to their respective sacrificial acts.
This sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) is for the purpose of setting aside that [previous position].
Regarding that [assignment] of the titles *ādhvaryava* and so forth even to the ritual action (*karman*):

there is a specification by means of both direct instruction (*upadeśa*)—such as "Therefore the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions and recites after" (*tasmān maitrāvaruṇaḥ preṣyati ca anvāha ca*), and "The Pratiprasthātṛ offers the oblation in the fire" (*pratiprasthātāgninam juhoti*)—and by means of titles (*samākhyāna*), such as *naiṣṭrīya* and *potrīya*.
By this as well, the specific determination [of roles] is to be understood.
In the *Kutūhala*, it is stated that the explanatory term in the Sūtra has the sense of an exception (*apavāda*).

Regarding this, the *Sudhā* states: "Since the collection of rites possesses designations such as *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu), if there were any sublation [of these], it would follow that the designation itself would be invalid everywhere; thus, one might suspect that a specific designation cannot be sublated. However, this is avoided by noting that the sublation occurs through sentences such as those concerning the *Maitrāvaruṇa*, because the duties of the *ādhvaryava* and others are indeed performed [by him]. Just as in the case of the statement 'he places the *sudhī* brick,' where the *ādhvaryava* and other monthly rites are made manifest through their abundance, so too—because it has a specific scope and the power to contract—this [designation] extracts from the general Vedic texts those [rites] that are specifically denoted, just as the instruction for the *Maitrāvaruṇa* extracts [certain rites] from other rites that lack a specific instruction."
"The instruction regarding the intervening region" (*kārṇnantaradeśanā*)—such is the statement of the teaching (*upadeśokti*).

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* (on Pāṇini 3.7.124) states: "But when there is a conflict between two designations (*samākhyā*), the sublation of the general designation by the specific designation will occur just as in the case of the *sūtra*: 'The indication [of that] is by means of its instruction and designation' (*tasyopadeśasamākhyānena nirdeśaḥ*).

On this point, Somanātha explains: "By the instruction—that is, by the verbal statement—and by the specific designation, there is an indication; that is to say, a determination, which amounts to an exception (*apavāda*)."

The Prābhākaras have explained this sūtra as a separate topic (*adhikaraṇāntara*) for the purpose of setting aside the general designation (*sāmānya-samākhyā*) by means of specific scriptural statements (*vacana-viśeṣa-samākhyā*). That is untenable; since it has been established elsewhere that a general designation is weaker than a scriptural statement, and a general one is also weaker than a specific one, this [interpretation] merely follows the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Therefore, this is indeed a supplement to the topic under discussion.
And that is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).

By stating that in sacrificial rites there is a fixed rule for the Adhvaryu and others based on their designations such as "Adhvaryava" and so forth, it was asserted that the specific [assignment] is determined by both direct instruction (upadeśa) and designation (samākhyā). When this established conclusion (siddhānta) has been stated, the following sūtra provides another reason: "But that [designation], like the specific designations such as *potrīya* and so forth, shows the Hotṛ priest in the case of the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), even though the designation would have applied [there] by virtue of the indicative mark (liṅga), namely: 'where one might overhear the Hotṛ reciting the morning litany. Thus, although the designation [of the rite as *ādhvaryava*] would have led to the Adhvaryu's performance of the morning litany, the indicative mark shows that the Hotṛ is the one who performs it.

Likewise, there are indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as: "The *udnīya* belongs to the *udgātṛ*s; the *praṇava* of the *ṛc*s belongs to the *ukthaśaṃsin*s (the *hotṛ*s); the *pratigara* belongs to the *adhvaryu*s; and the *udnīya* [belongs to the *hotṛ*s]. Furthermore, there is the mark: "He who knows what is the property (*sva*) of the *adhvaryu* becomes possessed of his own property; that which he causes to be recited is the property of the *adhvaryu*. These indicate specifically that particular officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are connected to those respective rites. Therefore, based on specific designation (*samākhyā*), there is a restrictive rule for the distribution of duties among the specific officiating priests.

On this point, the *Sudhā* states: Just as the restriction of the *adhvaryu* and other priests to specific roles arises from the designation of the ritual (*karma*) itself, and just as the instruction regarding other performers arises from specific designations, so too is the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) a specific regulator [of application].
As it is said: "That [function] should be assigned to each respective [person]" (2.3.16).

Although both the morning extraction (*prātaḥsavana*) and the sequence following the *āśvina* cup are enjoined by the statement "having taken the *āśvina* cup," nevertheless, because the injunctive [word] follows from a single word, there is no such contingency as "it would be taught for each of those.

In the case of "its [is] a cow" (*tasya dhenur*), since [the cow] is enjoined as distinct in the archetype (*prakṛti*), its modification (*vikāra*) should be [understood] through that similarity, just as by a word expressing a quality such as "desire" (*iṣṭaguṇa*).

"Now this Bhū-sarvadeva sacrifice is entirely threefold; its stotriya verses are those containing the word *viśva*, and a cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Thus is heard the eleventh ritual (*kratu*) named Bhū. In that context, "a cow is the sacrificial fee" is the specific instruction.
This cow that is heard of as "his cow" (tasya dhenuḥ) is a substitute only for the cows among the ordinary sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), not for the horses and so forth.

This is because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the sacrificial fees are enjoined in such a way as to be distinct—for instance, it is stated that "the horse is the fee" and "the mule is the fee," thus assigning the status of a fee to each individually.
In this sacrifice named Bhū, however, the cow itself is specified as the particular feature by the term "cow" (*dhenu*); therefore, it is none other than a cow.

And thus, by virtue of that commonality—that is, the commonality of being "cow" (*go*)—the word *dhenu* (milch cow) would denote a modification of that [cow]; it would be a modification of a cow. Consequently, there would be a sublation of non-milch cows among the cows. This is just as in the case of the *iṣṭi*: the injunctions pertaining to the *iṣṭi*, such as "one should offer a *caru* to Sūrya," are restricted by the word *nirvāpa* (offering), which is a term denoting a subordinate quality (*guṇaśabda*). Therefore, all the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma should apply to the sacrifice named *bhū*; however, the specific distinction is that the cows must be milch cows (*dhenavaḥ*) that yield milk.
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Alternatively, because of the singular number in the phrase "his cow" (*tasya dhenuḥ*), a single cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) takes the place of all the cows belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma; however, the horses and other items remain according to the original model (*yathā-prakṛti*). This is the prima facie view. Or rather, the entire [set of cows] is substituted because of its connection with the sacrifice, since the purpose of the sacrificial fee is one. Because the functions of the subordinate elements (*guṇa*) are identical, that which is heard in the scripture regarding the modification (*vikṛti*) would apply; for by that [substitution], there is a conjunction with the ritual acts.
The cow that is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the sacrifice named *bhū* excludes every other sacrificial fee for any sacrifice lacking a specific fee.

This is because of its connection with the sacrifice, as seen in the sentence containing the elliptical reference, "Its sacrificial fee is a cow," which establishes the relationship between the cow as the fee and the specific sacrifice situated within that ritual context.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the status of being the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belongs to the collection of ten substances—ranging from cows and horses down to sesame seeds—as a single unit, and not to each substance individually as separate fees. This is because the words "cow," "horse," and "ten" designate the entire collection of all these items and thereby enjoin them as a single sacrificial fee. In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) named Bhū, that original (*prakṛti*) sacrificial fee is set aside by the single cow prescribed for it; the singularity pertains to the purpose of the fee—that is, the purpose of the fee is the approach of the priests—and there is no plurality in that purpose.

Because the functions of the qualities are one; that is, because the functions of those qualities belonging to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—from cattle and horses down to sesame and māṣa beans—are also one, due to the unity of their function as being a "sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇātva*), a single cow prescribed by the scriptural injunction "its sacrificial fee is a cow" (*tasya dhenurdakṣiṇā*) would be sufficient for the purpose of hiring the priests (*ṛtvigamana*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). For since there is a connection through association with the priests via those ritual acts performed with that cow as the sacrificial fee, the cow is the sublater (*bādhikā*) of everything else that constitutes the sacrificial fee in the archetype (*kratu*).
Thus, there would be a restrictive rule based on not relying on other injunctions.

In the sūtra "tasya dhenuḥ," the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) presented the modified sacrifice (vikṛti-iṣṭi) as an example by means of the term "according to one's desire" (*yatheṣṭaguṇaśabdena*). The proponent (siddhāntin), however, [rejects this] because of the disparity between them: since the injunctions for modified sacrifices such as the *saurya* are not based upon—that is, are not dependent on or accepted by—the original archetype, and because there is an absence of specific properties explicitly prescribed [for the modification], there should be a restriction [of details] from the modified sacrifice to the archetypal sacrifice by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the pouring out (*nirvāpa*).
This is logical.

In the sacrifice named *bhū*, however, there is a single function for the cows and other items, namely, the status of being the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). And in that regard, a single cow is directly enjoined by the scripture (*śruti*); it is therefore capable of displacing the entire sacrificial fee as established by the general injunction (*codanā*). Therefore, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that a single cow displaces the entire archetypal (*prākṛtī*) sacrificial fee.
(Ke.)

Regarding the statement "his [gift] is a cow" (*tasya dhenur iti*), since it is enjoined as a specific modification within the archetype of cows, it would—by virtue of that commonality—be a substitute for the whole, just as in the case of a word expressing a quality such as "desirable.

In passages such as, "This *Bhūman* sacrifice belongs to all the gods; it is entirely threefold; its *stotrīya* verses are those of the *Viśvavat* [sacrifice]; a cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," does the cow exclude only itself, or does it exclude the entire sacrificial fee?

Thus, in this doubt, according to the principle that "the connection with the word *yat* (that), primacy, and so forth, are the characteristics of the subject (*uddeśya*"), since the cows and other items are first mentioned in relation to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), they possess the status of being the subject; and because the conjunction [of the cows] is not intended to be significant even though it is expressed by the word, each individual cow possesses the status of the sacrificial fee. Consequently, by the word *dhenu* (milch-cow)—which denotes the milking capacity of the cows as a whole—the cessation of only those cows that are milch-cows is understood. Furthermore, by the singular number, the cessation of the number one hundred and twelve is understood. Just as in the injunction "one should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," the details of the sacrifice are restricted by the word denoting the accessory quality (*guṇa*) which is the act of offering (*nirvāpa*), so too, by the word *dhenu*, there is the cessation of cows in general, but not the cessation of horses and the like. Having thus presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established that the entire sacrificial fee is set aside.
Su. Pṛ. 435:

*Tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ* (1.1.3). The section concerning their meaning (*arthādhikaraṇa*) is "The investigation of its cause" (*tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ*). By means of the sūtra "That which is characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇa*), the nature of the Vedic meaning—both as expressed by the words and as implied by the sense—was established, and therein the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was asserted.

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the nature [of the means of knowledge] should first be stated in terms of its difference and non-difference, or whether it should be stated by way of its being a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since the nature [of the means of knowledge] is primary, it follows that it alone should be described through both difference and non-difference. To this, the Sūtra states: because the determination of difference and non-difference is independent [of anything else] and depends upon itself, the reason for its validity—which depends upon the grounds of validity—must now be stated.
Therefore, the Sūtra provides an exposition by expressing the reason for validity, which consists in its independence.

*Ṛjuvimalā*, page 33. 🜂 *Tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ* | 1.1.3 | By this sūtra, the promise to investigate the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Dharma is made. The "investigation" (*parīṣṭi*)—meaning the search and thorough examination—of the "causes" (*nimitta*), that is, the indicators or means of valid cognition for that Dharma, "will be performed"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. What is this "investigation of its causes"? It has been stated that the Veda is the means of valid cognition for Dharma.

The meaning is that the investigation as to whether that [validity] is possible or not is conducted by way of determining the possibility of perception and other means of knowledge being authoritative with respect to *dharma*.
(Maṇi, p. 19). Beginning with "Of that, first," it is heard in scripture: "One should not look at the rising sun.
The word *mata* is a name for a ritual act (*karman*).
*Duṣ*.

🜂 *Teṣām arthena saṃbandhaḥ* (3.1.4). In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the vegetable oblation (*auṣadha*)—such as pouring out (*nirvāpa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and threshing (*avaghātana*)—are prescribed; those of the clarified butter (*ājya*)—such as heating (*upavāpa*), melting (*vilāpana*), taking up (*grahaṇa*), and placing down (*āsādana*)—are prescribed; and those of the *Sāṃnāyya* milk offering—such as fetching the branch (*śākhāharaṇa*), extracting the fat (*vasāpākaraṇa*), and driving forth the cows (*gavāṃ prasthāpana*)—are prescribed.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether all these [properties] must be performed everywhere, or only those that have a specific purpose should be performed there, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
There would be a connection with the purpose—the objective—of those primary rites.
That which serves as the means to accomplish the purpose in a particular context should be performed there.
However, every rite would become prescribed for all [contexts], because there is no distinction in the connection and no distinction in the context.
Setting aside the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the word "but" (*tu*), he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
Whatever property (*dharma*) is prescribed as a means to the *apūrva*, all of that would be a universal property (*sarvadharma*), belonging to all *iṣṭis*, *upāṃśuyājas*, and *sāṃnāyyas*.

This is because there is no distinction in their connection with the *apūrva*—that is, because it is the same—and because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*), since the recitation within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is identical for all.
Now, [the opponent might argue that] due to the disappearance of the purpose, there would be no performance of the action.
He refutes this prima facie view:

because of the disappearance of the purpose—that is, the absence of the visible result—the properties of the clarified butter (*ājya*), such as purifying (*utpavana*) and so forth, would not be performed in the case of the vegetable offering (*auṣadha*) or the *sāṃnāyya* milk; the properties of the vegetable offering, such as threshing (*avahanana*) and so forth, would not be performed in the case of the clarified butter or the *sāṃnāyya*; and the properties of the *sāṃnāyya*, such as the removal of the fat (*vasāpākaraṇa*) and so forth, would not be performed in the case of the clarified butter or the vegetable offering. Thus, due to the disappearance of the purpose, there would be non-performance (*akarma*).
Not all [causes] should be applied everywhere;
rather, a cause should be applied only where its fruit occurs.
For the fruit arises together with the activity, since the meaning of the word would otherwise be absent in the case of separation.

If it is argued that, in the case of threshing and other such acts, an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*) should be postulated for the sake of the injunction regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth, he says in response:
the word "but" (*tu*) indicates the removal of this doubt.
A result such as coarseness and the like is perceived together with the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), that is, concomitant with the action, or at a time subsequent to its occurrence.

When, in the case of rice and other grains mentioned in the Vedic texts along with actions such as threshing, a visible result— such as their softening— is perceived, then, since a visible result is possible, there is no assumption of an invisible (transcendental) one.

However, when the visible result is absent— that is, not perceived— and because the non-existence of the visible result cannot be definitively established, the meaning of the word must be determined by the injunction itself as providing an invisible benefit.
In the present case, however, since what is perceived exists, there is no assumption of the unperceived.

If it is argued that, because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*), all intermediate apūrvas (*avāntarāpūrva*) would necessarily be the motivators of religious duty (*dharma*), the author says in response to that as well: "In the absence of the intermediate apūrva due to its dissociation [from the result], and because the supreme apūrva (*paramāpūrva*) lacks the capacity to determine the application of the religious duty, the meaning of the word—such as rice and so forth—would also have to be considered as applicable to clarified butter (*ājya*) and the like, since there is no difference in their being means to the supreme apūrva."
This is not so.

Rather, as stated in the *Kutūhala*: "In the case of rice and other materials mentioned in the scriptures in connection with actions such as threshing, there exists a result called the *apūrva* produced by those respective sacrifices, mediated through the stages of rice-grains, flour, and so forth."
What is that?

It is their section on the purpose (arthādhikaraṇa), [Sūtra] 3.1.4.7. Because of the rule of what is required (*apekṣitavidhi*)—namely, that [the threshing] is not required by the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the curd-mixture (*sāṃnāyya*)—and because of the weakness of prescribing what is not required (*anapekṣitavidhāna*), it is thereby shown that the threshing has as its remainder only the medicinal substance (*auṣadhadravya*). That the support from the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) is merely an additional argument is clear in that very same place.
Parākrama 4012–4111. 🜂 Their section on the subject matter: The logic of rice (*vrīhi-nyāya*).
In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the ritual properties (*dharma*) of rice, clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *sāṃnāyya* offering are strictly fixed; they do not become intermingled.
The connection is by way of their purpose.
The Bhāṣya states: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices].

In that context, certain ritual duties (dharmas) are heard, such as pouring out [the grain], sprinkling it with water, threshing it, and so forth; these are the duties pertaining to the vegetable offerings (auṣadhadharmas).
Likewise, there are the properties of clarified butter (*ājya*), such as purifying (*utpavana*), melting (*vilāpana*), taking up (*grahaṇa*), and placing down (*āsādana*).
Similarly, there are the properties of the *sāṃnāyya* offering, such as bringing the branch (*śākhā-āharaṇa*) and driving forth the cows (*gavām prasthāpana*).

Regarding these, a doubt arises: should all of them be performed for the vegetable offering (*auṣadha*), the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *sāṃnāyya*, or should only those which serve a purpose when performed in a particular context be performed there?
But surely these [actions] are heard as being connected only with specific intended objects (the qualified subjects), such as "he threshes rice" and "he grinds rice. Certainly, they are so connected.
However, actions such as threshing are enjoined by direct Vedic statement (śruti),
whereas their connection with rice and other materials is established by syntactical connection (vākya).
Therefore, a doubt arises.
What, then, is the conclusion reached? They have a connection with a purpose—that is, with a motive.
Those things which, when performed in a particular context, serve a purpose, should be performed there.
Since threshing and so forth are not contributory to the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the *sāṃnāyya* offerings, they are not to be performed in that context.

Likewise, the fetching of wood and so forth are not for the vegetable (*oṣadha*) and *sāṃnāyya* offerings, and the bringing of the branch and so forth are not for the clarified butter and vegetable offerings.
[Objection: But are they not all heard of as being applicable everywhere?
We do not even know this: whether they are heard or not heard. That must be investigated.
Even if they were heard, they would still have to be performed because of their lack of utility.
Or rather—the remainder [of the discussion] has been stated along with its reason and its full scope.
Now, the section concerning "how they are applied" is investigated.
In that regard, the application of consecrations (*saṃskāra*), substances (*dravya*), and qualities (*guṇa*) is explained in three topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) in succession.

Regarding that, some maintain that application occurs there by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) in the first [section], by syntactical connection (*vākya*) in the second, and by direct assertion (*śruti*) in the third.
However, the Teacher does not accept this.

Although this section involves a consideration of the operations of various types of evidence, it has been stated that application by direct assertion (*śruti-viniyoga*) alone pertains to this [first] section, whereas application by indicative power and the rest will begin from the second section of the Mīmāṃsākośa (II.1.1).

The statement that "the properties of the medicinal herbs (auṣadhadharma) apply even to *ilā* and so forth" is also stated with the intention of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), even though it is something yet to be established in this particular section.

The proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) challenges the doubt by means of the authority of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), stating: "But surely these [grains] are already connected [to threshing].

On the other hand, the opponent, considering the connection with rice and so forth—which is produced by the relationship with another word—to be set aside by the injunction for pure threshing, says: "But the ritual acts such as threshing are enjoined by direct revelation (*śruti*). However, this too seems improper.
Why? Because "no word whatsoever is employed without another word;
and in the section concerning sentences, the remedy for the sublation of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) has already been stated."
For threshing and the like, even when connected with rice and other materials, do not cease to be threshing and so forth.
If they were otherwise, then the syntactical connection (*vākya*) would be sublated because it would contradict the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
In this case, however, since the necessity of performing threshing and the like applies to each name individually, they must necessarily be connected with something else.
For even in the absence of a specific [textual] injunction, acts such as threshing are not performed independently;
in that case, a connection with the mere substance obtained through the context would have to be postulated through great effort.
Even if some connection with a direct statement (*vākya*) were established, there would still be such effort.
If, on the other hand, a connection with the primary act is desired by way of being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), even then there is remoteness.
But if it is not connected with anything at all, then the consequence would be that the injunction has a single purpose.
Therefore, this belongs to that.
Therefore, it should be explained as follows: "The doubt here arises from uncertainty regarding whether there is a difference in the sentences or a unity [of action];
for this [doubt] is caused by whether [the act] is prompted by the ultimate apūrva or the intermediate apūrva."

In this case, the prima facie argument is not valid: "The ritual acts such as threshing are enjoined by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) as independent entities; their connection with rice and other materials is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), not by direct statement.

If that sentence, which has the nature of indicating the means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), is [determined] according to the specific context (*prakaraṇa*)—as it is for the vegetable offering (*auṣadha*)—then it is no different for the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the milk-curd mixture (*sāṃnāyya*).

In this way, through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, the connection of the *utpanna*, *vilāpana*, *śākhāharaṇa*, and so forth with other oblations not explicitly mentioned in the text must be demonstrated.
In that regard, is a single instance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice the motivator (*prayojaka*) of these ritual details (*dharma*), or are multiple instances?
And even if it is multiple instances, is it every new transcendental result (*apūrva*) in general, or only some specific ones?

If there were a single *apūrva* for all [rites], or if all [apūrvas] were the motivators (*prayojaka*) for all [the constituent acts], then there would be a confusion (*saṃkara*) of the ritual properties (*dharma*).
But if, in the case of multiple *apūrvas*, only a specific one is the motivator, then there is a distinct determination (*vyavasthā*) for each.
Regarding this, the author begins with the final conclusion itself: "Their connection is by way of purpose" (*teṣāmarthena saṃbandhaḥ*).

Even if the items denoted by words such as "prokṣatā" (those to be sprinkled) were to be mentioned in isolation, when the question arises as to where they should be performed, they must be performed where, being performed, they serve a purpose.
And these items do not serve a purpose when mixed with everything;
therefore, [the rule] regarding their purpose and locus applies.
The purpose of their legal proceedings (*arthādhikaraṇa*) can also be inferred elsewhere, because it is recorded there;
for just as there is an injunction for the *sāṃnāyya* and other offerings even when the specific substance to be offered (*pradeya-viśeṣa*) is not mentioned.

There is a lack of comprehension because it is a means to an unprecedented result (*apūrva*) that has never been known before. Likewise, even when there is a connection to a single *apūrva*, the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) alone [are the material], because they lack the character of being for that specific *apūrva*. Alternatively, on that basis, these [rites] would be prescribed everywhere; if there were no taking of the *kṣuga* and other [grains].

As for the fact that, within that very same *apūrva*, by virtue of having the same grammatical role (*kāraka*), they are prompted by the ultimate *apūrva* (*paramāpūrva*), or rather prompted by all *apūrvas*: in that case, it will be of service, and its property (*dharma*) will indeed belong to it, just as in the case of barley (*yava*).
They would be thus [auxiliary] if the *apūrvas* produced by the rice-oblations and so forth were distinct; and we shall explain all this in detail in the ninth [chapter].

[However, they would not be auxiliary] if there were no *utpattyapūrvas* produced by the Āgneya and other sacrifices; and if these [Āgneya-produced *apūrvas*] were the motivators (*prayojaka*) for the sake of accomplishing a single *phalāpūrva*. (That is, if the *utpattyapūrvas* were the motivators.)
However, those [apūrvas] are to be postulated, and not others, because the properties (dharmas) have that as their purpose; otherwise, there would be confusion.
There exist distinct apūrvas for each respective action, serving as the motivators. In that regard, there are indeed intermediate apūrvas.

Why? Because it has been established in the section concerning the *apūrva* (2.1.12) that the ritual details (*dharma*) belonging to the Āgneya and other sacrifices do not produce the supreme *apūrva* by their own nature in the absence of those [subsidiary] elements.

And although these [meditations] have direct results, nevertheless, because the establishment of their own nature is otherwise impossible, the fact of being a means to attainment enters as the motivating factor. Furthermore, this inquiry does not occur after the knowledge of the nature of Soma has been acquired.
[They are] fruitless.
