Therefore, it does not follow that [a rule] is non-injunctive simply because it is fruitless; for regarding the meanings of the Sūtras—namely, with respect to the purpose of those ritual preparations (*saṃskāra*) based on their visible utility—that which is absolutely fruitless is independent [of such purpose] (i.e., independent of the knowledge of its purpose), and thus the determination of the relationship [is established].
Or rather, [the relationship] consists in the fact that the substance and so forth have attained their own essential nature.
The properties of the *vrīhi* grains and the *sāṃnāyya* offering, though heard in the context of the intermediate [apūrva] such as that of the Āgneya sacrifice,
lead to the final fruit through a traditional succession, because they serve to establish the ultimate *apūrva*. This is the view of the followers of the *Gāmin* school.
Or rather, there must be an ordainer [of the sequence], because in the case of confusion, there is a connection with the *apūrva* of the result;

nor are the intermediate *apūrvas* established prior to the ritual acts (*dharmas*), for they are not directly connected with it, as their utility is already known through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Therefore, they are employed solely for the sake of attaining their own form. That context (*prakaraṇa*) which arises from the subject matter is established;

that *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) is the most excellent and powerful among those [means of proof] when, while certain properties are being enjoined, something new (*apūrva*) presents itself. Thus, that [contextual connection] is superior by virtue of its context.
It is that which is the motivator (*prayojaka*), not just anything whatsoever.

And from [the discussion on] rice and so forth, the Bhaṭṭa [school] concludes: Thus, when subsidiariness (*aṅgatva*) has been determined, the six means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—direct assertion (*śruti*) and the rest—establish that the *apūrva* is accomplished solely through its own action, and nothing else, because there would otherwise be no connection.
This is what was stated regarding the means of knowledge.

In this context, the Vedic injunctions (*śruti*)—which constitute the factor that establishes the subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) of elements such as *avaghāta* (threshing)—become meaningful by denoting, primarily through either the state of being the objective (*uddeśyatva*) or the state of being a causal factor of the action (*kṛtikārakatva*), that very same single *apūrva*. They do not denote a supreme *apūrva* or the *apūrva* of another ritual act. Furthermore, that [denotation] takes the form of case-endings such as the accusative (*dvitīyā*) and so forth;
in the case of verbal derivatives (*kṛdanta*), they depend on these.
He demonstrates this:

because, along with the activity such as threshing (*avahanana*), there is a lack of being grasped as a primary factor (*prādhānya*) due to its status as a completed action (*niṣṭhātva*) and so forth.

For that [threshing], among the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and other materials mentioned in the scriptural injunctions as *kārakas*, there is no status as a *kāraka* by way of primacy, since it is enjoined as a means to one's own *apūrva* (unseen potency) by virtue of denoting a specific substance.
It is observed.
Therefore, there is no transference elsewhere.

However, if for that very reason [the rule] "they thresh with the sprinkled mortar and pestle" were not a new (apūrva) injunction, then an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) would have to be postulated by implication; whereas in cases such as "the sacrificial cake is made of rice," the application is based solely on the scriptural statement, and even if the benefit is not presented by the words themselves, it would be postulated as the motive.
It has not been heard [in that sense].

Here, the second [case-ending] exists as the state of being the objective (uddeśyatva) in the case of sprinkling and so forth when they are subordinate members (aṅga); however, that [state] is indeed present here. This is the reason.

In reality, however, because it is that which is most desired (*īpsitatva*), it is the objective (*uddeśyatā*) and thus possesses the status of being the goal (*sādhyatā*). The Sūtra itself is likewise [intended] in this way. Furthermore, in the case of separation (*viprayoga*) regarding rice and other such items, since the accusative case—which expresses the mere object—denotes the verbal root's meaning, there is no primary direct denotation (*mukhyā śrutiḥ*) here either. Because there is no purpose for the *apūrva* (unseen potency), even the connection with the *sāṃnāyya* offering and so forth is remote; rather, the usage of the term "direct denotation" (*śruti*) in that context is merely figurative (*bhākta*). Regarding the aspect of being "most desired," the meaning of the word is established through the mediation of the supreme *apūrva* or the mediation of the *apūrva* of another rite, since one must admit *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Therefore, even the term "objective" (*uddeśyatā*) would not exist at all [in the primary sense].
Or, if it were at a previously unmentioned gate nearby, one would not have to exert such effort regarding the definition.
Likewise, in the case of the five [factors] and so forth, since they lack the capacity for the status of a *kāraka*, their status as objects belongs to the section on meaning (*arthādhikaraṇa*).
For them, the linguistic usage regarding the locus of the object (*arthādhikaraṇa*) is merely figurative (*bhākta*).

Likewise, even in cases where the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*) alone is intended to be expressed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), and not the presentation of another *kāraka* characterized by a specific delimitation of that means, there too [the expression] is merely syntactic (*vākyīya*).
Therefore, just as in the case of the sacrifice, there is no application for the sake of obtaining the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the rice (*vrīhi*), nor is it so stated in the scripture.

The same applies to cases where the substance is identical and so forth. And this should be understood in the same way regarding the lack of difference in their causal status (*kāraṇatā*) between rice and barley.

Thus, regarding the application of the *śruti* [scriptural injunction], its commonality [with other means of proof] is established by the very *tadbhūta* section (*PMS 1.1.25–30*); this is explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*.
Having established that in the ninth book (*adhyāya*) and others, the utility of the application of *śruti*—which applies to both primary and secondary meanings—is now demonstrated.
An investigation is conducted into the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) for [the status of being] an auxiliary to knowledge (*jñāna*) and an auxiliary to action (*kriyā*).

Maṇḍana: "The threshing of rice and so forth. Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [the texts state]: "One threshes the rice" and "One purifies the clarified butter. Śaṅkara: "There is no confusion regarding threshing and the like.
Thus, the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) for the clarified butter, the medicinal herbs, and so on, which are designated as *ājya*, are prescribed in the Śruti.

Among these, what is common to all [the subsidiaries] such as threshing? Is the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*) the capacity to be the means for the *utpattyapūrva* (originative apūrva), as in the case of the properties of clarified butter (*ājya*), herbs (*oṣadhi*), and the *sāṃnāyya* offering; or is it something different in the case of clarified butter and the rest? Such is the inquiry, which applies elsewhere as well. Having accepted that the determination according to the specific application is established by the third [chapter], rule 1.4, it is argued therein that the directly stated rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth cannot be the delimitor of the objective. This is because the capacity to be the means for the *utpattyapūrva* exists even in things like pleasure (*sukha*), which would lead to the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, there would be the consequence of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*).

Even setting aside [the necessity of] threshing, sprinkling, and so forth, a potential objection (*prasaṅga*) is raised and refuted by the statement, "by the section on their purpose" (*teṣām arthādhikaraṇena*). This is because [actions such as] threshing, which are delimited by *vrīhi* rice and the like, belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), and because [otherwise] there would be no application [of the action] to the *iṣu* (arrow).
Furthermore, the fact that [the action] serves a purpose is indicated.

Soma. 1.1.5. By the arguments in the "sections on *timira*"—such as "therefore, by the principle of the section on the agent (*namāyādhikaraṇa*), there is a connection with the *apūrva* through the desire for *vrīhi* rice"—it is established that the definition of substances as means of purification (*saṃskāra*) is necessary.

In that regard, the effort concerning the fruit is as follows: the establishment of the qualities (*guṇas*) as being subordinate to the revealed text (*śruti*) has been stated. Because [the sacrifice] is a single entity and because the capacity for being a motivator (*prayojaka*) has already been determined in the case of the indirectly contributing factors (*ārādupakāraka*), the status of the supreme *apūrva* as the means is established through its connection with the constituent part of the offering substance (*pradeya*). Consequently, the application of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) is explained; and that [application] is indicated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). *Ku.* 3.1.7.13: "In the section on their purpose (*arthādhikaraṇa*, 3.1.4.7–10), since they possess that [motivating] nature, the status of the supreme *apūrva* as the means is indeed [established] through the relationship of being a constituent part of the offering substance; thus the application of the purificatory rites is stated. And that is characterized by the indicative mark."
And although the status of being a means belongs to the Āgneya and other rites, some [hold that this is so] by way of the actual entity;
however, in reality, it is by the Vedic text itself.
Or [as stated] at Vārttika 3.1.4, page 665: for this very reason, there is no fault even regarding external restriction.

Therefore, because it is impossible for [the threshing] to function as an instrument by way of being delimited by the objective status (*uddeśyatā*) of the "formless" (*ārūpya*), and because it is common to all [grains], the threshing and so forth would apply even to clarified butter (*ājya*) and other substances. Regarding this, in the section beginning with "Their connection is with the purpose" (*teṣām arthena saṃbandhaḥ*), it is said: "But the mixing of all is prescribed;
nor is there a restriction based on specific designation."

If it were so, the *dharma* would apply [to all] because there is no distinction in their connection; this is because, with reference to the *vrīhi* and other grains mentioned in the *pūrvapakṣa-sūtra*, they are not applicable to *nīvāra* and the like due to their being mandatory.

According to the logic—having reached the position that "all *dharmas* apply everywhere except for the means of accomplishing the specific *apūrva* under discussion"—even if the injunction were made without distinction (*aviśeṣaprayukta*), it is proper that they should be restricted to the substance alone that serves as the means for the *apūrva* at hand. They are thus connected.

Nevertheless, even though the purpose is perceptible (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), one follows the principle of simplicity regarding restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi-lāghava*) to establish a specific [application], as stated at *Ku.* 3.1.6.12, p. 252. Where, however, there is a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) regarding rice (*vrīhi*) and other materials—how much more so when that too is a specific effort?

In a sentence where two causalities are established by means of proof, it will be explained in the *Arthādhikaraṇa* that, in the case of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, the term "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so on, through proximity (*pratyāsatti*), designates precisely the status of being a means to the unique transcendental result (*apūrva*) produced by the *Āgneya* sacrifice and the like;
for that is what is to be indicated (*lakṣyatvāt*).

Since that [dharma] also possesses the nature of being non-dependent (*aniśrita-prakāraka*), it is established as a means characterized by a single definition within the sentences concerning rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth (Kauṣṭubha on PMS 2.1.4.9, p.

67). Because there is no lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*), there is no reason to bypass it; furthermore, in order to avoid deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the dharma is pervasive even in the Āgneya, Upāṃśuyāja, and other sacrifices, because it possesses fruit through a traditional succession.
Therefore, it has been stated in the *Kaustubha* under the section on the purpose (*arthādhikaraṇa*, 3.1.4.7–10) that those things which have rice as their means are [the objects of the injunction].

Regarding those intermediate apūrvas (unseen potencies) arising from the Āgneya and other sacrifices up to the Aindrāgna—namely, that which is understood from the scriptural injunction "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) as the *sādhana* (means) for the apūrva by virtue of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) defined by the agency residing in the sacrifice and so forth, which is co-located with the modehood (*prakāratā*) specified by that [rice]—in that context, because the status of being the material cause culminates in the threshing (*avaghāta*), the state of being the means for the operation upon the rice-grain substance (which is the material cause of the *puroḍāśa* cake) is intended as the delimiting factor (*uddeśyatā'vacchedaka*) of the objective. Consequently, there is no confusion (*saṅkara*) [of functions], either according to the method in the *Arthādhikaraṇa* regarding their proximity, or because in the case of clarified butter (*ājya*) and the like, they are prompted by their own intermediate apūrvas.
*Soma* 1.1.1. *Atiprasaṅga* (over-extension).

And here, even though there is no single unifying factor for the quality of being "unprecedented" (*apūrvatva*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because all [elements] such as the threshing of the *sāman* are set aside from being unprecedented by virtue of being mentioned within a single word.

It cannot be suspected that their purpose is heaven through those respective operations, because by means of words such as "rice-grains" (*vrīhi*), they are proximate to the subject matter of the purpose (*arthādhikaraṇa*).
By means of logic (*nyāya*), there is the definition of the very status of being a means for the production of [the sacrifice] to Agni and others;

this is stated in *Bhāṭṭa* 1.2.1. Their systematic arrangement of ritual properties (*dharma-vyavasthā*) will be explained in the section on the purpose (*artha-adhikaraṇa*), as noted on page 730 of the *Sūtra*.

Among these, those whose metrical feet are established according to the sense are called *ṛc* (verses). This is attested in the Veda: "O Ahi Budhnya, protect my mantra—that which the seers of the *ṛk* know;
[protect] the *ṛc*s, the *sāmans*, and the *yajus*s."

Having concluded the incidental discussion on the definition of *ṛc*—namely, that "those which possess the characteristics of a verse (*ṛk*) are *ṛcs*"—we shall now, as a secondary point, define the specific categories of mantra known as *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman*.

Herein, the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: it was stated that the definition of an *ṛk* is "that in which the division into quarters (*pāda*) is determined by the sense";
however, this is not possible.

In the case of the verse "agniḥ pūrvairṛṣibhiḥ," since there is an absence of a finite verb (kriyāpada), the meaning of the *ṛc* is established even beyond the fixed arrangement of quarters determined by the delimitation of sense;

therefore, it follows that the referent of the term *ṛk* cannot be defined. This being the position reached, it is replied: this would indeed be so if a mantra composed in metrical quarters were the *ṛc*.
Regarding that [grinding], "In that [case] there is Soma"— this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The word *tu* (but) is for the purpose of excluding the alternative position.

"In that [work] consisting of the Mantras and so forth"— this is clear from the *Subodhinī*. Alternatively, [the author] states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the word "apivā" (or rather), thereby setting aside the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached through the Sūtra by way of removing the possibility of [these texts] being equal to the Veda.

These dharmas would proceed together with the means of initiation (*upanayana*), because, being equal to the Vedas, they are the prescribers of the Smṛti. Vedic matters occur subsequent to initiation;
and these [Smṛti] matters are indeed Vedic.

Therefore, these duties apply to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*), not to one who has not been initiated. Which ones? [The answer is: "In that case, there should be grinding because the purpose is not lost.
In that case—in the *saurya* oblation mentioned in the preceding sūtra—there should be grinding.

Because there is no loss of purpose—since there is no loss of the object [of the offering] and no absence of a purpose for the deity as the recipient—because even when grinding is performed, it is still possible to give to the deity;
such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Alternatively, there is non-performance [of the grinding], because it is a cause for the cake (*apūpa*).
In the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), there is neither performance nor non-performance—that is, no obligation—regarding the grinding (*peṣaṇa*).
This is because grinding is a cause for the sacrificial cake (*apūpa*);
when a *puroḍāśa* cake is to be prepared, grinding is its necessary cause.
But it would not be the case for the *caru* (oblation of boiled rice).
For the *caru* consists in having a very clear form by virtue of its internal consistency;
however, once grinding is performed, that clarity would not exist, and it would become crumbly.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that when the *caru* is to be prepared, there is no grinding (*peṣaṇa*).
This principle— that "when that is known, everything becomes known"—
was adopted by the venerable Vallabhācāryas in their *Subodhinī* commentary on the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*.
The meaning is this: Vidura went into the presence of Maitreya and asked many questions for the sake of attaining omniscience.
In that regard, it was said: "By the maxim that when one thing is known, everything becomes known, once the deeds of the Blessed One are known, everything becomes known. Thus he spoke boldly.

58.9 Oṃ. In that [fire], the rites of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*) are to be performed because they have been prescribed for it. In that fire—namely, the one brought from a blazing tree or from a vessel used for roasting chickpeas and the like, or having been taken from a forest fire and placed in a cooking pot (*ukhā*)—the rites of consecration, such as the formal installation (*ādhāna*) and others, must be carried out. This is because all ritual acts (*sarvakarmāṇi*) are prescribed as consecrations (*saṃskārāḥ*), and at present, all ritual acts are performed specifically in the *ukhya* fire.
Therefore, the preparatory rites for the *ukhya* fire must be performed;
this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
However, due to the displacement [of the fire], they would be omitted.

In place of the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*) consecrated by the *ādhāna* rite, this unconsecrated *ukhya* fire is prescribed. Because of this [substitution], the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the *ukhya* fire would be omitted from that point;
they should not be performed.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). [Question: Why? [Answer: Because the Soma must proceed in that [fire], since it is unmanifest (*avyakta*).
In the discussion as to whether the *darvihoma* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *soma* sacrifice or an independent rite (*apūrva*), he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
in that *darvihoma*, the *soma* sacrifice would apply; its ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) would be that of the *soma* sacrifice, because it is something else [distinct from the model].
The *soma* sacrifice has a different injunction (*codanā*), and the *darvihoma*, such as "he offers in the *darvi*-ladle," also has a different injunction.
Due to the commonality of the injunction, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *soma* sacrifice applies.
Furthermore, "difference" (*anyattva*) consists in the absence of both a material substance (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*) in the injunctive statement.

Or rather, [the Soma ritual procedure does not apply] because of the connection with the utterance of *svāhā* and because of the specific mention of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance; for there is a contradiction between that [Soma ritual] and this [Darvihoma].
The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view.
The Soma ritual procedure does not apply to the Darvihoma.
Because of the connection with the utterance "svāhā" in the formula, "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!
whereas in the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Soma sacrifice, there is the prescription of the *vaṣaṭ* call;
for in the Soma sacrifice the *vaṣaṭ* call occurs, while in the *darvihoma* (ladle-oblation), the *svāhā* call is found.

This being the case, since the Soma-related ritual procedure (*tantra*) is accepted, there would be a conflict with the *svāhākāra* due to that *vaṣaṭkāra*; because such a conflict would arise, the Soma-related subsidiary rules (*vidhyanta*) do not apply to the *darvihoma*.
Rather, this [offering] is a new, independent rite (*apūrva*).
In this regard, the reading in the *Kutūhala* is: "In this case, because of this conflict."
The meaning of the *tantra* is that because of the contradiction between the *svāhākāra* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) pertaining to the Soma sacrifice does not apply there;
this is because they are distinct verbal forms (*śabdāntaratvāt*).
He states another reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the *darvihoma* is indeed an original rite (*apūrva*) and not a modification of the Soma sacrifice.
In this context, "word" refers to the word *yajati* as it pertains to the Soma sacrifice;
"another word" refers to the different word *juhoti*.
That which is enjoined by the root *yaji* is the Soma sacrifice, while that which is enjoined by the root *hu* is the *darvihoma*.
Therefore, the *darvihoma* is a new (independent) rite.
This is because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
In the *darvihoma*, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Soma sacrifice does not apply; rather, there is the observation of an indicative mark showing that it is a new rite.

Having prescribed the utterance of *svāhā* in the *audumbarī-homa*, there is a statement concerning the procedure for the clarified butter (*ājya*) which says: "With the words, 'O Heaven and Earth, may you be filled with ghee,' he offers between his ears; having caused it to flow down to the root [of the tree], when it has reached the ground, he utters *svāhā*.
If the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) were that of the Soma sacrifice, then there would be the *vaṣaṭkāra*, not the *svāhākāra*.
Therefore, it is prior.
The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the preceding reason.
Clarified butter (ājya) should be offered between the two ears of the Audumbarī sacrificial hall.
Just as the clarified butter (*ājya*) that has been offered might reach the ground through the branch, so it must be offered again.
The meaning of the Śruti is that the utterance of *svāhā* should be recited once the butter has reached the ground, and not prior at the time of the offering itself.

As for the subsequent *svāhā*, however, it is like the *sāmada* [chant]; there, a renewed application is not prohibited, as seen from the indicative mark (*liṅga*), just as in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).

Regarding the statement that there is no *somavidhyanta* (procedural sequence of the Soma sacrifice) in the *darvihoma*, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) has cited an indicative mark (*liṅga*); the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) now refutes that.
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the position of the final view.

The utterance of *svāhā* is for the sake of what follows; whereas the *vaṣaṭkāra* is for the purpose of offering in the *udumbarī-homa* and other such rites, serving as the means for the modified forms (*vikṛti*).
Just as the *sāmidhenī* verses recited outside of a specific context (*anārambhādhīta*) belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*),

and being set aside there by the *pāścadasya* verses belonging to the specific context (*prākaraṇika*), they proceed to the ectype (*vikṛti*); in the same way, the *svāhākāra* recited outside of a specific context— according to the rule "the oblation is offered to the gods with either *svāhākāra* or *vaṣaṭkāra*"— having established itself as the archetype for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the *homa*, and having been superseded by the *vaṣaṭkāra*, applies to all other offerings except for the *soma* sacrifice.

This being the case, the application of the *saumika* archetype injunction (*vidhyanta*) to the *audumbarī-homa* and similar rites is neither prohibited nor contradictory. Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) here is redundant; this is the [author's] commentary (*bhāṣya*). [The opponent argues: "Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), as in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*)."

Just as in the case of the animal sacrifice accompanied by the *sāmidhenī* verses as heard in scripture, the application of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* ritual details is not contradictory because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as the *prayāja* offerings, since that [animal sacrifice] is expressly enjoined by a direct statement (*vacana*); similarly, in the case of the *audumbarī* oblation, because it is expressly enjoined by a direct statement, the application of the Soma-sacrifice ritual details regarding the utterance of *svāhā* would not be intended by the observation of indicative marks. Alternatively, for the sake of what follows, there must be purposefulness; otherwise, due to meaninglessness, there would be an obstruction of the archetypal (*prakṛta*) rule.

Regarding the *darvihoma*, the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) asserts that "the procedure of the Soma sacrifice applies, but the utterance of *svāhā* is for the sake of what follows"; it is precisely in this context that [the author] says:
the word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of setting aside the prima facie view.
The utterance of *svāhā* is not for the sake of what follows—that is, it is not for the purpose of producing the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.
In the archetype itself, in the *nāriṣṭha* oblations and the *pārvaṇa* oblations,
the utterance of *svāhā* possesses purpose and is effective.

If the utterance of *svāhā* were not meaningful in the archetype, then— because it would otherwise be purposeless, whereas the archetypal *saumika* *vaṣaṭkāra* is powerful due to having its own scope— the latter would be obstructed and set aside by the former.
However, the utterance of *svāhā* is not purposeless;
therefore, it serves a subsequent purpose.

And because the *darvihoma* offerings do not have a subsequent purpose, the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "he utters *svāhā* when [the offering] has reached the ground"—remains valid even in the absence of the *soma* sacrifice being performed first.
"If it is argued that [the rule] does not apply to the primary rite," the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) says:
"Even in the case of the primary rites, the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa, just as in the case of the modified rites (vikṛti), their application to the Nāriṣṭha-homas and so forth is not possible."
In that case as well, since there is no distinction made, the *vaṣaṭkāra* alone would apply;

however, while the *svāhākāra* is obtained through the textual recitation (*pāṭha*), the *vaṣaṭkāra* is what is actually prescribed (*vihita*). And a direct injunction (*vidhi*) is more authoritative than mere textual recitation.
Therefore, the utterance of *svāhā* serves only for the subsequent [rite], that is, for the sake of the modified form (*vikṛti*).
It has been stated that in a case of conflict, there is weakness of the latter.
To this, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies:
In the case of the *svāhākāra* in the *nāriṣṭha-homa* and similar rites, there is no sublation by the *vaṣaṭkāra*.
For here there is a convergence of syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).

By context, the *vaṣaṭkāra* is obtained for the *nāriṣṭha-homas*; however, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the mantras of the *nāriṣṭha-homas*, the *svāhākāra* is obtained through syntactical connection.

Thus, when there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), it was stated in the third chapter, in the *sūtra* on "Direct Assertion and Indicative Power" (*śrutiliṅga*), that in a conjunction [of authorities], the latter is weaker. It was therefore stated that syntactical connection is stronger than context.
Consequently, because the utterance of *svāhā* is inserted into the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), it does not serve the purpose of the modified rite (*vikṛti*).

And therefore, in the case of the *darvihoma*, it is not a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *soma* sacrifice. Since the injunction for that [sacrifice] has already been applied to the *iṣṭi*, its procedure (*vidhi*) would apply.
He states another position: let the procedure of the *nāriṣṭha-homas* apply to the *darvihomas*.
The word "or" (vā) excludes both the position that the details of the Soma sacrifice apply and the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position.

The injunctions pertaining to the *iṣṭi*—namely, those belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), specifically the injunctions for the *juhoti* offerings and the *nāriṣṭha* offerings—should constitute the rule (*vidhi*) in that case, namely in the *vāstu-homa*, because they are operative in all [sacrifices] and in all animals; "rule" (*vidhi*) means that which is enjoined (*vidhīyate*). Thus, the meaning is that the injunctions for the *nāriṣṭha* offerings belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices would apply to the *vāstu-homa*, since they are already operative elsewhere.
And because of the force of the word.
He states another reason for the alternative view that "in the *darvihoma* offerings, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *nāriṣṭha* offerings should apply.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction.

The prohibition that pertains to the capacity of the word would be a rule prohibiting *imā* and the others which are obtained from the *vyambaka* offerings by virtue of their having the *nāriṣṭha-homa* as their archetype;
and this prohibition, by demonstrating the prior application [of those elements], establishes that the *vyambakas* are indeed modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *nāriṣṭhas*.

Therefore, regarding the *darvihoma* offerings, when the properties of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations are extended [by analogy], the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that was stated—namely, "If an insect should fall [into the fire]," "One should pour [the offering] within the enclosing sticks," and "Standing within the altar, one offers the *sāvitra* oblations," and so forth—is indeed appropriate.

It is not [appropriate] because of being a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), nor is the resolution for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) tenable if there were a plurality [of applications]. Regarding the *tryambaka* offerings, he refutes the doubt—that the injunction such as "They are not performed with the *imāvāha* formulas" and "They are not sacrificed with the *prajā* [formulas]" is a prohibition of the *imāvāha* and other elements obtained through their application to the *nāriṣṭha* homas—by means of the third alternative (*pakṣa*).
A prohibitive injunction is not appropriate here because it serves as a supplementary part of another sentence.

The statement, "The *tryambaka* offerings are indeed unstable; they are not joined with the *iḍā*," and so forth, is a supplementary sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*)—an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)—to the injunction, "One should offer a *caru* oblation of rice in clarified butter to Āditya upon returning to one's home.
It may serve as an alternative (*vikalpa*) to either a traditional text (*smṛti*) or established practice (*ācāra*), but not [as a prohibition].
They consult together.
In that regard, some apply the word *yava* to long-awned barley; this is due to the weakness of linguistic usage. (Su. p. 212).
Some [apply the term] to *priyaṅgu* plants;
some apply the word "boar" (*varāha*) to a pig; and some [apply it] to *oṃ*, because no contradiction is observed among them, the disagreement is equal.
[The word *varāha* is also used] for the black bird (the crow).
Some take the word *vetasa* to mean the *vañjulaka* plant, while others take it to mean the *jambu* tree.
In that regard, since the meaning of the word is understood in both ways— as in "a cake made of barley," "boar-skin sandals," and "on a mat of *vetasa* grass"— [the rule applies].
[This is] a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Thus, here, out of a desire for systematic connection (*saṃgati*), Prabhākara [cites] what is heard in various places [in the scriptures]: "He collects the *prājāpatya* offerings."
In that regard,
the word *vikalpa* is explained as referring to the *kāryya* [the object to be accomplished], being intended in the sense of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*).
Some apply the word *yava* to long-awned barley, while others apply it to groats.
For he thinks as follows: when two independent scriptural injunctions prescribe rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding *priyaṅgu* grains;
likewise, some apply the word "boar" (*varāha*) to a pig, while others apply it to a black bird.
Thus, an option arises.

But here, in the single passage "the sacrificial grass consists of barley" (*yavamayaś carurbhavati*), some take the word *vetasa* to mean the *vañjulaka* reed, while others take this sentence as not being restricted [to that], [interpreting it] as referring to both the long-beaked parrot (*dīrghaśuka*) and the *priyaṅgu* plant. As for the *jambū* tree, [it is used] in its literal sense.
In that regard, when deliberating on what is to be adopted as certain for the performance,
it is possible [to interpret] it as an injunction;
however, if both were stated [simultaneously], there would be the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*).
He does not state a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Regarding those meanings of words such as "barley" (*yava*) and so forth, since they are used in both ways, it is impossible to determine that one is primary (*mukhya*) and the other is secondary (*gauṇa*), because the contradiction is equal due to the authority [of usage]. Thus, there is indeed a conflict of opinions.
It is possible [to accept both], because there is no evidence for a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā-pramāṇa*).
Nor would the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) be an option (*vikalpa*);
by way of an option, both meanings are to be accepted.

The determining authority [is found] in the statement, “The sacrificial post is made of barley,” because of its status as a scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) and because it is the cause for that [act],
due to the hearing of the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*).

However, according to the view of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by setting aside the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding Varuṇa with the word "or" (*vā*).
Because it is part of the scripture (*śāstra*).
This specific statement regarding the *karambha-pātra* made of barley—which is the primary substance—is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
It is precisely that distinguished understanding which is perceived as existing within the scripture.

According to the view of the author of the Vārttika, however, the establishment of the *yavamata* (barley-measure) should be accepted in the sprinkling of the *audumbarī* post, because that [measure] is the cause for it; this is what was stated [in the sūtra]. 1808.
It must be stated that because the usage [of the word] is observed even in the case of *priyajña*, a capacity (*śakti*) must be postulated for it as well through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

For, by the very logic of establishing that [capacity], since the usage in *priyajña* is established otherwise—namely, by the principle of figurative application (*gauṇaśāstranyāya*)—the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) would be exhausted.
(Vaitā.)
In the mantra "tattai śrutam," the modification (ūha) beginning with "tasmai śrutam" and so forth must not be performed; this applies to the *trivatsa-khaṇḍa* mantra as well.
Bhāṣya 9.1.15.42–44, Section 2:
For her, the benediction and the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) are only as prescribed, because of the inequality [of the two cases].
It is understood that husband and wife have joint authority regarding ritual action.
In that regard, whatever ritual act in the sacrifice is accompanied by mantras and is designated as "pertaining to the sacrificer" (*yājamāna*), all of that does not belong to the wife;
the wife has no authority therein.

However, as for the *āśis*—the mantras expressing blessings (in the *Vārttika*, it is stated that by the word *āśis*, purificatory rites such as the tying of the hair (*keśadharmya*) and so forth are indicated)—such as "O Agni, you are life; grant me life," and likewise *brahmacarya*; and whatever has been prescribed concerning the wife, such as "the wife ties [the sacrificial cord]" and "he makes the wife recite"—all that must be performed by the wife.
This is not the case [for other rites], because the wife is not equal to the sacrificer.
For a woman is indeed unequal to a man.
The sacrificer is a learned man;
the wife is a woman who has been deliberated upon.
Therefore, regarding that wife, her entitlement is only to that which has been prescribed: the benediction and the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Who [is the deity] for these? Fire should be [the deity], by virtue of the archetype (prakṛti), just as in the case of the fore-offerings (prayāja).

Regarding the Agni used for the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, there arises the doubt: should it be one consecrated by both the fire-installation (ādhāna) and the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, or one consecrated by the fire-installation alone? This is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) view. The pronoun "of them" (*tāsām*) in the eleventh sūtra points to the ritual elements of the iṣṭis; that Agni which pertains to those Pavamāna-iṣṭis should be understood according to the archetypal model (*prakṛti*).
In the archetype of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, Agni is indeed not yet consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis through the mere act of installation (ādhāna).
And since the ectype is like the archetype, whatever kind of Agni exists in the archetype, that very same kind of Agni is obtained from the archetype for those [ectypal] fires.
This is like the Prayājas: just as the Prayājas exist in the archetype, so too do the Prayājas exist in the Pavamāna-iṣṭis by virtue of being like the archetype; the same applies to Agni.
The term *vasti* here follows the first case ending, like the *prayāja*s, as in "like the *prayāja*s.
Or rather, it is not so, because they are for that purpose.

The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the fire in the *ādhāna* would be consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭi*s, such that the fire would be one refined by the *pavamāneṣṭi*s.

The fire for the Pavamāna sacrifices is not prepared by the Pavamāna sacrifices themselves; rather, it is the fire prepared solely by the *ādhāna* (consecration) ceremony that belongs to them. Why? Because those [Pavamāna sacrifices] exist for the sake of that [fire], as they would otherwise be impossible, since their purpose is the consecration of the fire. If one were to perform the Pavamāna sacrifices for the sake of the Pavamāna sacrifices, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the fire (*agni*) [required for the *darśapūrṇamāsa*] must be one consecrated solely by the act of *ādhāna* (the formal installation of the sacred fires). However, regarding the question of whether those *pavamāneṣṭis* exist or do not exist—just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings according to the logic of the section beginning with "But in that [case], it should be like the *prayāja*" (*ke. tasyāṃ tu syāt prayājavat*)—there is an inquiry into whether the fire is consecrated by the *pavamāna-havis* offerings.
Or rather,
in that case, it should be like the *prayāja* offerings;
in that [sacrifice], the *ārambhaṇīyā* ought to be performed.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "without doubt.
Just as there are *prayāja* offerings in the *ārambhaṇīyā*, so it is here;
for the purpose of the *ārambhaṇīyā*, there should be an *ārambhaṇīyā*.
"Repetition according to one's capacity does not entail an infinite regress";
such is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
[The response is: "Or rather, it is not so, because it is a subordinate element (aṅga)."

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), namely "it should not," is refuted. There should be no *ārambhaṇīyā* for the sake of the *ārambhaṇīyā*, because it is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; indeed, it constitutes their commencement.
Furthermore, for that which is a subordinate constituent (*aṅga*), success consists precisely in the commencement of the principal rite.

Therefore, because it belongs to the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, this *ārambhaṇīyā* is to be commenced many times; such is the established position. Consequently, there is no *ārambhaṇīyā* for the sake of the *ārambhaṇīyā* itself; this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Some [hold this view] because of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatvāt*).

Regarding the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is only one injunctive sentence that prescribes the commencement as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for both: "One desiring to commence the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu."
There is no second [performance].
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering] need not be performed for the sake of the Ārambhaṇīyā [itself].
Ke.

According to the principle that "it [the subsequent element] ends with that," just as there is a displacement (apakarṣa) of the Āghāra and other rites when the Prayājas are displaced (the meaning of this principle being stated as:
"tadanta" means ending with the Prayājas), so too, when the Abhiṣeka is displaced, there is a displacement of the Videva and other rites; such is the prima facie view (pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ).
Regarding those [mantras] ending with that [word], 1809: their repetition;

in the even [verses], there is an extraction (apakarṣa) of those mantras ending with that [word], which conclude with the *prayāja* offerings and include the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *āghāra* libation.
[This applies] to the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma.
(In this same way, there is a displacement of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s) together with their respective subsequent *sūkta* and *ākā* [verses].
This applies to the *savanīya* animal sacrifice.)
The principle of the removal of the final element (tadantāpakarṣanyāya).
This is indeed the same as the principle of that which begins with it and ends with it (tadāditadantanyāya).

In the *Adhvarakalpa*, regarding the injunction "one should offer [the oblation] before the utterance of speech," the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that, by the principle of the "retrogression of the end" (*tadantāpakarṣanyāya*), since there is a retrogression of all [elements], the constituent parts ending with the offering (*nirvapa*), which belong to the entire performance, are to be performed collectively (*tantra*).

(Bhāṭṭa 11.2.13). Regarding the statement "one cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) during the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu*), the prima facie view is that the [post-cutting], being thus retrogressed, causes the retrogression of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice and others, according to the principle of the "retrogression of the end. (Bindu 5.1.12). In the *Rājasūya*, [there are] the *abhiṣecanīya* and the *daśapeya*.
In that context, at the time of the purchase of Soma for the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, the purchase of Soma for the *daśapeya* is drawn forward.

Since that [purchase] is being drawn forward, by the principle of drawing forward up to its end (*tadantāpakarṣanyāya*), it also draws forward the ritual items preceding it. Thus, because both [sacrifices] share a common commencement (*ārambha*), they have a common ritual framework (*samānatantra*), and so forth—this being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

According to the *Bhāṭṭa* school (11.2.13), the very sequence of the preceding and succeeding ritual items is what determines the "ending with that" (*tadanta*) and "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) relationship.

Therefore, in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an anticipation (apakarṣa) of the rites up to the Prayājas for the Agniṣomīya animal victim; and in the Savanīya [offering], there is an anticipation of the rites up to the Anuyājas.
"The absence of that [dreaming] occurs in the channels and in the Self, because of scriptural statements regarding them. (Soma. 3.2.7).
By the principle stated in *Brahmasūtra* 3.2.7, the purity of the self (*ātman*) is being established as consisting of the *prāyaṇa* (the path of departure).

The absence of that [purity] results in the existence of the waking and dreaming states within the channels (*nāḍīs*), and by the word "and" (*ca*), also in the city (*purī*) and the self (*ātman*). This does not occur when one has become fully absorbed in the individual soul (*jīva*). Why? Because of the scriptural texts: "Then he is asleep in these channels," "He lies in the city," and "In that space which is within the heart, he lies. Such is the literal meaning of the words.
Śārīraka Rāmatīrtha, Chapter 3, Verse 120:
The principle is "because it is non-different from that, it is non-different from that.
For example, since all the gods beginning with Brahmā are non-different from the Lord due to His being their sovereign, the sense is that there is likewise mutual non-difference among them.
It is impetuous (sāhasī). 71. Its repetition should occur in equal [verses].
It is understood that in the Agniṣṭoma, one *sāman* is to be sung, completed for each verse (*ṛc*) within a triplet (*tuc*).

Now, regarding the inquiry as to whether the *geya* should be performed on two verses (*tuca*) that have the same meter or if there is no fixed rule, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

"The repetition of that"—meaning the repetition of that *sāman*—should be performed verse by verse upon three verses that are equal, i.e., of the same meter; it should not be done optionally, either on equal or unequal verses.
For the conventional usage of the number "three" occurs in the term *tṛca*;
and the conventional usage of a number applies when [the items] are placed upon some common basis.
Therefore, the repetition occurs in a *tṛca* consisting of verses of identical meter.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Regarding the fact that in the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice the *sāman* to be sung is completed verse by verse and should be sung upon three verses of identical meter, there is the observation of an indicative mark: "They say that a friend is established in a shallow vessel; when the *bṛhat* [sāman] is performed on *gāyatrī* verses."

Regarding the statement that the *Bṛhat* Sāman, which arose upon the thirty-one-syllable verse beginning with "tvāmiddhi havāmahe," should be sung on *Gāyatrī* verses consisting of twenty-four syllables: this would be like placing a large thigh (*ūru*) intended for cooking into a small pot (*sālī*).
For it has been stated therein that a large thing cannot fit within a small one.
Therefore, it is established that the Sāman should not be sung upon verses of dissimilar meters.
[Question: What is that?
[Answer: Its practice should be performed during the equinoxes (*samā*).
Now, in this very context, there is another interpretation (*varṇaka*) by means of the mixed-syllable (*miśradhūrmī*) sūtras beginning with "its practice" (*tadabhyāsaḥ*).
Another interpretation regarding the commentary should be seen under the section "Not [a case of] unevenness in meter" (*naikoccavikaraṇam*).

On the fourth day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there is a *sāman* called *naikocca*, which arises upon the *atijagatī* verse beginning, "The hero who overcomes all enemies" (*viśvāḥ pṛtanā abhibhūtaraṃ naram*).
The two subsequent verses, however, are *bṛhatīs*: "They bow down with their eye" (*nemi namanti cakṣuṣā*) and "The singers have sung together" (*samī rebhāso akṣaran*).
But this *tuca* consists of uneven meters.
In this regard, it is deliberated: should the final two *atijagatī*s, having been taken from somewhere, be chanted with a combined evenness of pitch, or rather, while remaining uneven?
Regarding this, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The practice of that [chanting]—the practice of that *naikoccasāman*—should take place upon even verses.

One verse, "viśvāḥ pṛtanāḥ," is itself an *ati-jagatī*; two others, being likewise *ati-jagatīs*, are to be brought from the *Dāśatayī* collections. Upon these three verses, the *naiśoka* should be sung.
This is also because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
But the occasional (naimittika) [application] is understood from its proximity to what follows.
By the word "but" (tu), he sets aside the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) and states the established conclusion (siddhānta).

Because of the proximity in the sequence of the subsequent text, the [application] of the two [verses] alone should result from what follows; therein, the occasional [application] is based on the cause of the sequential recitation as heard in the scripture (śrauta-pāṭha).
That very [text] is what is understood;
here, two *atijagatī* verses are not recognized from any source of tradition (*āgama*), because the direct hearing of the recitation (*pāṭhaśruti*) is more authoritative.
Therefore, the singing of the *naiśoka* [sāman] occurs only over its own subject matter.
And because they have a single purpose, there is repetition of that [sāman].

Now, if the Naiśoka is sung over a *tṛca* (a triplet) consisting of verses in different meters, then the word "triplet" (*tṛca*), which denotes a specific number, would be inappropriate; if this is argued, it is not so.
Because they have a single purpose—that is, because they share a single deity—there is the justification for the term "triplet" despite the difference in meters, due to their having a single purpose.
If it is objected that even so, the plural form of the word *atijagatī* in the expression "they praise with the *atijagatīs*" is not justified, he replies to that: "It is due to its repetition.

In the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, as in the rule "the *ṣoḍaśin* is twenty-onefold," all the stotras become twenty-onefold; thus, when the *naiśoka* sāman is being prepared through repetition, it attains the number seven while existing as *atijagatīs*.
This being the case, the plural form "with the *atijagatīs*" is indeed justified.

Therefore, there is no authority for *atijagatī* verses from any other source; rather, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *naiśoka* hymn should be chanted in uneven meters. Why? Because of the explanatory treatise (*arthavāda*).

Now, what is intended here: are the mantras meant to convey their expressed meaning, or are they not meant to convey their expressed meaning? Do they assist in the sacrifice by illuminating the purpose, or merely by their utterance?

In this regard, Prabhākara, out of a desire for systematic consistency (*saṃgati*), has described the topic as follows: "In the injunction, 'He spreads the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with the mantra, "O wide-expanding one, expand wide!"', if the meaning of the mantra "O wide-expanding one, expand wide! is intended to be expressed, then its application (*viniyoga*) to the spreading of the cake would be established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of that very meaning; consequently, the scriptural statement of purpose, "He spreads the cake," would be redundant regarding an unintended meaning."

Now, if that explanatory treatise (*arthavāda*) intends its literal meaning, then the mantra would have no intended meaning; thus, due to this mutual contradiction, the injunction (*codanā*) lacks authority.
This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: that which effects something is employed for a certain purpose through a specific action.
Just as in the case of threshing, which produces a specific effect, the accusative case in "vrīhau" (in the rice) denotes its status as a recipient of the result by means of the action;
therefore, where these three factors are understood from the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), there the application (*viniyoga*) is understood from the direct statement itself.

Here, however, in the statement "iti puroḍāśaṃ prathayati" (with this [mantra] he spreads the sacrificial cake), it is understood from the direct statement that the mantra produces a specific effect through the act of spreading.

Regarding the statement "he spreads the *puroḍāśa*," the spreading of the *puroḍāśa* is understood from the direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) as being both some kind of effect and a specific action of manifestation.
However, from the indicative power (*liṅga*)—which consists in the capacity of the mantra to denote—it is understood that the denotative mantra performs some function:
namely, that the object to be denoted is an effect to be brought about, and the act of denotation itself is a specific action consisting of manifestation.

Since the triad [of word-meaning, syntactic connection, and context] is presented by the indicative mark of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*) itself, the sequence for the application of the mantra to the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is established by that very *mantraliṅga*. This being the case, the scriptural statement (*śruti*), "He spreads the sacrificial cake," is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). However, where the triad is presented by *śruti* itself—as in "He worships the Gārhapatya fire with the *aindrī* mantra"—there *śruti* alone is the applicator. This is because the *aindrī* mantra has some specific function, and since he worships "having approached" (*upasthāya*), worship consists of making manifest; thus, making manifest is a type of action. Therefore, in such cases, *śruti* alone is the means of application.

Nor is the *śruti* redundant here because the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra performs the application (*viniyojaka*), for it possesses its own purpose precisely by conveying the action as already connected (*anvitakārya*).
Indeed, there is no other purpose whatsoever than the conveyance of the action as connected.
Even in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), that [purpose] remains unassailed; thus, the injunction (*codanā*) does not lack authority due to mutual contradiction.
This is inconsistent because of mutual contradiction; for there can be no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) in the absence of [an opposing view].
Indeed, contradiction occurs only between two positions of equal strength.
However, the application of a mantra should be determined according to its inherent capacity;
the application by means of a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is itself the primary applicator because it possesses the nature of a direct revelation.
Thus, since the mantra is a direct Vedic statement, its literal meaning is certainly intended.

As for the mutual contradictions stated by the opponent, from where do they arise? Nor should it be argued: "Even if study is prompted by the injunction to teach, nevertheless, because the meaning understood as an inseparable concomitant is more internal (antaraṅga) and because the injunction to study culminates in the qualification of the student, that meaning is required; thus, since the entire mantra has its meaning intended, there is no contradiction. This is not so, because even in the *nirvāpa-mantra*, such as "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ... (*devasya tvā savituḥ prasave*), we observe that the names [of the deities] have meanings that are not intended to be expressed.

Nor can these [mantras] be considered mere explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), because they lack syntactic unity with an injunction (*vidhi*). Just as the utterance of these mantras and the utterance of words such as *hum* and so forth serve the purpose of indicating fitness (*arha*)— since they lack any meaning integrated into the performance (*prayoga*)— so too, since their nature is determined by the science of grammar (*śāstra*) which teaches their specific forms, it is logical that the utterance of the mantra here also serves the purpose of indicating fitness alone.

Or, let it be granted that the application of a mantra is indeed caused by its intended meaning; even so, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning its purpose does not have an unintended meaning. For it has been established in the section on *arthavādas* that "even an *arthavāda* which restates what is already obtained through a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) has its meaning intended precisely as a restatement, by virtue of the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*)."

Therefore, since this has already been traversed by that very same reasoning on account of the equality of the logic, the objection regarding contradiction raised when either of two things of equal purpose—the mantra or the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—is intended to have its meaning as a restatement (*anuvāda*), is merely the product of one who has failed to attend to what precedes and follows;
thus, this section should be described exactly according to the *Vārttika*.

Once it has been established that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) possess authority by virtue of their utility in relation to what is enjoined, it must now be demonstrated that mantras possess authority by virtue of their utility in illuminating the meaning of what has been enjoined. To this end, it is investigated whether mantras have an intended meaning or an unintended meaning.

Here, the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: First of all, the utility of mantras for the performance of the ritual (*kratu*) in the illumination of the enjoined meaning is not possible, because that [illumination] can be accomplished even through meditation and other means, rendering the mantra useless; furthermore, [the mantra] would be contrary [to the purpose].
For when this [meaning] is first understood, there occurs a recollection of the word that denotes it. If that meaning is already understood at the outset, what is the use of the mantra?

Nor is it possible to maintain the restrictive rule that "the assistance to the ritual (*ṛtūpakāra*) is accomplished only through the meaning recalled by the mantra," because if the mantras possess an intended meaning, one would have to resort to the assumption of restrictive factors (*niyāmakakalpanā*), as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such rites.
Nor is it intended that the meaning [of the mantra] be expressed in this way; for that would contradict the rule regarding the teaching of purpose (*tadarthaśāstra*).

For if the mantra "O wide one, spread wide" were intended to convey its literal meaning, then its application to the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) would be established by the very capacity of that expression to denote it; consequently, the scriptural injunction of application—"one spreads the sacrificial cake with this mantra"—would be rendered purposeless.
Therefore, it is understood from this that "mantras do not have their meanings intended to be expressed."
This has been stated in the Bhāṣya (p. 145): "If one with eyes is led by another, he surely does not see the objects.

Furthermore, the application of a mantra by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is sometimes seen to be contrary to its indicative power (*liṅga*), as in the case of the *aindrī* mantra being applied to the *gārhapatya* fire.
That too would not be possible if the intended meaning of the mantra were [strictly] followed.

Thus, in the case of the *nirvāpa-mantra* beginning with "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," one must state that the meanings of the constituent parts as they occur in the application are not intended to be significant (*avivakṣitārthatva*). Likewise, since words such as *hum* and so forth lack any referent, their lack of intended meaning is already established.
Therefore, even where a meaning is perceived, because it is stated as something already established elsewhere, the lack of intended meaning of the mantras is indeed established.

Therefore, regarding the mantras recited in the context (*prakaraṇa*), which are assigned as appropriate by means of direct statement (*śruti*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth, their very form (*svarūpa*) alone is accepted as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) by the principal injunction (*pradhānavidhi*). Although that form, being non-actional in nature, does not itself constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), nevertheless, for the sake of its own purpose, it must necessarily be admitted as a factor (*kāraka*) by way of the act of utterance (*uccāraṇa-kriyā*).
Since a visible result is impossible, this utterance serves a purely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.

Objection: Is it not the case that the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), for the purpose of understanding the intended meaning, would contradict the fact that a mantra has an unintended meaning by establishing that the entire *svādhyāya* (Vedic corpus) possesses an intended meaning? Reply: Not so.

For, just as with the sounds *hum* and so forth, the study of a mantra is logically justified solely for the purpose of achieving mastery over the *svādhyāya* itself, which is invariably connected to its recitation.
Even for mantras, the injunction to study exists solely for the purpose of understanding their required meaning;
for it is the primary sense that is the natural rule (*autsargika*) for words.
When that is possible, even a word used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*) retains its status as a word.

Therefore, here too, since the primary meaning is untenable due to the existence of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and other such factors, the mantras indicate their own form (*svarūpa*) as the means of conveying [the ritual action]. And that form, because a visible purpose is possible, serves the sacrifice through its utterance by way of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, even in this case, the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) achieves its purpose through the attainment of the required understanding.

[Objection: But surely the relationship between the indicated (*lakṣya*) and the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) occurs when there is a difference in meaning, as in the case of the praise found in *arthavādas*.
But here, that very nature of the mantra cannot possibly be both the indicated (lakṣya) and the indicator (lakṣaka) within itself, because of this contradiction.
Not so;
for even in the case of mantras, both forms are accepted.
For just as its nature is that of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*), so too its being an object of valid cognition (*prameyatva*) certainly exists.

Therefore, it is entirely untenable to claim that it possesses the character of a defining characteristic (*lakṣakatva*) by virtue of its nature as a means of valid cognition, while possessing the character of the defined (*lakṣyatva*) by virtue of its being an object of valid cognition.

By this, the argument—"How can there be a connection with the verbalized contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of a mantra that is itself non-verbal, based on the connection with what is verbal?"—is also refuted.

Since it has been stated that even for a single mantra, its status as "verbal" (śābdatva) exists through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) in the form of the relationship between the expressed and the expresser, [the opponent argues that] by means of the *tadarthaśāstra* and other criteria, the mantras have no intended meaning and thus serve only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"The sentence-meaning is indeed not distinct [from the literal]."
This is the intended meaning: this would indeed be so if the mantras were devoid of intended meaning;
nevertheless, by the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), they are indeed distinct [from other texts].
Because of that specific injunction;
because of that specific injunction,
the study of the mantras— whether already performed or not yet undertaken— is prescribed.
In that case, there is no status as a "lord" (nātha) in its own right, because its establishment is achieved solely through the recitation associated with the mantra.
Therefore, it is determined that this [recitation] is intended only to indicate the application of the *ṛc*.

And the application of the *ṛc* for them is not by way of conveying a meaning—as in the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings—because the meaning of those [mantras], whose logic has ceased [to apply], is already obtained from the very explanation of the injunction (*vidhi*).

Therefore, their application in the ritual (*ṛta*) must be stated by way of their own essential form (*svarūpa*). And although that essential form, being non-action in itself, is not grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) as a constituent of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it can nevertheless be grasped in the form of a factor of action (*kāraka*).

When the question arises as to how it functions as a factor of action, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs through the consideration of the assumption of a visible result, according to the principle "whatever it is capable of doing."
Its function is thus indicated.
Furthermore, the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*) requires the existence of the enjoined items to be carried out.

Since the meaning of a mantra sentence, once understood, is capable of reminding one of those items even by recalling a single part, it is through its producing the knowledge of the sentence-meaning—which has as its fruit the recollection of the enjoined items—that the mantra is grasped as a factor (*kāraka*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Therefore, it is the mere recitation of these [mantras] that is intended as their essential nature (*svarūpa*), which must necessarily be performed at the time of ritual application; however, this is not the case for the sentences of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, because their essential nature is not lost when they are grasped through the context (*prakaraṇa*). This is the distinction. If, on the other hand, one were to require a result in the form of a traditional injunction (*smṛti*), the visible result of understanding the meaning would not be perceived; in that case, the mantra’s status as a causal factor (*kāraka*) might indeed consist solely in the act of recitation with an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*). But since a visible result is obtained even indirectly, the postulation of an invisible result is not tenable; thus, mantras have precisely the meanings intended by them.

Nor is the mantra useless even when recollection can be achieved through meditation (*dhyāna*) and other means, because it possesses purpose solely by virtue of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*).

For just as the injunction for threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth is purposeful as a restrictive rule—even though the state of being dehusked (*vaituṣya*) could be accomplished by other means—so too is this [case]; thus, there is no inconsistency.
Therefore, since the purpose of mantras is intended [to be recollection], the study of mantras is not for the sake of preventing the loss of one's Vedic learning (*svādhyāya*).
Nor is it the case that the mantra has its own form (*svarūpa*) as its meaning through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because the primary meaning is untenable.
What then? [Its purpose] is solely for the sake of understanding the sentence-meaning required for the effort toward the mantra’s purpose.

But how, then, even in the Siddhānta, can a mantra that is not directly denotative (*aśābda*) be connected with the ritual productive operation (*kratu-bhāvanā*)? In this regard, some say that even in the Siddhānta, the mantra has its own form as its meaning through secondary indication in order to establish its status as being denotative; that is incorrect.

The nature of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) consists in abandoning the primary meaning and postulating another related meaning that serves as a justification. However, in this case, there is no abandonment of the primary meaning even in the final position (*siddhānta*), as is the case in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the mantras have their intended meanings.

Rather, since the efficient force of performance (*prayogabhāvanā*) is untenable without a recollection of what is to be performed, the context (*prakaraṇa*), for its own sake and for the sake of the mantra’s purposefulness, accepts the mantra itself as the cause of recollection, provided it is capable of producing such recollection.

And since that [denotative function] is not possible if the mantra were non-verbal, it is appropriate to postulate a word directed toward that [meaning] through *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard) for its sake.

This is not untenable, because—as in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others—one may postulate a word directed toward that meaning for the sake of the object itself, which is inferred as the means of accomplishment (*upapādaka*).

Nor is there a lack of intended meaning due to the "scriptural statements of that purpose" (*tadarthaśāstra*) and so forth, precisely because such scriptural statements do not even exist here; for in cases such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," there is not even the possibility of such a statement occurring.

Even where there exists the possibility of that [connection]—namely, in the case of the taking up [of the reins] through the mantras—even there, it is not the Vedic text (*śruti*) that assigns the mantras.

What then? By virtue of their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), the mantras are already applicable to that taking up; however, by the text "He takes it up with four," the number four is also enjoined for the taking up.

Thus, when there is a mutual restriction according to the principle of the single-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī-nyāya*) among the others in the set of eleven, the meaning of the sentence results in: "The taking up must be performed with all four mantras used in combination."
Therefore, the hearing of the number four in that context is solely for the purpose of indicating a quality (*guṇa*).
This has been stated by the author of the Sūtras: "The repetition is for the sake of a quality.

Similarly, in the case of the mantra, "With this [mantra] he takes up the reins, saying 'O Death, this is your rein,'" there would be an application of the mantra even to the donkey's rein by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Nevertheless, because the application of a mantra through *liṅga* (indicative power) involves a remote process of inferring a *śruti* (direct Vedic statement), the mantra is applied to the *aśvaraśanā* (horse-halter) solely on the basis of the direct *śruti*: "With this [mantra] he takes it up. Since both the mantra and its context (*prakaraṇa*) are thus satisfied, there is no need to postulate a general *śruti* by means of *liṅga*.
Therefore, only the direct *śruti* is the applicator of the mantra.

However, one might ask: "If [the mantra] is obtained even without an injunction, what is the use of an injunction? In order to investigate this purpose, it is established that since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has as its object only the girdle in general, the application of the mantra would result in its being used for the donkey's girdle as well; therefore, the injunction itself serves as the necessary purpose. As it was stated in the *Grahādhikaraṇa*: "Just as in the case of a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), [the application] is determined by means of the form and the instrument" (as the root text says: "as long as it is being inferred...").
Until that inference is reached, the injunction is more quickly completed by means of the directly perceived Vedic statement (*pratyakṣā śruti*).
When the age for the injunction has not yet arrived and there is uncertainty regarding the mantra,
a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) is stated by way of its result, rather than through the repetition of a specific [word] in the text.
This is when one investigates what the purpose of the injunction might be.
"The fruit does not arise from the utterance of the word 'donkey,' but from the performance of another [act]. Thus it was stated by the author of the Sūtras: "Exclusion" (*parisaṃkhyā*).

"O thou who art wide, spread out!"—with these words he spreads out the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). [He does so] thinking, "I shall sacrifice," for by that spreading he causes offspring to prosper through cattle; it is because of that prosperity. It is because of that prosperity.

In the case of the phrase "he spreads" (*prathayati*), however, only the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is enjoined as something not previously established. Nor can it be argued that this spreading is already established by the necessity of preparing the sacrificial cake otherwise; for we observe the production of flour-cakes even without spreading, due to the force of a particular haste.

But when spreading is enjoined, since it must be performed with a specific purpose, the mantra also becomes applicable through its indicative power (*liṅga*) because it is composed of the relevant words.
Other examples are easily understood from the Bhāṣya and Vārttika themselves, and thus are not presented here.

However, where the capacity of a mantra to express its own identity [with the ritual act] arises solely by virtue of its scriptural application (*śrauta-viniyoga*), and no other means need be postulated, only there does the scripture possess the power of application (*viniyojakatva*).
This is as in: "With the *aindrī* verse he worships the *gārhapatya* fire," and "Saying, 'Thou art grain, satisfy the gods,' he pours that [grain] onto the millstones," and so forth.

However, in the case of the *nirvāpa* (offering) mantra and others, even though the [words] such as "devasya tvā" do not have a directly relevant meaning (*asamavetārthatva*), it must be assumed—following the principle of observed utility—that they serve as a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*) for the performance of the enjoined acts, by means of manifesting such a meaning through the force of being part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyabhāva*). Just as the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is also included as a restrictive factor because the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) produced at that very time from the *ulūkhala* and *musala* which have been sprinkled and from *hiṣ* grass with its awns removed is the means to the *apūrva*, so it is here as well.

Therefore, since the *hum* and other such sounds lack a desired meaning in the sense of being expressive of a further purpose, their application is solely for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, the recitation is performed by the injunction for study for the purpose of mastering the Vedic text itself, and not for any other purpose.

Objection: Grant that they possess a desired meaning; however, how can they have authority (*prāmāṇya*)? For they merely restate a matter already understood from the enunciation (*uddeśa*), and thus do not convey an unestablished fact. Reply: Not so.
Indeed, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of every Vedic sentence—defined as the capacity to convey a previously unapprehended object—is not what needs to be established.

This is because in such passages as "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the full moon" and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the new moon," that [definition] is absent due to their nature as restatements (*anuvāda*).
What, then, is to be established? It is their utility for the cognition of *dharma*.
And since that [efficacy] belongs to the mantra itself through a traditional lineage (*paramparā*), what is there that is illogical?

As for the purpose: if mantras have their meanings unintended (*avivakṣitārtha*), then there would be no performance of rites based on those [deities] remembered merely through meditation and so forth;
whereas if the meanings are intended (*vivakṣitārtha*), then [performance occurs] only when they are brought to mind by the mantras.
The Sūtra, however, states: "There is indeed no distinction between worldly sentences and mantra-sentences such that the meaning, though being perceived, would not be intended.

"Whoever here—whether by writing or speaking—records this summarized subject matter in another work, or does so himself, may he, having disregarded this [work], be deprived of fame and remain childless for hundreds of births."
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Tautātitamatatilaka*, the work of Bhavadeva, also known as Bālavalmī-bhujaṅga.
[The word] "tautā" [is derived] from the *tadvyākhyāna-śāstra*.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that mantras do not intend their literal meaning and assist merely through their utterance, he first states the reason: "Because there is no injunction regarding them, the mantras have no purpose [beyond recitation]."
The meaning of that mantra is "its meaning" (*tadartha*). A treatise concerning that meaning is "a treatise on its meaning" (*tadartha-śāstra*); [the word *mantra* is used] because of that.
By the term "recitation" (*abhivacanena*), the mantra-treatises are stated to have been recited from their initial commencement.
And those deities indicated by the indicative marks (*liṅga*) which are already present at the act of taking up are enjoined by the verbal statement: "He takes it up with four [verses].
Because they are specifically enjoined by the statement, it is made known that the mantras do not have their literal meaning intended.
