*Sūtra* 3.17, p. 49: Since the *iṣṭi*, *paśubandha*, and other sacrifices would naturally fall under the same original accentuation (*svarabhakti*)—consisting of the low (*mandra*), middle (*madhyama*), and high (*uttama*) pitches—the application of the primary Vedic accent might follow by way of direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*). However, according to the principle "Because of the inclusion of that [original], it should have its own property" (*tadgrahaṇāt svadharmaḥ syāt*), the injunctive statement of the performance (*prayogavacana*) is weaker because it depends on the extended application (*codaka*). Therefore, it is desired that one should adopt the accents obtained through that extended application (*codaka*). *Bhāṣya* 3.2.3, p. 811: But now, what scope will there be for the accents of various Vedas? It is said: it should be understood as being similar to the case of "because of the inclusion of that" (*tadgrahaṇāt*).

When a novel subsidiary (aṅga) belonging to another Veda is enjoined in a modified ritual (vikṛti) that is connected with the original accents, that [term] among the injunctive texts is called a mantra.
That which is designated as a mantra among those injunctive texts...
It has been deliberated whether the word *bhāva* occurring within a mantra is injunctive or not.
In that regard, what indeed is this thing called a "mantra"? Furthermore: "O Agni, protect for me the mantra which the seers know through their wisdom."
"Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus—for she is indeed the prosperity of the virtuous!"—thus the mantra is mentioned here.
What is this so-called mantra? It is said in reply:

The designation "mantra" is known among those injunctive passages (*codaka*) which enjoin that very [rite] and reveal the meaning to be performed; that is, the name "mantra" is understood in those motivating sentences.
Thus, the definition of a mantra is: being a Vedic sentence containing the essence of the meaning to be performed.
However, the general definition is: those which are called "mantras" by the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
The principle of the force of specific scriptural injunctions (*tattadvacanasāmarthya-nyāya*).

At the time of performing a ritual action, even if the specific cause for that action is no longer present, that action must still be performed by taking into account such a property (*dharma*) on the basis of the force of the specific scriptural injunction, even if it existed previously.
(Bhūti, p. 274)
Because that [quality] exists even in the Brāhmaṇas for the sake of establishing the capacity of their respective words, yet is absent in some of the mantras;
therefore, since it deviates from all of them, the word "mantra" must indeed have multiple meanings.
This being the position reached, it is replied as follows:

This would indeed be so if there were no instruction from elders (vṛddha) in this matter. For instance, in those sentences which elders employ— such as "he is studying the mantras," "he is teaching the mantras," or "the mantras exist"—
the determination of word-meaning is rooted in the authority of those who are proficient [in the tradition].

Therefore, even though there is deviation regarding the recitation of the *mantra-saṃhitā* and so forth, the established rule is that those things upon which the learned teachers employ the word "mantra" are mantras.
As it has been said: "Among those [texts] being recited in one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), those in which the word 'mantra' occurs are mantras;
for this designation is established as the definition of mantras."
(In the phrase "padaṃ sthitam," the reading in the root text is "padaṃ smṛtam. (Vākyapadīya, p. 437).
Furthermore, there is no purpose here other than the brevity of the definition and its comprehension.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "In the case of an objection (*ākṣepa*), a counter-exception (*apavāda*), that which is reached (*prāpya*), or a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇakarma*), as well as that which operates after having performed [another operation], the purpose (*prayojana*) need not be stated.
(The reading *ākṣepāpavādeṣu* appears in the root text for the first quarter.)
(Bhāṣya, p. 435) | As for the Sūtra: those sentences whose purpose is the designation of that which is being performed are so described.
The meaning is that among them, the application of the word "mantra" constitutes what is called a mantra.

This too, because it is merely common, is simply characterized by the state of being a teacher during the time of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). (Tautā. As for the *tatpuruṣa* compound [in *svādhyāyakālādhyāpaka*], it is not understood as such in its true sense. 1895.
"The rule of interpretation is: 'In the absence of a present [application], one resorts to what has occurred in the past.
(Śekhara, p. 274). An object that is performed without being fully understood in its true nature brings ruin upon the performer;
however, when performed after having been understood, it unites one with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
*Bṛhatī*, page 15: "Or rather, because the collection of those [subsidiary acts] is not enjoined.

Having cited the passage, "This [whispering] is indeed the voice of the sacrifice; therefore, whatever is prior to the *Upāṃśuyāja* is performed in a whisper," there arises a doubt as to whether this quality of whispering (*upāṃśutva*) is a property of the sacrificial portion (*yajñabhāga*) or a property of the individual ritual act (*padārtha*). [The conclusion is: Because the sacrifice possesses a fruit, [the whispering] is for the sake of the seventh case-meaning [i.e., the substratum] upon which the property rests.

Having raised the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view that—since the word *prācīna* (“eastern”) is understood to connect with the word *yajña* even though it is separated by other words in the phrase "that which is *prācīna* of the sacrifice" (*yajñasya yat prācīnam*), and since the word *prācīna*, which denotes the eastern direction, refers by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the ritual items belonging to that region—the rule regarding the eastern part pertains to the properties of the sacrifice's components—[the author] establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) as follows: because the word *prācīna* involves repetition (*vīpsā*) through its connection with the word *chandasi* (in the Veda), and because repetition is impossible in a single location as it applies to many objects, it is logical that by implication it refers to the ritual items in the eastern part of the *āmīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice]; thus, it is a property of the ritual items. To this end, in the sūtra "tadeśānām," [it is argued that] since the word *yajña* does not denote a mere collection of primary and subsidiary acts, but rather the collection of the primary act together with its subsidiaries, here the eastern part belongs to that entire collection; for it is impossible for a subsidiary alone to possess the status of being a part of the sacrifice, and thus, despite the connection with the compound *prācīnayajña*, the term refers to the whole.

Regarding the *tatpuruṣa* compound [Pāṇini 2.1.22], the fact that it is another treatise is stated here: "In the case of *khapati*, on page 150. Because the *tatpuruṣa* has predominance in the meaning of its own constituent members (*svapadārtha*), its requirement for the fourth case (*caturthī*)—which has predominance in the meaning of a different member (*anyapadārtha*)—is stronger."

Su. Pr., p. 1141: "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the first member retains its original accent] when it signifies similarity, or when it ends in a third or seventh case-ending, or is an object of comparison, or [is followed by] 'anya', or a second case-ending, or a *kṛtya* suffix" (*Pāṇini* 6.2.2).

In the *Niṣādasthapati-adhikaraṇa* (Bhāṭṭa 3.1.8), it is stated that because it would otherwise necessitate a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), the *karmadhāraya* compound is more powerful than the *tatpuruṣa*.
Maṇi, p. 149. The definition of the *tatpuruṣa* compound and an investigation into its meaning should be consulted in the *Samāsavāda* section of the *Maṇi* treatise.
Furthermore, there is another work on the principles [of grammar] titled *Tattvanyāsa*.

"Let one desiring heaven perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," and "He pours the *āghāra* libations"—thus they prescribe. In this regard, there arises a doubt: are the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra* injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)?

Having established in the *Udbhid* section that derivative (*yaugika*) words and in the *Citrā* section that conventional (*saṃvijñāyika*) words are names, [the author] now specifically raises the objection that certain derivative words are injunctions of accessory qualities and establishes their status as names.
And in that context, the very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice," is the example.

Even though the qualification-injunction (*adhikāravākya*), which consists in the connection with a result, was mentioned previously, the originative injunction was cited here merely because it is not connected to the subject matter of the discussion in the *Mādhyamikakaraṇa*, lest its purpose be rendered redundant.
Herein lies the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Let it be that words such as *udbhid* are names (*nāmadheya*) because they avoid the fault of implying possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

However, in the case of the word *agnihotra*, even according to the final view (*siddhānta*), since it can be derived from a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*)—namely, "that in which there is an oblation (*hotra*) for Agni"—it does not incur the fault of implying possessive meaning; therefore, the dative case ending itself serves as the injunction of the deity (*devatāvidhi*).

And since it is a prescription of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), in the case of the injunctions, "He offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati" and "He offers in the morning to Sūrya and to Prajāpati," because the two oblations obtained through the context are already established, and because Agni is already present in the evening oblation, this [injunction] prescribes Agni as the deity specifically for the morning oblation.

Nor should it be said that the sentence regarding the morning oblation alone is the prescriber of the accessory, while the *Agnihotra* sentence is intended merely for the originative injunction (*utpatti*).

Since in this case the adoption of multiple qualities is perceived, and because it is impossible to enjoin those qualities once the ritual action has already been established, the production of the action occurs here itself through a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), and the injunction of the qualities pertains to the *agnihotra* sentence alone.

Now, one might object: "But since even the morning oblation (*prātarhoma*) is bound to deities such as Sūrya and Prajāpati who are enjoined at its very origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), the injunction of Agni as a deity is not possible.
This is not so.

Regarding the phrase "to Sūrya and to Prajāpati," two *ca* particles are heard here. Since the conjunction of either one [of the two] would be established by a single *ca*, there is no other recourse but to conclude that the two *ca*s in the sentence for the evening oblation (*sāyahoma*) intend a mutual conjunction (*itaretara-samuccaya*). However, in this case, since a separate sentence exists that introduces Agni as a deity, the hearing of the second *ca* must indeed be for the purpose of conjoining him [Agni] with those [other deities]. Thus, the injunction of another deity is not untenable.

Alternatively, the injunction regarding Agni as the deity applies only to those *davi-homas* (libations with a ladle) that are devoid of other distant deities mentioned in the sentence, "If one were to offer with a single [ladle], one would make it deficient.

Similarly, in the passage "He pours the *āghāra*," the term *āghāra* is understood to refer to substances such as clarified butter (*ājya*) that are fit for pouring, based on the etymological derivation from the root *ā-ghṛ* (to pour).

And that [substance], being understood through the direct statement of the accusative case as "the *āghāra*" (the poured libation) to be the object of the act of pouring (*āghāraṇa-kriyā*), requires a purpose—just like the fruit associated with eating or the state of being intoxicated by drinking liquor. Furthermore, within the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is the action of the *upāṃśuyāja*, which lacks a specified substance and thus stands in need of an expectancy.

Therefore, it is enjoined for that very purpose by means of an injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) inferred through the principle of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the direct scriptural statement. As it has been said: "The connection with the refinement of the directly heard [substance] is consistent with the implication of its primary purpose."
"Otherwise, because of its connection with that, there would be a lack of coherence with the *prakṛti*.
(This is an ancient verse cited by the author of the Vārttika; Vārttika-pṛṣṭha 333).

Nor should it be argued that the prescription of the substance for the *āghāra* (libation) by the sentence [regarding the *āghāra*] is purposeless, because the *ājya* (clarified butter) is already obtained for the *upāṃśuyāja* by the very statement, "Indeed, this *ājya* is taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice.

This is because the statement, "Indeed, this is taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice," has its scope elsewhere—namely, in reference to the principal acts (*pradhāna*) which lack a specified substance—whereas this [sentence regarding the *āghāra*] refers specifically to those principal acts within the context that lack a substance; therefore, it is by this [latter sentence] alone that the substance for the *upāṃśuyāja* is prescribed.

Nor should it be argued that the direct mention of the accusative case (*dvitīyāśruti*) is contradicted in the case of single-pot offerings (*ekakapāla*) and the like, where it serves only for the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*); therefore, how can it be that by virtue of this [accusative], the clarified butter (*ājya*) and other substances serve the purpose of consecration, and how can its being a *puroḍāśa* (cake) be applicable to another function? For in those cases, because the substance is destroyed without leaving a trace (*niranvayavināśāt*), it cannot possibly be employed for another function. Here, however, since the pouring (*āghāraṇa*) consists in the non-performance of a portion of the substance, it is not illogical that the substance which has flowed out as a portion may be employed for another function.

And this is desirable: even in worldly activities such as drinking, there is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the desire for and the preservation of the substance being consumed; thus, the injunction is indeed of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the *upāṃśuyāja* itself.

This being the case, the fact that it serves to clarify what is already established, its status as a qualification for the ritual context, and its function of specifying a particular course of action follow as corollaries; therefore, it is simply an injunction of a subordinate quality.
This being the case, it is replied:

this would indeed be so if the term *agnihotra* were derived through a dative compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) according to the rule "the offering (*hotra*) for Agni is in this [rite]," namely as *agnaye hotram asmin*. However, since the possibility of genitive and locative compounds—namely *agner hotram* (the offering of Agni) and *agnau hotram* (the offering in Agni)—is also present, the ambiguous term *agnihotra* does not serve to establish Agni as the deity who is the object of the injunction.

Rather, it can be a name for the injunction of the oblation (*homa-vidhi*), taking as its basis of application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) the fact that Agni has become the deity as obtained from some other sentence; thus, for that purpose, it requires another sentence.

Furthermore, the mantra sentence "agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā," enjoined by the injunction "one offers the evening oblation with [the mantra] 'agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā'," serves to present Agni as the deity.

Therefore, taking that very definition of Agni as the basis, the term *agnihotra* is a name; thus, the oblation qualified by that name alone is what is enjoined, and not a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) elsewhere.
Now, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers this to be an injunction of a subordinate quality either in the morning oblation or in the curd-oblation (*dadhi-homa*).

First, in the case of the morning oblation (*prātarhoma*), the conclusion that Agni is the deity based on the wording of the mantra is not accepted as the final view, because it would entail the consequence of there being three deities.
Nor is it so in the *dadhi-homa* (curd-oblation), since that lacks a connection with the mantra due to its nature as a substance (*dravya*).
Therefore, how can the term *agnihotra* be established as a name (*nāmadheya*) by virtue of that scriptural injunction?
It is said in reply:

We do not say that in every case where there is what the proponent considers to be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), that [quality] is already established by something else; rather, when an injunction is uttered for a quality because of the power of its inclusion within the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*), that fire—which is already established by another scriptural source through the very sense of the direct Vedic statement—is capable of being faultlessly accepted as the ground for the application of the name. Why then abandon the direct Vedic hearing (*śruti*)?
This alone is the true meaning of the treatise on reality.

As it has been said: "Since there is another scripture here for the purpose of obtaining the qualities intended to be enjoined, therefore the attainment of those [qualities] would be redundant; thus, [the passage] is accepted as a name.
(Vākyapadīya, p. 334).
The reading in the Vārttika is "prāpi śāstra" (the scripture is reached).
For this very reason, this is not an injunction for a *homa* qualified by a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
As it has been said: "If a qualified [action] were to be enjoined, then this would be considered an alternative action."
"If they were not enjoined by another [text], then that would be the purpose," such is the reply (Vārttika, p.

Therefore, the sentence "He offers the Agnihotra" merely serves to establish the action denoted by the name; it does not, however, enjoin the morning offering, nor the offering with curds as the substance, nor does it prescribe the deity through a qualified injunction.
Nor should it be said that only the two sentences beginning with "yad agnaye ca" constitute the injunction for the oblation (*homa*);

for since they specify a qualified object of reference through the addition of unambiguous and non-redundant attributes, it is possible for them to enjoin an oblation characterized by those specific qualities.
Rather, they serve solely to enjoin the accessory (*guṇa*) by way of restating the oblations already established by the *agnihotra* sentence.

In that case as well, since it is impossible to enjoin multiple qualities regarding an action already established by another source, and because the mantra itself establishes the fire and the sun, and because the two times—evening and morning—are already established by the two sentences "He offers in the evening" and "He offers in the morning," it is *Prajāpati* alone who is enjoined as the single deity in both sentences, while everything else is merely restated (*anūdyate*).

Similarly, in the case of "He pours the *āghāra* libation," the verbal root *ā-ghṛ* (to pour) implies a substance such as milk or the like, which is suitable for pouring and whose specific nature has not yet been determined.

Therefore, the term *agnihotra*, being itself a subject of doubt, cannot—like the term *agnihotra* [in another context]—function as a provider of a specific substance for the *āghāra* offering which is subordinate to the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Furthermore, if the purpose is to specify a particular substance, then upon examining the context, a specific substance would already be obtained either by the force of the sentence, "Spreading [the grass] and sprinkling [the butter], he sacrifices with clarified butter alone," or by the statement, "Indeed, that which is the clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel is taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice. Since those two [statements] are themselves unambiguous and provide scope [for the substance], this injunction would be entirely redundant for obtaining a specific substance in the *upāṃśuyāja*. However, it is possible that the term *āghāra*—which is ambiguous regarding the deity of the *agnihotra*—does not enjoin the pouring (*āghāraṇa*) as qualified by a specific substance for the *āghāra*.

Likewise, since the substance of clarified butter (*ājya*) is already obtained by the very statement, "Having poured the *āghāra* libation of that which has become fourfold," the injunction of it would be redundant.
As it has been said: "It serves to obtain the quality intended to be enjoined."
Furthermore, because the term *āghāra* can be derived in the sense of an action (*bhāva*)—meaning "the act of pouring"—it is a name for the ritual action itself.
Therefore, even here, it is the action delimited by that [name] which is enjoined.
And that action acquires a connection with Indra as its deity through the power of the application of the mantra: "O Indra, let the sacrifice rise; he pours the *āghāra*."

Thus, being connected with the substance understood from the sentence regarding the fourfold-grasping (*caturgṛhīta*), it is determined that the name "āghāra" refers to a libation of ghee (*sarpis*) intended for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), Agni is the deity of either the morning oblation (*prātarhoma*) or the *davihoma*; according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he is not.

The Sūtra, however, states: "That which makes known the reality is the means of attaining it; by the terms *agnihotra* and *āghāra*, that which possesses the quality of being an injunction is what is meant by 'injunctive'—that is to say, if there exists another scripture, then these two [terms] must be names (*nāmadheya*) [of sacrifices]. (Tautātita).
And another treatise on the true nature [of these matters] is as follows.

Regarding the inquiry—namely, whether the words *agnihotra* in "He offers the *agnihotra*" and *āghāra* in "He pours the *āghāra*" are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)—the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
It is held that [these are names], because they are intended to be enjoined [as such]. (Mīmāṃsākośa 238)
And there is another treatise situated therein;
the logic situated therein;
the logic situated therein.
The principle established therein is as follows:
whatever quality—whether it be "handsome" (*abhirūpa*) or "consisting of clarified butter" (*ājyarūpa*)—is enjoined in the context of a ritual procedure, that quality is prescribed;
however, one might suspect that it is already known from another source.

"If [the author] intends that [Yājñavalkya] will prescribe [the deity] for all *darvī*-offerings (*darvihoma*) where no deity has been specifically mentioned, then this is for the sake of that [prescription].
This is the purpose of that [statement].
And by the rule "ātac śrauṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 3.1.106),
there is an injunction regarding the deities: "He offers in the evening to Prajāpati," because of its syntactic connection.
Likewise, that which is "placed" (ādhīyate) is called an "adhāra" (locus), meaning it is capable of containing.
What is it? It is that which makes known and establishes the quality intended to be enjoined, such as fire and so forth.
"Since this was [originally] taken four times, therefore one should take hold of the essence"—this refers to the *ādhāra* (support).
The term "substance" (*dravya*) denotes the clarified butter, water, and so forth;
and that is because of the second-case (accusative) designation.
Another scripture states:
"Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā!
And this is a prescription regarding the substance.
And that which is the experiencing of what was previously unknown is called "injunction" (vidhi).
Furthermore, since it is a state to be brought about by the action of perishing,
and because such an action is impossible without an instrument, it [requires] an effort (kṛti).

Due to their inherent connection (*samavāya*), the second case-ending denoting the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) attains grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verbal root, which characterizes the means (*sādhana*). This is because the action characterized by the agent’s effort (*kṛti*) proceeds toward its own accomplishment for the sake of the effect defined as the object to be accomplished; thus, there is no contradiction. Through the medium of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), when there is a requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is the meaning of the verbal root itself that [serves as the instrument] for the production (*utpatti*)...

Regarding *soma*: even though this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because it is connected as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of being an accessory (*upādhi*). Thus, the connection [of the two] is established through the fact that the effort is directed toward another [purpose].
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: indeed, instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) consists in being that which is pervaded by the intended injunction.
And it is possible for the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) to be so pervaded.

Furthermore, where there is another scriptural authority (*śāstra*) that grasps a quality (*guṇa*) not previously known, that too constitutes instrumentality, insofar as it is pervaded by the activity proceeding in that specific place.
Therefore, they say: "The meaning of the verbal root should be the name;
it is connected [to the result] both as the object and as the instrument."

[He] refutes that view [which holds that] "one offers the *agnihotra* and pours the *āghāra*"— namely, that the two [acts] are either the primary objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as the means (*karaṇa*) of the verbal root's meaning,
or else they are qualities (*guṇa*) and preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), or finally, they are names of rituals (*karmanāman*).

Those who maintain that [the word *hotram*] is connected with the verbal root-meaning as its object (*viṣaya*) and with the instrumental [suffix] as its instrument (*karaṇa*), as in "this is the oblation for Agni" (*agnaye hotram etat*), are refuted by this very [analysis] through the exclusion of such a connection. For if it were a name (*nāman*), there would be no [grammatical] form [to support] the quality being enjoined; thus, it is established that it is a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *-ada*.
For [the accusative] is used in the sense of being an object; as it is stated in the *Kharadadhṛti*:
"The second case ending is employed when it is said, 'He pours the Āghāra libation.'"

How is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the names of instruments and [the action]? If it is argued that in the case of "one should offer the *āghāra*" and "*agnihotra*," these two are names of actions derived etymologically (*yaugika*), and that there is coreferentiality with the word "*agnihotra*" through an instrumental sense based on its purpose (*ārthaka*); [we reply: no.

The deity is obtained from the mantra, and the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is obtained from the statement regarding the fourfold taking (*caturgṛhīta*). Since the status of being the object of accomplishment (*sādhyatva*) also exists for that purpose, even the injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is possible;
however, this is the way the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) functions here.

For if the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) were not already established, its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*)—which is characterized by being the meaning of the verbal root—could not exist without a discrepancy in form; thus, the entire presentation of the name would be untenable. Therefore, its state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*) must be expressed, and it is not at all to be doubted that this refinement (*saṃskāra*) [is what is meant]. Even if, according to that school’s view... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
Because it is an action (*kriyātva*). The status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is based on the primary sense (*aupādānika*), and not an implied disparity (*ārthika vaiṣamya*).

Bhaṭṭa: Here, whether the words are conventional (*rūḍha*) or etymological (*yaugika*), and even if they involve the possibility of [other] attainments, nevertheless, since [the action] would be inexplicable without the status of being an instrument, the injunction itself establishes the status of being the goal (*sādhyatva*).

In such passages as "He offers the Agnihotra," "He pours the Āghāra libation," and "He sacrifices with the Samidhs," since the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is untenable without something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the state of being an end (*sādhyatva*) is also implied.

Thus, the sense is that even if the words *Agnihotra* and so forth were names of rites (*karmanāmadheya*), their status as qualifiers of a substance (*guṇavidhi*) would be established through the very fact of their being enjoined (*aupādānika*). Therefore, when considering whether these are names of rites or qualifiers of substances, it is more appropriate that they be qualifiers of substances due to their well-known conventional meanings (*prasiddhi*).

Nor, moreover, is the word intended solely to express instrumentality by means of its being an object; otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because there is no plurality of things to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
In the term *agnihotra*, the status of being an object—which is presented by the subsequent scriptural injunction merely as a means—is not the actual meaning of the scripture.
By the etymological derivation "he whose offering (*hotra*) is in this [Agni]," Agni would be the deity only in a secondary sense, because the text is not primarily concerned with that.

(In the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*, it is established that [the action] is the subject matter; it is not enjoined [here], and furthermore, there would be the contingency of contradiction because [Agni] is not mentioned as part of the scriptural meaning in the passage: "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati"). Now, [if it is argued] that it is the word itself [that is the deity].

By this [statement], its [the act's] being already established is indicated; therein, having first denoted it as the object (*viṣaya*) by means of the mention of multiple qualities, he then denotes it again as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

This is because the injunction of a distinct, qualified action is necessary; otherwise, how could that which is uttered once in the ritual act enjoined by this sentence denote it twice? Or, if it were so denoted, there would be no attainment of the status of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Therefore, in cases such as the *dadhi-homa*, even though the *Āgneya* mantra is recited again, there is no restrictive rule stating that "it must be recited twice" or "it must not be recited thrice. Since it has already been recited, such a recitation is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *dadhi-homa*, and by this [recitation], only the deity is enjoined. What is the use of a veil for that which has already occurred once?
Nor is the attainment of that [result] possible through that [means], according to the principle that "that which is established by the wording of a mantra need not be further postulated.
And in that case, it has been stated that there would also be an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). This is because [of the aforementioned reason].
Or [it refers to] another distinct ritual act.

Even regarding the word *āghāra*, it has been stated that the connection with the second-case ending must be understood as being through the sense of instrument (*karaṇatva*), and not through the sense of object (*viṣayatva*).
By the word *āghāra*, the primary substance intended for the means of pouring is meant.
First, with respect to the *dhātu* (verbal root):

it is a formative action (*saṃskāra*) denoted by the root *kṣar* (to flow). It is enjoined with reference to that [flowing]. How can there be an indication by means of the accusative case for something not yet employed [as a subordinate element]? [In the phrase] "he pours the *āghāra*" (*āghāram āghārayati*), [the accusative is used] because it is suitable for being a formative action (*saṃskāra*).

It should be stated that, by means of a sentence constructed through the context (prakaraṇa)—as in the case of "he offers the Āghāra-oblation" and "he performs the Agnihotra"—[the following is established].
To this it is replied: two substances are enjoined.

"This was indeed the fourfold-drawn [oblation]; of that, there is the pouring (āghāra)—namely, the state of being something to be accomplished (sādhya) which belongs to the root-meaning (dhātvartha), for that which is not accomplished cannot function as an instrument.

By this statement, there is the presentation of a specific fourfold-drawn portion that serves as a subsidiary to the *prayāja* offerings, because otherwise its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) would be untenable.

Therefore, since both the quality to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the connection [with it] refer to a single object, the term *āghāra* in every respect refers to a substance and is not a name. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: since its possibility exists through the rule of the mantra-text (*mantravarṇa*) and the ritual injunction (*kalpavidhi*), this preceding injunction—
Because it would result in futility; and because [the word *vaiśvadeva*] can possibly apply to that which has prosperity as its culmination, first...
(of the word *vaiśvadeva*).

Since the injunction of the verbal root that brings about the ritual act is already assisted by the inclusion of the qualities previously accepted, its status as an injunction of something else is not even remotely possible.

This is because, by way of establishing the possibility of an injunction of a quality through the principle of *tat-pralaya* (the sublation of that), there is first an injunction of the deity by way of restating (*anuvāda*) the oblation already established by itself;
nor is it an injunction of a qualified action.

Or rather, [the deity] is to be understood through the accomplishment of the natural cause (*prakṛti-nimitta*), and not by means of the pure formula "Agnijyotirjyotiragniḥ svāhā" according to the principle of *tat-pratyaya* (that-connection). Page 250, (Viśva-): The attainment of the deity occurs solely through the word of the mantra that is appropriate [to it].

In the passage, "That which [is offered] to Agni and Prajāpati... having understood that the word *deva* (god), though already established [in usage], indicates a specific deity, one offers in the evening; and that which [is offered] to Sūrya and Prajāpati in the morning," here, by accepting that the word [*deva*] is a synonym for the word *sarva* (all), there is the injunction of Prajāpati alone as qualified by the conjunction of the deities belonging to both the evening and morning times, with reference to all subjects under discussion.

Having accepted that the word *deva* refers to a deity and having established the [deity-status] of the fire and other deities under discussion, for this very reason—just as the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) arises in sacrifices even from the mere indicative mark (*liṅga*) of a mantra dedicated to a single deity, so too does it arise from the syllables themselves as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Thus: "Agni, light, light; Sūrya, svāhā! etc.

In the view that [the mantra] is accepted [as applying to both], there is no contradiction; for it is prescribed: "One offers in the evening with 'Sāyam juhoti, sūryo jyotiḥ, jyotir agniḥ svāhā,' and in the morning with 'Prātaḥ juhoti, agnir jyotiḥ, jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā'.
Since the name [of the deity] is also present, it must be admitted that the application [of the mantra] occurs through the introduction [of the name].

This is because of the mixed indicative marks (*liṅga*) found in the wording of the mantra, which indicates a mixture [of deities]. Thus, even for those [mantras] containing a mixture [of names], that [application to both times] holds true.
Page 251: Nor is there [the word] *samit* in the case of *saṃjñā* as well.

Consequently, because the sentence "And that which for Agni" (*yad agnaye ca*) is established by the same logic [as the previous], the repetition [of the term] serves to indicate the deities belonging to the evening and morning [offerings]. 10) *Tanūnapāt*.
It should not be said that [the requirement] depends on the performance of the sacrifice at the times of morning and evening, because there is an absence of such dependence; rather,
it is the apprehender in the case under consideration.
Even though there is a connection of the conjunction (*samuccaya*)— brought forward by the word *ca*— with Prajāpati,
because it is established as being [merely] a prefix (*upasarga*) or the like rather than a primary suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*), it does not constitute a single injunction (*vidheya*).
And therefore:
Because it is a binding factor (bandhaka).
[Sūtra 2.2.2, p.
160] Because Agni is the deity and so forth, it is prescribed for the Agnihotra oblation; therefore, it applies to the Agnihotra oblation.
The nature of that principle is as follows: "The meaning of the sentence [in 'agnihotram juhoti'] is not that the word 'agnihotra' is a name [of the rite] due to etymological derivation;
the same applies to the āghāra [offering]. Rather, when it is possible to enjoin the meaning of the verbal root, [the word] must be enjoined as such."

Śābarabhāṣya 1.4.4: "In the Upāṃśuyāja, that which is taken is for the sake of the entire sacrifice; since the nature of the substance has already been established by the rule 'the clarified butter from the Dhruvā vessel is for all sacrifices,' the injunction for the Prayāja offerings is therefore accomplished."

Therefore, its status as a name (*nāmatva*) is accepted because it is obtained [from the context] "as it is," since if a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) were enjoined by means of a location, there would result the application of a second injunction; this is due to parsimony (*lāghava*).
(Vārttika 1.4.4, p. 334)

The term *āghāra* is a name (*nāmadheya*) by virtue of being that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*); and that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is indicated by the verbal root (*dhātu*). Now, those entities which are established through the principle of the suffix *-tavya* are indeed part of the *homa* itself.
"One pours the *āghāra* libation with [the mantra] 'indra ūrdhvo'dharaḥ'.
The constituent elements of the ritual act are indicated here in bold type according to their sequence of description,
but not by means of the deity mentioned in the wording of the mantra, as is suggested by the phrase "four times taken" (*caturgṛhīta*).
[This is done] by means of the sequence of the initial syllables of the *bindus*,
and because of the acquisition of the substance.
In this same way, it will also be explained regarding the *samidh* (sacrificial fuel) and other items.
In all cases,
there is no contradiction; for in the passage, "Then, therefore, they follow with the oblation mixed with fire," the accusative case of *agni* indicates its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*),
and thus the word is understood to refer to the sacrifice.
And there exists the *āhavanīya* altar, which is the locus for the *agnihotra*;
the principle [of application] is to be reached.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Kau. 2|3|10|21 Śaṃkara: "The name [is established] by the *tavya*-rule. (p. 65). Regarding the word *agniṣṭut*, because of the statement "They praise with verses dedicated to Agni" (*āgneyīṣu stuvate*), it follows that after the establishment of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) through the *tavya*-rule, the name—which was not present prior to that—indicates [the rite]. This is because [the rite] has as its constituent part a hymn of praise (*stotra*) to be accomplished by mantras addressed to the deity Agni.
Kau. | It is a name according to the principle of *tavya* [suffix]. 2|2|126, p. 208; 2|2|8|21, p. 250; also by means of a cause for application based on a single part.
In the *tavya*-suffix section (*tavyādhikaraṇa*), it is established that the name "Agnihotra" is valid by way of the *tavya*-suffix logic, wherein fire and the sun alone are the primary referents.
In the section concerning the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice,
the nature of the deity has already been determined.
Ku. 3|4|121; the *tavya*-rule will be explained at 1|4|14, p. 290:
"Even the ground for application [of a word] is not [the basis];
by this rule, words such as *agnihotra* are proper names (*nāmadheya*)."
The rule is that [the injunction] must be established according to the principle of *tavya* (the suffix denoting obligation).
However,

regarding the statement "He offers the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*), its status as an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) consists in its capacity to bring about the possibility of a pure injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), whether accompanied by auxiliary factors or not.

And it has been stated that [passages] such as "He offers with curd" (dadhnā juhoti) are injunctions of accessories (guṇavidhi); this is merely a point. If it is argued that they are indeed names (nāmadheya), let it be so. [Śābarabhāṣya 1.4.11.4, p. 251].

Regarding the statement "one performs the Agnihotra," although its specific form and the principles governing it are not perceived there, it has nevertheless been stated that the word *agnihotra* is a name (*nāmadheya*) according to the principle applicable therein.

[The term] *sāhasī* [is used]. 823. Because a *caturthī-tatpuruṣa* or a *upacaturthī-garbha-bahuvrīhi* is impossible [in the case of the word *agnihotra*], its possibility exists under the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*) for the obligatory rite; this has been explained there in detail regarding the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Soma. 7131. Regarding the statement "the cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*), since the deity cannot be obtained through the wording of a mantra (*mantravarṇika*), this word (*āgneya*) is not a name according to the principle established there.

Kau. 1.4.7.9, p. 230: The word *vaiśvadeva* is the name for the eight sacrifices beginning with the *āgneya* [in the first of the Cāturmāsya festivals], because of the restrictive principle (*tatra-nyāya*) arising from the difficulty of accommodating deities already enjoined by the originative injunctions (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-devatā*). Bhāṭṭa. 1.4.11: There will be a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the word *āgneya* and so forth is the name of the oblation (*homa*) as heard in the scriptural text, "He offers the fourfold portion" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*).

Having raised the objection as to how the terms *āgneya* and so forth can be names of those [offerings] even when the oblation is accomplished by means of the "four-fold recitation" (*caturavatta-vākya*), [the author replies: because the deities are obtained through the mantras applied according to their sequence, their status as names is established by that very same principle. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 448). Furthermore, since the substance and deity of the *āvāra* rite are stated there in a different grammatical case (*tatravyadhikaraṇe*), we have already explained that in that context the word *ādhāra* is understood to mean "it exists" (*vartate*) because it has "alkali" (*kṣāra*) at its head. (Page 761).

Ku. 2|3|12|20. Furthermore, the fact that the "grahaṇa" (the act of taking) is a name [for the *adābhya* and other vessels] is established because it is well-known as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the object to be taken (*grāhya*). Since it is understood from its injunction within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice to be for the purpose of refining the Soma belonging to that sacrifice, the literal meaning [of the term] is obtained there by the principle [of the *tatra-nyāya*]. Ku. 2|1|12|20, p. 63. Now, an objection is raised: since this *dākṣiṇahoma* (the offering pertaining to the sacrificial fee) is enjoined at a time subsequent to the giving of the Dakṣiṇā, the time for the Dakṣiṇā is obtained precisely through the sequence [of performance]; therefore, by the aforementioned principle, the word *dakṣiṇā* is a name [for the offering], and thus it cannot be an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). This is the doubt.

Su. Pṛ. 701: Now, since the word *dadhi* (curd) is also optional—just like the *agnihotra* and other such terms—it is established as a name (*nāmadheya*) by the principle applied there [in the case of *aindrendriyakāmasya*], because it is unfit to be an injunction for a purpose.
Pṛ. 844: By the principle applied there, the status of the term *dadhihoma* as a name is established;
and precisely because its status as a name is established by that same principle, its being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) has been stated.

*Soma*. 8|4|1. Here, the term *navarātra* is a name for the ritual (*karmanāmadheya*), according to the principle applicable therein [namely, that it denotes the sacrifice itself rather than its time].
(The *Navarātra* is to be performed in the month of Āśvina.

*Vratarāja*. The words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are names [of the sacrifices], because they are connected with the times of the full moon and the new moon as obtained from the two scriptural injunctions: "One should sacrifice on each full moon" (*paurṇamāsyā paurṇamāsyā yajeta*) and "One should sacrifice on each new moon" (*amāvāsyāyām amāvāsyā yajeta*), according to the principle applicable therein.

*Kau.* 2.3.13, p. 163: Since the term *vahiṣpavamāna* is already established by the injunction of the location in the form of the *āstāva* situated outside the *sadas*, it is a name (*nāmadheya*) there even according to the *tatravya* principle.

*ŚBh.* 1.4.13, p. 187: According to the *tatravya* principle, although the *vājina* substance is merely enjoined for the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, the deity *Vājin* is also enjoined by the explicit statement [of the text] (in the *pūrvapakṣa*).
*ŚBh.* 2.1.122, p. 258: Even the names *vaiśvadeva*, *darvihoma*, and so forth, are names according to the very same *tatravya* principle.

Page 218, 1|4|15: Since the deities such as Samit and others are already established through the wording of the *yājyā* mantras themselves—just as in the case of "he offers the *agnihotra*"—it is appropriate that they fall under the scope of that [preceding] principle; for since the deities such as Vasanta can be established by the *anumantraṇa* mantras beginning with "I gratify the season Vasanta," there is no necessity for the constant establishment of Samit and the others. Page 144, 2|1|2: By the aforementioned principle, the words *samit* and so forth function as names (*nāmadheya*).

Regarding the section beginning with *prayājādiṣviti cet* (9|2|20|58): since there is no possibility of the mantras enjoined by direct revelation (*śruti*) functioning as indicators for the presence of their own literal meaning, and because the principle [of *māntravarṇika*-deities] does not apply there due to the absence of such deities being obtained through the wording of the mantras, the status of being a name (*nāmadheya*) is untenable. *Sudhā*, p. 1309: In the section concerning the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*)—namely, "The application [of the term] would be to the quality" (8.1.8.15)—it will be stated that the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule for the set of eleven animals (*ekādaśinī*) applies to the *prājāpatya* offerings; since that [extended application] pertains to distinct sacrifices. *Sudhā*, p. 813: "The application [of the term] would be to the quality, because of the observation of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for each animal."
In the case of the animals belonging to the *ekādaśinī* (the set of eleven), there is a separate sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for each. Here, groups (*gaṇa*) of animals are intended; for example:
"In spring, one should sacrifice three spotted bulls," and "One desiring union with the waters and plants should sacrifice a white animal to Mitra and a black one to Varuṇa," and so forth.

In this case as well, having prohibited the use of three sacrificial posts by stating, "If one were to bind [the animal] to three sacrificial posts, it would place sensory power and vigor outside of him and produce an enemy for him; therefore, one should bind it to a single sacrificial post," the text prescribes one sacrificial post for the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
However, in other cases involving groups of animals, the sacrificial post is divided for each individual animal.
Thus, even in the Sautrāmaṇī, the division of sacrificial posts is established by common practice.

Likewise, in the case of groups of animals (*paśugaṇa*) and those consisting of eleven (*ekādaśina*), the differentiation of sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) for each individual animal is a common indicative mark (*liṅga*). Thus, since the term "sacrificial post for each animal" is observed, by virtue of that indicative mark, the application [of the rule] would occur in groups—that is, in groups of animals; the application of the injunction regarding the eleven animals would occur there.
And in this way, the eleven animals constitute the archetype (*prakṛti*) for groups of animals.
In that case, there would be a restriction of the *tantra* by its application, just as the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) is [restricted] by the *sūktavāka*.

Alternatively, since it is possible to introduce even a substance by means of its primary mention and subsequently present that which is to be accomplished through it, these cases as well serve as examples.
In that case, there is an injunction regarding qualities (guṇavidhi) based on those very [meanings] such as conventional usage (prasiddhi) and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no basis for the application of the word to the ritual action here;
if one were to adopt [a primary meaning] for the sake of applying it to the ritual action, there would result an extreme remoteness from the secondary sense (gauṇatā).
In that case, it is better to assume that the suffix *matup* has been elided.

For a means of proof (*sādhana*), because of its absolute invariable concomitance (*atyantavinābhāva*) with the cognition, indicates the action to be accomplished by itself even without the elision of *matup*, through a mere trace of its own form.
Furthermore: "The meaning of the *matup* suffix would arise here from the force of the sentence at the time of the utterance."
This meaning, when grasped at the time of the word, is extremely weak.

For in the case of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the word *śyena*—having abandoned its own primary meaning—indicates that which is characterized by it (the hawk) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, at the time of its own utterance, it employs its own primary meaning.

For you, on the other hand, since the meaning of the hawk is not applicable, the word would have to be employed from the very beginning with the intention of expressing similarity; thus, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) being sublated by a mere comparison (*upamā*).
It is said that the subject matter, which is not itself to be enjoined, is always praised by means of the simile of the hawk;
for it is not accepted that a thing can be praised by that very same thing.

For in sentences such as those concerning the *śyena* sacrifice, praise is not obtained from the simile "just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so does this [sacrifice]"; and thus, there must be praise for that which is being enjoined. Furthermore, if it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), then the substance *śyena* would be what is enjoined, and therefore that alone would be the object of praise.
And it is not logical for that [comparison] to be made with itself alone.
It might be argued that praise arises from the state of being a "sūtra" (aphorism) through non-difference, because of the absence of any connection with another;
just as one says, "The battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa was like that between Rāma and Rāvaṇa."

For in the world, even when there is a figurative state involving the expression of a distinction based on conditions such as [the bird's] flight-path, praise is possible; however, it would not be appropriate [as praise] if there were an actual difference.

(Considering that the *Bhāṣya* statement—"for if it were a name, [the word 'śyena'] would be literal, whereas if it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it would involve figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)"—is untenable as it stands, he explains it otherwise: But if it is a name for this sacrifice, it is straightforward because the comparison with the *śyena* bird is applicable to the substance [of the offering]. Otherwise, two meanings—the primary sense and the figurative sense—would have to be indicated, and there would be the complication of a conceptualized difference.
Furthermore, the praise of the sacrifice does not logically result in the praise of the substance dependent upon it, because the injunction of the sacrifice has not been set aside.

For while praise residing in the expressed meaning might be transferred elsewhere, here the sacrifice itself is the object of the injunction; thus, neither the substance is praised nor is it enjoined.

Moreover, since the substance is remote from the sacrifice due to indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the primary denotation of the word is that of the sacrifice itself, based on its direct syntactic connection (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the substance.

And in the injunction (*vidhi*), there would be a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding you; in the restatement (*anuvāda*), however, in the case of a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*), the elision of the suffix *matup* is possible—according to the Vārttika on Pāṇini’s sūtra "tad asyāsty asmin" which states "there is elision of *matup* after words expressing qualities"—but not after words expressing substances (*dravyavacana*).
As for the sense of "like" (*iva*), it arises by itself from the very use of the word "para" (other).

Furthermore, a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) based on the literal meaning would have to be postulated by oneself; however, the purpose [of the passage] beginning with "Just as the hawk" (*yathā vai śyenaḥ*) has already been established.
Moreover, the previously mentioned defects regarding verbal roots, nominal stems, suffixes, case-endings, and so forth, will be explained later.
In this context, the examples are exclusively conventional words (*rūḍha-śabda*) that are free from syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) and possess a designation of that [conventional meaning].
(Here, the word *tadvyapadeśa* is an imitation of the wording of the Sūtra.

In the Sūtra, by the word *tat*, the quality (*guṇa*) under discussion—defined as "that in which there is designation" (*yasmin guṇe vyapadeśaḥ*)—is indicated. Furthermore, the prefix *vi-* has the sense of "distinct" or "different.")
And therefore, from that quality which is intended to be enjoined, there is a designation—that is, a distinct mention.
5. The meaning of the Sūtra regarding *soma* is as follows: that word, such as *śyena*, in which there is a designation of that quality, should also be a name (*nāmadheya*).
For example, in the Vedic text, "One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the *śyena*," the *śyena* is heard as a quality.
Or rather, it is prescribed that his name shall be "the one in the form of a bird" as a result of that action.
The term "śyena" denotes an optional accessory belonging to the Soma sacrifice;
it does not, like the "citrā," result in a syntactical split (vākya-bheda), because it favors the primary rite when the [Soma] has been restricted.
Just as it is said, "Like a hawk," the relationship between the metaphor and the object of the metaphor is established;
therefore, because [the term] does not apply to a single entity, its application to the ritual action must be understood through secondary (gauna) usage.

5. The Bhāṭṭa [position]: In passages such as "One desiring to practice sorcery (abhicaraṇa) should sacrifice with the Śyena," since there is no sublation of the previously mentioned [reasons] and because of common usage, the words *śyena* and so forth must indeed be injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*).
An accessory based on the current Soma-sacrifice is enjoined for the sake of a result, or else a distinct qualified action [is enjoined].

Nor is it the case that, in this way, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"Just as a hawk swoops down upon its prey, even so does this [sacrifice] swoop down upon the hater"—would involve the impossibility of a thing being its own simile; for the concluding explanatory passage must be interpreted otherwise in accordance with the injunction determined by the opening statement.
"Those [movements] are like his playful gestures"—as in such examples, this would be appropriate as a figure of non-difference (*ananya*) because it conforms to non-distinction.
This being the position reached, we reply: this is not the figure *ananya*.
For if that were the case, it would follow that all these words of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) would result in the postulation of an absence of any other point of comparison (*upamāna*).

Therefore, since this is more logical, it is proper to accept that the name functions as a designation by resorting to a secondary (gauṇī) application— either through metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) or by treating it as a partial simile (*luptopamāna*)— in the case of a single word, thereby establishing its status as a name which necessitates a second injunction.

As for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), however, since its purpose is to provide the necessary accompaniment required for the metaphor, it may refer to the sacrifice being enjoined by means of a complete simile (*pūrṇopamāna*) based on proximity to that [sacrifice], even without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The purpose of the praise is not contradicted.
Thus it is established that in all cases, the status of being a name (*nāmatva*) occurs through exactly four modes.
5. Maṇḍana: "Furthermore, the word *śyena* is a name..."

Śaṅkara says: "Such is its designation. [Regarding] the phrase "and its designation," it has been stated in the section on the locus that this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) based on a comparison, as in: "Just as a hawk swoops down upon its prey, so does this [rite] performed with the Śyena swoop down excessively upon the hater whom one practices sorcery against."

*Bāla.*, p. 58: If the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) lacked the capacity to convey a meaning for their constituent parts, there would be a contradiction with the section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] beginning with "and because of the designation of that" (*atad-vyapadeśaṃ ca*).

For in that section, the status of a name (*nāmadheya*) is established by relying on a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) proven by specific sentences. [This is so] because in cases such as "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni at the new moon," since there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) when treating it as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*), it is necessary to even raise the doubt regarding the principle of "designation of that. (*Ku.*, 1.2.188).
Kau. 1.4.79: The word *tat* [is used].
The two words *yat* and *tat* function as the indicator (*uddeśya*) and the referent (*pratinirdeśaka*).
Vā. 6.3.16: The word *tat* refers back to what has preceded it.

Bhaṭṭa (on PMS 4.1.10): The relative pronoun *yat* necessarily requires the referent of the demonstrative pronoun *tat* presented within its own sentence, as seen in such cases as "one should offer the Jaya oblations in that rite which one desires. Such is the linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) by implication;
however, the demonstrative *tat* does not likewise require the relative *yat*.
Consequently, there is no rule that the demonstrative *tat* must refer exclusively to what is presented within its own sentence.

*Kau.* 3.3.14, p. 358: "The repetition [of the word] is for the sake of a subordinate quality due to proximity" (2.3.16). In this context, since the possibility of the action [of placing bricks] being enjoined has been excluded by the rule "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), the injunction regarding the sacrifice is found in the Soma-sentence.

*Su.* p. 790: Although other authors of commentaries have stated that even in the absence of results and so forth, there is a distinction [between acts] because they constitute a different context (*prakaraṇāntaratva*), we do not see such statements as "due to proximity, because of the lack of separation in its vicinity," or "the repetition is for the sake of a subordinate quality due to proximity."
Vā. 2|3|13|16. "When there is contact with that [object], the arising of cognition in the person through the sense organs is true perception" (Sūtra 1.1.4).

That which is called this "cognition" (*vijñāna*)—the cognition produced in the person by the sense organs when they are in contact with their respective objects—that is true perception (*sat-pratyakṣa*).
For example, the cognition "this."
As for that cognition which, during contact with one thing—such as a mother-of-pearl shell—is said to grasp another object, namely silver: that is not perception.
What then? It is merely memory.
But how is it determined that "this [cognition] occurs during contact with one thing" and "this does not occur during contact with another"?
For the mother-of-pearl is indeed in contact [with the sense organ];
therefore, this cognition also has the mother-of-pearl as its object, since one designates the mother-of-pearl itself as "silver.
This is because, when the eye is in contact with the mother-of-pearl, one thinks, "My eye is in proximity to silver."
(Tatprayoge—regarding the application of that; there is a difference in the reading based on different opinions, such as *satsaṃprayoge* or *sat pratyakṣam-tat pratyakṣam*).

*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 46. By the principle stated in *Tatsaṃyogāt ṛtudharmāḥ* (2.3.10.23), since the meaning of the root *cinoti* (to pile/build) consists solely in its proximity [to the fire], [the word] "Agni" denotes the sacrifice (*yāga*) called by that name, because of its connection with the fire consecrated by the act of piling (*cayana*). This is the literal meaning of the words of the Nyāya-sūtra.
*Saṃkalpa*.
And because it belongs to that same series;

furthermore, since there is a figurative praise (saṃstava) based on the distribution of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) performed at the fourth [pressing], it should be understood as being figuratively applied.
This is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
Su. Pṛ. 1544: The principle is that "by virtue of its similarity to that, the others possess the same nature.
[The designation] is based on that terminology due to association, as in the case of the *audumbara* tree.

The principle is that "that which is the locus of the accomplishment of something receives its designation through association with it. This principle is clearly evident in such expressions as "Bring in the spears" (*kuntān praveśaya*) and "Bring in the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*).

Because of their association with the spear-staff (*kunta-yaṣṭi*), the term [“thousand”] is applied by metaphorical designation (*tācchabdyam*) to the spear-staffs themselves; enough of this. (Sāhasrī 487). Its accomplishment (*tatsiddhiḥ*) is the accomplishment of the task (*kāryasiddhiḥ*).

The *prastara* (grass-bundle) is more important than the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) for the accomplishment of the ritual task; [this is expressed by] the aphorism itself or a portion thereof: "Its accomplishment" (*tatsiddhiḥ*), Śābarabhāṣya 1.4.18.
"Its accomplishment" means the accomplishment of the primary [agent], that is, the performance of its function—meaning, the performance of that specific task.
Soma. Its establishment [is as follows]: therefore, in some cases, the purposelessness of a word is the cause for its application.

In the statement "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), the quality of being a means to the sacrifice is the attribute of the sacrificer, and since that [quality] exists in the sacrificial grass-bundle, the word "sacrificer" is applied to the grass-bundle. (Vi. 1.4.18)

(Symbol) *Tatsiddhiḥ*. "The genus (*jāti*), coexistence (*sāhacarya*), context (*prasaṅga*), acceptance (*abhyupagama*), proximity (*sannidhi*), mark (*liṅga*), and inherence (*samavāya*)—these are called the indicators of qualities (*guṇākhyāḥ*). This is indeed a single aphorism (*sūtra*).
Regarding its interpretation and application, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) provides the presentation of each [indicator] in the nominative case.
Thus it is stated in the *Kaustubha* and other works.
In that context, "the establishment of that" (*tatsiddhi*) is the first member [of the syllogism].
It is heard in scripture: "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) and "The sacrificer is the single-pot-sherd offering" (*yajamāna ekakapālaḥ*).
In the inquiry as to whether this is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:
"Its accomplishment" (*tatsiddhiḥ*) means the accomplishment of that quality of the sacrificer—namely, his being the instrument of the sacrifice—by means of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*).
This occurs through the mediation of the *juhū* ladle and other implements.

Thus, the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is applied to the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*), by virtue of the quality of being a means for accomplishing the sacrifice.

In that context, there is praise of the sacrificial grass-bundle by way of its being the sacrificer; therefore, this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In this way, the praise of the "single potsherd" (ekakapāla) is to be understood.
Here, the quality consists in the form of praise. One ground for the figurative mode of expression (gauṇī vṛtti) has been stated.
Ke.
(Symbol) The section concerning that accomplishment:
the praise of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) and so forth by means of the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*).
The establishment of that [point].
The Bhāṣya states: "The sacrificer is the *prastara* (grass-bundle)," "The sacrificer is the *ekakapāla* (single-pot-sherd cake)," and so forth, is recited in the scripture.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the statement "the sacrificer is the *prastara*" an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), or should it be considered an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)?
Likewise, regarding the statement "the sacrificer [is] the cake on one potsherd," what is initially understood is that this is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi).
What would be the result of this? In this way, it would enjoin a previously unknown matter;
otherwise, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) would be purposeless.
It may be so; moreover, it is logical that [the passage] possesses a purposeful meaning. Therefore, it is an injunction (vidhi).
This is not so;

for if it were an injunction, the sacrificer would be restricted to the function of the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara), or the sacrificial grass-bundle would be restricted to the function of the sacrificer.
Regarding the injunction, "He places the *juhū* on the *prastara*, or all the *sruks*," this would mean that either the *juhū* or all the *sruks* should be placed on the *prastara*.

If that were the case, it would be impossible for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) to perform his duties, because the Brahman and the sacrificer sit to the south while the ritual action is being performed.
Furthermore, the *prastara* itself cannot perform the duties of the sacrificer.
Likewise, if the sacrificer were to be employed in the function of the single-potsherd cake (*ekakapāla*), it would have to be offered entirely;
in that case, there would be a total abandonment of the entire ritual system (*sarvatantra*).
Furthermore, the single-potsherd cake is not capable of performing the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
Therefore, it is not an injunction.
What then? It is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*); for the sacrificer is already known, and the *prastara* and the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) are also already known.
But how is their grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) understood?

For neither is the *prastara* (grass-bundle) or the single-potsherd (*ekakapāla*) the sacrificer, nor is the sacrificial cake prepared on the single potsherd the sacrificer, nor is it the first handful of *kuśa* grass that has been cut.
How, then, can a word denoting another entity refer to the *prastara*,
and for what purpose is the mention of the sacrificer made?
It is said:
he is mentioned as being known in order to praise him.
The *prastara* (grass-bundle) is to be placed above the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), because it represents the sacrificer.
Likewise, the sacrificer is to be made into a single-pot-sherd offering entirely consumed by fire; the Āhavanīya fire becomes his garlanded head when established therein.
How then does the word "prastara" (grass-bundle) function?
It is a figurative expression (guṇavāda).
The designation arises solely from the quality.
How can that which does not denote a quality express a quality? We reply: by denoting its own primary meaning.
All of these [words] are indeed secondary (gauṇa).

Words do not function with respect to their own primary meanings when applied to secondary qualities (guṇa), for in that case there would be the abandonment of what is well-known and the assumption of what is unknown. Moreover, even a companion who is sometimes afflicted by disease does not thereby become a lion simply because he is the son of a lion; he remains a lion [only in name].
Furthermore, a term denoting a whole cannot properly apply to a part.
In all established doctrines regarding the sacrificer, the logical principle remains fixed that the word denotes him [as a whole]. This should be understood as a refutation of the opposing view.
Nor does it function as a conceptual construction when [the object] is already established, because conceptualization would then be impossible.
If it is asked, "How then does it produce a cognition through the expression of its own meaning?
[The answer is: "Through its connection with the object."

When "lion" is determined [as the meaning], it is understood that the word functions as a cause for cognition because, in that context, it generally brings about the idea of a stone-thrower; this is due to the power of the cognition of the object.
For one who thinks, "I shall cause the cognition of a stone-thrower," if he utters the word "lion," his desired goal is accomplished.
Since the meaning of "lion" is cognized as being connected to a stone-thrower, it causes the other meaning to be understood through that association.
Thus, by means of the expression of its own meaning,
there is the section on the establishment of that;
the section on the establishment of that.
In those cases, a connection with a quality is perceived.

But here, in the statements "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) and "the sacrificer is the single-pot-sherd" (*yajamāna ekakapālaḥ*), what kind of connection with a quality is perceived? It is the connection as that which effects its accomplishment.
For everyone effects the accomplishment of their own purpose.
Furthermore, anyone else who accomplishes his task comes to occupy the same place in the heart as he does, just like the royal record-keeper (*paṭṭigaṇaka*).
The record-keeper carries out the king's business;
therefore, when the word "king" is uttered, he is understood [to be included].

In the same way here as well, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the *ekakapāla* (single-pot-sherd cake) accomplish what is to be done for the sacrificer; when those two are understood, they are understood as being the sacrificer.

Therefore, those two are indicated by the word "sacrificer. How could they [be so indicated] if they were not heard [in that sense] during the placing of the *barhis* grass and the complete offering (*sarvahoma*)?
Consequently, such passages are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), not actual injunctions (*viṣaya*).
Or rather—its establishment [is as follows].
Since the discussion of *arthavāda* was underway, the definition of the injunctions (*vidhi*) consisting of qualities (*guṇavāda*) that assist it was not stated there; it is now being stated.

Furthermore, the grounds for those [injunctions] were already explained there by the sūtras "on account of form" (*rūpāt*), "on account of majority" (*prāyāt*), and "on account of distance and abundance" (*dūrabhūyastvāt*) [Jaiminisūtra 1.2.1.11–12].
The truth has been stated, but not as a definition.
How then? That which was established here has been applied there for the sake of conventional usage regarding the subject matter of illustrative explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Here, however, the definition of all the functions of the qualities (*guṇavṛtti*) is being stated.

Furthermore, other secondary causes such as association, location, and so forth, which are employed by followers of Akṣapāda, have not been mentioned [in this system] (one should refer to the note in *Nyāyadarśana* 2.1.60 regarding "causes for figurative application").
Yet, such usage is observed in the world, as in: "Bring in the staffs," "The platforms are crying out," and "Such-and-such a king was defeated by the number of horses.
These [secondary causes] ought to be included [among the grounds for metaphorical designation].

Some maintain that [the properties] are subsumed solely through the inherence in the indicative mark (*liṅgasamavāya*). Here, there arises the cognition of the staff-bearer, the umbrella-bearer, and so forth, even though they are not inherent in the umbrella itself. Alternatively, it is the basis for figurative usage (*gauṇī vṛtti*) that is being stated here, not indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, is there also a distinction between these two (indication and secondary usage)? Certainly there is.
Why? "Indication is said to be the application [of a word] to that which is invariably connected with its primary meaning;
whereas here, secondary usage consists in the connection of the function [of the word] with qualities."

In this regard, just as a word denoting a form indicates the individual entity associated with it, so too words such as "staff" or "platform" have as their referent the person connected to them. However, in the expression "the boy is fire," the boy is not understood through an inherent inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); rather, because the word's primary meaning—such as "possessing heat"—is intended, that which is perceived is the quality of being tawny (*paiṅgalya*) and so forth. Through that [quality], the cognition of the boy arises by way of similarity (*sādṛśya*).

And in all cases, the application of words such as "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) and so forth is precisely like that of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the *yaṣṭī* (staff); thus these have been cited as examples. Here too, due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there are only three possible positions: first, that one of the two terms is a name (*nāmadheya*); second, that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) because the other options are untenable—due to the absence of a basis [for the former], the impossibility of assuming multiple potencies, and the fact that the purpose is served through the indication of a ritual action (*kāryalakṣaṇā*); or third, that it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) because the other is impossible due to incapacity.
Among these, the proponent of the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhivādī*) holds the following view:
No praise whatsoever is perceived through the mutual association of the grass-bundle and the sacrificer;
nor does a word for one thing function with reference to another even for the sake of praise; nor is there any ground for its application.
Furthermore, for one who is already engaged [in a primary action], there can be no other purpose than that characterized by the function [of the primary].
Therefore, as in the case of "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu," one or the other must be characterized by the function.

In that regard, according to the principle "The primary [sense] indeed [prevails] because of the prior injunction" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.1.12–13), the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) functions in its own primary sense, while the word *prastara* (the sacrificial grass-bundle) serves to characterize the function of holding the *juhū* ladle and so forth; thus, this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
To this it is replied:
"First of all, even for a single entity, connection with [multiple] effects is not tenable;
because of contradiction, there is no injunction for both the sacrificer and the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), etc."

Regarding the statement, "He offers the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*, like the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*)," if it were applied while the sacrificer is being offered [into the fire], there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the entire ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Therefore, the purpose of the scriptural mention of the offering (*homa*) is to establish that the *sūktavāka* functions as a subsequent means (*uttarasādhana*) through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
But how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) here with another word, or what is the form of the praise?

For the sacrificer is the one for whom all things are intended; since the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) exists for his sake, the *prastara* bundle must be placed upon it. Furthermore, when the *āhavanīya* fire is praised as heaven, the entire sacrificer is thereby metaphorically placed within it. The praise [of the cake] as being "on a single potsherd" and "unbroken" is figurative.
