As for the question in the Bhāṣya, "How can that which does not denote a quality [express a quality]?", this is a question posed by one who assumes that the word possesses direct denotative power (*vācakatva*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: all linguistic functions (*śabdapravṛtti*) do not abandon their own primary meanings (*ajahatsvārthāḥ*). This is because, when it is possible to proceed according to a prior capacity (*pūrvaśakti*), there is no evidence for postulating a further capacity (*śaktyantara*). In that case, the cognition of Devadatta arises from the cognition of the delimiting property (*avacchedakadharma*)—namely, being the agent who fashions the stone exactly as prescribed and obtained; thus, the prior capacity serves as the cause. Therefore, one must not resort to abandoning a well-known [capacity] and postulating an unknown one on the grounds of causing doubt, which would result in the cessation of linguistic usage (*vyavahāroccheda*).

However, the view of others is as follows: indeed, all words such as "lion" (siṃha) and so forth denote a collection of genus, quality, and action. Since these [qualities and actions] exist in their entirety in the actual lion, they are applied metaphorically to Devadatta and others due to the presence of only a few qualities and actions.
To this, it is replied:
If a word denotes a collection, there can be no comprehension of it in a single part;
this is the section [establishing] that the word "hundred" [denotes the whole], and not [just] five.
The locus for the establishment of that [universal] is understood through the form of the sixfold [classification].
However, usage occurs even with respect to a mere genus (*jāti*) when its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), qualities (*guṇa*), and perceptibility are most evident.
This [word] is primarily denotative of that very [universal], and is not figurative—as in the case of the word "lion" applied to Devadatta and others.
Furthermore, its status as denoting a universal, which was established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, would be contradicted [if it were figurative].
Moreover, because actions and qualities are infinite, it is impossible to experience a relationship [between the word and the object] for every individual instance.
Furthermore, within a single individual, qualities and actions such as childhood and so forth are distinct at each stage;
they cannot be denoted by a single term because of their lack of identity.
Nor can a universal be postulated on the basis of what is not a universal, since some [qualities] may exist in some degree even among different classes of things.

"In that case, it would be 'lionhood' itself that serves as the delimiter in this [expression]. Yet, since that is not explicitly stated, and because it has been stated in this manner, it denotes something else.
For lionhood, when not explicitly stated, cannot serve as the delimiter of qualities and actions, because it is not perceived."

If it is argued that [the word] indeed conveys [the meaning] because there is an understanding of all its qualities and functions due to the connection with the power of denotation (*abhidhānaśakti*), then figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) is impossible for parts of a whole.
However, some say: "The figurative is that whose existence is superimposed."

His view is this: a word denoting another object (*paraśabda*) cannot apply to something else without a genus (*jāti*) serving as its own basis, nor without the mediation of an action or quality that is otherwise absolutely inexpressible.
Furthermore, if the word "lion" does not apply [to Devadatta], the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Devadatta is a lion" would not be possible.
How then [is it possible]? It is by superimposing an interval upon the object; that is, it is established through superimposition (*āropa*).
Having reached the object to be expressed, words proceed of their own accord;
for, by observing qualities such as the performance of actions associated with lions and the like, Devadatta and others attain a state of similarity through the conceptualization of totality.
Consequently, the word is employed in its very own primary sense.
And by this much, there is no loss of primacy for the object, because it is superimposed.
However, where that very object is not superimposed, there it is primary; thus, there is no fault. To this, it is said:

No, because such a conceptualization is impossible. For it is said: "How could an entity that exists with an unmixed nature be superimposed as having the nature of another entity for the sake of verbal designation by those who are free from error?"

When, first of all, another [person] superimposes water upon a mirage and employs a word [for it], then, because the cognition of water occurs in both [the speaker and the listener] by way of establishing the primary meaning, it is "primary through delusion" (*bhrāntimukhya*).

[The compound *bhrāntimukhya* is a *madhyamapadalopa* compound—meaning "one whose middle term has been elided"—like *śākapārthiva*, analyzed as: "that which is primary (*mukhya*) by means of delusion (*bhrāntyā*) is 'primary through delusion'. (Su., p. 501).

Furthermore, even if the speaker, being discerning (*vivekī*), employs [the word] for the sake of another horse, and the listener does not discern [the distinction]—(here, although both the Ānandāśrama and Caukhambā editions read *itaravacanārthe*, nevertheless, based on the clarity of the *Sudhā* commentary which reads *śrotṛpratāraṇāya* and *śrotṛjanārthenaiva*, the reading *itaravaśvanāthe* is determined)—nevertheless, because there is no superimposition (*adhyāropa*) due to the discernment of one [the speaker], while there is superimposition (*adhyāsa*) due to the delusion (*bhrānti*) of the other [the listener]—(here, in the Ānandāśrama edition it is printed as *itarasyānyādhyasānāt*, and in the Caukhambā edition as *itarasya anyādhyasānāt*, without applying the sandhi).

Nevertheless, because the *Sudhā* (the commentary on the *Vākyapadīya*) states in its subsequent section, "Now, even if both [the speaker and the listener] are mistaken, or even in the absence of superimposition (*āropa*), the use of a word for one thing in reference to another is possible through error or for the sake of deception," it is determined that in the reading of the *Vārttika*, "because the other is determined through error" (*itarasya bhrāntyā adhyavasānāt*), there is not even a slight justification for secondary metaphor (*gauṇa*).
However, when both are mistaken, then because both determine the object based on a cause such as similarity, there is an absence of superimposition (*āropābhāva*).

The meaning is as follows: similarity—whether included by the word "ādi" (and so forth) or being the cause of similarity—is the quality-conjunction (*guṇayoga*) which serves as the *nimitta* (grounding cause) for a certain object [namely, the object of the suffix *-vat*]. Because this [quality] is determined (*adhyavasāna*) as the cause for the application of a word denoting another [object] to that [other object], the postulation of superimposition (*āropa*) is not tenable. (Su., p. 501) For instance: "Both perceive the distinctness of the lion and the man;
therefore, the capacity to superimpose [one upon the other] does not exist even for one of them."

For just as there can be no superimposition based on recollection regarding objects that have not been perceived—such as bitter or sweet tastes—because they lack any mode of cognition whatsoever, so too, discriminative knowledge is not possible for things that are similar.

Indeed, no cognition other than the determination of the object itself can serve as a basis for practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore: "When even the word [itself] does not function as the cause..."
How could the intellect (*buddhi*), being weak [and] transparent, be without an object there?
Furthermore, it was stated in the *Śrutiparīkṣā* that "the intellect does not arise for the Arhat as experiencing merely the form of a self.
Moreover, "first, the previously experienced object is remembered from the word."
Therefore, once the primary meaning has been understood, there will be a superimposition [of the secondary].
In every respect, this distinction between the primary and the secondary functions to determine the specific meaning for the listeners.

And at the time of the word, when the application of the word's own primary sense has not yet been superimposed—just as in the case of determining the word "lion" and so forth—they postulate its secondary nature because the coreferentiality with words such as "Devadatta" would otherwise be untenable.

Regarding that locus of establishment, in that very locus of their establishment, their state of being lions occurs as being essentially identical to the form of the lion itself; from this, there arises the cognition of similarity and so forth.

For those investigating whether that [cognition] arises from the word or from the object, the determination that it arises from the object is produced through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.
How so? "Indeed, even when the word 'lion' has not been uttered, [the cognition] arises because the object 'lion' is present;
but it does not arise for us when the object is absent, even though the word 'lion' is heard."

And when the listeners themselves have no superimposition [of the qualities], then it must be said that they do not form such a conceptualization as, "This simianity has been superimposed as something deficient. How then? [The speaker thinks: "A collection of various actions and qualities invariably concomitant with lionhood is intended by me; however, out of fear of being tedious, I do not express it through its own specific designations. And since there is no single word that denotes this entire collection, how could the listener, failing to grasp it, derive the meaning from the term "lionhood"? Therefore, that [collection] is first expressed [by the word].
For human linguistic usage proceeds by relying on the power of words (*śabdaśakti*), and it does not involve the production of some other capacity for perception.
Furthermore: "If a figurative function (*gauṇī vṛtti*) is postulated for this [word] by a speaker, how could such a function exist in the Veda without someone to superimpose [the meaning]?"
Therefore, the definition that "the secondary (gauṇa) is that whose purpose is the application of a quality" is the only logical one, and not otherwise.

Since here [in this context] the application of a word is considered secondary precisely because it is caused by a connection with a quality, that [word] is secondary whose purpose—that is, the cause for its application—is the connection with qualities belonging to the primary object in another sense.
By the etymology "that by which something is employed," the word *prayojana* expresses the cause.

But if this were so, it would follow that there could be no figurative application (*gauṇayoga*) for things such as "sky-flowers," because they lack qualities that are invariably concomitant with their own referents (and thus such usage would be impossible).

Furthermore, in the negation of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by the Sāṃkhyas and others, Buddhists and others would be unable to employ such terms without resorting to superimposition (*adhyāropa*).

For if [the object] is not admitted [by the opponent], the negation is purposeless; if it is admitted, there is a contradiction [with one's own tenets]. However, in the case of negating what is merely superimposed, there is no fault.
This is what is intended here:
likewise, this fault remains.
Why? "How can the state of being a sky-flower be superimposed upon a non-existent thing?"
"Or would that which possesses known qualities and existence be superimposed, or not?
(The analysis of the compound is: "that whose qualities and existence are known.

Because there are such usages as "the sky-flower is its own self" and "the sky-flower is the established doctrine," therein, which other sky-flower have you determined to be like a lion, such that it might be superimposed? Therefore, the very nature of the sky-flower is [itself] of the nature of superimposition. (Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s *Kośa* 240)
This must be accepted.
Furthermore, there is no perception of this [term] as being figurative in common worldly usage, because it possesses a distinct meaning from "friend" (*sakhi*).
For the essential nature of things such as "sky-flowers," being perceived first, does not depart from its primary status.
If it is asked how that which is non-existent can possess primacy, this is equally true in the case of secondary (gauṇa) usage as well.
For that upon which something is superimposed is the secondary [subject], not that which is superimposed.
And since a sky-flower is being superimposed, and there is no other object [to serve as its locus], it is either superimposed upon itself.

In this regard, it might be argued that the form of an existing jar or the like is superimposed there—(that is, the existent nature of an existing jar or the like is superimposed there upon a sky-flower or the like)—and thus it is not a figurative usage (*gauṇatva*). This is incorrect, because in the case of a sky-flower or the like, there is no perception of an existent nature. For necessarily, whatever an object was experienced to be at the time of its connection [with a cognition], it must be apprehended as being exactly like that at the time of its utterance.

Furthermore, the object such as a rabbit’s horn has never been previously experienced as existing; nor is a relation perceived between a rabbit’s horn and other things, such as flowers, when those other things are not apprehended.

For those two—the rabbit and the horn—whose relationship as real entities has never been experienced, there can be no figurative application (*gauṇatva*), because they are understood in their primary nature.
How then is it said that "a rabbit’s horn does not exist"? [For] since that which has not been perceived as existing is not even presented [to the mind], its negation is not tenable.
If it exists as a real entity (*sadpadārtha*), it has not been previously perceived.
Or, if its existence as a real entity is not perceived, how can an absolute negation be established?
For it is said: "An object whose existence is known elsewhere is what is excluded elsewhere."
But it is not the case that existence and non-existence are perceived in one and the same place.

If it is argued that "it is superimposed by that very [means]—[that is, for the reason that existence and non-existence are contradictory in this object, for that very reason existence is superimposed]"—no;
for superimposition likewise depends precisely upon the existence [of the locus] in another location.
Nor can there be a superimposition of one thing upon another by virtue of the existence of that other, because of the lack of a connection.

If it is asked, "How then can the form of water be superimposed upon a patch of saline soil? the answer is that this case is dissimilar because of the cognition of the actual existence of water in another location.

How, then, is the expression "the horn of a hare does not exist" employed? Some say that once non-existence has already been understood, the word "does not exist" is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*). [According to others, since non-existence is understood through the word "hare's horn" itself, the employment of the word "does not exist" is redundant.]

Alternatively, the word "non-existent" (*nāsti*), which generally applies to antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like, is qualified by the term "hare's horn," rather than the hare's horn being qualified [by non-existence], because there is no deviation [in this usage]; thus, there is no fault. Or else, for one who has grasped the two members [of the compound] and for whom a recollection of the genitive sense has arisen through general observation—just as in the case of *rājapuruṣa* and similar compounds—but who has never previously determined that a hare is devoid of horns, it is this application of their connection that is precluded.
(The meaning of "there is no rabbit's horn" is that there is no connection between the rabbit and a horn.

According to our own view, since the word "non-existent" (*nāsti*) functions as the meaning of the compound, its status as a referent is indicated by being manifested [by the compound]. Alternatively, even without a compound, the rabbit is specified as the locus and the horn as belonging to a cow or similar animal; without any superimposition, it is stated that "there is no connection between the two. By that very fact, for a person who has experienced the [usual] relationship [between horns and animals], the word "rabbit's horn" will convey that very absence (and thus the use of the word "non-existent" is for this purpose).

Because the present tense suffix *laṭ* in the rule "when a verb denoting action is used as a subordinate element for the sake of another action" (*kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*) is conditioned by the presence of a subordinate action intended for the sake of another action, the sense of "for this purpose" is obtained from the form "he will cause to go" (*gamayiṣyati*).
(Sukhabodha, p. 510).

Alternatively, the downward accumulation of the particles of earth existing within the hare’s swoon—which are piled one upon another and transformed into a specific solid mass—is the state [of that mass] without the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of this sentence ("the hare’s horn does not exist").

In the case of the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, an injunction (*vidhi*) is not heard; nor can one be inferred—unlike in cases such as "he who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu"—on the grounds that no other alternative is possible. This is because an alternative is indeed possible through its being an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), as in the passages: "He places the *prastara* above the *barhis*" and "He makes the cake on one potsherd entirely offered. Such being the case, since the purpose is fulfilled by means of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), there will be no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Nor should it be argued: "How can a word denoting another [entity] (*paraśabda*) be applied to something else without a ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)?
For the connection with a quality (*guṇayoga*) itself serves as the ground for its application.
[Objection: But was it not stated that there is no common quality whatsoever denoted by the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*)?
True.

Through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a word causes its own denoted meaning to produce a cognition of another object that is not even present [in the primary sense], just as the word "Ganges" [produces the cognition of] the bank which is connected to its own meaning.

The figurative (*gauṇa*) [use], however, produces another object solely through the connection with qualities (*guṇa*) indicated by the relationship between the denoted meaning and [that other object], as in "The boy is fire."

As it has been said: "Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is stated when there is a cognition of that which is invariably connected with the denoted object (*abhidheya*). Furthermore, since the word is understood as having a collective referent (*samudāyaviṣayatva*) by virtue of its collective substratum (*samudāyadhāra*), and since the collective is common to both sentient (*prāṇabhṛt*) and insentient (*aprāṇabhṛt*) beings, even if the word *prāṇabhṛt* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*), there is no abandonment of its own primary meaning (*svārtha*).
In this way, since *suṣida* also has a collective (*samudāya*) as its object, there is indeed an abandonment of its own primary meaning.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, if the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) holds, the inclusion [of the term] must be made by way of the well-known meaning of *suṣida*; if it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is by way of the sense of "the vital breath of one who is well-seated" (*suṣida-suṣida-prāṇabhṛt*).
Thus, regarding *tatsiddha* and the others, the purpose stated for the prima facie view should be inferred accordingly.
This has been stated in the Sūtra: "On account of the connection with the indicative marks" (*liṅgasamavāyāt*).
The meaning is that, because of the connection with the indicative marks of both living beings and non-living beings, it refers to the aggregate as a whole.
By this very Sūtra, [the term] *tatsiddhi* [is established], since words such as *aṣṭakapāla* have their application based on a quality (*guṇapravṛttinimittaka*).

Kau. | 4|1|4| 24 pṛ. 280. ⚴ This term *tatsiddhipeṭikā* refers to a specific technical meaning. A single sūtra (1|4|23), which reads: "The bases for qualities (*guṇāśrayāḥ*) are: accomplishment of that (*tatsiddhi*), genus (*jāti*), similarity (*sārūpya*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), majority (*bhūman*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and inherence (*samavāya*)," is called *tatsiddhipeṭikā*.

In this regard, having performed a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules), the six causes of secondary application (*gauṇavṛtti*) are stated across six topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*); thus, it is called a "box" (*peṭikā*). Ke.:
By means of demonstrating the causes of secondary application, the definition of secondary application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) is expressed by this sūtra (*tatsiddhi-*).
Kau.

Page 268, Sūtra 1.4.132: This sūtra (*tatsiddhi-sūtra*) is intended to raise an objection to and resolve the issue regarding the figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*) established in the *Vaiśvānara-adhikaraṇa*.

Since the figurative sense (*gauṇa*) was established in the *tatsiddhi-sūtra*, and its various causes as well as its nature of functioning through the abandonment of its own primary meaning were explained therein, this discussion [in Sūtras 3.2.1–2] must be understood as having preceded it. Vārttika 3.2.1, page 746: Because, in the *tatsiddhi-sūtra*, it will be stated that both indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and figurative usage (*gauṇa*) are preceded by the power of another meaning.
Kau. | 1|3|84, p. 110. One should observe nine secondary (gauṇa) interpretations along with those stated in the *Tatsiddhi* sūtra.
(The secondary function [gauṇīvṛtti] is to be seen under the word *iti*).
Or, in that context, by implication, the measure of the agent is 1920; in that regard, names such as "utpatti" (origin), "iva-bhakta" (as if divided), and so forth, come into being.
For those [priests] are prescribed by their very origin;
therefore, they are not causes for a division of the ritual action into separate parts.
Consequently, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that sixteen priests are to be chosen according to the requirements of the purpose.

On this point, the *Sudhā* [commentary] states: "The distinction of titles such as 'Adhvaryu' and so forth is not caused by a difference in the ritual acts, such as those of the Adhvaryu; for that distinction of titles is traditionally taught (āmnāta) at the time of the initiation (*varaṇa*), which serves to designate the performer during the original injunction (*utpatti*). Such is the meaning of the sūtra.

Furthermore, [the author] says "sudhā": Even though there is a repeated choosing (*varaṇa*) of a single person, because there is no difference in the act of choosing—since the rule "he chooses the priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*) is an originative injunction for the choosing (*varaṇotpattividhi*)—there can be no conjunction (*samuccaya*) of those to be chosen who are prescribed by the sentences regarding the Adhvaryu and others within a single act of choosing. Moreover, the plural number in the word "priests" (*ṛtvijaḥ*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) as a qualification of the object to be enjoined (*uddeśyaviśeṣaṇa*). And since, by the logic of "presumption based on the impossibility otherwise" (*kalpanānyathānupapatti*), the priests are like the *camasādhvaryus* (who are not included among the primary priests), they lack the status of being an unintended qualification of the object to be enjoined; thus, the words "Adhvaryu" and so forth designate distinct individuals, and therefore, because each is the basis for a specific function, they designate different persons. Alternatively, if there were no designation of different persons, then a single individual would have to perform everything that is to be done.
In that case, you [should hold] the subsidiary parts of the sacrifice, because there is no distinction among all [of them];
likewise, the *apūrva*.
In this regard, [the result follows] from all [desires], because there is no distinction.

Regarding the statement that the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices fulfill all desires—namely, "The Darśapūrṇamāsa for all [desires]" and "The Jyotiṣṭoma for all [desires]"—there arises an inquiry as to whether these results accrue from a single performance or by way of succession. This is the sūtra presenting the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view:
in that case, when the rites known as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Jyotiṣṭoma are performed once, all desires would be fulfilled simultaneously.
Because there is no distinction and because no specific qualification has been stated, the word "from all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*) is employed [in the scriptural passage].
Now follows the second interpretation (*varṇaka*).
In that regard, this is the meaning of the sūtra according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

In the optional rites such as the Saurya sacrifice, whatever desires such as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) are mentioned in the scriptures, all of them would pertain to the next world and not to this one,
because they are no different from heaven (*svarga*).
Just as heaven is not obtained here, so too spiritual luster and the like are not perceived in this world.
Therefore, [the opponent claims] that desires pertain to the next world.
[The author] refutes this on the grounds that the object of the power of yoga cannot be connected with what has not yet arisen.
He establishes his own position as follows:
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view.
It is not that all desired objects are obtained through a single performance; rather, they are obtained successively.
"Yoga" means connection, and by "succession" (paryāya), a sequence consisting of priority and posteriority is intended.
Success (siddhi) occurs through yoga by way of alternation (paryāyeṇa), which is the attainment of its fruit.

Through one application there is the accomplishment of one fruit, and through another, another; thus, by alternation, there is the fulfillment of all desires, because the fruit is connected with its production.

All desires are simultaneously unconnected by way of origination. "Unconnected by way of origination" means that a connection—that is, a relation—by way of origination is not possible; because there is no simultaneous origination of all [desires], they are "unconnected by way of origination. It is not the case that they are not so; rather, they are "unconnected by way of origination. The state of being such is "unconnectedness by way of origination"; therefore [the term is used].

Alternatively, because there is no connection in the *utpatti*—that is, in the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*)—there is no relation to all the desires; the meaning is that [the connection] is not heard [in the text].
Therefore, there is a conjunction (*sāhitya*) of the desires. However, in the second interpretation, the meaning of this sūtra is as follows:

Regarding those desires for *brahmavarcasa* (Vedic luster) and so forth that result from ritual actions (*karma*), they are not obtained in this world in the same manner as heaven; therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—established by the preceding sūtra—is that they are obtained only after death in another birth.
In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: if there is no obstacle to the connection with the fruit of yoga, perfection is attained in this very life.

However, as for the object—the fruit of ritual action—since it is not connected to the present birth when it is imminent, and because no such connection has been stated, the desired fruit is obtained in another birth provided an obstacle exists.
Thus [it is said].
Which [are those]? Likewise, those things employed within the sacrifice.

In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One offers when [the rice] has turned sour" (*mīḍhe juhoti*) and "One offers when [the rice] has spilled" (*skanne juhoti*).

Just as the *agnihotra* oblation and other rites are repeated whenever their respective times—such as evening and morning—arrive, so too the occasional oblations (*naimittika-homa*) employed within the sacrifice, such as the offering for souring, must be repeated whenever their respective occasions—such as the souring or spilling of the rice—occur; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
This concludes the section on extended application (*atideśādhikaraṇa*).
The reading "antaḥkratuyuktāni" is found in the *Subodhinī*, while the reading "antaḥkratusaṃyuktāni" is found in the *Kutūhala*;
however, the meaning is not different.
— Ke. (Keśava Miśra)
Thus, there is the maxim "as something not previously existing" (*apūrva*). This is the principle regarding the construction of the altar (*vedikaraṇa-nyāya*).
The literal meaning, however, shall be seen shortly.
There is a displacement of the consecration alone, but not of anything other than that, according to the principle "so too the unprecedented" (*tathāpūrva*).
(In the Rājasūya, this displacement of the consecration for the *abhiṣecanīya* and *añjana* [anointing] rites following the deities has been stated.)

Regarding the statement "But for the former [sacrifices], the details are established," since there is a description of the displacement (apakarṣa) of even non-archetypal elements such as the *vidhi* (injunctions), the term "as before" (*pūrvavat*) is explained as having a specific scope.
Likewise, there is the case of the *apūrva*.
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the altar (*vedi*) is prescribed to be prepared after the covering of the sacrificial offerings (*havirabhivāsana*).
However, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), it is brought forward [to the previous day] by the injunction: "On the day before the new moon, one prepares the altar."

In the inquiry as to whether that [modification], being withdrawn, also withdraws the items belonging to the preceding stage or not, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it does withdraw them because of its connection with the ritual application.
Therein, he establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of extension (*atideśa*).
The meaning is that the modification is preceded by the archetype (*prakṛti*).
"Apūrva" means that which does not exist previously; thus, the *amāvāsyā* is the primary (archetypal) action.

Although the altar (*vedi*) is [prepared] on the *amāvāsyā* by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it does not, like something obtained by default (*autprāptika*), cause the subsequent items to be drawn back [to an earlier time].
Therefore, the ritual items ending with the covering of the sacrificial oblation (*havirabhivāsana*) are not to be postponed.
The altar-sized [space] is to be cleared away.

The covering of the oblation consists of the surrounding flaming of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with *darbha* grass and its heating on all sides with firebrands (*ulmuka*), as well as the scattering of ash together with its embers over it.
After that, the construction of the altar (*vedi*).
Likewise [is the rule] for the sprinkling with clarified butter;
likewise [is the rule] for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Likewise, regarding the *abhighāraṇa* (sprinkling with clarified butter), it is heard in the scripture:
"In the *dyāmākāmayana*, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a garment," and "In the *nīhāragrayaṇa*, the sacrificial fee is a first-born calf.
It has been stated that for those two—the garment and the calf—the duties pertaining to the *anvāhārya* (the rice mess) must be performed, but cooking is not to be done.
Likewise, the pouring of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*) is not to be performed for the cooked offering (*pāka*).
This is because it is "caused by food" (*annakāritatvāt*), meaning it is brought about by food and is dependent upon food; this phrase is to be supplied from the preceding sūtra.

For the purpose of the pouring of clarified butter is to produce sweetness in that which is to be eaten; however, since clothing (*vāsaḥ*) and the calf (*vatsa*) do not possess the nature of food at all, the conclusion is that the pouring of clarified butter is also not to be performed for them.
By such a designation.
This is the sūtra of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position concerning the locus in the form of the *antarāgarbhaṇī*.
From the preceding sūtra, the word "because of being connected" (saṃyogitvāt) is carried over; from the sūtra prior to that, the word "of the primary" (pradhānasya) is also carried over.
The subject passage here is: "One should touch the full moon sacrifice with the Caturhotṛ [formula], and the new moon sacrifice with the Pañcahotṛ [formula].
The mantra beginning with "The earth is the Hotṛ" is named the Caturhotṛ.
The mantra beginning with "agnihotā" and "adhvaryur adhvaram" is named the Pañcahotṛ.
By the words "Paurṇamāsī" and "Amāvāsyā," the principal oblation belonging to each respective sacrifice is designated.

The meaning of the subject-sentence is that the sprinkling (abhigharśana)—that is, the touching with the hand—of the principal oblation (*pradhānahavis*) offered at the Full Moon sacrifice should be performed with the *Caturhotṛ* mantra; and the sprinkling of the principal oblation offered at the New Moon sacrifice should be performed with the *Pañcahotṛ* mantra. Regarding the doubt as to whether this sprinkling pertains solely to the principal [sacrifice] or to both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the principal, the conclusion is that the sprinkling pertains only to the principal, not to the subsidiaries.
Why? The word *pradhānasya* (of the primary) should be repeated.

The meaning is that by the naming of the primary—the naming of the *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* as the primary—it is the primary alone that is named. Because of the naming of the subordinate (*guṇa*), there is a naming for the sake of all [the subsidiaries].
When it is argued that the touching (*abhigharśana*) pertains only to the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated:
"One should touch the *paurṇamāsī* [offering]; one should touch the *amāvāsyā* [offering]. This designation is for the sake of all the primary sacrifices, not for the primary sacrifice alone.
Why? Because of the mention of the subsidiaries (*guṇa*).

Having stated that the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), as indicated by the accusative endings, are the objects of refinement for both the primary rites and their subsidiaries, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the act of anointing (*abhigharṣaṇa*) serves all purposes.

In this regard, one should observe the division: there is one topic (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting of two sūtras in the seventh chapter, and a third topic [of this section] consisting of the eighth and tenth [sūtras].
(Ke.)
Likewise, there is the act of heating.

The heating of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with bundles of *darbha* grass is performed for the purpose of baking it on top. However, in the case of the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), such heating should not be performed.
"For indeed, the ripening [of karma] occurs above; it cannot be spoken of as occurring below"—this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Who? [The author of the *Siddhānta*].
Likewise, there is the principle: "The *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath] follows after the *soma*" (Jaimini Sūtra 7.3.4.13).
The meaning of this sūtra will be explained immediately below.
Who [are the subjects]?

Likewise, regarding the statement "The *avabhṛtha* [is] from the *soma*," although there is no application of extension (*atideśa*) for the *anavabhṛtha* because of the discussion in the seventh section concerning the extension of the properties of the *audumbarī-avabhṛtha-bhāvanā*, it is nonetheless appropriate to speak of the time of extension by means of the name *avabhṛtha*. This is because, even in the absence of an extension, the name *avabhṛtha*—being taught by its own word—functions as a cause for extension by bringing to mind its own specific properties, just as the *Agnihotra* and other rites serve as the basis for optional qualities (*kāmyaguṇa*).
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 155).
Thus, "The *avabhṛtha* [is] from the *soma*."

In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "They go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the scrapings of the Vāruṇī offering and with the husks. Regarding this, there arises a deliberation: is this an injunction for the pouring of husks and scrapings into the water—which is already obtained through the *codaka* (extended application) from the Darśapūrṇamāsa—as a secondary detail? Or rather, is there an extension of the ritual characteristics (*dharma*) from the *avabhṛtha* of the Soma sacrifice? To address this, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Just as there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *pṛṣṭha* chants from the [Soma] sacrifice of sixteen days, so too, in the case of the other [Vaiśvadeva] offerings belonging to the Varuṇapraghāsa, the *avabhṛtha* or the *avabhṛtha*-dharma is extended by the name "avabhṛtha" from the [Soma] sacrifice, due to the commonality of the word *avabhṛtha*. If it is argued that this refers to the archetype (*prakṛti*),

then in the Varuṇapraghāsa rite— where it is stated, "They go to the *avabhṛtha* with the scrapings of the *vāruṇī* [offering] and the husks"— this is an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇa*) consisting of the scrapings and husks, in place of the pouring of water which is obtained through the archetypal rule (*codaka*) from the archetype, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
"It might be so"—this is the prima facie position.
If this is argued, we say:
no, because it is figurative.
That [interpretation] is consistent with the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because it is figurative (bhakti).

Regarding the pouring out of water and the carrying away of the *praṇītā* waters at the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the status of being a final purificatory bath (*avabhṛthatva*) is stated there figuratively; for this is merely a praise, as in: "This indeed is the *avabhṛtha* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
However, there is no actual *avabhṛtha* in the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Therefore, from the *avabhṛtha* belonging to the *saumika* sacrifice, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of certain ritual properties (*dharma*) to the *avabhṛtha* of the *vāruṇapraghāsika* sacrifice;
likewise the invocation (1926), likewise the invocation (1927), and likewise the origin of the others, as shown by the indicative marks (*liṅga*).

Regarding the extension of ritual characteristics (*dharmātideśa*) from the *saumika-avabhṛtha* of the Adhvaryu engaged in the *Varuṇapraghāsa*, the text—stating "He does not offer the *āyadī* oblation, he does not sing the *sāman*, nor does he mutter the mantra for going"—prohibits certain characteristics of the *saumika-avabhṛtha* while thereby indicating the application of other characteristics.

From this observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the characteristics of the *saumika-avabhṛtha* are extended to the Adhvaryu in the *Vāruṇapraghāsika* through the name *avabhṛtha*.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the reasons.
If it is argued that the invocation is likewise [to be performed], [we reply:
in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the proximity is indicated by the two Ājyabhāga offerings.

In this regard, if the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) should argue: "The *ājyabhāga*-fire is Agni in the form of the deity of the *ājyabhāga* offering; likewise, as stated in the preceding section, it must be a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), like the *aprayāja*. It is a preparation for the sake of the primary rite, namely the *ājyabhāga* dedicated to Agni."
No; because of the distinct designation, it is a separate deity.
The *ājyabhāga* offering belongs to Agni [of the *ājyabhāga*], not as a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*) for the primary fire, but rather as a directly contributory act (*ārādupakārakaṃ karma*).
Therefore, the fire of the *ājyabhāga* must be a separate deity from the primary fire.
Because of the specific designation: "Bring Agni, bring Soma, bring Agni. Here, two Agnis are designated as separated by Soma.
Therefore, the conclusion is that the Āgneya Ājyabhāga is a remote auxiliary (ārādupakāraka), and the Ājyabhāga-Agni is a distinct deity from the primary fire.
This is also because of uniformity.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, Agnīṣomīya is sacrificed.
Therein, Soma is indeed the deity of the sacrifice;
Agni as well, being distinct from the principal fire, is likewise the deity of the sacrifice.
Because of their equality— that is, because of the similarity in being deities of the sacrifice—
furthermore, since the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are designated as acts that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*),
the *ājyabhāga* belonging to the *āgneya* [offering] must likewise be an act providing indirect assistance.
Because their status as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakārakatva*) is equal.

Therefore, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *ājyabhāga* for Agni is distinct from the fire of the primary sacrifice, and the *ājyabhāga* dedicated to Agni is not a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), but rather a remote auxiliary.
In the preceding sūtra, "designation" was stated as the indicative mark (*liṅga*); in this sūtra, "equality" is stated as the logical principle (*nyāya*).
If it is argued that the invocation is likewise [not part of the Vedic text],
the status of the particle *iti* as scripture (*śruti*) has been refuted in the section on this point in the *Śāstradīpikā*.

Bāla, p. 460: "If it is argued that the invocation is likewise [for a secondary purpose]—that is, just as the *aindrī* verse is employed for a secondary purpose, so too the *haviṣkṛt* mantra used for invocation is employed for a secondary purpose—this is the meaning of the sūtra of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The meaning of the third part of the sūtra, ‘because of the statement drawn by the word *tathā*’ (*tathāśabdānukṛṣṭasya vacanāt*), is ‘because of the direct scriptural statement (*śruteḥ*)’ (Śruti, p. 1092)."

[Objection: "Oṃ, let it be that there is also an invocation. In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He invokes three times while threshing, saying, 'O preparer of the oblation, come! Here, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is either:

"While threshing—i.e., while performing the act of threshing—he says, 'O preparer of the oblation, come! (with *haviṣkṛdehi* being part of the mantra); or alternatively: "While threshing—at the time of threshing—he invokes [her], saying, 'O preparer of the oblation, come! (with *haviṣkṛdehi* being the act of calling).
The suffix *-śāna* has the purpose of indicating time.
Thus, when it is taught that "the mantra [is used] while threshing," one considers whether it indicates the time; regarding this, he states the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view.
Just as the *aindrī* verse is taught in relation to the *gārhapatya* fire, so too the invocation mantra, "O preparer of the oblation, come! is taught in relation to the act of "threshing."
If this is argued,
we say no, because it is taught as an injunction regarding time.
Having refuted the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), he states the established conclusion (siddhānta).
This injunction does not enjoin the mantra for the act of threshing; rather, it is an injunction regarding the time, preceded by a restatement of the time, and is an injunction for triple repetition.
This is because both the time and the mantra have already been enjoined elsewhere, and thus [the repetition] is obtained by implication alone.
Thus say Kaṣṭūrīraṅgācārya.
There is no injunction regarding the mantra for the act of threshing, because it is the threefold repetition that is enjoined in this sentence.

Nor is there an injunction regarding the time; for in the case of the invocation, the time of threshing need not be enjoined, since the invocation of assistants—which is required—is already established by the very fact of the necessity of the time for threshing.
Thus, it is a matter of curiosity.

The mantra is not for the purpose of threshing. Nor is there an injunction regarding the collection of time by indicating the time of threshing through the repetition of the negative particle (*na*) with the word "threshing" (*avahanani*); for if one were to enjoin the collection of time—which is to say, the threefold repetition—there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Regarding the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation): since the invocation at the time of threshing is enjoined by worldly custom and is already known, the injunction merely prescribes its repetition three times.
Thus says the *Subodhinī*.
This is because there is no [other] subordinate quality (*guṇa*) [to be enjoined].

[Objection: "But surely, just as the wife prepares the oblation (*havis*), so too does the act of threshing prepare the oblation; therefore, by the very nature of the action, the mantra would apply to the threshing. Thus, the statement ‘He calls out thrice while threshing, saying "O preparer of the oblation, come! will merely prescribe the threefold repetition. [Response: This is not so, because the mantra cannot apply to the threshing. The word *ehi* ("come") is in the form of an imperative command directed toward another, and the vocative address *haviṣkṛt* ("O preparer of the oblation") is in the second person; since these are impossible for an insentient object like the act of threshing, the mantra cannot be applied to it.
Therefore, because of the absence of qualities—specifically, because the quality of consciousness is absent in the act of threshing—this [act] does not have threshing as its object.
This is also because of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Since it is expressed by a word with a feminine gender-mark in the scripture, "Speech indeed is the preparer of the oblation; he thus calls Speech," the preparer of the oblation can be praised as being Speech itself on account of that indicative mark.
In this context, it is appropriate for the mantra to be for the purpose of summoning the wife, but not for the purpose of threshing.
[Objection: But surely, even in the case of threshing, there exists a word in the feminine gender which is employed. To this we reply:

The feminine gender is not necessarily restricted to the act of threshing (*avahanana*), for the term "threshing" (*avaghāta*) can also be masculine, and the term "action" (*karman*) can also be neuter.
Furthermore, the wife's similarity to the act of threshing is based on her essential nature (*svarūpa*), whereas the similarity of the word is based on its external form (*pararūpa*).
Therefore, the feminine gender of the wife is more appropriate.
Therefore, the mantra belongs to the act of threshing.
There would be a contradiction of the injunction if it were taught [as belonging] to the instruction [of threshing].

For when the mantra is taught as being for the repetition of threshing by the rule, “He calls out ‘O preparer of the oblation, come! three times while threshing,” there would be a conflict—a contradiction—of another injunction, namely: “Then he threshes with the words ‘May the enemy of heaven be struck down! and “He threshes with the words ‘Struck away are the sorcerers!’”
In that case, because [the action] does not exist [at that time], the scriptural statement would be like [a description of] something eternal.

Therefore, "while threshing" (*avaghnan*) has the purpose of indicating time; the meaning is that at the time of threshing, one calls the wife three times with the mantra, "O preparer of the oblation, come!
Oṃ; likewise, in the case of the subsequent [rite], it is because of its being of that same nature.
It is heard in scripture: "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a rice-oblation to Sūrya. In that instance, Sūrya is heard as the deity in the injunction.
"Sūrya," "Āditya," "Bhāskara," "Savitṛ," and "Divākara" are the well-known names of the Sun.
In the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), all the *nigadas* (invocatory formulas) are obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) as being archetypal (*prākṛta*).
Regarding the deliberation as to which word among these should be used for the designation of the deity, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In that modified (vikṛta) form, because it has the Saura [offering] as its archetype (*prakṛti*)—that is, because it has the Āgneya [offering] as its archetype—the utterance of the word "Sūrya" would occur as it is found in the original injunction (*codanā*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Therefore, from the root *tanu* in the sense of "to extend," *vitati* means extension; that is to say, modification (*vikṛti*).
[Objection:
"The origin of the others is likewise.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "Rising up, [the Adhvaryu says] 'O Agnīdh, spread the fires,' and 'Perform the vow'—with these words he releases his speech."
Regarding the question here— whether the instruction by means of the mantra pertains to the rising or to the release of speech, or whether the connection is for the purpose of indicating the time—

the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that one should rise with the mantra, "O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires," and the release of speech should be performed with the mantra, "Observe the vow. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated by way of extension (*atideśa*) from the preceding section.

Just as the mantra "O preparer of the oblation, come" (haviṣkṛdehi) is applied to its primary meaning, which is summoning, so too here the mantra "O Agnīdh, spread the fires" (agnīdagnīn vihara) is applied to its primary meaning, the command to spread the fires, and the mantra "Observe the vow" (vrataṃ kuruta) is applied to the command to undertake the vow. Regarding the phrase "in that [which consists of] rising and dismissal": "rising" refers to the statement concerning rising, and "dismissal" refers to the statement concerning dismissal; the meaning is that the mantra heard in those respective statements is applied to their primary meanings.
At the time of rising, he issues the command, "Distribute the fires," and at the time of releasing speech, he issues the command, "Observe the vow.
Thus, the conclusion is that this conjunction is for the purpose of indicating time.
Ke.

The same applies to rising and releasing speech. Just as with the threshing, so too regarding rising and releasing speech, there is an extended application (*atideśa*): in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), for the purpose of obtaining the mantra; but in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), for the purpose of its non-obtainment. It is not the case that the *agnīdh*-vow mantra is enjoined by the names "rising" and "releasing"; rather, by virtue of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being a direction (*preṣaṇa*) during the shifting of the fires (*agniviharaṇa*), the time for the fire-mantra—which was already obtained—is prescribed as the occasion for rising. And by virtue of being the completion of the restriction of speech (*vāgamanīyama*), the time for the release of speech—which was already obtained—is prescribed as the occasion for the utterance of the mantra known to the one who knows the directions for the consumption of the vow (*vratabhakṣaṇa*).

The application of the Siddhānta-sūtra is as follows: because the time for both the *utthāna* (rising) and the *vrata* (vow) mantras is understood through the sequence of the ritual injunction (*vidhi*) and the recitation (*pāṭha*), and because they are thus enjoined, they possess the functional capacity characterized by the dismissal of the *agnīdh* priest after the fire-mantras have been recited.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the mantra is applied to its secondary sense (*gauṇa*) based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); in the Siddhānta, it is applied to its primary sense (*mukhya*) based on indicative power (*liṅga*).
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1097).
Likewise, the origin [of the rule] for others follows from the sense of "mine-ness" (mamātva).

Furthermore, as for the fact that the rites prescribed by the Veda serve all purposes in both the archetype (prakṛti) and the ectype (vikṛti), that too is not to be questioned, because it has been determined by citing examples such as "they praise after having removed the fire," in the sūtra: "In case of doubt... not the Vedic... thus its origin."
Likewise, when there is a modification of a single object (tathaikārthavikāre). And likewise, there is an indicative mark (liṅga):
"In the case of a modification of a single object, the archetypal rule does not apply; for if it were to apply, there would be an option."
It is heard in the scripture: "In the sacrifice to Soma and Pūṣan, the sacrificial post (yūpa) is made of Udumbara wood.

In this context, "modification for a single purpose" (*ekārthavikāra*) means that there is a single common purpose or result; the Udumbara wood shares the same purpose as the *khadira* wood, namely the fivefold fruit (*pañcavadana*).

Regarding this modification for a single purpose, just as in the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) the original substance and deity do not apply when the modified ones are employed, so too, when the Udumbara post is employed in the sacrifice to Soma and Pūṣan, the original *khadira* wood and its characteristics do not apply—that is, they are not applied.
For indeed, there would have to be an option (vikalpa) between that which is obtained through the general rule (codaka) and that which is directly stated in the scripture;
and this is not logical.
Therefore, there is no application of the archetypal (prākṛta) element.
Such is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
"As far as the scripture [extends]," if it be so argued—
the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises this objection.
"As many as there are scriptural texts (śruti).

The text 'The sacrificial post (yūpa) is made of Udumbara wood' is a modified (vaikṛtī) scriptural text, and 'according to the archetype' (prakṛtivat) is the scriptural text of the extended application (codaka).
Thus, 'as many as are the scriptural texts, so many are the sacrificial posts'—this is an avyayībhāva compound."
And if it be argued that, in accordance with the two scriptural texts, there should be a combination of the *audumbara* quality and so forth— such that the animal should be tied to both together—
the answer is no, because such a combination is not explicitly stated in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
The proponent says:
This is not so;
because in the archetype (prakṛti) the udumbara wood is not mentioned by word, and in the ectype (vikṛti) the ladle (sruc) is not mentioned by word.

There is no combination. That which lacks an enjoining word is "non-verbal" (*aśabda*); because it is such, due to the absence of an enjoining word, there is a sublation of the original sacrificial post material by the modified *audumbara* wood.
Some [hold that] desire [is the motive], because of its connection with wealth;
and there is also an indicative mark to that effect.
Having explained all of this as a supplement to the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is now also explained in the Bhāṣya as a separate section. It is explained here as a distinct section;
this is an extension (*atideśa*) of the section concerning the singularity of the cup (*graha*).
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt.
Likewise, the gender (*liṅga*) is also intended to be significant, just as the number (*ekatva*).

Having prescribed three cows—namely, "In spring, in the morning, one sacrifices a black-necked [cow] dedicated to Agni," and similarly in summer and autumn—the remainder of the passage states, "They become pregnant."
And the *garbha* (the embryo) is feminine.

Likewise, [in the text] "The horse, the bull, the ram, and the ewe belong to Prajāpati"—why? Because of the connection with the purpose (*artha*), that is, because the fruit (*phala*) is connected with the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

And thus, even through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) in the stated scriptural passage: "If the sacrificer should desire [something], then the Adhvaryu priest should measure [the altar] low."

If, while the master desires [the result], the Adhvaryu should desire it for the sake of the master, then a single syntactical unity is possible even through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the one who possesses the desire is indeed the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

In this case, although the measuring of the *sadas* (the sacrificial shed) belongs to the *adhvaryu*, because the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) qualified by the qualities inherent in that [measuring] has the capacity to serve the purpose of the master (*svāmin*) by being based on the *sadmāna* for his benefit, its status as serving the master's purpose is understood through the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the text; since it is he alone who desires [the result], and because the name (*samākhyā*) restricts the agent to the primary performer and thus lacks connection with the subordinate, the performer of the *bhāvanā* is not restricted [to the *adhvaryu*].
From the designation and other such factors, it would belong to these others.

In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, regarding the desire expressed in such passages as "if he should so desire," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) stated in the preceding sūtra was that the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the one who desires. By this present sūtra, an exception to that is stated: "The Udgātṛ priest procures for himself or for the sacrificer whatever desire he may desire. Here, by the distinct term "for himself" (*ātmane*), the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is designated separately from the sacrificer. Therefore, based on such a designation, the desire should belong only to the other priests, those distinct from the sacrificer.

But in the absence of such a designation, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the desire belongs to the sacrificer alone. Having enjoined [the rule] with "ke," it is stated in the supplementary portion of the passage (vākyaśeṣa): "They are without testicles for the sake of possessing virility."

*Muṣkara* means "possessing the male organ" (*puṃstvaliṅga*). [According to] Pāṇini 5.2.97, *ra* is added in the sense of possession after the words *uṣ*, *tuṣ*, *muṣka*, and *madhu*. [The form is derived as: *muṣka-ra*. The elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*lopa*) occurs by Pāṇini 6.4.148. *Upasramiḥ*. Etc.
The *Kaumudī* states: "The word *muṣkaraḥ* means 'testicular' (*aṇḍaḥ*).
The word division is *madheḥ* and *raḥ*; [the suffix] *ra* is applied after *madhu*, resulting in *madhuraḥ*.
Therefore, it is certain that both femininity and masculinity are intended there;
thus, for example, is the Soma-cup.

In the context of the *ṛtapeya* sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "A wooden cup made of *udumbara* wood is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); it is to be given to a dear Brahmin of the same lineage.

This *soma*-cup, by virtue of its connection with the *brahman* priest, excludes only the portion belonging to the *brahman*, not the entire sacrificial fee of the rite. Just as, for example, in the rule "The *khaja* [ladle] is for the *udgātṛ*," the *khaja*—by virtue of its connection with the *udgātṛ* priest—excludes only the portion belonging to the *udgātṛ*. So it is here.
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Or rather, it is a modification of everything, because there is a prohibition regarding animals for the sake of the ritual. With the word "or" (*vā*), the author sets aside the prima facie view that the Soma-cup mentioned as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the *Ṛtapeya* sacrifice does not merely exclude the portion of the Brahman priest.

The *somacamasa* (Soma-cup) is a modification of everything and sets aside the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sacrifice. This is indicated by the scriptural sign (*liṅga*) that prohibits the giving of animals when making gifts for the sake of the sacrifice. Thus it is recorded in the tradition: "Soma is indeed truth, and animals are untruth; if one were to give animals, he would commit untruth; therefore, a Soma-cup made of Udumbara wood is the sacrificial fee."
In this context, having set aside the gift of animals, the *somacamasa* (Soma-cup) is prescribed. It is understood that when the *somacamasa* is given, the animals are not given.
If it were to exclude the gift of the Brahman priest alone, then animals would still be given to the others, and by that, there would be a falsehood.

Therefore, it is a remover of the whole [of the prohibition]. If it is argued that it is not distinct from the gift to the Brahman—just as in the *Ṛtapeya* sacrifice, where it is said: "Soma is indeed truth, and cattle are untruth; if one were to give cattle, he would commit untruth; the sacrificial cup for Soma made of Udumbara wood is the fee"—here, although the giving of cattle to the Brahman is accepted, because of the prohibition regarding cattle, the remainder is exactly the same.

Therefore, animals should not be given to the Brahman priest, but rather only the *somacamasa* (Soma-cup). Even if one accepts that the *somacamasa* excludes the Brahman’s share, the prohibition of the animals remains logically consistent.
If the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) should argue that the *somacamasa* excludes only the Brahman’s share and not the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), [the reply is:

because the general rule (*utsarga*) is for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), there would be a performance of what is prohibited; furthermore, the purpose of the secondary [substitution] would not be the meaning intended for the sacrificial fees.
In the midday pressing of the sacrifice, whatever is given upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), all that constitutes a single sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Since it is stated, "The Soma-cup is the sacrificial fee," at the *ṛtapeya* sacrifice, that entire sacrificial fee is indeed the Soma-cup alone.

Thus, because the relinquishment—the gift of the Soma-cup—is for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), and because it serves as the appropriate sacrificial fee for the entire sacrifice, the Soma-cup becomes the displacer (*nivartaka*) of the sacrificial fee of the whole sacrifice.

If, however, animals were to be given away other than to the Brahman priest, then it would constitute the act of giving animals—which is prohibited by the injunction, "If one should give animals, he would commit a falsehood. Therefore, [the gift] must be made to him.

Furthermore, that which is the portion of the Brahman is not the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) itself, but rather a certain part of the sacrificial fee. If the word *dakṣiṇā* were applied to a mere part, it would be used in a figurative sense.
Furthermore, that figurative meaning cannot be the purpose of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
The purpose of the *soma*-cup is the displacement of the sacrificial fees;
the gratification of all the officiating priests is the purpose of the sacrificial fees, not the gratification of the Brahman priest alone.
Therefore, the conclusion is that the *soma-camasa* (the cup for Soma) replaces the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of the rite, and not merely the portion belonging to the Brahman priest.
For if it were a modification of that [portion] belonging to the Brahman, [it would replace only that].
He states the purpose of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"If, however, the Soma-cup were the displacer of only the Brahman’s share, then that deficiency—the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) being deficient by that Brahman’s share—would be a modification of the sacrificial fee of all sacrifices, acting as its sublater; [consequently], excluding the Brahman’s share, all other sacrificial fees would have to be given to the other priests, while to the Brahman only the Soma-cup itself would be given."
Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Or rather, everything [belongs to the sacrificer] because of the removal of the person, since those [rites] have the sacrifice as their primary purpose.
He states the practical application of the established conclusion:

Or rather, all [the priests] receive the seasonal sacrificial fee (*ṛtudakṣiṇā*) by means of a single Soma-cup, because of the exclusion of the person [as the recipient], which results in the exclusion of the fee from all the other animals.
Why? Because those fees serve to gratify all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and thus the sacrifice is the primary concern.
Therefore, only one Soma-cup should be given as the entire sacrificial fee.
And that [permission] too is for Brahmā alone, and not for anyone else;
for the cessation of all worldly [impediments] occurs thus with respect to substances. (Mīmāṃsākośa 2.42)
Likewise, because it is heard that "one should offer for you, for the year,
and for the Lord at the same time," the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that there is a common performance (tantra) for all the auxiliary rites (aṅgas).
Furthermore, there is a singular scriptural statement [referring to it] as "the *iṣṭi*.

Although in the *adhvarakalpā* there are three sacrifices—namely, those performed in the morning, at midday, and in the evening—nevertheless, there is a scriptural hearing (*śruti*) of it as a unity, as in the passage: "This very sacrifice is called the *adhvarakalpā iṣṭi*. This is logically possible through the *tantra* (common procedure) of its constituent parts (*aṅga*).
Therefore, it is a *tantra*.
This is another reason stated for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Alternatively, because the rites are distinct and because there is a *tantra* arrangement for them, there should be an instruction for [the rites] together with their auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*).
He establishes the conclusion:
by the word "not" (avā), there is the exclusion of the five [other sacrifices].

Because the rites of the Āmāvaiṣṇava, Sārasvata, and others are distinct, and because for those rites the collection of auxiliary elements (*tantra*) is prescribed at various times—namely morning, midday, and evening—the instruction must be understood as pertaining to the three sacrifices together with their auxiliaries.
Therefore, it is a *tantra*.
Although the two sūtras— the sixteenth and the twentieth— possess an identical sequence [of syllables] and are indeed identical in their phonemes,
they differ due to the difference in their subject matter (*viṣaya*).
Alternatively, this is a statement regarding the time of the first [offering].
Regarding what was said—that because there is a single time for the specific [rite]—he replies:
this is a statement of the time for the offering (*nirvāpa*) of the first rite, which belongs to the morning, namely, "one should offer before the utterance of speech."
Not so for the second and third sacrifices.
Therefore, there is a distinction of ritual procedure (*tantra*). This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The word "sacrifice" (*iṣṭi*) is used in the singular just as in other cases. Regarding what was stated, namely "it is a sacrifice," he says: the word "sacrifice" ends in the singular because of the singularity of the result; that is, because there is a unity of action due to the singularity of the result.
Just as elsewhere there are the *sarvapṛṣṭheṣṭi*, the *mṛgāreṣṭi*, and so forth,
or as in the case of the *rājasūya*,
so too in the *adhvarakalpā*, among the three [sacrifices] to be performed at different times such as morning and so on, the constituent parts (*aṅga*) are to be performed separately.

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Why? Because the fruit is inherent in the master (*svāmin*), since the fruit is connected with the ritual action. Just as there is no substitute for the deities or for the sacrificial materials, so too there is no substitute for the master, that is, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Because of the inherence of the fruit (*phalasamavāyāt*), that is, because of the connection of the fruit with the owner alone through its inherence in him; since the fruit is connected with the action, the fruit is joined with the action.
This is the commentary beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth, for the purpose of explaining the action.

For the purpose of dispelling the equality of faults in both positions, [it is said] that because of the student’s syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) through the indication of location (*deśalakṣaṇayā*), the commentary beginning with "half within the altar, half outside the altar" (*ardham antavedy ardhaṃ bahirvedi*) is intended to explain the exclusion of the vowel *a*. This is suggested in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vārttika*, and other works in the section concerning "the altar for the sacrificial post" (*yūpavedinyāya*), where it is stated that by the collective expression "half within the altar, half outside the altar," a specific location is indicated. (The *Yūpavedinyāya*).
Kumārila [says]:

Likewise, because the vow has already been undertaken, the vow pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (dārśapūrṇamāsika), which is extended by the rule of transfer (codaka) to the Soma sacrifice in the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites, need not be performed; it is just like the fire-kindling (agnyanvādhāna).
Because it has already been undertaken for the sake of initiation (*dīkṣā*),
that which has been undertaken cannot be undertaken again as long as it has not been relinquished.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the vow (*vrata*) is obtained separately.
They say that the understanding is that "ownership" (svatva) is the meaning of the secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix in the word *tantra*.

Others, however, maintain that in certain cases, the suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) has its denotative power (*śakti*) upon the co-referentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) of two qualifiers that delimit the meaning of the word-base; this is seen in worldly usage in examples such as *pācakatvam* (the state of being a cook), *aupagavatvam* (the state of being Upagu’s descendant), and *nīlotpalatvam* (the state of being a blue lotus), where there is co-referentiality between the two qualifiers—namely, humanity and the relation to Upagu, blueness and lotus-hood, and the state of having Viśvedevas as deities and the state of being a Niṣāda chieftain—and in Vedic usage in examples such as *vaiśvadevītva* and *niṣādasthapatitva*, because co-referentiality is perceived as a qualifier [of the base-meaning]. This is what they say.

Others, however, maintain that there is the manifestation of co-referentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) as a qualifier of the delimitor of the denotatum of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārthatā’vacchedaka-viśeṣaṇatayā*). The expressive power (*śakti*) resides in co-referentiality alone; for there is a rule that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and the rule regarding the predominance of the suffix-meaning applies to cases other than compounds and so forth, excluding the meaning of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*).
They say that in the case of "nīlotpalam" (blue lotus), the cognition is: "lotus-ness is the substratum of the inherence of blueness.

Others, however, say that there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "blue" and so on in that which is the inherent locus (*samavāyin*); the relation is identity (*abheda*); and the cognition is: "the state of being inherent in something distinct from that which is denoted by the compound [term] 'blueness'.

As for the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) "paiśvadevī" and others, they have their primary denotative power (*śakti*) in the sense of a pronoun qualified by the status of being a deity (*devatātva*).
Since the referent of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is a specific mode of the object as it appears in the intellect, [the suffixes] *yat* and so forth are applied.

And thus, the divinity (*devatātva*) of the Viśvedevas—the meaning of the nominal stem—is construed with the substance that is the referent of the pronoun by way of being its qualifier, through the relation of the defining property (*nirūpakatva*).
Even when there is no substitution for the case-ending expressing a relationship (*saṃbandhavibhakti*), there is no fault.
Regarding the word *āmikṣā*, however, the wise hold that the *taddhita* suffix functions to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*) once the specific mode [of the referent] has been presented.

Some, however, maintain that the *taddhita* suffix possesses a primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the meaning of a pronoun, whereas its application to "divinity" (*devatātva*) is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*). They further state that in the case of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes which denote a substratum—such as the nominal base *viśvedeva*—its connection with the divinity indicated by the *taddhita* occurs through a unique feature of grammatical derivation (*vyutpattivaicitryāt*).
Others, however, maintain that the meaning of the *taddhita* suffix is specifically the substance (*dravya*),
while the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and its relation to the meaning of the *taddhita* is a case of semantic connection (*saṃsarga*).

Still others maintain that the status of being a deity alone is the meaning of the *taddhita*, and that the referent of the pronoun is expressed according to the principle of individual instantiation (*vyaktinyāya*).

Others, however, maintain that because a general substance whose specific nature is not determined is not perceived through a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), it does not denote a specific substance; rather, they say that in the word *āmikṣā*, it functions as a qualifier of the substance. (Maṇi, pp. 161–162). There is no connection with that which requires a complement for the meaning of the secondary derivative suffix; the same applies to a compound (*samāsa*).
(Mānameyodaya 314/174).

The rule regarding the deity [indicated] by a *taddhita* suffix is set aside by all [other types of rules]. The rule regarding a deity based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*) is the very weakest of all.

Vārttika 4.1.41–46, p. 341. Regarding the conflict between a *taddhita* suffix and the accusative case, there is a doubt as to whether the *taddhita* is more authoritative or the accusative; this is discussed in the section concerning Indra (3.2.13).
Su. Pr. 1087: For by the indication of a secondary derivative (taddhita), the specific number of the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) is expressed.

In that case, because the meaning of the nominal stem cannot be otherwise [accounted for], the analysis (vigraha) is made with a word ending in the singular number. Vārttika on 3.2.15: 37. Having heard of the divinity of the gods in the indication of the secondary derivative.
Bhāṣya:
There is a syntactical split (vākyabheda) characterized by the repetition of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*).
Bālakrīḍā, p. 181: Just like a secondary suffix, a compound does not apply to words that are dependent [on another].

For indeed, regarding those meanings which are expressed by case-endings (*vibhakti*), the formation of *taddhita* suffixes is observed only from those bases that are semantically equivalent to those case-endings, as in the rules: "purchased with that" (*tena krītam*), "beneficial for that" (*tasmai hitam*), "come from that" (*tata āgataḥ*), "offspring of that" (*tasyāpatyam*), and "existing therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*) (Vārttika 2.4.10, p.

492). Since the hearing of a *taddhita* suffix is weaker than the hearing of a grammatical function (*kāraka*), in the case of the mantra "aindrāgārhapatyam," the quality of being addressed to Gārhapatya alone belongs to the mantra, not the quality of being addressed to Indra.
This [definition] applies to the remainder. Kauṣītaki-Śrautasūtra 3.1.14, p. 350. *Tanuśiras* is the *uṣṇih* [meter].
In its feet, there are [syllables] 8, 8, 7, and 6. Example: *pra yā ghoṣe bhagavān* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.120.9).
The *tanūnapāt*-type [formulas] are differentiated according to the lineage (*gotra*) of the Kṣatriya, Atri, Vadhryaśva, Vasiṣṭha, Vaidya, Śunaka, Kaṇva, and Kaśyapa.
(For these, the second [deity] is *tanūnapāt*; however, for the Kṣatriyas and others, it is *narāśaṃsa*).
Bhāṣya 6.1.6: The principle of the thread (tantunyāya). This is applied when one intends to express that a collection as a whole is the accomplisher of an action.

The sense is that just as many threads joined together accomplish their function, so too even great beings, when united, accomplish their own purpose. (Sāhasī 994). This is the "Thread-and-Cloth" analogy (*tantupaṭanyāya*).
According to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), even when the threads have perished, the cloth remains for a moment; likewise is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

This is the establishment of the principle that when the cause is destroyed, the effect is destroyed. This is the summary. (Regarding the term *tantra*: *Tantra* is that by which, having been performed once, [the procedure] benefits all [subsequent instances].
But where others provide assistance to one another through an improper method, there is *prasaṅga*.
Ratna. 12|2|7|24. *Tantra* is that by which, through a single performance, assistance is extended (*tanyate*) or spread out for many; this is it.
Just as a lamp benefits many Brahmins [standing] together;

*Tantra* (the principle of extension) occurs in two ways: either with respect to each individual or with respect to the whole, depending on whether the verb is subordinate or primary in the completion of the sentence.
In some cases, the *tantra* (common application) is directly perceived:

"The *tantra* would be common; however, when there is another purpose, it is not the motivator. In this very way, through *prasaṅga* (extended application), [it applies] when its own injunction already exists."

(The meaning of this verse, which provides the definition stated in the Bhāṣya, is as follows: When an auxiliary (*aṅga*) being performed is common to many subsidiaries because its specific application is not apprehended, that is *tantra* (simultaneous performance), as for instance the *prayāja* and other rites in relation to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices.
