However, when an auxiliary being performed serves to benefit another, even though its specific application is apprehended as being for the sake of that other, then the state of being dependent upon that other is the determining factor (*prayojaka*). As, for example, the preparation of the whey (*vājina*) and the husks (*tuṣa*) are for the purpose of the bringing of the curd (*dadhyānaya*).

The meaning is that *prasaṅga* (incidental application) occurs where, although the power of one's own injunction to be the motivator (*prayojakatva*) exists, there is a dependence on another [injunction] for its purpose.

And thus, in the statement "But for another's purpose, it is not a motivator" (*parārthe tvaprayojakaḥ*), it should be understood that the sense obtained is "others [are motivated] by the power of one's own injunction to be the motivator. (Somaprabha 12.14)
The *tantra* is the common group of ritual elements,
as in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
The portion beginning with the *ājyabhāga* offerings is the first, and that beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is the latter.
The *tantra* is the common collection of duties (*dharma-grāma*). Those primary rites for which this [collection] exists are the *tantrins*.
Bhāṣya 12.1.1:
(That which is performed by way of a common procedure (*tantra*), or that for which there is a common procedure, is stated according to the order of the phonemes;
however, the word "not" (*na*) is placed after that.)
The *tantra* (common performance) applies to all rites when there is no prior distinction.
Bhāṣya 1.13.1.26. The *tantra* [applies] to the subsidiaries because of the conjunction of the three principal acts at a single time on the full moon day.
Ṭupṭīkā 1.4.4.11.

*Tantra* (the principle of ritual extension) applies to the mantra for increasing growth, "He bestows strength" (*undvīra ojo dhatte*), at the point of continuous pouring in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice.
(Bhāṣya 1.14.1, 50). *Tantra* applies to the mantra for looking at impure things, "May the eye descend" (*avacche cakṣuḥ*), when several impure objects are seen at once in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice.

(1.14.17, 50). *Tantra* applies to the mantra for threshing, "I shall strike down the demon, the rival from heaven" (*ava rakṣo divaḥ sapatnaṃ vadhayāsam*), in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, even though there are multiple blows with the pestle.
1|1|12|42: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the *tantra* (common procedure) of the *āghāra* and other subsidiary rites is not differentiated for each primary act (*pradhāna*).

1|13|10|21: In the Rājasūya, the *ulūlala* chant is a *tantra* common to the various *iṣṭis*.

5|2|6|12–15. The *tantra* (common application) of the mantra for scratching (*kaṇḍūyana-mantra*: "May we be ploughers in the ploughings") applies even when scratching is performed by many [people] simultaneously.
1|14|16|48–49. Another view in the *Bhāṣya* is that the *tantra* applies to the performers in the *Rājasūya*.
The *Vārttika*, however, states that when possible, those same [original] performers are the ones [to perform it].

Ke. 1.14.24–47: The *tantra* (common procedure) applies to the officiating priests—the Hotṛ, Āgnīdhra, and Brahman—at the two sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) during the Varuṇapraghāsa rites; however, there is a distinction between the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ due to a specific scriptural injunction.

In a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), there would be a state of *tantra* because of the sufficiency (*vibhutva*) of the cauldron, the spit, and the omentum-roasting spits.

Commentary: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, there would be a state of *tantra* for the cauldrons, the spit, and the omentum-roasting spits, because of their sufficiency.
A single pot is sufficient for the cooking of all the sacrificial animals and the offerings of food; a spit is used for the hearts; and a fat-roasting fork is used for the omenta.
Therefore, these should be common (tantra) to all. [Objection:

Since the cooking of the Soma is performed separately, it is argued that the pot and other implements, which serve a visible purpose, do not function as a common ritual element (atantratā). This is the connection [of the discussion].

Nor should it be argued that even when there is a single deity, the performance of the *avadāna* (cutting of portions) and so forth cannot be treated as a *tantra* (common/shared procedure) because it depends on preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
For, according to the method to be explained later, that [dependence] is severed even by means of making a mark.
As stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "In the case of the *Prājāpatya* offerings, is there a difference between the pot and so forth, or not? [There is] due to the difference in the limbs."
[Objection: "Do not fear; for there is authority [to act] regarding cooking and so forth. [Bhāṭṭa:

In the case of animals such as those dedicated to Prajāpati, which have a single deity and belong to the same class, the cooking and other rites must indeed be performed *tantra*-wise (simultaneously). This is because the simultaneity of cooking and so forth, understood from the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), would be contradicted if one did not accept large-sized vessels such as the *kumbhī*, *śūla*, and *vapāśrapaṇī*.
For no specific size was prescribed for these items in the archetype (*prakṛti*); therefore, a distinction of vessels like the *kumbhī* and so on cannot be accepted on that basis.
Maṇḍana: "The tortoise is the bestower of cattle.
Tantra.
Śaṅkara: "And the tortoise is the giver of cattle."
The *tantra* [is performed] at a separate time; the *tantra* is the initiation (*dīkṣā*), because it lasts for twelve days.
(The commentary says: "like the initiation.")
Bhāṣya 1.13.10.21: Regarding the *tantra* of place—
the *tantra* under discussion is now being explained.
The definition of *tantrāvāpa* has been proposed;
that is now stated:
in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the principal rites are those beginning with the *āgneya*.

It is heard that heaven is their fruit, as in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Does that [fruit] accrue to them through a single performance (*tantra*), or through separate performances? The same should be observed regarding the Cāturmāsya and other such rites.
But surely, heaven is not heard here as the fruit.

By the word *svargakāma* (desirous of heaven), a person is denoted; by the word *yajeta* (one should sacrifice), the performance of the sacrifice is denoted; and their connection is established by the sentence.
By what, then, is the fruit now stated?
He says: "By this very word *svargakāma*.
[Objection: But surely this speaker is a person (*puruṣa*).
[Response: Indeed, there is no such thing as a person called "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).
But surely, one who has a desire for heaven is "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). We do not even know this: whose is the desire for heaven?
For he who is a desirer of heaven becomes, at that very moment, a non-desirer of heaven.
In that case, this is merely an instruction regarding time:
"When one desires heaven, then one should sacrifice.
Even here, there is no specific time at which one would necessarily desire heaven.
At all times, all desires arise without restriction;
in that regard, there is no specific time.
By this, it can be designated.
In that case, then, this is neither an instruction regarding the person (*puruṣopadeśa*) nor an instruction regarding time (*kālopadeśa*).
What, indeed, is it? It is the desire for the fruit as the occasion (*nimitta*);
namely, "one should sacrifice" when a desire for the realm of heaven has arisen.
As in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice when the potsherd is lost," the refutation of this position has been stated by the Sūtra itself:
"If it is argued that the desire for a fruit is the occasion [for the rite], we say no, because of its obligatory nature" (6.2.110–11).

The Agnihotra and other such rites are obligatory (*nitya*). If these were prescribed as contingent upon a specific occasion (*nimitta*), their obligatory nature would be undermined. In that case, the injunctions regarding their obligatoriness, which state "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*), would be contradicted.

And there are indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as: "Verily, he who, being engaged in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, should let the full moon or the new moon day pass by, is indeed excluded from the heavenly world," and so forth.
By the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), this must be a connection with a result.
But how can a result be enjoined by this [sentence]?

That is stated as follows: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice. This may mean that one desiring heaven is instructed to perform the sacrifice, just as [the rule] "those wearing red turbans proceed" [instructs the performers]. Or it may mean that the sacrifice is for the sake of one desiring heaven, just as [the rules] "one who is dirty should bathe" or "one who is hungry should eat" [instruct the agent].
In that case, if one desiring heaven is instructed to perform an action, even having been so instructed, he would not engage in it;
for who would undertake exertion for the sake of another?
Thus, the instruction regarding the action would be entirely purposeless.
Now, if the sacrifice is for the sake of one who desires heaven, then it benefits that person, and the person performs it for his own purpose;
thus, the injunction regarding the ritual action becomes meaningful.
Furthermore, the meaning of the sacrifice will be grasped as being for the sake of the person, and the meaning of the sentence will be "one who desires heaven."
Therefore, sacrifice is beneficial to one who desires heaven.
For one who desires heaven, there are many benefits, such as the acquisition of cattle, sons, villages, and so forth.

If it were to bring about an end to those [desires] for sons, villages, and the like, then the word "one who desires heaven" would have its literal meaning disregarded and would become a term denoting merely any person.
And thus, it would indeed be purposeless;
for even without that statement "it comes into being," the mere person [as the agent] is understood from the verb itself.
Therefore, [the meaning is simply that] heaven arises from the sacrifice.

In that regard, when there is a conjunction of multiple rites, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and others, a doubt arises: is the fruit of these [rites] common (tantra), or is it distinct for each? What is the prima facie view? That it is distinct.
What is the reason? These principal rites, beginning with the Āgneya, having arisen as distinct entities through injunctions that are mutually interdependent, each individually require a fruit.
When a fruit such as heaven is heard in proximity to them, because they are required individually, it is connected to them individually.
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that there is a distinction of fruits for each principal rite.
This being the case, the following is commenced:

"Because of the connection with a purpose, there would be a separate existence for these [acts]; therefore, due to their conjunction with a single ritual action, there would be oneness of action even for these [rites] such as the Āgneya, which are otherwise distinct.
That is to say, despite being separate entities, these rites beginning with the Āgneya would constitute a single unified action because they are joined with one and the same ritual purpose.
Why? Because of their connection with a purpose. "Purpose" means the fruit (result).
The meaning is: because of the connection—that is, the conjunction—of these [factors] when they are combined for the sake of that [purpose].

Regarding the term *aikakarmyam*: here, by the word *karman* (action), the result (*phala*) is meant, because it is "produced" (*kriyate*). The state of those for whom the action is one is *aikakarmyam*, which means having a single result.
How, then, is it known that the combined [rites] such as the *Āgneya* and others are connected with a single result? It is known from the connection with the word "one" (*eka*).

That single word which denotes these [sacrifices] when they are combined is used to express them, and through it the connection with the fruit is established by the injunction: "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa. Therefore, the fruit is understood as resulting from the sacrifices taken together, not individually. Just as in the case of the injunction, "A tank should be dug by the village," where the well is enjoined in connection with the word "village" denoting a collective, the single well is dug by the people acting together, and not a separate well for each individual; so it is here as well.
In the tenth chapter of the *Ṭup-ṭīkā*, the two topics of sublation (*bādha*) and addition (*abhyuccaya*) are treated.
Among these, "addition" (*abhyuccaya*) does not refer to the existence of some positive entity (as is the case with what is to be known through scripture).
Rather, addition is said to be the mere absence of sublation, as in the statement: "The *anuyāja* offerings do not sublate the *upahoma*s."

In this tenth [book], the limit of the constituent elements— both those obtained through extended application (*codaka*) and those directly prescribed— has been considered. But here, in the eleventh [book], a specific limit is now being heard.

Where three sacrifices (which are the primary elements) are heard [in scripture], there is this question of their number (*iyattā*): does it occur through *tantra* (common performance), or through *āvṛtti* (repetition)?

Now, one might object that the consideration of *tantra* and *āvṛtti* regarding subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) is appropriate immediately after the tenth book, because it is precisely in the tenth book that the determination of their number is established.
In the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), however, the result (*phala*) is considered, and that is not a matter of number.
Therefore, there is no connection between that [the ninth] and the tenth.
For, whether the fruit belongs to each one individually or to them collectively—what kind of connection with the tenth could there be? It is said in reply:

If there is a single fruit for the combined [factors], then the consideration of *tantra* and *āvāpa* is appropriate. But if each one has its own separate fruit, then *tantra* does not exist at all (since there would be a distinction due to the fruits being different). Therefore, the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), which serves as an introduction, is commenced for the sake of establishing *tantra* and *āvāpa*. The second and subsequent sections are also commenced by way of that same context: do the auxiliary acts (*aṅga*) perform the benefit for the sacrifice (*ṛtu-upakāra*) collectively, or are they independent?
Alternatively, the first section is considered according to the general method of "insertion into the system" (*tantrāvāpa*).

(The Commentator, setting aside the discussion based on the Sūtra, raised the objection: "Indeed, heaven is not heard of here as a fruit"; he explains the meaning of that as follows: By the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), an agent is implied, and that agent is qualified by the term "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*), which expresses a person, just as in the case of "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya" (where "king" is the qualification).
And the qualification (such as desire or kingship) becomes an auxiliary element of the ritual action.

(He states the meaning of the subsequent commentary: "In this very way" (meaning, when it is accepted that [the word *svargakāma*] is a qualification of the agent), if heaven alone is eternally desired and not other things such as Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) and so forth, then, because of its uniqueness, the qualification is appropriate (in the sense of "one who desires heaven alone").
Yet, no such person exists.

Or, if heaven is never desired by anyone, even then, with respect to such a person (who does not desire heaven), the qualification is still applicable (in the sense of "one who indeed desires heaven").

However, there is no one who does not desire heaven at some time or other. To this it is replied: at the very moment one is "desirous of heaven" (i.e., desires heaven alone), one will perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices; thus, its status as a qualification is appropriate by way of [specifying] that time.
This too is not tenable.
As long as a person brings about the primary ritual according to the scripture, so long do various desires arise over a long period of time.
And if one should desire only the pure heaven, then—such being the case—the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices must be performed exactly as they are heard in the texts, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, no such person exists who desires heaven alone for as long as he lives.

Therefore, qualification by way of time is appropriate. (The author of the Bhāṣya stated, "Let one who desires a fruit be the occasion [for the rite]," and offered a rebuttal on the grounds of the contradiction between the permanent and the non-permanent; regarding that, he says: This contradiction between the permanent and the non-permanent that was mentioned is not tenable.

How so? Even for one who holds that the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) denotes the result, there certainly remains the contradiction between the permanent (*nitya*) and the non-permanent (*anitya*). For instance, it is known that the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices must be performed as long as one lives, yet they are also enjoined to be performed by one desiring [a specific result]. Due to this contradiction, there is no distinction regarding the result based on the occasion (*nimitta*). Nor does such a contradiction between the permanent and the non-permanent arise here. Why? Because in the case of the *Āgneya* and other [sacrifices], their permanence is not understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), nor is their character as being for a desired result (*kāmyatva*) [understood therefrom].

However, those [rites] which are contrary [to the natural state] by their very nature are enjoined for life-long performance by one sentence, and for the sake of heaven by another; nor is there any mutual dependence between the injunctions for "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) and "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), such that one would understand that whatever is to be performed in the life-long application must also be performed in the optional (*kāmya*) one—by which a contradiction might arise. Therefore, since the origination [of the rites] from the optional and the obligatory [injunctions] requires different [sets of subsidiaries] (without mutual dependence), there is no contradiction. Consequently, this refutation [of the view] that they are like occasional (*naimittika*) rites is improper.
Therefore, the refutation of [the view that it is] a contingent cause (*naimittika*) is explained otherwise:
the word *svargakāma* does not denote a contingent cause.

A contingent cause is expressed either by an absolute locative, as in "he offers when [the vessel] is broken" (*bhinne juhoti*), or by a conditional particle, as in "if he desires both, [he should offer]" (*yadi kāmayeta ubhayam*).
And this [injunction] is not a statement of fact (*tattvārtha*), nor is it connected with what has already been stated.

Therefore, by means of this [injunction], a person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is denoted. (Even in that case, since—by the previously mentioned reasoning—it is untenable for it to have the person as its primary referent, it must have the qualification as its primary referent.)
And as for that person, does he desire heaven as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), or as a means (*sādhana*)? There are thus two types of desire.

If he desires heaven as a means, then—given that [the word] refers to a qualification according to the previously stated logic (namely, the logic of the *svargakāma-adhikāra* person)—the sacrifice must be performed by one characterized by joy (*prīti*). And in that case, the principle of the *tantra* (the single performance serving multiple purposes) applies.
There is no word whatsoever by which the fruit could be intended.

For this term *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) expresses the means (*sādhana*), not the fruit. By this reasoning as well, the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) is not commenced, because without a fruit, the consideration of *tantra* and *āvāpa* would be untenable.
But this has been refuted in the sixth [chapter]:
desire does not exist for heaven as a means.

What is the reason? For everyone desires in this way: "May heaven be mine! Desire is primary with respect to the goal (*sādhya*), whereas it is merely incidental with respect to the means (*sādhana*), because the goal cannot be realized without the means.
Therefore, the desire directed toward the means [of accomplishment] is secondary (*gauṇī*).

Alternatively, the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), which expresses the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), implies a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) after [the activity] has been performed. Why does that implied [goal] fulfill [the requirement] first? For if it were fulfilled by the sacrifice itself, then no one would perform the sacrifice even when it is enjoined.
In that context, the injunction would be nullified.
Therefore, the means to heaven is what is desired; by that, the method is implied.
Therein, the sacrifice is enjoined as the means.

On this point, the text of the *Bhāṣya* states: "That single word which is the designator of these [acts] when they are combined—by means of that, having denoted them, the connection with the fruit is established;
namely, the term 'Darśapūrṇamāsa'.
This is the principle of the *tantra* (common application): "In the case of a common occurrence within a *tantra*... (Tantravārttika 1942).

In the *Tantrasamavāya* (19.43), it is stated: "The fruit [arises] from austerity and [the ritual], because of the single performance according to the direction of the [deities] beginning with Agni, as there is no difference between the two heterogeneous [substances], such as curd and [milk]. Thus says the text.
But when the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) has been placed as the oblation, the *prayāja* offerings take place; this is because they also belong to the two milk-offerings (*payoyāga*),
and by virtue of their being elevated (*udvāttatva*), they pertain to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
They are sacrificed.
Thus, there is a modification even by way of time.
Likewise in the case of the animal sacrifice, the *paśupuroḍāśa*—
When there is attachment to many principal acts beginning with the month, what [fruit] is there even from the six sacrifices?
And in the case of the *caru* offering, there is a modification by way of both quality and time;
therefore, it belongs to the *tantra*.
Furthermore, it must be considered whether the fruit is distinct and different for each respective sacrifice;
there would indeed be such a distinction.
This additional reason is stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
For, since they are connected here by a single injunction of performance (*ekaprayogavidhi*) within the delimited fruit, there is no [separate] injunction;
and because they are prescribed in the midst of a *tantra*, their accomplishment is achieved through the primary *tantra*.
This is the possibility of a *tantra*.
In that regard, in those various originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) of the respective sacrifices, [the accessory] would apply [to all],
because the purpose of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is common to them all;
for it is enjoined as an independent means, and is thus prescribed by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to those [sacrifices].

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there should be a difference in the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice and the *puroḍāśa* offering; [however,] in the sentence stating the result, there is a connection with the result [of the action] characterized by the concomitance (*sāhitya*) inherent in what is to be restated (*anuvādya*).

By the word "or" (*vā*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the Sūtra and Bhāṣya have been obtained; because [the former] is not intended as primary, it is understood as applying to each individually.
And for this reason:
by means of the *tantra* of the animal sacrifice (*paśutantra*), the *tantra* of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśatantra*) would be accomplished.
Why? Because—
The injunction for their performance is found precisely in the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) themselves:

"On the full moon day," because the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) is prescribed within the *tantra* (the central ritual framework), the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*) is likewise situated within that same *tantra*.

And in such passages as "One should sacrifice on the full moon day," there is an injunction for the full moon day alone, because it is that which is being prescribed. [Regarding the sentence] "Having performed the offering of the omentum of the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma, [one should offer] the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma..."
Therefore, by that sentence prescribing the first half and so forth which is generally applicable, it is in that very same [offering] that one says:
"He offers the animal-cake on eleven potsherds.
And thus:
This sacrifice is to be performed;
such being the position reached, even the name serves as an indicator in the originative injunctions,
for the purpose of the ritual system remains undifferentiated.

The meaning of the *tantra* is "the purpose of the *tantra*. Because the injunctive rule (*viniyoga-vidhi*) establishes a connection with the result in the statement of the result, the assistance rendered by the subsidiaries is established.
Thus, in this case, it is undifferentiated and non-distinct from the animal sacrifice,
because it is the object of the rules for yoga, because the sacrifices themselves are what are enjoined as desired for the fruit,
and because of the *puroḍāśa* cake.

The limbs of the animal sacrifice are proximate to those of the *puroḍāśa* cake, because of their commonality of location and because the concomitance (*sāhitya*)— which has arrived through the expression of the ritual procedure— is intended for that same place. Therefore, there is a single performance (*aikatantrya*).

Because it is intended to be expressed, there is only one single manifestation of the fruit for all of them; there is no distinction among them because the object remains unchanged despite the modifications.
Because their status as causes is established through a combination [of factors], like a staff, a wheel, and so forth;
and therefore,
it is logical that their arrangement within a single injunction for performance (*ekaprayogavidhi*) is also established in the manner that will be explained hereafter.
Regarding what was stated by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) beginning with "because of the modification of the accessory and the time" (*guṇakālavikārāt*), he says here:
"There is a commonality (*tantratva*). Furthermore, in this way, [the application of] the sentence "on the full moon day, with the Paurṇamāsī [offering]," and so forth—
The proponent [of the Siddhānta] says:
There would be no distinction between modifications;
for the purpose of one thing is the purpose of the subsidiary.

Furthermore, it would be redundant; for if there were a necessity of desiring the respective true fruits from each sacrifice simultaneously, there would be no basis for the benefit produced by the means of knowledge,
because that benefit remains unmodified— indeed, lacks any modification—
and thus it would be impossible to perform three sacrifices on a single full-moon day.

The animal sacrifice (*paśu*) and the cake (*puroḍāśa*) possess the status of archetypes (*prakṛti*), and their auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) are performed. However, since it will be stated later that this [text] serves the purpose of prescribing a single performance for both,
those very rites performed for the animal sacrifice also provide assistance for the cake.
And because they are qualities, they would be purposeless;
therefore, in the sentence stating the result, [they relate] toward a single manifestation of the result.
Even when there is a change in time, there is no division of the *tantra*;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*),
because the six [factors] are understood as being combined, like a staff, a wheel, and so forth, according to the method that will be explained.
And because it is impossible for some [to perform them],

and because the three [offerings] can be accomplished by a single performance, the Veda [is established] among the subsidiary elements not prescribed by the scriptures that produce curd, milk, and cake of different classes.
The principle of *tantra* (common performance) applies to sacrifices and the like;

likewise, it applies to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth belonging to the same class, as well as to the carrying forward of the fire (*agnyuddharaṇa*) and the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*), according to some authorities.
Even in this distinction, there is a commonality (*tantratva*).

Furthermore, because it is impossible to perform the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*)—such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—again, Maṇḍana [states]: "The fruit of the six sacrifices is indeed one and the same."
The state of being a tantra.
This is the established conclusion (siddhāntapakṣa). Śaṅkara says: "In this context, the fruit [arises] together with the primordial nature (prakṛti)."

He shows that there is a single fire for both the animal sacrifice and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) on the day preceding the Khaṇḍaparvan, beginning with the cooking of the *caru* for the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*), [stating]: "In the middle..."

The entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belongs to the *śrāddha*, whereas the *pitṛyajña* takes place on the following day; this is because the application of the principle of *tantra* (common performance) occurs due to the difference in time, as stated: "He offers the oblations to Agni, the oblations of the *puroḍāśa*, and the oblations of the animal sacrifice."
*Samayamayūkha*, page 75.
By this, there is a distinction regarding the extraction of the fire;
as in "of one fire," that is, of a single fire.

Just as there is an option regarding the *tantra* in the case of "either the *tantra* belonging to the Vaiśvadeva," so too should the observation of the *prayāja*s and other such elements be understood in the context of the *darśa* sacrifice.
Therefore:
From the maternal grandfather's brother.
(Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.288;
Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 163).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) applies to the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*). Regarding this subject of the *tantra*, there is a further discussion in the eleventh chapter (*ekādaśādhyāya*).

The word "gāna" (song) is used even for stringed instrumental music (*tantrīgāna*), as in the expressions "śārīrau" and "gītau"; this should be seen in the *Bālagrantha* under the section beginning with "yārtheḥ."
That which has another meaning within its own system is *sa-tantrī*.
For example: the austerity consisting of fasting performed by the sacrificer in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
"All [are included]."

In the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), there are the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), because of the scriptural statement: "The *savanīya* [cakes] exist," and because of the statement: "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) fast. Thus, in some cases, the two ritual procedures—the animal sacrifice and the [cake-offering]—are combined.
VI. 12|1|2 | Also:
In the case of a collective performance (tantrī), there is a single application for those who are equal because of the injunction;

and because the fruit is accomplished through austerity, it is like the world. But in the case of unequal [performers], there is a distinction, because the commencement of the injunction is for their specific purpose.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites, it is heard as austerity: "He does not eat for three days," "He does not eat for four days. This is because the time is specified by a scriptural injunction intended for that purpose.
That austerity is prescribed in the *Ādhvaryava* Veda;
having performed the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, [one performs] the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for Agni and Soma.
Since it is stated that this belongs to the *Ādhvaryava* by virtue of its designation (*samākhyā*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being thus established:
Regarding the statement, "He offers the cake on eleven potsherds," [the author] establishes the conclusion concerning the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa):
like the purificatory rites, the austerity (tapas) also belongs solely to the sacrificer.
Why?
Because the organs of knowledge are not to be performed separately from the animal sacrifice, but rather they are themselves the limbs of the animal sacrifice,
since they result in the accomplishment of the fruit.

Since the accomplishment of the fruit arises from that [asceticism] consisting of the emaciation of the body and fasting, [the opponent] states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the investigation [of whether] wisdom (*prajñā*) also assists that [accomplishment]: "The state of being the accomplishment of the fruit is *phalasiddhitva*."
*Tantra* means common property; those who possess it are *tantrins*, meaning the principal factors. Therefore.

Because it yields fruit by destroying sin through the giving of the experience of suffering; and because, in the assembly of those possessing authority (*tantrins*), that is, in the gathering of the principal officiants at one time,
the fruit belongs to the patron (*yajamāna*).

As in the world, so in the Veda; regarding the results of austerities such as *kṛcchra* and other forms of penance, there would be no fixed restriction by the Veda, because austerity is characterized by its excellence.
"He shall give.
The accomplishment of the fruit is the duty of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), not that of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Regarding the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is stated that austerity consisting of fasting belongs to the sacrificer because of the designation; therefore, "the austerity belongs to the sacrificer."

This third [section] of the *adhikaraṇa* is for the purpose of refuting what was stated by the opponent regarding the office of the *adhvaryu*. It begins with the word "third" (*tṛtīyā*)—because austerity (*tapas*) is of the nature of suffering, the agent is subordinate; this sūtra establishes that very point.
It removes the doubt that the designation (*samākhyā*) might be restricted by the fact of being hired as a servant (*parikrīta*).

Because austerity is subordinate, even though it belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), who is the primary agent as the means of attaining the fruit, it produces in him a fitness for receiving the fruit, just like a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).

Because of the designation "of the sacrificer" (*yajamānasya*), by means of the Veda and the office of the *adhvaryu*, the restriction established by the title *ādhvaryava* is that the duty must be performed by one whose capability is unimpeded, and not by the *ṛtvij* priests [in general]; therefore, there should be the performance of sacrifice (*yājana*).
Consequently, austerity (*tapas*) is not *ādhvaryava*, but rather belongs exclusively to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). This is the authoritative conclusion.

Furthermore, fitness (*yogyatā*) everywhere is of two kinds: it arises either through the removal of defects—or as this Sūtra also indicates, through another topic—or by the production of a superior quality (*guṇātiśaya*). In that regard, purification (*saṃskāra*) consists of the superior quality and austerity, while the accomplishment of the fruit is the result.

In the section [Jaimini Sūtra] 3.8.13, it is stated that [the *tapas*] produces [results], and austerity (*tapas*) effects the removal of defects. For one who performs the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites—such as the austerity of emaciating the body by the rule "one does not eat here"—there may be defects arising from the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited during this birth, whether in this life or another. Regarding such a person, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the ritual action belongs to the *adhvaryu* priest; the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
There exist defects caused by the failure to perform prescribed duties and the indulgence in forbidden acts within one's birth.

Since it is possible for austerity (*tapas*) to have as its fruit the cessation of obstacles, it need not be postulated as having the purpose of producing an unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) in the form of a new transcendental potency (*apūrva*); for even when such [obstacles] are not removed, they obstruct the fruit of the sacrifice by bestowing a result contrary to that of the rite.
This is stated in the *Parimala*: "They obstruct the fruit of the sacrifice even when it is performed entirely without defect."
This very austerity (tapas) effects the removal of defects;
for it is possible that it requires some cause connected to the sacrifice (kratu).

In this context, the removal of unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is heard of in the relevant section (*prakaraṇa*) as the cause of suffering and is opposed to its effects, occurs through austerity (*tapas*). It must be understood that austerity necessarily assists the sacrifice in some way; thus, austerity is that which destroys the sins which obstruct future auspicious results. (Kalpataru, Vākyārtha section 3.8.13)
In that case, because of dependence, proximity, and capability, there is no assumption of defects;
rather, as in the case of the refinement through austerity, the fruit belongs to the sacrificer himself, which is superior. *Viṣayavākya* 3.8.4.
For it is possible that through the destruction of suffering, one renders unrighteousness unfit to produce its effects. (Vārttika 3.8.13) The removal of opposing factors occurs through austerity.
Just as the performance of penance constitutes the basis for austerity (*tapas*),
so too is the principle of fasting (*upavāsa-nyāya*).

Since even a small amount of suffering in the form of fasting leads to the cessation of great suffering, that austerity belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) and not to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

It is understood from the statement "unrighteousness destroys" that it is to be seen in this very way; likewise here, the accomplishment of the fruit of austerity is like [the case of] the world. Regarding those austerities heard in scripture as being connected with fruits because they are not produced by ritual action (*akarmaja*), such as: "He does not eat here," or "He does not eat for three days"—since there is no other means for the accomplishment of their fruit, [it must be through austerity]. Commentary: Austerity is heard in scripture: "He does not eat here," or "He does not eat for three days. Since these are not produced by ritual action, and because there is no other means for the accomplishment of their fruit, [it follows that the fruit arises from austerity].

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is penance for the sake of the patron (*yājamāna*), such that there is no dependence on the removal of obstacles, and thus it is assumed to result in heaven and the like? Or is it for the priest (*ārtvija*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? On account of the designation (*samākhyāna*), those which are penances belong to the priest; their fruit consists merely in the removal of the fault. Thus, it is concluded that penance belongs to the priest.

This is indeed praise:

Bhāṣya 7.3.8.19:
Here we say:

the word *tīrtha* also denotes merely a member of a religious order (*tīrthya*). However, after stating "he has gone on a pilgrimage" (*tīrthayātrāṃ gataḥ*), certain sacred sites (*tīrthas*) are enumerated, from which it is understood that he intends the specific objects belonging to that region.
But where it is used alone, it expresses merely the sense of "toward" (*tīrthya*);
as in: "He bathes at the *tīrtha*; he becomes the *tīrtha* among his peers.
"Tumo ha muñjamaśno nemedhe rayiṃ na kaścin mamava avāhāḥ."
"Moving through the back of the atmosphere with those [rays] that are wearying,
rushing, and self-sustaining" (Ṛgveda 1.116.3).
This is the nature of the narrative concerning him.
O Aśvins, a certain king named Mujya carried his own son, named Tama, across the sea Umedha; that is, he brought him out.
Here, the second person is used for the sense of the third person according to the rule *tiṅāṃ tiṅo bhavanti*.
The particle *ha* is used for the purpose of emphasizing what is well-known.
Because the syllable *na* has the sense of comparison (*upamārtha*), it is like someone who, being near death, carries away his wealth (*rayi*) to the ocean—this is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).

You two carried that Mujyu out from the ocean by means of *ātmantī* refreshments (*iḍā*), which travel through the back of the atmosphere (*antarikṣapṛṣṭha*), that is, moving through the sky, and which are waterless (*apodakā*) rivers. Thus, you two brought him across.
The suffix *tumun* is prescribed by the rule "The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* [are used] when one action is for the sake of another action" (Pāṇini 3.3.10).
Maṭṭa Āgeśvara maintains that this is the *śruti* of application (*viniyoga*).
In the opinion of Pārthasārathi, however, this is not a Vedic injunction (*śruti*).

[Rather,] these two suffixes [denoting purpose and agent] will apply when there is an action for the sake of another action, or when the meaning of the verbal root is not [directly] applicable—as in the examples "he goes to see Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ draṣṭuṃ yāti*) and "he goes as a spectator of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ darśako yāti*).
(Bālam Bhaṭṭī, pp. 45–46).
This is the analogy of raising one end: by the single action of raising one end of a student, the lowering of the other student also occurs;
it is just like that.
Summary:
The analogy of the balance beam. Just as a balance beam rises slightly and descends slightly; so too does it move up and down with the slightest variation.
In this way, even a sinner rises slightly by a small amount and falls slightly by a small amount. This is the case for the reckless person; it is the same for one who follows the tradition.
The word "ca" (and) serves to exclude the suspicion that [the passage] is a careless reading and to indicate the addition of another reason for understanding its meaningfulness.

Alternatively, by the words "athavā" and so forth in the Vārttika, this very sūtra—"because of being a single syntactical unit with the *vidhi* through the *vicī*"—is applied to the exclusion of the suspicion that it is a careless reading as well. Since its meaningfulness is understood through its equality with the *vidhi* by virtue of being a single syntactical unit, the word "ca" in the phrase "tulyaṃ ca" (and it is equal) has the purpose of adding another reason for the exclusion of its status as a careless reading.
The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice is common to all [the deities], because there is no distinction in the context.
In the Agniṣṭoma, there are three animals: the Āgnīṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya.
Among these, the Āgnīṣomīya animal is sacrificed on the day preceding the Sutyā day, namely the Upavasatha day;
and it is precisely in that context that the ritual details for the animal, such as the binding and so forth, are prescribed.
And in that very same section on the Dharma, prior to the discourse [on the *dīkṣā*], the *savanīya* animals are also prescribed by such statements as "the animal for Agni is to be obtained.
However, the performance of the *savanīya* offerings takes place on the day of the *sutyā*;
the *anūbandhya*, on the other hand, is performed at the conclusion of the *avabhṛtha*.

In this regard, as for those animal-related rites such as the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) that have been prescribed, do they apply to all three animals, or only to two—the *āgnīṣomīya* and the *savanīya*—or indeed to the *āgnīṣomīya* alone, while for the other two they would occur by virtue of the *codaka* (extended application rule)?

In this matter, the first position (*pakṣa*) was introduced by the first sūtra under discussion, namely, "because there is no distinction in the context" (*prakaraṇāviśeṣāt*). Some maintain that, for the same reason—that there is no distinction in the context—the second position was also introduced.
It is clear that, according to the commentary as it was heard [from the teacher], the first position follows the Sūtra, while the second position is presented as being outside the Sūtra (utsūtra).
However, the author of the Vārttika has demonstrated that the first position is outside the Sūtra, whereas the second position is established by means of the Sūtra.
We, for our part, shall present [the matter] by way of the Sūtra exactly as it was heard.
In the sutra, the word "animal" (paśu) indicates the animal-ritual duties (paśudharma) by way of secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Alternatively, since it is enjoined for the sake of another by means of an injunctive term, the equipment and so forth are understood as constituting the animal-ritual duties.

And likewise, the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice—including the preparatory rites and other such animal-related duties—would apply equally to all animals, because there is no distinction in the context;

that is, the context of the Agniṣoma sacrifice is the same for all three types of animals. Therefore, the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the injunction regarding the animal sacrifice pertains to the ritual duties for all animals.

The first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated in the preceding sūtra was that the implements and other such items should belong only to the sacrificial animals, as they are properties of the animals.
Having stated the distinction therein, the second position is now expressed by this sūtra.

On account of context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), and proximity (*sādeśya*), the animal-related ritual duties (*paśudharma*) should belong to the first [animal sacrifice], namely the *agnīṣomīya*.
It is clear that they are not enjoined for the subsequent [animal sacrifice], because even though it resides within the context of Agni and Soma, it lacks [the required] position.

Although it might be possible in some way for the *savanīya* to share the same location, nevertheless, since there is no identity of performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*), those duties do not belong to it either; rather, they belong to the *agnīṣomīya* alone.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhāntapakṣa*).
Let it be that for some, the repetition there is for the sake of a secondary quality (*guṇārtha*);
it can be argued that the ritual requirements (*upakaraṇa*) and other characteristics of the animal sacrifice belong to the *agnīṣomīya* alone, and not to the *savanīya*.
How so?
Let it be for some; however, the word "tu" (but/however) is intended to highlight the distinction from the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice].

According to some [recensions] of the Śākhins, on the day following the *aupavasathya*—the day of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice—it is prescribed by the scriptural statement: "Having drawn the *āśvina* cup, having encircled (*parivīya*) the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with a triple-stranded rope (*tridhṛt*), one dedicates (*upākaroti*) the *savanīya* animal to Agni.
Therefore, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) of the animal sacrifice do not belong to the *savanīya*.
But then, for what purpose is the scriptural injunction for the *savanīya* animal sacrifice recited on the *aupavasathya* day? It is said in reply:

In that context, since there is already an injunction regarding the Savanīya animal, this repeated mention is a restatement; it is a scriptural reference to the Savanīya as being of archetypal (prakṛta) origin, and its mention on the Upavasatha day is for the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality (guṇa).

By way of censure, it attains syntactic unity with the passage, "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing, with the cake at the midday pressing, and with the limbs at the third pressing," and thus serves to enjoin the subordinate quality consisting of the performance of the omentum offering.

And the scriptural passage expressing censure, having mentioned the animal to be offered at the Soma-pressing (*savanīya-paśu*), reads: "Just as a month-old calf, not being recognized, kicks away people, so too these [animals], not being properly identified, kick away people."

The meaning of the scriptural censure is as follows: just as a fish moving on dry land, its movements unperceived by people, mocks the onlookers and casts doubt upon them, asking, "Where has it gone? Or from where did it come?", so too do these [animals] produce uncertainty through a lack of determination, such as, "What should be done with these animals? How do sacrifices become 'possessing animals' (paśumat) by means of these? This is the sense of the censure.

This scriptural passage containing a censure, although heard on the day of the *aupavasathya*, is displaced from that context and, forming a single syntactical unit with the scriptural statement, "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing," becomes subordinate to the injunction of the quality consisting of the performance of the omentum-offering. By this it is known that the animal-related duties pertain only to the *agnīṣomīya* animal and not to the *savanīya* animal prescribed for the [subsequent] pressing. For some reciters of the Veda, the *savanīya* animal is prescribed for the following day.

Furthermore, the meaning of the sūtra is that the repetition of the same [text] is for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa), being a supplement to the injunction of the subordinate element consisting of the performance of the omentum-offering (vapāpracāra).
If it is argued that this is an injunction of time for what has been displaced [from its original context],
the established position (siddhāntapakṣa) is set forth by the nineteenth and twentieth sūtras.
It has been stated.
Furthermore, this sūtra is for the purpose of presenting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

Since the Agniṣoma [animal sacrifice] is prescribed on the Upavasatha day and the ritual requirements and other duties pertaining to the animal (paśudharma) are mentioned in that very context, it follows that those animal duties should belong only to the Savanīya animal; or rather, since they are recited in that same manner, should they belong to both—the Agniṣomīya and the Savanīya?

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the purpose of the statement: 'Having taken the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted cord, he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni'?
It is replied:
By means of that accessory—the performance of the omentum offering (vapāpracāra)—the Savanīya animal is postponed, that is, brought forward, to the second day of the Soma-pressing (sutyā).

And since there would otherwise be no fixed time for the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of that preeminent animal, the injunction regarding the specific time is established by the sentence beginning with "Having taken the *āśvina* cup," which prescribes a particular time; thus, by that sentence, a fixed time is ordained.
Consequently, that sentence serves the purpose of prescribing a specific time and is not redundant.

However, the ritual duties pertaining to the animal—such as the preparation of the equipment, tying it to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), leading it to the slaughter-hall, immolation, dismemberment, and extraction of the omentum—belong exclusively to the *savanīya* animal.
If this is argued, [we reply]:
no, because it is a part of the [injunction regarding] the day.
This is not an injunction concerning time.
Nor is there a displacement of the offering of the omentum (*vapā-pracāra*), nor is there a displacement of the animal (*paśu*) by that [offering].

Even if there were a displacement of the offering of the omentum, since the omentum is but a single part [of the animal], there might be a displacement of the subsequent rites such as the offering of the omentum; nevertheless, there would certainly be no displacement of the preparatory acts and so forth, ending with the extraction of the omentum, which precede the offering of the omentum.

However, by the sentence beginning with "Having taken the Āśvina cup," etc., the performance of all [the rites], including the preparatory acts and so forth, is enjoined as equal for all; for the connection with the *vrīhi* grains is indeed equal for all, and the performance of the subsidiary acts on the day of the *sutyā* is prescribed.

Therefore, the ritual requirements for the animal sacrifice, such as the preliminary preparations and so forth, which are prescribed on the day of the fast (aupavasathya), cannot pertain to the *savanīya* animal; rather, they belong exclusively to the *agnīṣomīya*.
As for the *savanīya*, these requirements are obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*).
If it is argued that this is because of the purpose (*artha*), [we reply: no.
The opponent’s objection:

But surely, when the displacement of the accessory—the *āśvina* cup—is ordained for the day of the Soma-pressing by the injunction "the *āśvina* cup," the displacement of the entire Savanīya animal sacrifice, including the omentum and other parts, is established by virtue of each respective purpose.
And thus, the injunction "the *āśvina* cup" can be understood as a prescription of the time for the Savanīya animal sacrifice.
It is heard in the scripture: "Having enclosed the omentum with his fist, he should remain seated until the offering of the omentum.

Now, it is not possible for one to remain seated from the previous day—having enclosed the omentum with his fist—until the morning pressing on the day of the Soma extraction, for the priests must necessarily attend to their food, movement, and other such needs.

And likewise, if it is argued that all the ritual accessories and so forth should belong exclusively to the *savanīya* animal of the pressing day (*sutyā*) at its highest degree of excellence, and not to the *agnīṣomīya* animal of the preceding day—
this is not so, because it would contradict the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

"If there were a contradiction with the Vedic text stating, 'Having performed the extraction of the omentum with the fist, one should remain [seated] until the offering of the omentum,' then the injunction of time for that which is displaced by the sense of the matter would be respected; however, there is no contradiction with the Vedic text.
But because there is a contradiction with the Vedic text, it is not an injunction of time.
There is a contradiction with the Vedic text."
There is a contradiction of scripture; there is no contradiction of scripture, there is no contradiction of scripture.
Because there is no contradiction of scripture, there is no injunction regarding time.

If the preparatory rites beginning with the *upakaraṇa* and ending with the *visahana* were performed on the day of the fast (*aupavasathya*), and the offering of the omentum (*vapāpracāra*) were to be carried out at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) on the day of the Soma extraction (*sutyādina*), then—even though the slaughterer (*śamitṛ*) would be unable to remain sitting after covering the place where the omentum is extracted with his fist for a period of five watches (*pañcaprahara*)—there would nonetheless be a contradiction or conflict with the scriptural injunction "having covered it with his fist."

However, it can be said that having performed [the rites] with a handful of grass or a handful of leaves as the *śamitr*, one should remain indifferent until the performance of the omentum (*vapā*) on the following day; in that case, there would be no contradiction with the Vedic text.
Thus, it is not a prescription of time for something already established by its purpose.
Consequently, the preparation of the implements and all such items for all the animals must be performed on the very day of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), which is the following day.
Thus, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) maintains that all these animal-ritual characteristics do not belong to the *savaniya* animal, but rather to the *agnīṣomīya* animal.
[He argues] that by virtue of position (*sthāna*), they belong to the former, because the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is for its sake. It is the proponent himself who says this.
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of rejecting the view that [these rites] are for the sake of the *savanīya* sacrifice.
By virtue of position—that is, from their common location—the preparatory rites (*upakaraṇa*) and other such duties belong to the preceding *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice alone;
this is because the purificatory rite consisting of those preparations and so forth is intended for that [sacrifice], namely, for the purpose of the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*).
These properties are employed in the animal sacrifice, not in the Jyotiṣṭoma;
therefore, they are the properties of the Agniṣomīya—this is the conclusion of what was stated previously.
This is also because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).

For in the Siddhānta, this is the supreme Sūtra: "The ritual duties of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*), which are prescribed on the day of the Upavasatha for the Agniṣoma [sacrifice], do not apply even to the *savanīya* animal sacrifice prescribed on that very same day; rather, they apply only to the Agniṣomīya. To this effect, there is seen on the day of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the form of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), namely: "They proceed with the omentum (*vapā*) at the morning pressing, with the cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the midday pressing, and with the limbs (*aṅga*) at the third pressing.
For the cake-offering is intended for the consecration of the deity.
And he is able to consecrate the navel with that which has been prepared by the Agniṣomīya [offering].

Therefore, on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of seeing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the animal-ritual duties belong to the Agniṣomīya alone; for when two things are equal, [the ritual details] such as the husking and the release from the wooden pin (*tuṣkaraṇyavipramocana*) apply to one part of the whole.
The maxim is: "When one part of two equal things is elevated [and the other is lowered], the other part is also elevated.
The connection with the *śruti* regarding the *paurṇamāsī* is: "Whatever oblation there is from this *paurṇamāsa*.
Whatever is stated is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*).
In that regard, the rule does not apply [to the case] of "unequals in one part" (atulyayor ekadeśe).

Bhāṣya 4.4.4.11. Furthermore, there is an equal-like arrangement (*akramaṇa*) for equals, as in: "The gods, the seers, and the Gandharvas were on one side; the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the Piśācas were on the other. Bhāṣya 4.4.1.18. There is also an equal-like arrangement even for unequals, as in: "The gods, humans, and the ancestors were on one side. Bhāṣya 4.4.1.18.
In the section *Tulyānāṃ tu yaugapadyam* (JS 5.1.18), the principle of the common performance (*tantratā*) of subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) will be explained.

And because that [common performance] is not established without the common performance of the principal rites (*pradhāna*), the common performance of the principal rites is implied by the sense of the matter.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 733). In the sūtra *Tulyeṣu nādhikāraḥ syāt* (9.1.5.19), [it is stated... that there would be no entitlement [to perform the rite] among those who are equal...
This is connected with the aforementioned [principle]; for this being so, the action is enjoined by means of the number three.

In that case, something pertaining to the word *sva* (itself) is enjoined by the injunctive element. Otherwise, the relationship between the *ṛc* and the number would be expressed by a word situated in another [syntactic] position, and there would be a remoteness of meaning (*arthaviprakarṣa*) due to that.
Therefore, it is stated that [the word] "three" refers to the accomplishment of the *sāman*.
An objection is raised: "But surely the word 'three' is connected here only with the word 'verse' (*ṛc*);
otherwise, in the absence of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), there could not even be a compound."
To this it is replied: we do not say that it is not connected; indeed, it is connected, and a compound is formed.
However, that word "compound" (samāsa) is taught in the context of the production of the *sāman*.

In that case, the meaning of the word *tri* (three) and the word *ṛc* (verse) would be taught in terms of completion (*nirvṛtti*). The *sāman* is to be brought into completion within the *ṛc*; thus, those *ṛcs* become three, not fewer.

On the other hand, in the alternative view, the repetition (*abhyāsa*) is connected with the number three; in that case, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) such that "the *sāman* is performed [therein]," because the term "completion of the *sāman*" would apply even when the completion of the repetitions has not yet occurred.
Therefore, the chanting of Vyāsa must be performed.
The Sāman that is to be sung upon a triplet (tuce) and which serves as the means for the Stotra is called "stotrīya."
Furthermore, the *sāman* lacks the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *stotra*, because it is consecrated as a means for the *stotra*;
the discussion regarding its being a means for the *stotra* applies to each [verse] individually, not collectively.
Therefore, it should be sung according to its own [original] form (*pratyakṣa*).

The connection (*saṅgati*) here is one of the relationship between that which is depended upon and that which depends (*upajīvyopajīvakabhāva*), because the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) proceeds by relying on the principle stated in the preceding section concerning Soma—that the *sāmans* serve as ornaments for the *ṛc*s—namely, that they should be sung having completed them according to their own form.

As for the meaning of the *sūtra*: the singing should be performed by setting down [the verses] in a triplet (*tṛca*), because the accomplishment of the *sāman* is heard in scripture as "the *sāman* is made," and because the number three is prescribed therein.

However, if [the injunction] were "when it is performed on three," then by enjoining the relationship between the meaning of the word *tri* (three) and the word *ṛc* (verse), there would be a syntactical split (*vākya*) because it would also enjoin the connection of the words themselves. But if, through the sense of the verbal root in "is performed" (*kriyate*), the number three is enjoined with respect to the performance of the *sāman*, then there is conformity with direct audition (*śruti*). Regarding this, [the opponent says]: "The *sāman* is either entirely [performed] upon the verses or verse by verse, because of the direct audition of the word 'three'. [The author replies]: "Not so; it should be verse by verse, since the praise is accomplished by means of the verses."
The word *tṛca* [indicates] existence at that time;

and in cases such as "he has come with his son," [it indicates] the state of having a single connection, and so forth— this should be understood according to the requirements of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).
*Rahasya*, pp. 99–100:

Regarding *Pāṇini* 1.3.20, *yenāṅgavikāraḥ*: the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in connection with a word denoting a body part (*aṅga*) that possesses a deformity (*vikāra*), when it is employed in close proximity [to the word expressing the state of being deformed].
For example: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye").
Thus [it is said].
Here, the meaning is that [the object] is qualified by its relation to the eye.
And in this case, the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) of Caitra with respect to the state of being a part residing in the eye is through a mediated relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*).
Maṇi, p.

133: According to the grammatical rule *yenāṅgavikāraḥ*, which means that the instrumental case should be used for that limb by whose modification the modification of the whole (*aṅgin*) is indicated, we have the instrumental in examples such as *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye"). Here, the word *akṣi* refers to the eyeball (*cakṣurgolaka*) in its relation [to the whole]; the meaning of the instrumental suffix is "subsistence" (*vṛttitva*); and the word *kāṇa* refers to the state of having a defective visual organ (*cakṣurūpatvadīlaka*).

The understanding is that [the eye] possesses the nature of being an eye because it resides in the eyeball (*cakṣurgolaka*), just as [the term "eye"] denotes the state of being an eye. This is because the sense of "residing in" (*vṛttitva*), which is the meaning of the third case suffix, connects with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) through that relation.
(Rahasya, p. 100).
[This is an example of] the "indicator of such a state" (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the desire for livelihood (*vṛttikāma*: 1966), in the case of [injunctions] such as "one who desires livelihood should cook" (*vṛttikāmaḥ pacet*), the Guru maintains that the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which is the meaning of the suffix, is construed with the cooking (*pāka*), which is the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*).
Thus says the Guru.

Maṇi, p. 84: [Objection: "Because the mantra that reveals satisfaction (*tṛptiprakāśaka-mantra*) forms a single syntactical unit with the *bhakṣa*-mantra, the deity is one who bestows satisfaction; thus, Indra, being satisfied, satisfies the animals through the *praṇītā* waters. If this is argued:
Because explanatory passages (arthavādas) lack the intentionality to convey their own literal meaning.
Vi. 4.1.4. The *tejas-kāmeṣṭi* is a separate ritual: "One desiring splendor (*tejas*) should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni.

"By that [is meant] association with them; association with the radiant ones. (Bhāṣya 6.6.2.14). 'Tepānāḥ' means performing austerity;
the sense is 'by those [who are performing austerity]'."

The Taittirīyas, while studying the *Kārīrī* passages, practice eating on the ground, whereas other scholars do not. (Bhāṣya 2.4.2.8, p. 632). This very practice is established by the Taittirīyas themselves in the *Dharmasūtra* and *Gṛhyasūtra* of Āpastamba and Baudhāyana. (Vārttika 1.3.7.15, p. 244). The Taittirīya is one distinct branch (*śākhā*) belonging to the Yajurveda.
The Taittirīya school has internal subdivisions consisting of six distinct *sūtra* traditions: the Baudhāyanīya, Āpastambīya, Satyāṣāḍhīya, Vaikhānasīya, Bhāradvājīya, and Vāghula.
According to the *Taittirīya-ekavākya*, the *samidh-yajus* constitutes the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*).
[Vārttika 3.1.2.16]: By the statement of the *Taittirīya* branch, the acceptance of the sacrificial vessel is established as belonging to the giver.
But for the Maitrāyaṇīyas, it is accepted [as authoritative]:
"This will be like the drinking of oil" (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 3.4.1.131, p. 169).
Just as the drinking of oil or the drinking of ghee, even though it has been consumed, produces results such as memory, strength, and nourishment at a later time.
Bhāṣya 7.1.2.5: Here, there is a misconception; even for the drinking of oil, the fruit does not arise at a later time.
Its fruit is equal to that of ghee, and that occurs at that very moment.

And as for the fruit, such as strength, nourishment, and so forth, that arises from the proper digestion of food. 7.1.2.17. Regarding the term *toya* (water): "The word *toya* is accepted [as denoting] both a drop and a collection."

Commentary: Let this point remain for the moment unresolved; now, another section of the treatise is introduced.
In the Sādyaska sacrifice, there is the injunction: "The purchase-price for the Soma is a three-year-old steer that has not yet been castrated.

There are also substances for the purpose of purchase obtained through the rules of extension (*codaka*), such as: "He purchases with a goat, he purchases with gold, he purchases with a bull, he purchases with a horse-hoof, he purchases with a garment," and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: does the three-year-old steer exclude only the bull, or does it exclude all the substances intended for purchase?
What is established? That the bull (*ṛṣabha*) is the one who turns back.
Why? Because of its nature as a bull.
By the commonality of being a bull, this bull is enjoined.
Whence [is] the status of being a bull? From the mention of "castrated" (*sāṇḍa*).
Therefore, it is a substitute for the bull.
This being the position reached, we reply:
And the three-year-old [bull]—what is it? It is the displacer of the entire purchase.
It is directly perceived as connected with the verb "to buy" (krīṇāti), and by that, it displaces what is obtained through the extended application (codaka).
Therefore, it is the sublater of the entire purchase and its purpose.
And there is a scriptural indication (liṅga) to this effect.
The Bhāṣya states: "And having established this, [the scripture] shows the indicative mark."
What is the indicative mark? It says this:
"In another *sādyaska* sacrifice, a female cow is the one for purchasing Soma, for this rivalry has been excluded.
If the female cow were the displacer of every purchase, then there would be a similar rivalry in that case.
In this context, while this competition is ongoing, it is not tenable to say, "This competition has ceased.
Therefore, [the three-year-old calf] is the one that causes everything to turn back;
even the three-year-old calf shares the same sacrificial fee (*bhṛti*).
And he too is the displacer of everything.
Or rather:
if the three-year-old bull were the displacer of all, then the female cow mentioned in another *sādyaska* sacrifice would be an exception (*apavāda*) to that [rule] and would stand alone.
In this regard, the view that "this rivalry has indeed ceased" is logically consistent.
For otherwise, if one were to turn back a three-year-old calf that contradicts a solitary bull, the rivalry would still persist;
in that case, the statement "this rivalry has indeed ceased" would not be tenable.
Therefore, [the word] "of the entire purchase-price and the sacrificial fee" [is used].
Soma—[the meaning of the sūtra is: "And the three-year-old bull is the displacer of the entire [purchase-price].
Vi— "The bull is to be set aside by the three-year-old; or rather, the entire means of purchase [is set aside]."
The term *ṛṣabha* (bull) [is used] because of its status as a pre-eminent male (*puṃgavatva*), not because of its being prescribed as the place for purchase.
The entire means of purchase (*krayasādhana*) must be set aside.

In the *Bhāṭṭa* school’s view regarding the *Sādyaska* sacrifice, in the passage "A three-year-old castrated bull is the means for purchasing Soma" (*trivatsaḥ sāṇḍaḥ somakrayaṇaḥ*), since there is no explicit verbal form such as "it should be done" (*kartavyaḥ*), one must supply it. Consequently, in the context of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) involving that [purchase], it is necessary that the three-year-old bull (*trivatsa*), which was previously unestablished, be the object of the injunction (*vidheya*).

Furthermore, if that [quality] were enjoined with reference to the purchase (*kraya*), then since the female gender would apply even to goats and the like when they are accompanied by a bull, the word *sāṇḍa* (castrated male) would result in being a redundant restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already known. Moreover, since the act of purchasing is already established for the Soma-purchase by the sentence "he purchases," the phrase "Soma-purchasers" (*somakrayaṇaḥ*) would be a mere restatement. Nor does it follow that the word *sāṇḍa* would also be a redundant restatement because it applies to the *abhīṣomīya* animal and others where the three-fold cutting (*trivṛttva*) is applicable; for when one of two necessary restatements must be made, it is more appropriate to make it of the subordinate element (*jaghanya*).
And therefore, since the three-year-old state (*trivattva*) is prescribed in every instance, there would be no exclusion (*anidhuti*) of any substance whatsoever.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: it is not merely the possession of the three-year-old state that is enjoined with reference to the purchase (*kraya*), such that there would be the contingency of a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the castrated animal (*sāṇḍa*) and so forth.

Rather, the injunction is of another substance—remaining after the three-year-old female and the bull—with reference to the purchase, because the three-year-old female and other substances serve as the instruments (*karaṇa*) for the act.
Or rather, because [the injunction] is prescribed by means of the delimitation of the substance for those things characterized as a single substance,
it is indeed a sentence (*vākya*).
And therefore, since the masculinity [expressed by *puṃgava*] also sublates the femininity.

Section on the Three-Year-Old [Animal] (Trivatsādhikaraṇa): The *trivṛt* Agniṣṭoma with a bull as the sacrificial animal is a restatement of what is already established (*nityānuvāda*), not a restatement for the sake of etymological derivation (*avyutpatty-anuvāda*).
For this very reason, because it is enjoined by a single designation, the status of being a three-year-old animal and so forth does not apply individually to each of all the sacrificial animals.

Nor is the status of being a single substance established for all purchases merely by applying a counter-argument to even a single case; for if that were so, because there would be a plurality of substances, the use of the plural number would follow, and since oneness is to be enjoined only with respect to the sequential aggregate—just as in the case of the eleven *prayāja* offerings—the status of being a single substance is thereby established.

For this very reason, although there is an exclusion of gold and other substances in accordance with the requirement of masculinity, between these two—masculinity and cowness—it is logical that cowness should be favored because it serves as the means for multiple purchases. Thus, since the requirements for subsequent purchases are fulfilled through that [cowness] alone by way of *prasaṅga*, even the quality of being a goat (*ajatva*) is set aside. It is clearly stated in the *Kaustubha* that "only a male three-year-old [goat] delimited by cowness is to be understood as the one [animal] for all purchases.
Therefore, there is an exclusion of other substances.

For this very reason, in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—which constitutes a single ritual complex (*nikāyabhūta*)—the reference to those competing, as in "The cow for purchasing Soma is set apart; let her compete with those who hate," is also consistent, because there is no other substance [present].

"Because it is non-contradictory.

However, where the adoption of a meaning well-known in the Veda is simply not possible—as in such passages as "Having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-stranded cord, he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni"—there the meaning well-known in common worldly usage alone is to be accepted.
But it is not so in other cases as well.

Thus, by the same reasoning, for the words *caru* and *aśvavāla* as well, only the meanings established in the Veda are the means for establishing the *apūrva*, not the worldly meanings. Accordingly, having prescribed "The *prāyaṇīya* oblation is a *caru* made of rice" and "The sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is made of *aśvavāla* grass," the scriptures state "Aditi [is satisfied] with the *odana*" and "Those hairs have become *kāśa* grass. Since the *odana* and *kāśa* are thus understood from the revealed texts (*śruti*), and because there is a rule that the subject matter of the injunction and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) must be identical, those two alone constitute the meaning of the words *caru* and *aśvavāla*.

Nor will it be stated that, by relying on a figurative sense, the praise of a horse's foal well-known in the world— such as "the Trivṛt is like a chariot" or "the Traidhātavīya [is like] a young colt"— is [merely] a figurative application.
Therefore, the word *trivṛt* can refer to the nine-verse hymn (*ṛc*) contained within a chant (*stotra*), but not to triplicity;
the word *caru* refers to boiled rice (*odana*), but not to a cooking pot (*sthālī*);
