In this regard, the following observation is appropriate: if there were a repetition like that of a "man with a staff" (daṇḍakalita), then the sequence would begin again with the cup for Indra and Vāyu (aindravāyavāgra).
How so? When the days are calculated starting from the Trivṛt and proceeding in groups of nine, six days remain over in the first fortnight.

In that case, in the seventh [day], the sequence begins with the Aindravāyava; the Vijuvān has the Śukra first; the first Kharasāman has the Āgrayaṇa first; and then follows the Viśvajit—thus the *jyanīkā* is completed.
However, it reaches the Trayastriṃśa day with the Aindravāyava first, which contradicts this observation.
Therefore, it is an expansion in its own place.
For that [view] in which there is a repetition like a "measuring-stick" (*daṇḍakalita*), this observation—that the *Āgrayaṇa* cup is first on the thirty-third day—is not tenable.
How so? Because in this *Gavām Ayana*, the first fortnight consists of one hundred and eighty days.
In this way, the subsequent [fortnight] is also a [sacrificial] side;
in the middle [of the year], there is an additional day (*adhikamahaḥ*). Therein, on the first part of the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *jyānīkā* is established.
(The *jyānīkā* is a collection of three days, like a triple fruit.)
Because it belongs to the *ajādi* class—an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*)—the suffix *ṭāp* is also applied to a *dvigu* compound.
The word *anīka* signifies a multitude.
And that [multitude], when situated there, occurs excluding two days.
(Why so? Because in those two [cases], the sequence beginning with the Aindravāyava cup is directly perceived.
Furthermore, as it is being inserted into the remaining days—having been repeated nineteen times—seven days remain.
Among them, on the seventh day, the sequence begins with the Aindravāyava.
On that [seventh day], the first section is completed;
however, the *jyanīkā* is not yet finished (because two remain),
and it must necessarily be measured out.
Then (the eighth) is the *vijuvān* with the *śukra* cup first.

Then (the ninth occurs): the first *kharasāman* has the *āgrayaṇa* cup first; the second *kharasāman* has the *aindravāyava* cup first; the third *kharasāman* has the *śukra* cup first; then the *viśvajit* has the *āgrayaṇa* cup first; then the *ṣaḍaha* (six-day period), being reversed (*āvṛtta*), is employed.
Of that reversed [period], the first day is the thirty-three-fold (*trayastriṃśa*) day; it receives the *aindravāyava* cup first.

Thus, this view is not tenable if there is a rotation like the "beating of a staff" (*daṇḍakalitavat*) on the preceding side; however, it is tenable if there is an expansion in its own place (*svasthānavivṛddhi*).

This explanation provided by the author of the Bhāṣya is not tenable. Why? Because in this *Gavām Ayana* sacrifice, the *jyānīkā* (the sequence of sacrificial days) is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), neither from the name nor from an explicit statement, according to the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra.
Consequently—by virtue of the name "Viśvajit," the precedence of the Āgrayaṇa vessel is obtained;
likewise, by the name "Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha," the precedence of the cups associated with the well-known Ṣaḍaha is obtained;
and similarly, in the Abhiplava [Ṣaḍaha], by the names [such as] "Jyotis," "Gauḥ," and "Āyuḥ," the ritual procedure of the one-day sacrifices (*aikāhika*) is obtained.

The Abhiplava ṣaḍaha consists of [the days]: Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus; Gauḥ, Āyus, Jyotis. In that [six-day period], the Bṛhat [Sāman] occurs on the days designated as Jyotis, and the Rathantara on the days designated as Ayus.
In that regard, the ritual rules of the Ekāha [sacrifice] beginning with Jyotis are applied.

In the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*), following the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the *aindravāyava* cup comes first when the *rathantara-sāman* is used, and the *śukra-agratā* (the precedence of the *śukra* cup) occurs in those with the *bṛhat-sāman*.
Therefore, in the six-day *abhiplava* sacrifice, these two proceed by way of alternation (*vyatiṣaṅga*), not by way of the *jyanīkā* sequence.
It is logical that the application of the name [of the archetype] takes precedence over what is obtained through the general rule (*codaka*).

(Thus, because there is no *jyānīkā* here, this [position regarding] the locus is untenable. Even if one were to concede the possibility of a locus, he states the impossibility of the indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Even if there were an application of the *jyānīkā* by means of the *codaka*, nevertheless it has been stated (at 10.5.4.12) that the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *daśarātra* are extended (*atidiśyante*) to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
And when the *daśarātra* is applied, even in the case of the first fortnight (the *bhāgadheya* fortnight), a tenfold division would necessarily follow."
For if the nine-night period were not commenced, a ninefold division would result—namely, that nine nine-night periods would proceed.

But when the ten-night period is commenced, within the first fortnight divided into ten parts, the state of having the Aindravāyava cup first occurs in the tenth part. Consequently, when the subsequent fortnight is undertaken in reverse order, that very same part is commenced as the first.
In that case, the precedence of the offering to Indra and Vāyu (aindrāvāyavāgratā) would apply on the thirty-third day (even according to the Siddhāntin);
and consequently, there would be no distinction between the preceding and succeeding [days].
(Even though the nine-night period proceeds, what is this distinction made by the Commentator?)

For one [the proponent of the prima facie view], the calculation begins from the day following the *abhiplava* series, excluding the first two days; for the other [the proponent of the established conclusion], it begins from the *prāyaṇīya* day. (The distinction arises as the sixteenth day is being accomplished.
Therefore, the calculation must be performed identically.

For just as in the prima facie view the calculation begins from the *trivṛt* because the precedence of the *aindravāyava* cup for the *caturviṃśa* day and the *prāyaṇīya* is ordained by an explicit scriptural statement, so too is it in the established conclusion.
Furthermore, in the case of an equal calculation, the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would simply be untenable.

For even according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the three-day sequence (*jyānīkā*) is not completed in the first fortnight; it reaches two days or one day in the second as well, for the sake of equality of the portions.

Furthermore, another distinction has been shown by the author of the Bhāṣya while demonstrating the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the two positions: for one [the *pūrvapakṣin*], the calculation is made with reference to the entire Gavāmayana, having disregarded the statement regarding the three-year period (*tryanīkā*); for the other [the *siddhāntin*], however, the calculation is made within the first fortnight (*pakṣas*) alone.
(Having thus critiqued the Bhāṣya, he himself now establishes the topic and the indicative mark here: To this it is said:
if the three-year period were obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), then these defects would indeed arise.
This [rite], however, is enjoined by an explicit scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*) in the context of the Gavāmayana.

And the ritual details (*dharma*) being enjoined in the Gavāmayana are situated within the preceding sub-context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the first fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), not in the entire [Gavāmayana].
This is because it would be impossible [for them to apply to the whole]; [otherwise, they] would set aside the sub-context and apply to the entire Gavāmayana.
Moreover, there is the possibility of inserting the *jyānīkā* within the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) in that very first fortnight (*pūrvasmin pakṣasi*).
For the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), however, the repetition—like the movement of a staff (*daṇḍakalitavat*)—is not completed in the first fortnight.

This is because his counting proceeds starting from the *trivṛt* [stoma], excluding the first two days; for the precedence of the *aindravāyava* cup is directly enjoined (*pratyakṣaśruti*) for those two initial days, namely the *prāyaṇīya* and the *caturviṃśa*.
And for one who begins [the sacrifice] on the first day, there would be the precedence of the *śukra* cup on the second day;
and this would be in direct contradiction with the precedence of the *aindravāyava* cup.
But is not the precedence of the *śukra* cup also directly perceived, since it is taught here as part of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sequence?
It is said:
the precedence of the *śukra* cup is prescribed in a general sense by the rule, "Now [the sacrifice] begins with the *śukra*" (*atha śukrāgram*).

This remains applicable even in the second performance (*āvṛtti*). However, the precedence of the *aindravāyava* cup is prescribed specifically (by its own independent injunction). And the specific is more powerful than the general.
Therefore, its counting begins from the third day (and thus it is not completed in the preceding fortnight, but rather reaches the first day of the second fortnight).
However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because there is no contradiction, the counting is correctly performed starting from the very first day (the *prāyaṇīya* day).

Here an objection is raised: sacrifices such as the *Jyotiḥ* and others, at the very moment they are being produced, take on their ritual characteristics by virtue of their specific names, just like the *Agnihotra* in the case of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*.
But here, the *jyotiṣṭoma* would be subject to the nature of being a composite (*saṅghāta-dharmatva*).
And that [composite nature] is weaker because it occurs later, due to its connection with arising (*utpatti-saṃyogitva*)—[the alternative reading being:
"because it occurs later due to its connection with what has already arisen" (*upapanna-saṃyogitva*)].

It is said that by virtue of that name, the *āgrayaṇāgratā* is obtained for the proponent of the *pūrvapakṣa* even on the thirty-third day. In this regard, there is both a sequence and a conflict; just as in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the [new] rule, having been established, sets aside the original (*prākṛta*) rule obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) because of the contradiction. This is the section concerning the *tryanīkā*.

In the same way here as well, [the later rule] enters by setting aside that which has attained the name "threefold array" (*tryanīkā*), just as in the case of the *apaccheda* (simultaneous or successive disconnections), where a prior conditional rite is set aside when it is in conflict with a subsequent conditional rite.

Alternatively, as for the posteriority of the name: when the sacrifice is enjoined with respect to the fruit, it is at that very time—and not at the time of its origination—that the requirement for ritual properties (*dharma*) arises. In this state, where there is a requirement for properties due to the [sacrifice's] lightness of result, when considering whether the properties are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) or through the name, the acquisition of properties occurs by means of the name because of its direct perceptibility.
And that name effects the acquisition of properties through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

But by taking the *tryanīkā*, one does not effect the acquisition of the properties [of the sacrifice] called *āgrayaṇa* through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), but rather takes them through direct injunction (*upadeśa*) alone;
and because it is based on direct scriptural statement (*śrautatva*), direct injunction is stronger than extended application (*atideśa*).
By virtue of the explicit statement, there is a transposition among the eleven sacrificial animals (*aikādaśina*).

Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that it is "like the case of the eleven [animals]"—it is appropriate that there should be repetition in the case of the eleven animals, like a staff being paraded back and forth; for there is indeed a scriptural injunction to that effect.
"An Āgneya [offering] is at the end of the Vāruṇa," and "because of the repetition, one should take up the Āgneya itself on the first day";
because of this statement, there is a rotation like a measuring-stick (daṇḍakalita), as it is said, "and because of the repetition.
Since that [rotation] is impossible in a twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha), it enters into the Gavām Ayana.
Who here would not act according to the word? For there is no overstepping of the word;
and because of the observation of indicative marks.

The Commentary states: Furthermore, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) also shows this purpose, as in the case of "they repeat [the cycle] like a measuring-stick (*daṇḍakalita*)," [referring to] the set of eleven (*ekādaśinī*).
[It says]: "The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the set of eleven"; "when they reach the set of eleven, the days are in excess, or the five-fold [verses] are.
When there is purification in their own place, there is no excess; however, in the repetition like a measuring-stick, there may be either a deficiency or an excess.
Therefore, we see that in the case of the *ekādaśina* animals, there is a repetition [of the procedure] like the striking of a staff (*daṇḍakalitavat*).

The author of the *Bhāṣya* has deliberated upon this by taking as his basis the twelve-day sacrificial sequence (*dvādaśāhikī tryanīkā*) obtained through extended application (*codaka*), which lies between the *Prāyaṇīya* and *Udayanīya* days: Is it to be repeated like the striking of a staff, or is there a purification of each of the nine sequences in its own respective place?
(For that purpose, are these ritual properties (*dharmāḥ*) connected to the *prakṛti* as preceded by the individual days, or are they connected to the supreme apūrva?)
And regarding that purpose, is it a property of the object (*artha*) or a property of the portion (*bhāga*)?
Furthermore, in that context, what is intended by "non-mention" (*agrahaṇa*), or is it not? This is the formulation of the doubt.
If there is an intention despite the non-mention, then on the second day, the properties such as having the *śukra* cup first (*śukrāgratva*) and so forth would apply.
"The section on the three series:
first the *śukrāgra*, then the *āgrayaṇāgra*,
then the *aindravāyavāgra*, then the *śukrāgra*, and then the *āgrayaṇāgra*."

Regarding the attainment of nine *agrās* (priority offerings), since many [days] would not be completed [otherwise], there arises this consideration: in the rotation (*āvṛtti*) of the three-day sacrificial session (*tryaha*), should one perform nine *agrās* on the first nine days and then perform another nine on the subsequent nine days—thus following a "staff-measured" (*daṇḍakalita*) rotation? Or, having divided the first half-month into nine parts, should one perform one *agrā* in each part, with twenty [days] remaining for the final [part] (180 ÷ 20 = 9)? This is the question of "purification by its own place" (*svasthānaviśuddhi*). Upon such reflection, because the word "day" (*ahar*) is heard [in the text] and because that [day] alone is the means of accomplishing the result, the *agrā* is prescribed specifically with reference to that [day].
But this is not with reference to a collection of days.

Nor does it follow that, in this way, all forms of *āgrayaṇa* would apply to all days; for by virtue of the order of position (*sthānakrama*), these are obtained as the first *āgrayaṇa* in the first day, and so forth.
Therefore, since the words "first" and so on are merely restatements (*anuvāda*), they are indeed qualified restatements.
For this very reason, these *amrta* offerings are indeed connected with the days (*ahaḥ*).

Consequently, when the nine *ahīnas* have been performed by means of these nine *amrta* offerings, this same statement applies once again; therefore, there is a rotation (*āvṛtti*) like that of a measuring rod (*daṇḍakalita*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the correct conclusion is as follows]: because there is no evidence for restricting either the word *ahaḥ*—which denotes what is to be given—or the context (*prakaraṇa*), according to the order of position (*sthānakrama*).

Otherwise, the restriction that rice is for the sake of the Āgneya sacrifice and barley is an auxiliary to the Āmīṣomīya would be undermined; consequently, the state of having a single *agratā* (priority) would apply to all days.
This is not an acceptable conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would result in the injunctions for the first day and the two subsequent days, as well as the word "new" (*nava*), becoming redundant.
Therefore, by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), the word "first" (*prathama*), the word "now" (*atha*), and the second past foot [of the verse] serve to present the subject matter (*uddeśya*).

Therefore, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), having divided the period into nine parts, one-pointedness (*agratā*) is enjoined for each single part consisting of twenty days. Furthermore, the word "day" (*ahaḥ*) is a figurative restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the accumulation of days. Thus, in the *tryanīkā* passage of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the injunction regarding one-pointedness is made precisely with reference to the first and subsequent parts.

The "portion" (*bhāga*) consists essentially of the day; thus, the word "day" (*ahar*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). And since, in the present context, this is a property of the portion, it is applied to the supreme apūrva (*paramāpūrva*); therefore, there is purification at its own place.

Consequently, on the fifth day of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) during the latter fortnight (*uttare pakṣasi*), the observation that the Āgrayaṇa cup comes first becomes appropriate, as it is said: "The meters (*chandas*) descend in reverse order; the Āgrayaṇa is first, the Bṛhat is the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], and the Stomas are threefold. Thus it is established.
For instance, in the purification of one's own position (*svasthānaviśuddhi*), the *tryanīkā* sacrifice is completed within the first fortnight (*pakṣas*).

Furthermore, that which was performed in the first fortnight in direct order (*ānulomya*) is prescribed to be performed in reverse order (*prātilomya*) in the subsequent fortnight by the scriptural injunction: "They enter the fortnights.

Here, what is enjoined is not merely a repetition (*āvṛtti*) consisting of doing it again; rather, in accordance with another scriptural statement—"In six months they go the way, and in six months they return"—it takes the form of a reverse sequence.

For this very reason, in the six-day period (ṣaḍaha) of the first fortnight, the days proceed in the sequence: "Gāyatra, Traiṣṭubha, Jāgata, Gāyatra, Traiṣṭubha, Jāgata"; when these are reversed, the day of the six-day period becomes Jāgata.

Likewise, in the six-day period of the first fortnight, the Rathantara [Sāman] is on the first day and the Bṛhat on the next day, proceeding in this sequence through the six days; when that is reversed, the Bṛhat occurs on the first day.

Likewise, within that same six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), there is a sequence of stomas consisting of the *triṣṭubh*, *sadas*, *ekaviṃśa*, *trivṛt*, and *tryaviṃśa*; [specifically] the six-day period has the *tryaviṃśa* stoma. When this is performed in reverse order (*prātilomya*), it results in the same configuration at the beginning. Consequently, even when the *tryanīkā* is performed in reverse order, the fact that the *āgrayaṇāgratā* (the precedence of the Āgrayaṇa cup) arises in the first twenty-day portion of the latter wing is a logical indicative mark (*liṅga*).

However, in the case of a repetition according to the "stick-measured" (daṇḍakalitavat) pattern, because the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup is specifically prescribed again on the first two days of the preceding fortnight, the *tryanīkā* sequence begins from the third day.
Consequently, through nineteen repetitions of that sequence, the seven-day connection is distinguished once more; thus, the appearance of the *tryanīkā* occurs in the preceding fortnight.

Therefore, by this indicative mark (*liṅga*) of functional capacity, the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the preceding fortnight is set aside, and by virtue of the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), this [rule] pertains to the entire Gavāmayana sacrifice.

And at that time, the rule of retrogression (*prātilomya*) does not apply to this [period], because the rule for retrogression is prescribed from the second fortnight (*uttara-pakṣas*) onwards, starting from the first fortnight (*pūrva-pakṣa*). Consequently, having taken the *viśvavat* and the *svarasāman* as the first [days], there is the completion of the *tryanīkā*.

Furthermore, if the *tryanīkā* were performed in that same manner [as in the opponent's view], then the second day would have the *aindravāyava* cup first, and the third day the *śukra* cup first; consequently, the *viśvajit* day would result in having the *āgrayaṇa* cup first, which would be a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) beginning with the *aindravāyava*. Thus, there is an inconsistency with the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Nor should it be argued that, according to the Siddhāntin’s position, the injunction of the *tryanīkā* itself already establishes the *aindravāyava*-first status for the two days included in the first part—the *prāyaṇīya* and the *caturviṃśa*—and therefore the further injunction of the *aindravāyava*-first status for those two days is redundant. This is because, while the former establishes the status, the latter serves to remove any doubt regarding its application to those specific days.

Although the *aindravāyavāgratā* (the precedence of the cup for Indra-Vāyu) is obtained by virtue of its being a constituent property (*bhāgadharma*) according to the procedure of the three divisions (*tryanīkāvidhi*), it is nevertheless ordained as being prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of each respective day. The result of this is that the rule of *aindravāyavāgratā* is established even in cases such as the *ekāha* sacrifices—which are modifications (*vikāra*) of that [model]—where, despite the absence of the *rathantara-sāman*, there is no need for extension (*atideśa*) from the model sacrifice. Therefore, because the *aindravāyavāgratā* is established as being based on direct injunction (*aupadeśikatva*) within the twenty-day division through its purification in its own place (*svasthāna-viśuddhyā*), it serves the purpose of sublation (*bādha*) since the same [rule] applies to those specific days here as well.

As for the fact that the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having first described the instructional *nyūnīkā* and then, as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), cited the twelve-day (*dvādaśāhika*) nine-day-related *nyūnīkā* belonging to the Gavāmayana, established the prima facie position through repetition like a "measured staff" (*daṇḍakalita*), and explained the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)— which, as before, is characterized by its own specific place— and the observation of indicative marks (*liṅgadarśana*):

therein lies the reason that since it has been established that [the procedure] starting from the ten-day period within the twelve-day sacrifice applies to all modified forms (*vikṛti*), there is a valid basis for the application of the nine-day-related *nyūnīkā* alone.

Therefore, in the first ten-fold division of the ten *āgrayaṇa*-preceding [days], the tenth part, consisting of eighteen days, would have the *aindravāyava* as its first [cup], because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the tenth day has the *aindravāyava* as its first. Consequently, in the subsequent fortnight, according to the principle of reversal (*prātilomya*), it follows that the first part would have the *aindravāyava* as its first; thus, even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the precedence of the *āgrayaṇa* is untenable.
In reality, however, there is no evidence for the application of the extended injunction (*atideśika*) regarding the *anīka* [sequence] prior to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
For that [result] is obtained in its entirety only in the Gavāmayana sacrifice.
Therefore, a division of that entire [sacrifice] into nine or ten days is more meritorious, provided that this [other] defect is not taken into account.
Likewise, [it is said]: "If one were to offer oblations, he would be offering oblations that have not been previously offered; if he were to offer them [in the ordinary fire], Agni would fly away.
Thus, the silent oblation (*tūṣṇīhoma*) is praised because, when it is performed, both faults are avoided.

Since the internal validity of the option here is established as being like that of the Soma sacrifice, there is no pointlessness to the prohibition; such is the connection of this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
In Mādhavīya Vedabhāṣya: "In this silent oblation (*tūṣṇī-homa*), the well-known ritual characteristics of the Agnihotra are extended by means of the term 'Agnihotra.
In that regard, if the oblation is performed according to the option involving a Yajus formula, the mantra 'Sūryo jyotiḥ' should be used.

Since the well-known Agnihotra begins in the evening, in its first performance one offers in the evening with the mantra 'Agnir jyotiḥ,' and subsequently at the morning time, the oblation is performed with the mantra 'Sūryo jyotiḥ'; such is the sequence."

However, it has been explained here that "since the sun is indeed the light at the very beginning, by this [statement], because there is an absence of a sequence established by nature, it would be unlike the original. That is to be considered;
for in the silent oblation (*tūṣṇīhoma*), the word *agnihotra* which is heard does not serve as a transfer of ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*).

For here, unlike the Agnihotra occurring within the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice, the word "Agnihotra" is not heard in its primary sense, which would allow for the extension (*atideśa*) of ritual properties (*dharma*). Rather, it occurs in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); and a name found in an *arthavāda* does not effect an extension of properties, because its purpose is mere praise (*stuti*). Just as in the case of "This indeed is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices," where the word *avabhṛtha* refers only to the pouring out of the water and does not extend ritual properties;
or as in "Soma is indeed the *vājina* [gruel], the *surā* [liquor] is Soma," and "The *upaśaya* is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," and so forth.

Furthermore, this *tūṣṇīhoma* belongs to the *agnihotra*; thus, because there is no etymological basis for the term [in the sense of] "the offering (*hotra*) for Agni in this," it does not possess the character of an extended application (*atideśaka*), just like the *prāpaṇīya* and other such rites.
This point is made explicit in the fifth book of the *Tantraratna*.

Consequently, since it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) oblation, the performance of its specific ritual details (*dharma*) by the practitioners of sacrifice (*yājñika*) must also be considered.

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: by means of the examples previously cited—namely, that *homa* (offering) and *abhighāraṇa* (sprinkling) occur at the same time, involve the same action, and are subordinate to another—it is concluded that here too it must be an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise).
Furthermore, in the case of the sprinkling, the two options of performing the *homa* or not performing the *homa* are to be considered as alternatives.
Alternatively, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the two [possibilities] because the scriptural texts are equal;

for here, the negation is described as being subject to investigation (*mīmāṃsā*). In the case of a collection of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) whose purpose is the experience of that very investigation, the injunction (*vidhi*) remains established.
"When the purpose has been established, both [the injunction and the explanatory passage] are considered an *arthavāda* along with the *mīmāṃsā*.

Regarding the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), it is heard in scripture: "The exponents of Brahman deliberate: 'Should the *agnihotra* be offered, or should it not be offered? If one were to offer it with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*), one would be offering unprecedented oblations; if one were to offer it [with a formula], Agni would depart. Therefore, one offers it silently. The Bhaṭṭas [hold that] this is an *arthavāda*.

Likewise, with reference to the Tryambaka oblation in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, they deliberate: "Should one sprinkle [the butter] over it, or should one not? If one were to sprinkle it, one would cut off the cattle from the mouth of Rudra;
if one were not to sprinkle it, one would not offer the cattle to the mouth of Rudra.
However, they indeed say that one must certainly sprinkle it."
For it is heard in the scripture: "Indeed, an oblation is not [properly] offered if it is not sprinkled with clarified butter.
Even there, this entire supplementary portion pertains only to the final injunction, and not to the oblation and its absence, nor to the sprinkling and non-sprinkling.

There is an option (vikalpa) based on the hearing of injunctions and prohibitions, such as "it should be offered" versus "it should not be offered," or "it should be sprinkled with clarified butter" versus "it should not be sprinkled.
This is because the power of the injunction is obstructed by the specific nature of the inquiry (mīmāṃsā) into those two.

Nor should it be argued that since the inquiry is possible at the time of performance by relying on both sides during an option, the inquiry would be untenable if one side were to be enjoined, as that would involve reliance on only a single alternative.
Because prior to the final injunction, there is room for inquiry (mīmāṃsā) due to the presence of doubt;
and since that [inquiry] results in a definitive conclusion at its end through deliberation, the praise is logically justified.
Such is this oblation and the sprinkling of clarified butter that, even though they have been enjoined, they must indeed be performed because they possess many more excellent qualities.

The statement "but at home there is no fault whatsoever" is a praise. Furthermore, since the Tryambaka-homa is a *darvī-homa* (ladle-oblation) and is thus an original (*apūrva*) rite, it is prescribed that the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) must indeed be with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). For in a silent oblation (*tūṣṇī-homa*), there is no status as an *agnihotra*-oblation, due to a lack of authoritative evidence.
Nor does it possess the nature of the *agnihotra* ritual, because a name occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) cannot effect an extension (*atideśa*).

Even according to the method of the *Śāstradīpikā*, although it is a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), that [nature] would have to be extended like the *prāpaṇīya* and other offerings; however, since it is connected specifically as the motivator for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) by way of that [consecration], and because it cannot effect an extension, this *homa* is indeed something new (*apūrva*) enjoined as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *ādhāna*.
In that regard, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence for a mantra, the statement "silently" is a mere restatement (anuvāda).
As for the deity, if there is no beginning [to the ritual], it is Prajāpati;
however, the ritualists (yājñika) consider this to be an extension of the rules (dharmātideśa) from the Agnihotra.
In that case, there is also an injunction for silence;
however, in that instance, the authority for other ritual acts must be sought elsewhere.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The recitation ending with *tryambaka* is a praise."
"Śaṅkara [states]: 'The oblation and the sprinkling are constant; the entitlement to perform the ritual belongs to Tryambaka alone, and not to anyone else. Mānava Śrautasūtra 6.1.9.143.
The section on the *ārṣeya* (lineage). One who is capable of establishing the *ārṣeya* status has the entitlement [to perform the sacrifice].
There would be a loss of the *ārṣeya* status.

Commentary: In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He chooses the Ārṣeya; he chooses one, he chooses two, he chooses three; he does not choose four; he does not exceed five. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the Ārṣeya have the qualification [to perform the sacrifice], or not?
What is the prima facie view? That even the Ārṣeya is qualified.
Why? Because there is a general statement: "He chooses, saying, 'May I bestow [the reward].
Therefore, he chooses one or two.
And that is shown by the text: "He chooses one; he chooses two."
Likewise, it prohibits: "He does not choose four, nor does he choose more than five.
For a prohibition of that which is not already established is not possible.
Therefore, even one who belongs to the Ārṣeya lineage is entitled [to perform the sacrifice].
This being the case, we reply:
he who cannot appoint [three] is not entitled [to perform the sacrifice].
Why? Because of the specific statement: "He chooses three."
And it is an injunction because [the matter] has not been previously established.
Now, one might object that there is a specific statement, "He chooses one.
This is not accepted, because there is no injunctive case-ending.
But surely, by means of praise, they are enjoined, as in the passage "he chooses three.
It is replied: the praise applies to the number three alone.
"She shall ordain three;
she chooses one"—this is a restatement of the parts with reference to the three alone.
Even there, it is the number three itself that is praised for the purpose of being ordained.
Thus, there will be an injunction by means of a single sentence.
The statement, "He does not choose four, nor does he choose more than five," will be a restatement of what is already established (nityānuvāda).
Therefore, the entitlement belongs to the Ārṣeyya alone, and not to anyone else.
The injunction "I would choose him whom I might appoint" is a general injunction regarding the act of choosing for appointment.
As for the singular number and so forth, since they are already established by that same general rule, they serve the purpose of praise (*stuti*).
Furthermore, the prohibition of four or more [priests] is only logical within that very same framework.
Alternatively, when the act of choosing (*varaṇa*) is enjoined in a general sense, it is qualified by the number one and so forth.
This being the position reached, we reply:
the general statement "he chooses for the sake of the Ṛṣis" is expectant of a specification, and is therefore qualified by the number three from the sentence "he chooses three."
Oneness and so forth, however, are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the constituent parts.

Otherwise (if oneness and so forth were also enjoined), there would result a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), the postulation of eight [injunctions], and the postulation of an injunction not heard in the text.

If it is argued that the injunction is general while oneness and so forth are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), even so, because of the prohibition of four and more, the split of the sentence remains inevitable.

Furthermore, in the case of the opponent's position—that one should offer [the verses] and that [the sacrificer] chooses [them]—there is no fault, because of the syntactical unity [of the sentence], namely: "How many? Three.
Thus, he who is capable of accomplishing the three *ārpayeyas* is qualified;
and one who receives four [verses] possesses the capacity to accomplish three.
Nor does the statement "one is authorized only if one has such [a number of pupils]" imply that one is restricted to exactly this many.

[Objection: But is it not the case that the text says, "He chooses three"? [Response: The choosing of three is prescribed for one who is able to provide for them. It is not the case that the teacher's statement "I shall entrust [the pupil] to you" is intended for someone for whom the relationship is otherwise unnecessary. [Objection: From the prohibition against exceeding five—namely, "He does not choose more than five"—it is understood that there is indeed a choosing of five. [Response: This is not so.
That selection is inferred solely from inference;
however, the meaning of the scripture cannot be carried out through inference alone.
In the case of selecting three, five [of the remaining] are excluded, nor are they transgressed.
Thus, when praised for its brevity, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is established;
otherwise, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and other such defects would necessarily follow.
Therefore, one who is capable of accomplishing all three [requirements] is entitled to perform the rite.
One should not perform the act of choosing merely by saying "O Bhārgava.
However, in the case of the formula "like Manu" (*manuvat*), whether one chooses one girl or even five, there is only a single utterance: "like Manu.
When it is argued that one who chooses one, two, three, or five [girls] is entitled to the rite, the following is stated in reply.
"In that case, regarding the injunction of the three [sacrifices], because of the reliance on two prohibitions for each, two sentences would result; or rather, three [sentences] would result.
Furthermore, the injunction of one, two, or three [sacrifices] would likewise result, and from that, there would be three sentences."
Therefore, since there would otherwise be an option (*vikalpa*), the number three alone is prescribed.

[Objection: Since there is no incapacity (*asāmarthya*) that cannot be remedied regarding the offering of five *soma* vessels, there is eligibility (*adhikāra*). This is the connection of the counter-argument (*pratyavasthāna*).
[Response: The acceptance of four, five, and so forth is intended; in the case of the selection of the seers (*ṛṣipraya-varaṇa*), eligibility is accepted in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The prefix *vi-* may occur either at the beginning of each [word] or only at the beginning of the triad, as there is no distinction between them. The first [option] results in five [syllables], while the latter leads to a split in the sentence.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that the sacrificer, when undertaking the ritual action, should utter exactly three [syllables], neither fewer nor more.

In the Bhaṭṭa school’s view regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the following is heard in the scripture: "He chooses the Ārṣeya; he chooses one, he chooses two, he chooses three; he does not choose four; he does not exceed five.
In this regard, there is no dispute that one [clause] is an injunction and the others are restatements (anuvādas).

Otherwise, the injunction would apply to all [the gods], as in the section concerning the bowstring (jyārdha); however, one should rather characterize it as pertaining to Tvaṣṭṛ, because otherwise there would result both a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) and an option (vikalpa).
Therefore, "he chooses three" alone is the injunction (*vidhi*).
"He chooses one," "he chooses two" are partial restatements (*avayutyānuvāda*) for the purpose of [emphasizing] the substance of "three.
"He does not choose four," and so forth, are likewise constant restatements (*nityānuvāda*) for that same purpose.
And for this reason, just like one who possesses half of a bowstring (*jyārdheya*), one who possesses half of five (*pañcārdheya*) should also choose only three *śrīs*.
However, those who possess one or one and a half *dadhis* have no entitlement under this view;
rather, they follow the rule of the *manuvat* option as prescribed by another scriptural statement: "Now some, according to Manu, prescribe the one-and-a-half *dadhi* option for all classes."
This view of the venerable Jaimini has been accepted by other sages as well.
Accordingly, Kātyāyana says: "Or rather, [he chooses] after the *bādhriṇī*. Āpastamba also states: "He chooses three mantra-composers according to their respective purposes."
They have also stated other alternatives:
"Or as many as there are mantra-authors," says Kātyāyana;
"Or rather, one chooses one, two, three, or five; one does not choose four, nor does one choose five."
He establishes [the offering].
Here, the number of clarified butter offerings constitutes a separate sacrifice (*yāgāntara*) itself, and is not a substitute (*pratinidhi*) for the *tvāṣṭra* [offering].
Bhāṣya 9.4.14.16–60. *Oṃ*, the section concerning the *pālīvat* [offering] related to the *tvāṣṭra*.
In the *Tvāṣṭrapālīvat* sacrifice, there is an injunction regarding the secondary qualities (*guṇa*) of the ritual release (*utsarga*).
But in the case of the *pālīvat* [offering], there is a delimitation by priority.

The Bhāṣya states: Having prescribed the *pālīvata* [offering] belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, it is said here: "That which has been roasted all around (*paryabhikṛta*) as the *pālīvata*, they do not discard. In this regard, there is a doubt: is the discarding of the roasted [portion] belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ being enjoined, or is it a separate sacrifice from that?
If the two words "aparyabhikṛtam" and "utsṛjanti" are mutually connected, then it is the abandonment of the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ.
If, however, the word "pālīvataḥ" is connected with the verb "utsṛjati," then it is a separate sacrifice.
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is a separate sacrifice.
Why? Because it exists previously and because it is a *pālī* (a sacrificial vessel).
How could that which is qualified by both attributes be referred to by the word "because it is a *pālī*"?
Furthermore, if the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ were being enjoined as the act of pouring out (*utsarga*), the qualification "cooked all around" (*paryagnikṛta*) would not be appropriate.
Therefore, we say that the status of being a *pālī* (an enclosing stick) is enjoined for that which has been consecrated (*paryagnikṛta*), and that alone constitutes the sacrifice.
This being the prima facie view, we reply:
it is not a separate ritual action; rather, by means of the term "releasing" (*utsṛjati*), a specific portion of the previous [action] itself is enjoined as a delimitation.

What, then, will be the result? First, it will not be necessary to assume a measure (*mātrā*). Furthermore, the word *utsṛjati*, enjoining the act of relinquishing (*utsarga*) by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), will not be sublated by the syntactical connection (*vākya*).

On the alternative view that this is a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), the relinquishing—which is already established by implication because the *pālī* is being enjoined by the syntactical connection—would be merely restated (*anūdyeta*) by the verbal root.
Moreover, since the state of being "roasted all over" (paryabhikṛta) is already known from the preceding [text], it cannot be enjoined [again].
Therefore, there is a restriction (avaccheda) of the previous action.
As for what was said—that when the sacrifice to Tvaṣṭṛ (tāṣṭra) is being enjoined, the qualification "roasted all over" would not be applicable—that is not so.
This is not a fault.
Here, the suffix *-tva-tas* [in *pālītva-tas*] is not the primary factor (*atantram*); it does not qualify the object (*nāśau viśeṣyate*).

Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that the son of Tvaṣṭṛ (*tvāṣṭraḥ*), who is qualified by both attributes [being the son of Tvaṣṭṛ and being *pālītva-tas*], is referred to by means of the word *pālītva-tas* alone through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*).
Therefore, it is established that this is a case of exclusion (*avadhāraṇa*).
Or rather—by means of this very same context, it is further deliberated whether the verb *utsṛjati* (to release) also denotes a sacrifice (*yajati*) or not.
Thus, after a sacrifice has been enjoined as "He sacrifices a Pālīvata animal dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ," it is subsequently recited: "They release the Pālīvata animal once it has been roasted all over."

In this regard, since a doubt arises due to the appearance of two possible interpretations—whether this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*)—the distinction is established as being a distinct action by means of specific indicators (*viśeṣaka*), namely the subject matter of the connection between the material (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*). Furthermore: "And it is not recognized here as being identical with the [sacrifice] for Tvaṣṭṛ."
Furthermore, due to the connection with the term *paryabhikṛta*, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result.
For if, in this case as well, both qualifiers were to be relied upon just as before, then it would be understood that it is the very same ritual action (*karman*).

However, here there is no recognition whatsoever of Mahendra as being the same as Indra; therefore, due to the connection with a different deity, the action is distinct, just like the *vājina* sacrifice.

Furthermore, if the purpose of the offering were enjoined by means of the designation "pātnīvata," the sentence would be split because of the lack of distinction from the state of being a *pariṣeka* (sprinkling).
Furthermore, the term "utsṛjati" (he releases) would be connected [to the animal] by virtue of its being for the sake of the sacrifice (*vyadhahitakalpatayā*).
Since the release of it is already established by its own originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the repetition [of the word] would be purposeless.
Nor is there any lack of purpose in the injunction regarding the roasting over the fire (*paryabhikaraṇa*), because that is already obtained through extension (*atideśa*) alone.

Nor can the rule regarding the *tvaṣṭrapālī* offering be taken as optional, because that would contradict its status as a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the introductory passage. Furthermore, it is impossible to demonstrate novelty (*apūrvatā*) on the grounds of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice being mentioned again despite the *paryagni-karaṇa* (circumambulatory fire-purification) already having its function established by the archetypal model; for the *paryagni-karaṇa* is referred to here as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) as if it were already established.

Furthermore, the word *paryagnikaraṇa* is not a designation for the ritual procedure ending with that [act], such that by the force of grasping only that, the restriction to subsequent rites would be understood; nor does it denote time, such that one might assume "he releases [the animal] only at the time of the *paryagnikaraṇa*.

Nor is there any reason to resort to indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since the connection of the sentence is established even through direct statement (*śruti*). [This applies] to all injunctions (*codaka*).

Doubt: Is the clarified butter (*ājya*) a substitute for the previous [substance], or is a different rite (*karmāntara*) enjoined with clarified butter as its material because it follows the previous one? What is the prima facie view? It is a substitute. Why? Because the term "pātnīvata" denotes a substance.
Regarding the phrase "he discards," the act of discarding (*utsarga*) is understood to take place right there.

By the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*), that which remains after what has been used and is still present is meant. Thus, by the statement "he completes it with clarified butter (*ājya*)," it is declared that clarified butter serves as the functional substitute for the animal.
But has it not been stated that the preceding rite is completed?

To this it is replied: the statement regarding the relinquishing of the substance is made with reference to the purpose; however, as long as the word "remainder" (śeṣa) has not been employed, there arises the suspicion that the preceding rite is not yet complete.
Therefore, it is suspected that clarified butter (*ājya*) is substituted [for the *sāmnāyya*].
Furthermore, the expression "he brings to completion" (*saṃsthāpayati*) is not applicable to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result),
because it denotes the conclusion of the rite.
Commentary: We suspect it is thus.
This statement regarding completion occurs in the form "he concludes" (*saṃsthāpayati*).
By this we understand that what was previously commenced with an animal sacrifice is completed with clarified butter (*ājya*) once the animal has been released.
In this case, when a new ritual action (*apūrva-karman*) is being enjoined, its very commencement must be stated.

However, since the completion is mentioned without first stating the commencement, we understand that it is the completion of a previous [action] that is intended, and no new ritual action is being enjoined.
Alternatively, there would be a connection through the enjoining injunction (*codanā*), because there is no distinction from the general rule regarding the performance of the ritual action.
Commentary: Or rather, it is an injunction for another ritual act.
Why? Because the previous ritual act has been completed.
But was it not stated that, when the disposal of the substance or the mention of the remnant has not yet occurred, the completion of the previous ritual act is suspected?
To this it is replied: this substance is set aside;
"he establishes" is connected with the word *pātnīvata* as it occurs in the context.
In this regard, the meaning is as follows: one concludes with the Pātnīvata offering. This very sacrifice is enjoined; and the verb "to conclude" (sthāpayati) is used in its full sense.

Necessarily, some verbal root that expresses a completed state must be employed. In this context, when a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is being expressed, the root *saṃsthāpayati* (he establishes) is used by implication, as it is not incompatible with that activity, just like the root *ālabhati* (he immolates).
And the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is used in this way due to its similarity [to that which remains].

Furthermore, the disposal of the substance is entirely consistent when the sacrifice is being enjoined. Therefore, just as other terms such as *nirvapati* (he pours out) occur in the injunction of distinct rituals, so too the term *saṃsthāpayati* (he completes) ought to be understood as not differing from them.
Moreover, he indicates that the non-sacrificial nature of the *vanaspati* is well-known through that very [term].

The Commentary: It demonstrates for this very reason that the worship of Vanaspati is not well-known [in this context]. How so? "When you invoke Tvaṣṭṛ and Vanaspati, or when you will sacrifice to these two—the ninth fore-offering (prayāja) belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ, the tenth to Vanaspati; one should know these two deities to be present right here. By thus declaring the favor through another subsidiary rite, it shows the absence of the worship of Vanaspati.
Only when the remaining rites are completed does the worship of Vanaspati take place, as in the injunction: "He offers to Vanaspati."

Now, when the preceding action has been completed, then [the subsequent action] would be offered; in that case, the perception of non-existence is logically consistent. Therefore, the preceding action is completed, and this too is a distinct action.
The *saṃsthā* (conclusion) would [occur] at that very moment because of its essential nature (*tattva*).

The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that "the expression 'he concludes' (*saṃsthāpayati*) is not applicable to the *apūrva* (transcendental result)"—that must be refuted. To this, it is replied:

This statement regarding "conclusion" (*saṃsthā*) refers to that which is not actually concluded; nevertheless, because it was previously protected [by the ritual], a similarity of completion is recognized due to the identity of the deity.
In that case, it was the beginning of the *pātnīvata* offering, whereas here it is brought to completion.
Thus, this verbal expression "he concludes" (*saṃsthāpayati*) is appropriate on account of this similarity.

Soma: In the preceding section, this observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "He completes the remainder with clarified butter" (*ājyena śeṣaṃ saṃsthāpayati*)—was indeed raised; and since that indicative mark is only logically consistent if it prescribes a different sacrifice, there is a connection [to the present discussion] because that [previous section] established its status as a prescription for a different sacrifice. The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: In the statement "He completes the remainder with clarified butter," clarified butter should serve as a substitute (*pratinidhi*) for the animal substance, because the ritual action, having been interrupted, requires a material substance.
Vi: "When it is said, 'He completes the remainder with clarified butter,' a substitute for the substance is established."
Or other actions, [are accomplished] by means of discourses and utterances concerning the remainder of a gift to the fire.
Because it is accepted as being completed [by the previous], because it follows from the mention of the deity,
and because of its similarity, the remainder [of the action] is a sacrifice in the case of the "confinement" (saṃkṣiti), just like the "touching" (ālambhana) and other such acts.
Bhaṭṭa: There is a further objection regarding the *pātnīvata* passage.
For there, after stating, "He releases the *pātnīvata* having performed the *paridhi*-making," it is heard: "He completes the remainder with clarified butter (*ājya*).

Since the completion of the remainder would be impossible if [the *pātnīvata*] were an entirely new act (*apūrva*), the duty to perform the principal sacrifice is enjoined by extracting it immediately following the *paridhi*-making sentence.

And since there is no evidence for the omission of other [substances] when one trusts in that performance— even though substances such as the *viśvajit* have been omitted— it is enjoined that "one should complete the remainder, such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *prayāja*s, with clarified butter (*ājya*).

Although clarified butter is already established for the *prayāja*s and so forth in the case of the *tvāṣṭra-pālīvata* animal sacrifice in the southern fire, nevertheless, the injunction regarding clarified butter for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *anuvākyā*, and the *yājyā* is not contradicted.

Nor should it be suspected that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering also obtains clarified butter (*ājya*) by the very rule "for whom all oblations [are destroyed]," on the grounds that the *jyāṅga* (the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt*) is impossible due to the absence of trust; for its obtainment occurs because of the absence of causes such as destruction, and because the obtaining of trust is logically established even for the sake of the *jyāṅga*, since trust applies equally to both the subsidiary and the principal acts. Furthermore, the injunction regarding clarified butter in the *vanaspati-homa* and other rites is also thus explained. Indeed, there is no evidence here for any separate ritual act; on the contrary, there would be an inconsistency regarding the remaining portions and the completion of the rite.

This being the prima facie position, it is replied: when asked, "That you invoke Tvaṣṭṛ and Vanaspati—will you sacrifice to these two as well? the reply is, "The ninth fore-offering (prayāja) belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ, and the tenth belongs to Vanaspati; it is precisely here that these two are to be placed. Since this statement regarding Vanaspati—which is a subsidiary part (aṅga)—is made for the purpose of favoring [the sacrifice] through another subsidiary, it is understood that [Vanaspati] does not exist [independently]. And since that [existence] would be untenable without a new transcendental result (apūrva), the preceding sentence does not enjoin merely the principal act; rather, it is an injunction of the subsidiary ending with that [act], which results in a new transcendental result (apūrva).

And although the invocation of the deity (*devatā-āvāhana*) is not even applicable to the *vanaspati* offering when it is not being performed, nevertheless, because of the mention as if it were already established and because [otherwise] it would be inconsistent, an injunction for the invocation must be inferred.

However, Tvaṣṭṛ is excluded from the invocation precisely because he is the principal deity (*pradhāna-devatā*), and the inclusion of the ninth [verse] is intended to refer to the absence of the act of casting [the oblation].

Consequently, since there is no remnant (*śeṣa*) in the preceding rite, the prescription of clarified butter (*ājya*) is untenable; therefore, this is indeed a distinct rite characterized by the substance of clarified butter, following the model of the *upāṃśuyāja* like the *anuṣakta-nīvi*.

However, the two words *śeṣa* (remainder) and *saṃsthā* (conclusion) are somehow merely restatements (*anuvādaka*) of the previous ritual action, referring to its state where the effort [of performance] has not yet been completed. Thus, the threefold modification (*ūha*) is established.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The *saṃsthā* is a separate sacrifice performed with clarified butter (*ājya*)."
94. Śaṅkara: "Even by the words 'the remainder of the clarified butter,' the sacrifice [is indicated]."

Because the previous ritual act of the Tvaṣṭṛ-Pātnīvata animal sacrifice is concluded by the injunction, "He releases the Pātnīvata [animal] after it has been made *paryagni-kṛta*," which prescribes the completion precisely at the end of the *paryagni-karaṇa*, the use of the fifth verbal suffix (*liṅ*) in the word *saṃsthāpayati* (he completes) for the sake of favoring the remnants is understood—just as in the case of the injunction of a distinct ritual act qualified by clarified butter (*ājya*) in the passage "He performs [it] with clarified butter"—to refer to a different ritual act characterized by clarified butter. This is because the word "remnant" (*śeṣa*) applies according to the principle that it belongs to those parts other than the single part already employed; and since it is a sacrifice qualified by clarified butter, it is a different ritual act from the previously employed Pātnīvata animal sacrifice, as indicated by the instrumental case ending. Alternatively, the use of the word "remnant" may apply to that portion [of the sacrifice] due to the similarity in having Tvaṣṭṛ and the Patnīs as deities. Bhāṣya 12.1.17:

Because of the difference in location, there is a distinction between the two locations, namely "southern" and "northern";
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
If it is argued that [this is] not an injunction (*acodanā*), [we reply: no.
The proponent says:

Regarding the fruit of the *māsya* and *āmiṣā* offerings to be performed in the southern sacrificial hall (*dakṣiṇavihāra*), there is no injunction (*codanā*), nor is there a mandate (*vidhāna*). Rather, there is only a mention (*audanā*) of the *mārutī* offering in relation to the Varuṇapraghāsa rites. Thus, since there is no injunction for the ritual action itself, there is no attainment of its constituent parts (*aṅga*); how then could there be a unified performance (*tantra*)?
If this is argued, it might be so; [it would be] the full moon day (paurṇamāsī). The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says:
There may be the attainment of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) in the southern sacrificial hall (*dakṣiṇavihāra*).

Just as in the case of the full-moon sacrifice, where it is said, "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī [offering] on each full moon," the ritual action is not enjoined merely with respect to its fruit, yet it is nevertheless performed on the full moon together with its constituent parts; so it is here as well.
In the southern fire, [the offering is made] with the *dakṣiṇā*.
"If it is argued that this is an injunction for the performance," the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies again:
"It is appropriate [to apply it] on the full moon day."

By the verbal suffix in "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), there is an injunction for performance; an injunction for the performance of the Full Moon sacrifice is thus made, and performance consists of the primary and auxiliary rites.
Therefore, in that case, it is performed with its auxiliaries.
Thus, the illustration is dissimilar.
If this is argued, then here the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) says:

Likewise, as in the case of the *paurṇamāsī*, here too in the *mārutyā* sacrifice, by the word "places down" (*āsādayati*) in the passage, "He places down eight offerings for the Aśvayuj constellation in the northern [altar], and those dedicated to the Maruts alone in the southern," a sacrifice itself is enjoined through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as in the cases of "he offers" (*nirvapet*) or "he touches" (*ālabheta*). And thus, there is a distinct ritual action for each of the various deities.
If it is argued that this refers merely to the act of placing down (*āsādana*), [we reply: no.
The opponent says:

By the word "one should sacrifice on the full moon day" (paurṇamāsyāṃ yajeta), a sacrifice is expressed. But by the word "he places down the offering dedicated to the Maruts" (mārutīṃ pratiprasthātā āsādayati), a sacrifice is not expressed; rather, it expresses placing or setting down.
And if it is argued that, in that case, there would be no attainment for those who are ignorant, we say:
no, because [the rule] forms a single syntactical unit with what follows.
The proponent says:
This is not a fault.
Even though the word "āsādayati" (he places) denotes the act of placing, nevertheless, that [placing] is solely for the purpose of the oblation, not for some unseen transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*).
Because the sentence concerning the southern altar— “The offering to the Maruts alone is placed in the south”— forms a single syntactical unit with the sentence concerning the northern altar,
“He places the oblations in the northern hall,” the act of placing (*āsādana*) expressed by the word *āsādayati* in both cases is solely for the purpose of the oblation (*homārtha*).
Therefore, there is the attainment of the subsidiary elements (*aṅgānām*) in both locations.
Because it is not directly expressed.

In reality, however, by the word *āsādayati* (he places down), the placing down for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*) is not expressed; for the placing down of the sacrificial materials (*havīṃṣi*) on the altar (*vedi*) is already established by the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, by the word *āsādayati*, just as in the cases of *nirvapet* (he should offer) or *ālabheta* (he should seize), the sacrifice itself is denoted through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And thus there is the attainment of ignorance.
Therefore, let there be non-difference between the two meditative states (vihāras). The scriptural statement is likewise.

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) states the following as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) that the word *āsādayati* refers, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to the performance of the sacrifice:

"Whatever the Adhvaryu does, the Pratiprasthātṛ does in response. Just like that [performance] in the northern sacrificial area (*uttaravihāra*), this scriptural statement of the Veda declares that the same performance applies to the southern sacrificial area (*dakṣiṇavihāra*) as well.
Therefore, the word *āsādayati* denotes the performance of the sacrifice itself through secondary indication.
Consequently, there is the acquisition of the *ajña* offerings.

That alone is what is to be given;
because of its connection with that gift—namely, because of its connection with the act of giving while it is specifically characterized by one's own ownership.

this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [The view of] Ke.
is that in the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is a gift of only one's entire property as it exists at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇākāla*).

In that context, they recite this: "A cow, a horse, a mule, a donkey, a goat, sheep, rice, sesame seeds, and beans—this is its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), consisting of one hundred and twelve [animals and items]."

In that regard, there is a doubt: is the giving merely a religious duty (dharma), or is it the giving [of a fee] to the officiating priests? What is the prima facie view? The giving to the officiating priests would be merely a religious duty.
For its performance is indeed heard [in the injunction].
From this word, the performance of giving is understood:
"The gift to the officiating priest (ṛtvij) is to be performed; then he gives to them. Thus, by the very force of the context, it does not include the hiring [of priests] and so forth.
Moreover, courtesy (dākṣiṇya) is heard of in some cases as being according to the specific ritual action: a thousand [cows] in the Vaidhātavīyā sacrifice, and Soma-pressers at the Ṛtapeya.
Furthermore, a purchase is made through the high or low value of the sacrifice; that constitutes a barter, not a gift where the quantity is fixed.
Therefore, a gift is merely a religious duty (dharma).
Moreover, it is performed with observances and with mantras;

thus, it is understood to have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). And in some cases it is heard [in scripture]: "The staff, the sandals, and the dry [leather]—this indeed is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
For who indeed would bend [the mind] by means of a staff?
Therefore, the gift is merely for the sake of the Dharma;
or rather, it is for the purpose of hiring, because of its connection with the ritual action, as is seen in the world.
Commentary: Or, the gift is for the purpose of hiring.
Why? Because of the connection with ritual action.
It is heard in scripture regarding those connected with ritual action: "He gives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij)."
In this regard, it is impossible for me to imagine a purpose other than the visible one.
Even that "unseen" merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction is indeed for the sake of a visible purpose:
by means of this restricted gift characterized by specific qualities, the priests, being gratified, become the cause of prosperity.
How so? Renunciation is understood as being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), not as being primary (*pradhānabhūta*).
The meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) must necessarily be accepted;
otherwise, the phrase "to the priests" (*ṛtvigbhyaḥ*) would be devoid of syntactic meaning.
When something is not seen, the scriptural statement is all the more sublated;
for it is said that "the sacrificial fee (dākṣiṇya) is not in accordance with the ritual act.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating "he whom one intends through an action is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*)," the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is indeed pervaded (*vyāpyamānatva*) by the object-case-factor (*karmakāraka*) which is itself pervaded by the action. Thus, when any pervaded entity is considered as that which is most desired to be reached (*īpsitatva*), then by the maxim "that which is pervaded by the unpervaded is all the more pervaded," the Maitrāvaruṇa alone possesses the status of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*).
However, in the case of Vedic knowledge and the like, because of sublation, heaven and so forth alone are the intended objects (*uddeśya*).

If this is so, then the grasping of the staff has that [heaven] as its purpose, and thus it does not have an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) as its purpose either. Nor is there any inconsistency in the accusative case in "the staff" (*daṇḍam*); for, as in the case of the *saktu*, it has the sense of indicating instrumentality (*karaṇatva*).

To this we reply:

Even though [the substance] is an object of action (*karman*) according to the Vedic injunctions, a restriction of its function is possible in the present case as well, by way of being an intermediate disposal (*pratipatti*) for the purpose of giving, following the logic of the sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings (*prayājaśeṣābhighāraṇa*).

Nor is this case distinct from that principle because of the absence of a requirement for a subsequent performance due to the lack of an occasioning factor (*kalpaka*); for, out of fear of assuming a power in the injunction of giving to necessitate another staff, one accepts a contraction of its function, whereby the requirement for it arises in the interim.
It is observed in the world that even when complying with another's request, one may—by contracting one's own duty regarding a necessary object—bring that object forward prematurely.
And here, since it cannot be said that this [staff] assists the Maitrāvaruṇa priest by virtue of its own sentence, its status as a means of disposal (*pratipatti*) in that respect can be asserted.
Even though there is no relinquishment of one's own ownership, the performance of the *preṣa* and *anuvacana* is possible through mere surrender.
Consequently, because it is subsumed under the act of disposal (*pratipatti*), the status of the consecrated person’s staff (*dīkṣitadaṇḍa*) as being for that purpose is established.

In this very context, there is the giving of all staffs to all [officiants]; and thus, since the Vedic injunction for giving is intended for those who live by the staffs employed by others, and because of the *preṣa-anuvacana*, the consecrated staff does not imply other staffs when its purpose is fulfilled. However, in cases such as the *tantra-aśāda*, the implication of other staffs is indeed accepted, according to the logic of the "anointing of the axle" (*akṣāmyañjana-nyāya*) [Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.10].

In the Śrauta rules for the giving [of the staff], because only one eye is mentioned, the giving of only a single staff serves as an auxiliary to the Maitrāvaruṇa; thus, it should also be understood that there is only one staff during all the *preṣa* and *anuvacana* recitations.

This statement was made with the intention of there being no such rule, since the statement prescribing the staff for the initiated (*dīkṣita*) has been written by some followers of Pārthasārathi in their Mīmāṃsā works.

In reality, however, since the Taittirīya recension contains the statement "When he gives the staff to the consecrated one" (*yadīkṣitadaṇḍaṃ prayacchati*) along with its explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there is no harm even if one assumes that the disposal (*pratipatti*) is optional in the sentence "when [the Soma] has been purchased" (*krīte*), which lacks mention of the consecrated staff; for by the Taittirīya sentence itself, since the word *maitrāvaruṇa* is not heard, the giving is established as a disposal.

But in the "purchased" sentence, because the word *maitrāvaruṇa* is heard, it sublates the former, and according to the principle of subsidiarity (*tadanyāyaḥ*), it serves solely for the benefit of that [officiant].

Therefore, since the *taittirīya* sentence requires a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) for the verb "to give" (*yacchati*), and because the assumption that the staff mentioned in the *krīta* (purchase) sentence is independent would involve the fault of excessive complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*), it is established—by virtue of mutual requirement—that the staff of the initiated (*dīkṣita*) alone serves as a subordinate aid (*upakāra*) for Maitrāvaruṇa.

Nor should it be argued that, since the connection with initiation (*dīkṣā*) can be enjoined regarding the very staff already prescribed in the *krīta* sentence within the *taittirīya* passage, this [latter] sentence is not a disposal (*pratipatti*) injunction. For if that were the case, even if the initiated one were enjoined with reference to the staff, there would be a violation of the principle of "single thrust" (*ekaprasaratā*).
The Principle of Bestowing a Staff (Daṇḍadānanyāya): 2003.

There is no evidence for the view that giving is a purposeful action (*arthakarma*) because it would result in a syntactical split (*bhaṅga*). Furthermore, if one were to enjoin both the time and the Maitrāvaruṇa priest by way of restating the gift of grass (*prāsada*), it would entail a syntactical split.

Therefore, the injunction for giving applies in both cases. Among these, in the sentence concerning the staff of the initiated (*dīkṣita*), it is indeed an injunction for disposal (*pratipatti-vidhi*), because no recipient is mentioned and the word "initiated" is heard.
In the sentence concerning the purchased [Soma], however, by the reasoning already stated, it is simply a primary act (*arthakarma*).
The purpose in both cases is as previously explained.
In reality, however, even in the sentence concerning the purchase (*krīta*), because the *preṣa* (direction) and *anuvacana* (recitation) are appropriate,
the word *dadhi* [in the context of] *dadhi* signifies the sacrificial portion (*bhāgadheya*).
"Devoted to Tathatā, devoted to Kaṅkaṭaka, devoted to the barber"—this means "devoted to the gods," that is, having the gods as one's portion (*devabhāga*).
Bhāṣya 10.8.2.32. Curd is of two kinds: both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) in the Agnihotra oblation.

Vārttika 3.2.7.4, p. 722: In the statement "One desiring keen senses should offer curd," because of its connection with the oblation, the fruit results from the accessory (*guṇa*) of curd and so forth, and not from a separate oblation characterized by curd as its accessory.

Vi. 5.1.1, varṇaka 2: From the two sentences "one should offer with curds" and "for one desiring sensory power, [one should offer] with curds," both the optional (*kāmyatva*) and the obligatory (*nityatva*) nature of the curds in the Agnihotra are established. 4.3.3: In such cases as "one should offer with curds" and "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), there is an injunction of curds and rice-grains as subordinate factors (*guṇatvena*), because it is possible for them to be the names of the sacrifice (*yāganāmatvāt*).

Bhāṣya 5.4.2.4–4: Regarding the single substance *dadhi* (curd), when it is stated that its being for the purpose of purchase (*kraya*) and its being for the purpose of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) are due to the principle of "separation of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*)—as in the injunctions "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and "one desiring sensory power should offer with curd" (*dadhendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*)—an objection is raised under the sūtra "If it be said: [it is] a subsidiary" (4.3.6). This objection suggests that because the curd enjoined by "he offers with curd" has an expectancy for a result, and because the statement regarding the result of sensory power forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the former, there is no "separation of connection. In response, the sūtra "Not so, because of the separation of purpose" (4.3.7) will state that since the curd enjoined for the sake of the oblation (*homārtha*) has an expectancy for a result, there is no single syntactical unity [between the two injunctions].

Su. Pṛ. 827: This is the nature of curd, that what was commenced by previous [agents] is brought to completion on a subsequent day. Bhāṣya: It would be so because of the commonality of its formless nature.
It has been stated that the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya-paśu) is a modification (vikāra) of the Sāṃnāyya offering.
Now, a specific detail regarding that must also be stated:
this animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma should be a modification of the curd (dadhi) which is contained within the Sāṃnāyya.
The concluding rite (*vidhyanta*) [of the *dadhigraha*] applies to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*),
because of the commonality of form (*mūrti*).
Form (*mūrti*) means the state of being solid or dense (*ghanarūpatva*).
"The animal is thick, and the curd is also indeed thick.
Or rather, it is milk, because of the commonality of time.
By using the word "or" (vā) to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Curd is not the primary material; rather, milk is the primary material because of the commonality of time.
Milk is of the same time-period [as the sacrifice], and the animal victim is also of the same time-period.
Thus, milk is the more proximate (antaraṅga) factor.

But curd (*dadhi*) is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) because it is the time for grasping [the material], due to its sequence following [the animal sacrifice]. He states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Milk has immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) to the animal, whereas curd is separated from it by milk.
For this reason as well, milk is the more intimate (*antaraṅga*) factor; thus, it alone is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the animal, not the curd.
Furthermore, liquidity (*dravatva*) is common to both.
If it is argued that the milk of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma is not its "prakṛti" (original material), because milk is liquid while the animal is solid—
this is not so; for even though some parts of the animal are solid, some parts are indeed liquid as well.

Thus, the liquidity of the milk and the liquidity of the animal are indistinguishable and identical. Therefore, the conclusion is that the procedural details (*vidhyanta*) of the *sāṃnāyya*—which is a portion of the sacrificial milk used in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*)—apply to the milk of the *agnīṣomīya* animal. [Question: Do the ritual properties of the *praṇītā* water, intended for the sacrificial offering, assist in the cooking of the curd?
The principle of the curd-and-sugar (dadhnisitānyāya): the curd-offering (dadhigraha) is occasional (naimittika). The principle of the curd-and-sugar.
Regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses, because of the injunction, "One places the *praṇava* at the beginning of the *ṛc*," the *praṇava* must be employed when they are being recited.

And as for that [application], it may be either mixed with the syllables of the *ṛc* according to the analogy of a jujube fruit in a bowl, or mixed with them according to the analogy of curd and sugar; thus, it is possible even through the medium of curd.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In *Saṃkarṣa* 4.1.11, regarding the rule “the last [element] of curd” (*dadhnas caram*) in the sacrifice to Candrāmbudita,
the ritual requirements (*dharmāḥ*) pertaining to the offering (*ijyārtha*) must be performed upon the curd.
In *Bhāṣya* 9.4.14–42, it is stated that by the rule “the last of curd,” the ritual requirements for the substance to be offered (*pradeyadharma*) would not apply to the curd.

9|4|14|43-44. In the absence of curd, [curdled] milk (*payo dadhi*) is also produced by means of another acid, such as sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and the like. In that case as well, the term *āmikṣā* applies.
(Bhāṣya).
Curd and other such substances serve both as obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) requirements.

In the context of the Agnihotra, while the injunction "he offers with curd" serves the obligatory purpose, the injunction "one desiring sensory power should offer with curd" serves the occasional purpose.
(Bhāṣya 4.3.3–7). The bringing of the curd is employed for the purpose of the Āmikṣā offering.
That which is pervaded by an action directed toward a specific object belongs to that [object] as its "instrument" (*prayojya*).
