*Bhāṣya* 4.1.1. This is the maxim of curd and milk (*dadhi-kṣīra-nyāya*). Now, if it is argued that the nature of this maxim consists in a transformation into another state through the relinquishing of their respective original forms:
The transformation of milk into the form of curd occurs through the relinquishing of the form of milk, yet not by the relinquishing of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Śrīkara, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad-bhāṣya 1.4.26; [this is] the apprehension of curd.
It is internal to the constituent part, but not prior to it.
It has been stated that the *dadhigraha* (curd-cup) is obligatory.
Furthermore, it must be drawn prior to the *upāṃśu* and other cups.

This is because, regarding this unprecedented (*apūrva*) matter, its placement earlier [in the text] and the scriptural statement, "This is indeed the eldest of the cups," declare that it is to be drawn before all other cups.

Since it might be argued that the first to arise is designated as "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*), we reply: because the order of mantras is stronger than the order of the Brāhmaṇas, and since the *dadhyaham* mantra is recited immediately after the *upāṃśu* and other mantras, the designation "eldest" is intended merely as a praise—as in passages such as "these Brāhmaṇas are indeed the eldest"—where "eldest" does not denote actual priority of birth. Therefore, the worship of that [deity] occurs only after the *upāṃśu* and the others.

This very point is for the purpose of showing that the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) does not exist in the context of the *Gavāmayana*. Thus, this [scriptural passage] beginning with, "Just as cows, coming together and gathering, strike one another," becomes consistent.
Saṃkarṣa. 2.3.8. The *dadhi-graha* occurs at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) of the *Agniṣṭoma*.
‘He proceeds with the *dadhi-graha*.
According to the *Satyāṣāḍha-śrautasūtra* 8.2.1: at the time of the *dadhi-graha*, he takes the *dadhi-graha*;
he carries it (toward the *āhavanīya* fire for the purpose of offering).
He offers [the oblation] twice.
The cup for the curd-offering (dadhi-graha), the cup for the soma-stalks (aṃśu), and the cup for the adābhya have a common vessel.
The vessel for the curd-offering is made of udumbara wood and has four corners.

A *graha* (libation) is that which is to be taken with a substance; [in this case] it is a *dadhi-graha* (curd-libation). What is the *dadhi-graha*? It is indeed obligatory (*nitya*) in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. As stated: "Whatever deity the Adhvaryu may omit, he becomes subject to harm from her; in that he takes the *prājāpatya dadhi-graha*, he pacifies her. And: "This is indeed the eldest of the libations. These statements regarding the disturbance of the deity and its remedy are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) for the injunction of the *dadhi-graha*. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 4.4.15). The *dadhi-graha* is both obligatory and optional, due to the principle of distinct connection (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*).

In this regard, although the injunction “one desiring cattle should take the *dadhi-graha* [curd-cup]” might—by the principle of *utkarṣa* (transference)—be considered a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), it is more parsimonious to hold that it is merely an injunction of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) with reference to a result; the word denoting the substance (*guṇapada*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Since what has been enjoined is again enjoined for the sake of a result, it possesses both obligatory and optional status (*nityakāmyatva*) by virtue of the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), as in the case of the *aindravāyavya* cup. Saṃkarṣa. 3.3.10: The *dadhi-graha* is occasional (*naimittika*) because of its connection with a scriptural statement.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "He takes the Dadhigraha cup dedicated to Prajāpati. The inquiry is whether this Dadhigraha is obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*).
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states:
the Dadhigraha is occasional, intended for the purpose of removing defects arising from the deity.

Because of the connection with the Vedic text: "Whatever deity the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer may exclude, they are separated from it; when he draws the cup for Prajāpati, he indeed pacifies it"—since this is stated by the scripture as a cause (nimitta), and because it is constant due to the word "eldest" (jyeṣṭha).
He states the second prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

The *dadhi-graha* is both constant (*nitya*)—indicated by the word "and" (*ca*)—and occasional (*naimittika*), because of the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*). This is because the word "eldest" is applied to the *dadhi-graha* in the passage: "This *graha*, namely the *dadhi-graha*, is indeed the eldest of the *grahas*."
It is praiseworthy as the most excellent;
therefore, it is both obligatory and occasional,
and because it possesses all forms.

In the second prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states another reason: "This cup (*graha*) is indeed the form of all the gods. Since it has been stated that the *dadhi-graha* (curd-cup) possesses the nature of all deities, it is permanent (*nitya*). Therefore, this [rite] is both permanent and occasional (*naimittika*).

The *dadhigraha* (curd-offering) is occasional (*naimittika*). [Objection: The section concerning the *dadhigraha* holds that it must be obligatory (*nitya*), because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) which shows that the two [the curd and the soma] are not connected to the ritual action, and because there would otherwise be an obstacle to obtaining the result.
The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the second prima facie view.

The *dadhigraha* (curd-offering) must indeed be permanent (*nitya*), because of the form of the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*), and because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) which shows its similarity to all other deities.

As for what was stated in the first prima facie argument regarding connection with the Vedic text (*śruti-saṃyoga*), he replies: here, by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word "karma" as "that which is performed," the fruit is understood as the action itself.

Since there is no connection between the two—the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer—and the occasional fruit consisting of the removal of defects caused by other deities during the ritual, and since there is an absence of such a relationship, there is a contradiction between the permanent and the occasional.
And because the obstacle has the nature of being occasional (*kādācitkatva*),
it is therefore conditional (*naimittika*).
Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *dadhi-graha* (the curd-offering) is indeed obligatory (*nitya*).
The *dadhi-graha* is occasional (*naimittika*) because of its connection with a scriptural injunction (Jaimini 4.4.18).
It is heard in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: "If the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer have bypassed a deity, he should pour out for her this *dadhi-graha* dedicated to Prajāpati; thus he pacifies her."

Regarding this, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that "the obstacle caused by other deities is the occasion [for the rite], because it is expressed by the word 'if'. To this, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is stated:

since a word beginning with "if" (yat-śabda) that does not stand in grammatical apposition with the agent lacks the power to establish an occasion, the mention of the obstacle is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda); therefore, the *dadhi-graha* offering is obligatory. Thus, based on the explanatory passage, there is no injunction of an occasion.
Bāla, p. 55: The offering of the Dadhigraha must indeed follow after the Upāṃśu and other [libations].
Saṃkarṣa 13.8:
Om, the section concerning the Dadhigraha.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Dadhigraha is obligatory;
[however, it is argued that] the Dadhigraha is occasional because of its connection with a specific scriptural injunction.

Commentary: Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "Whatever deity the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer have offended by omitting [her], when he draws the Prājāpatya Dadhigraha, he pacifies her."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the *dadhi-graha* (the curd-offering) obligatory (*nitya*), or is it occasional (*naimittika*)? What is the prima facie view? The *dadhi-graha* should be occasional, because of its connection with a scriptural statement;
it is heard in scripture as being contingent upon the occurrence of another deity.
Nor is the obstacle permanent;
therefore, it is occasional.
And it is permanent because of the word "eldest" (jyeṣṭha).

Commentary: As for what was said—that it is occasional (*naimittika*)—that is accepted; however, it is also obligatory (*nitya*). Why? Because of the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*). The word "eldest" occurs [in the scripture]: "This cup is indeed the eldest of the cups; for whomsoever it is drawn, he goes to the highest rank."
And the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) may signify either preeminence or priority.
This [self] is neither the first nor the preeminent.
If it were eternal, then it would be appropriate [to call it so] because of its excellence.
That which is neither wavering nor fixed is never praised;
therefore, it is both constant (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*).
It should be undertaken even without an occasion, and furthermore, it should also be undertaken on an occasion.
And because of similarity.

The Commentary states: "It is heard in scripture that it possesses all forms: 'This cup is indeed the form of all these deities; for whichever [deity] this cup is drawn, all the forms of the sacrificial animals attend upon it.
Indeed, no other form of the deity is perceptible to us, since there is nothing else [that could be its form] than this [perceptible form], owing to its eternality."

Therefore, for this reason as well, it is both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*). Or rather, it must be obligatory because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), since those two [occasions] have no connection with the ritual action, and because an obstacle is possible. The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): As for what was stated—that it is both obligatory and occasional—in that case, it must be exclusively obligatory.
Because of the word "eldest" (jyeṣṭha) and because of its universal form;
as for what was said— that it is heard [in scripture] when the intervention of another deity is the cause—
it is not understood that the intervention of another deity is the cause.

This is because of the connection between the duties of the Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer through an intervention; for it is not heard in the scripture that "the deity [is placed] by the Adhvaryu" or "by the Sacrificer," since the intervention is indeed non-permanent.
But there is no such scriptural statement as, "When an obstacle occurs, the curd-cup (dadhigraha) is to be drawn.
Rather, the drawing of the curd-cup occurs even without such a conjunction; its purpose, however, is the removal of obstacles.
Therefore, this drawing is established as if it were permanent (nitya); it cannot be conceived as occasional (anitya).
In that regard, if it were taken as a statement of purpose (*prayojana*), the declaration of permanence would be contradicted by the teaching of impermanence.
However, if it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), it is not contradicted;
for it is not taken up in order to remedy that [contradiction].
It is stated that this [act] has a different purpose altogether, namely, for the sake of praise;
however, the purpose of the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) is solely its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Soma sacrifice.
Furthermore, there is an indication (*bhaṅgi*) regarding the obstacle.
And the breaking [of the sequence] is an obstacle; the wind is mixed with that which is to be constantly expelled.
Therefore, there is no fault: the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) is indeed constant.
Dvivedagaṅga says: it must indeed be constant.
Why? Because of the absence of a connection with a cause (*nimitta*).
For it is by means of the locative case that a cause is expressed—whether by the word *uccais* or by the particle *yadi*.
But here, these [words] are not heard.
Therefore, he says: "And there is no such word that expresses the cause. The cause...
Section 2007: On the Curd-Grasp (Dadhigraha). The modification of the curd-grasp is for the sake of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.
Therefore, whenever the Jyotiṣṭoma takes place, the grasping occurs because the occasion (*nimitta*) exists.
And [the phrase] "for the sake of an impermanent [obstacle]" does not connect the preceding with the subsequent.

If there were no such statement as "an obstacle must be performed," by which the ritual action (*karman*) might be grasped, then it has already been stated that neither of those two exists. Śā— "This [rite] is enjoined on the occasion of a sacrifice being obstructed by a deity."

Therefore, it is occasional (naimittika); yet it is true that, by virtue of the word "eldest" (jyeṣṭha), it is also permanent (nitya). Consequently, it should be considered as having both forms. But is it not the case that it is indeed permanent and not merely occasional? No; why? Because the status of being an occasion (nimitta) is not heard [in the scripture].

The hearing of the mention of obstacles is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise); thus, [the rite] would be obligatory (*nitya*). Soma [objects]: Since there is no connection with a statement of fruit (*phalaśruti*) regarding the *āmana-homas*, even though they lack the status of being for the sake of a fruit, the *dadhi-graha* is occasional (*naimittika*) because of its connection with a statement of a specific occasion (*nimittaśruti*). This rebuttal constitutes the transition (*saṃgati*). "Excluded from the interval" means set aside from the sacrifice; it has been forgotten.
It is seen as being restricted.

In the Sūtra, "due to connection with Śruti" means due to connection with the Śruti text concerning the occasion of an obstacle from a deity. As stated in the Vi— "In the case of both obligatory and occasional rites, the *dadhi-graha* is indeed fixed."
The eldest son shall be the one eligible for the *devāntarāya* sacrifice, provided he possesses the nature of a Soma-drinker;
however, in this case, there is no word such as "if" (*yadi*) to indicate that it is contingent upon a specific cause.
Therefore, this [qualification] does not function as a condition; rather, its perpetual obligation (*nityatā*) alone is appropriate.

Bhaṭṭa: "In the *homā* sacrifice, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer should take the *dadhigraha* for Prajāpati when there is a repetition due to an intervening deity"—thus, the *dadhigraha* is indeed occasional (*naimittika*).

Although this word "yat" (if) does not establish [the rite] as being occasional (*naimittika*)—because it establishes the status of being an occasion for an obstacle (*antarāya*) when used in conjunction with the word for the deity, and because a deity, being eternal and connected to obstacles, cannot logically be an occasion by its very nature—nevertheless, since the rite has as its fruit the removal of defects that serve as occasions for obstacles to the deity, and since that [removal of defects] occurs only occasionally, it is occasional.
Furthermore, it is occasional because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) otherwise necessitates the meaning of the other words [of the injunction].
"Indeed, this cup (graha) is the eldest of the cups"—this statement, even when taken as being for the purpose of avoiding deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), is justified by its excellence and so forth.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: first of all, a fruit mentioned in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) cannot be accepted, because it would contradict the nature of the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite.

Furthermore, in cases other than those of explanatory passages—where, in the absence of a deity, there would be the loss of the primary act itself, and thus even the deficiency caused by that [absence] is avoided—the possibility of avoiding deficiencies in other subsidiary parts, or the perfection of the primary act, simply does not arise; therefore, such a [result] is not tenable here.

Nor should it be argued that since the destruction of the deficiency caused by an obstacle is already established, it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to assume that the *āghāra* and other rites are the causes of that destruction alone, rather than assuming an intermediate *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit). For [otherwise] the *ājya* consisting of praise for seniority (*jyeṣṭhatva*) would be inexplicable; because in both positions, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the other [rite] must necessarily be treated as non-injunctive, it is more appropriate to assign that status specifically to the explanatory passage concerning the obstacle, in order to avoid making the recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa-pāṭha*) merely optional. Furthermore, parsimony is of no avail when it contradicts a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which must be supported by such a means.
Therefore, since the deficiency caused by the intervention of other deities cannot be remedied by the *dadhighraha* (curd-draught), the *dadhighraha* is indeed obligatory.
Maṇḍana states: "This *dadhighraha* is desired as obligatory.
Sūtrakāra Śaṅkara says: "The *dadhighraha* is certainly obligatory."

"Oṃ. A modification of the *dadhighraha* (curd-cup) is a distinct ritual act involving clarified butter (*ājya*) and Soma, which is taught with reference to the *dadhighraha* itself: 'One desiring splendor should take the *ājyagraha*'; and 'One desiring Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should take the *somagraha*'. Since these two would otherwise be obtained as permanent requirements through the use of curd, these two are injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*) for the sake of a specific result, by way of setting aside that [permanent requirement], just like the sentence concerning one who desires sensory power (*indriyakāma*)."

In such a case, as seen in the passage "For one desiring sense-power, [he should offer] curds" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya*), even though the third case-ending indicates that the accessory (*guṇa*) itself is the instrument for the realization of the result (*phalabhāvanā*), and even though this constitutes an injunction of the connection between the accessory and the result, the two—clarified butter (*ājya*) and Soma—are both grasped by the term "cup" (*graha*). Since they function as the instrument in that very context, and because the curd-cup (*dadhi-graha*) is a modification (*vikṛti*), these two optional cups (*kāmya-graha*) are enjoined as distinct rites (*karmāntara*), just like the modifications of the curd-cup. (Saṃkarṣa 3.1.9). Therefore, in the Soma-cup which is a modification of the curd-cup, the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the Soma-cup do not apply.

Even in the case of a modification (*vikāra*) of the *dadhigraha* (curd-cup), the properties (*dharmāḥ*) of the *soma*-cup should apply; for in the injunctions regarding *soma*, such as "He buys *soma*," the properties are prescribed by way of reference (*uddeśena*) to the *soma* that is the means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*). This is because there is a rule that the delimiting factor of the status of being the object of reference (*uddeyatā-avacchedaka*) must pervade the individual instance (*vigraha-vyāpyatva-niyama*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: in the injunction "One should sacrifice with *soma*," the very status of being the means to the transcendental result is the delimiting factor of the object of reference. Thus, the properties are obtained for that which has entered into the procedure. Furthermore, since the sacrifice has an expectancy regarding its manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*), the properties of *soma* apply therein.
*Saṃkarṣa* 3.1.11: *Oṃ*. In the modification (*vikāra*) of the *dadhigraha*, when there is an absence of Soma-attributes in the Soma-offering, water is used for the pressing.

Since, by the very logic already stated, even the act of pressing is not obtained [in this case], the sacrifice should be performed with the stalks of the Soma-creeper itself. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is replied: because the drawing [of the liquid] into the four-cornered cup is obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*), and because that [drawing] is established as having the substance as its means according to the principle of "the first [instance]" (*prathamānya-nyāya*), and precisely because of its nature as a vessel, [it applies] to the archetypal [offering].

Regarding *dadhimahāvikṛti* (2008): Since it is appropriate to restrict the term "curd" (*dadhi*) to mean curd that is more solid than milk, this restriction is implied by the sense (*ārthikatva*). Consequently, even according to the general rule (*codaka*), because the vessel must serve as a receptacle for the substance, the vessel is obtained through the inclusion of the *abhivatsa* offering.
Saṃkarṣa 3.3.2. The two *mahāvikṛtis* consisting of curd are optional rites (*kāmyau*) that constitute distinct rituals (*karmāntara*), namely the *somamahā* and the *ājyagraha*.

Saṃkarṣa. 3|3|9. "Om, the maxim of fever caused by *dadhitāpuṣa*. It is understood that this refers to the cause of fever. (When the fruit named *dadhitāpuṣa* is eaten together with curd, fever arises due to the resulting imbalance of the bodily constituents.)
The *Sāhasrī*.
Oṃ. The fact that curd is the substance [of the offering] is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the sacrifice.
*Bālakrīḍā*, page [number].

By the principle of the curd-offering (*dadhi-nyāya*), even in the case of a *kratvartha* (rite for the sake of the sacrifice) such as the *mahāvrata* performed with a desire (*kāmya*), the recitation of the hymn (*sūkta*)—namely "Agni naro dīdhitibhiḥ" (*agninaraḥ...*)—is established through the application of the *āśyaka* scriptures for the sake of the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). Thus, the dual purpose of the hymn, by virtue of both the general injunction (*codaka*) and the direct statement (*pratyakṣa-vacana*), is not contradictory.

The principle of the distinctness of connection (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva-nyāya*) should be observed here (AiĀSā. 1.3.12–14). For in this case—specifically regarding the rule "The *agniṣṭut* is an *agniṣṭoma* [sacrifice]; its [stotras] are on verses addressed to Vāyu"—the quality does not possess the fitness for connection in its production according to the *dadhi-nyāya* (as discussed in 4.3.15–17).

Kau. 2.1.12.6, p. 280: [The first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that] even though one has merely obtained the *revatī* verses, since there would still be the same problem of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*)—namely, that both the injunction of the *miśra-stotra* by way of restatement (*anuvāda*) and the application of the sacrifice toward a specific result must be enjoined—it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) here to follow the logic of the curd (*dadhi*) example and enjoin the relationship between the quality (*guṇa*) and the result. [The second *pūrvapakṣa*: Because of parsimony, it is the quality itself—the *vāravantīya* chant associated with the *revatī* verses—that is enjoined toward the result, as it is not already established. Therefore, according to the logic of the curd example, it is proper that only the relationship between the quality and the result is enjoined.
Bhāṭṭa 2.1.12. Oṃ. Regarding curd and milk: the properties of the *praṇītā* water are not perceived [as applying] for the purpose of the sacrifice.

(In the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*, although the curd and milk are for the sake of the sacrifice, because of the injunction in the context—"he cooks them together with the rice"—that they are to be cooked together, they incidentally take on the status of performing the function of the *praṇītā* water, and thus its properties apply to them).
Vārttika 2.1.12.27, p. 555. Oṃ. The maxim: "Curd and milk are a manifest fever."
Because it produces fever, the combined mixture of curd and milk is designated as "fever.
This is the summary.
[Regarding] curd and milk, [the verse number is] 2009. [The garment] made of *darbha* grass.
From the recitation of the number [of mantras] in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;

*dadhi* is a weapon that causes destruction (Vi. 3.15.9); *damayantī* was the wife of Nala (Vā. 3.4.119); even for a poor person, there is eligibility for ritual acts after acquiring wealth (Vi. 6.1.8); the maxim of the reflection in a mirror (*darpaṇapratibimbanyāya*).
This principle has been elucidated by the teacher Sureśvarācārya.
For it is said: "Within this [Self] are these two worlds; within it is this entire universe.
Yet the external world appears as consisting of the Self, like a reflection in a mirror."
Thus [ends] the *Sāhasrī*, verse 106. The maxim of looking at one's face in a mirror (*darpaṇamukhāvalokananyāya*):
this applies to the case where whatever form one sees in a mirror, that very same thing is seen [as it is]. Thus [ends] the *Sāhasrī*, verse 886. There are ten kinds of *darbha* grass.
Kuśas, kāśas, barley, duvas, uśīras with their bulbs, wheat, rice, muñja grass, and wild-growing darbha— these are the ten types of sacred grass.
(Dharmasindhu, Śrāvaṇa section): "Kuśa, kāśa, śara, gunda, yava, dūrvā, and then valvaja;
gokeśa, muñja, and kunda—each subsequent one is used in the absence of each preceding one."
*Nirṇayasindhu* (regarding items for the *śrāddha*):
Vi. 3|12|1. For the purpose of spreading the altar and so forth, the *pavitra* must be made from separate blades of *darbha* grass.
Bhā. 3|17|132: No other ritual application is performed with those same *darbha* blades.
In rites where darbha grass is to be offered with its tips pointing eastward or downward, it should be so placed;
however, in ancestral rites (paitṛka), it should have its tips pointing southward (Vi.
3.4.4). At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, during the cutting of darbha grass, the mantra for cutting—“I cut the barhis, the covering for the gods”—is to be repeated with each successive cutting.

Bhāṣya 1.1.144–45: "He purifies with bunches of *darbha* grass. Here, even though the number is mentioned within the sentence (*ativākya*), it does not pertain to the action (*karman*); therefore, there is no division of the action (*karmabheda*) in that case. Soma 2.17: The purification is performed by a collection of twenty-one *darbha* bunches, equal to the place of purification.

Bhāṣya 5.1.4–6: Regarding the *darbha* grass and the mantra—in the archetypal (*prākṛta*) Vājapeya sacrifice, the sound of the chariot and so forth supersedes [the *darbha*] which serves as the means for performing the Māhendra-stotra.
Bhāṣya 10.4.12.1–2, Section 3: He girds [the sacrificer] with a girdle made of *darbha* grass.

Even though it is made of *darbha* grass and so forth, and even though it possesses the quality of being a girdle (*kāpāśādivattva*), it must be girt because it serves a transcendental purpose (*apūrvārthatvāt*).
Vi. 6.8.9: At the Mahāvrata rite, the wife girds herself with a garment made of *darbha* grass.

In its original form, there is a combination with the *ahata-vāsas* (unwashed garment). Bhāṣya 10.4.13–15. Bhaṭṭa: "He who desires cattle, having performed the New Moon sacrifice, should drive away the calves; those that are sixteen-month-old, for them he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Saniṣṭhā; those that are middle-aged, for them a pap of boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; those that are three-year-old, for them a curd-mixture to Indra Dātṛ. Although it was established in the sixth [book] that this constitutes a separate rite (*karmāntara*) due to the absence of a rule for removal (*apanaya*), nevertheless, because of the scriptural mention of the *abhyuditeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one by whom the moon has risen) and the scriptural mention of driving away the calves...
Regarding the *darvī*: if it is argued that the *darvihomas* of the worldly [rituals] are unprecedented (*apūrva*) and do not apply even to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

The Commentary: If you view it thus—that "the placement of the *svāhākāra* occurs neither in the *nāriṣṭha* oblations nor in the *pārvaṇa* oblations"—then its placement would not be possible even in the archetype (*prakṛti*) at the *nāriṣṭha* oblations and so forth.

In those cases as well, only the *vaṣaṭkāra* would apply; for that is prescribed for the New and Full Moon sacrifices by way of an exception [to the *svāhākāra*], as in the rule: "The *vaṣaṭkāra* consists of two syllables."
Thus indeed he obtains it,
because of the word "dependent on another" (*anyāyatta*).
But is it not the case that the *svāhākāra* is also explicitly recited?
The *satya* has been recited, but the *vaṣaṭkāra* has been prescribed.

Therefore, in these cases, the [result] obtained through the recitation of the *svāhākāra*—namely, "his sacrifice is not interrupted; it is established in Prajāpati"—is set aside. For an inferred injunction (*ānumānika-vidhi*) is sublated by a directly perceived injunction (*pratyakṣa-vidhi*).
If there is no insertion even there, then the utterance "svāhā" serves solely for the sake of what follows, that is, for the sake of the modified ritual (vikṛti).
It has been stated that in a conflict (samavāya), there is weakness of the subsequent.
The Commentary says: Here [an objector] says, "This is not tenable—that 'the *svāhākāra* is set aside by the *vaṣaṭkāra*.
Why? Because, in the case of a Vedic verse (*ṛk*), when there is a conflict among the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest, there is weakness of the subsequent."
And here there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).
By virtue of context, the *vaṣaṭ* call would apply to the *nāriṣṭha* oblations; however, because [the mantra] forms a single syntactical unit with the words of that mantra, the *svāhā* call applies.
And syntactical connection is stronger than context.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is employed after the *svāhā*-utterance for the purpose of offering? [As it is said: "The *svāhā*-utterance is the eighth. [Reply: Certainly, the offering is not accomplished by the *svāhā*-utterance alone; how could the *svāhā*-utterance, which is not prescribed for the purpose of offering, effect the offering?
[Answer: And it is indeed prescribed.
How so? [Because it is said: "The oblation is offered to the gods either with the utterance of *svāhā* or with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.

Now, since both *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* are prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) would be purposeless; therefore, it is replied that this will prescribe these two as being for the purpose of offering.
Consequently, the *darvihoma*s do not have the Soma sacrifice as their archetype.
"Or rather, it would be an injunction for that [sacrifice], because the impulsion for the *iṣṭi* has already occurred.
Commentary: The word "or" (*vā*) is used to adopt an alternative position.
Or rather, it is an injunction for that.
By the word "tat" (that), the *darvihomas* are referred to.
Those specific subsidiary rites (*aṅgakarma*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) which are enjoined by the injunction "he offers" (*juhoti*) are to be applied to the *darvihomas*.
Which ones are they? They are the *nāriṣṭha-homas*.
For what reason? Because they are observed to be active in all sacrificial rites involving all kinds of animals and sheep.
And when a characteristic is generally observed in someone, it is inferred even when it is not currently perceived;
just as one who generally performs services for others is considered capable of doing so even in another instance of performing service for others.
Therefore, their performance [occurs].
And because of the capacity of the word.
The Commentary: Furthermore, the capacity of the word consists in the commonality of the injunction (*codanā*) for the *darvihoma* offerings.

For in the case of the *nāriṣṭha* oblation as well, there is an injunction consisting of the verb "to sacrifice," namely: "He sacrifices the *nāriṣṭhas*" and "He sacrifices when [the vessel] is broken.
Because of this commonality of injunction, the application of the ritual properties (*dharma*) follows;
and it is also because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
The Commentary states: "And the indicative mark (liṅga) shows this in the case of the *caitayajña*, namely that the *darvihomas* are preceded by the *nāriṣṭha-homa*.
What is the indicative mark? It is heard in the context of the *agnihotra*: 'If an insect should fall [into the fire], one should pour it out within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Likewise, regarding the *agni*, it is heard: 'Standing within the altar (*vedī*), he offers the *sāvitra* oblations.'"

The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) belong to the altar (*vedi*), because they serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the primary acts; they are not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations.
If their ritual properties (*dharma*) were to apply [to those oblations], then this view would be tenable.
Therefore, they do apply.
In that case, because non-existence is the cause, there would be no perception for the sake of the subordinate element (*guṇa*).

The Commentary states: "That which was taught as the perception for the sake of the subordinate element—that is, for the purpose of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations, meaning at the commencement of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations—is non-perception; the meaning is that it is not a proof [of their existence].
Why? Because non-existence is the cause in those cases. Regarding the *tryambaka* offerings, it is said: 'The *tryambakas* are indeed unstable.'"

"The fuel-sticks (*idhma*) are not gathered, no offerings are made for the subjects (*prajā*), no after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are made, and he does not recite the *sāmidhenī* verses"—having thus asserted the lack of establishment (*apratiṣṭhitatva*) of the *tryambaka* offerings, these [absences] are taught as the reasons for establishing that [lack of establishment], because of the absence of the fuel-sticks and so forth.

If the *nāriṣṭha-homas* were to proceed, then, since they serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, the duties such as the fuel-sticks and the *sāmidhenī* verses would indeed exist in the *tryambakas*.
Therefore, this absence of them cannot logically serve as a reason, because they do not exist [in that case].
Therefore, there is no application of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations.
If it is argued that this is a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), the Commentary states: "If you view it thus, [we reply] that this is merely a descriptive observation (*darśana*)."

Now, why is it not an injunction (*vidhi*)? Because, being an injunction that prohibits the *nāriṣṭha* oblations and the primary materials such as the sacrificial grass (*prastara*), the fuel (*idhma*), and so forth—which have those oblations as their archetype—it would enjoin a previously unestablished matter. As a restatement (*anuvāda*), it would not produce any specific activity and would therefore be purposeless. This objection is raised by means of the Sūtra once the proposition has been established: "The *darvihoma*s are archetypal (*apūrva*). [That is, they do not follow the archetype of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations.]

No, because it is a supplementary part of a sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), and a resolution regarding the purpose of the quality (*guṇārtha*) is not possible if there were multiplicity [of injunctions]. The Commentary states: This injunction is not appropriate. What is the reason? Another injunction is recited here: "One should offer a rice-oblation (*caru*) in clarified butter to Āditya upon returning to one's home"; this [text under discussion] is a supplementary part of that [injunction].

How is this known? Because it is required by that [preceding passage]. Having proclaimed the defect in the words, "The three-faced ones (*tryambakas*) are indeed unstable," the following is heard: "Having returned home, one should offer a *caru* oblation of clarified butter dedicated to Āditya; for Aditi is this earth, this is stability, and since Āditya is this [oblation], he is established in her.
This is understood to be for the purpose of remedying that defect; therefore, it forms a single syntactical unit with it.

Furthermore, those statements regarding the existence of fuel and so forth within that [context] are also rightly understood as belonging to that very body [of the sentence], because they are uttered therein.

If these were assumed to be injunctions, they would become separate sentences; in that case, the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*) would be subverted, and there would be the assumption of an interrupted connection (*vyavahita-kalpanā*).
Nor do these possess injunctive force, because they are of the nature of restatements (*anuvāda*).
Therefore, they are not injunctions (*vidhi*).

Now, what is the distinction here, such that while the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the same, the observation regarding "within the enclosing sticks" (*antaḥparidhi*) is non-probative, whereas the other is probative?
We shall explain the distinction later on.
(Thus it has been stated that for *darvihoma*s, the *nāriṣṭha-homas* are not the archetype;
however, for those [rites] where there is an offering of curd and milk, they would indeed apply, provided there is no contradiction.)
Commentary: The meaning is that for those sacrifices in which the oblation is offered in the two rear fires, there should be the performance of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Why? Because there is no contradiction.
In this case, the contradiction that was stated regarding the performance of the *nāriṣṭha-homas*—namely, "because of the absence [of the rear fires] being the cause"—does not exist here.
For them, indeed, the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and the kindling verses (*sāmidhenī*) are not auxiliary parts;
thus, the observation of their absence there is not contradictory.
They also possess the duties of active engagement and the injunctions for oblations, such as "he offers the oblation together with his wife."
Therefore, their application [occurs]. In that regard, medicinal herbs are mentioned; they would be understood by way of their location.
Commentary: This is not tenable.

What is the reason? Because medicinal herbs are mentioned there in connection with the ladle-oblation (*darvihoma*), such as: "In the *tryambaka* offerings, there is a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), bowls of groats (*karambhapātra*), rice grains (*taṇḍula*), and so forth.
These would be understood through their position (*sthāna*). By virtue of the displacement of the clarified butter (*ājya*), the properties of the clarified butter (*ājyadharma*) would be obtained.
They are not capable of being performed there;
or, if they were performed, they would serve a purpose other than their original one, whereby the injunction (codaka) would be sublated.
Therefore, there must be some purpose for their performance.

The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are also performed with other mantras, and the *vaṣaṭkāra* is replaced by the *svāhākāra*. (By these two sūtras, the status of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings as the archetype is set aside).
Or rather, due to indicative mark (*liṅga*), it applies to the two remaining oblations.
[Bhāṣya]: Or rather, there may be the application of the flour-smeared oblation and the *līkaraṇa* oblation (in the case of ladle-oblations).
Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), that is, because of the commonality with the medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*).
That defect which was stated regarding the application of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings—namely, the futility of the ritual properties (*dharma*)—does not exist here.
In that case, the properties of the medicinal herbs, such as pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*) and so forth, can be performed.

Therefore, it is said that the activity of those two [occurs]. However, since those two are actually cognitions (*pratipatti*), the Bhāṣya states that they are not modifications (*vikāra*); yet this is not so.
Why? Because these two oblations are acts of disposal (*pratipatti*), whereas *darvihomas* are primary acts (*pradhānakarman*); thus, there is a vast difference between them.
Furthermore, the acquisition of ritual properties (*dharma*) is desired through general similarity (*sāmānyat-sādṛśyena*).

As it has been stated: "The properties of the medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*) can be performed [here]. Since they are acts of disposal, the properties such as pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*) and so forth are prompted by that very [similarity].
Therefore, by that same reasoning, its status as an act performed [by a priest] is not established, nor is it endowed with ritual properties (*dharma*), nor does it possess a purpose.
Consequently, this too is untenable.
Thus, in no way whatsoever is the acquisition of ritual properties for *darvihoma* offerings logically justified.

Therefore, in the case of a conflict, the non-occurrence of the contradictory [element] should be understood in the prior [instance], because the purpose cannot be altered due to the statement regarding the application of the injunction; thus, there would be an extension (atideśa) by virtue of that statement.
The Bhāṣya: Now, why is it that when both types of indicative marks (liṅga) are present, only non-occurrence is perceived, and not occurrence?
It is said in reply:
When there is a combination [of factors], it is not logical to recognize the manifestation of these conflicting symptoms. Why? Because of the necessity of the origin of the injunctions;
for the injunctions, too, have their own textual recitation.

And it is established that there is no transfer [of mantras]. For some [mantras] are recited in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, while others are recited in the Soma sacrifice. Since the meaning [of the mantra] cannot be transferred, when they are recited in one place, the *prakaraṇa* (context) is set aside when they are transferred elsewhere.
Therefore, non-application is understood.
To this he says: "What is the purpose of this prefix [a-], that there is non-attainment everywhere?
This being the case, it is replied:
There would be an extension [of the rule] by virtue of a statement,
as in the case of the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings in the duties of the *udgātṛ*.
In the absence of such a specific statement, it is something new (*apūrva*).
Now, regarding those [rules] mentioned as indicators (*liṅga*) which are not previously established for *davihoma* offerings— such as "If an insect should fall into the *davihoma* offerings,
one should pour them out within the enclosing sticks" and "Standing within the altar, he offers the *sāvitra* oblations"— what is the resolution for these two? It is said:
Because it is preceded by an improper method, that discussion is understood to be figurative (*lakṣaṇayā*),
referring to "the region within the enclosing sticks" (*antaḥparidhideśe*) or "the region within the altar" (*antarvedideśe*), since neither the enclosing sticks nor the altar exist there.

"Just as people say, 'The night itches for me' or 'My mole is throbbing,' even when there is no redness or when the mole is absent, speakers use such expressions by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) regarding that location.

Soma: Having concluded this incidental discussion, the examination of exceptions (*apavāda*) is now commenced. Ci: "In the *dravihoma*, are the properties of the *soma* sacrifice [applicable], or is it a case of *apūrva* (novelty)? The first [view]..."
Because they are unmanifest (*avyakta*) and because they constitute a sacrifice, there is the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the utterance of *svāhā* and so forth.

According to the Bhaṭṭa school: in those [rites], due to their unmanifest nature, there is generally eligibility for the Soma-sacrifice; however, in some *darvihoma* offerings, the unmanifest nature refers to the essential form (*svarūpa*) of the *darvihoma* itself.
Bhaṭṭa: It is heard in an independent injunction (*anārabhya-vidhi*): "The oblation to the gods is offered either with the utterance of *svāhā* or with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.

By resorting to a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in that case, the injunction of both *svāhākāra* and *vaṣaṭkāra* as auxiliary elements of the rite for the gods and their mutual optionality are established by logic alone.
Furthermore, in certain *darvihoma* offerings, the utterance of *svāhā* is heard: "To the Earth, *svāhā*; to the Atmosphere, *svāhā*."
That too should be restricted according to the previously stated principle.

This being the position reached, since it is impossible to restrict the two prescriptive mantras by their own form, the restriction of the mantra-ritual must be stated to be by means of the injunction of the *ahavaniya* fire.

And because that *vaṣaṭkāra* is highly effective, and since it is possible for it to serve the purpose of regulating the word, it is illogical for it to serve the purpose of restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*)—which consists in excluding other unmentioned subsidiaries.

It is not that there is an option (between the two), but rather that there is a restriction to the word *svāhākāra* alone; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, in reality, because of the scriptural injunction "He utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call over the *yājyā*," which prescribes that the *vaṣaṭ*-call must occur subsequent to the *yājyā*, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is restricted to those sacrifices where the sacrifice is performed by means of the *yājyā* alone.

But where the sacrifice is performed by means of a mantra other than the *yājyā*, then, by elimination, it is the *svāhākāra* alone; thus, there is a fixed alternative (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) between the two.
And thus, in cases such as "To the Earth, Svāhā" (pṛthivyai svāhā), the recitation of the word *svāhā* is for the purpose of establishing its status as a mantra.

For this very reason, where the word *svāhā* is not recited, even if the word *svāhā* were to be enjoined there according to the aforementioned rule, that [textual unit] would not possess the status of a mantra; nor would there be a penance for a deficiency in the mantra within that specific work. However, it is not the case that the word *svāhā* is absent from that [mantra] by its very nature.

For this very reason, even though the mantra lacks such [an expression] in cases like the Audumbarī-homa, the injunction regarding time—stated as "having performed the Audumbarī-homa with the mantra, one utters *svāhā* when it has reached the ground"—is appropriate as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *svāhā*-utterance once that utterance is already established. Furthermore, in certain specific homas, the prohibition "one does not utter *svāhā*" is also appropriate as a restriction (*paryudāsa*) ending at that point.
Therefore, there is no [need for] subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) here.
The Sūtras also should be applied to this very same meaning:
Maṇḍana says, "In the Darvihoma and others, [it is] svāhā";
Śaṅkara says, "The utterance of svāhā is for every oblation."

In the case of offerings made with a ladle (*darvihoma*), regarding the injunction "he offers what has been taken four times" (*caturgṛhītaṃ juhoti*), since the offering can be accomplished even with what was first taken, the number is restricted by the very principle of that which is mentioned first.
(3.4.16) The number is restricted.
Saṃkarṣa. 2.4.16.
In *darvihoma* offerings, the oblation must be performed only after placing a fuel-stick (*samidh*) for each subsequent offering.
Although the rekindling of the fire is mandatory in *darvihoma* rites, there is no rule requiring the insertion of a fuel-stick therein,
as there is no restrictive authority present, as there is in the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses.

This being the prima facie position, [the following is stated]: In the context of the *agnihotra*, after prescribing, "When one has taken a single fuel-stick (*samidh*), one offers two oblations," there follows the question, "On which fuel-stick does one offer the second oblation? Since this implies that the placing of a single fuel-stick for each oblation is established as necessary, there is no lack of restriction. For it is frequently observed that a matter established through non-restriction is subsequently restricted by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) or similar means; otherwise, even the rule "one cuts off [the portion] with the *sruva* ladle" and so forth would not constitute a restriction.

For this very reason, the view held by some—that because this [passage] belongs to the context of the *agnihotra* and is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), it cannot serve as a restrictive rule—has been refuted in the *Bhāṣya* itself (Saṃkarṣa.

This is because, in the case of the *darvihoma* offerings prescribed by injunctions such as "he offers in the *darvi*," even though no specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) has been prescribed, it is impossible to extend a fixed set of ritual details (*vidhyanta*) since no specific archetype (*prakṛti*) can be determined.

Since both non-restriction (*aniyama*) and universal application (*sarvātideśa*) have been refuted within the discussion of the eighth [chapter], and since the *apūrva* (transcendental result) will be discussed later at the end of the section on the inferior [rites], it follows that for all the materials, deities, and so forth, as well as the entire class of procedures (*itikartavyatājāta*), mentioned in the scripture—functioning as direct auxiliaries (*saṃnipatyopakārin*)—their purpose culminates solely in the production of the *karaṇāpūrva* (the transcendental result of the instrument) by means of the restrictive *apūrva*. Consequently, even for those [procedures] performed elsewhere, there is no other recourse but to assume that they serve as the means for assisting the instrument, which is itself accomplished by the remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*). (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 35–36). In the case of the *darvihoma* offerings, in the absence of a specific scriptural statement, that which is taken up once is fixed as the rule.

In the case of *darvī-homas* (ladle-offerings), since no restrictive rule such as "one offers with what has been taken up four times" (*caturgṛhītaṃ juhoti*) is perceived, and because an offering could be accomplished even with what was first taken up when an unlimited number of takings had not yet been established, the number is restricted by the very principle of that which is mentioned first.

For this reason alone, after prescribing "he offers four times" (*caturjuhoti*) and "he offers twice" (*dvirjuhoti*), the necessity of another set of four offerings is established and justified by the passage beginning, "Now, how do two oblations come to be?
(Saṃkarṣa. 2.4.16).
In all *darvihoma* offerings, the rule "the *yajus* formula is to be recited in a low voice" (*upāṃśu yajuṣā*) is meaningful.
Vārttika 3.1.2, p. 813.

In all *darvihoma* offerings, the utterance of *svāhā* occurs (Bhāṣya 10.8.10.20–22). In *darvihoma* offerings, no ritual activity other than the mere pouring of the oblation is heard in the scripture, nor is such an activity obtained through extended application (*atideśa*). This is because there is a distinction between the characteristics of sacrifices (*yāga*) and those of oblations (*homa*), based on their respective generic classes (*jāti*) and locations (*deśa*).

Nor does it belong to the *darvihomas* [in general], because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for determining the specific distinction as to "the duty of which *homa*? or "in which *homa* does it apply?

(The sense is that this is because [the rule] applies only to those *homās* such as the Agnihotra, Traiyambaka, and Nāriṣṭha, just as in the case of the *caturhotṛ* and others). Therefore, since it is not obtained through the general property (*dharma*), the principle of the *darvihoma* is stated as: "How should one effect [the result] here by means of the *darvihomas*? This is the *darvihoma-nyāya*.
Even when it has arisen, the expectancy is satisfied merely by the production of its own form. Mīmāṃsā, p.
192–93. [This establishes] that the word *darvihoma* is a name for a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*).
The term *darvihoma* is a designation for a sacrifice because of its connection with the act of offering (*homa*).
The Commentary states: "It is heard [in scripture]: 'If one should offer with a wooden ladle (*ekadhā*), one should perform a *darvihoma*.
Regarding this word *darvihoma*, there is a doubt.

Is this an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or a name for the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*)? What is the prima facie view? That it is a designation for the sacrifice in the *darvī* oblation; that is to say, it is the name of the ritual action.
Why? Because of its connection with the term "oblation" (*homa*).
The word "homa" (oblation) is heard here. In that context, it is completed for the sake of the primary rite;
the *darvihoma* is subordinate, and the *homa* is the ritual action.
Alternatively, "one should offer" (juhuyāt) denotes an action;
therefore, it is combined with that [action], as in "one should offer with one.
Consequently, it is the name of an action.
Let that which has been established remain for now; next, the process [of the categories] is undertaken.
Since there was instruction on substance (*dravya*), the mention of qualities (*guṇa*) should follow. Commentary: That which follows after what has been established is now being stated.
As for what was said—that "darvihoma" is a name for a ritual act—that is not so; rather, it must be a designation of a quality. The meaning is that it is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).
Why? Because there is an instruction regarding a substance (*dravya*).
An instruction regarding a substance is understood, as in "the *darvihoma* is a substance-offering.
In this way, the term "*darvihoma*" will be established according to its conventional usage.
Therefore, it is an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*).
No; because [the rule] adopts worldly practices and because purity is enjoined for another purpose.
The Commentary states: "It is not logical that this should be an injunction of a subordinate element."

What is the reason? First, for those following worldly practice, it is established by custom that one offers with *darbha* grass, as in the injunction: "That which one offers with a *darbha* stalk having roots and a handle.
That [practice] need not be enjoined.
Furthermore, for those following the Vedic tradition (*śrauta*), other vessels for the purpose of offering have been prescribed.
"One offers with a ladle," "One offers with a cup"—
with these, there would be an option regarding the wooden spoon (*darvī*),
and that is improper.
The reason is that there exists an injunctive word for the *sruva* ladle, namely, "He offers with the *sruva*," but not for the *darbha* grass.
In that case, the injunctive word would be merely inferential;
furthermore, another vessel is actually observed [to be used].
Commentary: Furthermore, another vessel is seen in the *darvīhoma* sacrifice, as it is said:
"He first lifts up the *sruva*-ladle with the words, 'To the Bhṛtas'.
Therefore, this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Mīmāṃsākośa 253:
"Likewise, [the rule applies] to the fire and the oblation.
Commentary: Now, it might be argued that the function of the *darvī* (ladle) will belong to the fire and the oblation.
A *darvihoma* is an oblation offered with a ladle (*darvi*); that is, an oblation performed by means of a ladle is a *darvihoma*.
Regarding this, we say:
the same applies to the *āmikṣā* and the *havir* as well.
Just as a ladle is not suitable for a vessel, so too it is not suitable for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*agnihaviṣ*). In that case as well, the *āhavanīya* fire is prescribed as the substratum,
as in "when one offers into the *āhavanīya*," and furthermore, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and the like are prescribed as the substances to be offered.

Therefore, even in the case of the fire-oblation (*agnihavis*), there is no entry of the ladle (*darvi*) into its function; there is no connection for the purpose of displacement. The Commentary states: "And it has been stated by us previously that another substance is incapable of performing the function of the fire."
In the statement regarding burning, the primary object is the fire;
and it is not possible to produce any other substance in place of that effect. Therefore, the ladle is not the effect of the fire.
Therefore, it is not an injunction of a quality;
the word *darvihoma* is simply a name for the ritual action.

Soma: Here, [the objection] was raised that there would be an exception to the extended application (*atideśa*) about to be made by the Prābhākaras, and thus it was said that this is a discussion regarding the injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*). That has been stated;
for since the word *darvihoma* occurring in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is itself subject to extended application, it cannot—by way of incidental mention—serve as an exception.
Therefore, the connection here is indeed a *prasaṅga* (a logical consequence).

Let the sūtras be as follows: "The word *darvihoma* is a designation of a ritual (*karmanāmadheya*) denoting a sacrifice (*yajña*), because of its connection with the act of offering (*homa*). Vi [tarka]: "In the *darvihoma*, is it a subordinate element (*guṇa*) or a name? It is a subordinate element, like the *dadhihoma*."
Because of the impossibility of [other] qualities, that name would exist in both worldly and Vedic usage.

Bhāṭṭa: Thus, the method of extension (atideśa) having been established, the meaning of the term *darvihoma* is now defined in order to state its exception (*apavāda*) regarding the *darvihoma* offerings.

In this regard, it cannot first be suspected that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), because—unlike the case of Soma and other substances—the absence of a direct hearing of an injunctive suffix (*vidhivibhakti*) makes the suspicion of its being injunctive untenable.

Furthermore, in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the injunction of qualities for the *vāstu-homa*—namely, "If one were to offer with a ladle (*darvī*), one would perform a *darvī-homa*"—it is impossible for the term *darvī-homa*, which is heard there, to function as an injunction by implying another word (such as *ghṛta*), as is the case with the word *ghṛta* and others. This is because there is no need for an injunction of qualities consisting of two *ṛc*-verses, such as "one offers with the *yājyā* following the *puro’nuvākyā*. Nor can the term *darvī-homa* be understood as an injunction regarding the location of the offering based on the necessity of explaining the established mention [of the act], as in the case of the sentence "He holds it above, for the gods are above. (Note: The text discusses the hermeneutical principle that a term mentioned in an *arthavāda* cannot be assumed to be an injunction unless there is a specific requirement for it, such as the need to explain a subsequent established statement.)

First, regarding the *vāstu-homa*, since the *sruva* ladle is directly prescribed [in the Śruti], it is impossible to enjoin it [as a *darvi*]. Furthermore, even in other *smārta* oblations, its employment is established by the *smārta* statement itself: "He offers with a *darbha*-blade from the root-stalk of a *nyagrodha* tree.

Moreover, the term *darvihoma* applies to *śrauta* rites as well, because of the presence of various other vessels in those contexts, such as the injunctions: "He offers with a *sruva*, he offers with a *camasa*, he offers with a *juhū*," and so forth.

Therefore, since it is impossible for that [term] to be an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) according to that logic, one must accept that the word *darvi* is a figurative designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other vessels, or else that this is the name of the first oblation alone, based on its partial application as a ground for usage.
Maṇḍana says: "The term *darvihoma* is a name. Śaṅkara says: "And in the case of the *darvihoma*, it has the status of a name."

If we do not obtain [the authority of] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through some instruction, then, according to the principle of the *darvihoma* (8.4.11–19), we shall assume the capacity of the injunctive statement itself. (Vārttika 1.2.17, p. 115). The word *darvihoma* is a name for a ritual action.
Domestic and Vedic oblations such as the *sthālīpāka*, the *aṣṭakās*, the *agnihotra*, and the *nāriṣṭahomas* are all *darvihomas*.
Thus, the *jyās*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* are indeed *darvihomas*. (Vi.
8.4.1, 4). The term *darvihoma* is the name for both Smārta and Śrauta rites.

It would apply to worldly [rites], because the name belongs to the agent. The Commentary: When this is a name for ritual actions, it is then considered whether the term *darvihoma* is the name for these worldly, Smārta rites, or for all rites—both worldly and Vedic. What is the prima facie view? It would apply to worldly [rites].
Indeed, that term "darvihoma" should be the name for worldly rituals. Why? Because the performer is designated by that name;
the performer of those [rituals] is designated by the term "darvihoma."
‘Among the Śinīs, there is a Brahmin who performs the *darvihoma* sacrifice; among the Ambaṣṭhas, there is a Brahmin who performs the *darvihoma* sacrifice.
And whatever one does, by that he is designated—just as, for example, a ‘reaper’ (*lāvaka*) or a ‘purifier’ (*pāvaka*).
If this were the name for the *akā* and other such implements, then their maker would deserve the designation "wood-burner" (*dāvahomin*).
Therefore, it is the name of common worldly things;
or rather, it applies to all of them, because it is observed in the case of the *vāstu-homa*.
Commentary: This is the name for all [offerings], both worldly and Vedic;
it is not for worldly ones alone. Why? Because it is seen in the case of the *vāstu-homa* (the house-consecration oblation).
For in the Vedic *vāstu-homa*, it demonstrates the nature of a *darvihoma*:
"If one were to offer with a single [verse], one would perform a *darvihoma*;
by reciting the *puro'nuvākyā* and then offering with the *yājyā*, it becomes possessed of a deity."
[The opponent says: "But this view is contrary [to reason]: that one should perform a *darvihoma* with a single offering-spoon; for it would then result in what is not a *darvihoma*.
If the *darvihoma* is indeed defined by the first [case], then even when being offered with one or two spoons, it remains a *darvihoma*."
In this regard, the following scriptural observation is not tenable:
"One should perform an *ārvihoma* with a single ladle.
To this, it is replied:

If the name "darvihoma" applied only to worldly (laukika) acts and not to Vedic ones, then even when an offering is made with a single ladle, it would not be a *darvihoma* because it would lack the Vedic character; in that case, the statement "one should perform a *darvihoma* by offering with a single ladle" would be inexplicable. Therefore, this [statement] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that Vedic acts possess the nature of *darvihoma*. Even so, what is the source for this indication? It is said: [the source is the aforementioned scriptural statement].
Because the word *homa* denotes a general category, it applies [to all such acts].
Therefore, this is the name for both worldly and Vedic [acts]. As it is said: "It is the name of every worldly [act], according to the sentence."
Because it shares the same basis [of denotation], the word "all" (sarva) also applies to what is expressed by that [word "everything"].
Bhaṭṭa: (This was originally included in the first section (*prathamādhikaraṇa*) of the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* for the sake of the formal topic (*adhikaraṇa*).
Here, having extracted it from its context in that second section, it is inserted at this point.

In that regard, just as the name "Dārvi-homika" applies to the performers of the *smārta* *Pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* sacrifices—both because such usage is observed and because the etymological basis (*pravṛttinimitta*) exists—so too does it apply to the performers of the *śrauta* sacrifices, due to the usage of the term *vāstuhoma*.

Nor should it be argued that this ritual procedure is contradictory because it would entail the status of a *darvihoma* if performed with a single *ṛc*, since in reality there is no status of a *darvihoma*. For if the term *darvihoma* were merely a name for Smārta rites, then even when the *vāstuhoma* is performed with a single *ṛc*, it would follow that it lacks the status of a *darvihoma*.

Because this explanatory passage (arthavāda) serves as an indicator (jñāpaka) establishing the application of the term *darvihoma* even to those oblations prescribed in the revealed scriptures (*śrauta*), it is therefore a name for all [such acts]. Maṇḍana states: "It applies to both the worldly and the Vedic."
That is the locus for the *darvihoma*.
Śaṅkara says: "This name belongs even to the Vedic [rituals].
The term *darvihoma* is the designation specifically for *homas*, not for *yāgas*.
Or rather, it is the name for those [acts] enjoined by the injunctions of *juhoti*, because of their connection with that.
The Commentary states: The word *darvihoma* is the name for both worldly and Vedic acts.
It has been established that [the term] "darvihoma" is a name.
Now it is considered whether this is the name for all injunctions of *yajati* (sacrifices) and injunctions of *juhoti* (offerings), or only for the injunctions of *juhoti*.
Because there is no distinction, [it applies to] all.

Regarding the Darśa sacrifice [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.3.1]: "The Darśa belongs to Agni because of its nature" (*darśabhāvāt*). There is no definition of the *tarka* (logical reasoning) here. Nor is the *pañcaśarāva* (five-platter offering) enjoined by setting aside the Darśa.

Just as when the *girā* word is prohibited and the *irā* word is prescribed, there the *irā* word indicates the function (*kārya*) of the prohibited *girā* word; however, in this case, there is no such prohibition (by which a function could be indicated). Therefore, even in the case of the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*), since it is merely a metaphorical application of the function, there is no non-performance (*anāpatti*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*).

Because it is performed with the substance as heard [in the original injunction], whatever defect arises from the failure to perform the *darśa* sacrifice, the rite enjoined for the purpose of removing that defect attains syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the *darśa* by way of remedying the occurrence of that defect.
(Therefore, it is established that it is an auxiliary [*aṅga*].
Śabara: The five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) should be a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*).
"This might be so if the new moon (amāvāsyā) were ceased; however, it is not so.
For even upon the destruction of the previous substance, another substance is possible.
Soma—this is the contextual connection (*prādhvikī saṃgatiḥ*).

"One should drive away the calves for the subsequent oblation"—thus it is stated regarding the *darśa*. Regarding the driving away of the calves in the *darśa*: "In the *sāṃnāyya*, [the rites] beginning with the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) are first performed for the *āgneya* [offering], or else..."
According to the sequence of the performance of the ritual, the Sāṃnāyya offering is first accumulated.
The offering (*pradāna*) comes first, and likewise the cutting of portions (*avadāna*) in the Āgneya sacrifice is appropriate;
because the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyatantra*) governs those performed out of ignorance, it is recorded according to the order of the principal elements.

[Objection: But has it not been stated that the single ritual act (padārtha) begins with the cutting (avadāna) and ends with the offering (pradāna)? In that case, how can there be an inquiry into the order [of its constituent parts]? [Response: In that case, let this be a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*).
Or rather, let this inquiry proceed according to the injunction regarding the cutting of the portions for oneself (*sviṣṭakṛt*).
[The Bhaṭṭa concludes: Thus, by the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), the order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*) is sublated.

Just as, for instance, in the case of curd and the *pāṭha-dārśya* [offering], first come the constituent acts such as milking, and afterwards the acts such as the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) for the *āgneya* [oblation].

Then, although by the order of the text (*citakrama*) the placing of the oblation (*havirāsādana*), the sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* (*prayājaśeṣābhighāraṇa*), the cutting of the portions (*sviṣṭakṛdavadāna*), and so forth, are all obtained as things to be performed, they must first be performed for the *āgneya* according to the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), and afterwards for the *āgneya*’s counterpart.
For indeed, by the very order of the text, the performance of the *āgneya* comes first among the principal acts, and afterwards that of the *sāṃnāyya*.

Even though it might follow that the performance of the *āsādāna* (placing) and other rites must also occur in the order of the *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses, and thus, since there would be no fixed rule regarding the sequence of past and future activities, the primary order (*mukhyakrama*) would merely serve as a restrictive factor— therefore, this cannot be an instance of resolving a contradiction— nevertheless, another such example must be sought. The underlying reason for the refutation, however, is that in the primary order there is the favoring of proximity to the principal rite (*pradhāna*),
whereas in the order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*) there is mutual proximity among the subordinate elements themselves.
Therefore, there is a sublation of that [secondary application].
In this case, the primary act is not the illustrative example, because it has been established that the offering (*pradāna*) constitutes a single ritual element (*padārtha*).
Maṇḍana [states]: "The primary [act] is to be accepted; there is no application [of the secondary] when there is a contradiction."
In the case of Śaṃkara, there is likewise sublation by the order of the primary [rite].
In the Darśa sacrifice, the sequence of the two offerings to Agni follows the order of the primary [rites].
It is established by implication that the curd for the *darśa* sacrifice is to be prepared on the preceding day, as it serves as the material at the time of the drawing of the portions (*graha*).
The New Moon sacrifices (darśa) are established as being performed by distinct persons for Indra-Agni, Indra, and Mahendra.

Regarding the milk-giving (doha) for the sake of curds at the New Moon sacrifice: since it must be accomplished at the time of drawing the cup (graha), it is not established that it should take place on the previous day. [Vi.
6.1.9] The milk-giving at the New Moon sacrifice must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavītī) during the obligatory Agnihotra and other rites.
In the *Pretāgnihotra*, however, it should be performed with the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).
(3|4|2,4) Regarding the *Darśa* sacrifice, there are two milkings on the previous day in the evening; that [milk] is for the purpose of making curds.
On the day of the sacrifice, there is also a milking in the morning; that is solely for the purpose of [fresh] milk.

3|6|8: In the case of the loss of one or both of the milkings for the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is a five-pot-sherd rice-offering (*pañcaśarāva odana*) dedicated to Indra. And that [offering] is a subsequent rite (*karmāntara*); furthermore, it is part of the New Moon sacrifice itself, not a substitute (*pratinidhi*) for the New Moon sacrifice.

6|1|10: At the Darśa sacrifice, the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) of rice is optionally performed on the previous day. At both the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, only one of the two purificatory oblations (*pāvana-homa*) is to be performed.

Mā. 9|1|156–57: At the Darśa, the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) is prepared on the previous day; on the day of the sacrifice, the rites beginning with the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and ending with the covering (*abhivāsana*) are performed.
There is no such thing as "diminution" here.
[Vi.
5.1.16] There is a difference in time between the two primary rites of the Darśa sacrifice, because of the scriptural statement: "On the preceding day, on the new moon, one prepares the altar."
Bhāṣya 11.3.1.1: In the injunction "one should bring a branch facing east" at the Darśa sacrifice, it is the eastern direction of the tree that is indicated by the term "branch.
This is the statement regarding the *śālā* (branch).
At the Darśa sacrifice, there is the connection with the vow regarding the driving away of the calves, even in the case of one who does not maintain the sacred fires.
If it is time [that is intended], then because of the connection with its characteristic mark, [it applies] to the side of the restrained.
Commentary: It has been established that the connection is for the purpose of indicating time.
Now there is a doubt: does this time apply only to the side of the restrained, or also to the unrestrained?
What is established? That it belongs to the restrained side.
Why? Because it is heard thus: "He drives away the calves before [the time].
And there is no driving away of calves by one who is unrestrained.
Therefore, the time [for the *apākaraṇa*] is indeed within the period of restraint (*saṃyatapakṣa*).
The *apākaraṇa* is an indicative mark (*liṅga*). Alternatively, because it serves the purpose of indicating the time, it may be understood as applying to both.
Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
It is not only in the case of one who is self-restrained;
this time-period would also apply to one who is unrestrained.
Why? Because it serves the purpose of time.
There is no purpose for the removal of the calves or the vow itself;
rather, the purpose lies in the time.
And that for which there is a purpose therein is indicated.
But how is the removal of the calves for the sake of time? Because it is for the sake of another; for they are removed for the sake of the milk.
For in this way, there is a visible purpose;
otherwise, there would be an invisible purpose. And therefore, the driving away of the calf is heard of in scripture as something to be adopted.
As for what was said— that [the fruit] occurs only on the side of the self-restrained due to connection with those signs—
that is not so;
for even one who is not self-restrained may experience it through the power of time.
Even for one who does not perform the *sāṃnāyya* offering, there would be no drawing away of the calves at all, and certainly not even the time for drawing away the calves.
For us, it is the time that is required, not the drawing away of the calves;
just as when it is said, "One should arrive at the time of the conch-blast."
Even in a village where a conch-shell does not exist, at the time when the sound of a conch is heard, one says "it exists"; thus, its presence does not make one subject to ridicule.

Just as in the case of the *darśa* sacrifice, there is the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) and the fetching of the branch (*śākhā-āharaṇa*), so too here, even though the driving away of the calves does not actually take place, because it exists at that time, the vow (*vrata*) is not made ridiculous by its absence at that time.
In the *Soma-sūtra*, "due to the connection with its indicative mark" means due to the connection with that mark or sign of that time.
[The verse states: "That time would belong to the *sāṃnāyya* offering, or perhaps to the other as well;
for the time characterized by the calf's sucking belongs to this other [offering] as well."

Bhaṭṭa: Although the driving away of the calf (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) is an indicator of time (*kālopalakṣaṇa*) and not itself a constituent part (*aṅga*) because it serves another purpose, nevertheless, since the time itself cannot be known in its absence, and since the driving away of the calf exists only for one who performs the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice, the vow (*vrata*) is required.

For this very reason, even in the case of a single-cake offering (*ekapuroḍāśā*), although the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is absent, the *āgneya* sacrifice is present; thus, because the indicator of time exists, there is no deficiency even in the *upāṃśuyāja*.

This being the position reached: in cases such as "one should arrive at the time of the conch-blast," even though [the time] is merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), because that indicator has ceased [to apply], and because the specific time—consisting of the sequence following the *anvādhāna*—has not lapsed even in the absence of the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), the vow must indeed be performed even in the absence of the *sāṃnāyya* offering.
Maṇḍana says: "For one who is not self-restrained, the time is exactly thus.
Śaṃkara says: "That [time] would exist even in the case of no *sāṃnāyya*."
In the case of the Darśa sacrifice, even on the preceding day, there is no displacement of the rites ending with the removal of the oblation from the altar;
this is the principle of the *vaidikaraṇa* (preparation of the altar).
Bhāṣya 9.1.16.9 states: "In the Darśa, the cutting, bringing, and trimming of the branch are the motivators [of the subsequent acts]."
The section concerning the secondary piercing (*upavedha*).
In the *Darśa* sacrifice, it is stated: "With a branch, he drives away the calves" (Vi. 4.2.2). Thus, the bringing of the branch in the *Darśa* is a property of the milking.
The purpose is for both milkings.
The ritual duties such as fetching the branch at the *darśa* sacrifice are indeed for the sake of both milkings, not merely for the sake of the evening milking alone.
Because of the difference in time between the two milkings, they would have been heard [in scripture] as being connected.
Commentary: There is the evening milking, and likewise there is the morning milking.
However, there are duties pertaining to the milking, such as the preparation of the shed, the driving forth of the cows, the sprinkling [of water], the milking of the cows, and so forth.
Do these have the evening milking as their purpose, or do they serve the purpose of both?
What, then, is the established position? The ritual duty heard [in the scripture] would apply to those two milkings separately.
Why? Because on the day of preparation (aupavasathya), they prescribe the fetching of the branches and other such acts in the sequence of the evening milking;
and the evening milking occurs on that very same day.
Therefore, by that sequence, [the acts] for the sake of milking in the evening possess the characteristics of milking.
Or rather—having thus shown the non-contradiction of the sequence, he now shows the contradiction:
