because of the commonality of location on the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*) or because of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), the acts beginning with the fetching of the branch would result in being for the purpose of the curd (*dadhi*).
Or rather, because there is no distinction in the context, the scriptural injunction regarding time applies to that which is connected with it.
The Commentary states: For the context is common;
just as it is for curd, so it is for milk.
Furthermore, context is more powerful than sequence;
therefore, the duties of milking (dohadharma) serve both purposes.
Moreover, there is no scriptural injunction for the milking on the previous day.
What then? On the following day. How so? For they prescribe thus: "The curd for Indra on the new moon day," and "The milk for Indra on the new moon day.
Indeed, both [offerings] together with their constituent parts are enjoined for the new moon day.
This very evening milking is, by implication, performed on the preceding day.

This is the inherent nature of curds: that which was prepared on the previous day reaches its completion on the following day. Therefore, it is simply not the case that these [mantras] are prescribed in the sequence of the evening milking.
Therefore, the characteristics of *dohada* serve both purposes.
Alternatively, when performed in the context of the teaching of Dharma, it follows the sequence;
and while being recited, it constitutes a subordinate section (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).
The Dadhi-sacrifice, however, is prescribed and performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
Therefore, it is equal to the milk [sacrifice].
Certain ritual acts (dharmas), intended for the accomplishment of the state of being curd, are performed on the preceding day.

Furthermore, those [acts] such as the fetching of the branch are not the "apprehenders" (grāhaka) of the subordinate elements (guṇas), because it has been established that "subordinate elements exist for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*), and thus their [direct] connection is impossible.

Therefore, since the fetching of the branch and so forth are prescribed for the sake of both [the curd and the Soma], their performance on the previous day is due to this dual purpose, and not solely for the sake of the curd; hence there is no fault.

Regarding the purpose of the Soma: there is no restrictive rule (*niyamābhāva*) that the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) must be performed specifically for the sake of the morning milk on the previous day.
Likewise, for one who milks in the evening, another shed need not be prepared for the morning milking; however, according to the Siddhānta, both [milkings] pertain to that same location.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: because of the difference in time between the two milkings, the location belongs to the evening milking, not to the morning milking. Therefore, the milk mentioned in the text would remain unconnected with the ritual properties [of the morning milking].
The ritual properties such as the cutting of branches and so forth are established for the evening milking;
they either exist for the morning milking as well, or they remain as before due to their position in the evening.
Because there is a connection through the context of having no other subject of discourse, they exist on the previous day;
therefore, by virtue of this strong contextual indication (*prakaraṇa*), they are present even at the morning milking (*prātardoha*).
In the Bhaṭṭa view regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, curd is produced on the previous day and milk on the following day; furthermore,
the duties pertaining to the milking, such as the fetching of branches and so forth, are performed on the previous day.
"Because of the instruction for their performance, there is the sequence of the mere curd.
Thus ends the section on the throwing away of the branch in the Darśa sacrifice.
Even if there were a position [of *sthāna*] when [the time] has arrived, it would nevertheless be bound by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
For here, unlike in the previous case, the existence of a context cannot be set aside by one who asserts that the assistance [of the subsidiaries] is already established.
Nor does the *sthāna* of the curd-offering exist, because its performance occurs on the very next day.

Even though *dadhi* (curd) is already present [in the context], its [re-statement] does not fall into redundancy; rather, its purport is to characterize it as a means to the *apūrva* (unseen potency).

Nor can there be a suspicion that it merely serves as a reminder (*smāraka*) of the sacrifice through *dadhi*, because for the Naiyāyikas, such a reminder cannot function as a "grasper" (*grāhaka*) [of the relationship].

Furthermore, the properties of the *dohada* (the milk-offering) are enjoined on the very next day; since there is a requirement for the *bhāṣya* (commentary) precisely there, these properties, being understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) as serving both purposes, are established accordingly.

Even though the specific duties being performed on the previous day are carried out with the status of being "on the previous day," they do not exist solely for the sake of that [previous-day status].
However, the distinction is that acts such as milking recur by virtue of their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Maṇḍana states: "In the case of milking, the group of milking acts [recurs], because of their equality."
Śaṅkara: "The procedure for the two milkings is the same.
9. The cutting of the branch and so forth is not the motive for the *upaveṣa*; rather, the driving away of the calf is the motive.

In the case of cutting the branch for the Darśa sacrifice, the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) alone is the motive for the acts of removing [the calf from the mother] and separating [the milk], not the placing of the potsherds (*kapālopadhāna*) as well.
Likewise, the acts such as cutting have only the [milk] as their purpose, and not the root [of the branch] as their purpose either.
The throwing away of the branch at the Darśa sacrifice is a *pratipatti* (disposal), not an *arthakarma* (primary act).
This is the section concerning the throwing away of the branch (*śākhā-praharaṇādhikaraṇa*).
In the Darśa sacrifice, the throwing of the branch is performed together with the *prastara* bundle into the fire.
(Vi.
4.2.3) [This occurs] at the time of the throwing of the *prastara* bundle in the Darśa sacrifice.
The branch [is placed] on the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara), like the act of mixing [the curds].
Commentary: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]."

In this regard, it is heard in the scripture: "He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] along with the branch (*śākhā*). Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the branch a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the *prastara*, such that there is a relationship between them based on the purpose of the subsidiary? Or is the connection for the sake of time—that is, the branch is to be thrown at the time of throwing the *prastara*? What is the prima facie conclusion (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? The branch is [subsidiary] to the *prastara*, like the act of pouring (*āśrayaṇa*).
The branch is a subordinate constituent of the grass-bundle (prastara). Why? Because of the rule: "When used with *saha* (together), the third case ending occurs for the non-principal element.
And that third case ending is applied to the branch.

Therefore, the branch is subordinate to the grass-bundle (prastara). Furthermore, the accusative case is used for the grass-bundle, while the instrumental case is used for the branch in the sense of accompaniment; the accusative denotes the primary element, whereas the instrumental denotes the subordinate.

But surely no visible benefit is conferred upon the grass-bundle by the branch? True, no visible benefit is conferred; however, an invisible benefit (adṛṣṭa) is conferred, just as in the case of the mixing [of the soma].
As in the case of "He mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk," the second case ending,
through its connection with the third case ending, indicates an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭopakarā*).
"Thus it is here as well.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: This is commenced by way of the occasion of the connection with the calf (*vatsasaṃyoga*).
Alternatively, the connection is: "What is the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the throwing away of the branch (*śākhāpraharaṇa*)?"
But is it not established in the fourth [book] (4.2.4.12) that the branch is for the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*)?
It is replied:
even though the grass-bundle (*prastara*) is for disposal, its existence serves as a well-known illustration.

Therefore, that very same [consequence] might also occur here. To address the doubt as to how this could be so, this undertaking is appropriate for the purpose of establishing that [point], since both are subject to temporal regulation.
Commentary: Or it may be an injunction regarding time.
Why? Because both are present.
Since it is a sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara), its existence is already established by the requirement for the protection of the Soma vessels.
Its striking is also prescribed by another sentence at a specific time;
therefore, this is a restatement of it for the purpose of conveying [the application of] the hall.
It is said:
"Let there be a restatement of the sacrificial grass;
however, it is the hall that is enjoined here. To this it is replied:
Because both are already present.
For the branch was previously enjoined for the purpose of separating the calves;
now, however, is it enjoined as a subordinate element, or is it being disposed of?
When [the action] is being performed, a visible purpose is observed:
there would be space for movement due to the specific location;
and as for the degree and extent of the conjunction with another location, nothing visible exists [beyond that].
Therefore, the striking is the performance of the sacrificial post.
Consequently, because there is no further purpose [for it], the rule for the time of its disposal is established.
Now, one might object: the third case ending occurs when something is subordinate, and that [subordination] resides in the branch.
To this it is replied: that which is the third case in the passage concerning the branch functions as the second case;
and that which is the second case in the passage concerning the grass-bundle functions as the third case.
How is this understood? This is a conjunction [of two acts]; both are to be performed at one time.
In this regard, for that whose time is fixed, there is a restatement (anuvāda); but for that whose time is not fixed, there is an injunction (vidhi).
And [the mantra] for the branch is unsharpened, while that for the prastara-bundle is sharpened. Furthermore, its repetition is not for the sake of the meaning; thus it is subordinate.
The utterance of the other [word] is primary. Primacy is the meaning of the accusative case; in that context, the third case [is used].
The word *pāda* also has the meaning of the third case; in that context, the second case [is used].
Therefore, the case-ending is used in the sense of "today.
The *Ṭup-ṭīkā* states: "The injunction regarding time applies to both [the day and the night], because both exist [in the context].
But surely, according to the rule "when joined with *ahaḥ*, the third case is used for the subordinate element," the third case occurs only in connection with the word *saha* (together with).
It is said:
if that were so, then the *yajus* would also be subordinate to the branch, just like the *prastara*.
As it is said: "The *sūktavāka* itself is the *yājyā*; the *prastara* is the oblation."
If it is argued that this applies only to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [we reply that] it serves the purpose of indicating the time.
This is said.
Because of the mention of the *sūktavāka* in relation to the *prastara*;
or rather, because the *prastara* is mentioned as being a constituent part of the sacrifice, it possesses the nature of a sacrifice.
Otherwise, there would be no *yājyā* verses and so forth.
It is not so here;
therefore, it is well said that there is a connection with the "pure" [state] immediately upon the striking.
This is because it is for the purpose of purification (*saṃskāra*).
Commentary: Nor is a visible benefit to the *prastara* (grass-bundle) produced by the branch;
for grass being burned does not provide a benefit to wood, whereas grass would indeed benefit wood that is being burned.
Therefore, the branch is not for the sake of the *prastara* (grass-bundle).
And for that reason, it should be present even when [the *prastara*] is separated [from the ritual].
The Commentary asks: "What is the purpose? Even if the branch is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the *prastara*, nevertheless, at the time of throwing the *prastara*, the branch is also cast away."
It is said:
if the branch is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *prastara* as it is being thrown, then it must not be thrown without the *prastara*;
but if it is not an auxiliary, it may be thrown even without the *prastara*.
The act of throwing [the branch] is without a sacrificial fee (*asāmiṣkarma*), and it is to be performed at the time of the *prastara* (grass-bundle).
Therefore, even in the event of separation, for that very reason, the throwing of the branch should take place even when separated from the *prastara*.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: If the branch were a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*) of the *prastara*, then one would have to explain that the *prastara* must not be thrown without the branch.
On the full moon day, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) should be used for the *śālā* (shed).
According to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should be thrown away even without the *śākhā* (branch).
Alternatively, the example may be explained otherwise.
Regarding the *prātaḥsavanīya* cakes, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the branch should not be discarded without the *prastara*;
in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should be discarded.
Furthermore, the *upaveṣa* would be present only optionally.

Commentary: If it were as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) maintains—that the branch exists both when the *sāṃnāyya* offering is present and when it is absent—then the *upaveṣa* (the wooden splinter used for clearing embers) would likewise exist both when it is present and when it is absent.

However, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), since the branch is prescribed as being disposed of (*pratipādyate*) specifically on the path of the *sāṃnāyya* offering, the *upaveṣa* exists only in that case and not otherwise. Ci:
"By the injunction 'one should carry the *prastara* [grass-bundle] together with the branch,' the branch is prescribed."
Or rather, time is indicated here as the purpose for the engagement of one who has already begun the practice.
The first [case] is due to the fear of being a mere subordinate part (*aṅga*); they seek its disposal (*pratipatti*).
Since the branch (*śākhā*) is employed [in the rite], it is not distinct from the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), because of its disposal [along with it].

(412) And that [concomitance] is not by way of equal primacy (*samapradhānatva*), because the throwing of the branch (*śākhā-praharaṇa*) is likewise a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the sacrificial post-shed (*śālā*); rather, in the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara-praharaṇa*), the branch is subordinate (*guṇatva*). This is understood from the grammatical rule "when joined with *saha*, that which is not primary [is the object of the suffix]" (*sahayukte 'pradhāne*), which establishes its subordinate status, just as milk is subordinate in the sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇagraha*).

This being the position reached: although the branch is heard [in the text] as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) in the verbal cognition, nevertheless—by means of postulating an additional injunction for a secondary understanding (*ārthika-pratīti*) according to the logic of the sprinkling of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings—the branch, like the *prastara* grass-bundle, possesses the same status of having its purpose fulfilled; therefore, it is to be disposed of (*pratipādya*). For this very reason, it has been stated that even the mention of the branch as a subordinate element in the verbal cognition is for the sake of its disposal at the time of the throwing of the *prastara*, and not because it is itself an independent ritual act (*tantra*). Consequently, for one who does not perform the *saṃnayana* (the preparation of curd and milk), the throwing of the *prastara* occurs even without the branch.

And at the Full Moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī), when it is performed according to one's capacity, even in the absence of the *prastara* (grass-bundle), the throwing of the branch (*śākhā-praharaṇa*) takes place by the principle that "when a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted [the primary act remains]. Maṇḍana says: "One should throw the branch at the time of the *prastara-homa*. Śaṅkara says: "Therefore, the branch is indeed to be disposed of."
Therefore, at the time of the throwing of the *prastara* bundle, the meaning is that the sacrificial hall (*śālā*) is to be assigned [to the fires] and the fires are to be cast into them.
Regarding the cleansing of the branch (*śākhā-mārjana*) in the *darśa* sacrifice, the mantra is "ūrjaṃ tvā" (Vi.

2.1.19). Regarding the milking of the *sāṃnāyya* milk in the *darśa* sacrifice, by the word "the northern one" (*uttarā*) in the injunction "she milks the northern one," all the cows currently present—those other than her own three—are to be milked.
1|1|12: In the *darśa* sacrifice, during the sprinkling of the *sāṃnāyya* vessels, [the action] occurs through the application of mantras such as "be purified" (*aśundhadhvam*).
This is the section on Order (*krama*).

3|1|5: In the *darśa* sacrifice, the *sāṃnāyya* offering belongs to one who has performed the *soma* sacrifice; however, for one who has not performed the *soma* sacrifice, there are the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni and Indra.
The words *darśa* and *amāvāsyā* have the same meaning. Bhāṣya 4.1.11.134:
The commencement of the *darśa* sacrifice takes place before sunrise, not during the day.
The intention [is the cause]. The performance at midnight is by means of the new moon sacrifice.
Bhaṭṭa 12.1.15.
The New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Having established the sacred fires, everyone resolves: "At every lunar festival (parvan), the New and Full Moon sacrifices must be performed by me.
(Bhāṣya 1.1.1)
Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa):

even though the charcoal embers [of these sacrifices] are not employed anywhere in the single-mantra-brāhmaṇa of the Jyotiṣṭoma, this non-utility does not exclude one’s eligibility [to perform the Jyotiṣṭoma], because fitness is established precisely through the distinction of the *iṣṭi* sacrifices.
Vārttika 3.8.8.18. The New and Full Moon sacrifices are prescribed to be performed for thirty years.
*Sañkalpa* 1.3.7: The *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), yet by another scriptural statement they are also optional (*kāmya*). Thus:

"One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*. Regarding these *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the texts further prescribe: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *Sāṅkapraśāyīya*; one desiring prosperity should sacrifice with the *Saṃkramayajña*. Here, the fruit is stated to arise from a subsidiary element (*guṇa*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* itself, not from separate rituals.

Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.2.14–16: The view that the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are not distinct rites every month is maintained because there is no difference in their connection, form, injunction, and name.

In this regard, the connection with the result is "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*); the form consists of the cake on eight potsherds for Agni (*āgneyāṣṭākapāla*) and so forth; the injunction is "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*); and the name "New and Full Moon sacrifices" is one and the same. Thus, there is no division of the ritual action (*karmabheda*). Viṃśatikā 2.4.2: The New and Full Moon sacrifices accomplish the result collectively, according to the principle: "Because of the purpose [of the whole], [the parts] are connected" (*prayojanābhisaṃbandhāt*). (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.3.1).
Su. Pṛ. 544: The New and Full Moon sacrifices have a common ritual framework (samānatantra).
Mā. 1.3.1.16: 54. The New and Full Moon sacrifices are for the sake of all desires;
one who is fit for the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

4|3|1|25-26: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma. Here, [the connection] is for the purpose of time; Soma is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the Darśa. Vi. 4|3|16: The modifications of Soma, such as the Gavya and others, which are single-day rites (*ekāha*), should be performed only after the Darśapūrṇamāsa, not before.

Mā. 5|3|1|26: Regarding "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the word *Darśapūrṇamāsa* indeed denotes a sacrifice (*yajña*); here, the state of being the instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) is heard in relation to the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
One should perform something else by means of the collection of sacrifices known as the Darśapūrṇamāsa;
that which is other than that is what is stated as being to be performed, not the sacrifice itself,
and that is the apūrva.

"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*)—this is an injunction concerning the qualification of a person for an optional rite (*kāmyapuruṣādhyādhikāravidhi*) that pertains to the connection between the ritual action and its fruit (Bāla., p. 14). From the statement "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," it is understood that the fruit of the primary rite along with its subsidiaries (*sāṅgapradhāna*), which consists of the animal sacrifice to Agni (*āgneyapaśu*), accrues to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) (Vi., 3.8.24).

Regarding the fruit heard in the text "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," heaven is the fruit of the six primary rites beginning with the *āgneya* collectively (*tantra*), and not separately for each primary rite.
Regarding the lapse of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa): [Section 2027] the threshing of the grains for the Darśapūrṇamāsa;

regarding the lapse of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, there is the prescribed procedure for the Vaiśvānara and Adhvaradīkṣita offerings. This is the section [establishing] that expiations (prāyaścitta) are for the purpose of removing defects.

VI. 12|3|15: Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the term *adhicāpa* is used in the statement, "He scatters [the grain] upon it (*adhi*) and places the potsherds (*kapālāni*) upon it (*upadadhāti*).
*Adhicāpa* refers to the placing of the rice grains upon the sacrificial oblation for the purpose of grinding.

III. 8|10: Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, concerning the *yeyajāmaha* formula which is established by a general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*), there is the rule: "One does not perform the *yeyajāmaha* in the *anuyāja* offerings."

In that context, the negative particle (*nañ*) is used for the purpose of determining whether there is mutual exclusion (*anyonya-bādha*) or an alternative (*vikalpa*). When considering whether this [negative] signifies a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) or is called an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that, because the negative particle primarily functions as an injunction according to the *śruti* (direct Vedic statement), it must signify a prohibition. However, even though a prohibitive sense is understood, in the case of "one should not look" (*nekṣeta*), since it stands in grammatical apposition with the word "vow" (*vrata*), one does not accept the prohibitive sense; rather, by the principle of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it is accepted as an exclusion, functioning as a subordinate element.

Su. Pṛ. 8. Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: the third after-offering (anuyāja) is a directly contributing auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) because it effects the consecration of the deity Sviṣṭakṛt.
This is the section concerning the third after-offering.
Ke. 10|4|19|38. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one who speaks untruth shall attain hell, yet he shall also obtain the fruit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa without any alternative.
PMS 4.3.1.43 (p. 112): In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the prohibition against speaking untruth is an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

PMS 3.4.8: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the *anvādhāna* preparatory mantra beginning with "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations" (*mamāgne varco vihaveṣvastu*) is to be recited by the Adhvaryu; however, the fruit mentioned therein belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) alone, because it is [the sacrificer] who is to be addressed.

3|8|14. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* [iṣṭi] makes the person who is about to undertake the commencement of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* fit for the undertaking of the ritual action.
Bhāṣya 9|1|10|34–35, Section 2: At the beginning of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is performed only once. This is the *ārambhaṇīyā-nyāya*.
9|1|12|34-35, Section 1: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the *anvāhārya* (subsidiary rice-offering) is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the purpose of hiring.
It must be performed by the master (*svāmin*), not by the *adhvaryu* priest.
This is because the hiring of priests is an act belonging to the master.
Ke. 3|8|12–2. In the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the cooking of the *anvāhārya* (subsidiary rice-offering) is subject to option.
This rule is made known in the context of the *āgneya* sacrifice involving a cloth and a calf.
Vi. 10|3|9. In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, regarding the *anvāhārya* sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), only Brāhmaṇas are seen [to be eligible], as it is said: "These indeed are the gods."
"Whenever [the Brāhmaṇas say]...
(Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.4.15.47). In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is the practice of sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) upon the anvāhārya rice; this is for the purpose of making it savory.
However, in the case of the Āgneya sacrifice, the sprinkling of the cloth and the heifer—which serve as the sacrificial fees—is set aside.

VI. 10|3|10. Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it has been stated (3|2|15–6) that the mention of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) in the rule, "When about to carry forth the water, one restrains speech; one releases it together with the *haviṣkṛt*," is for the purpose of indicating the time. Bhāṣya 11|3|1|15. In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the carrying forth of the water is done with a cup (*camasa*).
VI. 1|4|2. In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the pouring out of the water is the motive (*prayojaka*) for the act, whereas the pouring down (*ninayana*) is a disposal (*pratipatti*).
The *ninayananyāya*:

Ke. 4.2.14–15. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, regarding the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the waters, the *godohana* vessel serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), not the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Vi.
4.1.2, Section 3: In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, regarding the carrying forward of the waters, the mantra for the *godohana* and other vessels is [recited] because it is optional (*kāmya*).

4|1|2. Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is a figurative statement (*bhakti*) identifying the sprinkling of water (*apāṃ vyutseka*) as the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), as in: "This indeed is the *avabhṛtha* of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Bhāṣya 7|3|1|44. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is fourfold. That which is called the "fruit-*apūrva*" (*phalāpūrva*) or "supreme *apūrva*" (*paramāpūrva*) is that which generates heaven (*svarga*).

On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), there is one composite group consisting of three sacrifices, and another composite group consisting of the sacrifice of the cake for Agni (āgneyapuroḍāśa), the low-voiced sacrifice (upāṃśuyāja), and the sacrifice of the cake for Agni-Soma (agnīṣomīyapuroḍāśa). These two composites constitute the two parvans of the composite [sacrifice]. Within each composite, there are three originary apūrvas (utpattyapūrva) produced by the three sacrifices.
There are also subsidiary apūrvas (aṅgāpūrva) produced by the subsidiaries such as the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and those produced by acts such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).

In that regard, those [actions] produced by proximate auxiliaries (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) are required for the accomplishment of the *utpattyapūrva* (the original apūrva), whereas those produced by remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) are required for the accomplishment of the *samudāyāpūrva* (the collective apūrva).

Vi. 2.1.2. Regarding the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [the rule] "He offers while stepping forward" establishes that actions such as the stepping forward are auxiliary to the *prayāja* offerings, and through them, they are also auxiliary to the Darśa sacrifice.
This is the section concerning the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇādhikaraṇa*).
3|1|10. Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is the act of pouring [clarified butter] over (*abhighāraṇa*).

This is performed at the time of offering the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) into the ladle (*sruk*), for the purpose of preventing the sticking together of its parts; this includes both the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*).

10|2|12. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the act of sprinkling (*abhigharśana*) is connected only with the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), and not with the collective group of rites such as the *paurṇamāsī*.
Bhāṣya 9.2.11–19: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the sprinkling (abhigharṣaṇa) is for the purpose of all sacrificial materials (havir-mātra), both primary and subsidiary.
This is the section concerning sprinkling (3.7.4.10).

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the spreading [of ashes] (abhyūhana)—expressed by the rule "He spreads the ashes with the Veda"—is a property of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); it would not apply to the rice-oblation (caru) dedicated to Sūrya.

Ke. 10|2|18|19. Regarding the *avaghāta* (threshing) in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices: the *avaghāta* in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices continues until the production of rice grains (*taṇḍula*). 2028. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it should be performed repeatedly even when there is no *soma*.
The section beginning with "of actions such as threshing," etc. (Vi.
11.1.6): In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, threshing does not produce an *apūrva* (transcendental result), because its purpose is perceptible;
however, it is enjoined as a restrictive cause for that *apūrva*.
2|1|3: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, threshing is the primary motivator [of the ritual action].

4|2|11: Just as the injunctions for threshing and other rites in the Darśapūrṇamāsa apply to *vrīhi* rice, they apply directly to *nīvāra* millet—which serves as a substitute for *vrīhi*—because, although deficient in the *vrīhi* species, *nīvāra* possesses the essential characteristics of the primary substance.
3|6|14: A determination regarding the injunctions for threshing and grinding in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
This is the section concerning the determination of the rules for purificatory rites such as threshing (Bhāṣya 4.2.11.26).

Regarding the threshing mantra used in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—namely, "I shall strike down the Rakṣas, the rival from heaven"—it should be recited only once at the first stroke, and not with every subsequent stroke.
This is known as the *avaghātanyāya* (the principle of threshing).

1|1|4|12|42 (45). In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the shaking [of the sacrificial vessel] is a characteristic of the *puroḍāśa* cake: "He shakes it with bunches of *darbha* grass. This [shaking] would not apply to the *caru* offering dedicated to Sūrya.

Ke. 10|1|2|160: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is a simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) from the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) up to the offering (*pradāna*), but not merely by the cutting of the portions alone.
The sequence beginning with the *avadāna* (cutting of portions) and ending with the *pradāna* (offering).
5.2.14. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) consists of the pouring of water; it is figurative.
"This is the *avabhṛtha* of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*."
VI. 7.3.4. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the injunction regarding threshing is for the purpose of restriction, not a mere restatement (anuvāda).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mention of two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) for one who does not sacrifice with Soma is a restatement.

"By means of the two *puroḍāśas*": this is a specification of the form of the two *puroḍāśas* for those who are already entitled [to the sacrifice], because it is heard in that context, like the *Vaiśyastoma*.
Commentary: Regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, this is taught: "One should cause a non-soma-sacrificer to sacrifice by means of the two *puroḍāśas* alone—the *Āgneya* and the *Śrautāmana*.

In that very context, there arises a doubt: Is this a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction of entitlement, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*s," such that a non-soma-sacrificer should sacrifice with these two *puroḍāśas*?

Now, what is the subject of this further discussion? Is it an injunction for the origination of another ritual act—namely, "one should sacrifice with two other cakes of this same kind"? Or is it an instruction regarding the performer of the rite, stating "having said 'with these two cakes,' one should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice"? Or is it an injunction regarding the time, stating "one should sacrifice with these two at the time of the non-Soma sacrifice"? Or is it a restatement (anuvāda) of the injunction for the Indra-Agni offering? Or is it a restatement of both? These are the possible positions.
What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? That it is a supplement to the qualification (adhikāra).
Regarding the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," this is its supplement: "one who has performed the Soma sacrifice and desires heaven should sacrifice with these two *puroḍāśa* cakes.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement of that [Soma sacrifice].
For the two *puroḍāśa* cakes are described by the word as being accompanied by that scriptural statement.
Therefore, these two are not additional; because they must be performed even by one who has not sacrificed with Soma,
they are connected to these two [sacrifices] by direct scriptural statement (śruti), not by time.
For that [latter] would have to be indicated by secondary implication (lakṣaṇā),
and direct statement (śruti) is more authoritative than secondary implication.
In that case, either one who has performed the Soma sacrifice would not have the two cakes, or one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice would not have the Sānnāyya.
If the non-Soma-sacrificer is enjoined with reference to the two *puroḍāśa* cakes, then the non-Soma-sacrificer does not [participate] in the *sānnāyya*.
In that case, the particle *eva* (only) provides support:
[the meaning is] that the Soma-sacrificer [participates] by means of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes alone, and not by means of the *sānnāyya*.
Now, two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśau) are prescribed with reference to one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice; thus, there are no sacrificial cakes for the Soma-sacrificer.
In that context, the word "eva" (only/just) occurs in this very place: "only for the non-Soma-sacrificer [there are] the two sacrificial cakes.
Just as: "One should know this very person—pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with celibacy (brahmacarya)."
O Brahmin, you should speak of me to that guardian of the treasure who would not deceive anyone whatsoever.
Thus [he said]. (Exit, 2.4).
Those who should have said, "Know him alone as pure," instead said, "Know purity as him."
The same applies here as well.

Since the statement of both [the *vaiśya* and the *rājanya*] constitutes a supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the scriptural injunction regarding eligibility (*adhikāra-śruti*), the initial [conclusion] occurs in both ways.

Just as in the case of the Vaiśyastoma, there is a supplementary portion to the scriptural injunction regarding eligibility stating, "A Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma," so too here, it is precisely a supplementary portion to the scriptural injunction regarding eligibility.
But there is no authority for impermanence, because an injunction is connected with what is permanent; therefore, it is a supplementary part of the sentence.
Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that this is merely a supplementary part of the sentence concerning authority.
For the New and Full Moon sacrifices are obligatory, as it is said: "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices for as long as one lives. And they are indeed obligatory.
In that regard, these two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) are auxiliary factors for the fruit [of the sacrifice].
It is untenable to say that these two are prescribed for one who is non-eternal and has not performed the Soma sacrifice.
Why? Because the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are indeed eternal, and they will be performed by one who, though not having performed the Soma sacrifice, intends to do so.
Thus, it is not tenable [to claim otherwise].
The injunction regarding the *puroḍāśa* cake has a constant connection with the entire complex of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Therefore, the scriptural statement concerning those who do not perform the Soma sacrifice is a supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) [of that injunction].
What then? It is the origination of two other distinct rites for those two [persons] who are entitled.
This connection is not made in such a way that "for as many cakes as are prescribed for the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the non-soma-sacrificer is enjoined with respect to them."
How, then, is it? For one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice and desires heaven, it is these two rites—the Āgneya and the Aindrāgna—that are enjoined.
If they are indeed enjoined, they are distinct rites from the previous ones.
In that case, the statement "these two" will be a restatement (anuvāda) with reference to the ritual properties (dharmas).
For example: "Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman upon these very Revatī verses.
In this way, the word *eva* (even/just) will have this meaning here;
just as in the case of: "Having eaten with milk, Devadatta should eat with milk."
The word "again" (punar) is understood to mean "he should indeed eat.

In this very same way, although the two *puroḍāśa* cakes are already prescribed for both the Soma-sacrificer and the non-Soma-sacrificer by the injunction for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), they are prescribed again for the non-Soma-sacrificer with the rule: "One should cause the Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with these two *puroḍāśas* alone.
Thus, it is understood that [the eating] is by means of one or the other.
And it does not apply by way of a partial connection, because the agent is the primary factor.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, as long as there remains a portion of the entitlement (*adhikāra*), a connection between the two *puroḍāśa* cakes and an agent who is a non-Soma-sacrificer is not tenable;
for when there is a remaining portion of the entitlement, it is the agent who is indicated as the primary factor."
Furthermore, in the absence of a fruit, the status of being the principal element is not logically tenable;
nor do the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), which constitute parts of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, become the means of accomplishing the fruit;
nor can the fruit be postulated on the basis of the authority of the scriptural statement.
Because there is an internal implication of the word "of the statement," for this reason also there is no remainder of an injunction;
likewise in the case of the *stoma*, because it is complete.
Commentary: As for what was described—that it is like the Vaiśyastoma—it is appropriate in the case of the Vaiśyastoma.
The entire Vaiśyastoma is intended, not merely a single part;
in that case, the result is possible.
And no fruit is possible here;
nor is anything single and eternal connected with that which is impermanent.
Therefore, one should perform the Vaiśyastoma sacrifice for these [purposes].
If it is argued that it must belong to the agent—the commentary says:

if you think that it cannot be understood as a supplementary part of the scriptural injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra*), then it is replied: [The objection: If it is argued that it must belong to the agent—the commentary says: if you think that it cannot be understood as a supplementary part of the scriptural injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra*), then it is replied:
The arising of another action is not possible here;
rather, the expression "these two" is understood as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a dependent relationship.
How then is this [to be explained]? It is an instruction for one who marks the parts.

O Agni, he who is the agent [is not the primary one]. The direct statement "he should cause to sacrifice" (yājayet) refers specifically to the causal agent; for the root *yaj* [in this context] functions through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
[It would belong] to the agent.
Furthermore, a contradictory relation between the eternal and the non-eternal would not be admitted;
nor could it possibly come to be.
For one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice, the *sāṃnāyya* is already obtained by means of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes;
therefore, one need not strive for it.
Therefore, the hearing [of the injunction] is not for the purpose of [specifying] time; rather, it is an injunction for a distinct ritual act.

Furthermore, since there is doubt regarding a repeated hearing intended for a subordinate quality because it has already been enjoined, the scriptural statement would have a dual purpose, just as in the case of the Āgneya sacrifice, which is seen to have a single deity despite being unintended [as such].
Commentary: The word "apica" (furthermore) serves to exclude the previous position.
This is not an injunction for a separate ritual action;
it is a restatement (anuvāda), because the Āgneya sacrifice has already been prescribed.
For that [sacrifice] has indeed been prescribed in both cases by the text: "The cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni is constant on the new-moon and full-moon days."
The rule regarding the Aindrāgna [offering] applies because it is not prescribed for both occasions.
Wherever it does not otherwise obtain, this scriptural statement (śruti) is for the purpose of prescribing the Aindrāgna on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī).
Just as it is not intended [for other times], so too the Āgneya is uttered.
And there is an injunction for both cases;

its manifestation is seen in the rule, "One divides the cake dedicated to Agni (āgneya) into four parts," as well as in the Sāṃkalpāyīya rite, "Having performed the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga), [one offers] with the cake dedicated to Agni."
"But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] the injunction.
Commentary: This also sets aside the aforementioned position.
It is not so.
Regarding the statement that "the offering to Agni is a restatement (anuvāda), while the offering to Indra-Agni is an injunction (vidhi)," both would be injunctions regarding time.
Why? Because the teacher Bādarāyaṇa held the view that the injunction for the Sāṃnāyya offering applies even prior to the Soma sacrifice.
The *sāṃnāyya* offering is also prescribed for one who does not perform the *soma* sacrifice, in the text: "He should prepare the *sāṃnāyya*.
Likewise: "In that very same way, for those who do not perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice, there is only the *sāṃnāyya* for one who does not perform the *soma* sacrifice.
Therefore, the connection [of the two offerings] is for the purpose of [specifying] time.
Or because of the cognition of what is prohibited.
The Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
This is not the case; it is not an injunction regarding time.
Nor is there the production of two additional rites, nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *āgneya* and an injunction (*vidhi*) for the *aindrāgna*.
What then? It is a restatement of both.
How so? This sentence is for the purpose of enjoining the *sāṃnāyya* offering for one who has performed the *soma* sacrifice.
Therefore, there is no injunction even for the offering to Indra-Agni;
for in that case, the sentence would be split.

The connection is made thus: for one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice, [the offering] is by means of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes alone, whereas for one who has performed the Soma sacrifice, there is also the *sāṃnāyya*.

"One should cause a non-Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with two *puroḍāśa* cakes—namely, the one dedicated to Agni and the one dedicated to Indra—and a Soma-sacrificer with the *sāṃnāyya*. Thus, by one sentence the *sāṃnāyya* is prescribed for the Soma-sacrificer, and by another sentence for the non-Soma-sacrificer.
Therefore, both are restatements (*anuvāda*).
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, this other passage also demonstrates this very point—that it does not refer to a separate ritual action.
How so? It says: "Fourteen oblations are offered at the full moon, thirteen at the new moon.
For if a separate ritual action were being produced, there would have to be more oblations.

Regarding the *Soma* sacrifice: although there is an absence of the fourfold portioning (*caturavadāna*) in what is called the *upāṃśuyāja*, the connection [of this topic] arises from the discussion of whether, for one who does not perform the *Soma* sacrifice (*asomayājin*), there is a displacement of the *sāṃnāyya* offering, or for one who performs the *Soma* sacrifice (*somayājin*), there is [the displacement] of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "By means of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes alone"—this refers to the instruction regarding the *puroḍāśa* cakes for those who do not perform the *Soma* sacrifice (*asomayājinaḥ*), that is to say, the instruction concerning the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the two *puroḍāśa* cakes for those who do not perform the *Soma* sacrifice.
This is because of the scriptural statement (*tacchrutitvāt*), since it is specifically those who do not perform the *Soma* sacrifice who are mentioned in the scripture.

Just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," where the qualification [for the rite] belongs to the Vaiśvadeva alone because it is explicitly mentioned in the scripture (*śruti*), so it is here as well. Vi— "There are seven positions: (1) the qualified persons are those who [sacrifice] with the two *puroḍāśa* cakes alone."
[Objection: It should be the remainder, because of the scriptural statement to that effect; [Response: Not so, because it exists eternally in its entirety.
(3) It is not the case that there is an injunction for another action; rather, it is simply recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
(4) It is not the case that there is an injunction of the causative sense (*ṇij-artha*); because it lacks a fruit, its own meaning is abandoned.
Let it be an injunction regarding time—no, for that would entail the fault of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Let it be an injunction regarding the offering to Indra and Agni—no, because of the inequality and the force of the particle *eva*.
"Let time be both a defining characteristic and [the subject] of its own meaning"—this is not so;
because it is a sentence prescribing an injunction through praise, it is not a mere restatement since it possesses its own purpose."
(Here, having refuted each preceding prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), each subsequent position is established; and the seventh position is the final conclusion [*siddhānta*].

Bhāṭṭa: In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there is a scriptural prohibition regarding those who have not performed the Soma sacrifice: "One who has not sacrificed with Soma should not perform the *sāṃnāyya* offering. This is the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the *sāṃnāyya* for one who is not a *somayājin*.
And because of that connection, it is heard in scripture: "One should cause a non-Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with two *puroḍāśas* alone—the one for Agni and the one for Indra-Agni.
This is either an injunction of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

Regarding the offering to Indra-Agni, since it has been prescribed specifically for one who does not perform the *sāṃnāyya* rite on the new moon day—namely, "one who does not offer the *sāṃnāyya* should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Agni on the new moon day"—its praise is appropriate by virtue of its suitability.

When it is considered what kind of person is intended by the injunction, the first position is that only the non-performer of the Soma sacrifice (*asomayājī*) is entitled to the two *puroḍāśa* cakes, and not the *sāṃnāyya*.

This is because his eligibility is established through the rule of exclusion (*paryudāsavidhi*). Furthermore, since the *sāṃnāyya* is prescribed for the non-performer of the Soma sacrifice as well—based on the statement from another recensional branch (*śākhā*) that says "he should offer the *sāṃnāyya*"—the *puroḍāśa*... [is thus restricted].

Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*): [The first view is that] only one who has not yet performed a Soma sacrifice (*asomayājī*) is entitled to perform the *āgneya* and subsequent offerings of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and not one who has performed a Soma sacrifice (*somayājī*).

This is because it would follow that there is no *āgneya* offering for the Soma-sacrificer, and since the *sāṃnāyya* is mandatory for the Soma-sacrificer, there is no possibility of the Soma-sacrificer performing the *aindrāgna* offering prescribed in the absence of the *sāṃnāyya*; thus, this position is untenable. [The second view is that] a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is being enjoined. This is the third [view].

The fourth [view] is that it is an injunction for officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), because there is no evidence for it being a separate action and because its propriety is established by the hearing of the particle *eva*.

The fifth [view] is that it is merely an injunction regarding time—namely, "the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśau*) at the time of the non-Soma sacrifice"—because the fruit is heard in the text and because this position is untenable since [officiating] is already obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*).

Furthermore, since that [offering] to Indra-Agni is already established at the time of the non-Soma sacrifice, and because if the time for the Agni offering were prescribed for the non-Soma sacrifice, it would result in a prohibition for the Soma-sacrificer, and because it would result in the loss of its status as a constant offering and the status of having all deities as its recipients, this is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise); thus, it is treated as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*) based on what is established in the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*. In certain alternative views, there is also the application of sublation (*bādha*) due to the sublation of the time for the Agni offering during the non-Soma sacrifice.
Maṇḍana states: "There are not two additional *puroḍāśa* cakes."

Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), in the passage "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo'ṣṭākapālaḥ*), the word *āgneya* is not the name of the ritual action, but rather an injunction regarding the deity. This is the section concerning the Āgneya (*āgneyādhikaraṇa*).
VI. 1.4.7: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is the offering to Agni on eight potsherds (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*).

In that context, within the ritual formulas (*nigama*), the designation of Agni must be by the word "Agni" itself as prescribed by the injunction, and not by any other term such as "the Pure One" (*śuci*) and so forth.
The section concerning the word "injunction" (vidhi-śabdādhikaraṇam). Ke. 10.4.12–14.

Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, after enjoining: "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni is constant on both the new moon and the full moon," it is further heard: "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni is [to be offered] on the new moon."
In that context, there is no double repetition regarding the *āgneya* [offering]; however, the repeated mention of it has the same purpose as that of the *aindrāgna*.

Bhāṣya 2.3.14.27–29. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the offerings (*yāga*) are: the *āgneya* cake (*puroḍāśa*), the *upāṃśuyāja*, the *agnīṣomīya* cake, the curd for Indra (*aindraṃ dadhi*), the milk for Indra (*aindraṃ payaḥ*), the *āghāra* libation, the two *ājyabhāga* portions, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the *patnīsaṃyāja*s.
Among these, those ending with the milk offering are the primary acts (*pradhāna*), while the *āghāra* and others are auxiliary acts providing indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*).

In the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, after having cut and offered the portion for Agni (āgneya), the cutting and offering of the portions for Agnīṣomīya and the others follow; thus, there is a simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) with respect to the principal acts of cutting.
This is the section concerning the principle of simultaneous performance from the cutting up to the final offering.

(Vi. 5.1.4). Furthermore, in the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, regarding the rule "one divides the portion for Agni into four parts" (*caturdhā karoti*), this fourfold division applies only to the *āgneya* cake, and not to the *aindrāgna* or *agnīṣomīya* cakes.
The principle of the fourfold division of the Āgneya [offering]:
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) for the Āgneya [oblation] is "Agnirmūrdhā divaḥ" (Bhāṣya 8.1.16.31).
In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *adhvarakalpa*, and the *upāṃśuyāja* is a modification of the *sārasvata-mājin*.

5.1.10). In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) of the remnants of the *prayājas* for the *āgneya* offering comes first according to the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), and after that, that of the *sāṃnāyya*. (Ke. 5.1.7.4).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Āgneya offering comes first, not the Āgnīṣomīya, even though the Brāhmaṇa text is otherwise;
this is because the Āgneya mantra appears first in the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Yājamāna sections (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.2),
and because the recitation of the mantras depends upon the recitation of the Brāhmaṇas (Jaiminīya Sūtra 5.1.9).

In the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), regarding the taking of handfuls, the placing of the potsherds, and the portions for the *āgneya* and *āgnīṣomīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), there is "concomitant performance of the whole" (*samudāyānusamaya*); this is the principle of concomitant performance of the whole (*samudāyānusamayanyāya*).
Bhāṣya 5.1.3.4. In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the *āgneyājyabhāga* (the butter-portion for Agni) is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*);
this is the principle of the *āgneyājyabhāga* (*āgneyājyabhāganyāya*).

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, although there is a distinction between the primary offerings such as those dedicated to Agni and others, the performance of the preparatory rites (āghāra) and other rituals is carried out collectively (tantra), because they share the same location, time, and performer.
Because the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*) exist for the sake of the principal acts (*pradhāna-karman*), there would be a difference in their performance according to the distinction between them.

**Bhāṣya:** Regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the principal acts are the *Āgneya* and others, while the *Āghāra* and others are their subsidiaries. Concerning these, it is considered whether the subsidiaries are to be performed separately for each of those principal acts, or whether they are to be performed collectively (*tantra*) for all of them. What, then, occurred in that regard? [It was stated: "And like the seasons, this [subsidiary] should be inferred to be for the sake of the fruit" (1.1.1.29).
In that case, the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice was performed with reference to [the whole] collectively;

but here, each respective primary act is considered individually. What is the prima facie view? Since the subsidiaries are for the sake of the primary acts, there would be a division of the ritual procedure according to the distinction between those primary acts.
There would be a distinction in the application of the subsidiaries; why? Because they are for the sake of the principal action.
That is to say, because they are for the sake of the principal.
For the subsidiaries are taught for the purpose of the principal.
How is it that the primary acts possess subsidiaries?
And when there is a connection with the subsidiaries, the simultaneity of the primary acts is not intended to be expressed.
For in that case, the principal acts are not being enjoined; rather, it is the subsidiaries. And a quality of a matter that is already being enjoined is not intended to be significant.
Just as there is oneness in the thought "I am the cleanser," so too,
if each primary rite were to be connected with its subsidiaries,
then if those subsidiaries were performed only once, they would not be connected with [all] the primaries individually.

As it was stated in the section beginning with "vidhistvevaśrutitvāt" [JS 2.2.13], that there must be a connection between the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices and the entire set of eleven sacrificial stakes (*ekādaśinī*), therefore there is a distinction of subsidiaries for each primary act.
[Objection: But surely, in the section "anabhyāso vā prayogavacanaikatvāt" [JS 11.1.17–19], the simultaneous performance of the subsidiaries was established?
What is to be considered here? To this he says: The procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is connected [to the sacrifice] by favoring the instrument (*karaṇa*) through its cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Therefore, it has been stated that there is no tautology even for the primary acts (*pradhāna*) which have already received assistance [in the form of the abundance of results].
Now, however, it is deliberated whether the procedure assists the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices collectively (*tantra*), or individually (*bheda*).
In this regard, we say: [the procedure applies] "individually.

How so? First, the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) assists all the primary rites, beginning with the *Āgneya*. And at the time of providing that assistance, their collective unity (*sāhitya*) is not intended to be expressed, because it resides in the objective element (*uddeśya*).
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it benefits each individual [action] alone, and not the actions taken together.
However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: he will state that the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary acts (*pradhāna*) share the same location, time, and agent.
Consequently, because no distinction is perceived, [the auxiliary act], being performed only once, benefits [them all].
Therefore, there is the performance of the subsidiaries according to the *tantra* (simultaneous) method;
otherwise, due to the violation of the sequence, there would have to be simultaneity.
The Commentary states: "And the principal acts possess a sequence."

And these [rites] must be performed with their respective auxiliary parts in the proper sequence. In that regard, if the *tantra* were the auxiliary parts, then the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice would commence without having first performed the *āgneya* sacrifice; and thus there would be a disruption of the sequence of the principal rites.

But if there is a distinction, then having concluded the Āgneya sacrifice along with its subsidiaries, the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice is commenced along with its subsidiaries; thus, there is no violation of the sequence.

Another says: if the subsidiaries were to belong to the common ritual framework (*tantra*), then as long as the *Tanūnapāt* offering benefits the Āgneya, so long would the *Samidh* offering have to benefit the Agnīṣomīya. This would indeed be a violation of the sequence of benefits (*kopa* meaning contradiction).
Moreover, [substances] such as charcoal and cows, as well as [qualities] such as touch and so forth, are understood to be distinct for each primary element (*pradhāna*).
Through these, there will be no lack of distinction among the substrates (*ādhāra*) and the rest.
However, for those that are identical, there would be simultaneity due to being taught by a single word, because no specific difference is perceived.
The commentary states: The word "but" (tu) introduces an alternative position. This position—that there is a distinction—is not the best;
what then? There should be simultaneity, that is, a single performance.
The auxiliary elements (aṅga), when employed once, are connected simultaneously with all the primary rites (pradhāna).
This is because there is no perception of any distinction among those that are equal and taught by a single term.

These [rites] are equal in terms of agent, place, and time, as expressed in the injunctions: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," "One should sacrifice on the full moon day with the Paurṇamāsa," and "One should sacrifice on the new moon day with the Amāvāsyā."

And he will state that the subsidiaries (aṅga) share the same place, time, and agent as the primary acts (pradhāna) in the passage: "But the subsidiaries, because they are enjoined, are taught along with the primary act" (JS 11.1.1). Furthermore, by a single word, the primary acts are taught with respect to the fruit: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. What follows from this? From this, it follows that they (the primaries) act in combination toward the fruit.

Therefore, for one desiring heaven, there is a simultaneous desire to perform all [the rites], not just one. However, when the Āghāra-libations and other such acts are performed with the desire to perform them all, no distinction is perceived among those having the same agent and so forth as to whether these belong to the Āgneya sacrifice or to the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice.
And all [of these] are applicable;
therefore, all [the paths] exist.
Therefore, there is no returning.
"There would be a connection because of the single purpose.
Commentary: As for the statement, "And there would be a disruption of the sequence if there were simultaneity," to that we reply:
Because of the single purpose, there would be no intervention; there is no disruption of the sequence.
Why? Because they have a single purpose.
It has been stated that these are "conjoined performers" (sambhyakārīṇi); their action is simultaneous, not individual.
For in that case, no purpose is served by what is performed by one alone;
rather, there would be a sequence in the performance of the single act of connection. Therefore, there is a sequence in their employment; how then could there be a violation of the sequence?

As for the argument that there would be a disruption of the sequence in the case of assistance (*upakāra*), even there, the substratum does not assist the primary acts (*pradhāna*) merely by being performed;
for at that time, the primary acts themselves do not yet exist.
Rather, when all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) have been performed, then the *apūrvas* produced by them combine and assist the primary acts.

For it has been stated that even the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) possess the quality of performing their function collectively, according to the rule: "Now, because they have a single deity, there is a single performance" (JS 11.1.16).
Therefore, even with respect to the benefit (*upakāra*), there is no violation of the sequence.
And thus, Kāmukāyana cites a scriptural observation regarding another matter [to support this].
The Commentary states: And likewise, there is the observation of another fact which accords with the principle as taught; this is what the teacher Kāmukāyana held.
What, then, is that? "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, and thirteen on the new moon day.
If there were repetition [of the rites], neither thirteen nor fourteen would be fixed.
Because of the specific nature of that rule, it should apply first, since the preparatory rite (saṃskāra) is for that purpose.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "And as for the claim that there should be repetition even for those [rites] that assist from a distance (ārādupakārin), just as with those that are in contact," we reply:
that rule applies to those that act in combination, namely, "those that act together perform their action simultaneously."
By that same principle, the action should be performed by all together.
However, due to incapacity regarding the points of contact with the ritual duty (*dharma*), there may be a sequential performance; the action would be performed separately.
For it is not possible for the cooking of all [grains] to be accomplished from a single removal of embers.

Nor do all [cakes] become spread out when a single *puroḍāśa* is spread out, because the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is for the sake of that [specific object]; this refinement is prescribed for the purpose of cooking. Therefore, there should be a repetition with respect to each primary act (*pradhāna*), as it provides visible assistance.
Otherwise, it repeats as many times as the [main rite] is performed;
even though not directly touched, it is repeated for that purpose.
The Commentary states: "Even though not directly touched, the substratum and so forth repeat with each main rite."
Why? Because it is for that purpose.
It is understood as a distinction that whatever is performed in proximity to something is for the sake of that thing.

When the specific difference is grasped—that the rites beginning with the *ādhāra* and ending with the *ājyabhāga* belong to the *Āgneya*, while those beginning with the *snigdhakṛt* belong to the *Agnīṣomīya*—then there is a distinction.
Therefore, the Āghāra and other rites should be performed before the Upāṃśuyāja and others, and the Sviṣṭakṛt and others after them.
In this way, there will be a distinction between these and the others through their contact.

(Although the reading here is "asaṃspṛṣṭaḥ" in the Sūtra and at the beginning of the Bhāṣya, and likewise in our Mīmāṃsādarśana, nevertheless, since the Bhāṣya states "saṃsparśibhiḥ," the reading "asaṃspṛṣṭaḥ" is indeed necessary.)
Even in the Vivaraṇakāra’s commentary on the Sūtra and Bhāṣya, it is stated that [the self] is "unaffected" (asaṃspṛṣṭa); this is also the view accepted by Viśvādarśa, Vṛtti, and Yaśas (Ke.).

Commentary: As for what was stated—"The distinction is understood that these [rites] belong to him in whose presence they are performed; therefore, there must be a repetition of them"—this is not tenable.
Why? Because of their capacity (vibhava).
Even when performed in the presence of only one person, these will be capable of benefiting all.
It is like a lamp.
For example, a lamp lit in the presence of one Brāhmaṇa who is eating in a certain place provides benefit to all of them.
Therefore, there is no repetition.
But in common worldly usage, it would apply to each principal element according to the injunction.
The commentary states: the refutation of the objection raised previously has not yet been made;
therefore, that shall now be explained.
As for what was described as being "like a lamp," that is incorrect;
for in the world, the action of a lamp occurs either simultaneously or sequentially.
If it illuminates everything once it has been produced, then it is produced only once.
If, however, it does not illuminate [everything], then it must be produced repeatedly;
and thus, its capacity for direct perception [is established].
In this case, assistance or imitation is understood through an injunction (*vidhi*), not through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor is there an injunction stating, "it assists this.
Rather, from proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), the apprehension of a specific relation is understood: "it assists that in whose proximity it is employed."
Therefore, there is repetition.
Kāmukāyana maintains that one should recite [the mantra] once, because of the contradiction regarding the prescribed measure.

Commentary: Now, as for what was stated—"The teacher Kāmukāyana maintained that one should recite [the mantra] once, because of the contradiction with the measures such as fourteen or thirteen"—what is the resolution for that? The sūtra ends with the word "ābhāṣā" (addressing).
Because the injunction is for the sake of a purpose, there would be a transgression of the Vedic text by performing [the subsidiary] only once.
Commentary: That which is enjoined is called an "injunction" (vidhi) in the sense of a subsidiary (aṅga), because the subsidiary exists for the sake of another.
When it is established that "whatever is performed in the presence of something is for the sake of that thing alone," then there would be a repetition of the performance of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*).
In that case, numbers such as fourteen or thirteen would not be applicable;
rather, it is with respect to the oblations (*āhuti*) that there are fourteen or thirteen.
Their statement is justified by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*):
"There are fourteen oblation-substances on the full moon day, and thirteen on the new moon day.
This is not an injunction regarding number, because the number is already established through accumulation itself.
This, however, is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
It is justified by the function of restatement (*anuvāda-lakṣaṇā*);
it pertains to that which is already known.
And this number prescribed is for the *vidhis* (injunctions) of the offerings, not for the offerings themselves;
therefore, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of them.
Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] the performance [of the rites] occurs according to the division of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

The Commentary states: Bādarāyaṇa considers the performance to be by way of a single application (tantra). Why? Because of the non-division of the context. It has been stated that for all primary rites, the procedure is undivided due to their being performed together.
In this regard, no distinction is perceived within the middle [section]. As for the claim that a distinction is apprehended through the application of proximity,
that is incorrect.
What is the reason? Any specific detail that exists by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is set aside by the context (*prakaraṇa*), just as in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Just as in an injunction, because the context is common [to all], all these are understood here to be subsidiaries (*aṅga*); they do not belong to that for whose proximity they stand, because the sequence (*krama*) is sublated by the context.
Moreover, proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) by itself is not a non-differentiating reason.
Even when all objects are present, proximity must necessarily be established for at least one of them.
Therefore, it is impossible to definitively establish a distinction based on proximity alone.
Therefore, the application [of the rule] is according to the text.
The mention of Bādarāyaṇa is for the sake of honor, not for the sake of adopting his specific opinion.
If it is argued that this is because there is an injunction in some places, [we reply: no.
Commentary: This is not logical, for it is performed only once. Why? Because in some cases, simultaneity (*sahatvam*) is enjoined, as in: "They bind together; they grind together."

Since there is no restriction [otherwise] regarding its performance in all respects, this statement is for the purpose of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), meaning: "Conjunction occurs only here, not elsewhere.
No, for the injunction has already been established.

In the two months [of the rainy season], the rule "one desiring cattle should construct an altar with removable soil" (āhāryapurīṣāṃ vedim kuryāt) serves the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha), not the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha).
