By the principle of the fourfold means, since the sacrifices belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa alone possess primacy and the others do not have the status of subsidiaries, the establishment of equal primacy is achieved.
Su. P. 923. Oṃ. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, all the offerings are principal acts because there is no distinction [between them].

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the following sacrifices are heard in the scripture: the cake for Agni (āgneya-puroḍāśa), the cake for Agni-Soma (agnīṣomīya-puroḍāśa), the low-voiced sacrifice with clarified butter (upāṃśuyāja), the cake for Indra-Agni (aindrāgna-puroḍāśa), the Sāṃnāyya consisting of curds and milk, the two libations of clarified butter (āghāra), the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), the fore-sacrifices (prayāja), the after-sacrifices (anuyāja), the Patnīsaṃyājas, the Samiṣṭayajus, and the Sviṣṭakṛt.
In the inquiry as to whether all of these are indeed principal acts or some among them are subordinate, the author states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

In the two sacrifices of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, all the acts of worship (*ijyā*) should indeed be primary, because there is no distinction; for all of them equally possess the nature of sacrifice (*yāgatva*) and the quality of having heaven as their fruit. Some [acts] are subsidiaries (*aṅga*), those in which praise occurs by way of being a subsidiary; for generally, there is praise directed toward the primary.

In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that sacrifices such as the *āghāra*, *ājyabhāga*, and *prayāja* should be considered primary—just like the *āgneya* and other offerings, as in the case of the *rājasūya*—this is the aphorism of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). It is not the case that all sacrifices occurring within a ritual complex such as the *rājasūya* are primary; rather, some, such as the *āghāra* and others, are auxiliary (*aṅga*) and not primary.
The word "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view.
In those sacrifices where there is praise as being constituent parts (*aṅga*),

such as "Among these [sacrifices] of this sacrifice, they are the Āprīs," or "These four, indeed, are the Āgneya-portions of the sacrifice," and so forth— because this praise by means of fire (*agni-saṃstava*) is common to the constituent parts, meaning that being praised by means of fire is a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*), that is, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the constituent parts.
It is indicated by repeated mention (*abhi-saṃstava*) that "this is a subsidiary" (*aṅga*).
Therefore, even sacrifices such as the *āghāra* libations and the *ājyabhāga* offerings are indeed subsidiaries and not the primary acts (*pradhāna*).
And thus there is the observation of another purpose (*anyārthadarśana*).
In the established conclusion (siddhānta), he states another reason:

there is seen an injunction regarding the *kṛṣṇala* grain for the Saurya sacrifice in the form "At each *prayāja*, one offers a *kṛṣṇala*," which is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *prayāja*s that serves another purpose—namely, the purpose of enjoining the *kṛṣṇala*.
And this cannot be a restatement of the primary sacrifice itself.
Therefore, some members [of the ritual] are subsidiaries, and not all sacrifices are primary acts.
However, the reason [for their status] is not distinct, because the quality [of being a means to a result] exists in the primary acts as well.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says:
The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the established position (*siddhānta*).
The *prayāja* offerings and so forth are not subsidiary (*aṅga*) elements; rather, they are themselves primary (*pradhāna*) rites.

As for the reason stated—that they possess the nature of praise (*saṃstava*)—which is intended to establish their status as subsidiaries, that reason is equally and identically applicable to the primary rites such as the *Āgneya* sacrifice, according to the scriptural text: "The *Āgneya* is indeed the head of the sacrifice," and so forth.
Because the quality of being a constituent part of familiarity exists even in the primary rites,
therefore the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are indeed primary.
It is not the case that there is a perception of another purpose when [the purpose] has not been stated, because [such a perception] would be for the sake of something else.
Regarding what was stated in the Siddhānta—"And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose"—the Pūrvapakṣin says:

when neither the statement of the subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, nor the underlying logic (*nyāya*) has been stated, the observation of another purpose does not establish that subsidiary status.
As for what was shown—namely, "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain"—that is for the sake of another purpose.
That [statement] is for the purpose of enjoining another *prayāja*—one that is non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*)—as distinct from the archetypal *prayāja*.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is once again that all [the *prayājas*] are principal acts.

However, the application of the designation [of "principal"] occurs in the case of separateness, both according to scripture (*śruti*) and through specific mention (*vyapadeśa*). Furthermore, that which possesses fruit is the primary characteristic [of a principal act]. That which is connected with proximity to it would be its subsidiary (*aṅga*), because of the participation [in the fruit]; there is no connection with an unmentioned cause.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie position that has been restated.
Not all sacrifices are equally primary;
among them, those that possess a fruit are primary, while the others are auxiliary members (aṅga).
In this context, there are two sets of three [rites] that possess fruit: one set of three consisting of the Āgneya, Upāṃśuyāja, and Agnīṣomīya sacrifices, designated as the Full Moon (Paurṇamāsī);
and a second set of three consisting of the Aindrāgna, Aindra, and Payasyā sacrifices, designated as the New Moon (Amāvāsyā).
By the dual number in the expression "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," both of these aforementioned sets are indicated in the stated order.

And by the phrase "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), the possession of a fruit is stated. This very point he expresses [as follows]: because it is heard from the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) that "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and because of the designation by means of the dual number in the expression "with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," there is a distinct application—that is, a separate performance—of the two names, "Darśa" and "Pūrṇamāsa," within two distinct triads of constituent parts.

That which is "possessing fruit" (phalavattva) is, moreover, the primary characteristic (mukhyalakṣaṇa), that is, the characteristic of the primary (pradhāna). "That, moreover" means "that [is the characteristic].
By this, possessing fruit is the characteristic of the primary.
The sacrifices of the New and Full Moon [rites] (2037). Regarding the New and Full Moon [rites], the fire-pan has been described;
likewise, there are two sets of three [offerings].
Therefore, that alone is the primary [act].
Now he states the definition of a subsidiary (aṅga): "In proximity to that"—meaning in proximity to that which possesses a fruit—that which is not connected with a fruit itself would be a subsidiary.
The meaning is: that which lacks a fruit when in proximity to something possessing a fruit is its subsidiary.
And such [rites] as the *āghāra* and *ājyabhāga* offerings are likewise;
therefore, in that case, it is the primary [act],
yet it is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) because it possesses the quality of being a cause for the status of being a subsidiary.
"Portion" (*bhāga*) means distribution or assignment;
because it has already been stated that [an injunction] is not connected [to another] "due to the manifestation of the purpose through context and so forth" (3.1.4.11), this is the meaning.
Regarding the "unheard connection with another," the connection of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth with some fruit—such as the primary result—is not heard in the text.

Thus, since the definition of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) has been stated as "that which is without fruit in the proximity of that which bears fruit is its subsidiary," and because the *prayāja* offerings and so forth lack fruit, they must be accepted as subsidiaries alone, not as primary acts (*pradhāna*).
Furthermore, qualities (*guṇa*) are enjoined in connection with names, and these are not applicable to the subsidiaries.
This is another reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), as set forth in the Sūtra.
The word "ca" (and) indicates a conjunction.

[In the passage] "One should mix the Paurṇamāsī with the Caturhotṛ [offering], and the Amāvāsyā with the Pañcahotṛ [offering]," qualities such as the touching [of the oblations] are enjoined in connection with names;
that is, they are prescribed in connection with the names "Paurṇamāsī" and "Amāvāsyā."
And those [offerings] without fear arise only in the principal acts, not in the subsidiary parts.
Therefore, the *āghāra* and other such offerings are indeed subsidiary parts, not the principal act.
Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding the cause is equal in its connection with both the principal and the subsidiary parts.
He refutes what was stated by the opponent, namely, "But the cause is not distinguished" (*aviśiṣṭaṃ tu kāraṇam*).

The scriptural statement regarding the cause—namely, the touching (*abhimarśa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*), that is, the constituent parts such as the *Āgneya* and others, of the Full Moon sacrifice (*Pūrṇamāsa*) as being "full of other human purposes"—is the same even if the *Āgneya* and others are primary (*pradhāna*).
The sense is that praise consisting of the comparison of the limbs of the sacrifice to the limbs of a person is appropriate even when the *Āgneya* and others are the primary elements.
And that praise is expressed as: "The Āgneya is indeed the head of the sacrifice, the Upāṃśuyāja is the heart, and the Agnīṣomīya is the two feet.
Because there is a connection at the time of origin, there should be an instruction regarding the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*).

This present sūtra is intended to provide a specific clarification regarding that which was stated in the preceding sūtra concerning the application of the connection, namely the sūtra *aviśiṣṭaṃ tu kāraṇam*, by means of the response *tulyā ca kāraṇaśrutiḥ*.
This connection that has been stated between the constituent parts of the Full Moon sacrifice and the limbs of the person must be justified.

Just as when a person is being born, the head is born first, the middle part in the middle, and the feet last, so too the offerings to Agni come first, the Upāṃśuyāja in the middle, and the offering to Agni-Soma at the end.
It is on account of this similarity that this praise is expressed.
Therefore, this instruction regarding the subsidiaries must be for the purpose of praise;
by it, there is no loss of the primary status of the Āgneya and other rites.
And thus there is the observation of another purpose.

In the Siddhānta, the final sūtra concerns another reason (*hetvantara*). Likewise, regarding the predominance of the Āgneya and other offerings and the subordinate status of the Āghāra and other rites, there is also the observation of another purpose (*anyārthadarśana*): "Fourteen oblations are offered at the Full Moon sacrifice, thirteen at the New Moon sacrifice.
[These consist of] five *prayāja*s, two *ājyabhāga*s, the Āgneya, the *pāṃśuyāja*, the Agniṣomīya, and so forth, and three *anuyāja*s.

Including the *sviṣṭakṛt*, there are fourteen [offerings] at the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*). At the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), there are thirteen oblations: five *prayāja*s, two *ājyabhāga*s, the *āgneya* offering, the *sāṃnāyya*, the *sviṣṭakṛt* (making three), and three *anuyāja*s. This being the case, if the *āghāra* and other such offerings were also primary rites, then there would have to be a double performance of them at each full moon sacrifice.
However, repetition is possible if [the acts] are subsidiary (aṅga).
From this observation of another purpose, it is established that the Āghāra offerings and others are indeed subsidiary.
At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there are two Iḍā portions: one before the after-offerings (anuyāja) and another after them.
VI. 10.1.13. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, regarding the *iḍā-nigada*:

although it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to those [sacrifices], it does not apply to a modified form (*vikāra*) involving multiple sacrificers (*yajamāna*), because its meter (*praticchandaḥ*) does not denote a meaning that is actually present (*samaveta*).
Bhāṣya: 9.1.13.40. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the consumption of the *iḍā*, the *prāśitra*, and other portions begins.
Now, regarding the destruction of the *matva* (the state of being a sacrificial vessel) for the purpose of consuming the *iḍā* and other portions, it remains in its very nature [of gold].

(Jaimini Sūtra 6.4.2). In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, four offerings (*upahāra*) are prescribed for the sake of accomplishing the fourfold consumption: the consumption of the *iḍā*, the consumption of the *prāśitra*, the consumption of the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), and the consumption at the time of the *śaṃyuvāka*.
However, in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* beans, the simultaneous performance of those offerings pertaining to the Brahman priest has been stated.
10.2.4: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the fuel (*idhma*) is accomplished by means of ritual acts accompanied by mantras such as "three enclosing sticks" (*trīn paridhīn*).

10.1.9: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, regarding the statements "He cuts the sacrificial shed with *iṣe tvā*" and "He strokes [the wood] with *ūrjaṃ tvā*," there is a distinction of mantras because of the distinction of purpose (*arthabheda*), which results in a distinction of sentences (*vākyabheda*).

2.1.16: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the placing of the fire-pot (*ukhādhishrayaṇa*) constitutes the first pair among the twelve pairs mentioned in the text: "He lets the calf stay near and places the pot on the fire."
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is an auxiliary benefit (upakāra). Regarding the ten potsherds (kapāla) in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices,
for those two sacrifices which require an auxiliary benefit,
either the Prājāpatya or the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice must be performed as a preliminary offering (prayāja).
Bhāṣya 5.4.6.19–21: And when the fires require assistance, it is the assistance in its very state [of being performed] that is intended.
Regarding the mortar in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices:
from the context (prakaraṇa), it is understood that "the mortar and the pestle" are for the purpose of those sacrifices.
[It is] merely because of the impossibility of anything else [being the case];
[it is] the sacrificial implement.

The assumption of the mortar and pestle as instruments [is made] by the statement, "He threshes with the mortar and pestle" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 3.1.2, p. 658). Its utility lies in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice.

3|1|9. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, two portions of four ladlings each are to be prescribed for the *upabhṛt* [ladle], and not one portion taken from elsewhere. This concerns the two sets of four ladlings for the mortar and pestle, as well as the grinding stone and muller, which are not previously enjoined nor otherwise employed.
This is the section concerning the two sets of four ladlings.
It is indeed so; it is not stated by means of *han* and *piṣ*.
This is the section concerning *han* and *piṣ*.
Ke. 46–48. In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the breaking of the potsherds and so forth is the occasion (the motivator) for the Māṣa-parvan rite.

As long as the occasion of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) exists, so too must there be the occasional rite (*naimittika*)—namely, the *homa* to be performed. (Why? Because the *homa* is prompted by the occasion, which is the *apūrva*. And in that case, the breaking [of the vessel] occurs only occasionally, not as a constant rule.

Nevertheless, what [is the problem]? To this he says: In that case, because the beneficiary (*upakārya*)—which is distinct—is non-eternal (*anitya*), while the motivator (*prayojaka*, i.e., the *apūrva*) is eternal (*nitya*), there is a contradiction between the eternal and the non-eternal. However, if the act of breaking (*bhedana*) is the efficient cause (*nimitta*), then when the oblation (*homa*) is performed by means of that distinct cause, the *apūrva* serves that purpose; thus, there is no fault (i.e., no contradiction).
And the seventh [case-ending] is used in its literal sense as indicating a cause;
if it were intended to express a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*), there would have to be an indication by secondary metaphor (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, it is only the cause that differs, not the preparatory refinement.

He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of that which was previously mentioned: "Because the status of being a cause and the purposefulness [of an act] are not constant, there is a connection [between them]. [Here,] "cause" (*nimitta*) refers to that which prompts performance, and "purposefulness" (*tādarthya*) refers to the fruit. For example, living (*jīvana*) acts as the cause that prompts the *agnihotra* oblation, and that [oblation] is for the purpose of destroying the faults already incurred.

(The reading here is: "Just as living is the cause of a person's fault, therein the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the vow (*vrata*), and the oblation (*homa*) are prompted; that [is] for the purpose of destroying the fault.")

However, it is not the case that [the relationship] does not exist there; for since the life [of the agent] and the personal fault (incurred previously) are present there, the connection is not contradictory.

There is a connection between both [the causal factor and the result], even though they are impermanent; just as Brahman-slaughter and so forth are impermanent causes, and the personal fault is impermanent, yet in that regard, the expiation prescribed for Brahman-slaughter serves to destroy the fault—and thus there is no contradiction. Therefore, as long as the beneficiary (the result) exists, there is a connection with whatever is the causal factor.

In this case, however, there is a contradiction: [the benefit] is occasional (*kadācit*), whereas the motivator (*prayojaka*)—namely, the *apūrva*—is eternal (*nityam*). (He explains the Bhāṣya: "It is not possible to benefit that which is eternal" means that the oblation (*homa*) cannot eternally provide a benefit, because of the absence of an occasional object to be benefited (*upakāryasya*).
Therefore, the statement "it would benefit it eternally" is mere idle talk; thus says the author regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

(How so? [The Commentator says that] the author of the Bhāṣya speaks of the *apūrva* as the object to be accomplished (*prayojya*) by the thought, "One should constantly provide assistance" (referring to the *homa*).
Therefore, since it is untenable for that which is assisted to have a permanent purpose, the breaking [of the vessel] by the potsherds (*kapāla*) and so forth constitutes the occasion (*nimitta*).
And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, their removal would follow from the scriptural statement.

Commentary: In the absence of an explicit statement, a subordinate element (guṇa) cannot exist for the sake of another subordinate element. According to the context, all [elements] serve the purpose of the primary action; thus, even though the oblation (homa) is distinct, it is not taught as having the nature of a substratum (ādhāra).
For if the broken vessel were the locus [of the offering], another oblation would not be prescribed;
rather, it would be understood that the broken vessel is merely an accessory (*guṇa*) of the primary act.

In that case, the connection with the *āhavanīya* fire would be contradicted. If it is argued that there is an option based on a specific scriptural statement, we say no, because the broken vessel can function as a conditional cause (*nimitta*).
And because the oblation (*homa*) is enjoined by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*);
when the oblation is enjoined, it is by *śruti*,
but when a distinct accessory (*guṇa*) is enjoined, it is by syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Therefore, the substratum is distinct.
If it were argued that even in the case of the word "occasion" (*nimitta*), there is no separate oblation, but rather the occasion is prescribed for the very oblation under discussion—
that is not so.
For that which is not being taken up is called a "condition" (nimitta).
If it were itself enjoined, it would no longer be a condition.
Furthermore, if the person for whom it is a condition were also the object of reference (uddeśya), then there could be no relationship between two things that both exist [simultaneously as objects].

And it is not prescribed here that one should perform the offering in the case of a breakage; rather, what is heard as something else when a breakage has occurred is enjoined [as a contingent rite]. [If it is asked: "How can both offerings serve the purpose of the primary sacrifice under the view that they are contingent?"—to this he replies: Because of the context, the offering serves the purpose of the primary sacrifice; even though the breakage is the occasion, the offering is to be performed for that very purpose through the mediation of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result). Therefore, the offering is not for the sake of the breakage itself.

Furthermore, there is no statement that establishes the oblation as having the potsherd (*kapāla*) and so forth as its purpose, because in the sentence "He offers when [the vessel] is broken" (*bhinne juhoti*), there is an absence of the accusative case-ending which would establish that relationship of being for the sake of something else (*tādarthya*).

Nor is a defect perceived in the broken vessel through direct perception, by virtue of which the oblation could be for the purpose of removing that defect—[which would imply a visible purpose even in this accusative case, and thus the oblation would be for the sake of the broken vessel]. Furthermore, it is not taught as the locus of the breakage (as the word *ādhāra* in the Bhāṣya implies).

[Objection: But since it was already established previously that "a quality cannot be for the sake of another quality," how can there be such a doubt? [Answer: To this he says: it is proposed merely on the basis of the possibility of the scriptural statement (*śrutisaṃbhavamātreṇa*).
For the locative case (*saptamī*) is possible both in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*) and as a locus (*ādhāra*).

[He now follows the *Bhāṣya* on the refutation in terms of its meaning: Being a locus, it would be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) only to the Āgneya and other primary rites (because of the context), not to the subsidiaries themselves.
Nor is the connection with the *āhavanīya* fire annulled by another action (since it is illogical for a qualified injunction to set aside another),
as in the case of the potsherds (*kapāla*) and so forth in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices;
this refers to an occasional annulment (*pākṣika-bādha*), not a permanent one.

(The opponent, however,) having admitted [the objection], says: "If it is argued that there is an option because of the scriptural statement"—[meaning] that an optional sublation based on the force of the statement, as in the case of rice and barley, is not a fault—[this] refutes the mention of the option: this option is improper because the two are distinct in their respective contexts (*prakaraṇa*), and because the *āhavanīya* fire is not enjoined in the context of the initial undertaking (*anārambhādhīyatva*).

Just as, by virtue of its very connection with the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), the similarity [of the *pañcadaśya*] taught as an isolated injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) is set aside, so too here, the *āhavanīya* fire is indeed set aside by the broken vessel (*bhinnena*), and there is no option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, because the *āhavanīya* has already served its purpose elsewhere (in other oblations),

whereas the broken vessel— being enjoined by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to the oblation under discussion— has no scope elsewhere, it finds its place only by superseding that [the *āhavanīya*], just like the word "foot" (*pada*).

Therefore, the mention of an alternative (*vikalpa*) was stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* as a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*). [For] even an alternative is improper when another course is possible, and such a course does exist: because it is possible [to connect the broken vessel] as a mere cause (*nimitta*). Some say: "This alternative is indeed proper, because both [the broken vessel and the *āhavanīya* fire] are connected with the act of offering (*juhoti*) by means of the sentence. [Objection: "But was it not said that the broken vessel has its own context (*prakaraṇa*)? To this he replies: "Nothing more than this is obtained from the context, because the sentence is stronger [than the context]."

Regarding the two numbers [fifteen and seventeen] in connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses: how then [should they be understood]? To this he says: since those two numbers would be purposeless if they were connected merely to the *sāmidhenīs*, a connection with the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) must necessarily be sought.

In that case, the connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) is established for one [the *pāñcadaśya*, fifteen-foldness] by way of its own context (*prakaraṇa*), whereas for the other [the *sādr̥śya*, similarity], it is established through the *sāmidhenī* verses which have already been connected to another sacrifice (*anyacirita-kratu*). Thus, because of this remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) of the connection, the similarity is set aside by the *pāñcadaśya* (since the similarity has already served its purpose in the modified sacrifices).

Furthermore, even if that were the purpose [of the scripture], the scripture would not be the cause of restriction, or rather, it would be due to the favor of the scripture. For the effort of discerning people is not for the sake of acquiring means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather for the sake of attaining what is desired.
Therefore, that which is perceived to be sublated by a means of valid cognition is indeed sublated.
And the sublation of similarity is also perceived.

In this case, however, the word *juhoti* is the same [in both instances, despite the difference between the common fire and the *āhavanīya*]. The locative case (*saptamī*) expressing the locus is likewise the same; therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

But surely, since the word *juhoti* and the locative case are identical even in the statement "he offers on the footprint" (*pade juhoti*), there would be an option between the footprint and the *āhavanīya*.
It is said:
that which is enjoined by another sentence is sublated by that which is enjoined by the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), and the word is enjoined by the originative injunction.
(The *āhavanīya* fire is enjoined by another sentence; therefore, it is sublated by that word.)
Thus far, the contradiction has been stated through an examination of the words and the sentence.

[The author] says that even the sentence concerning the *āhavanīya* fire does not apply there: furthermore, since the *āhavanīya* (the substratum) is not required by the *homa*, this [substratum], being brought forward (or "being assigned," according to the written reading) by the sentence, prescribes another *āhavanīya* as the substratum for those *homās* that are pure (i.e., those such as the *agnihotra* which have already arisen), but not for those [such as the *padahoma*] which are being performed and thus lack a substratum. If it is argued that this is for the purpose of distinction (*bhedana*), [we reply: no.

The Commentary says: It may be argued that in this manner that potsherd is joined together with the formula, "May the Gāyatrī of a hundred syllables join you. [Thinking] "I shall join that potsherd," one acts accordingly.
To this we shall reply.
Because it is not a subsidiary part of the whole.
The Commentary states: It is not logical for the breaking to be a subsidiary part [of the rite]; nor can that [break] be mended by means of an oblation or a mantra.
Even if it were mended with clay, the cognition of its being broken would not depart.
And it would be purposeless in the event of total destruction.
The Bhāṣya states: "In the case of total destruction, it is heard [in scripture]: 'If it breaks, he throws away the potsherd.
In that case, the consecration would be purposeless."
But is it not the case that what has been extracted is placed down? No, we say;
for they declare, "He places down something else."

Therefore, the action is a subsidiary element (aṅga) conditioned by a specific occasion (*nimittaka*), as stated in the scripture: "One offers when [the vessel] is broken. In this case, since a partial breakage is constant, it serves as the occasion;
however, only an occasional breakage of that which has been prepared can function as the occasion.
But the proponent of the second view maintains: "This oblation is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the broken vessel, because it removes the defect of the breakage."
If that were the case, the status of being a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāritva*) would indeed be obtained;

furthermore, the status of being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakriyātva*) would logically result in [the former] being a direct auxiliary. Moreover, that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*) must be capable of performing the function; once it has been joined with [the refinement], it becomes capable of that function.
Therefore, when there is even a slight degree of breaking, at that very moment the oblation should be performed.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"This would indeed be so if it were a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), but this is not a rite of purification for a broken vessel."

For if it were a *saṃskāra* (consecration), the status of being a causal factor (*nimittatva*) for that which is distinct [from the sacrifice] would not be obtained. Because of its status as a causal factor, the *homa* must always belong to the *agniṣṭoma*; [otherwise] there would be a contradiction between the permanent and the non-permanent regarding the object of consecration.
Regarding the *kapāla* and other implements in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices: how does the act of digging obtain a connection with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*?
Therefore, it is concluded that the oblation (*homa*) is enjoined as being contingent upon the breaking [of the *kapāla*].
And because there is no distinction [between the two cases], this [penance] would apply even when only a part is broken, as well as when the whole is broken.

Soma [objects]: "In the previous case, although other [participants] distinct from the priests were mentioned as being occasional, here only the breaking of the whole must be accepted"—this is the counter-argument; and furthermore, since eating is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the substance, whereas the oblation (*homa*) is a consecration of the broken [vessel], this is the connection [of the present topic].
According to the Sūtra: "Even when only a part is broken, there should be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because the purpose—the breaking—is present there as well."
Regarding the rule "In the case of the breaking of a skull, there is a *homa* offering when there is fear, or when it rains, or in both cases":

the first [case] is for the sake of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) because the breaking of the vessel is a subordinate part (*aṅga*); the middle [case] is because the consecrated [vessel] is not the occasion for the rite;
thus, there is no contradiction between the permanent and the non-permanent.

"Equal is the status of being a *nimitta* (condition) in both breaking and grinding; therefore, there is an oblation for both. Regarding the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta*) in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices according to the Bhaṭṭa school, it is heard in scripture: "He offers when [the vessel] is broken; he offers when [the grain] has spilled. In this regard, there arises a deliberation: does this [expiation] apply only to a complete breakage, or only to a partial breakage, or to both? Upon reflection, since a partial breakage is not something to be brought about (*arjanīya*) when two [halves] are joined together, and because it would then be a constant occurrence (*nitya*) rather than a contingent condition (*nimitta*), the first position is that this expiation applies only to a total breakage—that is, in the state where it has become powder.

Even when a few parts have become powdered due to a fracture (*saṃgharṣa*), because they are perceived as being distinct, the cognition of "breaking" occurs only upon the separation of gross parts such as potsherds (*kapāla*). Since that [separation] alone is impermanent, it is logical that the breaking of a single part can serve as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the entire breaking. Therefore, this *homa* takes place precisely there. For although this breaking is the occasion, since the *homa* requires a purpose, it serves to consecrate the broken potsherd in order to obtain the benefit of restoring the integrity of the vessel.

For if, due to the breaking of the *kapāla*, there were the contingency of a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) because the prescribed measure would be lost, then the consecration (*saṃskāra*) by means of an oblation (*homa*), which serves to remedy that deficiency, would not be inappropriate.

Since that [breaking] cannot be connected with a consecration that is already established, and since it is impossible to employ it in its entirety through a total breaking, only the breaking of a single part (*ekadeśabheda*) is the occasion (*nimitta*).
Or rather, let this locative case (*saptamī*) be intended solely for the purpose of indicating a consecration, and not even one signifying an occasion.

Nor does the occasional nature of what has been broken entail a contradiction regarding its connection with both the permanent and the impermanent; for even though the *Rathantara* [chant] is occasional, it is logically consistent with the injunction of properties such as "closing the eyes" (*saṃmīlana*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: whether for the sake of the sacrifice (*bhāvyopayogitva*) or for the sake of the material already used (*bhūtopayogitva*), since that [offering] occurs upon the breaking [of the vessel], there is a contradiction with the scriptural statements, "He throws this broken potsherd [into the fire]" and "He places another [on the altar]. Therefore, this is not an independent oblation that effects the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the broken [vessel]. Nor do the oblations mentioned in the context (*prakaraṇa*) serve to purify it.

By this, the view that—through a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the oblations belonging to the ritual context (*prākaraṇika*), there is an injunction for the breaking of a potsherd (*kapāla*) as the very locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of a worldly act, thereby setting aside the *āhavanīya* fire—is refuted. This is because the oblation belonging to the ritual context occurs after the placing of the potsherds; consequently, the statement "he places another" would result in a contradiction with the Vedic purpose, and a penance (*prāyaścitta*) would be untenable.

Therefore, this is a distinct ritual act; therein, it is prescribed as an occasional (*naimittika*) auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) for the purpose of remedying a deficiency in the sacrifice (*ṛtuvaiguṇya*), by virtue of its being a priestly function.
Consequently, both the breaking of the entire vessel and the breaking of a single part constitute the occasion (*nimitta*) here.
Maṇḍana [states]: "Even when there is a breakage, the *juhoti* offering should take place."
Śaṅkara: "The *homa* [is performed] when there is some slight difference from the whole.

Regarding the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is stated: "'He scatters [the grains] over them and places the potsherds upon them'; thus, the twelve pairs constitute one [unit]. (Vi. 3.8.10).

Bhāṣya 12.4.6.10: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood—that is, from the wood of the *palāśa* tree.

VI. 3|6|1: At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, clarified butter (ājya) is to be taken four times into the juhū ladle; at the time of taking the butter, it is stated: "He takes [butter] four times in the juhū. In that case, there is a repetition of the mantra with each taking. 1|1|4|15: At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra "Mayi dakṣakratū" is to be recited over the juhū.

And that recitation of the mantra is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), or rather, it is a duty of the person engaged in the sacrifice (*kratuyuktapuruṣadharma*), not a duty for the person’s own sake (*puruṣārtha*).
This is the topic [discussed] in the section concerning the one being born (*jajñyamānādhikaraṇa*),
namely *Kevala* 3.4.15.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle is for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings, while the clarified butter in the *upabhṛt* ladle is for the sake of both the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings.
In this regard, there should be a distinction based on their origin.
Commentary: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He takes four portions in the *juhū*, and eight in the *upabhṛt*."

In this regard, there is a doubt: are both the *jauhava* and the *aupabhṛta* [clarified butter] intended for both purposes—the *prayājas* and the *anuyājas*? Or is the *jauhava* for the *prayājas* and the *aupabhṛta* for the *anuyājas*?
Or rather, is the *aupabhṛta* for both the *prayājas* and the *anuyājas*? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Both are intended for both purposes.
Why? Because whatever is performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) ought to be for that very purpose, since there is no distinction.
[The discussion] begins by way of a digression from the relevant topic.

(Having established that the act of bringing together (*samānayana*) necessitates the clarified butter held in the *aupabhṛta* ladle, the question of its being for that specific purpose is considered in connection with it; and by way of a further digression from that, the same is considered regarding the *jauhava* and *śrauva* ladles.)
Since it has been established that the clarified butter (*ājya*) is the purpose of this [rite], the commencement of the preceding section follows;
however, it was commenced earlier because of the risk of an apparent lack of connection.
[The author states the prima facie view: Because they are not explicitly connected, the *ājyas* are not included within the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Therefore, whatever is to be accomplished by clarified butter (*ājya*)—such as the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings—in each of those cases, these [clarified butters] are used (the plural number is used with reference to the various vessels;

the mention of the *jauhava* and *aupabhṛta* in the Bhāṣya is for the purpose of indicating the *śrauvasa* as well). Among them, the *jauhava* is for the purpose of excluding it from the *anuyāja* offerings.
The Commentary states: It is not the case that both [portions] serve both purposes.
The *jauhava* portion is for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings, while the *aupabhṛta* portion serves both purposes.

How so? The statement regarding the *jauhava* [clarified butter]—namely, "In that he takes it with the *juhū*, he takes it for the seasons; the seasons indeed are the progeny"—indicates the *prayājas* for the purpose of prohibiting the *anuyājas*.
An objection is raised: "But there is no statement for the purpose of prohibiting the *anuyājas*.
As for this [statement], 'He takes it for the *prayājas*,' this is merely an instruction regarding the *prayājas*."
"It has no capacity to prohibit the *anuyāja* offerings.
To this it is replied: We do not say that this [text] is a prohibition; rather, in the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is simply no connection with a purpose for the *ājya* offerings.

By this statement, the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings is established for the *jauhava* [clarified butter]; however, its purpose for the *anuyāja* offerings is not understood precisely because there is no such statement. Thus, it is said that the statement is intended for the purpose of prohibiting [the use of] the *anuyāja*.

[Objection: In that case, while the injunction "he takes four portions in the *juhū*" is being presented for the purpose of prohibiting the *anuyāja*, the *jauhava* [butter] desires [to know], "What must I do?
And the *prayājas*, being presented, desire a substance.

In the case of the loss of the sacrificial substance during the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [the rite is completed] with clarified butter (ājya) because of a specific scriptural injunction (vacana). Bhāṣya 4.1.17 states that there are twelve pairs of duties pertaining to the Adhvaryu priest during the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, not those pertaining to the sacrificer (yājamāna).
"Because they are recited in the section on the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the rites should belong to the sacrificer.
Commentary: There are two [sacrifices], the New Moon (*darśa*) and the Full Moon (*pūrṇamāsa*).

In that regard, twelve rites are recited in the *Yajamāna-kāṇḍa*: "He lets loose the cow for the calf and places the pot on the fire; he threshes the grain and beats it with the pestle on the mortar; he scatters [the husks] and places the potsherds; he places the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the clarified butter (*ājya*) on the fire; he carries away the *stambayajus* and takes hold of the water; he encloses the altar (*vedi*) and girdles the wife; he sets down the sprinkling waters and the clarified butter."
"These indeed are the twelve pairs in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: are these the duties of the Adhvaryu priest, or are they those of the sacrificer? What is the prima facie view? Since they are recorded in the section concerning the sacrificer, these duties should belong to the sacrificer.

It is understood that these [rites] belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) because of their specific enumeration (*viśeṣa-samāmnāya*), just as in the cases of the *potrīya* and *naiṣṭīya*. For instance, regarding the twelve pairs of actions— such as placing the pot on the fire (*adhiśravaṇa*), threshing (*avahanana*), and so forth— which are recited both in the section for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) and in the section for the Adhvaryu priest (*ādhvaryava*), they must be performed by the sacrificer because they are employed through the mantras specifically enumerated in the *yājamāna* recension, just like those mantras that are explicitly enjoined there.
The Adhvaryu should perform it; for that is indeed the traditional recitation preceded by logical reasoning.
Commentary: It should be performed by the Adhvaryu.
For it is understood from the designation (*samākhyāna*) that the Adhvaryu is the one who has been hired for that purpose.
All these ritual acts are prescribed specifically for the Adhvaryu;
their performance as a pair is mentioned in the section concerning the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). And "pairing" (*dvaṃdvatā*) consists in the performance of the acts in conjunction.
In that case, it would be impossible for the Adhvaryu to perform the ritual acts while the sacrificer also performs them simultaneously.

Therefore, according to the principle "and in the conflict between a subsidiary and its quality, the quality must yield because of its subservience to that purpose," the quality of simultaneity (dvandatā-guṇa) must be set aside.
Consequently, these ritual acts belong to the Adhvaryu.
As for what was stated—that it is "due to the designation"—that must be refuted. It is replied:
the traditional recitation (samāmnāya) is preceded by logical reasoning; therefore, based on that recitation, the sacrificer must bring about the state of being a pair (dvaṃdvatā).
The sacrificer should say, "Prepare this and that.
Regarding certain ritual items, there is an accompanying recitation (*anumantraṇa*) by the sacrificer;
on account of that, the designation [of those items] will come to be.
As for what was stated—that "in the case of the *apūrva*, it would be performed separately," as in the cases of the *potrīya* and the *neṣṭīya*—the same would apply here.
To this, it is replied: that is appropriate in those cases, because of the specific designations (*samākhyāna*).

In this case, however, the state of being a *dvandva* (pairing) belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), whereas the constituent items (*padārtha*) themselves belong exclusively to the officiating priest (*ādhvaryava*).
Therefore, there is no fault.

Or rather—because there is no capacity to bring about the state of being a *dvandva* for those things that have not yet arisen, and because there is an absence of an injunctive word [to that effect], these do not originate within the *yājamāna* section itself.

What then? [The purchase] belongs to the Adhvaryu. And since there is a requirement for an agent therein, the purchase is for that purpose. Once the agent is thus determined, there is no need for expectation at the time of the dual mention; therefore, the status of the sacrificer as the agent is untenable.
In that case, since the essential nature [of the act] lacks a connection with the sacrificer, how could the dual nature (*dvandvatā*) pertaining to the sacrificer be established?
Nor is such a dual nature possible when the acts are performed by another agent. Thus, the dual nature is not established.
Furthermore, actions being performed by another agent cannot be made to belong to the sacrificer.
Nor is it possible for the very nature of the ritual action itself to belong to the sacrificer merely out of deference to the performance of the compound [of duties].
Therefore, according to the principle of the conflict between a subordinate element and its quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*), that too belongs exclusively to the *adhvaryu*.
The sacrificer, however, will cause [the priests] to remember [their duties] with the words "let them be paired"; thus the designation [of the *adhvaryu*] is purposeful.
Śā—Wherever rituals are enjoined, there they require an agent. And since the rituals are enjoined in the *Ādhvaryava* [section], they are *ādhvaryava* (belonging to the *adhvaryu*).

Soma: Since there was no fixed rule previously, whereas here there is a fixed rule for the sacrificer, this constitutes the connection through expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Vi: "One should let it set upon the *vasta* grass and place it upon the *taduhyā*";
this [procedure] belongs either to the master or to the other.
The first [type of purchase] is established by the textual recitation in the *Svāmikāṇḍa*, because the purchase is for that purpose;
in the *Mahākāṇḍa*, another [purchase] is intended, yet it is mentioned as being merely a compound.

Bhaṭṭa: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, twenty-four ritual acts—beginning with "He lets loose the cow for the fast" (*vastam upāvasṛjati*)—are enjoined individually, each associated with the designation *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu). Subsequently, those same acts are associated with the designation *yājamāna* (pertaining to the sacrificer), as in "He lets loose the cow for the fast and places the pot on the fire," and so forth, concluding with: "These indeed are the twelve pairs; having performed [them] in the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice. Thus, just like the recitation of mantras, it is not possible for these acts to have both persons as performers, because that would result in them serving two distinct purposes.
Nor does a different ritual act arise from repetition, because it is intended for something else.

For this very reason, since the acts belong to a single agent, the *adhvaryava* [section] itself is reached through its specific designation (*viśeṣa-samākhyāna*). Although they might thus fall under the *yājamāna* category, they are not enjoined in the *yājamāna-kāṇḍa*; rather, since they are enjoined in the *ādhvaryava* section, they are restated (referred to) in order to enjoin the form and qualities of the two [offerings], due to their mutual proximity within the *ādhvaryava*. Therefore, regarding these constituent elements (*padārtha*), the *adhvaryu* alone is the performer.
Furthermore, the sacrificer does not exist solely in the state of duality.

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is no possibility of a "five-portioned oblation" (pañcaśarāva) [for a single sacrificer], because it is impossible for one person to accomplish the state of duality when the rites are being performed by another.
What is called "pairing" (*dvaṃdatā*) is the bringing about of proximity between one primary action, such as the act of milking a cow,
and another [action], such as the threshing performed by both the mortar and pestle through a single act of striking.
The same should be understood regarding the twelve ritual actions (*kriyā*).

Nor does there occur a sublation of the agents of the principal constituent elements (*padārtha*) in accordance with the agent [of the subsidiary], because such a possibility exists through the principle of the conflict between a subordinate and its quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that [the sequence] "having performed those, one should sacrifice" implies a single agent for the sacrifice due to the gerund suffix (*ktvā*), which indicates a state of simultaneity (*dvandvatā*) [between the acts].
It should not be said that, by the mere mention [of the word], the designation (*samākhyā*) takes precedence over the ritual items beginning with the *agniṣṭha*;
for it is possible for the suffix *-kvap* to function as the motivator (*prayojaka*), and thus it is illogical for the primary designation to be sublated.
In this same way, even the designation residing in the *dvandva* compound should be explained solely with the intention of it being the motivator.
Therefore, the mere act of reciting [the mantra] belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), whereas the ritual acts themselves belong exclusively to the officiating priest (*ādhvaryava*).
Maṇḍana states: "The dual [acts] are not the work of the sacrificer. Śaṅkara states: "The dual [acts] are ours, belonging to the *ādhvaryava* [priest]."

12. In the performance involving two wives at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, regarding the formula "having girded the wife" (*apatnīṃ saṃnahya*), there is no modification (*ūha*) of the singular number.
This is the *Patnīsaṃnahananyāya*.
Śabara-bhāṣya 9.1.6.122. The ritual properties (*dharma*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), not prompted by the sacrifice itself (*yajati*).
Therefore, there is the accomplishment of modification (*ūha*) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
[Sūtra 9.1.1.14] The ritual properties (*dharma*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are connected with the fruit.
This is the section concerning the deity of the fruit (*phaladevatādhikaraṇa*).

9|1|3|4: In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the word "grain" (*dhānya*) in the mantra "Thou art grain; win over the gods" expresses that which is actually present in the performance. This is the section on grain (9|1|138–39, Section 2). For that purpose, the following is considered: Are these [mantras], when employed in a sacrifice whose deity is Svāhākāra, denotative of that [deity]?
"Does the statement 'He performs the svāhākāra offering' constitute an injunction regarding a deity, or is it a name? These [options] should be understood.
If that were the case, the well-known function of the sacrifice would be upheld."

In that regard, since the deity is obtained through the explicit statement, it is not appropriate to assume [the deity] from the mantra; [the mantra] provides assistance only indirectly. Therefore, the action that assists indirectly is the most excellent.
"Because this [latter] is of no utility, its assistance would be remote.
Thus [it is said]:
"The *prayāja* [is remote]."
To this it is replied: "In the injunction of a deity, there is no power [for the suffix] to denote the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
Nor does that which is exhausted in the injunction of the sacrifice enjoin the deity."
This being the case, we reply:
and [the rule applies] to the *prayāja* as well, because it follows that same principle.
This has been stated.
The rule:

"In the mantras for the *ājyabhāga* offerings and so forth, the deity about to be sacrificed [is named]; before it, there is a *svāhā* offering which is a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*). Here too, by the word "and" (*ca*), [the same applies].
Since they are recognized as being mixed together according to their respective order, they are thus indicated;
the final *prayāja* is a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*).
Therefore.
Since remembrance has its purpose clearly perceived, there is no assumption of an unseen result (adṛṣṭārtha); they consider this to be its very essence.
The deities who are to be worshipped in the *ājyabhāga* offerings and other rites—

namely Agni and the others— are those very same deities here in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *saurya* and others, even though the words "Agni" and so forth have lost their literal meaning [in that context].
Why? Because the utterance of *svāhā* is connected with the deity; [the other elements] cease [to apply], due to the absence of such a connection.

Or rather, the connection with a deity is understood through a secondary derivative (taddhita); for example, in "Soma-svāhā," let there be the status of a consecratory rite (saṃskāra) for the offering;
or [the deity is indicated] by that which ends in the dative case.
And here there is neither a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) nor a dative case;
therefore,
because it was previously connected with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
But here, in any case, there is the utterance of "svāhā";
it is not an injunction regarding a deity.
Furthermore, the accusative case ending is used because of its grammatical coreferentiality with the sacrifice.
It is said that because there is no state of being mixed together, there is no quality of being a consecratory act (*saṃskāraka*);
this is understood. Therefore, the word *svāhākāra* is a designation for the sacrifice (*yāga*), just as [the word *svāhā* is].
The connection is by way of an illustration. But the meaning of the fourth [sūtra] is this: "If it is possible for that which is desired, [then one should take] the *samit* and so forth."
He said:
"If that [second] is due to conjunction, then the conceptualization is not tenable; this is because it is analogous to the logic of the *svāhā* offering at the final oblation."
If you consider it to be a statement regarding sacrifice, then sacrifice is that which provides remote assistance; [it would apply] to that which is most desired to be attained,
yet even that would possess the nature of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāraka*).
Thus,
indeed, the second case ending occurs.
To this, it is said:
It is exactly so. [Question: Is another *prayāja* subsidiary to something remote? [Objection: This being the prima facie view, we reply:
"Because that same logic applies here. That very logic is the one [stated] here:
(u) "refinement" (*saṃskṛti*).
The mantra "svāhā" is for the oblation of *svāhā*, as it is stated by the gods in the *Mātṛbandha* mantra;
or rather, because it is a residual element (*śeṣabhūta*), it is understood as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that [oblation].
[Objection: Is it not so? [Response: No; for this is not the case, because of the absence of the dative and other such cases, since there is only the sacrifice [intended].
And it is a remnant in the *ājyabhāga* offerings and so forth.
Here, in rites such as the *saurya*, the names "Agni" and so on refer to the deities of the directions.
[The deities] are Agni and the others.
The sacrifice for that purpose becomes purposeful.
Bhāṭṭa: Even though the *svāhākāra-prayāja* exists, [the term] "svāhā"—in the other view.
This is because its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice is logically established.

For, by the mantra "May they partake of the clarified butter" (*ājyasya viyantu*), the meaning accepted is: "O Svāhākāra, indicated by the word *agni*, when you are satisfied, may all those principal deities and others who are to be worshipped become fully satisfied.

Therefore, in the aspect of the objective (*uddeśāṃśa*), the Svāhākāra would be a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*); however, it is not so even with respect to the meaning of the mantra itself, since it is established that it serves to manifest those respective deities through the very act of its performance.

In reality, however, the status of *svāhākāra* as a deity is not denoted by the accusative case; for since the word *svāhākāra* can also be analyzed as having a gerundive suffix (*ṇamul*)—meaning "so that there may be a *svāhākāra*"—its ending in the vowel *-ā* is ambiguous.

Therefore, it has been stated in the *Kaustubha* that, because of the desire to establish a primary distinction (*prathamavibhaktivipriyakāma*), the word *svāhākāra* is a name (*nāmadheya*) based on the occasion of its occurrence (*pravṛttinimitta*), just like the word *svāhākāra* which is already present in the meaning of the mantra.
In this sacrifice, the deities are precisely those such as Agni and others who are to be worshipped and are obtained through the wording of the mantra, just as in the case of the *sūktavāka*.

Therefore, this sacrifice effects the purification (*saṃskāra*) of each respective deity even in the aspect of the objective reference (*uddeśāṃśa*). This applies to the meaning of the mantra as well; it is not the case that it purifies only the already established meaning of the mantra. Rather, it is an established principle that while it is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) in the aspect of the objective reference, [it is a direct auxiliary] in the subsequent case.
This should be understood by means of the subsequent case endings.
Maṇḍana: "The *prayāja* offerings are auxiliary (*saṃskāraka*) to the *iṣṭi*.
Śaṅkara: "The utterance of *svāhā* is a direct constituent (*saṃnipātī*).
In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, both the *prayājas* and *anuyājas* are offered with clarified butter (*ājya*) alone.

In that context, the *juhū* is for the purpose of holding the clarified butter (*ājya*) for the first three *prayāja* offerings, and the *upabhṛt* is for the purpose of holding the clarified butter used as the substance for the final *prayāja* and for the *anuyāja* offerings.
(Vi. 5.2.8). In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *prayājas* are directly contributory acts (*ārādupakāraka*), because the words *samit* and so forth are names [of those acts].
[Objection: "Even in the case of the *prayāja*..."
The Commentary: In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there are the fore-offerings (*prayāja*):
"He offers to the *samidhs*, he offers to *tanūnapāt*, he offers to the *iḍas*, he offers to the *barhis*, he offers with the *svāhā*-utterance.

Regarding this, a doubt is raised: do the words "he offers to the *samidhs*" and so forth enjoin specific deities such as the *samidhs*—that is, "he offers to these [deities] named *samidh* and the rest"?

Or rather, why should a connection not be established with the *samidh* and other [deities] already under discussion? For it is not the case that deities denoted by the word "evam" are taught in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? A sacrifice is enjoined for the *samidh* and others who are already present in the archetype; and the *samidh* and others are the deities because of their syntactic connection within the sentence.
Thus, when a connection is made with the *samid* and other [deities] under discussion, there will be support for the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, it follows that even in the *prayāja* offerings, the deities under discussion must be the ones intended. Furthermore, the primacy of the deity is as seen in the case of the *pārṇahoma*.
"Because they are not enjoined. The Commentary says:
"No, it is not so; for here the *samid* and others are not enjoined as deities."
Why? Because of the mention of the accusative case.
A deity is enjoined either by the mention of a secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix or by the mention of the dative case;
for it is in those instances that the state of being for the sake of something else (tādarthya) is understood.
And it is by virtue of being for the sake of that [deity] (*tādarthya*) that something becomes a deity.
There is no such thing as a "deity" by way of genus (*jāti*).
That very same [entity] is the deity of a certain form, and that same one is not the deity of another.
That which serves as the purpose for someone with respect to something is the deity of that [person].
For the accusative case occurs in reference to the factor of action (kāraka) most desired to be reached;
in that context, the fact of being for the sake of a substance is not understood.
Therefore, there is no injunction of a deity by means of a word ending in the accusative case.
To this, he says:
"We shall assume that it exists for the sake of that [deity]."
As in the expressions "he sacrifices to Viṣṇu" and "he sacrifices to Varuṇa," neither Viṣṇu nor Varuṇa is the sacrifice itself,
nor is it another sacrifice distinct from the original one; rather, that which is the desired object (īpsita) among the factors of the sacrifice (kāraka) is denoted by the accusative case.
Therefore, in that case, its being for that purpose is either inferred or understood through another word;
but here, it is not enjoined by another word.
Nor can it be conceived in this way;
nor is it possible for [the word] to function as a factor (*kāraka*) of the sacrifice.
Because the terms *samit* and so forth are the names of the sacrifices, the words *samit* and so forth are appropriately established as denoters of those sacrifices.
When an action is desired for the sake of a result, the second case is employed, as in "he cooks the cooking" (*pākaṃ pacati*).
Therefore, the meaning of "he sacrifices the fuel-sticks" (*samidho yajati*) is: "the sacrifice of the fuel-sticks is to be performed."
And when the performance is enjoined with respect to the sacrifice, then the sacrifice becomes something already indicated.
If, however, the deity were taught here [independently],
then the deity would be taught once the sacrifice has already been taught.
In that case, if there were an instruction regarding what has already been instructed, the sentence would be split.
Therefore, it is an instruction concerning the deity.
When there is no instruction concerning the deity, then the injunction for the deity is derived from the wording of the mantra.
And because it is to be adopted [as the deity], they resort to a deity expressed by the word "evam.

Therefore, there is an injunction regarding the deity based on the wording of the mantra. [Duh]—In this context, within the section concerning the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the objection is raised: "He sacrifices to Viṣṇu; he sacrifices to Varuṇa."
In this regard, it is postulated that the purpose [of the mantra] is established, or it is understood as being enjoined by another word.
Regarding this, he explains the second resolution in two ways:
It is said here that the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice has been enjoined by a subsequent sentence; this [mantra] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that.
Alternatively, it is the sacrifice itself that is enjoined here.

In that case, Viṣṇu is obtained through the indicative power of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*) by virtue of the favor of the context; his application in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [is established] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, there is the performance of the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

The objection is as follows: Sacrifice is the primary meaning [of the root *yaj*], and here "Viṣṇu" is not a name, because that which ends in the accusative case lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb "to sacrifice.
(Having thus cleared up the example, he returns to the subject at hand: Even in the case of the *prayāja* offerings, there is an injunction regarding the deities based on the wording of the mantras.
By the word "abhi" in "abhisamidhaḥ," Tanūnapāt is indicated; in this very same way, Viṣṇu and the other deities are understood.
Or [the words] such as *samidh* and so forth are names (*saṃjñā*).

Even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (according to the principle of "being known from that"), nevertheless that name is not the differentiator; rather, it is the repetition itself that is the differentiator.
This has been stated in the second book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*, at 2.2.12].
Śālikanātha: "For the sacrificer, it is indeed taught that renunciation [of the offering] is preceded by a specific mention;
and in that act of renunciation, the deity never possesses the status of an object (*karman*).
Therefore, the *prayāja* offerings are *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly beneficial)."
Soma: As before, the connection arises from the context (*uddeśya*).
Viśvarūpa: "In the *prayāja* offerings, the *samits* and so forth should be either deities or sacrificial acts;
they do not have Viṣṇu and others as their true referents, because there is an absence of the dative case ending."

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the four *prayāja* offerings beginning with *samit*, if the words *samit* and so forth are intended as injunctions of deities—just as in the case of "he sacrifices to Viṣṇu"—or if, because of the impossibility of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the injunction of the deities *samit* and so forth is established solely by the wording of the mantras (*mantravarṇa*); then for the *upasti-yājyā*, the words *samit* and so forth are either restatements of the deities (*devatānuvāda*) or merely names (*nāmadheya*). In any case, in order to achieve the status of being an auxiliary that assists through direct application (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), they must serve as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of those deities, just like the *āghāra*, *anuyāja*, and other such offerings.

Nor is there an absence of the *samit* and other such materials, because since the words *samit* and so forth are seen everywhere in the Veda to be used in grammatical apposition [with the deity], their utility in the *Āgneya* sacrifice is possible. Alternatively, since even a mere *samit* has utility in the *samit* offerings and so on, it alone possesses the quality of being an auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).

This being the position reached, we reply: although the words *samit* and so forth appear in apposition in the Veda, it is untenable for those words to manifest that [deity], according to the principle of the section concerning Indra and Mahendra.
Because the word [denotes] the deity by its very nature, it would be illogical to employ another word for that same entity when there is a difference [in the ritual context].

Nor should it be argued that—just as with words like *pūrṇamāsa* and the like, or as with the *pārṇahoma*s—the word *samit* and others may function as a consecratory (*saṃskāraka*) element here as well; for even though the meaning of that [word] is related to the object of reference (*uddeśya*) through its connection with being denoted by the word in the specific portion of the reference within the *Āgneya* sacrifice (just as the *pārṇahoma* is a consecration), the status of being a consecratory element cannot be established here on the grounds that the word *samit* and others denote the deity.

In that case, even in the Vedic mantras such as "May the *samidhs* enjoy the clarified butter, O Agni; may *Tanūnapāt* enjoy the clarified butter, O Agni," since the *samidh* and other substances are perceived as being distinct from Agni through the vocative address to Agni and their subsequent connection with the ritual action, the words *samidh* and so forth do not denote Agni. Consequently, if they were intended merely as preparatory acts (*saṃskāraka*) for Agni, the extension of the ritual procedure (*atideśa*) to the animal sacrifice would be untenable.

As for the claim that, although the other *prayāja* offerings are directly contributory (*ārādupakāraka*), the *samit* offering is a preparatory act for the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) which serve as the material cause (*aṅga*) of the kindling, that is not correct.
If that were the case, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the passage, "He who indeed knows the pairing of the *prayāja*s sacrifices the *samidh*s as if they were the *barhis*," would be untenable.
For here, by the word "as if" (*iva*), it is indicated that the plurality is superimposed, since there is in reality no plurality [of deities].

And such [superimposition] is not appropriate for the *samidh*s, because they actually possess plurality. However, in the view that they are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), even though the word *samidh* has a deity as its referent, the superimposition of plurality upon the single *samidh*—established through the cognition of the nominal stem's meaning—is appropriate by virtue of the indicative mark.
Therefore, all four *prayāja* offerings are merely auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) rites; consequently, they are not to be modified (*ūhitavya*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
19. Maṇḍana: "In the case of the *samit* and other [offerings], there is an injunction of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice).
27. Śaṅkara: "The *prayājas* are for the sake of the purpose."

The status of the *prayāja* offerings and other subsidiaries as belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
This is the section concerning different contexts (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*).

[This concludes] the section on the *abhikramaṇa*.
