Bhā. 6|8|8|28. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, [the acts] are either performed by those who carry out the meaning of the commands or have different performers.

The meaning is that the ritual acts beginning with the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* waters [are performed] by the *agnīdh*. Furthermore, this is because the *praiṣas* (directions) pertain primarily to the *agnīdh*.
Commentary: The *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices exist.

In this regard, the following directions (*praiṣas*) are recited: "Place the sprinkling waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the very same person who issues the direction also the one who performs the action directed, or is the director one and the performer of the directed action another?
What is the prima facie view? That it is the same person for both the direction and the directed action.
Why? Because of the designation.
The word "another" shall not be a command (*praiṣa*). We shall explain that the *loṭ* suffix is used in the sense of the time having arrived.
He said:
Even when the time [for the use of a particular person] has arrived, the restriction of the second and other persons applies only when "you" (yuṣmad) and so forth are the governing words (upapada);
thus, there is no confusion of persons.
It is said:
when there is the intention to speak [of someone], the second person and so forth are used for "you" (*yuṣmad*) and the rest.
When it is intended to be expressed that "it is your time to attain," then the second person is used only for "you" (*yuṣmad*), and not for "we" (*asmad*) or for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

When indeed only this much is intended to be expressed—that the time for an action has arrived—and not "for you" or "for me," then the second person (*madhyama*) and so forth cannot occur by virtue of the inclusion of *yuṣmad* and the like.
Nor can these two be intended to be expressed simultaneously, namely, that "the time for the matter has arrived" and "for you. For if it were so, the sentence would be contradictory.
Therefore, whether it is said at the time of determining the meaning of the word, "this is your time," or whether "your" is determined first and then "the time of the object," in that case,
what must be stated is the time of the object, not the referent of the pronoun *yuṣmad*.
For there is a clear purpose in doing so.
For that [act] is understood as something to be performed, but your purpose is not so.
Therefore, based on the designation (*samākhyāna*), both the command (*praiṣa*) and the object of the command belong to the Adhvaryu alone.
This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply:
"One [word] applies to the *praiṣas* (directions), another to their meanings.
Why? Because of the governing context (*adhikāra*).
For it is appropriate in the case of a *praiṣa*, but not in the case of a name (*nāman*).
He says: "But was it not stated that it will apply when the time has arrived?
It is replied: "In the case of an injunction (*praiṣa*), it is not possible for the state of 'arrival of the time' to be logically appropriate."
Therefore, it is said that although the referent of the second person (*yuṣmad-artha*) is understood, it is not intended to be expressed (*na vivakṣita*).

Furthermore, the sense of an injunction (*praiṣa*) is possible here; therefore, there is an injunction. It is established that the sense of an injunction is distinct from the act of commanding (*praipya*).

Or rather—since both the command (*praiṣa*) and the object of the command are designated as belonging to the *Adhvaryu* by the technical name *Ādhvaryava*, it is determined that they must be performed by the Adhvaryu. If it is asked, "How then can there be a command directed at oneself?", he replies: "This is not a command at all; rather, we shall explain that the *loṭ* suffix is used here to express the 'arrival of the proper time' (*prāptakālatā*).

The proponent of the command (*praiṣavādī*), however, objects: "If the arrival of the proper time regarding the ritual action (*karma*) is intended, then alas, the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*) ought to be used!
For the second person (*madhyamapuruṣa*) is not obtained without the referent 'you' (*yuṣmadartha*), which pertains to another."
But in the case of a *praiṣa* (an injunction), because its nature is directed toward another, it is easily understood.

However, the opponent says: when the notion of a *praiṣa* has been removed due to the priority of the name (*samākhyā*) and the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛtva*), then that which is expressed as indicating the proper time—should it indicate the actions (*kriyā*) or the agents (*kartṛ*)? It is understood that it indicates the actions; for they, being enjoined, are purposeful and are primary.
Furthermore, for the sake of performing those [actions], the recollection of the appropriate time serves a visible purpose;
however, in the case of a scriptural injunction regarding the agent and the appropriate time, everything is the opposite.
Moreover, since in verbal forms (ākhyāta) one of the persons—namely the first person—must necessarily occur, the second person will follow as a necessary corollary.
And it is precisely an action that is said by you to be "the time having arrived.
If, however, it were said that the time has arrived for the agent, then the expression would remain expectant [of further specification], as in "What is to be done by the agent?

If one were to supply [the ellipsis] as "to perform the sprinkling of water, the placing of vessels, and so forth," then, because of the injunction of such a specific matter, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, even from this [usage], the fact that the time for action has arrived is made manifest.

Even if this is accepted as an injunction (*praiṣa*), nevertheless, by some means, one will designate oneself as both the sender and the sent, through the distinction between the body and the embodied, or between different states [of them]. Thus, since the identity of the agent is established, we reply:
"And in the case of the *praiṣas*, another [priest] should perform the other [function]"; this is the conclusion.
(Here, "and in the case of the *praiṣas*" refers to what is situated in the current sūtra;
regarding the *praiṣas* of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]... [the *phalīkaraṇa* of the Darśapūrṇamāsa]).

"Another [should do] the other"—this is understood from the preceding sūtra; the word "should perform" (*kuryāt*) is supplied by ellipsis. Why? Because by their very nature they have another as their object, just like the act of hiring (*parikraya*).
In that case, the objection that "this is not an injunction (*praiṣa* at all)" is incorrect, because the cognition of an injunction is established simply from the form of the mantra itself.
For if one were to subvert that [injunction] on the grounds of having a common agent, then the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would be subverted by the name (*samākhyā*).

Nor is the contradiction regarding gender in the expression "the time has arrived" (prāptakālatā) avoided, because the second person [suffix] is not present. Furthermore, it cannot be said that "the time has arrived for you" with respect to an action that is not conveyed by another word.
Even if it could be so stated, still no perceptible purpose would be served, since this usage of the word "you" (tvad) is intended to refer to a conscious being.
Likewise, even in the postulation of a distinction between the selves, no purpose whatsoever is observed;
here, the figurative sense remains established,
and it has been determined that the primary function belongs to the mantras (3.2.1).
And so, although the *loṭ* suffix occurs only when the time for action has arrived, nevertheless, since it is said that this [time] belongs only to another, the scope of the "other" (*para*) ceases.
Nor is there a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), because a command regarding a qualified object is given.
Furthermore, a qualified [object] must necessarily be admitted here, due to the taking up of the *prokṣaṇī* water.
Nor does a sentence, despite being a single word, split its meaning into many parts;

for in all verbal forms, it is unavoidable that action, agent, number, voice, person, and *bhāvanā* are simultaneously conveyed. Furthermore, such a qualified injunction must not be rejected as impossible anywhere.
Furthermore, if it were a matter of [the time] being appropriate for the action and the meaning of "you," then a distinct power would have to be postulated because of their difference.
But in the case of an injunction (*praiṣa*), since that [middle voice] always has the meaning of "you" as its object, the middle person is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
And in this way, this designation (*samākhyā*) of "injunction" is upheld.
Therefore, because the name (samākhyā) is set aside by the indicative mark (liṅga), the direction (praiṣa) is one thing and the meaning of the direction is another.

Soma [says]: Although in the previous case there was a setting aside of the agent obtained through the original name (prakṛta-samākhyā) due to the force of the statement regarding the assignment (ādeśa), here, in the absence of such a statement, there is no setting aside of the agent obtained through the name.
Thus, the connection [of the topic] arises from this counter-argument.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: in the case of commands (*praiṣa*), another person should perform the action intended by the command, because by their very nature, those [commands] have as their object another [person].
For example: "Should the Adhvaryu perform the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* water, or [should someone else do so]?"
The first [type of injunction] is by name (*samākhyā*); the other, sent as a command (*praiṣita*), is determined by its characteristic mark (*liṅga*).

Bhaṭṭa: Commands such as "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters" and so forth, as well as the objects of those commands—such as the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* waters and the like—are to be performed by a single agent, the Adhvaryu, on account of the name (*samākhyāna*).
Nor is it impossible for one to command oneself, for just as in the case of "Having fixed the mind, they pierce," an instruction directed toward oneself is possible even in one's own case.

In reality, this is not a *praiṣa* (an injunction); rather, it is according to Pāṇini 3.3.163: "The *kṛtya* suffixes and the *loṭ* [imperative] are used in the senses of *praiṣa*, *atisarga*, and *prāptakāla*. (*Kṛtya* suffixes and the *loṭ* occur in these meanings;
therein, *praiṣa* is an injunction [*vidhi*];
*atisarga* is permission for one's own will.)

Thus, because the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed by the rule *cakrāraḥ* even for the sense of "the time having arrived" (*prāptakālatā*), the *loṭ* occurs precisely when the time has arrived; that is, the time for the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* vessels has come. However, the second person, which refers to the meaning of the word *yuṣmad*, is to be understood as merely a formal usage (*sādhuvācya*).

Alternatively, in the case of "O Prokṣaṇyāsādana, this is your morning time," that [addressing] occurs through the superimposition of sentience upon the action. However, where there is an injunction such as "O Agnīdh, spread the fires," let the status of being addressed be accepted there in accordance with the requirement of the injunction, and let the object of the injunction be understood as having the Āgnīdhra as its agent. But in reality, since it can be explained as "O Agnīdh, this is the morning time for my spreading of the fires," even in that case there is no sublation of the designation (samākhyā).

This being the position reached, [we reply]: since there is no evidence for interpreting the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) as grammatically correct by following the name (*samākhyā*) and thereby superimposing consciousness upon the action; and since both the vocative and the second person would result in a loss of their primary meaning (*ahṛyārthatva*); and since it would follow that the name [of the section] "Injunction" (*praiṣatva-samākhyāna*) would be inappropriate because the sense of "time for action" (*prāptakālārtha*) is untenable; and since even the "injunction" (*praiṣa*) would have to be taken figuratively in this context—therefore, due to the contradiction with the name "Adhvaryu" in one instance, the agents of both must indeed be distinct. Maṇḍana: "In the injunction and its purpose, there is no identity of agent."

12. Śaṅkara: "Measured by the command, the purpose of the command, and the agent. [The word] *kartrī* means "the agent. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is not employed for the sake of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*), but rather for the sake of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result).

Bhāṣya 9.1.11–19: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, acts such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) are directly-contributing subsidiaries (sannipatyopakāraka) and are prompted by the transcendental result (apūrva). 9.1.12–13: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, in the injunction “Place the sprinkling-vessels” (prokṣaṇīr āsādaya), the word *prokṣaṇī* is etymological (*yaugika*).
Therefore, in some cases, clarified butter (ghṛta) serves as the sprinkling liquid (prokṣaṇa).

This concerns the section on the sprinkling liquid (prokṣaṇy-adhikaraṇa), Pāṇini 1.4.189: in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the ritual acts such as the placing of the sprinkling liquid are not performed by the Adhvaryu, but rather by the Agnīdh.
The *praiṣas* (directions) are for the sake of the purpose [of the ritual]; this is the section [on the subject].
3.8.1.24–25. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the mantras that reveal the fruit and the deity are connected with the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).
This is the section on the fruit and the deity (*phaladevatādhikaraṇa*).

9|1|34–5: In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the assistance of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is utilized for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the fruit, not for the production of a new transcendental result (*apūrva*).
If the *apūrva* were produced by the subsidiaries with regard to the fruit, then it would merely be a subsidiary itself.
11|1|17–35: In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *phalīkaraṇahoma* is performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire with the mantra beginning "O Agni, eater of food" (*agne'danvādyo*).
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) at the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
the husks and rice-grains (*phalīkaraṇa*) which are the remnants of the sacrifice at the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Therefore, [the rule applies] to the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa*. (Vi.
5.1.15) In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is cut more than once;
however, in the Pitṛyajña, it is cut only once.
Bhāṣya 1.1.17, 36–37: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is of two kinds: primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*).
The primary consists of *kuśa* grass and the like, which possesses the ritual properties and prohibitions (*dharma-adharma*) [of the sacrifice].
The secondary, however, is other grass called *ulapa*.

VI. 3|2|1. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and its ritual properties, as well as the altar (*vedi*) and its ritual properties, serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal rites; they do not serve the principal rite alone. This is the principle regarding the altar and the sacrificial grass. Bhāṣya 3|1|1|1–5. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the primary sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is prepared by cutting it with a sickle using specific mantras in the section beginning with "Thou art the announcer of the sacrifice" (*yajñasya ghoṣad asi*; Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1|1|2).

VI. 1.12. Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, concerning the mantras "barhir dūṇoti" and "ājya darśapūrṇamāsayoḥ," and among the *yājamāna* rites of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, when the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are embraced by a single performance-injunction (*ekaprayogavidhi*), there is an immediate succession (*anusamaya*). In the archetype (*prakṛti*), since the sequence of the preparation (*upaskāraṇa*) and the binding (*niyojana*) is established by the textual recitation (*pāṭha*), even if there is a sixteen-moment interval in accordance with the scriptural (*aupadeśika*) requirement for the simultaneous performance of the animal sacrifice (*paśu-sāhitya*), there is no authority for a greater interval. Therefore, it is logical that the order of procedure (*pravṛttikrama*) should be such that the binding follows the very same sequence as the bringing near (*upākaraṇa*).

In the present case, however, because the two consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa*) belonging to the single *prayāja* are not recited in various branches of the Vedic tradition, their sequence is not established by textual order (*pāṭha*). Furthermore, even though all *prayājas* are subsumed under a single performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), it is impossible to follow the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*). Moreover, since each pair of formulas belongs to a different *patnī*, the sequence of operation for the formula of one *prayāja* follows the sequence of the formula of the other *prayāja*.

Furthermore, even though there is no established order [of sequence] when [the mantras] reside in different recensional branches (*śākhā*), because the five mantras do possess a fixed order by virtue of being recited within a single branch, there is no contingency of subverting that order even when they occur in another branch due to the lack of restriction. This is because the five mantras, as subsidiaries of the five *prayāja* offerings, do not constitute a single residue (*ekaśeṣa*); rather, since they are encompassed by distinct intermediate performance-injunctions (*avāntara-prayoga-vidhi*), their order is unrestricted by the mere fact of their recitation.

And it is accepted that, even though there is unity of the great performance (*mahāprayoga*) for the five after-offerings (*anuyāja*) and for the oblation (*homa*) which effects the fruit of prosperity in the animal sacrifice of the *iṣṭi*, their sequence is not established because they are governed by distinct intermediate performance-injunctions (*avāntaraprayogavidhi*).
Therefore, this [is the case].
Maṇḍana says: "In other cases, there would be no fixed order."
4. Śaṅkara: "Because it is not included within the fixed order. This is the sequence.

5. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, by the force of the recitation of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras, one performs the rites for the cake (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni—from the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) up to the offering (*pradāna*)—and only thereafter does one perform those same rites for the *sāṃnāyya* (the milk-offering).

VI. 5.4.2: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the recitation of the *yājyā* verses should be performed while standing, whereas the recitation of the *anuvākyā* verses should be performed while sitting.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the recitation of the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses is for the purpose of consecrating the deity.
And the recitation [of the *anuvākyā*] is a primary action (*karma*), like the [main] ritual act, because of another injunction.
Commentary: Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in the scripture: "He recites the *yājyā*," and "He recites the *puro'nuvākyā*.
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the recitation of the *yājyā* and *puro'nuvākyā* a primary action, or is it a preparatory action (*saṃskārakarma*)?
What is established? That "he recites" (*anvāha*) must be a primary action (*pradhānakarma*).
Why? Because of a separate injunction (*codanā*).
If it were a preparatory action (*saṃskārakarma*), then the mention of those two would follow from their very nature; thus, the further statement "he recites" would be purposeless.
But if it were a primary action (pradhānakarman),
it would have to be stated that its performance is not understood otherwise;
therefore, because its status as something to be performed is understood through direct scriptural statement (śruti), it is a primary action.
It is permanent.

Just as in the case of the *stotra* and *śastra*, where they are understood to be primary acts because one understands them as things to be performed—namely, "he praises" (*stauti*) and "he recites" (*śaṃsati*)—so too should it be viewed here.
Or rather, it is a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*), because that which is enjoined has the purpose of expressing the verbal meaning.
Commentary: Or it may be a preparatory act (saṃskārakarma).
Why? Because the word for a purpose that has been enjoined serves the purpose of that [enjoined] object;
its visible purpose is that very [object].
If that [unmanifest] exists, there is no reason to postulate an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, it is the formative action (*saṃskārakarma*).
If it is argued that this is because it cannot be designated [as either manifest or non-manifest], [we reply:]...
Commentary: That which was stated must be refuted.
It may be so, because it is for the sake of a subordinate purpose (guṇa). Commentary: The statement "he recites" would thus be appropriate and consistent.
Why? Because they serve as subordinate qualities (*guṇa*).
The repeated injunctions, "Standing he recites the *yājyā*" and "Sitting he recites the *puro'nuvākyā*," are appropriate as referring to the qualities of standing and sitting.
Therefore, the *yājyā* and *puro'nuvākyā* are acts of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*).
Soma: [This is stated] because it is recited with a difference from the previous [case].

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: the non-recitation prescribed in the *anvāhārya* [rite] would be an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) action, because of the force of its prescription for an invisible purpose due to being enjoined by a separate injunction; thus, "always" (*śaśvat*). 21. Vi: "The *anvāhārya* should be a primary action (*arthakarma*) or a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*); [it is concluded that] it is a primary action."
[The opponent argues: "But since it always results from the cognition of an effect, its refinement (*saṃskṛti*) is for a visible purpose.

Bhāṭṭa: Although it is possible that the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras serve to manifest the deity based on their indicative power (*liṅga*), the recitation must have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), just like the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns, because otherwise the meaning of such injunctions as "he recites the *yājyā* while standing" and "he recites the *puro'nuvākyā* while sitting" would be rendered superfluous.

For a subsidiary injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhi*) cannot be established here by referring back to the recitation, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and the resulting logical fallacy.

If [the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*] were qualifiers, they would depend on a qualified locus; for if they were enjoined by means of the *yājyā* itself, the *yājyā* would remain unestablished, and this would result in the same contingency even in the case of the *kāmeṣṭi-yajūṃṣi* and the *praiṣas*. Furthermore, the explanatory reference (*anuvāda*) "he recites" (*anvāha*) would be untenable.

If both were intended as having perceptible purposes, there would be the contingency of an option between them; furthermore, in the case of the injunction "sitting [he recites] the *puro'nuvākyā*," if the *yājyā* and *puro'nuvākyā* were also enjoined, there would be the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices characterized by these qualities, the *yājyā* [is prescribed]; [likewise], the encircling of the altar (*vediparigraha*) pertains to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Since the recitation has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), when there is a change of deity in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the original *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses need not be recited; rather, if modified *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are available for recitation, they should be used in conjunction with them. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is replied: although this injunction regarding the fifth case-ending might constitute an injunction for a qualified recitation prior to the operation of the injunction inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*), nevertheless, since a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭa*) is possible, it is improper to assume an unseen purpose. Therefore, the recitation must serve the purpose of consecrating the deity (*devatā-saṃskāra*), and not have an unseen purpose.

In reality, however, by means of the *yājyā* instruction, there is here only the injunction of a mere accessory (*guṇa*). Nor does the consequence [of the *yājyā*] arise in the *praiṣa* (direction) whose object is the *yājyā*, because in the direction "he directs the *hotṛ*," the *hotṛ* alone is the object of the direction, and thus the *yājyā* is not its object.
Therefore, since the recitation is already established as a constant requirement, the instruction by means of the *yājyā* serves only to enjoin a mere accessory.

Since the combination [of the two] is understood through another sentence, namely, "Having recited the *puro’nuvākyā*, he sacrifices with the *yājyā*," there is no suspicion regarding the determination of the meaning of the word *puraḥ* in the *asīna* (seated) injunction.
Therefore, because it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), its sublation (*bādha*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is indeed appropriate.
21. Maṇḍana: "The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*)."
23. Śaṅkara: "The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras should be thus. This is the *saṃskriyā*.
There is a lifelong repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, because both are occasioned by life as qualified by the specific times of the full moon and the new moon."
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, he girds the wife with a yoktra (waist-band).
That [practice] is established by extension (*prasaṅga*) for the Soma-related rites within the iṣṭi-type rituals at the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Bhāṣya 12.1.129.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the spreading [of grass] is enjoined for the primary [sacrificial ground] using *kuśa* grass itself;
this is the *barhir-nyāya* (the principle of the sacrificial grass).
Vi. 3.2.1. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the driving away of the calves is performed with a *palāśa* branch.

"That he separates the calves with a leafy branch" (ŚB 4.2.2). This refers to the *vatsopāsarjana* (the driving away of the calves) during the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), which consists in releasing the calves from their mothers' side for the purpose of suckling.
This is included among the twelve pairs [of actions].
"He releases the calf and places the pot on the fire.
In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the twelve pairs consisting of the releasing of the calf, placing the pot on the fire, and so forth, are the duties of the Adhvaryu, not of the sacrificer.
Ke. 3.8.19–21. Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there is the restraint of speech: "When they are about to perform the sacrifice, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer restrain their speech."

In this context, the restraint of speech (*vāgyama*) is not the motivator for the supreme *apūrva*; rather, because the restraint of speech is enjoined specifically for the summoning of the *haviṣkṛt*, it is the motivator for the *apūrva* of those ritual acts such as the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) that precede the summoning.

(Vi. 9.1.7). In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the two "knowledge-utterances"—"He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon" and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon"—are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the collective whole.

2|2|3. In the two "Injunctions of the Knower" (*vidvadvākya*) regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), because the connection with time serves as the basis for the designation [of the sacrifices] by name, and because the relationship between the sacrifice and the connection with time is established, a collective whole (*samudāya*) is possible even for those acts enjoined by separate sentences, since they share a common connection with the same time.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 729). In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the *vidhṛtī* grass-bands and the *paribhojanīya* sacrificial grass must be prepared.
Bhāṣya 3.8.17.33: At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the *veda* (sweeping broom) is made of *darbha* grass.
[As it is said: "Having made the *veda*, one prepares the *vedi* (altar). Vi. 11.1.12.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the injunction "One desiring cattle should prepare the *veda* [grass-bundle] after the calves have been driven away" is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), not for the sake of the ritual act (*karmārtha*). Bhāṣya 4.1.21, Section 2. Regarding the subsidiaries prescribed by two different Vedas within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, when various Vedic accents are prescribed, the rule of "subordinate versus principal" (*guṇamukhyatva-krama*) applies such that the quality of the primary Yajurvedic rite—namely, being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*)—would prevail. Consequently, there is a specific scriptural prescription (*vācanika*) regarding the accent: "The rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings are in a low tone; those following are in the middle tone; and the *anuyāja* offerings and subsequent rites are in the highest tone. Vārttika 3.2.15, p. 811.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the acts such as the spreading of the altar and the two sacrificial grounds must be performed at their own respective times, and not at the time of the primary sacrifice.
This is because there is a rule that subsidiary (aṅga) and primary (pradhāna) rites may have different locations, times, and performers; this constitutes the governing principle (*adhikāra*).
At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [the priest] sprinkles the altar with water, saying, "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ... He encloses the Veda-grass-bundle by tracing around it with a spade.
With the spade, he digs up the upper layer of earth.
"Parilikha": "And the taking possession (parigraha) will be explained later," [in] Vi. 10|1|19.
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is stated in the Veda: "On the previous day of the new moon, one prepares the altar (vedi). Thus, the preparation is on the previous day. Bhā. 5|1|16|29.

Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the mantra "Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass, thee" is recited only once at the first sprinkling of the altar (*vedi*), and there is no repetition of the mantra with each subsequent sprinkling; however, because the altar is a single entity, the repetition of the act of sprinkling itself is based on a direct scriptural injunction (Vi. 11.4.16). Furthermore, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, during the construction of the altar and similar rites, the mantra "He who hates us and whom we hate" must be recited even in the absence of actual enmity, because it serves a transcendental purpose (*apūrva*) (Bhā. 6.8.28). Finally, the ritual properties of the altar in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices pertain to both the subsidiary and the primary acts.

The principle of substance and preparation (*dravyasaṃskāranyāya*): Regarding the enclosure of the altar (*vediparigraha*) in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—the initial measurement of the altar—"He encloses the altar by tracing around it with a wooden sword (*sphyena vediṃ parilikhan parigṛhṇāti*). [Then follow] the sprinkling of the altar (*vediprokṣaṇa*) and so forth in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; [and] regarding the vow (*vrata*) in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

*Parilekhana* means drawing lines all around. (Vi. 10.1.9). In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is the application of the mantra that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sprinkling of the altar (*vediprokṣaṇa*).
This is the *vediprokṣaṇa-nyāya*.

Bhāṣya 11.4.14.49–50: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the altar, the exterior [of the site], and other such items are properties belonging to all the subsidiaries and the primary rite (*pradhāna*), not to the primary rite alone. The altar belongs to the properties of the oblation (*havirdharma*). Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.7.1.19–25: Regarding the spreading of the altar in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is said, "He spreads the altar in three layers or five layers. In that case, there is a repetition of the mantra for spreading with each layer.

Regarding the *sāmidhenīs* in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the triple repetition of the *sāmidhenīs* was prescribed for the sake of completion; however, since completion occurs here even otherwise, [the repetition is not required].

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains that the fulfillment [of the required number] should occur through the addition [of mantras] from the traditional scripture (āgama), provided there is no sublation of what is intended to be expressed. For instance, in cases where an increase in the *sāmidhenī* verses is heard in the text—such as "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one"—the addition (*āgama*) that would otherwise be established by logical principle (*nyāya*) does not take effect.

This is because, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), by the injunction "He recites the first three times and the last three times," there is a prescription for the repetition of the first and last verses among those already listed as eleven, in order to complete the number fifteen; thus, due to this [inherent] fulfillment, there is an absence of addition (*āgama*).

Nor does this [text] imply that there are no recitations beyond those three, merely because it prescribes repetition for only the first and last [verses]; for if the limit were restricted to three repetitions, it would result in the verses serving a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). By this statement, following the logic of the sprinkling of the remains of the *prayāja* offerings, there is a prescription of mere repetition for the sake of achieving the number fifteen, as enjoined by the rule: "One should recite fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses."

For regarding the first and last of the eleven verses, when there is a repetition until the required number is reached, the principle that "it should be equal, as nothing specific is heard" (*samaṃ syādaśrutatvāt*) results in a threefold repetition for each.
Therefore, the argument of Pārthasārathi—that because the required number can be achieved even by repeating them twice or four times, a threefold repetition is redundant—is refuted.

Consequently, since the meaning of the sentence is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to be "one should repeat the first and last [verses] until the required number is reached," their repetition alone is to be performed even for the sake of reaching numbers such as twenty-one.

Nor does the fact that both the first and the last [repetitions] are intended as the objects of the injunction result in a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) caused by their multiplicity; for, as in the case of the rule "half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*), there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the state of being both, because that duality serves as the delimiting factor for the object of the injunction. This being the prima facie view, we reply: although the application of the principle of "each locus producing its own result" (*niṣpādaka-pratyadhikaraṇa-nyāya*) would lead to the contingency of an invisible transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), a figurative indication is nonetheless improper. Furthermore, by the very same reasoning as in the case of the sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings, even without the explicit mention of a verb of action, two distinct sentences are established here; thus, without intending the first repetition, only the third repetition is enjoined.

For this very reason, since the number fifteen is achieved by repeating the first and last of the eleven [verses] three times each, it is stated in the *Kaustubha* that, in reality, the number is not enjoined at all in the passage "one should recite fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses.

Therefore, because the number fifteen is not otherwise established, and because an injunction for repetition is justified as being for the purpose of achieving that number through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is precisely the triple repetition that is enjoined by this [text].
It should be understood that the statement "they become fifteen" is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the rule "he recites the first one thrice."

Therefore, it is established that even in cases such as the twenty-one-fold [recitation], there is the addition (*āgama*) of the remaining *prakṛta* (archetypal) verses beyond the first and last, which are subject to repetition (*abhyāsa*).

In that context, regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses, it is stated in the archetype: "He recites the first verse three times; he recites the last verse three times.

Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is this a property of the *ṛc* (verse) itself—that wherever the *pravovāja* verse is located, it must be recited three times—or is it a property of the position—that whichever other verse happens to be recited first must be recited three times?
Whence does this doubt arise? From the possibility of both interpretations.

If the intention is made thus—"That which is the first among the *sāmidhenī* verses uttered should be recited three times"—then the property of being recited three times belongs to the verse "pra vo vājāḥ.
But if it is understood thus—that the tripling and so forth are connected with the state of being first—then the property belongs to the position [of the verse].
What, then, is the established position? That the *dharma* belongs to the *ṛc*.
Why? Because priority is connected with the individual instance (*vyakti*), and the individual instance is connected with the repetition. How is this understood? From the use of the neuter gender.
For "woman" (strī) is indeed a particular individual.

If primacy were a qualifier of that [individual], then the specification of gender would be appropriate; for she too is connected with the repetition. If, however, it were first stated that "one should practice," then the particular individual would not be intended to be expressed, and in that case, the specification of the feminine gender would not be tenable.

Moreover, a syntactical split (vākyabheda) would result: it would follow that first, the [sacrifice] must be repeated three times, and then, the Ṛc mentioned first must be repeated three times. In my view, however, the property is stated for the Ṛc characterized by its being first; thus, since there is the injunction of a single object, there would be no syntactical split.
Moreover, by direct statement (śruti), the word "three" is connected with the first [verse], whereas by syntactical connection (vākya), it is connected with the repetition.
Therefore, the property of the Ṛg-verse is that the *pravovājā* verse, wherever it may be situated, is to be repeated three times.
This being the position reached, we reply:

This triple repetition of the first *sāmidhenī* verse that is prescribed applies to the first performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; it is a ritual duty (*dharma*) occasioned by the position [of the verse], not a duty occasioned by the genus (*jāti*) of any particular *ṛc*.

Why? Because in the *Ṛgveda*, which is neuter in gender, there exists no particular verse (*ṛc*) called "the first" that could be referred to by the word "three"; in that case, "firstness" would have to be taken as a mere secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).
In the other view, however, there is direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) rather than secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and direct scriptural statement is superior to secondary indication.
Therefore, [the *Ṛgveda*] is incomplete.

Now, as for what was stated—"Because of the neuter gender indication, the Vedic revelation (śruti) applies only to the view of repetition (abhyāsa), and thus neither the sentence (vākya) is split nor is the neuter gender untenable"—to this it is replied: For words that express qualities (guṇavacana), the gender and number are derived from their substratum (āśrayataḥ). Thus, even when the individual entity (vyakti) is not specifically intended, whatever gender necessarily occurs belongs to the quality by virtue of its substratum.
Even when that [gender] is not prescribed by rule, the mention of a specific gender remains indeed a restatement (anuvāda), as in:
"white male," "white female," "white neuter";
or "one white [thing]," "two white [things]," "many white [things]."

In the case of the injunction "Bring a white cloth" (*śuklāṃ śāṭīm ānaya*), although the bringing of the cloth and so forth is not what is being enjoined, but rather the inquiry into the property of its connection with whiteness, a qualification by gender is nevertheless not applied there; yet, the mention of the neuter gender still occurs as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) in the form "Bring [it] white" (*śuklām ānaya*).
And because it is a restatement, there will be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

This being the case, although the connection of the firstness with the neuter gender is based on direct audition (*śrauta*), nevertheless the connection of the firstness is with the repetition (*abhyāsa*), not with the gender.
If the connection of the gender (liṅga) with this [suffix] were intended, then the mention of "primacy" (prāthamya) would have to be assumed as a mere restatement (anuvāda).
Even if the connection with primacy were being expressed, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).

Furthermore, one should not dispute this point, for the neuter word is indeed a qualifier of the nominal stem (prātipadika), according to the rule: "The suffixes taddhita and others are applied to that nominal stem which refers to the feminine."
A qualifier does not enter into a syntactical connection with another word, as in the case of "the king's man goes" (*rājapuruṣo gacchati*).
However, when there is a connection between primacy and repetition, the neuter gender is employed there as a restatement of what has already been established;
for those words that are *sāmidhenī* verses, they are indeed *ṛc*s, and the word *ṛk* is neuter in gender.
In this context, that which is the first utterance has the *ṛc* as its substratum.
Since words expressing qualities take their gender and number from their substratum, even though the *ṛc* is not specifically qualified, it will be neuter.
That which is the first utterance is repeated three times; thus, that *ṛc*, being feminine, is called a *sāmidhenī*.
Therefore, the statement "He recites the first verse thrice" is a restatement (anuvāda) of a characteristic already established.

Since it is said, "He recites the first thrice, the last thrice; these amount to fifteen," this triple-recitation (tricatana) prescribed for the attainment of the fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses applies to the complete *ṛc*, not to a part of a verse.
Consequently, as it is a restatement of what is already established, the characteristic belongs to the primacy [of the position], not to the verse itself.
Śā [explains]: "In that context, it is denoted by the neuter gender;
here, its connection with the three repetitions is enjoined.
It is said: "By the word 'first' (prathama), primacy is denoted through direct scriptural statement (śruti)."

The *ṛc*, however, would be mentioned by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, the property of being first [belongs to the repetition]. Regarding "Soma": Just as it was stated previously that [the rule] ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* applies to the final sacrifice because of the requirement for a specific sequence, so too, for the sake of establishing the subsequent [rule], the repetition of the *ṛc* itself—which is required—is enjoined; thus, the connection [of this section] is established through this demonstration. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: Among the *sāmidhenī* verses, the repetition of the first and the last is a property of the position (*sthānadharma*), either because of its connection with being first, or because it is presented by the word "first" [in the context of the *sāmidhenīs*].
Vi— "Is the property [of repetition] due to the state of being recited thrice, or is it a property of the position?
It is [a property of] the neuter gender; no, because of the predominance of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
There is no repetition of this verse, 'pra vo vājāḥ,' which is recited in another position."

Bhaṭṭa: In the intermediate context (*antaraprakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "He recites the first [verse] three times; he recites the last [verse] three times.
In this regard, the recitation itself is merely restated as being already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), while only the triple repetition (*trirabhyāsa*) is enjoined.
Furthermore, there is no dispute that the word "first" (*prathamām*) serves to identify the object of reference (*uddeśya*).
In that case as well, the word "first" (prathama) denotes something qualified by priority for the purpose of specification, just like words such as "white" (*śukla*).
Therein, the qualificand is understood to be the *ṛc* itself, because of its neuter gender and because of the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses.

Furthermore, due to the connection with the qualifier in the form of priority, there arises the cognition of a specific *ṛc*, and not a presentation characterized by [the specific mantra] beginning with *pra vo vājā*.
It is not denotative (*śābdī*), because there is no word that expresses it.
For this very reason, primacy alone is the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*), just like "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.

It is not, however, the nature of being a horse and so on as characterized by that [primacy], because there is no evidence for secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) without a cause; such is the argument.
But this is now investigated.

When the contingency of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) arises regarding the first [verse], and when—by way of indicating the means to the *apūrva*—there is the indication of merely that *ṛc* which reveals the intention toward the means to the *apūrva*, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) results. To avoid this, there arises a deliberation: is it the status of being the first (*prāthamya*) that is intended as a qualifier of "being a *ṛc*" (*ṛktva*) within the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedakatva*), or is it the specific nature of the *pravovājādi* [verse] itself? In this deliberation, having accepted the unexpressed (*aśruta*) form of "being first" as the delimiting factor of the objective, and once the capacity for the indicated function of being a means to the *apūrva* is established through proximity (*upaśrīṇatva*), one settles upon the delimiting factor of the objective as consisting in the specific nature of being a means to the *apūrva* that has been thus determined.

Regarding the tripling of the *sāmidhenī* verses in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices: since there is no authoritative basis for a specific number of *sāmidhenīs* in the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the qualification "being a *ṛc*" applies specifically to those beginning with *pra vo jāḥ*. Consequently, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), wherever they may occur, it is precisely those beginning with *pra vo jāḥ* that are to be recited three times.
But it does not apply to a mantra that falls under the first position.

This being the case, in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because a qualification distinct from the mere absence of those respective substrates is presented by what is postulated for the parts—even though that [qualification] is exhausted [in its specific application], it qualifies only the *prāya* (the majority/primary), and not the *anuṣṭhiti* (performance) by virtue of being a *prayojya* (that which is to be employed).

In the case of threshing and so forth, however, since the status of being the intended object (uddeśyatva) is determined solely by the fact that these acts are the means for producing rice grains, there is no need to include "rice" (*vrīhi*) in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), even if one were to assume a restrictive rule (*vyavasthādhāraṇa*) establishing barley (*yava*) as a subsidiary element of the ritual (*dharma*). This is because there is no syntactic unity (*aikavākyatva*) [between the threshing injunctions and the rice-injunction]. In the present case, however, if one were to accept such an over-extension, it would result in a lack of syntactic unity between the two sentences containing the initial word *utpāda* (i.e., the injunctions regarding the *praüga* and *śyena* chants). Furthermore, because the statement "they become fifteen" (*tāḥ pañcadaśa saṃpadyante*) would otherwise be unintelligible, the intention to express the qualification (*viśeṣaṇavivakṣā*) is indispensable.
And for this reason, there is also the application [of the rule] that "whichever [act] occurs first, middle, or last" applies here as well.
Maṇḍana [says]: "The performance of the practice should be at the first [instance] of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
heaven [is the result]; in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, when the oblation is exhausted..."

In the context of the two-month [Darśapūrṇamāsa] sacrifices, the mention of the fruits of the *sruva*, *upabhṛt*, and *dhruvā* ladles is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the fruit, not an injunction of the fruit.

This is the *parṇamayī* principle (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 4.1.1.1–3). In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, heaven is the fruit; however, that is not something to be enjoined, because one engages in it spontaneously due to its inherent desirability.
VI. 4.1.2, Section 2: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *upahavya* oblation.
Bhāṣya 3.4.1.9: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Sviṣṭakṛt is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). This is the principle of the "upper half" (*uttarārdhanyāya*).
In the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is also a disposal (pratipatti).
Bhāṣya 3.2.5.16. In the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is a purificatory rite (saṃskāraka) for the sacrificial substance.
Ṭupṭīkā 10.1.3.11. In the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Sviṣṭakṛt has the purpose of removing the impurity from the oblation (havis).
The principle of the Āśvina cups (Āśvinanyāya):
Ke. 4.1.7.18–20. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the subsequent rites such as the Sviṣṭakṛt offering are to be performed from all the oblations, not from just one of them.
This is the principle of the Sviṣṭakṛt section (Sviṣṭakṛdadhikaraṇanyāya).

Regarding the subsidiary rites such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, if they belong to a single [offering], then the rule of the first presentation (*prathamopasthitanyāya*) applies.

Bhāṣya 3.4.16.46–47. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the subsidiary rite of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and others should not be performed with the northern half of the sacrificial cake, because there exists another purpose for that portion.
VI. 3|5|1. At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, this Sviṣṭakṛt [offering] is to be performed with the clarified butter from the Upāṃśuyāja and other materials.
Bhāṣya 3|5|1, 1–12: At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice is a purificatory act (*saṃskāraka*) within the Anuyājas, not a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
10|4|1|9|138: At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the cooking of the oblations (*haviṣām śrapaṇam*) is prescribed to be done on the Gārhapatya fire.
In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, when there is a failure of the sacrificial oblation, the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) is subsidiary to the Darśapūrṇamāsa;
beginning with the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the *idā*,
it will become purposeful by assisting them.
Otherwise, one would have to assume a result in the absence of a statement.
Therefore, the sentence is set aside precisely because of the absence of a result; thus, by means of the particle *iti*, the context will be upheld. Hence, this [section] begins.
The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Nor is it a modification (*vikāra*) of the Agnihotra or the Jyotiṣṭoma, nor a modification of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
If it were a modification of those, then there would also have to be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in that case when [the vessel] is spilled or broken.
The *Śābarabhāṣya*: Having concluded the incidental discussion (6.5.8–14), it resumes the section on expiation (*prāyaścittādhikāra*).

Soma: The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: the expiation (prāyaścitta) heard in the context (adhikāra)—that is, in the section on the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices—should apply everywhere because of the commonality of the fault. Viśvarūpa: "Whether it occurs in the Hotṛ’s portion or elsewhere in the archetypal rite (prakṛta), it applies everywhere due to the occasion (nimitta); for it forms a single syntactical unit with the archetypal rite for the sake of the fruit."

Bhaṭṭa: Although the expiation (prāyaścitta) such as "he offers [an oblation] when there is a breakage" is occasional (naimittika), it is nevertheless an auxiliary to the sacrifice (kratvaṅga) because of its dependence on a result and its context. Furthermore, the occasion (nimitta) for the rite—such as the breakage—is not that of an ordinary worldly potsherd; rather, since the general nature of expiation requires it, one must assume that the occasion is specifically the breakage of a potsherd used by the officiating priests (ṛtvij), which is unavoidable. This is because postulating an independent unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava). Maṇḍana: "In the case under discussion, the offering upon breakage should take place."
Śaṅkara: "If [the fire] is divided, the oblation is not all-pervasive.
At the time of fetching the fire for the purpose of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra that is an auxiliary to the milking for the Agnihotra should not be performed. No."
9|4|8|139: There is no performance of the *uddhāna* (carrying away) of the fire that has been drawn out for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, within the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

It is a single ritual action called *darśapūrṇamāsa* that acquires various designations such as *dākṣāyaṇa* and so forth through its association with unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) qualities denoted by terms like *ayana* and the like.
The desires for specific qualities (*guṇakāma*) associated with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such rites do not apply to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
[Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 8.1.14.23–25]. In the case of the rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, along with their constituent parts, the Adhvaryu is the performer.

There is a requirement for the performance of all constituent parts (*aṅga*) in the case of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). (Vi. 11.1.13). Regarding rites such as the Agnihotra, there is an oblation when a specific occasion (*nimitta*) arises. This constitutes the section [of the discussion].

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, the Bhāṣyakāra has stated that they are the instruments (*karaṇa*). In this regard, he says: By means of the sentence (*vākya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the name (*samākhyā*), there is also a restriction (*niyama*)—namely, "by these [priests] alone [the ritual] is to be performed"—and its visible purpose is indeed [this]:
a certain degree of satisfaction arises for the performers.

Thereafter, with reference to that which has been accomplished (*niṣpanna*)—namely, that which follows from the stated purpose—the Commentator says: "For that eating is for the sake of purifying the person.

However, the ritualists (*yājñikās*), adhering to a distinction [wherein] the purpose of the action is the purification of the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*) while the purpose of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is the purification of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*), have stated: "The eatings are purifications of the person," and so forth.
[Thus,] the specific mention [of the eatings] serves the purpose of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

Commentary: Now, as for what was stated [in the sūtra], "because of the specific mention," that is for the sake of the quality (guṇa). The others are obtained simply by virtue of being performers of the action (karmakara).

In that context, the sacrificer is designated as the fifth among them by virtue of the scriptural statement. Since this statement is intended for the purpose of including him, it does not constitute an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
"In the primary act, there is the indication by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Commentary: As for the fact that only the giving of the substance is specified in the primary act, it is treated as an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) on the authority of that statement;
for in that case, there is no injunction of anything previously unestablished (*apūrva*).
In this case, the sacrificer is enjoined.
When there is a doubt as to whether [a statement] is an injunction (vidhi), an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā), or a descriptive restatement (anuvāda), it is explained as an injunction;
in that regard, the word retains its own primary meaning.

In the case of exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), there are three defects: the abandonment of its own meaning, the acceptance of another's meaning, and the sublation of what has already been established.
Therefore, those who are present at the rite itself should consume [the sacrificial food].
If it is argued that this follows from the sense of the matter:
The Commentary: Now, as for what was stated—that there would be a contradiction in the Aśvamedha sacrifice because of the multiplicity of portions to be consumed—that must be refuted. [We reply:
No, because there is no distinction.
Commentary: In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, not everyone will eat [the horse].
By implication, if everyone were to eat it, they would not complete the Aśvamedha.
In that case, the scriptural injunction (śruti) for the Aśvamedha would be contradicted.
Being contradicted, that [restriction] sublates the eating of all [meat] obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).
However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no contradiction. Therefore, all those present at the archetype should eat.
Śālikanātha: This section [of the treatise] follows as a consequence of the remaining topic.
Somanātha: The meaning of the sūtra, however, is that the consumption of the remnants must be performed by others, because of the injunction: "The sacrificer is the fifth [participant] in this.
Just as when the offering of everything would otherwise follow, the offering is restricted to the mere giving of the substance by virtue of the specific injunction, so it is here.
Vi—Is the consumption of the remnant for the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or is it the consumption by someone else?
Since the officiating priests have already been excluded, and since ownership has not been established [for them], the final alternative is prescribed.
Bhaṭṭa—Regarding the consumption of the remnant here, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the consumption of the remnants is indeed heard in the scripture.

In that regard, regarding the *iḍā*-consumption, the agents are those heard in the scripture: "The four priests with the sacrificer as the fifth consume the *iḍā*. Likewise, regarding the *prāśitra*-consumption, it is heard: "He hands over the *prāśitra* to the Brahman priest.
Regarding the fourth-consecration (*caturthākaraṇa*) consumption as well, there are four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), according to logic, scriptural instruction, and direct measurement.

In the case of the consumption at the time of the *śaṃyuvāka*, however, all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) participate; for although the teacher’s statement and the designation [of the text] refer only to the sacrificer and his portion, the plural number in the scriptural injunction, "They consume the remnants of the oblation" (*haviḥśeṣān bhakṣayanti*), indicates that all are involved due to their role as performers of the ritual action.

Nor should it be argued that, since the repeated hearing of the rule here serves as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of what would otherwise be obtained by logic, those other than the aforementioned should be the ones consuming at the time of the *śaṃyuvāka*.

Even though the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are already established [in the sacrifice], their association with the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), which was not previously established, is enjoined therein; for this does not serve to exclude (*parisaṃkhyā*) the priests from other instances of eating.

For here, although there is an injunction of another instance of eating qualified by the agents of the *iḍā* and other remnants, at the time of enjoining the qualification, the act of eating—which is already established—is enjoined together with the association of the sacrificer through the principle of "distinguishing between what is already established and what is not" (*prāptāprāpta-viveka*).

Regarding the portion for the priests (*ṛtvij*), although it serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the performers according to the principle of the sprinkling of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings, it is not enjoined in the case of the eating of the *prāśitra*, because it would be purposeless (*ānarthakya*) since it is already being eaten by default. Since that [eating] is already established without need for an injunction due to its inherent purposelessness, what is enjoined is the accompaniment of the sacrificer (*yajamāna-sāhitya*), which was otherwise unestablished. However, if it is considered that the eating also serves to provide strength for the ritual about to be performed, then let there be the inclusion of the sacrificer as the fifth member for the purpose of including the wife (*patnī-parigraha*).

In every case, because the number of performers for the consumption [of the remains] is restricted by the *kartṛ-parisaṃkhyā*, only the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the performers at the time of the consumption following the *śaṃyuvāka*. On this view, the wife and the sacrificer are not excluded from that [consumption]; this is to be understood from the statement of the authors of the Kalpasūtras: "Right here, the officiating priests consume the remnants of the oblation. Maṇḍana says: "The consumption of the remnant should be for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Śaṅkara says: "All consumptions belong to the officiating priests."
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, there is also a portioning and consumption of the *iḍā* for the sacrificer; as it is stated:
"Having brought together [the portions], those with the sacrificer as the fifth consume the *iḍā*" (Vi.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, there is an optionality (*vikalpa*) regarding the remaining expiations (*prāyaścitta*) from among the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.3.15–16). In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites, the fruit mentioned in the *karaṇa-mantras* accrues to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). It should be increased for the one who desires prosperity.

The *karamamantras* and the *praipas* at the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices [are discussed in ŚB 13.2.6–28]. Regarding the nature of the *karamamantras* at the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, the fruit conducive to the ritual belongs to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
The section on transgression (Atikramādhikaraṇa).
Śābarabhāṣya 8.1.29–30: In rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the entitlement belongs to a single performer alone, not to one accompanied by a second.

6|2|12-13. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, the injunction regarding the agent, place, and time is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha). Vi. 4|2|9. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, there is a repetition of the mantras used for the pouring out [of the oblation] and so forth. This is the Nirvāpa-nyāya (the principle of the pouring out).

Bhāṣya 1.1.4.47–48: Even when substitutes such as *nīvāra* grass are used for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and others, the primary ritual duties (*mukhyadharma*) such as threshing (*avaghāta*) must still be performed.
3.6.14.37–39: In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and others, even after the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding *nīvāra* has been made, one must take only *vrīhi* rice and not *nīvāra*;
however, once the preparation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) has begun, the sacrifice must be completed using the substitutes themselves.
VI. 3.16: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, there is an option regarding the three mantras for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
I. 2.1.15: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, the context (prakaraṇa) is the factor that assigns the prayājas and other subordinate rites.
Or [the term may be] secondary (gauṇa), on account of the similarity of the action.
Commentary: It is not the case that the *preṣa* (command) belongs to the *agnīdh* and the *praipārtha* (the purpose of the command) belongs to the *adhvaryu*.
What then? The *adhvaryu* himself commands the *agnīdh*.
In this way, both the *preṣa* and the *praipārtha* will be performed by the *adhvaryu* alone.
In that case, the designation "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" (ādhvaryava) is upheld.
Therefore, the Adhvaryu alone should be the primary agent. What constitutes his primacy? That everything must be performed by him, on account of the designation.
Now, as for what was said—that "the Adhvaryu is seen to be the performer"—that is addressed here.
It is true that he is seen, but no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is found upon reflection to establish his performance of the *praipa* (directions).
Therefore, this is a false perception.
For that view which lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a delusion,
such as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
However, the Veda is a means of valid cognition for accomplishing human goals.
Therefore, the Āgnīdhra is the one who performs the ritual action;
and since the word *adhvaryu* is seen to refer to the performer, it must be used in a figurative sense.
Because he performs the ritual acts (padārthas) prescribed in the *Ādhvaryava* Veda, he is called the *Adhvaryu*, and [the other] is called the *Āgnīdhra*.
Therefore, the *preṣa* (command) belongs to the *Ādhvaryava*, while the *praiṣārtha* (the object of the command) belongs to the *Āgnīdhra*.

Alternatively, according to the principle "or rather, the primary one, because of the prior injunction," it is appropriate that the agent designated by the name (*samākhyā*) be the one who issues the *preṣa*, due to his priority.
For at that time, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
But when that [term] is employed, because of the contradiction, another [word] comes to be used in the sense of the *praipa* (directive).
And since the status of the agent is not obstructed even with respect to the operation of the one being prompted by the prompter, both [terms] are accommodated.
Otherwise, there would indeed be a total contradiction regarding the command (*praiṣa*);
for he would neither have performed it himself nor caused it to be performed by another.
Therefore, one who has been commanded by the Adhvaryu should perform the action.

And by the statement, "With the *vajra* [he strikes] the *adhvaryu*," that [act] will be designated as belonging to the *āmīdhra* due to the transfer of function (*kāryāpatti*). The Bhaṭṭa [school] says: Even there, since there is no evidence for subverting the designation (*samākhyā*) when there are many primary matters to be conveyed by the *praipa*, the act must be performed by another person through the agency of the *adhvaryu* in a single *praipa* such as "having taken up the *prokṣaṇī* waters. For this very reason, the text shows the distinction among those who hold [the implements]: "Having held the *sphyā* crosswise, he utters the *saṃpreṣa*; if he were to hold it otherwise, the *adhvaryu* would be struck down by the *vajra* of the *sphyā*. Thus, it demonstrates the difference among the holders.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: even though the acts denoted by the *praipa* (directions) have other agents, the designation (*samākhyā*) of the Adhvaryu is justified because he is the agent by virtue of being the instigator (*prayojaka*).
In some cases, others indeed perform the acts denoted by the *praipa*, while the Adhvaryu retains the function of issuing the directions.
Furthermore, in the case of the Soma sacrifice and the like, there are specific injunctions for the Pratiprasthātṛ and others.
That is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

However, in the case of the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*, [the *praiṣas*] belong to the *āmīdhra* alone; because he acts as both agent and object (*karmakartṛtvena*) in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites, the *praiṣas* belong to the *adhvaryu*.
"But the Adhvaryu [should give the command], because it is so observed.

Commentary: Now, this being the case (that is to say, once it is understood that the agents of the *praipa* and the *praiṣārtha* are distinct), this doubt arises: should the Adhvaryu send the command to the Āgnīdhra, or should the Āgnīdhra send the command to the Adhvaryu?
There is no fixed rule, as there is no specific distinction [stated].

This being the position, we reply: the Adhvaryu should be the one who performs the action according to the meaning of the aforementioned direction (praipa). Why? Because it is so seen [in the scriptures].
The instruction is: "One should hold the *sphyam* crosswise;
if one were to hold it otherwise, the *sphyam* is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the *adhvaryu* would be destroyed by that thunderbolt.
Thus, the *sphyam* is held in the hand of the one who issues the command.
"He would injure the Adhvaryu with the *spaya*," thus [the text] indicates that the Adhvaryu is distinct from the one who issues the command;
therefore, the Adhvaryu should be commanded—
or else, "if he were to hold it himself, the Adhvaryu would be injured by the thunderbolt."
Alternatively, there is the reading: "The *vajra* would injure the *adhvaryu*.
The holding of the *sphyam* belongs exclusively to the *āgnīdhra*;
by stating that "he [the *adhvaryu*] would injure," the text indicates that the *adhvaryu* is the one who commands the *āgnīdhra* while the latter holds the *sphyam*.

But what is its application? By the rule, "And in case of conflict with the thumb [measure], because it is for that purpose," it is logical that the *adhvaryu* is the performer of the *praipa*, not the principal [priest].
Furthermore, there are many purposes of the *praipa*, while the *nigada* is singular.

Therefore, by the principle "The majority should possess the same character" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.22), the *adhvaryu* is the performer of the *praipa* purpose; by process of elimination, the *āgnīdhra* is the performer of the *praipa* itself.

It should be understood that the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such rites belong to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, as this is well-established among practitioners of the sacrificial ritual (*yājñika*).

As for the indicative mark (*liṅga*), if the *adhvaryu* were to hold the *anvaya*, then the *sphya* would destroy him; since there is no such sublation (*bādhaka*), the holding and the command are appropriate even for the *ācārya*.
Furthermore, the claim that "holding the *sphya* is well-known in the *Kalpasūtras* as being exclusively the duty of the *adhvaryu*" is a boastful argument (*prauḍhivāda*) lacking in factual basis.
Maṇḍana [says]: "The *adhvaryu* alone should perform the command."
The remaining duties are to be performed by the Āgnīdhra;
the *śaṃsana* (invocation) should be performed by the Adhvaryu alone.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, if the substance that was cut off for the purpose of the *śeṣa-kāryas* (concluding rites) such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is lost, there is an omission of those concluding rites.
The section concerning destruction.

Commentary: Now, if [the substance] perishes while possessing the characteristics of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, should a remnant be taken from it or not? What is the prima facie view? That a remnant should again be taken.
Why? Because here, the entire [substance] is not offered to the deity of the northern half.
To whom, then? To one who is present.
For when there is a purpose, that which is present must not be taken [without permission]. By taking it from one who is present, what is prescribed by scripture is accomplished.
"Therefore, the remainder is not to be taken.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"There should be an omission for those who do not partake of the remainder" (the word *lopaḥ* is supplied in the sūtra).
(Śloka 1.4.14) Why? Because it is a distinguished cause.
For that [animal] is the distinguished cause in the act of cutting out the portions; how, then, could it be disposed of?

And the disposal (*pratipatti*) assists by means of creating separation (*viviktakaraṇa*). For that which is being disposed of so as to be separated, there is this rule: "It is to be disposed of with an oblation to *Sviṣṭakṛt*. In this way, it becomes properly disposed of.
If that [offering substance] which has been drawn out for the oblation should be lost after it has been separated [from the main portion], one should not perform a re-drawing.
Furthermore, since it is intended to be offered in the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation,
and because of the absence of anything to be offered, the *sviṣṭakṛt* itself would simply be omitted.
When the primary [portion] has been set aside, what remains is common to all the subsequent rites (*śeṣakārya*).
In that case, when one [portion] has been extracted, the remainder is to be offered elsewhere.

[The author of the *Ṭupṭīkā* objects to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): The *Sviṣṭakṛt* [offering] is not prompted by the fire (*agni-prayukta*)—[the reading in the Ānandāśrama edition is *anya-prayukta*].
[It would be] the apprehender of the substance.

If this were so, then since the apprehension of another's [substance] is excluded when [the substance] is present, the disappearance [of the original] upon destruction is established; what, then, is the purpose of this [section]? It is said: if it were the instigator (*prayojaka*).
(Then: Since that which was offered was of such a nature, it would not be something remaining from which another portion could be taken again.

However, as for that which is to be consecrated by the *aindra* [offering], even if it is destroyed in one part, because the remainder still exists, why is the consecration not performed again by taking another portion? Furthermore, in this context, the term "portion" (*abhava*) is not intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)—that is to say, it is not intended as an indicator for the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion.
What then? It is that which is being consecrated (*saṃskriyate*).
This being the case, we reply:
A specific location (consisting of the upper half of the entire *puroḍāśa* cake, which is the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering) is required as the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*).

Since that location no longer exists, who would perform the disposal (*pratipatti*)? If it is argued that a transcendental result (*apūrva*) [is produced], then in that case, the *apūrva* here is merely a byproduct of the disposal of the substance.
Therefore, that [the sacrifice] itself is not the motive;
rather, the preparation of the substance is what is intended to be performed (and thus the motive), not the accomplishment of the sacrifice.
(And this injunction for the omission of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering follows from logical necessity.)

Because of that statement, its completion with clarified butter (*ājya*) is indeed intended; however, in this case, there is the omission of the *ādī* offerings themselves. The connection [of the discussion] arises from the counter-argument that, as in the case of the Soma sacrifice, there is no absence of material to be cut off (*avadāna*) here, which would otherwise necessitate a further offering.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: "Furthermore, the cutting off (*avadāna*) depends on the remaining portion (*śeṣa*); because of the word 'retention' (*adhivāsa*), the word 'omission' (*lopa*) is also to be supplied [into the text].

And thus, for those who do not possess a remainder, when their own portion is destroyed, there is no cutting off; rather, there would be an omission, because the performance [of the ritual] has as its cause a specific purpose consisting of the disposal (*pratipatti*), and in the absence of that which is to be disposed of, there is no disposal. Vi— "When the portion intended for the *iḍā* and so forth is destroyed, another [portion] should be taken from the remainder, or the first [portion] should not be [taken]; this is the view of Īdima."
And the remaining sentient beings [are included] because they are encompassed by the other modes of practice.

According to the Bhaṭṭa school: where, however, the subsequent rites consist of the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, then in the event of the destruction of the northern half and so forth, the rite cannot be performed with the remaining portion because there is no other northern half and because the remainder has already been taken up for another disposal (*pratipatti*).
Nor does it entail the production of another oblation (*havis*), because that would not serve as the motive (*aprayojakatva*).
Rather, the rite is completed with clarified butter (*ājya*).
Regarding the rule stated for the destruction of a substance that has already been mentioned, it applies merely by virtue of the requirement for a substance.

However, according to the view of the ritualists (*yājñika*), this is absolutely necessary based on the statement of Āpastamba: "If [the substance] is to be offered, one should condense the remainder with clarified butter (*ājya*).
Since this rule applies without distinction, it pertains specifically to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in accordance with the requirement.

Therefore, due to the absence of any hope of abandoning [the primary], there is indeed the elision of "idam" and so forth; and this is stated by the proponent of the latter half [of the verse] regarding the prescription of multiple realizations as a subordinate element (*śeṣatvena*) in the case of multiple realizations.

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices (2074), regarding the injunctions for the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Cāturmāsya, and so forth, it should be understood that even if a portion of the remnant is destroyed, the entire disposal (*pratipatti*) is accomplished by means of the remaining parts alone. Maṇḍana [says]: "But there is no performance of the rites with the remnant when the remnant is destroyed."

Śaṅkara: "Thus, when there is the destruction of what remains (śeṣavat), there is the omission of the remaining rites. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, the Āgneya and other offerings, taken together, have a single collective result."
The principle of the Tantra [is as follows]:
