Bhāṣya 11.1.2.14–4. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, even if there is an injunction regarding the *parṇa*-leaf nature of vessels such as the *juhū*, there is no contradiction with the injunction that vessels such as the *ulūkhala* and *ulvala* must be made from a single piece of wood.
Su. p. 1062. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, the procedure is Vedic.

Bhāṣya 7.4.1.1: Place, time, occasion, fruit, and purificatory acts (saṃskāra), when heard in proximity to an injunction within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites, do not cause a division of the ritual action (*karmabheda*).

Vi. 2.3.13: A sentence such as that concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa prescribes the performance of the principal rite together with its subsidiaries only when it is accompanied by all means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), beginning from Śruti and extending to Smṛti and established practice (*ācāra*).

Su. p. 1186: There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the collection of fruits, restrictive rules, and logical principles connected with the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites to the Saurya and similar sacrifices.
Bhāṣya 8.1.12.20–22: The modified *dadhi* vessel and so forth are prescribed for the *āghāna* (fire-consecration) for the purpose of sacrifices such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Vi. 3.1.12: Among the ritualists, there is a well-known consensus that the *anvādhāna* and other rites constitute the first constituent act (*prathamapadārtha*) at the commencement of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Bhaṭṭa 9.1.11, p. 67: Even when the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is repeated, the *ārambhaṇīyā* (commencement offering) is to be performed only once at the beginning.

Bhāṣya 9.1.10.34–35: There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) to the Saurya and other rites for which no procedure has been specifically prescribed.

Bhāṣya 7.4.1.1: The New and Full Moon sacrifice (*darśapūrṇamāseṣṭi*) is the primary archetype (*mūlaprakṛti*). Vi. 8.1.3, Section 2: Only after the New and Full Moon sacrifices do the modifications of the Soma sacrifice, such as the Gava and others, become one-day rites (*ekāha*); they do not occur prior to that.
Bhāṣya 5.4.1.26: After the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Jyotiṣṭoma is to be performed.
4.3.15.13: Regarding that which is praised as being for the benefit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, a prohibition is enjoined against it;
likewise, wherever there is a connection with the purpose of a ritual act, falsehood must be avoided in all such cases.

Vārttika 3.4.4.13, p. 941: In the ritual of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the sacrificer (yajamāna) should perform only the act of relinquishment (utsarga); the performer of the remainder (śeṣa) is someone else, such as the Adhvaryu priest.
Bhaṣya 3.7.8.18–20: Because most sacrifices generally occur at the time of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

Bhaṣya 8.2.1.2, p. 1528: The sacrificial grass (barhis) belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa is not the archetype (prakṛti) for the sacrificial post-hole (yūpavaṭa), the wooden splinter (svaru), or the sacrificial grass used elsewhere.

And there is no extension of the ritual property (*dharmātideśa*). Vi. 7.2.7. Regarding the two mantras for touching the sacrificial oblation (*havirabhimarśana*) belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *cāhuta* and *aupabhṛta* mantras in the case of the Saurya and other sacrifices. Bhā. 8.2.1.5.26. There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the Agni-oblation material belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa by way of option (*vikalpena*) to the rice-porridge (*caru*) for Sūrya.

Bhāṣya 8.2.1.5.26: There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure ending with the injunction for the *Āgneya* [offering] belonging to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* into those modified forms (*vikṛti*) that have a single deity and *oṣadhi* as their substance; however, in the case of those with two deities, there is an extension of the *Agnīṣomīya* and similar offerings, and in the case of those having clarified butter (*ājya*) as their substance, there is an extension of the *Upāṃśuyāja*.

Vivaraṇa 8.1.16: There is no extension of the properties (*dharma*) from the clarified butter named after the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* into the *ājya* used for the *parvan* [joint] of the animal sacrifice, because it is not known [as such].
Bhāṣya 7.3.7.18: In the *iḍā-nigada* belonging to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word "sacrificer" (*yajñapati*) in the modified form.
1|1|2|13|40: There is no modification (*ūha*) of the word "owner" (*svāmin*) in the *nirvāpa* mantra belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices when applied to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
1|1|2|146: There is no modification of the non-controversial words in the *nirvāpa* mantra belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices when applied to a modified sacrifice.
9|1|2|116–37: There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the *parvan-homas* belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices to a modified sacrifice.
9|1|2|185–96. There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the *godohana* vessel and other such items intended for human purposes within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices to the *saurya* and similar rites;
for it is only the subsidiary elements of the sacrifice (*ṛtvaṅga*) that are extended.
Vi. 8|1|14. In the mantra for grinding belonging to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, there is an adaptation (*ūha*) of the word "grain" (*dhānya*) when grinding other substances, such as: "Thou art meatless."

Bhāṣya 9.1.2.38–39, Section 2: Regarding the *praṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire) belonging to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, there is an extension (*atideśa*) to the *praṇayana* occurring in the *Cāturmāsya* (where it is said, "they carry it forth twice"), and not that of the *Saumika*. This is the view of the Bhāṣya. The view of the Vārttika, however, is that it is neither the *Dārśika* nor the *Saumika*, but rather something entirely new (*apūrva*).
And this *praṇayana* occurs specifically on the middle *parvan*.
7|2|23-25: The animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya-paśu) is a modification of the sāṃnāyya belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
therein also, it is a modification of milk, not a modification of curd.
8|2|1|15-18: Modifications of the sāṃnāyya belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa and modifications [of the animal sacrifice] by way of the agnīṣomīya-paśu must take place after the Soma sacrifice.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Cāturmāsya, and other sacrifices, the primary rites such as the Āgneya and others share the same place, time, and agent.
Bhāṣya 1.1.2.12; Darśapūrṇamāsa—Darśapūrṇamāsa-Cāturmāsya etc., 2075; the Darśapūrṇamāsa principle.

In the Cāturmāsya and other sacrifices, there is repetition by name in accordance with the application of that specific term. This is the section concerning the *iṣṭi* and *rājasūya*. (Sūtras 11.2.12–18): There is a rule regarding the Upāṃśuyāja being performed with deities distinct from those included within the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

Bhāṣya 10.8.16.49–50: The extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual details (*dharma*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) to modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni.
Bhāṣya 8.1.12: There is no extension of the ritual details of the New and Full Moon sacrifices to the Soma sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 8.1.13–10: The principle (*nyāya*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

The Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Jyotiṣṭoma are for all desired objects (sarvakāmya). [Sūtra 11: "The attainment of all desires [is achieved] by means of those sacrifices not intended for specific desires, because of the context.

Commentary: This is recorded in the sacred tradition: "Other sacrifices are performed for a single desire; the Darśapūrṇamāsa are for all [desires]; other seasonal sacrifices (ṛtu) are performed for a single desire; the Jyotiṣṭoma is for all [desires]."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this a restatement (*anuvāda*) together with the desires for the subsidiaries (*aṅgakāma*) and the desires for the subsidiaries of the subsidiaries (*aṅgāṅgakāma*), or is it an injunction (*vidhi*)? What is the prima facie view? It is a restatement;
that which constitutes the "desire for all results" (*sārvakāmya*) is here being restated.
Together with those desiring the limbs (*aṅgakāma*) and those desiring the minor limbs (*aṅgāṅgakāma*).
For there exist both those desiring the limbs and those desiring the minor limbs, such as:
"One who desires cattle should construct the altar (*vedi*) with soil from a mine; one who desires stability [should construct it] with soil from a bathing place," and so forth.

Likewise, [there is the text]: "If one should desire that Parjanya should rain, he should erect the Sadas shed low"; we consider it logical that this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of the desired result, since it is already enjoined by the rule: "The Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed] for all [desires]. [Durga says: Because there is no injunctive statement such as "The Jyotiṣṭoma [is for] all," there is an absence of its being a means [to those results].
Therefore, disregarding the desire for the constituent parts (*aṅga*), the statement "the Jyotiṣṭoma [is] from all [these]" is a restatement (*anuvāda*);
or rather, it is an injunction of the result (*phalopadeśa*), because of its connection with the word denoting the primary rite (*pradhāna*).
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: Or it is an injunction of the result.
Why? Because the connection with the fruit occurs through the word denoting the principal [rite].
For instance, it is said: "The Darśapūrṇamāsa for all [desires]," and "The Jyotiṣṭoma for all [desires].
And by the mention of the principal, the possession of all fruits is enjoined for that principal rite.
Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda).
If, however, it were to depend upon both the desires for the subsidiaries (aṅga) and the desires for the sub-subsidiaries (aṅgāṅga), then the word would be used in a figurative sense (lakṣaṇā);
and direct denotation (śruti) is more authoritative than figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

Therefore, the injunction is by means of the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance). [Dvādaśādhyāya-bhāṣya: Only the primary act has its fruit directly heard in the text; the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the subsidiary-of-subsidiaries (*aṅgāṅga*) would have to be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Moreover, direct Vedic statement (śruti) is more authoritative.
Nor is this [passage] a subordinate part (śeṣa) of anything else, such that it would be restated as a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).

Therefore, in this case, the injunction arises from one of the following: the originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi), the injunction of performance (prayoga-vidhi), the explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), or the bringing together of these elements.
Does "all desires" mean all those desires achievable through ritual action (*karma*), or does it mean whatever desires there may be?

Since no distinction is made, others hold that it means "whatever desires there are. If it is argued that other seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*) accomplish a single result, whereas this sacrifice accomplishes all—meaning "all" refers to the results pertaining to the season—it follows that this is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the *Jyotiṣṭoma* being enjoined as having all results; therefore, there is no authoritative proof for its attainment of all results. To this, it is replied:
In cases such as "desirous of gold" (*hiraṇyakāmaḥ*) or "desirous of a son" (*putrakāmaḥ*), it is precisely in those instances that [the object] possesses the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*).
Why? Because they employ the word "desire" (*kāma*) in reference to those [objects], and not elsewhere;
for something becomes dear only when preceded by the act of perceiving it.
Furthermore, in that case, the result would never occur for all [of them] together;
therefore, there is no application of desire (*kāma*) therein.
Consequently, only those words expressing desire (*kāma*) that are uttered in the injunction (*vidhi*) are to be supplied (*anuṣajyante*).
Śā [explains]: "The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are for the sake of all desires"—this is a restatement (anuvāda), and the Darśapūrṇamāsa is the primary purpose.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"Even when [the term] functions in the sense of a mere connection, there is no fault."
And since the sense of "being for that purpose" (tādarthya) is expressed by the dative case, there is no proof for it from any other source.
The primary acts may have the fruit as their purpose because the subsidiary acts assist them;
however, the primary act can never, in any way, be subordinate to the fruit of the subsidiary acts.
Therefore, when all desired objects are attained, [the result] is enjoined;
and the word for the injunction and the efficient force (bhāvanā) must be brought in because of their necessity to be performed.
Alternatively, the injunction and the efficient force are established through the originative injunctions.
Here, only the connection with the fruit is enjoined by depending [on the sacrifice].
Therefore, it is an injunction of the fruit.
As for Soma: the connection is established because there is an objection that, as in the previous case, here too there cannot be the state of having multiple fruits.
Vi— "Is the [injunction] 'the Darśa and others [are performed] for the sake of all desires' a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the fruit, or is it an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the fruit?
Since desire is mentioned in connection with the primary and subsidiary limbs, it is restated because there is no separate injunction [for it].
[This occurs] by relying on the productive injunction (*utpatti-codanā*) which establishes the existence of the injunction and the mental realization (*bhāvanā*)."
Through the understanding of the connection with the fruit, there must indeed be an injunction regarding the fruit.

The Bhaṭṭa [school] holds: "For each individual desire, other sacrificial rites are prescribed; the Jyotiṣṭoma is for all desires; for each individual desire, other sacrificial rites are prescribed; the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are for all [desires]. By these two scriptural statements, through the principle of the distinctness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), [the rites] have all fruits as their purpose; however, this does not mean that even the desires for specific qualities mentioned within those respective contexts are to be employed by means of the Darśa and others.

In this case, it is generally a restatement (*anuvāda*) because it would otherwise be purposeless; for if one were to accept it as figurative (*aupacārika*), there would be no evidence for its being intended for that purpose.

Therefore, precisely because it refers to something not already established, it is an injunction (*vidhi*). This applies to what is heard within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
By supplying words expressive of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is an application [of the sacrifice] for the sake of all fruits.

Nor is the injunction indicating heaven as the purpose rendered useless in this way; for, according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the assumption of the *Mitra* and *Viśvajit* sacrifices is justified by the fact that it results in an exalted prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
And here, all fruits are to be understood without distinction.

However, because the word "nyāya" occurring in an *arthavāda* signifies similarity, the term "all" (*sarva*) in each respective instance refers merely to the fruits produced immediately following a *Soma* sacrifice similar to the Jyotiṣṭoma or the Darśapūrṇamāsa, as the case may be; for it is logically consistent that an *arthavāda* serves the purpose of praise. For this very reason, since the word "all" is a pronoun, it cannot be restricted solely to Vedic fruits, because even Vedic things were not previously established [in the mind], and furthermore, there would be no distinction against worldly things that might somehow have been established.
However, those things such as the horns of a hare which are not established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are not included by the word "all" (sarva).

As for the claim made in the *Tantrasāra*, the *Tantraratna*, and other works—that even omniscience characterized by the direct knowledge of supersensuous objects is not included under the term "all" (*sarva*) because no such means [of knowing all] is observed anywhere in either worldly experience or the Vedas—that is incorrect. For the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra] states: "Through the practice of throwing light [upon objects], there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the distant; through *saṃyama* on the sun, there is knowledge of the worlds"; and so forth. Furthermore, [the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* says]: "By joining the eyes with the sun, and the sun itself with the eye, while meditating upon Me there with the mind, one sees the universe with the eye."

In the Purāṇas and other texts, it is stated that the specific practice of *yogadhāraṇā* (yogic concentration) is the means for achieving mere supernatural powers (*siddhi*). This is required because, even if [the Lord] were not the unsurpassed omniscient one, the perception of the worlds and so forth would still be possible [for him].

Nor does this imply that the Smṛtis must be rooted in the Veda simply because mantras and the like could otherwise be considered omniscient; for if the eightfold means of attaining heaven are not established by any other means of knowledge, they cannot be known even through yoga. As Maṇḍana says: "Let there be an injunction for all desires."
Śaṅkara says: "The Darśa and other rites are for the sake of all desired objects.
The term *darśapūrṇamāsa* refers to two groups established by two distinct *vidvadvākya* (injunctions of the knower) and possesses a well-known meaning; it is not dependent upon its own name.
(And the *vidvadvākya* is: 'He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Darśapūrṇamāsa,' etc.)"

Mīmāṃsā: The term *darśapūrṇamāsa*—just as the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* is the delimiting factor for the group of eight sacrifices (*yāga-aṣṭaka*), so too, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the term *jyotiṣṭoma* is the delimiting factor for the group of sacrifices characterized by the *triṣṭad* and other *stomas*.
Bhāṭṭa 4.4.12:
There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *puroḍāśa* offerings of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* to the *surā* cups in the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 8.2.12–15: The context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices constitutes a "great context" (*mahāprakaraṇa*) that is not delimited by a "sandwiching" (*asaṃdaṃśa*).
Bālakrīḍā, p. 9: By virtue of the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, mantras such as the *anumantraṇa* for Pūṣan and others are displaced [from their original position].
For a mantra is a sanctificatory act (*saṃskāraka*); since it would be purposeless if there were no object to be sanctified, its application there [in the original context] is not desired.

In the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), with reference to the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāgau*), it is stated: "One does not perform them at the animal sacrifice, nor at the Soma sacrifice.
Here, the sentence "nor at the Soma sacrifice" is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the statement "one does not perform them at the animal sacrifice."

Bhāṣya 10.8.2.5: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the statement "He chooses the Āryeya" refers to the proclamation of the sacrificer's lineage name (*pravara*), and not to a specific Ṛgvedic verse.

Saṃkarṣa 3.4.1: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the scriptural passage regarding the *nivīta*—"The *nivīta* is for men"—is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the rule concerning the *upavīta*, and not an independent injunction.

Ke. 3.4.12–19: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, within the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, it is heard: "That which is cut at the top is for the gods; that which is in the middle is for men; that which has roots is for the ancestors."
In this context, the phrase "the two teeth" (*paśū*) is a reference (*anuvāda*), while the phrase "that which is between" is a restatement for the sake of praising that which has a root;
however, the state of having a root (*samūlatva*) is what is actually enjoined.

(Vi. 3.4.7). In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantras dedicated to Pūṣan and others, even though they are not part of the *asaṃdaṃśa* group, do not interrupt the context from the outset.

Vārttika 3.1.121, p. 733: In the section on the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the connection with time is enjoined by the statement "One should sacrifice on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyāṃ yajeta*), etc.; it does not enjoin a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*). Vi. 2.3.13: In the section on the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the statement "He pours the remainder into the Sviṣṭakṛt [offering]" (*śeṣaṃ sviṣṭakṛte samavayati*) is an injunction regarding the connection with a consecration (*saṃskāra*); it does not enjoin a separate ritual act. Vi. 2.3.12: The passage concerning the *nīvīta* and *prācīnāvīta* mentioned in the section on the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the injunction for the *upavīta*.

The section concerning the *nīvī* (3.4.9): In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the injunction regarding the wearing of the sacred thread around the neck (*anutat-avaniṣeva*) is prescribed as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).

The section concerning the mantra "mayi dakṣakratu" (3.4.8): In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the recitation of the mantra "mayi dakṣakratu" is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person who is engaged in the sacrifice and is being made aware [of it]; it is not merely for the purpose of the person (*kevalapuruṣārtha*).

The section concerning that which is being produced (jajñamyamānādhikaraṇa). Bhāṣya 3.4.6, 14–16. In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard: "That which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti," and so forth; this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the injunction: "It should be cooked without burning. The section concerning the tooth of a bird (pakṣidantādhikaraṇa).

11. Regarding that which is heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, [and] regarding that which is heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, 2077 [it pertains to] the procedure for the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
The prohibition against threatening (*avagoraṇa*) is extracted from its context because it serves solely the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). (JS 3.4.16–17).

The offering to Pūṣan (*pauṣṇeya*) mentioned in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is to be placed in a sacrifice where there is only one deity, not in one with two deities. (Bhāṣya 3.1.129–46).
The offering to Pūṣan mentioned in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is to be placed specifically in the *caru* offering dedicated to Pūṣan.

3|1|134–38. The displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *pauṣṇeya* offering—heard in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—to the sacrifice dedicated to Pūṣan. This is the section concerning the search for Pūṣan (3|1|134).

The prohibition against conversation with a *malladagdha*—heard in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—is displaced from that context because it serves solely as a human purpose (*kevalapuruṣārtha*).
The Section on Concordance (Saṃvādādhikaraṇa) | 3.4.18–19. There is no displacement elsewhere of the *jāghanī* (tail) mentioned in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
This concludes the chapter on the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.

The *jāghanī-nyāya* (the logic of the tail): 3.1.20–23. In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is stated: "Having concluded the *Paurṇamāsī*, he performs the *Vaiśvadeva* offering. This [offering] removes only the defects of the *Paurṇamāsī*, but not the defects of both the *Darśa* and *Pūrṇamāsa*.
Vi. 4.3.14. In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, the preparation of the altar (*vedi*) is prescribed as being for the purpose of receiving the oblation (*havis*).

Bhāṣya 12.1.12.139: Although the *prayāja* offerings are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), their intermediate context (*avāntarakaraṇa*) will be established in the section concerning transgression (*atikramādhikaraṇa*).
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 764: The *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites have the New and Full Moon sacrifices as their archetype (*prakṛti*).
Bhāṣya.
The commencement and completion of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices] occur every month. (Vārttika 2.4.13, p.
627). The Pavamāneṣṭi consecration is not employed for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, but rather for the sake of the fire (Agni).
(Bhāṣya 3.6.16–17). It has been stated (6.3.12) that in the lifelong performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the procedure consisting of the Prayāja offerings and so forth applies.
Or rather:

even if the moon rises after the pouring out [of the oblation] but before the subsequent rites beginning with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the performance of these should take place once it has risen.
Bhāṣya 6.5.12–16: Even when the New and Full Moon sacrifices are performed on the following day, the performance must take place during the day itself.
The sacrifice must also be performed on the following day, specifically at night.

This is because in the Śruti text, "Therefore, the gods are worshipped on nights similar [to others], on the new moon (amāvāsyā), and on the full moon (paurṇamāsī)," the use of the genitive case in the word *rātrīṇām* ("of nights")—as in the sentence "Among Brāhmaṇas, Yajñadatta is handsome"—indicates that the full moon and other such occasions possess the nature of being "nights.
Furthermore, in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa-anuvāka*, it is stated that the terms *paurṇamāsī* and *darśa* are names for nights.

This being the case, the sacrifice must be performed on the very day [of the full moon]; for the scripture states, "The morning libation cup," and as explained by the elder Śātātapa: "That which is the fourth part of the *parvan* day and the first part of the *pratipad* is the specific time for sacrifice, designated as 'morning' by the wise. This is because the concluding statement, "the following day," is based on the scriptural text.

Furthermore, the term *darśa* (new moon), which denotes the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), is of no use here. In this context, the expression "of the nights" (*rātrīṇām*) is appropriate because it intends to include the possibility that the commencement might sometimes occur even at night.

Moreover, the word *rātri* is seen to refer to a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*) in such instances as "one consecrated for twelve nights (*dvādaśarātrī*) should offer the *bhūti-vanīta*," and "impurity lasts ten nights (*daśarātrāśaucam*). As for the fact that the *Bhāṣya* cites only days (*ahaḥ*) in Vedic texts—such as "on an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) the divine rites [are performed]," and "those two days are indeed pure and fit for sacrifice; on the following day, one sacrifices to the deities"—that is used here as the supporting reason.

The word "night" (*rātri*), as used by the Sūtrakāra here, is established otherwise—primarily referring to the *ahorātra* (the full cycle of day and night)—due to the context of its own system and so forth; for even in the word "day" (*ahaḥ*), both [day and night] are possible. (Saṃkarṣa. 3.1.3). Indeed, the *sāṅkapraśāya* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. (Bhāṣya 3.1.12–13). Among the modifications of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is the archetype (*prakṛti*), because it shares the commonality of having a living being (*prāṇin*) as its substance.

In the *Saṃkarṣa* (2.4.4), there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the sacrificer’s mantras to the modifications (*vikāra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Regarding the modifications of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—excluding the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*)—all three [mantras, etc. are obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction). However, for the optional sacrifices, because the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is prescribed by specific statements such as "according to the color, indeed" (*yathāvarṇaṃ vai*) regarding the primary element denoted by the word "optional," the pitch (*svara*) is appropriate only at the eighth measure (*mātra*). (Su. pṛ. 1.78). Furthermore, even in the modification of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, [the mantra] is similar to the *śāmidhenī* verses. (Vi. 6.6.6).
In the modified forms (*vikṛti*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices when they possess specific conditions (*sopādhi*), there is a re-performance of the *ārambhaṇīyā* rite.
This is the section concerning the *ārambhaṇīyā*. Bha.

The *darśapūrṇamāsa* injunctions extend to the *āgneya* and *aindrāgna* [offerings] in the *āgneya-mahākalpa*, the *āgneya-paśu* sacrifice, the *aiṣṭika-dravya-devatva* (the deity and substance of the sacrifice), the eleven *prayāja* offerings, the *prayājatva* (the nature of being a *prayāja*), the *sruca-sammārjana* (cleansing of the ladles) and other such *āvaraṇa* (accessory) rites, the "approaching the animal" (*upaśumantikam*), and the "touching" (*ālambha*) as in "he touches the animal. The term *darśapūrṇamāsa* is used in common parlance for the *daśapeya* (the ten-day Soma sacrifice); this is the *daśapeya-nyāya*.
"Therefore, they enter [the water] as before," so it is seen in the case of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).
Therefore, it is a common ritual procedure (*tantra*). And this applies to the subsequent consecrations (*dīkṣā*) as well.
In the Siddhānta, there is another reason:

because the initiations (*dīkṣā*) for the subsequent Daśapeya are seen to be distinct from the initiations of the Abhiṣecanīya, there is no common procedure (*tantra*) between the two. Thus it is said: "They should extend the initiations of the Abhiṣecanīya so that the Daśapeya is completed on the tenth day," and "He initiates immediately; he purchases the Soma immediately" (here, the Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra reads: "They extend the initiations of the Abhiṣecanīya so that the Daśapeya will take place when ten nights remain of the year"). Therefore, there is no common procedure.
[The two rites are] identical because of the commonality of time.
As for the statement in Sūtra 58, "That which has the same number of recitations is like that," he says that this is not so.
In whichever year the Abhiṣecanīya [rite] is performed, in the year immediately following it, the Daśapeya is performed in that very same season.

And likewise, because of the commonality of time— that is, because of the similarity of the time characterized by the *kratu*— between the *Abhiṣecanīya* and the *Daśapeya*, the principle of the *Daśapeya* applies here in the statement, "This sacrifice is indeed the same. This is the principle of the *Daśapeya*.

In that regard, if "ten" were prescribed when there was an unrestricted possibility of "a hundred," then the term "each one" would be untenable; or, if "each one" and so forth were prescribed, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, since multiple cups (*camasa*) would be obtained for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterers, and since [the number] is possible as a restatement (*anuvāda*), the act of consuming would already be established by the preceding statement ("A hundred Brahmins consume the Soma"), making the word "cup" redundant; moreover, a qualified [phrase] would split the sentence.

Nor is it possible for the statement "ten for each one" to be a mere restatement (anuvāda), because even when a hundred [cups] are taken for the purpose of preparing the *camasa* vessels, they would apply in their entirety to each individual cup.

For if it were for the purpose of purifying the agent, then—as in the case of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)—there would be a requirement for distribution, and by the principle that "it should be equal," the result would be "ten for each one.
In that case, even if there were an injunction, it would be a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Alternatively, even in the case of many [vessels], ten consumers each obtain [their share].

Or, in the case of a single *camasa* (cup), ten shares are obtained for ten [consumers]; thus, by way of groups of ten, the hundred [shares] are established. This is the subject matter of the tenth chapter; it is the investigation of the meaning of the tenth chapter.

In the case of the statement "the altar has been prepared," there is a sublation of the *uddhāna* (uprooting) acts that produce [the altar], due to the loss of the means (*dvāralopa*) consisting in the completion of the altar. In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* berries, there is a sublation of the *avasthāpana* (placing) act, due to the loss of the means consisting in the act of husking (*vitubīkaraṇa*). In the second chapter (*pāda*), the brief mention of the loss of the means is expanded upon through numerous examples.
In the third [case], the subverting reason is the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*).
For example, in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), the purchase of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij-parikraya*) is the effect of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of cows, horses, and so forth.
Likewise, in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) consisting of the *bhūtāgni* one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), that same [purchase] is the effect of the sacrificial fee consisting of a cow (*dhenu*).
Consequently, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) such as cows, horses, and so forth, which have been obtained for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by means of the *veṇvā* [text], are set aside.

Regarding the fourth [chapter]: the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) prescribed for the *nakṣatreṣṭi* are combined with those [offerings] brought by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) through non-extension (*anātideśa*); such is the principle of combination (*samuccaya*). Regarding the fifth [chapter]: the *ṣoḍaśin* cup belongs to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

The discussion concerning the *graha* vessels and so forth occurs in the sixth [chapter], based on the contingency of sublation (*bādha*), such as the rule that "it should be drawn from the *āmrayaṇa* vessel" itself. The discussion concerning the *sāman* chants occurs in the sixth [chapter], based on the contingency of sublation, such as "the *sāman* is not to be sung for you.
In the seventh [chapter], regarding the animal sacrifices (*paśvagni*), there is no differentiation of the oblation (*havis*) for each individual limb.
Investigation of the subject matter of the tenth chapter:
[The conclusion is] that it must be produced exactly according to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Having thus understood what has been obtained in a general sense, one subsequently examines the individual items according to their own nature, thinking, "How was assistance rendered by this? How was assistance rendered by that?

In that regard, having observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) that threshing (*avaghāta*) provides assistance by means of its visible purpose, one considers that in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces, since such a state of affairs is impossible, there must be a sublation (*bādha*) of the previously arisen general knowledge.

Thus, even in the case of a substitution (*pratyāmnāna*), when ritual items (*padārtha*) are obtained through their functions, the external function of placing the oblation (*havirāsādana*) is first established [by the archetype]. When there is a requirement for its means, before the *kuśa* grass is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), the *śara* grass is prescribed by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavākya*) for that very purpose; therefore, the *śara* grass sets aside the *kuśa* grass and others. Similarly, in the case of a prohibition, there is a displacement (*utkālana*) of the general form of the *codaka* due to the specific scope of the object, as in: "He does not choose the *āpya* [priests]."

Therefore, since the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is established for other [elements] that are not sublated, prescribed as alternatives, or prohibited, the sublation (*bādha*) is proven. Regarding this, some declare: "Even though its purpose is lost, acts such as the *hanana* (striking) possess the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) in cases such as the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces; whether it exists or does not exist, such is their performance."
The *tantra* is established for the sake of accomplishing the slaughter at the village; otherwise, it would not be established.
When the attainment [of the result] is being obstructed, it would be as in the case of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth.
For the third [case] is indeed because [the rule] has not been reached, whereas the tenth is because it has been reached; such is the established position.

In that regard, if the *codaka* (the rule of extension) itself does not apply to those whose purposes have been sublated, then, since there is no reaching [of those elements] such as the *dhāyyās*, the expression "reaching what has already been reached" is stated because their purpose is not yet fulfilled; however, that is incorrect.
In this case as well, [the application of the rule] would be purposeless.

For it is not intended that the acquisition of the ritual object follows merely from the acquisition of an assistance common to all objects; rather, since the injunction of the ritual objects is desired by the scripture itself, and since those objects exist in a general form, if this were extended to each one individually, the scriptural injunction of threshing (*avaghāta*) would become purposeless in its non-performance.
Therefore, there is no other alternative than either the non-extension of that [threshing] or its performance.
Granted that it may be useless; however, one cannot postulate an unknown object on this basis alone. For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here to produce any beneficial result.
But surely, the very fact of not knowing [the object] and thus not having acquired it is itself the means of valid cognition?

If it is argued that this cannot belong to one who provides no assistance, and since there is no scriptural statement regarding the slayer being like the original material (prakṛti), and thus no other way for him to provide assistance,
therefore [the result accrues to] the performer—
then that is answered by what follows.

Because it would be like the original form (*prakṛti*), the scriptural injunction prescribing the use of *kṛṣṇala* seeds for the subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the *vaimṛdha* offering would become invalid.

Furthermore, if there were a sublation of what has been obtained, why would there be no permission for the *kuśa* grasses, which are the means of the sacrifice and are not [otherwise] permitted? If this is asked, the answer is no; for even by that, there is no loss of the status of being a subsidiary part.
They...
The discussion of the subject matter of the tenth chapter [concerns what] is sublated.
That performance which is sublated has not [previously] been established; thus, because it was not established, there is no impossibility [of its being sublated].
Therefore, what has been stated is indeed logical:
that in whatever [context] the *codaka* (the general rule) applies, it ought not to exclude anything.
Truly, this is its very nature.
But that inherent nature is obstructed by a powerful cause (3.6.12). [The reading] "na codanārthakāsyānt" (3.6.18) is not correct;
in fact, the reading of the sūtra is "na tulyatvāt" (7) and "codanārthakāsyānt" (8).
This very point under discussion was also previously stated as "codanārthakāsyānt" alone.

Therefore, it should be understood that even the suspicion that "the printing here might otherwise be due to the error of the scribe" is refuted by the very nature [of the case], which limits [the occurrence] to only a few instances.

And although, in this case, falsity cannot be perceived by one who knows the general rules of logic through a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*), nevertheless, it is indicated by another cognition that serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*).

For even that substance was mentioned merely as an illustration: "That cognition which has a defective instrument (*karaṇa*) and in which there is the conviction that it is false—that is a non-valid cognition" (Bhāṣya on 1.1.5, Vṛtti-text, p. 28).

In that context, since [defective instruments] are possible among Vedic cognitions, only the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) serves as the defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), and not the knowledge of a defect in the instrument, because such is impossible [in the case of the Veda].

And he says: "As for the second defining characteristic mentioned—the knowledge of a defect in the instrument—that pertains to worldly matters and is therefore not possible in the Veda; hence it was not set forth."

But how, then, is false knowledge produced by that which is not defective? For false knowledge is not produced by a sublater; rather, once it has arisen, the [Vedic statement] "That thou art" makes known its falsity. Its production, however, is due solely to a defect in the cause.
That is indeed true.
For even here, a defect in the cause certainly exists.

Although no inherent defect whatsoever exists within the Veda, which is not of human origin, nevertheless, due to the listener’s intellect being clouded by general ignorance and because fallacious arguments (nyāyābhāsa) proliferate without the identification of any sublation, false knowledge arises.
It is for this very reason that the Mīmāṃsā system is purposeful for the sake of correctly identifying right reasoning.

Furthermore, this defect cannot be determined prior to the sublation [of the cognition], just as one cannot determine [the nature of] death before it occurs; thus, it has been stated that falsity is to be characterized by a sublater (*bādhaka*).
This is entirely consistent.
Therefore, it is established that a cognition which is certain in the form "it is thus" is declared to be false by means of another cause.

"There is no injunction for those [elements] that have been elided," and "The *codaka* does not enjoin what has been elided or what serves no purpose in the archetype," because of such statements in the *Bhāṣya* (Bhāṣya on 10.1.12).
"Moreover..."

And because of the sūtra, "But it would be a supplementary statement" (10.8.14), the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) applies simultaneously to those auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) which are not prohibited by explicit scriptural statements or by the destruction of the purpose.
Thus, in cases such as the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces, acts like killing are not auxiliary; likewise, the action [of striking] is excluded.
However, the accomplishment of the restriction [is achieved] through the restriction itself in its essential form.

In this regard, it might be argued: "Even if the act of killing (*hanti*) is not obtained in the case of *kṛṣṇala* grains for the sake of a visible purpose, nevertheless, why should it not be obtained for the sake of fulfilling the restrictive rule (*niyama*)?
That is not so, because that [purpose] is impossible in that case.
For it is thus conceived: "The rice grains, being produced by threshing itself, accomplish the *apūrva*.
But this is not possible here, and because [the result] is not the motivator (*prayojaka*).
Indeed, the requirement for the rule (*niyama*) is not the motivator for the threshing.
Since the essential form [of the action] is already established by its very purpose, it is merely a restrictive rule (niyama) that is prompted by that [purpose].

Therefore, although grinding is not prohibited in the case of *caru* offerings—since the status of being *caru* is not impaired even when the grain is ground—nevertheless, because there is no purpose [for it], the essential form of grinding is not established; and since [the performance] depends upon that [establishment], there is no performance prompted by the restrictive rule.

Furthermore, even if a purpose existed, because the prompting agent is absent, the grinding is set aside in the case of *caru* and similar offerings, just as the *puroḍāśa* pan and other implements are set aside.

By this, the sublation of the original restriction regarding the material substance—namely rice or barley—in the case of the *citriṣṭi* sacrifice with respect to the rice grains is explained. For it is said: "When the employment of the original material has been established, a restriction is here enjoined; however, the rice grains used here are merely worldly (laukika), not those belonging to the original archetype (*prakṛti*)."

For there is no scriptural injunction in the archetype stating, "one should sacrifice with an oblation consisting of *māṣa*," by virtue of which, through extended application (*atideśa*), even rice-grains (*taṇḍula*) would possess that same nature.
Regarding the sacrifice, the status of rice as the instrument (*karaṇa*) is heard in the text, "One should sacrifice with rice-grains.
And an instrument is that which lies within the scope of the agent's activity.
As stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka*: "Having taken up rice grains (*vrīhīn*), one should prepare the oblation (*havyam*) with them.

And their status as instruments (*karaṇatvam*) is possible because they serve as the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the sacrifice, just like the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which is distinguished by its production [from those grains]. Thus, the meaning of the scripture is: "Having taken up rice grains and having prepared the oblation with them, one should sacrifice.
And here, having restated "having prepared the oblation and should sacrifice," only the phrase "with rice grains" is enjoined.
This being the case, the status of the oblation (*havis*) in the context of rice grains is based on implied meaning (*ārthika*), not on direct scriptural statement (*śrauta*).
Furthermore, this is not possible in the case of rice grains.

For it has not been established that the preparation of the oblation must be accomplished by taking up its raw material (*prakṛti*); rather, since it is possible to perform it by taking up rice grains already established in common worldly usage, the rule "with rice" (*vrīhibhiḥ*) serves as a restriction.

Now, one might object: since even in the archetype (prakṛti) it is possible to perform the sacrifice by taking a purely worldly sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), how can the procurement of the oblation through the adoption of the archetype be established as the subject matter for investigation in the tenth chapter?

If this is argued, it is replied: "For the status of being a *puroḍāśa* is held to be something accomplished by the cooking of the oblation (*havis*). Its self-agency (*svayaṃkartṛkatā*) with respect to that cooking is what is enjoined.
Indeed, the oblation in the form of a *puroḍāśa* cannot be realized without cooking."

For that [cake] must indeed be prepared either from worldly materials or from its own constituent parts; although an unrestricted option might have resulted from the originative injunction—"one should sacrifice with a cake on eight potsherds"—since it would be possible in either way, nevertheless, because of the statement "he cooks it on potsherds," one does not take what has been offered by another. Thus, its being prepared by oneself alone is what is enjoined, and all this is established by the force of the originative injunction itself.

The *kapālas* (potsherds) are established by the original injunction (*utpattivākya*). Furthermore, baking (*śrapaṇa*) follows from their functional capacity; for since words such as "sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśa*) denote a specific baked substance—given that there is no status as a sacrificial cake for what has not been baked—the act of baking must be performed by the agent himself. As the venerable Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) has said: "Because of the statement 'he bakes on the potsherds,' he does not take [the cake] baked by another" (1.4.6.9, p. 341). By the force of this, the employment of the primary material (*prakṛti*) is obtained.

For otherwise, it would not be possible to cook it oneself. Thus, when the employment of the material as prescribed in the archetype has been established, there arises the expectation: "In what state and of what form should the material be employed? In response to this, by means of the word *vrīhi* (rice), which denotes a specific genus characterized by its husk, that [employment] is restricted, thereby excluding the states of flour and rice-grains, as well as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like.

However, if it were enjoined by this very scripture that "the oblation should be prepared by employing the archetype" and "it should be made with *vrīhi* grains," then there would be prolixity (*gaurava*).
Furthermore, if there were an alternative course available, the injunction "he cooks it in skull-pots" would be rendered purposeless, which is improper.
Therefore, wherever there is cooking, there the agent must perform it himself;
and wherever that is the case, there the requirement for the material prescribed in the archetype (prakṛti) is obtained.
And where that [cooking] occurs, there is the restriction to rice (*vrīhi*).

However, in the case of husked grains (*taṇḍula*), because the purpose of cooking is lost, it is discontinued. Once that has ceased, how could there be an application of the rule of self-performance (*svayaṃkartṛkatva*)? How much less the taking of the archetype (*prakṛtyupādāna*), and how much less the restriction to rice?
Thus, the restriction to rice (*vrīhi*) is not possible in their case.
[Objection: But surely, by virtue of the capacity for threshing (*avaghāta*), the original material would be employed even in the case of rice-grains (*taṇḍula*).
[Reply: No, he says.

The injunction "he threshes the rice" (*vrīhīn hanti*) does not prescribe threshing with reference to the rice for the sake of establishing that the act is to be performed by oneself, because [self-performance] is not otherwise unestablished; thus, the rice does not attain the status of being the *prakṛti* (the material substrate) such that self-performance could be enjoined as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of it—meaning "one should thresh oneself and not have another thresh. This is because the removal of the husk (*vitupīkaraṇa*) can also be accomplished by means of pounding with a mallet (*nalaniṣvanana*) and so forth. By this, the case of grinding (*peṣaṇa*) is also explained; for even without grinding, the rice grains, once softened, become powdered.
Such is the sequence:

first, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is enjoined; then, when its material is required in some way or another, it is procured by itself through the use of the primary substance (prakṛti) due to the injunction for baking (śrapaṇa); next, when there is a requirement for a specific primary substance, rice grains (vrīhi) are enjoined by the rule "one should sacrifice with rice," which excludes the immediately preceding primary substance (piṇḍī), excludes the even more remote husked grains (taṇḍula), and excludes the most remote wild rice (nīvāra) and so forth; finally, when there is a requirement as to how the sacrificial oblation is to be prepared, the injunctions for threshing, grinding, and so on are prescribed.

In the case of rice grains (*taṇḍula*), when the act of cooking (*śrapaṇa*) ceases due to the disappearance of its purpose, there follows a sequential cessation of the threshing (*avaghāta*) and other rites, as well as the rule regarding the procurement of the *śrīhi* (rice) which is their fundamental material cause; this is established by worldly practice.
However, with the exception of certain types such as *varaka* and others, [other grains] may be used.

But where there is a purpose for cooking even without a sacrificial cake (*apuroḍāśa*)—as in the case of *caru*, parched grains (*dhānā*), groats (*mantha*), parched barley-flakes (*lāja*), flattened grains (*pṛthuka*), barley-gruel (*yavāgū*), and so forth—there the rule regarding *vrīhi* certainly applies.

The purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as threshing and so forth—this subtle exposition can be discerned by those whose mental eyes have been refined through the study of the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika*, but not by those of gross vision. Regarding this, the authors of the *Vārttika* sing in verse: "If the cooking [of rice] were to cease because half of the grains has been removed..."
How can there be self-performance of the act of cooking once it has ceased?
How much less, then, could the material cause be dependent upon that [act]?
And how, in the absence of that [act], could there be the restriction regarding rice?

Thus, because the archetypal elements are set aside due to the disappearance of their purpose and so forth, there is the production of modified effects; and since the addition of elements such as the *āmana-homa* has been declared, the manner of performance was considered in the tenth [book].
Thus ends the fourth chapter, "The Determination of Ignorance," in the *Śrī Nyāyaratnamālā*.

By the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the tenth book, the nature of the *sāman* established for the two subsequent [verses] is that it performs its function—whether sixfold, whether archetypal (*prākṛta*) or non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*), and whether seen or unseen—precisely in its unmodified form.
Śābara Bhāṣya 9.2.9.
The logic of the prima facie view of the tenth book is: "The transfer (*atideśa*) of ritual elements occurs by way of their essential form (*svarūpeṇa*)."
*Soma*. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the tenth book:

"In the *saurya* sacrifice and others, because there is an expectancy regarding the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*), there is an extension of the auxiliary benefit (*upakārātideśa*). This established conclusion of the tenth book does not apply here.

8.3.6) The commencement of the ten-night sacrifice occurs in the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) beginning with the two-night sacrifice.
(Bhā.)
In the ten-night [sacrifice], during the ten-night [rite] (2092), in the Dākṣāyaṇayajña, it is indeed twice.
In the Dākṣāyaṇayajña, there is no falsehood (2093). The section concerning the Dākṣāyaṇayajña.
In the *Daśarātra* sacrifice, the piling (*cayana*) can be performed.
In the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*, it is well known as a subsidiary element (*guṇa*) that "one should not speak untruth" and "one should not eat meat.
Therefore, according to the principle of the section on verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), [these lead] to the fruit.

There is no optionality regarding these various [elements], because of the injunction for sacrifice; it is a distinct sacrifice. According to the principle, the *daśahotṛ* is the *haṃkāra*, and the *sāmidhenī* verses [are prescribed]. — *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa* 1.3.9.
The intermediate vows recited in the Dākṣāyaṇayajña and the injunction for the performance of the rite are without subordinate qualities;
there is a specific sequence, not an alternative one.
(Saṃkarṣa. 4.1.1)

And because of the observation of an indicative mark.

otherwise, one may also sacrifice for only fifteen years."
"For it is indeed here that she is accomplished.

for it is indeed here that she is truly accomplished."
If the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves belong to Dākṣāyaṇa, then the purpose of the thirty steps is as follows:
consequently, it is appropriate that there be an inclusion of those thirty steps for him.
For this reason also, it is not a separate ritual action.
Alternatively, the mention of the "thirty-day fullness" of the *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* indicates a distinction [between these rites and the Darśapūrṇamāsa].
For the thirty-year period pertaining to the Darśapūrṇamāsa cannot be fulfilled by means of another ritual action;
nor can there be an extension (*atideśa*) of that specific rule.
By this, there would be the prescription of this fifteen-year option for a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Nor does the fifteen-year option arise for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves on the grounds of being a "Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice," because there is no such connection.
Furthermore, [the statement] "there are two full-moon days and two new-moon days" would be untenable [if it referred to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*].
But from the qualities (guṇas) arises the bondage of conjunction.

Commentary: Regarding what was stated—that it is a different ritual because of the connection with a distinct conjunction—if the term *dākṣāyaṇa* could not be interpreted in any way as denoting the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), then it might be said that it is a different ritual.
However, it is indeed possible to denote the same sacrifice because of its connection with the quality of repetition (*āvṛtti*).
"Ayanam" refers to a turning or revolution.
These belong to Dakṣa, thus they are "Dākṣāḥ"; their revolution is "Dākṣāyaṇam. But who is Dakṣa? He is the energetic one.
Likewise, in the *Sāṃkhyaprasthāyīya* as well: "Prasthāna together" means a connection with a quality (*guṇa*).
This applies everywhere.

If it is possible to state a connection with a quality regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices], why is that very sacrifice, being perceived [therein], said to be something else? Or why should the context (*prakaraṇa*) be set aside?
Or rather—when there is a connection with origin and a prior relationship, a name becomes distinct.
However, [the passage] beginning with "Now this Jyotis" is not thus connected with origin, because there is no introductory context;
rather, since it is possible [to understand it] simply as possessing qualities based on the preceding rite, it does not constitute a distinction.
For it is on account of the statement of Dākṣāyaṇa being a distinct sentence and because of the well-known meaning of its constituent parts that "repetition" (abhyasta) is expressed.
And by means of that [repetition], the fruit is accomplished specifically by relying upon the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, due to the context.
Dakṣa is a sacrificer who is energetic and quick-acting; his priests are the *dākṣas*.
Their performance (*ayana*) is called *dākṣāyaṇa* because it is based on the sacrifice (*yajña*).

In the case of the *sāṃkāprasthāyīya* as well, it is so designated because the *sānnāyya* offering is carried out simultaneously (*sākam*) from the very cooking-pots (*kumbhī*) without removing it [from them].
Therefore, there is no sublation of the recognition of the original form (*prakṛta*).
The conclusion is not distinct.

Commentary: As for what was stated—that the sentence is completed with respect to the result, and that the performance of the sacrifice is enjoined for one desiring offspring and so forth—it is not so;
the completion [of the sentence] with respect to the result is indistinguishable [from its completion with respect to the injunction].

Those other statements which, having removed all doubt, establish a result for a quality—that is, those which culminate in declaring a fruit for a quality—such as "One desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curd," and so forth; this [present case] is not different from them.
For here too, a fruit is stated to arise from a quality.
How so? It is not connected in this way: "One desiring offspring should perform the sacrifice."
How, then, is it? It means that one who desires offspring should perform the *āvṛtti*.
And *āvṛtti* here refers to a connection with the repetition of the sacrifice;
it is the act of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) that is indicated, not the sacrifice itself.
Therefore, in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices under discussion, a fruit is stated as resulting from an accessory (guṇa), and another sacrifice is not enjoined.
This should be understood likewise in the case of the Sāṃkāsthāyīya and the Saṃkramaṇa.

Or rather—even if a fruit is not enjoined with reference to the ritual act itself—nevertheless, because of the relationship between the ritual act and its fruit, it constitutes a different ritual act (karmāntara).

Just as it was established in the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* that "the fruit [arises] from the action," so too in the case of the statement "but because of the inequality of the two sentences" (*atulyatvāt tu vākyayoḥ*), there arises a doubt as to whether the sentence culminates in a connection between a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) and a fruit. To resolve this, it is established that for the sake of supporting other words, the fruit results from the subordinate factor alone, not from the action. This being the position reached—namely, that [the *Dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice and others] are distinct actions—it is now stated in reply: [The response follows: "But because of the inequality of the two sentences... etc. [The full argument is provided here]. Thus, it is concluded that the fruit arises from the subordinate factor, not from the action. Therefore, [the *Dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice and others] are not distinct actions. This is the final conclusion.
"It might be so if it were a mere name; in that case, a quality would be enjoined there—namely, the undertaking of the fruit, its repetition, and the like—so [the opponent] thinks."

Soma: The connection [of this topic] follows from the conclusion that, just as in the passages concerning the spring season (*vasantādi*) and others, a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is to be enjoined here as well.

As for the purpose: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since it belongs to the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there would be a frequent performance of the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* and so forth—just like the *Saurya* sacrifice and others—and thus, by performing the *Dākṣāyaṇa* for fifteen years, the thirty-year performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices would be sublated.

According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, it is merely a modified performance (*guṇavikṛta-prayoga*) of that very same sacrifice, and there is no sublation of the thirty-year performance.
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: In the sentences concerning the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice and others, because of the connection [of a new result], it must be a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Vi— "That one who desires heaven should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña:
is this a distinct ritual act, or is it a subsidiary quality (*guṇa*) for the sake of accomplishing the stated result?"
However, because it is well-known from the section concerning the Ādākṣāyaṇayajña that this is a quality (guṇavidhi), there is a difference of ritual action here due to the name.
[Objection: A quality (*guṇa*) cannot indeed be designated by the first name [of the sacrifice] because of its non-arising and its being subsidiary.

[Bhaṭṭa’s response: Regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is revealed in scripture (*śruti*) that "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*," and likewise, "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *Sāṃkāsthāyīya*."

In this regard, since the quality denoted by terms such as *dākṣāyaṇa* is not well-known in common usage, it is understood—like the term *udbhid*—to be a name (*nāmadheya*). Consequently, a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) is enjoined either by way of a designation (*saṃjñā*) or through repetition (*abhyāsa*), because the connection with a fruit is already established by the force of the *sārvakāmya* injunction itself, and thus there is no intention to enjoin anything else. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the following is stated in reply.

Although the term *guṇa* (quality/attribute) is not well-known in common worldly usage, nevertheless, these [priests] belonging to Dakṣa the sacrificer are the *Dākṣas*, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The performance (*ayana*) consisting of their activity is the ritual application (*prayoga*) of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; this is understood from the etymology to refer to a repetition (*āvṛtti*), and from the etymology "that in which there is a simultaneous departure" (*saha prasthānaṃ yatra*), it is understood to refer to simultaneity (*sahatva*). Thus, rather than assuming an additional power, the conclusion is reached that it is a name.
Therefore, it is precisely a quality—consisting of both the previously unestablished repetition and the form of "one thousand"—that is enjoined with reference to a result.

When the question arises as to how many repetitions there are, the specific injunction "one should sacrifice on two full-moon days and two new-moon days" establishes that there are exactly two repetitions.

Furthermore, when the question arises as to with what the simultaneity (*sahatva*) of the primary acts occurs, the statement "one should carry this [offering] together with the *kumbhī* vessels" indicates that it is with the *kumbhī* vessels.
By this very statement, which prescribes the simultaneity of the introductory rite (*abhikramaṇa*), its basis is established even in the absence of an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).
In these cases, by virtue of the context, the New and Full Moon sacrifices themselves are the substrate.

Therefore, since there is no [new] name here and because it takes the form of a connection between a quality and a result—wherein there is no repetition—it constitutes a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

In reality, however, because of the traditional rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.3), which states that "the *n* following a word ending in a *c*-suffix [or a word with a *c*-suffix as its cause] becomes *ṇ* when it is a name (*saṃjñā*), but not when there is an intervention by *g*—as in *duṇasaḥ* or *ṛgayanam*"—it follows that *dākṣāyaṇa* must necessarily be a name (*saṃjñā*). Even so, since one accepts a *yogarūḍhi* (a compound meaning based on both etymological and conventional senses) for the word *dākṣāyaṇa* because it possesses an etymological meaning (*avayavārtha*), the assumption of such an etymological meaning would result in a contradiction. Since [the practice] has not been previously established, it is enjoined for the sake of a specific result; thus, there is no contradiction. Maṇḍana says: "There is no difference in the case of the *Dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice."
Śaṅkara: "The fruit [is] the qualities of the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice.
Regarding this, there is curiosity: others do not tolerate this view.
For the injunction regarding the Dākṣāyaṇa and other sacrifices is not in proximity to the Darśapūrṇamāsa; if it were, then there would be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhāna) therein.

For in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, having set forth the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices in the third chapter, the fourth chapter prescribes the Vaimṛdha offering to be performed after the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice is completed, and the Aditi sacrifice after the Darśa is completed; then, having prescribed the Abhyuditā and Abhyudayeṣṭi offerings, it enumerates many rituals such as the Prasthāyī and others known as the Dākṣāyaṇayajña, beginning with the words: "Now, therefore, the Dākṣāyaṇayajña;
one performs this with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña on the full moon day of Phālguna," and so forth.

In this regard, because the word *atha* (now/then) marks a break in the context—just as in the case of "Now this is the Jyotis" (*athaiṣa jyotiḥ*) and so forth—and because it is impossible for another name to be applied to the ritual under discussion due to the presence of a different name already enjoined for its origination (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it is proper that this refers to a distinct ritual altogether. Furthermore, the term *dākṣāyaṇa* cannot denote the quality of repetition (*āvṛtti*) belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; for the etymological derivation—that "these belong to Dakṣa" (*dakṣasyeme dākṣāḥ*) refers to the priests, and their performance (*ayanam*) constitutes the repetition—is merely a figurative interpretation, whereby the term would have to refer to a quality well-known from another scriptural passage.

"Indeed, Dakṣa, having sacrificed with this [rite] at Pārvatī, obtained all his desires" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 4.4); and "He is indeed named Dakṣa because he conquered by means of this; therefore, its designation is the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice"—from the mutual etymological explanations found in these very words of the Kauṣītaki, it is understood that the word *dākṣāyaṇa* refers to a specific accessory injunction (*guṇavidhi*). Consequently, it is logical that this is indeed a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

Likewise, in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, after the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices have been set forth in the *Iyavākāṇḍa*, and after the *Ādhāna*, *Punarādhāna*, and *Agnihotra* have been set forth in the *Saṃbhara-kāṇḍa*, the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* is subsequently set forth.
Thus, because of the interruption of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is appropriate that this is indeed a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).

Even though the *Dākṣāyaṇa* and other sacrifices are heard of in the *Taittirīya* initiation within the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, nevertheless, the claim that the word *Dākṣāyaṇa* and so on refers to a mere accessory (*guṇa*) is untenable for the reasons stated above; therefore, it is appropriate that it is indeed a distinct ritual act.
The *adhikaraṇa*, however, should be applied to subjects such as the *ūrjāman* and others found in the context of the *Gavāmayana*.
Thus far, then, regarding these [sections].
Thus.

[The Bhaṭṭa says: In the *Soma* sacrifice, as a supplement to the injunction "he makes the hall with its beams facing east," there is this scriptural passage: "Gods, humans, and ancestors divided the directions: the gods [took] the east, the ancestors the south, humans the west, and the Rudras the north."

In that regard, concerning rites connected with humans, both the injunction (*vidhi*) and that which establishes an injunction (*vidhikalpaka*) are set aside—just as in the *nīvīta* and *audumbara* sections—because, as in the preceding section, in the case of Vedic rites to be performed by humans, the facing of another direction is already established by general and specific scriptural statements and thus is not something to be newly enjoined; and in the case of worldly (*laukika*) rites, the facing of the west is never established as a rule. Therefore, there is neither an injunction nor anything that establishes an injunction.

This being the case, although here in this context the western direction is mentioned merely in relation to human beings, because the injunction for all cases has already been refuted in that same manner due to the mention of specific ritual acts (*karma*), the connection between humans and the western direction is understood as pertaining only to such actions where facing west is established by worldly custom, such as the performance of sacrifice. Since the praise is thus logically established by taking this very connection, there is no basis for postulating an additional, separate injunction.

In the case of the phrase "upari hi," however, because "above" is heard in connection with the Agnihotra for the gods, and since that [offering above] was not previously established, there is the postulation of a separate injunction; thus, it is an injunction regarding the state of being "above" by way of restating the fuel-sticks (*samid*) which are subsidiary parts of the Agnihotra for the gods.

Bhāṣya 3.3.29, p. 812: The accent (the sound *uvāca*) in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] is prompted by the apūrva of the subsidiary (*aṅga*). This is the principle of the restriction of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering.
Bhāṣya 9.1.212–3, Section 2:
The fire of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice itself must be maintained until the end of the Soma sacrifice.
This is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
The section concerning the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiation sacrifice). The principle of the conflict between a subsidiary and its quality. Is initiation on a festival day (*parvan*) or not on a festival day?
Mīmāṃsā 12.1.129: At the conclusion of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, the status of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*) is established, and the duties of the initiated are to be performed.
This is the section concerning the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
The ritual duties beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* are prescribed with reference to the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice when it is concluded in the *agniṣṭoma* form, not for all forms (*saṃsthā*).
This is the section concerning the forms (*saṃsthādhikaraṇa*).

Bhāṣya 3.6.161–14: The *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are purificatory acts (*puruṣasaṃskāra*). They purify the person for the purpose of receiving the fruit and the *pavitra* [vessel], because they exist as part of the sacrificial performance. Dūṣaṇa 7.3.1436: The rites beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* have the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as their archetype (*prakṛti*) within the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

Bhāṣya 10.1.24: Since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such rites are not known as belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, they are extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the modifications of the Soma sacrifice (*somavikṛti*).

This is the section concerning the primacy of the Soma sacrifice (Soma. 4.4.122). In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such rites, the *agnyanvādhāna* (the placing of fuel on the fires) need not be performed even for the purpose of securing the deities (*devatāparigraha*).
The section concerning the term *agnyanvādhāna* (the placing of the fires):
In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, the *anvāhārya* sacrificial fee is established by *prasaṅga* (extension) from the fee of the *saumika* [soma] sacrifice.
The principle of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) pertaining to the Soma sacrifice:

in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites, the forest-food (*āraṇyaśāna*) is accomplished through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) by means of the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and other observances belonging to the Soma sacrifice.
(12.1.4–13). In the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites, the *Ārambhaṇīyā* offering is not performed.

PMS 10.1.24: In rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) belonging to the *Dārśapaurṇamāsika* [New and Full Moon sacrifices] is not established by *prasaṅga* (extension/application) from the vigil performed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the Soma sacrifice.
This is the *Jāgaraṇa-nyāya*.
Bhaṭṭa 12.1.8–137: In rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the kindling of the fire (*agnyānvādhāna*), which belongs to the *Dārśapaurṇamāsika*, need not be performed.
12.1.10 (19): In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, the presence of the wife is established by extension (*prasaṅga*) from the *saumika* [sacrifice].

12.1.12 (9): Regarding the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*) in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites with the mantra "O Agni, Lord of Vows" (*agne vratapate*), etc., it need not be performed again because it has already been undertaken previously in the *prayaṇīyā* and other *saumika* rites.
12.1.20–23: In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, the consumption of the remnants (*śeṣabhakṣa*) must be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) for the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*).
12.1.133–34: In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such rites, the consumption of the remnants (*śeṣabhakṣa*) must indeed be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others: 2104. The principle of the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyamanyāya*) in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth [applies].
In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, the selection of the *hotṛ* priest (*hotṛvaraṇa*) is not established by incidental application (*prasaṅgasiddha*) through the *saumika* [sacrifice].

Although the *parisāman* chants belonging to the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are included within the performance (*prayoga*) of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and others, they are performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) because there is no distinction in their being prior to the *Agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1183). In the modified form (*vikṛti*) of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and others, there is an annulment (*bādha*) of the *Anvārambhaṇīyā*.
This is the topic (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning the *Ārambhaṇīyā*.
Bhāṣya 10:

Regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* in the *asthiyajña* (sacrifice for the bones), [the discussion is] under the view that the qualification [for the sacrifice] has ceased (*luptādhikārapakṣe*), which is a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvācintā*).
Vi. 10.1.18: The consecration (*dīkṣā*) is accomplished through the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi*; however, the staff, girdle, and so forth, are merely indicators (*abhivyañjaka*) of the consecration.
5|1|11: The *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* and other such rites are subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, because they are taught within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma;

the Soma sacrifices are the primary acts (*pradhāna*). 4|1|12: From the conclusion of the rites beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* until the end of the *rukmapratimocana*, the ritual action [pertains] to the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*).
Bhāṭṭa 5.1.12: The principle of the restriction of speech at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice;
the restriction of accent.
Regarding those things employed for the sake of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), it should be prompted by that [rite], because they exist for its purpose.
Section 2: The Commentary—Or rather, there is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
In that context, this is handed down in the scripture: "With whatever degree of voice one desires, with that one should recite at the Dīkṣaṇīyā [initiation] offering."
"The mantra is [recited loudly] at the Prāyaṇīyā, more loudly at the Ātithyā, and in a whisper during the six Upāṃśus.

In this regard, there arises the following doubt: are these ritual properties (dharmas) prompted by the ultimate transcendental result (paramāpūrva), or are they prompted by the intermediate transcendental result (apūrva) of the Dīkṣaṇīyā?

What is the prima facie view? Since the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites are employed for the sake of the refinement leading to the ultimate transcendental result, and because the ritual property serves the purpose of that ultimate transcendental result, the Dīkṣaṇīyā and the others must indeed have the ultimate transcendental result as their sole purpose.
For it is the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) that possesses the fruit;
that which is enjoined as being performed by an agent is what is connected with the ritual duties (*dharma*s), not the *apūrva*.
For that [agent] is the locus of the injunction.

Regarding the *saṃskāra* known as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, whatever *dharma* (ritual duty) pertains to it is connected with the *paramāpūrva* (the ultimate transcendental result), not with its own essential form (*svarūpa*). Why? Because the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is prompted by the *paramāpūrva* and is itself fruitless.

Therefore, because of the connection of the sacrifice with that purpose, there is a relation of *dharma*; thus, it must be prompted by the sacrifice, since the *saṃskāra* exists for the sake of that [sacrifice].

In the case of a connection [with the primary], there is secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); however, when the connection with the primary (*aṅgin*) is intended, that *apūrva* must be indicated by means of the primary which has itself been indicated. But when the connection is with the *apūrva* of the subsidiary (*aṅga*), the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* indicates its own *apūrva* by direct denotation (*śruti*) alone.
