Thus, by this method, it has been demonstrated that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) there is "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) there is merely "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*).
[The mantras beginning with "atha vā" do not exist in the written *Upaṭīkā*.]
Since that has already been explained in the discussion of the *tanmantra*, it is indeed so.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the *vaidhātavyā* is a substitute for the *dīkṣaṇīyā*—specifically through the assumption of the function of the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* offering—it is endowed with those ritual properties (*dharmas*), just as wild rice (*nīvāra*) is endowed with the property of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the ritual properties are prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* offering, whereas in the *vaidhātavyā* there is a different transcendental result altogether.
Nor does one thing grasp another *apūrva* by means of the property of being another *apūrva*. (In the middle, he raises an objection: This purpose is untenable.
(How so? There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between these two [in the statement]: "The *dīkṣaṇīyā* is the *vaidhātavyā*."
In this regard, if even the primary term were taken as referring to the principal act (*aṅgin*), then grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not be possible.
Therefore, one of these two terms must be secondary (*gauṇa*) and the other primary (*mukhya*).

Between them, because of its priority and lack of contradiction, the term *vaidhātavyā* is primary; however, the term *dīkṣaṇīyā*, being subsequent and already subject to contradiction, indicates the fire-related assistance to the sacrifice (*ṛtūpakāra*).

When that [fire] is observed, the Vaidhātavyā [offering] is prescribed (meaning that the Vaidhātavyā takes over the function of the Dīkṣaṇīyā). Being thus prescribed, because it supersedes that function, it acquires its properties.

Even according to the Siddhānta, just as the threshing-block (khalevālī), being prescribed for the function of the sacrificial post (yūpa), acquires its properties (such as the ritual sprinkling and so forth).

Therefore, the application of ritual properties (*dharmaprāpti*) is equal for both positions. Now, it might be argued: "By the statement, 'The *Dīkṣaṇīyā* becomes the *Vaiśvadevī*,' the function of the *Vaiśvadevī* is set aside and [its place] is prescribed as the function of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*. And that [function of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*], the *Vaiśvadevī* will accomplish by means of its own established properties and its own *apūrva*, and it will not take on the properties of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*," so says the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādin*).

(He refutes this: Even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), if the function of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* were to be performed by the *vaidhātavyā* (as if it were already established), then that function would be accomplished by its own inherent properties (*dharmas*) because it possesses well-known properties. If, however, the *vaidhātavyā* does not perform the function of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, then all the more so do its own inherent properties belong to it. Furthermore, even when the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*) has been stated, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* sacrifice served as the specific means (meaning: the *āgnāvaiṣṇava-apūrva*).
Likewise, there is no such [door] here;
therefore, there is no restriction of speech in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

[Objection: But surely, by this same reasoning, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) would not apply to wild rice (*nīvāra*), [this being the objection of one who considers the term *āgnāvaiṣṇava* according to its literal sense].
It is said: True, rice (*vrīhayaḥ*) is a distinguished means (*dvāra*) for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

However, there is this much difference between the two (*nīvāra* and *vrīhi*): rice benefits [the ritual] through a visible intermediate effect (*apūrva*), namely the production of rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), whereas *nīvāra* grains are seen to accomplish that same function directly.
In that case, the attainment of merit through the agency of the speaker and so forth is logical.
But here, in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering], there is no evidence that the unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*, i.e., *apūrva*) exists as a means toward that effect;
nor is it the case that this unseen factor itself is the sole purpose.

(How so? Just as the Vaidhātavyā offering arose in that specific form, so too is it enjoined (as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* in the Aśvamedha); by the word "Vaidhātavyā," that very same [offering] is referred back.
Since there is no mention of the Āgnāvaiṣṇava [deity], it does not constitute a separate ritual action either.
Therefore, it must be performed as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) exactly as it was understood in that context.
Even if it were a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*), one would still grasp the properties (*dharma*) by means of the name (*nāmadheya*), and not by the extended application (*codaka*).

Śā—The supreme *apūrva* possesses a fruit; therefore, [the subsidiary] would be its subordinate element. Its own *apūrva*, however, is subordinate to the sacrifice because it itself possesses a fruit. It is logical for that which possesses a fruit to be a subordinate element, but not for that which is fruitless to be a subordinate element.
Therefore, a difference in accent is prescribed for the form that serves as its means of accomplishment.

It is said: "If this were relied upon, there would be a case of indirect indication (lakṣitalakṣaṇā); it would be merely an indication of its own apūrva. Therefore, it is better that it [the accent] be subordinate to that."

Soma: [The connection is as follows: Just as in the previous case, because the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) would be purposeless if it did not serve the purpose of the *apūrva*, it was held to serve the purpose of the *apūrva*; so too here, because the fruitless *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice would be purposeless if it did not serve the purpose of the *apūrva*, it is said that it serves the purpose of the *apūrva* of the fruitful Jyotiṣṭoma.

In the Sūtra, by the word "refinement" (*saṃskāra*), the refinement of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) consisting of the *Dīkṣā* is intended; and by the word "that" (*tat*), the ultimate *apūrva* (*paramāpūrva*) is intended. Vi: "Mantras and the like [serve] either the ultimate *apūrva* or the intermediate *apūrva*, depending on whether there is a fruit [from the former]; however, the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* is for the sake of the specific [ultimate *apūrva*]."
Bhaṭṭa: Or rather, it is thus.

First of all, it was stated that because there would otherwise be the contingency of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) regarding the nature of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), there must be a definition [of the subsidiary] as being a means to the *apūrva*.

In that regard, when considering whether only the *apūrva* produced by the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*) is indicated, or whether that produced by the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is also indicated: first, in cases such as the grinding of the husks (*avaghāta*) and the pounding (*peṣaṇa*), there is no other intermediate *apūrva* produced by the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth; for there is no dispute that the definition consists in the finality of the *apūrva* produced by the primary sacrifice.

Regarding the principle of the restriction of speech at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation rite]: by the principle of the restriction of speech at the *dīkṣa�ṇīyā*, since rites such as the *prokṣaṇī* (sprinkling) and others—which produce an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*)—are enjoined for the purpose of purifying the sacrificer (*yajamāna-saṃskāra*) produced by themselves, they lack a desire for further ritual properties (*dharmākāṅkṣā*). Therefore, even in those cases, there is no visible purpose; nevertheless, for those who are ignorant of that, the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule "with whatever degree of voice one speaks" applies to the *upavasatha* and other such stages.

Regarding such passages as "If one should desire [so much], one should recite at that many *dīkṣaṇīyā* offerings," Maṇḍana [states] that the accents—by means of indicating their previously established status as means (*sādhana*) produced in the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *jyotiṣṭoma*, and other sacrifices—are employed by the injunctions for the knowledge of the accents themselves;
thus, they serve solely that purpose.

However, Śaṃkara [argues] that even in the case of the *prokṣaṇīyā* and others, there is the status of being an accessory (*aṅga*) to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* based on the term *dīkṣaṇīyā* as it was previously produced.
8. [Otherwise] there would be pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) because even in that case, there would be an absence of possessing a fruit (*phalavattva*).
Thus, the principle of the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*) regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyā* does not apply here.

For although the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is a directly contributing factor (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), it is established as having a fruit for the sake of the *jyotiṣṭoma*'s own *apūrva* through a mediated succession; thus, even the *apūrvas* of the subsidiaries, being means to the undesired, lead to their own [result].
In the section on the excellence of initiation (dīkṣotkarṣa), 2108: there is a combination of the time for initiation with the oblations of the Soma-initiation by means of others;
this is the topic [of discussion] in the section concerning the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana).
When initiation (*dīkṣā*) is elevated, the *agnihotra* and other rites are likewise elevated.
Because the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*) remains, there is no consideration of transgression [of other rules], as that [initiation] has reached its proper time.
Commentary: This is heard [in scripture]: "Therefore, one who is initiated does not give, does not cook, and does not offer oblations.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they recite: "There are three initiations," and so forth.

If, however, because of the inability to recite the other initiation (dīkṣā), the time for initiation is postponed, there arises a doubt: is there a postponement of the giving, the oblation, and the cooking, or not? What is the prima facie view? There is no postponement;
for the giving, the oblation, and the cooking are obligatory by such scriptural injunctions as, "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives."
This is their refutation: on those days for which the Jyotiṣṭoma is prescribed by the scripture, [the other rites] should be performed on other days, excluding those many days;
they are not prohibited after the time of the Jyotiṣṭoma injunction.
Therefore...
The application [of the ritual] is seen through the verbal testimony. And the initiations are for the sake of the perfections of the initiated.
Furthermore, that state of being initiated, because it is something being undertaken, is intended as a subordinate factor (guṇa) in each respective context.
Consequently, there arises the possibility that [the dakṣiṇās] serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite.

Since the dakṣiṇās have the purpose of procuring the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and since the act of bowing down (*ānamana*) consists in providing assistance, they possess the fitness for being employed in the performance.

Therefore, by means of the principle of *kiṃcīryāna* (3.7.3), there arises the possibility that they pertain to the performance of the primary rite together with its subsidiaries—that is, the possibility that they serve all purposes.

(He strengthens the reasoning regarding the practice of the ritualists: Furthermore, this is directly perceived: the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), being acquired by means of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—this is the analysis of the compound *dakṣiṇopāttāḥ*—perform even the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*). Otherwise, having been hired for that purpose, they would perform only the primary act (*pradhāna*).
Yet, the sacrificer has no need for them being hired merely for that much.
Therefore, since it is determined that they will perform whatever [is required] once hired, the sacrificial fee is for that purpose.
And thus, the designation of [the fire] as the agent will be consistent with the eleventh [book], (1.2.1.8).
Therefore, it serves all purposes.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"The initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) of the Soma sacrifice," "the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for one initiated for the Soma," "food for one being initiated" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.6).

Regarding the absence of food for one who has been initiated, there is a regulation of the vow (*vrata*) according to the distinction of social classes (*varṇa*): "Milk is the vow for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel (*yavāgū*) for a Rājanya, and meat for a Vaiśya."
This vow is not for the sake of the human agent (*puruṣārtha*), but rather, by virtue of the context, it is for the sake of the ritual act (*kratvartha*). (Vi.
4.3.4) When the consecrated person (*dīkṣita*) sees something impure, the mantra beginning with "Food is the mind" (*annaṃ manaḥ*) is to be recited.
And that [mantra] is not to be repeated even if one sees several impure things at once.

8|4|7. Regarding the prohibition of giving, offering oblations, and cooking for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*): the prohibition of all acts of giving, offering oblations, and cooking would apply without distinction.

As for this prohibition stated concerning the initiated person in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—namely, "The initiated does not give, does not offer oblations, and does not cook"—since there is no specification (*aviśeṣāt*), that is, an absence of distinction, it would be a prohibition of all acts of giving, offering oblations, and cooking, whether they serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). Alternatively, it would be a rule (*dharma*) regarding those things not connected with the performance; for the [sacrificial] act is directly enjoined [by scripture].

He states another alternative: this prohibition would apply to those acts such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth that are not connected with a ritual season (*ṛtu*). However, this prohibition cannot be accepted for acts like giving that *are* connected with a ritual season, because such acts are directly enjoined—being prescribed by the verbal text itself—and because that [prohibition] would also be a specific [rule] based on inference.
Or rather—this introduces an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*).
The giving, offering, and cooking of that sacrifice, which are inferential and obtained through the *codaka* rule, are prohibited by such injunctions as "the initiated one does not give.
This is because there is no distinction between that which serves the purpose of the person and that which is inferential; they are equal in being objects of prohibition.
Therefore, there is another position: that this is a prohibition of what is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
However, it should rather be the exclusion of other [deities] based on the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), for if it were a prohibition, there would be an option (*vikalpa*).
With the words "However," he states another position.

The sentence "He should give every day," "He should offer oblations every day," or "He performs [the rite] upon obtaining a guest," has as its supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) the sentence "The initiated one does not give," and so forth.

Therefore, based on that supplementary statement, the phrase "the initiated one does not give" and so on constitutes an exclusion (paryudāsa) for the other—that is, for one who is not initiated—regarding the injunctions "He offers oblations every day," "He gives," and "He cooks.

If, however, this were accepted as a prohibition (pratiṣedha) in the case of "The initiated one does not give," then because it would be both enjoined and prohibited, there would be an option (vikalpa), which is improper.
In every respect, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the *agnihotra*, giving, oblations, and cooking are not to be performed by one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*).

The meaning of the section is that in the statement "the consecrated does not give" (*dīkṣito na dadāti*), the negative particle (*nañ*) does not signify a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), but rather signifies an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
— Ke. (Kaiyaṭa).

8|4|8. At the time of crossing a river, the initiated person (*dīkṣita*) must mutter the mantra: "O divine waters, O son of the waters" (*devīr āpo apāṃ napāt*). This should not be repeated even when there is a change in the intermediate current.
Vi. 11|4|18. At the time of sleep, the initiated person must first mutter the mantra beginning with: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows" (*tvam agne vratapā asi*).
And that [mantra] need not be repeated even when there is an interruption in the rain.
8.4.9. For one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), the mantra "udantīr varṇaṃ ghat" is to be recited during the raining of Parjanya;
and that need not be repeated even when the rain falls in many streams.

11|4|18. For one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), there exist the *vārūṇī* [offering] alone prior to the recitation, as well as the *sārasvata*, *āgnāvaiṣṇava*, and *bārhaspatya* [offerings]. There is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*) of these, not an option (*vikalpa*), because they perform different functions. 8|4|10. For one who has been initiated, until the completion of the intended journey—even if interrupted by rest in the interim—the mantra beginning with "O Agni, may you go to what is auspicious and excellent" (*bhadram agne śreyaḥ prehi*) is to be recited only once at the outset. This is the section (*adhikaraṇa*) within the *Jyotiṣṭoma* complex.
For the rule regarding the non-eating of specific foods until the end of the initiation is prescribed for those seeking spiritual welfare.
(The absence of specific food is restricted until the end of the initiation, as in the injunction: "One must not eat until the end of the initiation.

The exclusion of the offerings into the fire (*homa*), cooking (*pāka*), and other acts performed by one who has undergone initiation (*dīkṣita*) when they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
This is the section concerning those not initiated (*nadīkṣitādhikaraṇa*).
The duties of one consecrated for a sacrifice (*nadīkṣita*) include such rules as "he does not give, he does not cook, he does not offer oblations," and so forth (Vi.
8.4.11). When there is a displacement of the duties of the consecrated due to divine circumstances, that displacement indeed follows.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the vow of the initiated: "He scratches with the black antelope horn. It is further stated: "When the sacrificial fees have been led [to the altar], he throws the black antelope horn into the pit" (Bhāṣya 11.3.6.13). The application of the term *dīkṣita* (initiated) occurs at the conclusion of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* rite.
The consecratory rites (*dīkṣitasaṃskārāḥ*) are to be performed first; thereafter, the releasing of the gold ornament (*rukmapratimocana*) and so forth take place at the fire-altar (*agniyane*).

[AitBr 8.4.12]. The word "being consecrated" (*dīkṣyamāṇaḥ*) refers to the agent of knowledge; it is placed in the fire-altar. By the use of the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), the future time is indicated.

8|4|13. When a word signifying an action is used as an upapada (governing word) for another action, [the suffix] *dīp* is applied to the root *duh*, as in *dīkṣyamāṇavat*; [an example is] *duścikitsyavraṇa*.

The *luṭ* suffix [is used] in the sense of "one who intends to sacrifice with Soma," meaning "one who desires to sacrifice with Soma" (Ratnaprabhā 5.4.2). Because the capacity to illuminate the meaning of a word does not depart even when that word stands in an obscure position, the remainder [of the construction]—such as "give to the Brāhmaṇa" or "give, to the Brāhmaṇa"—is also [valid] (Saṃkṣepaśārīraka 2.4.17). A long duration becomes the *tantrī* (the governing rule).
Dp. 12|1|21|32: Long-tailed parrots (*dīrghaśukāḥ*) and *priyaṅgu* grains appear when the previous crop has been exhausted.
Bhā. 4|3|4|9: The *dīrghasoma* sacrifices—such as the *ukthya* and others—are modifications of the *soma* sacrifice due to the increase in the number of *graha* cups;
these include the eight beginning with the *dvirātra*.
The Agniṣṭoma, however, is not indeed a *dīrghasoma* (long soma sacrifice).
Vi. 3.3.16: The displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *saṃtardana* (the rite of pressing the stones close together) from the Jyotiṣṭoma occurs in the case of the *dīrghasoma*.
3.3.16: "All is indeed suffering for the discerning one"—this is the maxim.
In the *Pātañjaladarśana*, Mādhavācārya has stated that [pleasure] is of the nature of happiness even in relation to things such as the sky, sandalwood, and women, which are actually suffering.
(Sāhasī 870). For suffering is indeed torment.
(Bhāṣya 3.8.3.19). It is heard in scripture that unrighteousness (*adharma*) results in the experience of the fruit of suffering.
3|8|3|19, "possessing suffering.
That which ought to be done is possessed of ease; that which ought not to be done is possessed of suffering.
6|1|1|1, p. 1349. [The singing] of the *kāṇḍavīṇā* singers at the Mahāvrata is of the same class as the drum-singing (*dundubhigāna*).
And that [is] the name for the drum-song.

Vi. 10.4.16: By the sound of the drum, which serves as the means for the commencement of the Māhendra-stotra at the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is a sublation of the original (prakṛta) ritual elements and the mantra.
(In that case, there is a sublation of the two blades of darbha grass by the drum, and of the mantra by the sound.)

Bhāṣya 10.4.11–2, Section 3: This is the singing in accompaniment (*upagāna*) by the wives with *kāṇḍavīṇā* lutes and other instruments to the drum-shaped musical instrument during the Mahāvrata rite. Bhāṣya 10.4.18–9: The word *dunduṣṭa* denotes the act of joining together (*samāsa*).
Dup. 9|3|1|9, p. 1748: The word *duṣṭa* denotes a compound.

Dup. 9|3|1|9, p. 1748: The maxim of the wicked man and the donkey (*durjanagardabhanyāya*). This refers to the application [of a term] even when there is an intention to express the meaning "the donkey is in the place of the wicked man" or "the wicked man is in the place of the donkey."
This too is composed in verse:
"A wicked person, while defiling the armor of an honest man, becomes even more radiant;
even if he receives beatings and the like, the villain remains true to his nature."
The meaning of this is as follows: even so, he remains of that very character.
How so? He says: "Arjunavarman [follows] the white path.
According to Amara, "dhavala" and "arjuna" both mean white.

Furthermore, if wealth (*rāḥ*)—that which is to be stored—is accumulated such that it becomes fit for depositing, then one becomes intoxicated (*madī*); that is, one becomes possessed of pride (*madvān*). Moreover, if one receives beatings and the like, there is a connection to the nature of being intoxicated according to the maxim of the "lamp on the threshold" (*dehalī-dīpaka-nyāya*).
In the sense of a donkey, a *khala* is a *khara*, because of the non-distinction between the letters *ra* and *la*; nevertheless, he remains characterized by that very nature.
What is he doing? He is making turbid—by raising dust through trampling—the *arjunavarma*, the path of light.
Furthermore, he who is intoxicated by pride during the month of Vaiśākha, even if he receives beatings and the like, does not abandon his wicked conduct.

Moreover, the sense that Karṇa—the son of Rādhā—who defiles Arjuna, the middle Pāṇḍava’s armor on the road, becomes intoxicated, is also suggested. (Sāhasī. 972) Even a weak explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) serves as a basis for a definitive conclusion when it creates doubt regarding a powerful injunction (*vidhi*).
The determination of the injunction, "He places the smeared pebbles," is made by the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "Clarified butter is indeed splendor" (Vi.

4.4.19). Even a weak injunction attains equality with a prohibition that depends upon it for its own existence; such is the application of this very *paryudāsa* (exclusion), which is synonymous with the *mahanyāya* (the great rule).

Bāla, p. 98: Regarding the tenth [sūtra], *apratiṣedhaḥ pradeśe* (10.8.1.12), it is stated that by the principle—"even a weak injunction becomes equal in strength to a prohibition because its very nature is dependent upon it"—there is an establishment of an option (*vikalpa*) for the rule "not at the first sacrifice" (*na prathamayajñe prakṛtyāt*), whether it is treated as a prohibition (*pratiṣedhatve*) or as a restrictive injunction (*vaidhaparyudāsatve*).
P. 98: "Even that which is weak possesses the strength of being powerful."

Even though Smṛti is weaker than Śruti, it possesses greater force here because it is based on a powerful primary element (padārtha), namely the act of sipping water (ācamana). Therefore, rather than abandoning the heard action—which is subordinate as a quality of the primary element—one must perform the sipping of water itself immediately after the Veda has been made [from the mouth], provided that it is so enjoined by Śruti. For the strength of a weak means of knowledge (pramāṇa) consists precisely in its being supported by something stronger.
Valor. 6|2|2. It is logical that the weak should be sublated by the strong, not the other way around.
Bhāṣya 12|1|2|17. That which depends on the weak is sublated by that which depends on the strong, because it has not [otherwise] attained its status.
Vā. 13|1|7|4, p. 860. The maxim [is]: "The taking up of a surgical instrument by one who wishes to heal a wound in those afflicted by a wound difficult to treat.
Just as a physician cuts with a blade to alleviate the pain of a man suffering from a wound, he is called a physician (vaidya) because of that [act] (Mī. Ko. 265).
[The term] *duṣkulaprasūtatva* means being born of a low family (2114); *hatinavanīta* means butter produced from the milk of a female elephant.

It is not, however, by way of being a slayer; rather, it is for the sake of dissolution that Śiva possesses the quality of *tamas*, desiring to provide rest for those living beings who are weary from wandering through the continuous cycle of suffering-filled *saṃsāra* by means of the experience of the bliss of their own true nature, which is easily attained during the period of separation [from the world].
In reality, however, Śiva is simply an ocean of unsurpassed compassion.
For this very reason, there is no cruelty whatsoever on the part of a physician who knows the cause of the disease when he administers treatment to patients afflicted by illness.
"In this case, it is compassion alone that is the motivating factor," as explained in the *Śivapurāṇa*. Furthermore,
being born into a low family is the cause for a tendency toward unchastity, not poverty.

Su. pṛ. 12: Because defectiveness (duṣṭatā) consists in the destruction of the capacity for causal efficiency (kāryaśakti). Ṛju. pṛ. 227: It is logical that defectiveness results in incapacity for the [intended] effect; it does not, however, result in capacity for another effect.
Bṛhatī. pṛ. 53.
For [seeds] such as rice do not possess the capacity to produce sprouts when they are afflicted by defects and the like.

As for what was said—that because the defect of bile (*pittam*) has a different function, it cannot be called a "defect"—in that regard, the functions of the bodily fire (*vahniḥ*) are strength, nourishment, and so forth; however, those [functions] are simply absent there [in bile].
As for digestion (*jaraṇam*), that depends upon the fire, and with respect to that [digestion], bile does not constitute a "defect."
*Ṛju-vivaraṇa*, page 52: "Sexual intercourse with one's daughter is improper conduct.
*Vārttika* 1.3.17, page [number]: "There is also a certain case where there is a remote connection (*dūrānvaya*)."
Even that which is separated by another atom, if it revolves in the mind in immediate succession, is indeed sufficient to produce a specific [cognition].
For example: "From here you flee; you run toward a tree grown far away. I tell you, O large-eyed one: you are destroying your old age."

The construction is: "You step upon the foot of one who is running old" (Pāṇini 4.3.111). The phrase "due to being at a great distance" (Pāṇini 1.2.1.12) is stated as the basis for an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

[This refers to] the basis for the explanatory passage: "The gods saw only smoke, they did not see the fire itself. By this rule, the basis is stated: by day, fire is not seen because of its distance; but at night, it is seen because of the abundance of light emitted from the sun into the fire.

Or: Vākyabhāṣya 1.4.12.3, p. 354. The maxim is that an alternative (vikalpa) tainted by the eight defects is worse than the assumption of syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) due to being situated at a distance.
Ābharaṇa 3.1.5.26, first section:
In cases such as *durveṭaka* and others, the properties of bricks (*iṣṭakā-dharma*) must be performed.

Although the term *iṣṭakā* (brick) in its various contexts serves the purpose of the function of a brick, because a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is necessary regarding the door-component, the principle of the *camasādhikaraṇa* applies; thus, since the generic form (*ākṛti*) is not intended to be expressed in the case of bricks, and since the genus of "brick" (*iṣṭakājāti*) is absent in *dūrvā* grass, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and so forth, the properties of bricks do not apply to them. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: because the application of the word *iṣṭakā* in such expressions as "he lays down *dūrvā*-bricks" and "he lays down *ghṛta*-bricks" has the effect of bringing about those properties, and because of the all-pervasiveness enjoined in the rule "he builds even a thousand-fold altar," they [the *dūrvā* and *ghṛta*] would indeed possess those properties.

Even in the case of those made of clay, the properties of bricks apply (Saṃkarṣa. 2.1.8). In the case of the *hita* and *navanīta*, [the rule applies] to all the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), not only to those belonging to the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*).
Or [the rule applies] at that time because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The Commentary states: This is now being deliberated: is *navanīta* (fresh butter) for those subsidiaries performed at the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), or for all of them?
It should be for those at the time of the Soma-pressing, because of the observation of an indicative mark.
This is heard: "He obtains a thousand [cows].

In that context, there is a further statement: "In place of the *āmīṣomīya* [animal], there is a *puroḍāśa* cake for Agni-Soma; in place of the *anubandhyā* [cow], there is a curd-mixture (*payasyā*) for Mitra-Varuṇa. This indicates that two positions are vacant.
By this, it is understood that the statement ordains a specific modification of the subsidiary rites belonging to the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*).

Or—(due to the proximity of the preceding rule, as the word "due to specific proximity" was not taught [in the previous case], the logical connection is severed)—by means of specific proximity, having observed it generally, one establishes the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) through the observation of its characteristic mark (*liṅga*) at that time.

For the association with the animal (*paśu-sāhitya*) is indeed its own property; the time of the *sutyā* sacrifice is observed in the two rites called the *āmīṣomīya* and the *anubandhya*, because of the statement regarding their being assisted by another.
Therefore, this [rite] also, being of that same nature, belongs to the time of the *sutyā*.
Or rather, it belongs to all [the priests] because there is no distinction.
The Commentary states: Or indeed, the butter (navanīta) should belong to all the officiating priests (aṅgas).
Why? Because there is no distinction.

"In the absence of a specific distinction, [the rule applies] to all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*)"—or rather, as it has been said: "Or [it applies] to all, because they are subordinate (*śeṣatva*) and because of their connection thereto. This is an observation of an indicative mark (*liṅgadarśana*) stated in the *Nyāya*.
Commentary: As for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that was mentioned, it must be refuted.
There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which its statement could establish that [the *sutyākāla* rites] are subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the [main] sacrifices;
rather, there is only a direct observation (*darśana*).
But how is it that the animals are to be immolated in the middle?
By reason of logic. What is the logic?
This is the favoring of the sequence.
In this way, the sequence is favored even when devoid of verbal expression.
Therefore, [the term] "fresh butter" (navanīta) applies to all the constituent parts (aṅgas).
Or rather— this indicative mark (*liṅga*) is a means of proof for what is to be understood through reasoning (*nyāya*). However, this [matter] is to be understood through scripture (*āgama*),
and not because it is a property of the *sahālambha* [offering] from the time of the *sutyā*.
What then? From another reasoning alone.
And that [reasoning] is not possible in the case of "butter from a slain [cow]" (*hatinavanīta*).
He shows that reasoning (the Bhāṣya): "In this way, that sequence characterized by proximity, which has the meaning of an inferred scriptural statement (*anumeya-śruti*), will be favored."
For at the time of the *savanīya* offering, by sacrificing [the animal] at that very moment, the time of no animal would be transgressed;
nor does it become doubled. Otherwise, both [transgressions] would occur.
Therefore, the view [of the opponent] is established.
Regarding the *sāman*— which was mentioned in the context of the curd-butter (*navanīta*) applied to the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*)—
there is a contextual connection (*prasaṅgikī saṃgati*) arising from the deliberation as to whether it should be performed at the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyākāla*) or at all times.

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: this [procedure] would apply only to those subsidiaries belonging to the time of the *sutyā* (pressing), because the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the very nature of the *sutyā* time is observed in that subsidiary which is enjoined with the requirement of the concomitance of the animal sacrifice (*paśusāhitya*). Cinnabhaṭṭa says: "In all the subsidiaries occurring at the time of the *sutyā*, a quality is enjoined;
the first [subsidiary] is so due to a specific argument (*vaiśeṣikavāda*), while the connection with all subsidiaries is established through the syntactical statement (*vākya*)."

Bhaṭṭa: If this were so, then since we observe such [passages] as "he seizes a thousand [animals]" (*sahasraṃ nālabhate*) at the very time of the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing), the status of being fresh butter (*hatinavanītatva*) would also be restricted to that which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) belonging specifically to the *sutyā*-time.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the Siddhāntin replies]: because it is improper to restrict the scope of a scriptural statement (*vākya*) based on an inference from general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), it must serve all purposes.

For even the conjunction of animals (*paśusāhitya*) does not have its auxiliary status (*aṅgatva*) determined by its occurrence at the time of the *sutyā*; rather, it is determined by its relationship to the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*). Furthermore, there are three reasons for its inclusion: its being mentioned in the context of the primary rite, its being an excellence (*utkarṣa*) of the time already stated, and its being a cause for the removal of defects (*avaccharupahetu*).
And that [defect] does not exist here;
therefore, it is indeed the case that all parts are intended.
Maṇḍana says: "In every limb, fresh butter is desired."
Śaṅkara: "Even at the time of the *sutyā*, this [is the case].
25. 'At the *sutyā*, there is the slaughter of a hundred animals.
26. (Just as there is a collection of animals at the *sutyā*)."
(Symbol) The section concerning the elephant's butter (*hatinavanīta*). The term "elephant's butter" refers to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), not the primary rite (*pradhāna*);
for when a specific proximity (*saṃnidhānaviśeṣa*) is possible, it applies to those subsidiaries.
The Bhāṣya states: "By which it is heard: 'Fresh butter [is] clarified butter (ājya).
In that regard, there is a doubt: does the fresh butter belong to the primary sacrifice, or to the subsidiary rites?
What is the prima facie view? That it belongs to the primary."
For its context is as follows:
by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement, the primary rite is to be accomplished with butter.
This being the position reached, we reply:
In the absence of this [soma], there would be ignorance on the part of those who are ignorant [of the procedure].
How is there an absence? Because the primary substance consists of soma.
But surely, by virtue of the scriptural statement, butter will be used; no, for the meaning of the sentence is not that "butter is what it becomes."

With reference to what? By the statement "by which [substance] butter becomes clarified butter (*ājya*)," a connection between the butter and the clarified butter is enjoined; by this, the connection with clarified butter is restated, and it is not directly the case that there is a connection with clarified butter for this [butter]. However, such a connection does exist for certain [other] substances. For that [substance] for which it exists, the butter is enjoined after being restated, due to the specific context (*saṃnidhāna*).
Or rather—[the opponent] thinks that Soma will be set aside because of a qualified injunction within the context [of the passage]: "Clarified butter is the fresh butter of the elephant.
(The author states the final position: However, since it is possible to enjoin multiple objects, clarified butter (*ājya*) is restated (*anūdyate*) and only its specific quality is enjoined.
Furthermore, there is no attainment of clarified butter for the primary sacrifice itself.
Therefore, it is established by the principle: "Because of meaninglessness, [the rule applies] to its subsidiaries.

If it is argued that the same applies to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) as well, the Bhāṣya states: "If this is seen—namely, that butter belongs to those who do not know [the Pavamāna hymns]—then it would also apply to the *pavamāneṣṭis* within the *ādhāna*."
For those [other substances] also are produced by that [substance] which serves as the means for its preparation; even when prepared by that [means], they are accomplished by it.
Or rather—one must necessarily state that whatever is beneficial is clarified butter (*ājya*).
Consequently, since the *pavamāna* oblation is also beneficial, it would follow that it is clarified butter, and thus fresh butter (*navanīta*) would be required.

[The opponent argues: "No, because it is not part of the context (aprakaraṇatvāt), since that [fire-laying] is the cause for this [offering]. The Commentary (Bhāṣya) states: "For neither are the Pavamāna offerings heard of in the context of this [fire-laying], nor is the fire-laying itself [heard of] in the context of those offerings."
What follows from this? [The rule] "as desired" applies neither to the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the fires) nor to the fires themselves; there is no connection between them.
The *ādhāna* pertains to the fires, and the fires pertain to the sacrificer. Therefore, fresh butter (*navanīta*) is used in the *pavamāna-havis* offerings.
This is not the reason why [the fire-installation] is a subsidiary, namely that it assists the fires mentioned in the context of the installation.
If any one of the means such as *prakaraṇa* (context) were present, that would be the reason.
Therefore, there is no basis for a connection between the two acts of fire-installation.
Or rather—(he says this to explain the sūtra himself)—a connection [of a term] is not established merely by being helpful.

What then? By virtue of the context (*adhikāra*), that which is helpful to the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) is brought near by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), and not the *pavamāneṣṭis*. This is the settled conclusion. *Sudhā*: "That of which fresh butter (*navanīta*) produced from curdled milk is the archetype" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; thus, clarified butter (*ājya*) characterized by the fresh butter of curdled milk serves the purpose of the primary sacrifice alone, by setting aside the *soma*.
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the *dṛṣṭupalyau* are enjoined in the section concerning the curd-butter (*navanīta*) vessel.

Since a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the meaning of the final member is predominant is possible, whereas a *bahuvrīhi* where the meaning of the first member is predominant is not applicable, and because a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (a bahuvrīhi with non-co-referential members) is utterly improper due to the impossibility of a qualified injunction—which would result in the fallacy of enjoining multiple things—and because the words "fresh butter" (*navanīta*) and "ghee" (*ājya*) have distinct meanings and thus cannot enter into grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it follows that the secondary term "ghee" must be understood as indicating its function (*kārya-lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, since indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is incompatible with a direct injunction, one understands from the context that there is an injunction of fresh butter and curdled milk (*ghṛta-navanīta*) by way of restating the function of ghee. Since there is no function for the primary substance itself, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the injunction of curdled milk and fresh butter applies to ghee in general.

Śā [explains]: Since it is possible for *ājya* (clarified butter), even though it is not part of the primary context (*aprakṛta*), to be obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from the two specific injunctions (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the quality of being fresh butter (*ghṛtanavanītatva*) is enjoined as a subordinate attribute (*guṇa*) by way of referring back (*anuvāda*) to that *ājya*.
That which is *ājya* should have its source (*prakṛti*) in fresh butter obtained from this [skin-begging]. (The meaning of the *Ājyāpaniṣad* is "that which is *ājya*").

*Soma*: Just as in the previous case it was established through the syntactical connection (*vākya*) that [the term] has the primary sense, here, because it is directly perceived through the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is a connection [to the primary sense]. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: since it is impossible [to apply the term] to the primary [sense], it must belong to the subordinate elements; thus, by virtue of the injunction (*codaka*), the application of the butter (*ājya*)—characterized by its specific qualities—is justified as being clarified butter (*navanīta*).
This is the conclusion.

Although a *tatpuruṣa* compound is also possible for "fresh butter" (*navanīta*) in the sense of the function of clarified butter (*ājya*), nevertheless, if that were the case, there would be a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *ājya* in the sense of its function; and since even such a secondary usage is not appropriate, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is adopted (as the final conclusion in the *Śāstradīpikā*). Vi— "Fresh butter is the *śyena*, [the term] *ājya* [refers to] the primary [substance] or the subsidiary part; let it be the primary.
Only that which is to be enjoined and was previously unestablished—namely, the curd and fresh butter—is [the object]."

The primary modification is [the substitution] of the *mukhya* (principal substance); as for the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), clarified butter (*ājyaka*) is obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*). Following this is the principle of the accomplishment of perception (*dṛṣṭisiddhi-nyāya*).

The twenty-one-syllable *prajāpati* mantra beginning with "āsrava" has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Every rule of permission (*abhyanujñāvidhi*) has a visible purpose as well. This also applies to the rules concerning substitutes (*pratinidhi*) and restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*).

Page 23: An injunction whose purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*)—whether its object is already established or not—is in every case a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*); this must be investigated, because even when its object is not [otherwise] established, the unseen merit of restriction (*niyamādṛṣṭa*) necessarily arises. *Rasāyana*, page 213: The selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) has a visible purpose. *Saṃkalpa*, 2131: Even though there is a visible purpose, since the requirement for the "manner of performance" (*kathaṃbhāva*) arises for the sake of establishing the unseen merit of restriction, the context (*prakaraṇa*) exists.

Vārttika 3.1.12, p. 732: Even in the case of prescribed acts that have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is possible. Vi. 6.2.10: "In all cases where there is a visible purpose, an unseen merit is also accepted [as arising] from the restrictive rule. Rasāyana 2.13: Having observed the manner of the effect in those things with a visible purpose, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) by the modified (*vaikṛta*).
VI. 10|4|1: But in the case of rites with visible results, there is equality regarding the path, the characteristics, and the application [of the mantras].
Vārttika 1:
This is the principle of the *devasvata* mantra.
The principle of the mantra "devasya tvā... applies here;
therefore, [the words] would refer to what is perceived, because the mantra is required by way of manifestation.

If, however, they denote [their objects] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then they too would refer to what is perceived. Therefore, the words *savitṛ* and so forth denote that which is inherent [in the ritual].

Alternatively, even if the primary meaning alone is conveyed by the words "Savitṛ" and so forth, they nevertheless express that which is inherent [in each case]. How so? Because these mantras are distinct.
Therefore, there is a division of mantras for each deity, beginning with "Of the god Savitṛ, you... and so on.
And in those [mantras], the phrase "I offer the oblation" is to be supplied as an elided remainder (*anupaṅga*).
In this regard—) the injunction regarding the deities based on the wording of the mantras will serve as an optional alternative to Agni and the others in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice.
On this point, some say:

"The injunction of deities through the wording of the mantras cannot set aside those [deities] taught by the originative statements (*utpattivākya*) of the other [sacrifices], because they exist in different contexts."
Therefore, even on the basis of the wording of mantras such as "Savitṛ," other sacrifices are postulated;
and in those [sacrifices], words such as "Savitṛ" are both primary and expressive of what is inherent [in the ritual].
This is not tenable.
This being the case, because they would constitute distinct sacrifices, they would be equivalent to the *prayāja* offerings and the like.
Consequently, there would be an entitlement (*adhikāra*) even for those [elements] extended by the *codaka* rule, just as there is for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
In that regard, there would be no significant difference between the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions.
Therefore, that alone is the correct prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) wherein modification (*ūha*) is established.
[The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) says: This being the case, we reply:
in common worldly usage, terms such as Savitṛ are not well-known as designations for Agni and the other deities.

Nor are they capable of designating fire and the other deities by means of a quality (even as the substratum for the maintenance of that quality). Why? Because wherever a word refers to another thing by means of a quality (as a cause), it occurs in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that other thing; however, here there is no coreferentiality between the word "fire" (*agni*) and [the words] "Savitṛ" and so forth, because of the indication of different case endings. Furthermore, it is not possible to assume an injunction regarding a deity based on the wording of a mantra (*māntravarṇika*).
For it is said that [the rule] "he becomes [one]" applies when there is a difference of mantras;
yet, since this mantra is one, it has been stated [in the sūtra] "because of the unity of purpose" (JS 2.1.46).

Even if a difference of mantras were imagined, there would still be no option (vikalpa) between Agni and the others on the one hand and Savitṛ and the others—[who are indicated] by the words of the mantra (māntravarṇika)—on the other.
[This is] logical because of the unevenness of the command (*viṣamaśāsana*).
Therefore, their utterance is for the purpose of offering (*nirvāpa*).
Consequently, for that reason, no mention is made of those [deities] not explicitly heard by means of words such as *Savitṛ* and so forth.
For what reason, then, is it performed? It is employed for the sake of the other [offering], namely the pouring out (*nirvāpa*).
"In the impulse of the god Savitṛ"—that is, impelled by the god Savitṛ, or when the sun has risen;

"by the arms of the Aśvins"—referring to the act of circumambulation, [it is done] by the arms of the two sacrificers who are desiring [the goal]; for those two are "possessors of horses" (*aśvin*), since they have attained the fire and so forth through faith, or they have eaten, or they enjoy the fruit thereof.
He says this, pointing to his own two arms: "The two Aśvins are the deities; these two are the arms.
But he considers Pūṣan to be the sacrificer himself, from the root *puṣ* (to nourish).
Thus, everything is for the purpose of illuminating the specific distinctions of the extinguishing [of the fire].

An objection is raised: why are the words Savitṛ and the others not mentioned? In another context, they denote Savitṛ, the Aśvins, and Pūṣan. Being displaced from that [other] context by an indicative mark (liṅga), they ought to override the [original] context (prakaraṇa).
To this it is replied:

Savitṛ and the others are made subordinate qualifiers by the force of the case-ending (vibhakti) heard in the text; it is understood that they are distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha).
In that case, the gender (liṅga) is sublated by the direct statement (śruti).
For the gender (liṅga) serves to illuminate the meaning of the nominal stem for the sake of the deity;
since there is no deity here, it is said that [gender] is mentioned where a deity exists.
However, the hearing of the case-ending (vibhakti) indicates that the meaning of the nominal stem is qualified by another word-meaning.
And that [word] exists here as another word;
moreover, direct statement (śruti) is more powerful than indicative mark (liṅga).
Therefore, there is no displacement.
He asks: "When Savitṛ and the others have the sacrificer as their referent, then how can there be no modification (anūha) in the formula?
It is replied: This sentence is for the purpose of pleasing (joṣaṇa), not for the purpose of requesting permission (anujñāpana).
The act of choosing (*joṣaṇa*) that which has not yet been chosen must be performed; in that case, there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
The request for permission (*anujñāpana*) was previously performed by means of a quality (*guṇa*), which would result in having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Furthermore, in the phrase "I choose the *juhū*," the word "I choose" is expressed by the verbal noun (*bhāvaśabda*) "I offer" (*nirvapāmi*).
The permission expressed by the words "In the impulse of Savitṛ" is performed for the purpose of qualifying the subsequent act;

even though it is a permission, one must indeed perform it according to the meaning of the word *nirvāpa* (offering), for the sacrifice is not heard of as being [performed] by one who has not approved.
Therefore, because they serve the purpose of approval, the words beginning with "Savitṛ" are for the sake of another and will not be recited [in the *anuvacana*].
Śabara—(states the prima facie view): "In that case, because the visible purpose is obtained, the words should denote the deities.

The words *savitṛ* and so forth would attain the status of having an invisible purpose only for the sake of praising the act of offering (*nirvāpa*). Therefore, the words *agni* and so forth denote [the deities]."
Either by the indicative mark (*abhiñā*) or by the option (*vikalpa*), the [deity] is indicated by the words of the mantra.

(He states the established conclusion: At the time of production, [the deity] is indicated by that which is expressed by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), and it is not optionally [substituted] by what is expressed by the mantra, because of the disparity [between the two].
Consequently, their lack of explicit mention is employed for another purpose.

The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that deities are manifested here by means of words that convey [the meaning]—and that there is no purpose whatsoever in manifesting those who are not explicitly heard, that must be refuted. To this, it is replied:
The principle of the *devasvata* mantra;
the principle of the *devasvata* mantra is that terms such as Savitṛ and others are its designators.

These mantra-sentences are to be divided according to their respective deities; the words "juhoti" (offers) and "nirvapati" (pours out) are to be supplied by ellipsis everywhere. In every case, it is understood that there is a single mantra for the act of pouring out.

That which is prescribed once, such as the *juṣṭa* formula, cannot tolerate repetition; therefore, modification (*ūha*) is not applicable there. Having concluded the incidental discussion related to the introduction of Soma, the subject matter of this chapter—namely, *ūha*—is now considered; this is the connection (*saṃgati*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Since mantras function as subsidiaries (*śeṣabhāva*) toward a ritual action by means of denoting their meanings, Savitṛ and the other deities also function as subsidiaries through the denotation of their own respective meanings; because they thus denote meanings inherent in the rite, there should be modification (*ūha*). By the statement, "In the case of mantras, subsidiarity should exist due to the connection with the denotation of meaning," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established. To that, the reply is: Savitṛ and the others are not subject to modification (*acodita*), because they do not denote what is enjoined (*acoditārthaka*); since the mantra denotes what is enjoined, Savitṛ and the rest—which would otherwise be subject to modification—are excluded. [Verse]: "Should Savitṛ and the others be modified or not? Because they are connected with the meanings [of the rite]."
*Ūha*: Since the connection with the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is possible even when [the mantra] is not modified, there arises the doubt:
"Should *Savitṛ*, *Agni*, and so forth be modified (*ūhanīya*), or not?
The Bhaṭṭa school: Thus, by way of an introductory discussion (*utpoddhāta*), the subject matter of *ūha* is now considered.
Now, that very subject is considered directly.

In this regard, concerning the sūtra *phaladevatvayoḥ* (9.1.3.4), it was stated that in the case of mantras that reveal a deity which is the means (*sādhana*) for the *apūrva*, when there is a modification (*vikṛti*) involving another deity in that same position, there is a substitution (*ūha*) of other words for the purpose of revealing that [new] deity through its own expressive power.

Furthermore, it is not by their primary denotative power (*śakti*) that the words of the mantra reveal the presiding deity who is the means to the *apūrva*, but rather they reveal that deity through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Alternatively, the directly expressed meaning itself is employed for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). In that case, because the meaning is not directly connected to the ritual act, the directly expressed meaning becomes related to the means of the *apūrva* through its connection with the unseen result. This is indeed the case in the mantra "devasya tvā" and so forth, because the words such as "abhinirvapāmi" (I pour out) are connected to the act of pouring out.

In that context, regarding the recitation (*japa*) of mantras such as *śakṛt* (dung) and others, even though they are connected to such a sacrifice by way of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) with respect to their own possible meaning, they do not possess the quality of having a "conjoined meaning" (*samavetārthatva*).
Likewise, words such as "deity" (*deva*) and so forth do not have a conjoined meaning.

For it is not possible for words like *deva*, *savitṛ*, and *prajāpati* to denote the deity of the sacrifice under discussion; this is because the postulation of a deity based on the wording of a mantra (*māntravarṇika-devatā*) is untenable when it is obstructed by a deity already established by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-devatā*).

Nor can that [mantra] be applied to the *upāṃśuyāja* offering; for if that were the case, it would follow that the mantra constitutes a single syntactical unit with the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*), which would result in the fallacy of [the mantra being recited] while the action is already being performed. Furthermore, by means of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying the missing words), one may accept a division of the mantra as follows: "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I pour thee out for the *juhū* ladle," "With the arms of the Aśvins, I pour thee out for the *juhū* ladle," "With the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out for the *juhū* ladle," and "For Agni, I pour thee out for the *juhū* ladle. In this way, the unity of the syntactical whole regarding the act of pouring out is established.
It should not be argued that even if the fourth [mantra] is employed in the *upayāja*, it is possible for the three mantras beginning with *āghā* to have the deities and the fruit as their objects;
for it is precisely a defect to accept a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) through syntactic ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*).
Furthermore, there is no evidence that the words ending in the genitive case—when construed with *prasava* and so forth—serve to designate the deities.

For this very reason, even though it is possible to insert the names of the deities as a single unit, they are understood to constitute separate sacrifices. This doubt has also been raised because, if that were the case, those other sacrifices would necessarily become subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of the *Āgneya* and other primary rites, and since they would thus be modifications (*vikṛti*), the application of modification (*ūha*) would follow. By this, the position in the root text—which accepts that the words "Savitṛ" and so on refer to "Agni" and so on through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and thereby maintain a relevant meaning—is refuted; for if the reference to the modified deities could be established by the same relationship of denotation (*śakya-sambandha*) that refers to Agni and the others, there would be no need to rely on the contingency of *ūha*.

For this very reason, in the definition of "having a combined meaning" (*samavetārthatva*), only the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) is qualified. Alternatively, let it be understood as "that which is conveyed by the function of the word denoting the primary meaning"; nevertheless, even if there were a combined meaning, the aforementioned reasoning would still entail the necessity of formulating a modification (*ūha*).
This objection has been disregarded.

Therefore, since there is no manifestation of a meaning inherent within the ritual action itself, the entire purpose of mantras such as "devasva" (belonging to the gods) and so forth is simply to manifest the offering (*nirvāpa*) as qualified by whatever meaning is denotable by those words—such as "belonging to the gods" and the like.

In this regard, for those word-meanings where a visible purpose is possible, the purpose of manifesting them must be assumed to be purely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*). However, for those where that is not possible, the purpose of manifesting them must likewise be assumed to be purely transcendental.

Therefore, it should be understood that even the qualification of such items over the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*), as well as their being brought forth (*āhāryatva*), is merely for the sake of mental recollection.
In this context, the visible purpose of the pouring out is indeed separation;
and the purpose of the item "to Agni, thee" is its application to that [separation], while its independence serves the purpose of providing a clear mental impression.
However, it will be stated regarding the *juhapada* that it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), whereas for others [the words], it is the same.

Some, however, maintain that by means of words such as *devasvatva*, the glorification (*praśasti*) of the offering (*nirvāpa*) is conveyed through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And it should be understood that this [glorification] is intended to inspire confidence in the offering even at the time of its performance.

Let it be so; in any case, the words "devasva" (the property of the gods) and the others have been placed there with meanings that are not inherently connected [to the literal sense]. As for what the Bhāṣyakāra has stated—that the word "artha" (purpose/wealth) in the context of the Āghāra offering refers to the husband and wife because it is offered without faith (*aśraddhā*), and that "Pūṣan" refers to the sacrificer because of his quality of nourishing (*poṣatva*); and that since the office of the Adhvaryu is considered to belong to him, the god Savitṛ is also figuratively the sacrificer, [acting] at his instigation (*prasava*)—[this is the view]. Mīmāṃsākośa 266.

The principle of the *devasvāli* mantra (21.22): By accepting the meaning that the deities are Indra and others who "desire," it was established that they function as qualifiers of the sacrificial offering (*nirvapa*). However, since there is no person in the Veda who performs such superimposition (*āropa*), the intention here is that the absence of superimposition is understood from the fact that [the passage] is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) for another purpose.

However, when it is considered that—having established the distinction of the *āghāra* offering through the *svātmanidhana* of the *adhvaryu*—there is no obstacle to employing Vedic sentences (just as in the case of using worldly sentences) in order to manifest the *nirvāpa* performed by oneself, then, since there is no evidence for an unestablished secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and because there is no restrictive rule for adopting the views of the *abhyudaya*, the *brahmā*, or the *yajamāna*, it is indeed proper to follow the previously mentioned position.
Furthermore, in this way, in the *sattra* sacrifice, the modification (*ūha*) of the plural number is observed in words such as *devasavi*, *śriṣ*, and *puṣpa*.

Nor is the commentator’s resolution—that here there is no status as being for the sake of another (parārthatva), as in the case of the prosperity of the sacrificer (yajñapati)—correct. For even though such [a status] might be possible in the case of the Aśvin-flower, the sacrificer’s authorization (anujñā) regarding the substance belonging to another serves a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatva) by way of avoiding falsehood and so forth; thus, like the words "deva" and "savitṛ" in passages such as "udīcīnānasya pado nidhattāt," modification (ūha) is unavoidable.

Nor should it be argued that, even in your own view, since the deity Savitṛ accepts [the term] *prasave* (at the time of rising) and so forth as referring to his very nature, the injunctions such as "one should offer the oblations at midnight" would be contradicted by the word *aprasave* (not at the time of rising). Furthermore, it should not be claimed that on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), when there is no prior manifestation of light, there would be the contingency of the rite's omission;
for there is no contradiction in accepting the meaning as "when the rising has occurred" or "when it is about to occur."

Since the manifestation of the time of sunrise lacks a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), it follows that there is no modification (*ūha*) in words such as "devasva" and so forth; this is established. Maṇḍana states: "No modification should be made in words such as *saci* and the like."
Śaṅkara—inferring from the beginning:
Regarding the determination of the status of a single sentence in mantras such as "devasya tvā" (In the impulse of the god Savitṛ), there is the definition of a single sentence [Ke.

212|14|46]. In the mantra "devasya tvā savituḥ prasave," because the two words "agnaye nirvapāmi" (I offer to Agni) illuminate the meaning of what is to be performed, the words beginning with "devasya tvā" possess a meaningful purpose; thus, all [the words] are meaningful.
[The opponent says: It is an ornament.

Because it is impossible to abandon [the deity] since the deity is not an object of enjoyment, and because there is no physical form [to be abandoned], [the deity] lacks the capacity [to receive the offering]; thus, [the deity] has no entitlement.

Furthermore, due to the contradiction between the status of the object of the action (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*), it is impossible to abandon [the deity], because this [act of abandonment] consists in the cessation of one's own ownership with respect to that which is intended as the object of enjoyment.
Soma. 6|1|2. The divinity of the gods is established sometimes by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and sometimes by syntactical connection (*vākya*).

It is established by direct scriptural statement when there is an indication by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), and by syntactical connection when there is an indication by the dative case.
Bhāṣya 2|1|923, p. 523: the gods have no eligibility for Vedic ritual action.
6|1|2|5. The *devapatnyaḥ* (wives of the gods) are the deity of the third among the four *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
It is by means of them that the name of the rite, the term *patnīsaṃyāja*, is applied.
Vi.

Regarding the worship of a deity with sandalwood paste and so forth, suppose someone were being instructed on these matters and were to say: "Incense should be offered to the deity, flowers should be scattered, [the body] should be anointed with sandalwood paste, and this oblation should be presented;
when this has been done, it is the praise of the deity.
To him, another would reply: "It is not so; incense should not be given first; rather, flowers should be scattered first."

He thinks thus: that the offering of incense is mentioned first. Bhāṣya 5.1.4.4. *Devayajana* means a place where the gods are worshipped; it is a sacrificial ground. Regarding the statement in the chapter on the *devayajana*: "This should be made a *devayajana* because of its suitability"—this is the conclusion.
This must be performed prior to the commencement of the sacrifice (yajñābhrama). Ke.

Bāla. p. 72. For it has been established in the third [book] that even for a deity, there exists a mental resolve (saṃkalpa) termed "appropriation" (svīkāra), in order to establish its status as a legal entity (vyavahārasiddhi) such as ownership of property.
Bhāṭṭa.
The mantra "O divine waters" is for the purpose of crossing a river while the initiated person (*dīkṣita*) is away from home.

When he crosses a river with multiple currents, the mantra is recited only once at the beginning; there is no repetition of the mantra for each individual current. (Bhāṣya 11.4.17.50). Deities are to be understood through extraordinary means of knowledge (*alaukika-pramāṇa*), like the *apūrva*.
Saṃkarṣa 2.2.2: The deity is an indirect auxiliary; therefore, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) [is more proximate], while the oblation (*havis*) is internal.
Bhāṣya 8.1.132: When the deity has been invoked, it partakes of the oblation and is satisfied; being satisfied, it bestows grace.
When there is production, it connects [the agent] with the fruit;
this has been established in the ninth [chapter].
10.1.1.2 Section 3: Deities such as Indra and others do not exist as characterized by having a physical body, accepting the oblation, consuming it, being satisfied, or possessing a state of grace.

Since the fivefold [categories] beginning with *vigraha* (embodiment) lack *tātparya* (intentional focus) regarding their own literal meaning within the context of the *arthavāda* (explanatory passages), there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [for them].
Deities are either of the nature of sound itself,
or deities whose forms are conceived by the mind and understood through words.
They are to be accepted. Vi. 9.1.4. The deity is the intended object; 2123. Or the deity may be the motivator.
Because the deity is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) with respect to the substance—which itself is a subordinate factor of the act of relinquishment—the requirement for the deity is weak.
(Bhaṭṭa 4.1.7). "Since the deity alone is the primary [factor], it is the deity that attains the fruit; no one, while a master remains, requests the fruit from his servants."
(The meaning is that [the fruit] belongs to the deity precisely through the ritual act.
Vārttika 21.5.29, p. 441. The deity is subordinate to the ritual act; she is indicated by means of the *yājyā* and other verses for the sake of accomplishing the ritual.
Bhāṣya 12.4.2.4: The deity, moreover, accomplishes the purpose by way of being the object of reference (*uddeśa*).

6|1|1|18. "But the deity [is the referent] because it is the recipient of that [blessing], since [the ownership] has already been attained; otherwise, the master would be purposeless. By this sūtra, in the rule *āśāśānā meghapatibhyāṃ megham*, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the word *meghapati* refers only to the deity and not to the sacrificer. This is because the animal called *medha* is intended for the deity who is the lord of the clouds (*meghapati*), and such a blessing is logically possible for the sake of establishing the deity's ownership of the animal; whereas, since the sacrificer has already attained ownership of the animal, a blessing for that purpose would result in redundancy. Thus, it is concluded that the word *meghapati* refers exclusively to the deity and not to the sacrificer.
Su. Pṛ. 1534: In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is no substitution of deities in the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Bhāṣya 10.8.16.49–50: A deity is not designated by means of a word ending in the accusative case, because there is no authoritative basis for such a designation. Ṭupṭīkā 10.1.1.14: The deity does not go [to the sacrifice] individually.
In the act of sacrificing, however, one merely becomes the fire by means of the designation [of the deity].
Bhāṣya 11.4.78: "There is no deity whatsoever possessing a physical body.
[Objection: But Viṣṇu is praised; yet there is no benefit whatsoever from Viṣṇu being praised.

Indeed, Viṣṇu is not made an object of invocation. (ŚB 12.4.1.1). In the distribution-mantras such as "May they return according to their respective portions," the deity is not addressed; rather, [the address is directed] only toward the two lumps of food (piṇḍau).

Saṃkarṣa. 2.1.16. Furthermore, what is this so-called "deity" (devatā)? One view is that those who are celebrated in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as Agni and others, dwelling in the celestial realm (nākasad), are the deities.

It is said: among those deities, there is no inclusion of days and so forth, or tigers and so forth. Furthermore, it is recorded in tradition that things denoting time possess the status of deity, as in "the month is a deity," "the year is a deity.

Another opinion holds that those for whom the word "deity" is heard in the context of mantras and the like—such as "Agni is a deity," "Vāta is a deity," "Sūrya is a deity," "Candramas is a deity," and so on—are not what is meant here by the term "deity."
Even there, it is only when day and night do not overlap.
Therefore, let us magnify with our inspired thought Jātavedas, who possesses the hymns, as if [magnifying] wealth;
for his providence is auspicious in our assembly. O Yama, in your friendship may we never suffer harm.
"Thus [it is said in] Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.94.1].
Regarding those who partake of the oblation (*havirbhāj*), it is stated: 'One should offer a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, and one on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma.
Or rather, the deity is the recipient of the oblation, toward whom the oblation is intended; the same applies to the hymn (*sūkta*) as well."

In this way, whether they are corporeal or incorporeal, sentient or insentient, those things intended for a certain purpose according to the Veda shall possess the status of a deity (*devatātva*). That which is the object of the resolve, "I shall offer the oblation after having remembered the word that denotes it," becomes the deity in that context. (Bhāṣya 10.4.12.23, p. 1927). A deity is whatever is designated by a name.
For a deity is one who is invoked, not one who is not invoked.
"Deity" (devatā) is a term denoting a relationship, not a term denoting a genus. [Pāṇini 6.1.5.19] Deity.

Because it is the essence of the *Nyāyasudhā* treatise, even though the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expresses the meaning, one must accept a secondary indication (*lakṹ�aṇā*) of the meaning as qualified by the word in order for it to connect with the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*). Since there is the possibility of connecting the divinityhood expressed by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) to that [meaning], it is understood that "the meaning conveyed by the word is the deity. However, because the status of being the object of offering (*udeyatva*) is sublated in the case of a meaning qualified by a word—even if that meaning is what is to be expressed—and because the status of being a word, which serves as a qualifier, cannot be connected to another by virtue of the maxim "that which is subordinate to one thing cannot be connected with another," it should be disregarded due to its lack of relevance.

Or [it may be as follows]: Vārttika 3.1.2.1234 states that the deity is subordinate to the sacrifice;
