The word "or" (vā) serves to set aside the established conclusion of the preceding section.

The deity itself should employ the mantra, because the act of eating has that [deity] as its purpose—that is, it is for the sake of the deity. For this so-called sacrifice is indeed an offering to the deity.
The substance to be consumed is offered to the deity; she will consume it.
Therefore, the deity is the prompter (prayojikā), just like a guest.
Just as whatever service is due to a guest is prescribed for the guest alone,
so too is this [the case] with respect to the noble offspring.

Because the deity is the noble master (āryapatya) and the lord of wealth (arthapati), it is established that the deity is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of the mantras and other elements in the sacrifice.
Furthermore, they record in their tradition that "the deity rules over objects" (*arthānām īṣṭe devatā*).
Likewise, there is the common usage of terms such as "the assembly of deities" (*devatāgrāma*) and "the field of the gods" (*devakṣetra*).
He confirms that very same mindfulness:
"Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over the earth; Indra [rules] over the waters; Indra indeed [rules] over the mountains.
Indra is the strengthener of the mighty; Indra is the lord of the wise; Indra is to be invoked in peace and in exertion."
(Rigveda Saṃhitā 10.89.10).
And thus, there is a connection with that.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, regarding the mantra "By the victory of Agni, may I be victorious," the deity is the prompter [of the action].
This is because the deity becomes satisfied by the consumption of the oblation;
and for that very reason, through the grace of the deity, the sacrificial rite becomes connected with its fruit, such as heaven and so forth.

Therefore, the deity alone is the motivator and the primary element. Or rather, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the sacrificial act should be the primary element; the scriptural mention of the deity is subordinate.

The word *api vā* (or rather) is used to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In a sacrifice, the deity is not the primary element; rather, the sacrificial act itself is the primary element, because the fruit and so forth are preceded by the word [of the Veda].
Whatever the word declares must be accepted as authoritative.
And the word declares the fruit through the action, as in "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and so forth.
[Objection: But the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) consists in the connection between the material substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*).

This is true; however, there is a scriptural mention of a deity in the capacity of a quality (*guṇa*). For that which has come into being consists of substance and deity; the meaning of "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is that which is to be brought into being.
When something already existing is uttered, it is taught as a mantra for that which has come into being.
Consequently, when the ritual action (*karman*) is primary, the deity is subordinate.
Therefore, the deity is not the motivator; rather, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) alone is the motivator for the mantra and other elements—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
"That which has the word as its prior authority" means that the sacrificial rite has the word as its preceding means of knowledge; that is to say, it is based on the authority of the sacred word.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: its state is "having sound as its precursor" (*śabdapūrvatva*); therefore [the term is used].

The phrase "mention of a deity" (*devatāśruti*) means a word denoting a deity; the meaning is that it indicates the quality of being subordinate to the ritual action (*karmaguṇatva*). In the case of a guest, there is an absence of such primacy [of the action], because the guest has satisfaction as his primary concern.

Having demonstrated the disparity between the example "like a guest" cited by the proponent (*pūrvavādin*)—who argued that the deity is the primary factor in the sacrificial rite—the author concludes the established position (*siddhānta*).

When a guest is present, the primacy of the giving of food and so forth belongs to him; that is, it is the primacy of the guest (*atithipradhānatva*). That act of giving food and so forth, in which that guest is the primary factor, is "that-primacy" (*tatpradhāna*).
This is because that gift of food and so forth has the guest's pleasure as its primary purpose;

for in that case, the guest's pleasure—that is, his satisfaction—is the principal factor. However, in rites such as sacrifice, there would be an absence of that [guest's pleasure] being the primary purpose, since the primary purpose there is the deity's pleasure.
For in sacrifices and similar rites, the action itself is primary, while the deity is subordinate.
Therefore, the analogy "like a guest" is an inappropriate comparison.
Consequently, there is no primacy for the deity within the ritual action.
Consequently, the deity is not the motivator (*prayojikā*) of the mantras.

Here, in the *Sudhā* (p. 750), for the purpose of stating the disparity with the example [of the *Soma*], it is said in the Sūtra that even though there is the existence of a physical form (*vigraha*) and so forth, because the root *yaji* does not denote "worship" (*pūjā*), there is no predominance of the deity in the sacrificial act (*yāga-karman*). Thus, by means of the middle member [of the compound], it is established that the deity is predominant.
For those who wonder whether or not deities possessing a physical form and other attributes exist according to the Mīmāṃsaka school, there is an investigation in the *Kutūhala*.

In this regard: for those who hold that the deity is merely the word ending in the dative case, and for those who hold that the deity is the object itself devoid of consciousness and so forth, since the word or the object is insentient, their lack of qualification [for ritual action] is established; consequently, because there would be no other deity, the effort [to prove otherwise] would be futile, making the contradiction with the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya difficult to avoid.

As for the fact that in the ninth book, in the section beginning "Or the deity might prompt [the action]" (9.1.4.16), the fivefold attributes such as the corporeal form of deities are refuted, that is merely a statement of bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).
For this very reason, the Vārtika will proceed with that section [on the existence of deities] without even considering the fivefold set beginning with the corporeal form of the deity;
as for the claim that "the word alone is the deity, not the referent," it is merely the prattle of a Buddhist.

In the absence of an object, words such as "Indra" would be meaningless; consequently, the case endings (*suvibhakti*)—which express number and so forth under the governing rule that they denote the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) and its gender—would not occur.
As a result, entire sentences composed of words like "Indra" would become nothing more than the incoherent ravings of a madman.
Furthermore, the claim that a deity is an object devoid of the fivefold analysis (etymological derivation, etc. is merely the hidden prattle of a Buddhist.

For those who accept the authority of the Vedas cannot maintain that the deities lack the fivefold attributes, such as having a physical form, because it is precisely from the force of the injunctions for sacrifice that their possession of such forms and so forth is established.
Indeed, sacrifices consist in the propitiation of deities, according to the traditional rule: "The root *yaja* means the worship of the gods."
And in the case of those desiring results, just as in the statement "the king gives the reward," it is understood that the deities being propitiated through sacrifice are the givers of the result.
However, it is not possible for those who possess knowledge of the result to be the givers of that result;
nor do those who lack effort bestow a result.
Nor do they accept the oblation without being informed [of it], nor do they become pleased [without being informed].
And none of this is possible for those who are insentient and devoid of physical form.

Therefore, by the very force of the injunction for sacrifice, the fivefold attributes of the deities—namely, possession of a physical form, the state of being an enjoyer of the oblation, the state of possessing grace, the state of possessing sovereignty over the fruits [of action], and the state of being the bestower of fruits—are postulated.

Furthermore, because the fivefold attributes such as corporeality (vigraha) are clearly stated regarding the deities in mantras, arthavādas, itihāsas, and purāṇas, such as: "May the thousand-eyed, mountain-splitting god, the bull, bestow [blessings] upon us"; "Indra, being himself satisfied, satisfies the cattle with cattle"; "Indra is the king of the moving world and of men; whatever exists on earth in manifold forms, from that he gives wealth to the donor"; "For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant the desired enjoyments"; and "Being satisfied themselves, they satisfy him with auspicious fruits of all desires."
Even though these [mantras] are injunctive sentences, there is no reason for them to convey the corporeal form (*vigraha*) of a deity through the connection of their constituent words;

therefore, the Blessed Jaimini’s demonstration—through such sūtras as "But the meaning of the sentence is not distinct" (2.1.4.12) and "Because the purpose is otherwise, there is one sentence" (2.1.4.14)—that mantras possess the nature of sentences and possess meaning, is fully justified.

It is precisely by relying on the comprehension of the meaning of mantra-sentences that the discussion in the section beginning with "Or rather, the goat, because of the wording of the mantra" (6.1.1.13) proceeds.
The application (*viniyoga*) of mantras such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*) is established through their indicative power (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, those [passages] that contradict the meaningfulness of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and would otherwise conflict with the meaning of the scripture have been resolved through figurative usage (*gauṇī vṛtti*) in the section on *arthavāda* by means of such sūtras as "the statement of a quality" (*guṇavākya*, 2.1.110) and "from form and from majority" (*rūpāt prāyāt*, 2.1.111).

In cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), the meaningfulness [of the passage] is due to the connection with qualities such as performing its function; this has been demonstrated in the *Tatsiddhipaṭalikā* (2.1.121–123).

What need is there for more? The entire *Mīmāṃsā* of sacrificial ritual proceeds by depending precisely upon the indicative power (*liṅga*) of mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). If these were devoid of meaning, the system would fall into confusion. Nor should it be argued that their authority is untenable because they lack a definitive purport (*tātparya*) as prescriptive sentences; for mantras and explanatory passages do possess a purport regarding matters such as the embodied form of deities. Thus, how could they not be authoritative?

Although the mantras and arthavādas possess a great primary purport (*mahātātparya*) with respect to those [injunctions] through syntactic unity (*vākyaika-vākyatā*) with the injunctions for sacrifices and the like, they nonetheless possess an intermediate purport (*avāntara-tātparya*) regarding their own literal meaning, just as the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and so forth possess such a purport toward their own specific contents within the context of the principal injunctions. "That happiness which is unmixed with pain, which is not followed by its opposite, and which is brought about by acquisition— that is the state denoted by the word ‘heaven’ (*svarga*)."

This is the meaning: even though an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) has the purpose of praising that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), it is universally accepted that it also possesses an intermediate intention (*avāntaratātparya*) in conveying the meaning of the word "heaven" (*svarga*). Just like that, since there is no contradiction, one must accept that every explanatory passage possesses an intermediate intention toward its own literal meaning. Nor should it be argued that while the explanatory passage concerning heaven possesses an intermediate intention because it is required by the injunction regarding the fruit (*phala-vidhi*), other explanatory passages do not.
For instance, the injunction for invocation (*āvāhana-vidhi*), "He invokes the deities," requires the arrival of the deities, as this is observed [in the world].
Their arrival is for the purpose of accepting the oblations, and their acceptance is for the purpose of eating;
the eating is for the sake of satisfaction;
and the production of satisfaction in the deities when an act is performed with a desire for a fruit is for the sake of establishing their capacity to bestow that fruit.

Regarding the capacity to bestow fruits and the sovereignty over those fruits, since the arrival of deities and so forth—whether directly or through a lineage of succession—depends upon the requirements of the invocation (*āvāhana*), their possession of a physical form (*vigraha*) must necessarily be accepted. Furthermore, regarding the sacrifice of the creators of the universe (*viśvasṛjām ayāga*), a fruit is heard in scripture: "They attain union with Brahman (*sāyujya*) and residence in the same world (*salokatā*); those who perform this [sacrifice] attain such union with the deities (*sāyujya*), equal power (*sārṣṭi*), and residence in the same world (*samānalokatā*). Here, "residence in the same world" (*samānalokatā*) refers to the attainment of being in one and the same world; from that, "equal power" (*sārṣṭi*) means possessing a body and enjoyments identical to theirs.
There is a uniformity of meaning in this regard:

if the gods did not possess divine bodies and unsurpassed enjoyments in their respective specific worlds, then the injunction [of sacrifices] for the sake of those fruits would be nothing but the prattle of a madman.

Likewise, in the *Sāmavidhāna-brāhmaṇa*, it is stated: "One who employs the second [sāman] while thinking, 'This is not a sacrifice, but a slaughter,' sees the gods. From this vision of the gods, as well as from the power of the injunction for the recitation of specific *sāmans*, the fact that the gods possess embodied forms (*vigraha*) is established.
Nor should it be argued: "How is the vision of embodied gods possible when there are many sacrificers performing the recitation of the *sāman* simultaneously?
For precisely because of this, it is postulated that for them, objects such as food and drink are brought forth by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*).
Thus, it is not untenable that deities invoked simultaneously by many sacrificers are present at one and the same time.
Furthermore, the non-duality of deities within the sacrificial enclosures is possible through their sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), just as in the case of a yogin.

As for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "To whom indeed do the deities come? To whom, or to which of the many sacrificers? He who first dismisses the deities—he alone sacrifices to them when they have been heard," this is merely supplementary to the injunction, "Having offered the *agnihotra*, [one should not speak] in the morning," and its literal meaning is not intended to be taken as a factual statement.

Nor does the *Vājasaneyaka* contradict this, for it is heard there: "These two oblations, once offered, enter the intermediate space; they satisfy the intermediate space; they enter heaven; they satisfy heaven; they return and enter this earth; they enter man; they enter food; from that, offspring is born. And likewise: "The oblation duly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born; from rain comes food; from that, living beings."

Furthermore, based on such Smṛti passages as "Because the oblations offered return from the other world in due order," one might ask how the gods can be the enjoyers of the sacrificial offerings in the sacrificial wind (yajñavāta). However, this is resolved by the fact that two types of statements are accommodated: a certain portion of the offered oblation is consumed by the gods for their satisfaction, while another portion, having been transformed into the form of rain and so forth, returns [to the earth]. Nor should it be asked how gods with extremely gross bodies—as indicated by the verse, "Thirty yojanas is its [the earth's] extent; Indra bears it firmly upon his lap"—could be satisfied by a small amount of oblation.
This is because the increase of the offered oblation is heard in the scripture: "As many deities as one desires, and as much as is given, so far does the oblation expand.
Furthermore, there is no fault in this, for it is the subtle portion of that very oblation which has been offered and emerged [from the fire] that undergoes expansion.
Moreover, it is heard in the text, "Then, having made them unseen and fragrant," that the oblation is led to another state.

Even in the case of sacrificial offerings such as *kuśa* grass, *kāśa* grass, and the like, a certain edible portion undergoes transformation through the specific form of their respective ritual procedures (*āsādana-yoga*); thus, there is no fault of inedibility in them.
And the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this is: "This indeed is the middle [essence], which is the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

And it has been stated in the *Tantravārtika*, in the section on the Veda and the World (*lokavedādhikaraṇa*), verse 1.3.130, paragraph 1: "And if this clarified butter is indeed the honey of the gods for us..."
"In that case, there would be no contradiction between the meaning of the words and the ritual efficacy [of the mantras] such as *ṛk* and *vīrya*" (Vākyapadīya, p.

In those [rites] where there is the invocation (*āvāhana*) of a deity, the scriptural statement regarding the deity's arrival—namely, "having arrived, he partakes"—and the scriptural statement regarding the carrying of the oblation (*haviḥ*) would be contradicted.
Furthermore, because it is impossible to bring [the oblation] for the gods who are already present at the offering, those two [offerings] cannot be brought together.

Although in a *śrāddha* ceremony, an invitation (*āvāhana*) is not possible because deceased ancestors—having attained births as stationary beings, animals, humans, or denizens of hell—cannot possibly arrive; nevertheless, just as a pregnant woman, having eaten what is desired by her dear friend in the womb, becomes satisfied and thereby gratifies and nourishes the one in the womb while also repaying her friend, so too the deities presiding over the *śrāddha* food, being satisfied by eating it, gratify the ancestors such as the father of the performer of the *śrāddha* and bestow the fruit of the *śrāddha* upon them. Thus: "The ancestors, in the forms of Vasus, Rudras, and others, are the deities of the *śrāddha*."
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "Satiated at the Śrāddha rites, they gratify the ancestors of men; they bestow all desires by the hundreds and thousands," and so forth.
Regarding the mantra, "We grasp your right hand, O Indra," the meaning is: "O Indra, we shall take hold of your right hand as if it were a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thus, there is no contradiction with direct perception.
In such cases as "Svāhā to the plants, Svāhā to the roots," there is no contradiction because these refer to the presiding deities of those respective objects.

Nor should it be argued that there is no need to postulate an *apūrva* because the production of a result occurring at a later time from a sacrifice can be accounted for solely through the grace of the deity;

for even in the case of gracious deities, it is impossible for them to bestow a result that arises in another kalpa, and thus it must be admitted that even divine grace produces the result only by means of an *apūrva*. Therefore, the same [postulation] applies to the other case as well.

"Knowledge and action take hold of him, as does his prior cognition"—since this scripture declares that knowledge (*vidyā*), action (*karman*), and the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by previous experience depart together with the individual soul (*jīva*), one must necessarily admit the existence of the *apūrva* (unseen potential) born of action.
In this same manner, other apparent contradictions regarding the corporeal form of deities and so forth found in the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) are to be resolved.
A detailed treatment of this may be found in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā* and in great works such as Vācaspati’s *Pariśuddhi*, the *Parimala*, and the *Nyāyaratnamālā*.

However, the connection between the substance and the deity is not established by any [direct] means such as perception or verbal testimony; there is no assistance to the sacrifice [arising] from such discourse.
