In the mantra "of rice, O cloud," there would necessarily follow the exclusion (*ūha*) of words such as "barley" (*yava*) or "millet" (*priyaṅgu*). Nor should one suspect what was stated by the author of the *Mūla* (the *Tantravārttika*), namely: "Since the deity Sūrya is connected to the *bhāvanā* itself in the injunctive sentence according to the seventh and ninth chapters, and since there is no injunction for him in the sacrifice as a whole, he is connected to the performance; therefore, even though he belongs to the primary rite along with its subsidiaries, and although he is included in other subsidiaries through that connection, just as the word 'Agni' is fixed in the archetypal (*prakṛti*) mantras of invocation and so forth, so too the word 'Sūrya' is appropriately fixed in those same mantras in the modified (*vikṛti*) rite. This is because [the deity] is indeed enjoined in the sacrifice as a whole. Furthermore, since the deity is enjoined in the injunctive sentence within the *bhāvanā* itself, the word "Sūrya" must necessarily replace the word "Agni" in the archetype, and consequently, it must also necessarily replace it in the modification. Thus, the objection raised by the author of the *Mūla* is untenable.

Even though the substance and the deity have an initial connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), according to the principle of the "red [calf]" (*aruṇānyāya*), they are accepted as belonging only to the sacrifice itself at a subsequent stage; therefore, they do not apply to the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other such preliminary acts. Otherwise, the substance would also incur a connection with both the subsidiary and the principal rites. Furthermore, it will be explained later that substances and deities—which differ according to place, time, and agent—are established according to the state in which they arise.

Furthermore, since the deity is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) in the performance of the ritual with its constituent parts (*sāṅgaprāyabhāvanā*), and because [the mantra] serves the purpose of consecrating the deity through the act of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, the application of mantras such as the *āvāhana* and others can be established by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in expressions like "belonging to Agni" (*āgneyam*) or "belonging to Sūrya" (*sauryam*).

Therefore, since it is understood from the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the *āvāhana* and other mantras themselves that they serve the purpose of consecrating the deity, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the authority of the verbal testimony (*vākya*) expressing "Sūrya" when the word "Agni" has been removed in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*).

This being the position reached, [we reply: in the mantras for the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, there is no assumption of multiple indicative powers (*liṅga*) as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as: "One should manifest the deity connected to each respective archetypal limb by means of the words *gandha* and so forth. This is not the case, because that would entail the fallacy of assuming numerous scriptural statements. Rather, there is only one such statement: "One should manifest the deity connected to the archetypal limbs by means of the word prescribed by the injunction."
Therefore, for that purpose, even in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the use of the word [‘medha’] as prescribed by the injunction is mandatory; thus, there is no use of synonyms for ‘sūrya’.
For this very reason, it is impossible to assume such various types of scriptural authority (śruti) regarding the substance.
To illustrate: in the case of the primary sacrifice itself, such as “of the rice-grains, medha,” there would arise the contingency of using the word ‘yava’ [instead].
Furthermore, one might argue that the substance which serves as the juncture between the primary (prakṛti) and the modified (vikṛti) rites should be indicated by the word *vrīhi* (rice).

Consequently, when the word *vrīhi* is removed from the primary rites in cases such as the *kṣaṇa* sacrifice, there would necessarily follow the application of every synonymous term (*paryāyapada*) that denotes barley (*yava*). Alternatively, even if the meaning [of the word] is established as being inseparable from the primary rite itself, since one seeks its indication as a constituent part of the sacrifice, the very word that constitutes a part of the sacrifice must be remembered—either through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or even without it—by means of the remembrance of the object, just as the words *anvādi* found in mantras for invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth [remind one of the deity].

And thus, the Vedic text (*śruti*) is to be inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) as follows: "By means of the word *vidhitaḥ*, one should effect a refinement (*saṃskāra*) delimited by being the substratum of the deity who is the means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), through the power of proximity (*sannidhi*) which consists in the capacity to produce the cognition of the words employed [in the mantra]. For it is indeed possible that, by means of the perception of one proximate word—the object of such a verbal cognition—there occurs the recollection of another proximate word, through the relation of being the locus of the power that produces such a cognition.

And thus, there is also parsimony regarding the delimiter of the intended object (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). Consequently, even in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), there is no possibility at all for synonyms to apply.
Nor does it follow that the two words [‘Agnaye’ and ‘Pāvakāya’] would fail to be used in the *āvāhana* and other mantras within the modified ritual, as in the case of "To Agni Pāvaka."

Indeed, by accepting that the meaning alone is the intended object (*uddeśya*), its status as the illuminator (*prakāśakatva*) is established through recollection; otherwise, one might suspect [the application] to be "thus and so" in various ways. 14. Maṇḍana: "In the *Saurya* sacrifice, one should utter the word 'Sūrya'.
16. Śaṅkara: "That is likewise even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)."
16. That [mention of] the deity is likewise established by injunction.

There is also an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the deities of the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* offerings when the *sūktavāka* is displaced upward along with the displacement of the *anuyāja* offerings, following the *āgnimāruta* section.
(Bhāṭṭa)
Even in the case of the omission of actions involving deities and mixing, one may accept a substitute.
[Objection: Actions involving deities and mixing do not admit a substitute, because they are connected with another purpose.
Commentary: Deities are those such as "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ) and so forth.

“Fire”: [as in] “When one offers into the Āhavanīya fire, by that he gratifies the Ṣoḍaśin. “Word”: a mantra such as “I cut the grass, the seat of the gods,” and so forth. “Actions”: “He sacrifices the fuel-sticks; he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt,” and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: when there is a deficiency in the rites involving deities or mixed materials, should a substitute be employed, or not? What is the prima facie view? According to the principle of the preceding section, a substitute should be adopted and the performance carried out with something else.
This being the position, we reply as follows.

There should be no substitute for the deities when there is a failure in the mixed rites. Why? Because of connection with another purpose. A substitute being employed would be something other than the deities; it is not possible to perform [the rite] for those very deities [if a substitute is used]. (Note: This is the reading in the Vicalakarīyā; however, in the Ānandāśrama edition, the reading is "anyacca teṣām" instead of "anyadevebhyaḥ").

And what is their purpose? A deity accomplishes the purpose by means of that [offering]. An eight-potherd cake is offered to Agni on both the full moon and the new moon days. Furthermore, the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices do not consist merely of whatever other oblations have been prescribed.
In that case, when another [rite] is being prescribed, one should not perform the purpose of what has not been prescribed;
for when something else is being prescribed, the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices do not come into existence.

Therefore, a deity is not substituted. Likewise, when there is a failure of the Āhavanīya fire in the injunction "he offers into the Āhavanīya," neither another fire nor any other substance is to be substituted for it.
Why? Because of its connection with a different purpose.
That which is being substituted does not perform the function of the *āhavanīya*.
Why? Because the function of the *āhavanīya* consists in that which occurs when an offering is made upon the *āhavanīya*;
it does not occur when [the offering] is made upon something else.
For that [substitute] is not grasped by implication through the word "if" (yadi), because it is placed upon something else.
Indeed, the location upon which something is being placed does not provide any assistance to that which is being placed.
Therefore, there can be no substitute for others.
Likewise, in the performance of a mantra, nothing else may be substituted.
Why? Because it is connected with a different purpose.
For this is the function of a mantra: that it causes one to remember either the ritual action or its instrument.

In the absence of recollection, the ritual action does not come to fruition. Therefore, if the mantra has been mispronounced and one utters another word to fulfill its meaning, one should utter the very word previously perceived; one should not perceive the meaning through a different word. For if that which was already perceived were to be perceived again by means of a substitute word, it would constitute a verbal cognition [rather than the original].
(In this context, the passage beginning with "śabdāt" and so forth would be an explanation of the word "pratīyāt" itself;
and since that [explanation] was written outside [the main text], it is understood that it was subsequently inserted into the manuscript by a scribe.
Furthermore, in this way, the requirement for extraction (*uddhāraṇa*) regarding substitutes would be purposeless.)
There is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to the effect that "something must be made known by a word.
If there were such a means, then it would specifically be stated as "by this word, namely *barhis* and so forth.
In the absence of such a means, the adherence to other words would be purposeless.
Therefore, the word is not a substitute.
When an action is omitted, another action is not substituted for it,
because of its connection with a different purpose.
"One should offer the fuel-stick; the New and Full Moon sacrifices must be performed.
These two do not come to an end when another action is being performed [reading *vicalakarīya*].
Therefore, there is no substitute for the action."
[The Siddhāntin] says: Furthermore, when a deity is expressed by a direct scriptural statement (*vācanika-śruti*), it cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, how could there be a deity in the case of the boiled rice (*karambha*)? [Because] due to the absence of a means (*dvārābhāvāt*).
The removal of the husks and the preparation of the rice grains (*taṇḍula-nivṛtti*) are directly perceived, but the status of being a deity is not [directly perceived].
Furthermore, what constitutes similarity for the purpose of substitution?
It is the absence of the deity and the destruction of the word [expressing it].
Therefore, having recollected the word denoting the deity, one may subsequently take up [the substitute] for that [original substance].
That [substitute] is established as being primary; therefore, there is no substitute.
This same principle applies to the mantra as well (in the *Ḍupa* manuscripts, however, the reading is *prakṣaḥ*;
the reading *prakāraḥ* found in the *Ratna* is the correct one).
Let this be the distinction: there is no need for the deity to be remembered by means of the primary mantra itself, nor by another word similar to it;

nor is there any rule stating that the remembrance must be performed by means of the specific word [of the mantra]. Rather, through the power of the specific mantra's recitation (*ābhimaṃhana*), there is the exclusion of other observers and so forth, due to the restriction imposed by the mantra.
In the absence of that (due to the absence of that fixed mantra), who can prevent the *upadraṣṭṛ* and others? (Therefore, there is another word serving as a substitute.

He says: "There is no substitute for the fires. Because the *āhavanīya* fire is prescribed in the Vedic injunctions for the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the oblation (*homa*), it provides eightfold assistance (because it lacks visible assistance;

[as stated in] "one offers into the *āhavanīya*," it is enjoined for an invisible purpose). Therefore, in the absence of those two (the sacrifice and the oblation, along with the *āhavanīya*), there is no implication [of a substitute].
And because there is no displacement [of the original], there is no substitute.
(He shows this even regarding action: There is no authoritative means of knowledge for the claim that "whatever is performed by the *prasthā* and other [limbs] shall be performed by another action.
However, in the case of [actions such as] *havir-nirvāpa* and so forth, because they have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), a substitute exists.

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "Because of connection with another object" (*anyārthasaṃyogāt*), what is meant? It means "because of connection with a cause for substitution" (*pratinidhikāraṇasaṃyogāt*).
(This word *artha* does not denote a purpose, but is a synonym for a thing.
And [the rule applies] to the deity as well, because it is for that purpose.

Commentary: Even regarding a deity, that for whose sake something is enjoined is not to be substituted. That which is called a "deity" is that for the sake of which something is prescribed; another [entity] standing in its place as a substitute would not be the deity.
For a deity is indeed one who is invoked, not one who is not invoked;
and the word "deity" implies a connection. Whatever is mentioned for the sake of a particular [rite], that alone is its deity, and no other.
The term "deity" (*devatā*) refers to a relative [of the sacrificer] and is not a word denoting a genus;
therefore, for this reason as well, there can be no substitute for a deity.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: the deity and so forth are not subject to substitution, because they are connected with a different purpose, because they fall under the category of non-substitution, and because they involve a different principle of application.
Viśvarūpa: "Regarding the gods, in rites such as the sprinkling with mantras for Agni, is there a substitute or not?
As before, there is one here; however, since that which exists in the primary [substance] does not exist in this case, there is no such substitute."
Bhaṭṭa: Thus, although a substitute (pratinidhi) is prescribed in all other cases, it does not apply to the deity (*devatā*).

For if the nature of the deity consisted merely in the object itself—as defined by the form conveyed by the word that serves as the instrument for utterance at the time of renunciation (*tyāga*)—then, even though there is a restriction regarding the specific word taught in the injunction (*vidhi*), since the sacrifice and so forth would still be accomplished provided that meaning is conveyed (even if the original word cannot be used due to illness or other causes), a substitute might indeed be employed through the application of another word, whether primary (*śrauta*) or secondary (*lakṣaṇika*), capable of conveying that same meaning.

But when, according to the method to be explained in the tenth book (*adhikaraṇa*), the status of being a deity belongs either to that which is qualified by the word *vi-vigata* or to such a word alone, then what occasion is there for another word?

For the status of being a deity—which is established through cognition and linguistic usage, takes the form of an unobstructed limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and consists in being the object of an utterance at the time of the offering of the oblation—is not possible in another word, since it is necessarily restricted to the nature of the word *vi-vigata*.

If, however, the object (*artha*) is also somehow admitted to have the status of a deity (*devatātva*), then even in that case, one must accept that it is expressed by a word devoid of such [specific] grammatical gender; thus, the absence of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) must be justified.

For this very reason, even when the sacrifice itself is conceived as the deity, since that desired [deity-status] is constituted by its being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and because it cannot be implied (*ākṣepa*), the injunction regarding the deity is indeed an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).
And in the event of its impossibility, there is simply the omission of the sacrificial category (*yāgapadārtha*).

However, when there is a failure regarding the deity, the statement "Prajāpati" is authoritative as a prescriptive injunction in its absence; therefore, the performance should be carried out exactly in that manner. Likewise, there is no substitute for the locus of the oblation (the fire).

In that regard, since the Āhavanīya and other fires are established by the injunction for their formal installation (*ādhāna*), they fall within the scope of the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice; thus, they are understood to be qualifying conditions for the eligibility [to perform the rite].
Precisely because it is not an object of relinquishment according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*), there is no suspicion of a substitute (*pratinidhi*).

However, even in cases where the status of being a locus (*ādhāra*) is based on a scriptural injunction (*vācanika*)—whether pertaining to the ordinary world or to the sacrificial vessel (*pātra*) and so forth—even though that status falls within the scope of the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*), no substitute is permitted because it serves a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

For an oblation (*homa*), which consists merely of the act of throwing [the offering] into the fire in the form of an activity conducive to separation from the previous location, has no requirement for a locus.
For this very reason, even that injunction is indeed an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction).

Since the status of the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth as the substratum for the falling [of the oblation] is established by the word itself through its function of preventing such a fall—and since this purpose is accomplished by one [means] alone, a combination [of means] is impossible and thus not to be accepted.
Consequently, even in that case, there is no evidence for the existence of a substitute for it, provided it serves to produce that [specific result].
However, in some cases, there is indeed an explicit scriptural injunction regarding the status of the Brāhmaṇa’s hand and so forth.
Likewise, even in these mantras intended for the manifestation of meaning, there is no substitute for another word or another mantra.

For when the meaning has not been understood through other means such as meditation, the possibility of a substitute is not even to be considered, precisely because of the absence of anything that could convey that meaning.
Once that [object] has been understood, there is no recourse to it without depending on a reminder (*smāraka*).

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that the recitation of the prescribed mantra would not occur in cases where the object is already remembered by oneself; for in those cases, the recitation of the mantra is necessary because one assumes that it brings about prosperity (*abhyudaya*) through the very fact that the mantra is employed as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) to ensure the successful completion of the rite. However, there is a difference [between these cases and the case of a substitute]: since there is no evidence that a substitute constitutes a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for that which is implied by the injunction of the ritual action, there is no recitation [of a mantra for the substitute]. Thus, the two cases are dissimilar.

Thus, since there is no authoritative basis for the measure of another [substance] when the primary one is lost, there can be no substitute even for ritual acts such as the *āghāra* libation or the *prayāja* offerings, because they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

However, for those acts which have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), such a substitute certainly exists. As for the point raised by some here—that even in the case of the non-performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, which has an invisible purpose, there is no substitute—[that is not so].

When the intention for the performance endowed with the sixteen subsidiary parts has been formed, if by chance the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is also included therein, then—since there is no absence of the state of being endowed with the sixteen parts—it is stated that there is no need for a substitute for those eight [subsidiaries] beyond what is already present.

This is because, from the injunction "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* at the *atirātra* sacrifice," it is understood that even in the absence of taking the *ṣoḍaśin*, the benefit to the ritual (*ṛtūpakāra*) is accomplished through the mere presence of the other subsidiaries; thus, even when the *ṣoḍaśin* is taken, there is no evidence for its serving an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
For this very reason, if the *ṣoḍaśin* is taken there, only the prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for an unintended act must be performed.
Maṇḍana: "There is no substitute for the mantra and so forth.
Śaṅkara: "That [substitute] is not accepted for the deity and so forth.
That is the substitute.
The Section on Deities.
The deity is the primary factor.
Ritual duties are not prompted by the deity.
The deities do not exist as impurities such as physical forms.
Or rather, the deity should be the motivator [of the ritual], because the meal is for its sake, like that of a guest.
The Commentary says: This is not so; that Agni and the others are not motivators.
All deities ought to be the motivators of all ritual duties.
Why? Because eating is for that purpose.
For this "sacrifice," which is called *yāga*, is indeed the act of feeding the deity;
the substance to be eaten is offered to the deity with the thought, "She shall eat it."
For this sacrifice is heard in scripture as having the deity as its recipient (*saṃpradāna*). And a recipient is indeed that which is most desired by the agent even with respect to the action.
Therefore, the deity is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*); and with respect to the deity, both the substance and the action are subordinate.
The sacrifice to Agni is indeed the worship of a deity;
and in the world, worship is observed to be subordinate to that which is to be worshipped.
This should be viewed as being like the case of a guest:
just as whatever service is rendered to a guest is entirely prompted by the guest,
so it is with this as well.
He said:
"But by speaking thus, you have effectively admitted that the deity possesses a physical body and partakes of food.
It is replied:
And [it says] "cādam" (and so).
The deity possesses a body and also eats.
Why? Because of traditional scripture (smṛti).
Because of figurative usage and because of the observation of other meanings;
for thus they record in their tradition that "the deity possesses a body," and scripture (smṛti) is an authority for us.
Likewise, they treat the deity as if it possessed a physical body;
they depict Yama with a staff in his hand and speak of him accordingly,
and similarly, Varuṇa with a noose in his hand, and Indra with a thunderbolt in his hand.
We postulate a double measure even from figurative usage (*upacāra*) based on memory. Likewise, there is a statement with another purpose which shows a deity possessing a body:
"O Indra, [I have] grasped your right hand" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.47.1). For indeed, a person who has a physical body possesses both a right and a left hand.
Likewise: "O Indra, these two boundless worlds are indeed small for you when you grasp them as a mere handful, O Maghavan" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.30.5).
"Kāśiḥ" means a fist;
that too is possible only for one who possesses a human body.
Thus, with his thick neck, pot-bellied form, and strong arms, Indra, like a swan in his exhilaration, strikes down the Vṛtras.
Thus (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.17.8). There is a perception of the body of a person consisting of a neck, belly, and arms; therefore, it is said that "the deity possesses a physical form" and "it eats."
How is this understood? From scripture (smṛti), from figurative usage (upacāra), and from the observation of other meanings. Thus they remember: "The deity has eaten."
And thus they treat this [Soma] as if it were being eaten, in that they present various services to it.
Furthermore, there is a scriptural indication (*anyārthadarśana*) that leads one to understand the deity as eating:

"O Indra, drink and eat of what has been set forth" (*adīndra piba ca prasthitasya*), and likewise, "He holds all things within his bellies" (*viśvā sannāni jaṭhareṣu dhatte*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.95.10).
"Drink the thirty lakes at once with a single impulse" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.77.4).
He says: "The deity does not eat;
for if the deity were to eat, the oblation offered to the deity would be consumed."
It is said: the deity is understood to be a non-eater of food, like a honey-gatherer.
How so? When an oblation is offered to the deity, it becomes sapless;
therefore, it is understood that the deity consumes the essence of the food.
Regarding this, one who considers that the sacrifice is for the purpose of propitiating the deity advances the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
the sacrifice does not have a [future] result as its objective, but rather has the propitiation of the deity as its purpose.
Why? Because of the *taddhita* suffix [in the word *āgneyaḥ*, meaning "that which has Agni as its deity"].

The deity Agni is a qualifier of this word *asya* (this), and the word *asya* denotes a substance (*dravya*), while the other [word, *agni*,] is its qualifier. That [substance] becomes a qualifier of the word *agni* only if it is offered with reference to Agni; it is not otherwise. And when the substance is offered with reference to Agni, then Agni becomes the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
Furthermore, the recipient is more primary than even that which is most desired for the sake of the action (*karma*).

(How so? The act of sacrificing pervades the substance, and by means of the substance, the recipient [is reached]. Therefore, the sacrifice is for the sake of Agni, just as in the expression, "He gives a cow to the teacher."
[Regarding the statement] "a gift for the sake of the preceptor":
furthermore, they record that the root *yaji* is used in the sense of worshiping a deity (*devapūjā*) [as the grammatical rule states]: "The roots *yaja*, *devapūjā*, *saṃgati*, *karaṇa*, and *dāna*.
Therefore, in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), one should propitiate the deity through sacrifice; from that [deity], heaven will result.
By means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

Commentary: If a deity were the mistress of some object and, being worshipped, were to become pleased, then this worship of the deity would be undertaken for the sake of propitiating that object. Since neither of these two conditions exists, it is said that [the deity] is a "deity by implication" (*arthāpatti-devatā*). How is this understood? From traditional usage (*smṛti*) and from the observation of other purposes (*anyārthadarśana*).
For thus they remember: "The deities have mastery over these objects.

Likewise, there is the figurative usage of "village of the gods" (*devagrāma*) and "field of the gods" (*devakṣetra*), which demonstrates that very same traditional remembrance (*smṛti*). Similarly, another scriptural passage showing a different purpose indicates the Lord as the deity: "Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over the earth; Indra rules over the waters; Indra rules over the mountains."
Indra is the increaser; Indra is the lord of the wise; Indra is the one to be invoked in peace and in exertion.
Thus [it says in] Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.89.10:
"O Indra, lord of this world, beholder of heaven, lord of the waters.
Likewise, from the usage in the Smṛti, it is understood that he is pleased.
For thus they remember: "The deity is pleased.
Likewise, they speak figuratively: "Paśupati is pleased with him," "Merit has arisen for him," or "Vaiśravaṇa is pleased with him; wealth and prosperity have come to him.

Similarly, there is a scriptural observation regarding another matter: "By means of oblations alone he gratifies the gods who consume the offerings," and "Being pleased with him, they bestow upon him food and vigor."

And therefore, there is a connection with that. The Commentary: Consequently, there is a connection of the deity with that fruit; it becomes possible for [the deity] to be worshipped. He who worships the deity—that is, serves [her]—to him she imparts the fruit.
How is this understood? From both scripture (smṛti) and figurative usage (upacāra), as in the section concerning the deities (devatādhikaraṇa).
For they remember that "the deity bestows the fruit. He demonstrates that very same traditional recollection through figurative usage: "By him Paśupati was propitiated; by him a son was obtained.
By means of that [recollection], he shows here the observation of another purpose: "He, with his followers, with his sons, with his kinsmen, brings forth booty and wealth with his men."
"He who serves the father of the gods with a faithful mind and an oblation, [serves] Brahmaṇaspati" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.3.14.1).
Likewise: "Indra indeed satisfies him with offspring and cattle."
Therefore, the deity is propitiated by the offering of oblations and by words of praise;
being pleased, she bestows the fruit. How does she grant that specific fruit for which one desires it, having been propitiated by a particular ritual act?
The Sun is not capable of giving that.
From this statement it is understood who gives what;
as there is a statement regarding Agni, so there is none regarding the Sun.
"Because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the sacrificial act should be primary; the mention of the deity is secondary.
Commentary: The position beginning with "adhi" is set aside.
And not...

Regarding the section on the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*), concerning such passages as "in the Lord" (*īśe*) and so forth, we determine—having perceived that the deities lack actual sovereignty—that this word is used in a figurative sense.

To this, he replies: "The sovereignty of this [deity] is understood precisely from the authority of the scriptural statement; for whatever purposes people employ objects, we determine that it is solely due to the intention of the deity."
In this regard, the intention of those who attend upon the deity is understood from the means of valid cognition known as direct perception;
it cannot be denied.
Even those who describe the deity as sovereign do not deny the intention of the attendants.
What do they say? They say that the deity acts in such a way that the intention of the attendants is fulfilled.
And he is not truly sovereign who conforms to another's intention, for there can be no exercise of authority on his part if it does not proceed from his own intention.
Furthermore, this statement is not [to be taken literally], because it is an instruction regarding the present time.
Due to contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is understood to be a figurative praise (*stutivāda*).
And since a figurative praise is possible, it is not understood that [the Lord's] sovereignty follows from the authority of the verbal testimony.
Furthermore, the deity is not connected with the fruit—that [deity] which might be served for that purpose.

As for what was stated regarding "recollection," "conventional usage," and "the perception of another meaning"—namely, "he gives" and "he is pleased"—among those, the points concerning recollection and conventional usage have already been explained.
As for the perception of another meaning, namely, "to him he hands over the sharpened arrows," that too has been addressed.
Because another injunction is recorded: "He says, 'It is to be carried around on the right,'" and "In that way, indeed, Indra causes him to prosper with offspring and cattle.
Herein lies the prescription for the oblation dedicated to Indra.

Therefore, the deity is not the motivator. Dupa: "Alternatively, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the sacrificial act should be primary; the scriptural mention of the deity is subordinate. Regarding the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," from the latter half of the word "should sacrifice"—that is, from the expression denoting efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—three requirements arise.

In this regard, first of all, the object to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) requires an inquiry: "What should one cultivate? This is satisfied by the word denoting the result (*phala*). Then, a second inquiry arises: "By what means is that which is being cultivated cultivated? This second inquiry is satisfied by the first half of the verse.
The third expectancy, "How [is it to be performed]? is satisfied by the acts of adding fuel to the fire (*abhyanvādhāna*) and so forth, due to their proximity.
Thus, from this sentence, the fruit is heard as resulting from the sacrifice (*yāga*), not from the deity.
But was it not stated that the deity is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) [and thus primary]?
It is said:
sacrifice impels toward the accomplishment of a result (or "results," as in the Ratna edition of Ānandāśrama).
And that [sacrifice] is not possible without a material substance and a deity.
Furthermore, when substance (*dravya*) and deity (*devatā*) are required, they are required solely as *kārakas* (factors of action), not as the objective aspect (*bhāvyāṃśa*).

In that regard, the substance functions as a *kāraka* through the third case (*tṛtīyā*), while the deity [functions as a *kāraka*] through a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) or the fourth case (*caturthī*).
And if that deity-*kāraka* were not to attain primacy with respect to the sacrifice (*yāga*), then the sacrifice itself would not be accomplished.
Furthermore, because the sacrifice would not be accomplished, the causal factor (kāraka) itself would not even exist.
And if the sacrifice were not to receive those subordinate elements (guṇas), it would not even attain its own existence.
Therefore, the state of being a subordinate element must be understood as being inseparable from the sacrifice.
The status of being the primary factor is inseparable from the character of the deity.
Furthermore, an inseparable operation is not the cause for either subordinate or primary status, because it is not so enjoined;
for it is by means of the sacrifice that one is enjoined toward the fruit.
Thinking, "I shall accomplish the fruit, not otherwise," one must become subordinate to the deity through an action that is invariably concomitant [with it].
Therefore, in all cases, there is a desire for the result;
therein, it must be understood what is intended to be expressed and what is not intended to be expressed.
In that regard, in the world, the intention [of the speaker] is determined by the purpose;
in the Veda, however, it is determined by the word.
And because the sacrifice, being proximate through the word, is the means for accomplishing the fruit, its primacy is understood, while the deity is understood to be subordinate.
Furthermore, subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is not characterized by utility.

What then? It has been established that it is characterized by injunction (*codanā*). What is the purpose of this inquiry? If the sacrifice is for the sake of propitiating the deity, then the deity is the object of worship and the sacrifice is the act of worship.
Furthermore, worship is a worldly matter;
in that regard, what assurance is there that the Sun is worshipped in exactly the same manner as Fire is worshipped?
It could even be the opposite at times.
Furthermore, it is not possible that the Sun, being alone, is satisfied by worship, whereas Agni, when accompanied by other deities, is satisfied by the worship of Soma and Indra;
for Devadatta, though nourished by extremely sweet honey, milk, and the like, does not become a lover of sour gruel merely through association with Yajñadatta.

In our established conclusion (*siddhānta*), ritual properties (*dharma*) are connected with that which is being brought about (*bhāvyamāna*); therefore, in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice, the properties are required precisely for that which is being brought about.
In that case, the attainment of the ritual details (*dharma*) occurs through similarity, because the ritual details pertain to the non-worldly (*alaukika*).

Alternatively, when the sacrifice is for the purpose of propitiating a deity, then— as stated in the rule "in the event of a conflict, it shall be determined by the oblation" (*vipratipattau haviṣā niyamyeta*)— the conclusion of the Siddhānta is that in a conflict between the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*), the extension of the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) is determined by the commonality of the substance.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, because sacrifice is for the purpose of propitiating a deity, the commonality of the deity alone is more powerful than the commonality of the substance, since the latter is more remote.
[This concludes] the section concerning the deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*).
In the case of a guest, there is an absence of the primary nature of the ritual act, because that [reception of a guest] has satisfaction as its primary aim.
Commentary: That which was stated, "because of the guest-offering," must be refuted. The guest-offering (ātithya) should be associated with a guest.
For that principle is prescribed in the context of hospitality:
a guest must be honored;
one should act in such a way that he is pleased.
"Whether it be giving or providing food,
whatever is pleasing to him should be done; whatever is not pleasing to him should not be made to do by force."
But here, in this ritual action, there is an absence of the injunction for [offering] with affection;
therefore, it is not a case of "remaining in a discordant state.
Śā—(The prima facie view: "Because Indra and others are the recipients (saṃpradāna), the object (karman) also possesses primacy."
"Sacrifice (yāga) is worship (pūjā), and the guest-offering (atithi-bhājana) would be its subsidiary (aṅga).
This being the position reached, we reply: "The animal-nature of the sacrifice itself is declared to be the means for achieving the fruit;
and the deity is for the sake of that [sacrifice], because it is useful for its accomplishment."
Since the sacrifice is of the nature of that which is to be accomplished (sādhya), it accepts the deity as its means (sādhana);
and the deity, being of an established nature (siddha-rūpa), is the means for that [sacrifice].
Therefore, the ritual properties (dharma) are prompted by the *apūrva*.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: although *soma* is predominant, it might not be the motivator (*prayojaka*); thus, having raised an objection against the motivator-status of the preceding [element], the author now establishes it.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: the deity alone should apply all the ritual duties (*dharma*), because the sacrifice is performed with the thought, "This is the oblation for the deity; the deity shall consume it. The term "eating" (*bhojana*) is used here as a designation for the sacrifice.
Since the eating is for the sake of the deity, the example given for its status as "eating" is "the guest" (*atithi*).

Bhāṭṭa: Thus, having for the time being accepted the *apūrva*, the claim that the propitiation of the deity is the motivator [of the ritual] has been refuted. For the deity is either the motivator with respect to the *apūrva*, or it is [the motivator] through its bestowing the fruit upon that [apūrva]. Indeed, this [deity] is not a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) in what is to be enjoined; rather, it is appropriate for the *apūrva* to bear the fruit. Bhāṭṭa: In this manner, having provisionally accepted the *apūrva*, the status of the deity’s favor as the motivator has been rejected.
But here, setting that aside, the doubt is raised incidentally that the temple of the deity alone might be the motivating factor; this is addressed at length.

In this regard, because the deity is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and because that recipient is primary even in relation to the object (*karman*) as it is intended [by the agent], the sacrifice is understood to have the nature of an act of worship (*pūjā*). Furthermore, with respect to its utility, since the Veda bestows the fruit—following such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as "He alone leads him to prosperity" and "Indra, being satisfied, satisfies him with progeny"—there is no evidence for the sacrifice itself to be the producer of the fruit; consequently, there is all the more no evidence for it to be the means to the *apūrva*.

Or, even if the deity were intended [as the primary object], such an assumption is untenable because the Brāhmaṇa—mentioned in injunctions such as "he gives a cow to a Brāhmaṇa"—cannot possibly be the giver of the fruit, and thus cannot be the primary element; since his primacy is impossible, there is no justification for assuming him to be so. On the contrary, according to the principle of the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, when the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) which has the sacrifice as its instrument requires an objective to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), it is heaven alone that is construed as such. Furthermore, if the deity were merely the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), it would be the goal (*uddeśya*) of the action and could not in any way be considered the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Thus, the deity cannot be the primary object.

Even though the sacrifice is indeed called a "deity," nevertheless, since the sacrifice requires an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*) to produce its fruit, and because no such operation exists [in the form of a physical act], one must postulate it. Rather than postulating a prior [operation], as in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, one should postulate that the grace of the deity mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves as the medium. Thus, the fact that the result is produced by that [grace] is established. Furthermore, since the deity's grace is otherwise inexplicable unless it involves a body and the enjoyment [of offerings], there is no fault even if one postulates a body, enjoyment, and so forth, in accordance with the explanatory passages and other authorities.

This being the case, if *prasāda* (divine grace) consists of a desire (*icchā*), then, because it would follow as an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that it could be the cause of its own fruit merely by virtue of being a desire, it must be expressed as a desire of such a form that the person [the devotee] is the agent of the state [of grace] and thus possesses the status of being the cause of the fruit. And in that case, there is complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of causality. Furthermore, since the status of being the agent of that [grace] does not depart even when the enjoyment of the fruit produced by the [state of] *daśā* and so forth has occurred, there would result the production of a fruit for one person from the *daśā*-offering performed by another through the grace of that other. Therefore, [grace] is the cause with respect to a specific individual instance of the fruit (*phalavyakti*) delimited by the nature of being that specific instance.

The causality must be stated as being of the nature of a desire in the form "let there be the manifestation of that fruit. And thus, in the postulation of multiple cause-and-effect relations, there is complexity (gaurava) regarding the delimitors of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).
Furthermore, if such grace were at the end of the satiation of Brahmins, then there would be the undesirable consequence that sacrifices do not arise at all.

If, however, intermediate propitiations (*avāntaraprasāda*) arising from those sacrifices—such as those produced by the *Āgneya* or *Yatkiñcitvat* offerings—are desired [as the means], then, since the unfailing nature of the will of the deities is established in the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), the result would necessarily follow even if one were to perform an act that causes their displeasure by chance.

Now, having accepted this very [scriptural] explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the causality toward that which is delimited by a heterogeneous fruit belongs to such a "great grace" (*mahāprasāda*) precisely by virtue of its being a heterogeneous entity, just as in the theory of the unseen potency (*apūrva*). Furthermore, the intermediate graces (*avāntaraprasāda*) possess causality toward the great grace and its fruit precisely by virtue of their being heterogeneous instances of that [grace]. The delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the causality is the state of being performed by one who is initiated by a teacher who has himself produced [the grace]; and the delimiting condition for the effect-nature is inherence (*samavāya*) in the portion of the fruit.
Consequently, there is no production of the fruit in the agent [of the sacrifice].

If it is argued that there may be such a proximity (*pratyāsatti*) between the intermediate favor (*avāntaraprasāda*) and the great favor (*mahāprasāda*)—namely, that in their mutual relationship of cause and effect, the proximity consists simply in both inhering in the same sacrifice which produces them—[we reply: no, because the complexity of the relationship (*saṃbandhagaurava*) is a logical fault. [This is established] in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (Topic 2138), where the effectness (*kāryatā*) defined by the causality residing in the sacrifice [is shown to reside in the deity].
Furthermore, you are unable to provide a definition for the relation of "container and contained" (ghaṭaka-sambandha).
In my view, however, there is simplicity, as the relation for all causal factors (kāraṇa) and their effects (kārya) is simply inherence (samavāya).
By this, the position that *prasāda* is a specific kind of clarity (*saulabhyaviśeṣa*) is also refuted.

Nor should it be argued that this "gravity" (gaurava), once established in its function known as *prasāda* (favor) toward the meaning and so forth, possesses the character of being "result-oriented" (*phalamukhatva*).

For while an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) may be justified by its quality of being a praise (*stāvakatva*), it lacks the capacity for independent inference (*kalpakatva*) due to its inherent nature. When there is a requirement for a function, one must—following the logic of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice—infer another word expressive of that function; and in postulating that [praise] as the function, since the status of being a function is constituted by causality, that [causality] must be preceded by the apprehension of a relation. Consequently, it is untenable for the gravity of the relation itself to be rooted in the result.

Therefore, those [words] that convey qualities such as "serene" (*prasāda*) and so forth, being for the purpose of manifesting the specific deity—such as the mantra-deity Devī and others—are not untenable, because they serve to manifest the qualifying attributes by virtue of their meaningfulness.
Whether the relation constituting this qualification is adventitious (*āhārya*) or non-adventitious (*anāhārya*) is another matter.

Since the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) are eulogistic through that very same relation, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise even in them; thus, there is no need for any other [theoretical] construction.
Or let it be so; nevertheless, because that would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the injunction (*vidhi*), [the mantra] is for the purpose of invoking the deity.
Deityhood (*devatātva*)...

The *nigada* beginning with "O Agni, bring hither [the gods] for me" (*agnim agna āvaha*) and so forth, which serves the purpose of invoking the deities, is recited by the Hotṛ priest between the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *prayāja* offerings.
(Vi. 10.1.1, Section 3). At the time of invoking the deities, the invocation of Viṣṇu Urukrama should not be performed in the *vaiśvadeva-caru* offering.

(Bhā. 10.1.1.1–3, Section 3). A rule based on the deity is set aside by one based on the material, just as in the case of the *aindra-puroḍāśa*: although the procedure of the *sāṃnāyya* would apply due to the commonality of the deity, it is superseded by the procedure of the *āgneya* offering, which applies due to the commonality of the material.

Vāla-pṛ. 141: The *yājyā* verse serves to indicate the deity. Bhāṣya 1.2.3.15.35: When there is identity of deity in a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), there is a single performance (*tantra*) for the offering of the omentum (*vasāhoma*).
Bhāṣya 1.1.2.15.24: Similitude based on the substance is more powerful than similitude based on the deity.
Bhāṣya 8.1.12.32–34: "The nature of a deity (devatātva) consists in being connected [to a sacrifice] through the conjunction with Agni and Soma" (saṃsṛṣṭavṛtti).
Saṃkarṣa 4.4.6: "The nature of a deity is the state of being the object of an act directed toward the substance being relinquished.
Sūtra-pṛ. 749: "The nature of a deity is the state of being the intended recipient of the substance being relinquished."
*Mīmāṃsā*. Deityhood (*devatātva*) consists in being the object of the utterance of a word ending in the dative case at the time of renunciation (*tyāga*).

*Rahasya*, p. 102. Deityhood belongs to whichever [entity] is expressed by the word itself, whether it be suitable or unsuitable; thus, it is not caused by genus (*jāti*). *Vārttika* 2.2.123, p. 537. Deityhood is the state of being represented by a mantra.
*Saṃkarṣa* 2.4.2: Deityhood (*devatātva*) consists in the function of the *yajyā* [verse] and takes the form of an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).

*Bhāṭṭa* 3.1.16: Deityhood is refuted as belonging to the mere word. Now, one might object: "Since deityhood belongs to the mere word, and since the words 'Indra' and 'Bhendra' are distinct, how can there be identity of deity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... (The commentary on the ninth and tenth [chapters] states: "And the deity is not the mere word").

(Vārttika, p. 417). Now, an objection is raised: "But [in the sūtra] *api vā śabdapūrvatvād yajñakarma pradhānaṃ syād guṇatve devatāśrutiḥ* (9.1.9), since it has been stated that by the principle of the co-utterance of the past and the future (*bhūtabhavyasamuccāraṇanyāya*), the deity is subordinate (*guṇatva*) with respect to the sacrifice (*yajña*), one might suspect: 'Is it not the case that even for the ritual act (*karman*), the deity is understood to be intended (*abhipretatva*) because of its being the object of the sacrifice? To this, [the author] replies: 'We do not deny its status as the intended object.'"

In the Bhāṣya—“By the word *taddhita* or by the dative case, it is understood from the sentence that this [word] is intended to have the status of a deity” (Bhā. p. 1652)—it is refuted that mere sound (*śabdamātra*) constitutes the deity-status. This is because, if a collection of meaningless phonemes lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it lacks the fitness for connection with a *taddhita* suffix or a dative case; thus, by mentioning such a connection, the acceptance of meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*) is established, thereby excluding mere sound.

And in the tenth [book], under the sūtra *vidhi-śabdasya mantratve bhāvaḥ syāt tena codanā* (10.4.23), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that since the deity can be designated by any synonym whatsoever during the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, there is no need for respect toward the specific word for Agni and others found in the injunction (*vidhi*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) maintains that because the connection of the oblation with the deity is enjoined by the word "Agni" occurring in the injunction *āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*, the function of the mantra—the utterance of the word found in the injunction—is required for the purpose of designating the deity. Having asked, "What indeed is this so-called deity?", he sets aside two definitions: first, that the deity is whatever word such as "Agni" or "Vāta" is used in the Veda in connection with Indra and others (e.g., *agnir devatā, vāto devatā*), because this fails to include terms like "day" (*ahaḥ*) or "tiger" (*śārdūla*); and second, his own view stated in the Bhāṣya: "The deities are subtle, external, the oblation, and the clarified butter" (Bhā. p. 1927). He supports this by citing usage such as *āgneyaṃ sūktam* ("a hymn dedicated to Agni") and *āgneyaṃ haviḥ* ("an oblation dedicated to Agni"), as well as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating, "Some deities partake of the oblations (*āhutibhāj*), while others partake of the hymns (*stomabhāj*) and the meters (*chandobhāvāḥ*). From this, one understands that the meaning of the term "deity" consists in being the object of praise in a hymn and the object of designation for the oblation being offered; thus, whether they are embodied or unembodied, conscious or unconscious, anything that is intended as the goal of a sacrifice becomes a deity upon hearing of it. This is further supported by the Bhāṣya statement: "Whether it be an embodied or conscious entity, its status as a deity will exist provided it is intended as the goal of the sacrifice" (Bhā. p. 1927). Furthermore, the Bhāṣya states: "That [entity] becomes a deity when the intention is made that the oblation is to be abandoned after remembering or uttering the word that denotes it" (Bhā. p. 1927). Since the direction is for the sake of utterance, and since words like "Prajāpati" in passages such as *prajāpatiṃ manasā yajeta* are understood through their denotation (*vācya*), the denoted object is declared to be the deity. Anticipating the objection, "If this is so, then one might very well designate Agni by any word whatsoever," he begins: "This would be so if the word 'Agni' were merely for the sake of abandonment, and if the actual object were employed for the sake of connecting it with the oblation" (Bhā. p. 1927). He concludes: "The status of a deity as a means of sacrifice (*yajñasādhanabhāva*) does not occur by way of its form."

By what means, then? By the statement in the Bhāṣya beginning with "by the word [as] connected" (Bhā. p. 1928), the status of the word as the deity is refuted, because it is declared to be distinct from that which is connected to the word.
(Su. p. 643) Deity-status consists in being a recipient of the oblation and being a recipient of praise. (p.
669) It is the meaning, when heard and expressed by the verbal [form], that attains the status of the deity, and not otherwise.
Or rather: Pāṇini 6.3.1.18 states that being a deity does not consist solely in being the intended recipient of a substance;
such is the nature of deityhood.
Regarding the definition of a deity (*devatā*):

if it were merely the state of being an object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), then in such cases as "he gives a staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa" or "he gives gold to the Āgneya," the Maitrāvaruṇa and others would also incur the status of deity because they too possess the state of being objects of reference for the substance.

Furthermore, if deity-hood consisted in mere objectivity, then even that which is substituted could potentially be a deity; consequently, the principle of the non-existence of a substitute for a deity (*devatā-pratinidhi*) which will be stated in the sixth book would be contradicted.
*Soma*, p. 63 (4.4): The word itself possesses the status of a deity (*devatātva*).

*Bhāṭṭa*, 9.3.12: Having accepted the twofold nature of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), some maintain that although the recipient designated by "receiving" (*pratigrahaṇa*) lacks the status of a deity, the recipient designated by "not rejecting" (*anirākaraṇa*) does possess it; *Sūtra*, p. 832:
"Whatever object is enjoined as a deity in a particular instance..."
If there were even the slightest difference from that [prescribed form], it would not be understood as being "the deity.

Furthermore, if whatever [deity] he ordains, in whatever manner, and for whatever purpose, is accomplished exactly so during the performance, then it is determined that "this is measured by that [injunction]. However, if even a slight discrepancy occurs here, once the injunction has ceased its operation, another means of valid cognition must be sought.

"And that [object] does not exist; thus there is a lack of authoritative means of knowledge" (Vārttika 2.1.5, p. 422). In the mantras, Agni and others are designated as primary and are recognized as deities (1.4.6.9, p. 340), because the status of being a deity is something to be accomplished through ritual performance.

2|3|15|4|601. Because the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is restricted to a dual-deity [offering] due to its residing in a composite [deity] (vyāsajya-vṛttitvāt) 1|3|15|14. Having stated the definition of the status of being a single deity with the words "because the status of being a deity is based on the word" (*śabdanimittatvena*), etc., another definition was stated with the words "in the case of the term 'deity-status' of the object" (*arthasya devatātvapade*), etc.
(Bhāṭṭa 8|2|7). [Question:
How can the status of being a deity—which is characterized as the enjoyer of the oblation that is being abandoned—be the cause for the conceptualization of a sacrifice?
Su. p. 929: Because [the deity] is understood as having the nature of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛ).
p. 929: Because the status of being a deity is untenable without a sacrifice (yāga).
p. 928: There is an absence of the status of being a deity without an injunction (vidhi).

Page 775. And the indicators of deity-status (*devatātva*) are: the word "deity" (*devatā*), a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the dative case, the accusative case, and the wording of a mantra (*mantravarṇa*).

In passages such as "Prajāpati is the deity," "the deities," and so forth, as well as "some [say] the Night is the deity," and "some [say] the Nakṣatras are the deity," there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the deityhood that culminates in the status of being a deity—the deityhood consisting of the nature of the substance-deity (*dravyadevatātva*) which is denoted by the word "deity.
In cases such as the renunciation (*tyāga*) of the root-meaning, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Thus, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) such as *āgneya* denotes a specific substance qualified by divinity.
Nor should it be argued that its denotation of a specific substance is unestablished;

for if it were to denote a category existing in the intellect (*buddhistha-prakāra*), then the rule for secondary derivation, "this is its deity" (*asā 'sya devatā*, Pāṇini 4.2.24), would apply to the sense of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).

And thus, the expressive power (*śakti*) of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) resides either in the eight-pot-sherd-ness (*aṣṭākapālatva*) or in the individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) of that mode which is present in the intellect as qualified by the deity.
However, the [deity] delimited by that [mode] is obtained through the principle of the individual (*vyaktinyāya*).
There is no expressive power in "being present in the intellect," because there is no appearance [of the object] as being present in the intellect.

Even though there is a diversity among those types, the possibility of grasping the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) exists because "being present in the intellect" (*buddhisthatva*) serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). It is the direction [of this argument] that what serves as a secondary indicator for the grasping of potency does not possess the status of being the delimiting factor of the denotable meaning (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). (Maṇi, pp. 162–163). Two deities should not perform their respective functions together.
Bhāṣya 10.7.27: When there is a conflict between two deities, the substance is more powerful.
Bhāṭṭa 8.1.8: In a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), archetypal deities such as the pair of deities are set aside by the designated deity and other factors.
Bhāṣya 10.7.16, 58–60: The conjunction of two deities is the motivator for the injunction of the sacrifice.

"One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu"; "One should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya. (TS 2.3.15.1–2). The meditation on the deity must be performed by the Hotṛ priest prior to the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call; this is established in Saṃkarṣa 4.3.6. Meditation on the deity occurs before the *vaṣaṭ* call because of the use of the future tense in the injunction: "He should meditate upon that [deity] when about to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call" (*tāṃ dhyāyed vaṣaṭkariṣyan*).

Since the meditation on the deity is enjoined by the rule, "He should meditate upon whichever deity he is about to address with the *vaṣaṭ* call," one may perform it at any time, as no specific restriction regarding the timing has been prescribed.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: because of the capacity of the time immediately following birth—as seen in such injunctions as "he takes hold of the newborn with joined palms" and "he breathes over the newborn"—and because of the observation of a restrictive rule, meditation (*dhyāna*) is prescribed in the ritual of deity-worship; thus, meditation on the deity must occur prior even to the *vaṣaṭ*-call.

Furthermore, this restriction is established by another scriptural statement: "For whichever deity the oblation has been taken, one should meditate upon her; while about to offer it, he directly pleases that very deity" (Saṃkarṣa. 4.3.6). This is the son of the Deity.

The section concerning the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) should be consulted (*Brahmasūtra* 9.1.4.6–10). The status of being a deity (*devatātva*) functions only when there is no contradiction with other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Why should even one of the two [statements]—namely, the scriptural mention of distinction (*bhedashruti*)—not have its own primary meaning according to the logic of the section on deities? (*Saṃkṣepa-rāmatīrtha*, 3.283). The designation of the deities—such as "this is for such-and-such and for such-and-such"—should be performed by collecting [the offerings], where the *caru* oblations and the *puroḍāśa* cakes are intermingled (*Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa* 1.3.23).

The deity-abiding [form] (devatāniṣṭha) is the form of the deity; even for a word expressing qualities abiding in the deity, there is an invocation in the modification (vikṛti), because the deities of the auxiliary parts (aṅga) are also included. 12|1|124–28. There is no application at the beginning.

In the *pavamāna* [stotras] and others, there is the designation of the deity as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) alone. Bhāṣya 10.4.15.30–31: Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the worship of the deity (this is the prima facie view).
Since a word (*pada*) is a specific form of sound, it must be uttered [to be effective].
Saṃkarṣa. 9|1|14|16; 2|4|12. Furthermore, through the manifestation of the deity, there is a perceptible benefit, namely the accomplishment of the sacrifice.
Even when the word for the deity is joined [with other elements], there is no violation of the number seventeen.

rather, in the connection with each respective deity—as in "We sacrifice to Agni" (*yajāmahe 'gnim*)—there is the indication of seventeen general deities.

In such injunctions as "one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *puroḍāśa* (grain-cake), but not an extension of the properties of the *sāṃnāyya* (milk-offering).

Even for words such as *saṃcanti* (they gather), which require a correlative (*pratisambandhin*), there is no impairment of their semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*).

*Ratnākara*, p. 347. A word such as *Devadatta*, which denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*), does not express it through its power (*śakti*). *Vākyapadīya* 3.4.4.3, p. 933. The maxim of Devadatta’s son (*devadattaputranyāya*).

This is stated precisely when there is an intention to emphasize the father; however, when there is an intention to emphasize the mother, one says "the son of Devadatta. This is a summary [of the principle]. It is the maxim of "Devadatta’s killer" (devadattahananodattahana-nyāya).
Just as when Devadatta is killed by the hand of his slayer, the killing of Devadatta indeed occurs.
Regarding the place, the vessel, and so forth:
the characteristic of the place is that there is no fault even when vessels and other items already used in one application are taken up for another application.
In worldly matters, one may act according to one's desire, because the purpose of the ritual refinement is absent.
Commentary: Here, worldly matters serve as the examples.
For instance, regarding location: "One should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices on level ground."
The performers are the priests of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices— namely, "the four priests"—
as well as the vessels such as the *sruva* ladle and others.
Regarding these, there is an inquiry.
Should different materials be employed for each performance, or may one perform using those same materials or others?
What is the prima facie view? That different materials should be employed for each.
What is the reason? Because learned people do not perform a ritual again with the same materials used previously.
This being the case, we reply:

regarding worldly matters, one may act according to one's desire; there is no restriction as to whether those [materials] or others are used. Why? Because the purpose of the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) would otherwise be lost.

In the preceding application, there is no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent and other factors. Why? Because that which would be elided here in the case of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*) is not present;
nor is there an elision of purpose (*arthalopa*).
For indeed, the performance can be carried out by others as well;
therefore, there is no restriction.
As for what was said—that the learned do not perform the sacrifice with a *niriṣṭika* [offering]—that remains to be addressed.
And this very same fault applies here as well.
But surely they cite the text: "An officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and a teacher (*ācārya*) are not to be transgressed against"?
That is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*), not a duty of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).
Because of the absence of connection with ritual action and the absence of a specific context,
[the discussion] concludes with regard to places and agents. Regarding the vessels, the subsequent discourse will be undertaken.
Just as there is a distinction in the invocations of Soma, so too there is a distinction among the locations and other factors;
thus the connection [of the topic] is established.

(Regarding "niriṭyakena" as found in the Bhāṣya and other works: That which is used excessively here is *niriṭya*; that which is *niriṭya* alone is *niriṭyaka*, meaning it has been employed in a single ritual act. The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: In the case of worldly [objects] such as places and vessels, since there is no loss of the refinement (*saṃskāra*)—which was produced by a previous use and serves as a basis for subsequent use—even when another [object] is taken up; and since there is no loss of purpose because the performance of the rite can still be accomplished by others, one may act according to one’s desire (*yathākāmī*). In this specific performance involving different places, vessels, and so forth, others are superior.
If they were primary, the others would be like [the leaves of] Aparṇā; or, like a garment, they would not be desired.

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains that there is indeed a distinction between the sacrificial grass (kuśa), the ladles (darvī) and so forth, the officiating Brahmins, and the vessels for the Soma-juice, with respect to each ritual act and each performance.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) regarding the placement of the fire-altar (niriṣṭakopadhāna).
This being the position reached, [the author states]: "The Kuśa grass, the ladles and so forth, the mantras, and the Brāhmaṇas who are deeply learned..."
They do not become like discarded offerings when they are employed again and again.

By this statement, even though there is an application of what has already been applied (*viniyuktaviniyoga*), there is no restrictive rule because it contradicts the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

Nor can it be argued that there is a restrictive rule that "only those [the officiating priest and the teacher] are [to be served]" on the grounds of the prohibition against transgression in the statement, "The officiating priest and the teacher must not be transgressed against.

This is because these [rules] do not belong to the context of the sacrifice (*aprakaraṇasthatā*), and since there is no evidence for their being an obligatory duty in the form of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), performing them for another purpose does not result in a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) of the ritual.

Otherwise, if [the *varaṇa*] were to be deposited elsewhere, there would be the possibility of improper conduct arising from the logic of provoking anger; consequently, even the prohibition regarding the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) would not apply.

Nor is it the case that, on the view of oneness, since the individual instance (*vyakti*) is one, all subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) would have their requirements fulfilled by the consecrations (*saṃskāra*)—such as the selection (*varaṇa*) and sweeping (*saṃmārjana*)—performed only once, according to the principle of the sprinkling of the sacrificial grass for the guest-offering (*ātithyā-barhiḥprokṣaṇanyāya*). For if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the bringing of the *varaṇa* would not need to be repeated for each performance.

Because, according to the Naiyāyika view of the manifestation of oneness (*vyaktaikatva*), there is an absence of the logic of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇanyāya*) regarding the guest-offering (*ātithyā*) and so forth; and because, even in the doctrine of the manifestation of oneness, the selection (*varaṇa*) and other such acts would not achieve their purpose through *prasaṅga* (incidental application) in another performance, as is the case with the fire-altar (*agni*) and the path.
This is also determined in the case of the location of the clay-pots (*mṛtpiṇḍu*).
Regarding the vessels (*pātra*), however, it is considered as follows:
Maṇḍana states—“The place and the agent are different when there is a different application [of the rite]”;
Śaṅkara states—“Also the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the place.”
[This is] optional.
"Oṃ; because of the difference in location, the mantra is repeated.
In the *ātithyā*, the *upasads*, and the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is common.
The mantra for the spreading [of the grass], "I spread thee, O giver of wool," is repeated;
it is employed separately because of the distinctness of the locations.
The *prāgvaṃśa* hall is for the *ātithyā* and the *upasad* rites, whereas for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice it is near the *uttaravedi*.
Therefore, there is a repetition [of the ritual action];
this is the conclusion regarding the mantra for the spreading [of the grass].

Regarding the rule that "low-voicedness (*upāṃśutva*) is restricted to a specific place" (the reading *deśasaṃbaddha* is also found), according to the principle of the ninth section (9.1.6.20), since it is established that the accent belongs to the nature of the sacrificial portion (*yajñabhāga*), it would follow that even a subsidiary (*aṅga*) action not previously mentioned (*apūrva*), if it falls within the sacrificial portion, would incur the duty of the original (*prākṛta*) accent. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1182). For regional dialects and untrustworthy words are like heads split open; they cannot be distinguished [from the correct forms]. (Vārttika 1.3.5).

"The night itches for me."

Bhāṭṭa 1.2.17: The injunction regarding place (*deśavidhi*) in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices serves the purpose of restriction. An explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) having the same form as an injunction regarding place—namely, "Thirty-six steps toward the east, thirty by the foot-measure, twenty-four in front"—is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to that injunction.

"We are able to perform this [rite] in this [place]" (Bālakrīḍā, p. 57). By the statement, "He fixes half within the altar-ground and half outside the altar-ground," a specific location is indicated (Vyavahāramayūkha, p. 51). Proximity of place is not a differentiator of ritual acts.
