Regarding the rule "the low voice (*upāṃśutva*) is connected to the place" (in other texts, the reading is *deśabaddha*), the following is cited: "This is indeed the haste of the sacrifice; therefore, whatever is prior to the [offering] to Agni and Soma, they perform that in a low voice. Here, a doubt arises as to whether this low voice is a property of the sacrificial portion (*yajñabhāga-dharma*) or a property of the ritual act (*padārtha-dharma*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that it is a property of the sacrificial portion. This is because the sacrifice, being fruitful, possesses the capacity to motivate its constituent properties; thus, through the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*), even though it is separated, there is an understanding of its connection with the word "prior" (*prācīna*). Furthermore, since the word "prior" (*prācīna*)—which literally denotes direction—is used here by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to the ritual acts belonging to that region, it is concluded that the low voice is a property of the sacrificial portion. The final established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is a property of the ritual acts. This is because the word "prior" (*prācīna*) is understood as a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) due to its connection with the word "whatever" (*yat*) occurring alongside "anything" (*kiñcit*). Since a distributive repetition applies to many objects and is therefore untenable when restricted to a single location, it is more logical that the word "prior" refers by indication specifically to the ritual acts situated in the region prior to the offering to Agni and Soma. Thus, it is determined to be a property of the ritual acts.

Su. Pṛ. 730. The quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) should belong to those [rites] connected with the specific place, because of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), and because that [quality] exists there.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "This indeed is the haste of the sacrifice; therefore, whatever is prior to the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice], they perform that in a whisper.
That which is prior to the sixth part of the sacrifice from the Agniṣomīya is the haste; that is a deceptive gait—a slow placement of steps like the catching of a bird.
Therefore, it is heard in the scripture that at that time the mantras are to be recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the quality of being in a low voice belongs to those rites which precede the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, or whether it is connected with the preceding [general] context, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):
The quality of being in a low voice is heard as connected to a specific location; that which is prior to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is the location for that low-voiced recitation.
Therefore, that is heard as being connected [to it].

By the force of the ablative case-ending (*pañcamī-śruti*) in the phrase "from the Agniṣomīya," those rites which are indicated are such that low-voicedness (*upāṃśutva*) is their property, because of the indication by the ablative case-ending.
Now, the sentence heard as "whatever is prior to the Agniṣomīya" is what is referred to here by the word "scriptural statement" (*śruti*).
Because of the mention in the *śruti*; that is, because it is mentioned in the sentence by that [word].

Alternatively, by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word "prior" (*pūrva*) in the *śruti* should be understood as referring to the sacrificial elements such as those occurring prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.
With reference to such an *apūrva* thus specified, the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) being enjoined would be for the sake of that [apūrva].

And because that [subsequent *apūrva*] and the preceding intermediate one both exist there— namely, in those instances such as the sequence beginning with the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice— the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) is prompted by the *apūrva* of the actions preceding the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice;
or rather, it belongs to the sacrifice itself, because of its connection therewith.

The state of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) and the state of being like a sacrificial animal (*paśutatva*) connected to the region of fire (the heart) are fruitful through the piercing of the various types of bodily sheaths.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is indeed prompted by the transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*).

Hereafter, two sūtras (21–24), although explained in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) and other works as subordinate elements (*guṇa*) of the present topic (*prakṛta-adhikaraṇa*), have also been explained as constituting a separate topic (*adhikaraṇa*) because they are contained within the interval (*antarā-garbhīṇa*). Consequently, it should be understood that we shall explain them as a separate topic in another section.
Or rather, it belongs to those [actions] in that location, because the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is not enjoined.
By the word "or" (*vā*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is set aside.
The state of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is not prompted by the supreme *apūrva*, but rather by those actions located in that place.
That which has its location prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice refers to those rites whose place is before that point;

for those rites situated there, the state of being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*) would be prompted by the preceding ritual items—it is not connected to the aggregate of the cup-offerings (*grahayāga*), nor is it prompted by the ultimate *apūrva* produced by that aggregate of cup-offerings.

This is because the portion of the aggregate of cup-offerings that precedes [the *agnīṣomīya*] is not enjoined as being connected with the state of being performed in a low voice; that is to say, there is no such injunction.
"Or rather, haste indeed [is the fault] in the section concerning initiation;
for there is the defect of the *lililekhika*."
Having raised the objection that the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules for initiation (*dikṣā*) to the *anubandhya* and other sacrifices is not logical (Sūtra, p. 1180), [the author] replies:

because the *dārśapaurṇamāsika* *prayāja* and other rites are observed within the section on initiation, it is understood that the initiation inherits the characteristics (*dharma*) of the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices; thus, there is the perception of that which is accompanied by its auxiliary benefits (*sopakāra*), established by the original means of proof (*prākṛtapramāṇa*) within its own context (Sūtra, p.
1194). Rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva-karma*) should be performed during the rising of the sun, the first half of the month (*pūrvapakṣa*), the day (*ahaḥ*), and on auspicious days (*puṇyāha*).
6|5|123: Due to a divine cause, even if one [rite] is delayed from its own time, another [rite] should not be performed according to that [delayed] sequence.

For example, during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, even if the *saṃtāpanī* is delayed, the *agnihotra* must not be performed out of its own time. 5|1|130–34: The influence of destiny (*daiva*) is greater than that of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).

Su. Pṛ. 132: In rites for the gods (*daiva*), the ritual rules (*dharma*) require that [the grass] has its tips pointing east or north; however, in rites for the ancestors (*paitṛka*), the tips must point south.

Vi. 3.4.4: Regarding the portions for the deities (*daivata-avadāna*): there is a simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) of the portions for the deities, the portions for Sviṣṭakṛt, and the portions for the *iḍā*, in the case of a group of animals dedicated to a single deity in the Vājapeya sacrifice, specifically among the animals dedicated to Prajāpati.

Bhā. 5.1.6.10–12: The portion for the deity, the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt, and the portion for the *iḍā* constitute distinct ritual acts (*padārtha-bheda*), because of the injunction prescribing a different order of sequence, such as "having first taken the portion for the deity," and so forth.
Furthermore, when there is an intervention by other unrelated objects, the status of being a single object is not achieved.

Consequently, in a group of animals dedicated to a single deity, the sequence of the offering to the deity and so forth is performed individually for each animal; at the end, however, the oblation to the deity is performed collectively (*tantra*). As for the invocation of the *Sviṣṭakṛt*, it is likewise performed collectively.

In reality, however, even when there is an intervention by other unrelated items, since the portioning for the deity (*devatāvadāna*) also serves to accomplish the five-fold offering (*pañcāvattahoma*), it is logical that its presentation (*pradāna*) occurs immediately after [the preceding item]. Thus, even in a "multitude" (*khala*) involving different deities, there is *anusamaya* (sequential performance) from the portioning for the deity up to the presentation. But in the case of a single deity, there is *anusamaya* of the constituent parts of the ritual action itself; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Bhāṭṭa 5.1.6. In the case of portions for deities in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), there is *anusamaya* of the ritual actions.
Vi.

Just as in the case of the *daivatakya* [mantra], where in the statement "Agni-Soma are the deities" (*agniṣomo devatā*) it is called *daivatakya* because of the upward placement (*ūrdhvatva*) of the *nyāsa*, so too in the case of "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs to the couple as one and the same.

(In the sentence regarding the sprinkling of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings: By the maxim "there is no fault in that which is inferred," there is no defect in the status of being the motivator for the maintenance [of the vessel] within the implied injunction of comprehension (*pratipatti-vidhi*).

Regarding the sūtra beginning with "doṣātu lililekhike," the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is established that [the rites] are caused by the giving of worldly horses, based on the mention of defects. Then, by the sūtra beginning with "arthavādo vā," the final conclusion (siddhānta) is established that they are caused by the giving of Vedic horses. [This is] Parākrama, 2111–2. In the case of "doṣātu lililekhike," there is no defect in the Vedic context due to its inherent nature. The scriptural authority for the sacrifice performed upon receiving a horse is: "He who receives a horse receives something sharp; as many horses as he may receive, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should he offer. This refers to the sacrifice for the reception of a horse.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the *iṣṭi*—the sacrifice for receiving a horse (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi*)—should be performed in a worldly context or a Vedic one, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The sacrifice for receiving a horse should take place in a worldly instance, specifically in the case of the gift of a horse by a friend, because of the fault; for in that very case, there is the possibility of the fault consisting of swelling of the abdomen and consumption.

However, in the case of Vedic [acts] such as the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, if one does not give cooked rice, there would be no fault precisely because of the force of the scriptural injunction that ordains the giving;
therefore, this *iṣṭi* should apply only to the worldly acceptance or giving of cooked rice—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Alternatively, it is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because there is no possibility of a transgression, and it is understood from that very fact.

Regarding the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for receiving a horse): the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), which suggests that this sacrifice is required when a horse is received or given in a worldly context, is set aside by the word "or" (*vā*) in the Sūtra. The author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

the passage beginning with "He receives him [the horse] as Varuṇa" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). It is an explanatory praise intended to glorify the sacrifice, not an explanatory praise intended to remove a defect. Why? Because of the lack of connection; for the remainder of the sentence, "He releases him from the noose of Varuṇa," cannot be construed in its primary literal sense.

For, in reality, there is no acquisition of the seizure by Varuṇa (varuṇagraha)—which consists of dropsy—resulting from the acceptance of a horse; consequently, since dropsy does not follow from the acceptance of a horse and thus [the condition] is not established, that statement is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda) intended to extol the sacrifice. Therefore, it is only in the case of a Vedic acceptance of a horse that an expiation is understood by virtue of the injunction, and not in the case of a worldly acceptance of a horse.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In the section [of the *Tantravārttika*] beginning with "But because of the fault, there would be a scribbling," it was determined that the *iṣṭi* sacrifice for receiving a horse is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the act of receiving the horse, and not an independent rite.
This is the *parākrama*. 8.1.1.
By the removal of defects;
[this refers to] milking, pouring out, and so forth. Through the removal of defects, the sacrificer attains fitness for receiving the fruit [of the sacrifice].

And austerity effects the destruction of defects. (Vārttika 3.8.13) But a prohibition that does not have another purpose as its object is for the sake of [pointing out] a defect, just as: "In speaking falsely there is a defect; for one who speaks the truth, the harm is equal."
"And by speaking falsely, one incurs the fault of being deluded by falsehood" (Bālambhaṭṭī, p.

30). For the purpose of destroying such faults, there is occasional (*naimittika*) Vedic ritual whose cause is not fixed, such as: "He who should neglect the new-moon or full-moon sacrifice, he should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni Pathikṛt."

"And: 'He who should omit either the new moon or the full moon sacrifice shall offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. There is an option between these two. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 85). A conditional injunction (*naimittika*) to be performed for the purpose of removing a fault is of two kinds: that which is occasioned by the transgression of a prescribed rule, and that which is occasioned by the performance of a prohibited act. This is an injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāravidhi*).

3.4.4) There are two milkings:
on the night of the new moon, there is one milking; on the morning of the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), there is another.
Regarding the milking: it should be boiled in connection with the different times [of the sacrifice].
Two milkings are mentioned: the evening milking and the morning milking.
Furthermore, the ritual requirements for milking, such as the spreading of branches and the driving away of the cows, have been described.
Regarding the inquiry as to whether those ritual properties (dharmas) apply to the morning milking (prātardoha) or not, this sūtra presents the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
The milk of the morning milking that has been boiled would be connected with the properties of the milking-rite if it were unconnected [to other rites], but it would not be so if it were connected.
The meaning is that those properties would not belong to the morning milking.

and because the ritual details (dharmas) are recited in close proximity to the evening milking.
Curd is prepared from the milk of the evening milking.

Alternatively, the rule regarding time applies to that which is connected [to the context], because there is no division of the context—that is, due to the absence of a division within the context of the Darśa sacrifice.
The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Because there is no division of the context, there is no separation from the context of the Darśa sacrifice.
The context for both milk offerings is identical;
there is no division of the context therein.

By the injunctions, "Sour curds dedicated to Indra on the new moon day" and "Milk dedicated to Indra on the new moon day," both, along with their auxiliary parts, are enjoined for the new moon day without any division of the context.

This rule regarding time applies only to that which is connected with both [milking sessions], such as the *śākhāntara* and so forth, but not to that which is connected solely with the evening milking.
It cannot be said that the properties of milking are prescribed in the sequence of the evening milking;
therefore, the properties such as the *śākhāntara* apply only to the [sacrifice] involving both milkings.

Because of the observation of a mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the number of oblations—namely, "fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, thirteen on the new moon day"—the wooden sword (*sphya*) and other implements are not things to be offered as sacrificial portions.

Who [says this]?
Substances (dravya) are eleven: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, mind, darkness, and sound.
Some maintain that a substance such as earth is merely a collection of qualities (guṇasamudāya) and not something distinct from them.
In this regard,
since the destruction of the previous color-form and the production of a subsequent color-form in earth and other substances through baking and so forth are established by experience;
others, however, assert that the aggregate of parts itself is the whole.
That too is not correct,
because of such cognitions as "the jar has arisen" and "the jar has perished" (Maṇi, pp. 21–22).
For substances are of two kinds: stationary and moving.
Among these, disjunction occurs in the case of the stationary;

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): Regarding this, they recite: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu.
Here a doubt arises: should an uncastrated animal be used here as well, or a castrated animal?
It is said:
this word "white" has an innate connection with the quality of whiteness;
therefore, whatever is connected with the quality of whiteness is to be sacrificed.
For the word "white," being directly perceived, cannot be set aside by some inferential cognition that denotes a white substance.
Therefore, either a goat, a cow, or another white animal is to be sacrificed.
Thus it stands.
This being the case, we reply:
when this contingent substance is present—namely, the word "white" which has the quality of whiteness as its cause—it is merely the quality that undergoes modification.
For here, a substance qualified by a genus is not perceived.
From this sentence it is understood that "whatever is to be offered, that alone is to be delimited.

And as for its means of accomplishment (sādhana) which is obtained through the *codaka* (extended application) and is not explicitly heard, that [means] this word "white" (*śveta*) will delimit by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*).
Now, one might object: "Can it not also delimit other substances besides the goat? We do not say that it cannot; however, there is no purpose served by such a delimitation.
Therefore, even though the word "white" is directly perceived, it determines only the goat and no other animal.
Soma [says]: Even the word "white" does not have as its sole referent a mere quality;
for if that were the case, since there would be no connection between a substance and a deity, it would follow that the sacrifice itself could not be established.

Therefore, since the instruction is understood to extend only as far as the substance—because from the teaching one understands merely a substance possessing the quality of whiteness—the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the extended substance.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that even though the instruction extends to the substance, just as before, because a specific genus is required for the substance, there is no contradiction with the instruction even when the archetypal substance is taken; thus, it terminates in that very [substance], and there is no sublation.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: In the case of a contingent (naimittika) injunction where the word "white" (*śveta*) is based solely on the quality (*guṇa*), there should be the taking of the natural substance (*prakṛta-dravya*) itself; for it is only in that [natural substance] that the quality of whiteness can be produced, and because that [substance] alone is delimited by the quality of whiteness. By the term "contingent," he shows—as in the previous case—that there is no absence of a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*), but rather that the mere quality is the cause (*nimitta*), and that this is possible even when the substance is taken according to the general injunction (*codaka*).

And [the rule] regarding the non-action of a substance: "When substances are connected with an action..."—in the case of "A white [animal] for Vāyu," whether it be any [animal] or specifically a goat, since no distinction is stated, any [animal] may be used; however, by its very nature, it is indeed a goat.

31. Since the substance [the Gārhapatya fire] is established at a time not restricted to any specific rite, its application should be for all purposes, because it has its own fixed time.

In the discussion as to whether a separate *agnyādheya* (establishment of the sacred fires) should be performed for each individual rite—such as the *iṣṭi* sacrifices or the *pāśuka* animal sacrifice—or whether one single performance at its own time should suffice for the sake of all rites, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
This is because the substance, namely the Gārhapatya fire, is established at a time that is not limited to any particular rite.

The accomplishment of rites such as the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices does not occur at their [prescribed] times; rather, the accomplishment of the fire (*agni*) itself occurs independently at those respective times.

Therefore, because there is no accomplishment of the time for the ritual acts, the performance—the performance of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*)—should be for all purposes; it should be for the purpose of all ritual acts.
This is because it has its own time: spring, summer, and autumn are prescribed as the independent times for the fire-installation itself.
And thus, like one's own independent time [for performing rites], the installation (*ādhāna*) is for the sake of all ritual acts.

*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 172: Regarding the rule that "a Brāhmaṇa acquires wealth through acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*) and so forth," even if this [rule] has the purpose of establishing the utility (*kṛtyārthatva*) of such means, just as in the case of Vedic injunctions (*śrutivacana*), there is no evidence to prevent the assumption of indeterminate means for the purpose of eating; therefore, wealth is not necessarily the object of utility in every instance.
*Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 4.1.2, Section 2: There is no conjunction between two distinct substances because of the absence of a cause for conjunction.
Conjunction arises from the action of one, from the action of both, or from another conjunction.
Furthermore, there is no action in either of the two all-pervading [substances], nor does their conjunction as parts constitute a possible conjunction.

Nor is inherence (samavāya) tenable, because there can be no mutual inherence between two substances that lack the relationship of the produced and the producer. Thus, [conjunction] is produced by cognition; *Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 242.
In the connection of substances with ritual acts, there is a relationship as subordinate factors (*guṇatva*).

In such scriptural injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," when the relationship of substances as means for attaining heaven is perceived, there must be a relationship as subordinate factors because of the capacity of substances to produce the ritual act.
Thus, heaven and so forth are the two goals to be accomplished (*sādhya*), while the sacrifice is the primary means (*pradhāna*).
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Regarding the connection of substances with action (sūtra 6.1.48): "The undertaking [of the action] is in the substances; however, according to Bādari, it is not the means of accomplishment."

It has been stated: “One desiring heaven should sacrifice. In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the sacrifice is the primary element and heaven is the subordinate element; the word "heaven" refers to the means of attaining happiness, whereas a substance is the means for performing an action. Thus, according to the prima facie view, the sacrifice is what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and heaven is its means. The aphorism of the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) [answers this]: Because the sacrifice is for the sake of that [heaven], the sacrifice itself is the accomplisher of heaven. Since the sacrifice exists for the purpose of heaven, the sacrifice alone is the means of achieving heaven.
The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Because there is a connection with each object, the relationship is indeed through the action; therefore, it must be an instruction regarding the action.
Sacrifice is for the sake of heaven, but heaven is not for the sake of sacrifice.

Therefore, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that heaven is the primary [result] and the ritual action is the subordinate factor (*guṇa*), there arises the doubt: "By the single-word hearing (*ekapada-śruti*) of the term *yajeta* (‘one should sacrifice’), the sacrifice is the goal to be attained (*bhāvya*), whereas that which is expressed by the word *svargakāma* (‘desiring heaven’) is not the goal to be attained. This aphorism is intended to refute that doubt.
[In this context,] there is a division of words: *prati* and *arthe*.

That which is sought after or desired is called an *artha*, such as the state of heaven (*svarga*) and so forth. Because of the connection—that is, the syntactic relation (*anvaya*)—of the injunction (*vidhi*) with respect to that *artha*, namely heaven and so on, there is indeed a connection through action, meaning the relationship [of the injunction] is with the action itself as the means.

For this reason, in the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), the instruction regarding the ritual act is by way of its being the means to heaven and so forth; thus, the instruction would be for the ritual act itself, such as the sacrifice.

Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that heaven, which consists of the form of bliss, is the primary object (*bhāgyatva*), while sacrifice and the like are subordinate factors (*guṇatva*).

And so, since the performance of action by the agent is possible through the enjoyment of the fruit, the purpose of commencing the "Chapter on Entitlement" (*adhikārādhyāya*) is this: [the establishment of] such entitlement.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to exclude doubt while simultaneously collecting other intermediate points.
The allocation of substances to specific actions is as follows:

"They eat with the *sphyā*," "He cooks on the *kapālas*," "He pours out the oblations with the *agnihotrahavaṇī*," "He winnows with the *śūrpa*," "He spreads the black antelope skin over the mortar," "He places the grinding stone upon the *śamyā*," "He threshes with the mortar and pestle," and "He grinds on the lower and upper grinding stones.
The preparation of substances and actions is a seasonal duty (ṛtudharma).
But the preparation of substances and actions should indeed be a seasonal duty.
In the Agnihotra it is heard in scripture: "Milk is the vow for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel for a Rājanya, and meat for a Vaiśya.

Regarding the doubt as to whether this vow is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) or for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that it is for the sake of the person because it is enjoined by a direct statement (*vākya*)—is set aside by the word *tu* (but), and the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Here, by the word "substance" (*dravya*), persons—namely Brāhmaṇas and Rājanyas—are understood according to the logical principle [of the context].

For those actions intended for the sacrifice— those pertaining to the ritual— and for substances such as the Brāhmaṇa and others that have entered into the ritual, this vow (*vrata*) would be a sacramental refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the purpose of maintaining the body and for the purpose of providing strength.
And thus, by means of the person who has entered the ritual, it would become a property of the ritual (*ṛtudharma*),
not merely a property of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

It would remain distinct due to its separate nature. Since it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the observances (*vrata*) for the initiated (*dīkṣita*) Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, and Vaiśyas at the sacrifice—consisting of milk, barley-gruel, and meat respectively—are duties pertaining to the ritual (*ṛtudharma*) and not merely duties pertaining to the person (*puruṣadharma*), one might ask: "If that is so, for what purpose is the connection with the person stated in such passages as 'milk is the observance of the Brāhmaṇa'? In response to this doubt, he provides the answer.

Because the performances (prayoga) performed by Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, and Vaiśyas are distinct, the connection with specific persons is stated for the purpose of establishing the rules regarding the vows (vrata).
Milk is the vow for the Agnihotra performed by a Brāhmaṇa, gruel (yavāgū) for that performed by a Rājanya, and meat (āmiṣa) for that performed by a Vaiśya.

Thus, because the performances are distinct, the performance of the vow in the Agnihotra is established as being restricted to those respective performers; it is for this reason that the connection with persons is stated.
Therefore, the vow is indeed for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*).

Regarding substances—such as the *syādira* ladle, the *juhū* made of *parṇa* wood, the *upabhṛt* made of *aśvattha* wood, and the *dhruvā* made of *vaikaṅkata* wood—they are not prompted by [the attainment of] a fruit.

Bhāṣya 4.3.1.9–4: Among substances, even those whose very existence is perceived as having been produced, some are understood to be non-eternal, because a cause of their destruction is observed, as when one sees a newly made cloth.
Substances have no other purpose than the accomplishment of the action connected with the sentence, because [otherwise] there would be no connection with non-existence and so forth.

Just as a *homa* (oblation), being of the nature of an action, requires an object (*kim*) and is thus grasped by the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) of the primary rite as a means of assistance, a substance is not like that.
And there is no postulation of an unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*) for those [entities] such as the *apūrva*, which are established through action. Vākyapadīya 2.1.4.12, p. 411.
There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the substances used as means for purchasing the *soma*.
Regarding a substance, there is a scriptural statement of a result: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report."
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
It is established that when the prescribed substance is lost or spoiled, one should employ a substitute after taking it up.

Regarding the sūtra *dravyeṣvārambhāmitvādarthe vikārasāmarthyam* (10.4.14.29), by stating that "because [words] have the capacity for modification (*vikāra*) in their meaning due to the non-limitation of their commencement (*ārambha*) in substances," and because action resides in substances in their own form, even though there is modification, the mention of qualities (*guṇaśruti*) in substances occurs. By asserting this disparity— that there is capacity for the meaning in substances— the sense is that since one accepts the application of the action in substances as being in the form of the object (*artharūpeṇa*), there is no restriction on the use of words according to grammatical injunctions (*vidhi*).
Su. Pṛ. 461:
In the case of substances, the mention of a quality is for the purpose of prescribing a restrictive rule;
likewise, the mention of a quality in relation to substances is because of its connection with the originative injunction.
Commentary: This is an extension of the present topic.
They recite this: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu";
likewise, "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a caru-oblation of white rice in ghee to Soma and Rudra"; and likewise, "One should offer a caru-oblation of black rice to Nirṛti."
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the white color and so forth enjoined, or is it merely restated?
What is the prima facie view? It is restated, because it is already grasped by the mention of the substance.
"In accordance with the rule, it serves as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) for the color which is already optionally obtained.
This purpose stated for the alternative applies to both sections.
As for the meaning of Soma’s sūtra: even the mention of a quality regarding a substance is a restrictive injunction.

By way of origination, through conjunction with the substance that produces the action, because it serves to delimit that [substance]. [The *Viśva* commentary states: "Is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the white-colored object, or is it an injunction (*vidhi*) of the white color? It is the latter; for it is understood through the medium of the substance, and as in the previous case, it is restricted to that. *Raśmi*. Dravyadāreṇa tatyāteḥ; pūrvavat tanniyate. (As above.)
In the Bhaṭṭa school, however, this is unified with the preceding section.
Maṇḍana states: “The restriction of qualities regarding a substance is likewise.
Śaṅkara states: “And likewise the scriptural mention of qualities regarding a substance.”
Thus is the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).
Among substances and sacrifices, whatever refinement (*saṃskāra*) exists is prompted by the *apūrva*;
for substances and sacrifices, the connection with ritual duties (*dharma*) occurs through their belonging to that [apūrva], not by virtue of their own intrinsic nature.
Bhāṣya 9.1.1.1, Section 3:
Nor is there a restriction on the use of injunctive words regarding substances due to their inherent connection with a purpose;
(however, such a restriction does exist) in the case of a deity.
Or [the other way around]. Vārttika 2.4.8.11, page 345. The section on substance (dravyādhikaraṇa).
The section on *syāt* (syādhikāra).
The definition of the delimiting factor for the deity regarding the substance:
"And the substance, because of its connection with the originative injunction, is enjoined solely for that purpose.
Commentary: The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices exist.

In that context, they recite: "The winnowing basket, the potsherds, the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the winnowing fan, the black antelope skin, the *śamyā* pin, the mortar, the pestle, and the lower and upper grinding stones—these indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*).
Regarding this, a doubt arises:

are these items prescribed for whatever purpose can be accomplished by them, or only for that specific purpose with which each is connected? What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are for whatever they are connected to.
Why?
Because in the section concerning substances (dravyādhikaraṇa), [the rule] beginning with "danti" and so forth follows.
In this regard, one [type of statement] is an injunction (*vidhi*), while the other is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

If the former is an injunction, then, because it is directly connected to the sacrifice, it would—by the logic of the fourth section (*caturthādhikaraṇa*, 3.1.4)—be like the seventeen-fold [sacrificial post], and thus, due to the fault of purposelessness (*ānarthakya*), they would descend into that [context] because there is no distinction in their status as subsidiaries; consequently, it would be understood that they serve all purposes according to their respective capacities.
And thus, the doubts regarding the *uddhana* and so forth would result in the status of being unestablished restatements (*avyutpannānuvādatva*).

Furthermore, if only those [acts] connected with the *uddhanana* (threshing) and so forth constitute the primary subject matter (*viṣaya*), while the other is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), then, by the principle of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇanyāya*), the application (*vyavasthā*) is determined according to their respective connections.

What is the conclusion? Since there is no connection with a distinct transcendental result (*apūrva*) and since there is no difference in their having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), the application is according to their respective capacities (*yathāsāmarthya*).
In this way, the injunctions connected with the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*) will become meaningful.

And the plural expression found in the Bhāṣya intends to convey the multiplicity of words expressing the objects to be enjoined (for there is clearly a plurality of such words as "kapālāni" and so forth). Otherwise, however, because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), there would be only a single injunction.
Therefore, the application (*viniyoga*) occurs according to the respective capacities of the elements.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"The connection of this [text] with the established practice is due to its being obstructed by the injunctions regarding the sacrificial implements (*kārya*) and so forth;
therein, the phrase 'the sacrificial implements' merely restates what is already established."

"Indeed, these are the ten sacrificial implements"—because of the connection with the word "vai," this [statement] is of the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, there is no injunctive element here capable of enjoining or prescribing their application. Moreover, many sentences would become meaningless even if they were [taken as injunctions].
Furthermore, there is no purpose for these [sentences] being mere restatements (*anuvāda*).

Indeed, these are directly enjoined by their own designations (*svābhidhāna*) specifically for acts such as *uddhana* (striking), whereas they appear only indirectly in the sentence concerning the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*).

This is because the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) functions as an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the constituent parts (*aṅga*), and because the word "implement" (*āyudha*), which denotes an instrument of war, is used figuratively (*aupacārika*) with respect to other ritual actions.
And in this case, the principle of the seventeen *arattis* (the *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) is not applicable.
For here, unlike the expression "of the Vājapeya," we do not observe a genitive case following the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) that would merely denote a general relationship.

Furthermore, even if the principle of "uselessness [implying] subservience to its parts" were to apply, general injunctions—when restricted by specific injunctions connected with particular elements such as the *uddhana*—are not connected with other rites.

Therefore, at the very beginning of the summary (uddana), all those sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*) that have not yet been established—exactly as we perceive them—are restated by the passage "these indeed are ten.

As for the objection that there is no motive for a distinction between new (unestablished) things, we reply: in the case of the potsherds (*kapāla*) and so forth, the motive is precisely the distinction between the transcendental results (*apūrva*) of this particular cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*).
For the others as well, there is no confusion [of application], because they serve as the doors for the *uddana* and so forth, and because no benefit is produced by them elsewhere.

For example, even though [the acts of] killing and so forth are connected to the same *apūrva* in the case of the *sugā* and other [offerings], they are not performed [therein] because they are distinct causal factors (*kāraka*).
Therefore, it is established that the application of these too occurs precisely according to their respective associations (*saṃyoga*).
Therefore, because this is a restatement (anuvāda), the others are considered to be injunctions (vidhi).
Consequently, there would be no fixed rule regarding the actions such as covering and so forth, [if it were not for these injunctions].

Because the sentence beginning with "Soma-uddana" lacks injunctive force, there is no fixed restriction here due to the absence of a connection (saṃyoga), similar to the case of the *mīmāṃsakas* regarding the connection with threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth.
This constitutes the "relevance" (*saṅgati*) because it is directly perceived.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: even a substance, when connected with something, is understood as being for the sake of that very thing; this is because of the connection at the time of origin, as in the statement, "They scoop out with a spade."

Whether there is a confusion or a fixed determination regarding a substance such as a visible fruit and so forth, the status of being a sacrificial implement is equal for all; therefore, there is no confusion here.
If there were a confusion [of functions], the mention of the uprooting of the tree and so forth would be redundant;
for the mention of the weapons is merely a restatement (anuvāda). Therefore, as before, there is a fixed distinction (vyavasthā).

According to the Bhaṭṭa school, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, after enumerating ten substances in the passage "The *sphyu* and the potsherds," the scriptural statement "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhāni*) prescribes all ten substances as means for the sacrifice. Furthermore, since they cannot be directly the means for the sacrifice due to being subsumed under the *puroḍāśa* (cake), they descend to the subsidiaries. Thus, the substances are prescribed by that which is delimited by the action requiring substances that serve as means for the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the context; and because there is no application [of the term] in passages such as "They dig with the *sphyu*," it is not an unintelligible restatement (*anuvāda*).

This being the case, since the *sphya* and other implements are specifically enjoined by various direct injunctions (*pratyakṣa-vidhi*) established by the presence of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), the sentence regarding the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha-vākya*) alone is a single instance lacking an explicit injunction; it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) connected with the word "vai" (indeed), because multiple restatements would be redundant.
Furthermore, this [sentence] possesses purpose as an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the injunction: "He collects the sacrificial implements.

Therefore, having indicated by means of the term "uddhana" (digging) that which is the substratum of the status of being a means for the *apūrva* produced by the activity consisting merely of digging, the injunction of the *sphya* and others is made precisely with reference to that [activity].
Maṇḍana [states]: "The *sphyādi* (the *sphyā* and so forth) are for the purpose of driving away [obstacles] and so on.
Śeṣa [states]: "The function of the *sphyādi* is fixed.
Śaṅkara [states]: "The function of the *sphyādi* is established."
In the section on substances (*dravyādhikaraṇa*, 3.1.11), the application of a substance is discussed.
Some maintain that this [application] occurs through syntactical connection (*vākya*),
but in reality, it occurs through direct assertion (*śruti*) alone.

(Briefly stated: There is no confusion [of categories] because the assistance rendered by those [factors] does not exist elsewhere—namely, in the case of substance (*dravya*), number (*saṃkhyā*), cause (*hetu*), aggregate (*samudāya*), and substratum (*adhikaraṇa*).
Tā. pṛ. 669.
Description of the acquisition of substances (*dravyārjana-varṇana*): 2149. Substance. 2149. Description of the acquisition of substances.
It is understood that there exists a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) in those cases where, when one part is grasped and pulled, the whole is pulled along.
For instance, when a single piece of wood is being pulled from a bundle of wood, other pieces of wood are not pulled along.

Indeed, when a single cognition arises produced by mutual interconnection, such that no cognition of individual parts is perceived, nor can it be inferred by any means of inference, it is said that a distinct substance has come into existence there.
Wherever there is the cognition of a different substance, there is a different substance.
Where, when one part is being pulled, the whole composite is pulled along, it is as observed in experience.
Where one [substance] being used causes another to be used, there too it is according to what is observed.
(Ṭup. 27). Even when there is a deficiency of the substance, another optional substance should not be taken up.
(Ke. 6|3|128–30). Even when the rite is performed with another substance as a substitute, each [action] remains one and the same; there is no division of the ritual act.
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

[Sūtra 6.3.131–12]: Because its purpose has been fulfilled with respect to one substance, there should be a repetition of it upon the use of another substance, since the mantra is subordinate to that [action], and because it is enjoined for that purpose.

In the *rājasūya* sacrifice, during the *nānābījeṣṭi*, since the threshing (*avaghāta*) has fulfilled its purpose with respect to one grain—its objective, the removal of the husks (*tuṣavimokṣa*), having been accomplished—there must be a repetition of that threshing for the sake of removing the husks from the second grain; and since the mantra is subordinate to that [threshing]—being a constituent part of the threshing—it too must be repeated.
Because it is enjoined by the *codaka* (extended injunction) as being a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the threshing for that purpose;
therefore, there is a repetition of the mantra for each individual grain.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The principle of the arrival of another substance (*dravyāntarāgamananyāya*). This is precisely the principle of the substitute (*pratinidhinyāya*).

Even when the act of throwing [the oblation] (*prakṣepa*) is not desired, since the sacrifice (*yāga*) remains unaccomplished, although the throwing is no longer the motivator (*aprayojaka*), it can still be motivated by the sacrifice; therefore, there is no contradiction with the principle of the arrival of another substance in cases such as destruction.
Su. Pṛ. 1535: When there is a deficiency of the substance, the rite is completed with a substitute.
Ke.:
The designation of the substance [is used] in the nigamas according to the *ānuṣaṅga* principle; in the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is governed by the rule regarding the word.

Bhā [on Jaimini Sūtra] 10.4.16–33: The acquisition of wealth is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). This is because statements such as "A twice-born man should perform rituals with wealth acquired through righteous means" indicate that even the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice is understood through the gradation of eligibility regarding primary and secondary means of livelihood, as well as those who are permanently excluded. Thus, there is no fault even if it serves both purposes, according to the principle of the distinctness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*).

Bhāṭṭa 4.1.2, Section 3, p. 86: Since the acquisition of wealth falls outside the ritual performance (*prayoga*), even though it occurs within the context of one's own acquisition, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in seeing that it is performed at each individual performance (*pratiprayoga*), just like the hiring of priests, the winning of wealth, or the *prayāja* offerings. 4.1.3, Section 3, p. 85: There is a restriction regarding the means (*upāya*) for acquiring wealth, because using any other means would result in sin (*pratyavāya*).
In that regard, there is a textual passage describing the Brahmin’s means of acquiring wealth as receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and teaching.

In the *Tantraratna*, however, it is explained why this [the establishment of the fires] does not occur in this manner: he says, "It ought to be like the *ādhāna* (the act of establishing the sacred fires).
This means that it cannot be like the *āhavanīya* fire and others.

For in that case, the *āhavanīya* and other fires, having been produced by the *ādhāna* and being in need of a purpose (*prayojana*), attain their status as established through the scriptural injunction (such as "one offers oblations in the *āhavanīya*"), even without a specific context (*prakaraṇa*).

In this context [of the acquisition of wealth], there is no such statement that enjoins the acquisition of wealth as a ritual act. (The Bhāṣya beginning with "Now, as for the indicative mark that was mentioned" and so forth is restated. Even regarding the burning of the house, whether for the sake of non-destruction or for the sake of a fruit—[in that case too]—there is no authority for its being non-destruction. (But the mention of that [non-destruction] is merely a descriptive reference.)
Therefore, the acquisition of wealth is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
[Question: Is the acquisition of wealth for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person? [Answer:
In this regard, "the gathering of wealth is for the sake of the ritual, in order to give purpose to the restrictive rule (*niyama*)."
For if it were for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), the restriction would be meaningless; indeed,
the offering of a substance is seen even when there is a desire to prepare the substance itself.

"Due to the difference in causal dependence, there is a distinct conventional usage. (Vārttika 412/517, p. 424). Since nothing would be accomplished by the sacrificer if the disposal of the substance were performed by another, the sacrificer performs the disposal of the substance. (Vārttika 417/119). The injunction regarding the disposal (*pratipatti*) is indeed a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) with respect to the very object intended for disposal.
Bāla, p. 23: Even though substance (*dravya*) and action (*karman*) are one, [the substance] is that which is desired to be reached (*īpsita*).
Substance is the substratum (*āśraya*), and action is the dependent (*āśrita*).
Having accepted both difference and non-difference between the substratum and the dependent, their relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) is described.

Therefore, even when there is a difference in substance, the action does not differ. (Vi. 6.2.3) This is the expectation for the demonstration of the similarity and dissimilarity between substances and actions.
Bhāṣya 4.1.8.21: The principle of the conjunction of substance and action; "One should sacrifice an animal."

In the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), although the substance is not intended to be significant because it serves no purpose— just like the flour-grains (*saktu*)— nevertheless, the accusative case ending indicates it as a general grammatical factor (*kāraka*). Thus, even when there is a difference in substances,
whether through a difference in the substance itself or through a difference in number, no distinct transcendental result (*apūrva*) arises.

What then? The archetypal number and the archetypal substance are understood; however, the benefit remains the same. (Durmāpāra 12.1.14, p. 2221). Even when there is a difference in substance, the ritual act does not differ.
Because it depends upon an action, there would be a distinction regarding another substance.
The Bhāṣya states: The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is prescribed as being performed with a *puroḍāśa* cake;
and it is heard in the scripture that this *puroḍāśa* must be made of *vrīhi* rice.

In this regard, the following is considered: if a sacrifice were performed with an oblation (*puroḍāśa*) made of wild rice (*nīvāra*), would it be that very same sacrifice or another? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? There would be a distinction due to the difference in substance; it would be a different sacrifice.
Why? Because it is dependent. A distinction is understood from the difference in the substratum:
this one, which has *nīvāra* as its substratum, is different from that which has *vrīhi* as its substratum.
It is quite clear due to the difference in the substratum (*āśrayabheda*). In that case, even this form (*rūpa*) is understood to be distinct.
Therefore, the sacrifice is different when there is a different substance (*dravya*).

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively: "Because there is no distinction and because the word for form is inseparable, there would be oneness like that of 'cowness' (gotva); and the name would be like 'existence' (sattva).
Commentary: The word "api ca" (moreover) marks the fifth repetition.
The same action would occur even with respect to another substance;
when there is an action such as moving or falling, the object remains exactly the same at that time,
and no distinct excellence or deficiency whatsoever is observed therein.
It cannot be said that it is a different form, nor is there another word as its designator.
[Objection: But surely the difference in substrata is quite clear.
It is said: We indeed maintain that the substratum (*āśraya*) is distinct, but the supported (*āśrita*) does not become distinct because of that distinction, because they are different.
For when an axe or a saw is broken, a distinction in the person [wielding it] is not perceived on account of that distinction in the tool.
If it is argued that his self is also distinct [from the body], this is not so;
for such a thing can be asserted only by those who perceive a distinction,
and no such distinction is perceived in this case.
Is it not the case that this very distinction exists, namely, that one has perished while the other persists?
As for what is said—that "it has not perished"—that is not so;
for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence prior to its perception.

Therefore, [the substance] has perished. Nor is it recognized [as being the same], because it is perceived as distinct [from that substance]—[the phrase "distinct from that substance" is added in some versions; the meaning is: because the form of the stable [substance] is perceived as distinct from the form of what has perished]. If it is asked, "How then does the cognition 'it moves' arise?", it is said in reply:
Because we observe the attainment of another location;
for one who goes to or comes from that other location is said to "move.
In that case, both the mover and the other location are perceived.
Therefore, it is said that [the action] has gone, and it is also said that it has come.
(The passage beginning with "But surely this very... is intended to demonstrate the difference between actions based on the distinction between the cognitions of "destroyed" and "not destroyed.
It is true that what is destroyed is different from what is not destroyed.
Moreover, even that other [instance] is indeed denotable by the word *yajati*;
the generality of the act of sacrificing (*yajati-sāmānya*) does not differ,
nor is it not expressed by the word.

Therefore, even one who should perform a sacrifice with wild rice (nīvāra) has indeed performed what was enjoined; and for one who performs what is enjoined, the desired result follows, not that which is performed as something unprecedented. Furthermore, the name [of the rite] indicates this.

"Darśa" or "Pūrṇamāsa"—this is the common name for this very [sacrifice], not for individual instances. What is the purpose of this inquiry? This will be deliberated upon in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*). [From here until the end of the chapter, there is an inquiry into the specific details regarding performance according to one's capacity.]
As for the previous section, it was like a repository for the over-extension of the application according to one's capacity, being merely a supplementary matter.
He states the established conclusion: "Or rather, because there is no difference.
Just as the New and Full Moon sacrifices, when performed at another time, in another place, or by another person, are neither excessive nor deficient.
Thus, even with respect to another substance [the two rites remain] neither less nor more.
By this, the sūtra-word "because of non-difference" (*avyatirekāt*) has been explained.

He explains the non-distinction of form (*rūpāvibhāgam*): Nor is there any sublation of the perceptually apprehended cognition that "these very same are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices," even with respect to another substance, because of the absence of other words and so forth (which are the causes of difference).

For no distinction caused by differences in sound (*śabdāntara*) and so forth arises in that which is being performed with wild rice (*nīvāra*), whereby the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "this is that very same [act]" would be sublated.
(He explains the non-differentiation of the word: Even when it is performed with a different substance, its designation as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* remains this very same one.
Just as the performance [of the ritual] in Vaiśākha does not differ from the performance in Caitra,
and by virtue of that lack of difference, those two do not lose their designation as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices,
so too, by analogy with that, even when performed with *nīvāra* grains, they retain this very same designation.
If it is argued that "the universal of that very [entity] is stated to be in the result," that is incorrect.

For, unlike the *śāstra* and so forth, a universal (*gotva*) is not perceived here as being manifested; therefore, it is not the universal that is enjoined in relation to the result. What then? The six specific individual entities (*vyakti-viśeṣa*), such as the *Āgneya* and others, which have been produced, are enjoined in relation to the result.
Even though there is a difference in substance, [it refers to] the modification of the substance.
The individual instances alone are what is denoted by the terms *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*.
Therefore, even when the rite is performed with a different substance (such as *nīvāra* rice), the cognition of it being a "different instance" does not arise.

Śā: Hereafter, following the refutation of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the discussion on substitutes (*pratinidhi*) will be introduced as a subsidiary topic (*śeṣa*) to the performance according to one's capacity (*yathāśaktiprayoga*) established in the context of occasional rites (*naimittika*).
However, this is considered from the perspective of its being derived from that [substance]:
"In that case, action is merely a name and form of the substance itself, not something distinct from it;
since it is of the same nature as that, how could there be any difference when there is a difference in it?"
It is said: "Even for that [universal], there is a distinction from its own self, however slight it may be;
yet, because it possesses qualities just like a genus (*jāti*), it does not differ even when those qualities differ."
Therefore, since there is no difference in the action even when the substance is different, the substitution (pratinidhi) is established.
Soma: The meaning of the sūtra is that because actions are distinct from substances, there would be a division—that is, a difference—in the action when there is another substance.
Vi: "Due to the difference in substances such as nīvāra, would the ritual act be different, or would it be the very same?"
Since [the distinction] was previously established through the differentiation of substances, therefore it is not inferred here from a difference in those [substances].

Bhaṭṭa: Thus, when that which can be established according to the available means has been determined, and the discussion regarding substitutes—which follows as a subsidiary element—ought to be undertaken, this is first investigated by way of an introductory topic (upodghāta).

Regarding that, first of all, since there is no difference in substance other than through action, if there were a difference in substance, it would follow that there is a difference in the ritual act (*karma*); thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the prescribed action cannot be accomplished by means of *nīvāra* grain and the like. However, even though there is neither absolute difference nor absolute non-difference, because absolute difference is likewise absent, the action itself remains appropriate—just as there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as "this is the same movement" or "this is the same sacrifice"—even when there is a difference in the agent, place, time, and so forth, as well as the substance. Therefore, there is no fault even in the adoption of a substitute (*pratinidhi*). In this regard, there is only one single individual instance (*vyakti*) of the ritual act existing upon the surface of the earth; it is merely its manifestations (*abhivyakti*) that differ.

Alternatively, it is by means of such proofs as the use of different words that the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*) is established; whereas through [differences in] substance, place, time, and the manner of performance, there is merely a difference in the identity or non-identity of that very same individual instance.

Or again, let there be no distinction between individual instances even in those cases; rather, it has been established as the final position (*siddhānta*) that it is the universal classes (*jāti*), such as "belonging to Agni" (*āgneyatva*), that are distinguished by proofs such as the use of different words.

Even though action (*kriyā*) is dependent upon a substance (*dravya*), it is impossible to suspect a difference in its generic nature (*vaijātya*) when that substance differs; furthermore, under the doctrine of the identity of the individual (*vyaktyaikya-siddhānta*), this would result in the denial of the *apūrva*.
Moreover, if that [action] were produced by manifestation (*abhivyakti*), it would entail the necessity of resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *yaj* (to sacrifice).

Therefore, the investigation should be stated as follows: even given other means of knowledge such as distinct words (*śabdāntara*), since it is understood through [the principle of] "being enjoined" (*vidheyatva*) that the generic nature of being related to the *Āgneya* sacrifice and so forth is the cause for that which is delimited by a distinct class of sacrifice (*vijātīya-yāgatva*), just as rice (*vrīhi*) and other materials are causes for [the production of the *apūrva*].

In the same way, because there is the determination that it manifests that very genus (*jāti*), the accomplishment [of the effect] as delimited by that genus does not arise from taking *nīvāra* and other grains as the material cause.

This being the position reached: even though rice and the like possess causality toward that which is delimited by that genus, they do not individually manifest that genus, because there is deviation—since they also function as causes for other ritual acts by virtue of their being *vrīhi* and so forth.
Rather, they manifest it only as a causal totality (*sāmagrī*).
And the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for that which is capable consists of being rice (*vrīhitva*) and so forth;
however, for that which is incapable, it does not consist of those.

Consequently, even when *nīvāra* (wild rice) and the like are employed as the material, there certainly arises [an action] delimited by the nature of a sacrifice of a different class (*vijātīya-yāgatva*), the unmanifest potency (*apūrva*), and the fruit.

In the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), the supreme fruit indeed arises according to degrees of excellence; however, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), even if one who is incapable of the full undertaking completes them merely to avoid the fault of being censured by the learned, no fruit is produced, because that fruit arises only through the inclusion of all constituent parts (*sarvāṅga*).
This is because, by failing to complete the performance, one incurs the fault [of non-completion].

Some maintain that because there is no other fruit in the performance [of the rite], it does not involve the transcendental result (*apūrva*). However, since there is no distinction in the nature of the occasional rite (*naimittika*), one should consider that even when sin is postulated in that case, there is still a gradation (*tāratamya*) therein. Maṇḍana states: "Action is not a substitute for anything else.
Śaṅkara states: "There is no difference in the action, even when there is a difference in the substance."

Even one who has not acquired wealth has the entitlement to perform ritual acts, because it is possible for him to acquire wealth. Bhāṣya 6.1.8.39–40. The word *dravya* (wealth/substance) occurs three times in the *Upādāna* [section].
Saṃkalpa 4.1.12. The word *vṛhatī* denotes a substance.
"Sound is a substance"—this is the meaning [of Pāṇini 4.1.4].
The status of being a denotation of a substance belongs to words such as *piñjākṣi* and others [Vārttika on 3.1.6–12, p. 609].
"The metaphorical treatment is like that of a substance"—this is the logical principle (*nyāya*).
Furthermore, metaphorical designations (*upacāra*) would follow as if they were substantial entities (*dravyavat*).
"Metaphorical designations" means conventional usages (*vyavahāra*).

Just as one single person cannot simultaneously perform multiple actions such as fetching water with a single jar, so it should be understood in the present case as well; thus [it is said] "the elision (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth here."
Satya:
[The property of] being a substance belongs to the atoms as well,
because they are inherent in a substance [according to Pāṇini 6.1.14].
Thus, at the time of giving, there is this discussion: the commentary states, "In regard to duty (*dharma*), non-greed (*tyāga*), and desire (*kāma*), one does not exceed [the other].
[This is based on] the commentary on *Pāṇini* 6.1.16, which says, "[The suffix *matup*] indicates the existence of ownership.
And [this is also based on] the commentary on the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which says, "Or rather, the wife has authority over what is acquired through marriage (*pāriṇaya*)."

In the case of a group of animals, regarding the *patty-anuyāja* offerings, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the tails; however, there may be an option (*vikalpa*), for it is a modification of the substance (*dravyavikāra*), as in the previous case, and it would be a purposeful act (*arthakarma*). Alternatively, there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) because of its primary status. Thus, in a group of animals, there is a combination of the tails in the *patty-anuyāja* offerings, or else an option, as it is a modification of the substance.
Now it is deliberated whether [the act] is a modification of the substance (*dravyavikāra*).

"Modification of the substance" means that in which the tail (*jāghanī*), which is a part of the animal substance, is the modification; such an act of joining the tail would, as before, be a purposeful act (*arthakarma*) like the previous one in the archetype (*prakṛti*), namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and not a disposal act (*pratipattikarma*).

And thus, when there is an option regarding the natural state (*prakṛtitva*), and an option between clarified butter (*ājya*) and the tail-tendon (*jāghanī*) has arisen, there would be a restriction (*niyama*) of the tail-tendon by means of the repeated scriptural statement (*punaḥśruti*) in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice: "They join the wives with the tail-tendon.
Because the ritual action is primary, the joining of the wives with the tail-tendon [is established].
Therefore, the joining of the wives with the tail-tendon in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is a purposeful act (*arthakarma*), even though it occurs during the animal sacrifice itself.
Furthermore, in a ritual action where a single purpose is served, the combination (*samuccaya*) of multiple tails (*jāghanī*) is not appropriate.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the tails in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings at the animal sacrifice.

Even though they are substances, there would be a combination because the substance effects the completion of the rite; since the rites differ for each animal, this remains as it was in the archetype (*yathāprakṛti*).

In the ritual of the *patnīsaṃyāja*, the tail (*jāghanī*) is the sacrificial substance (*haviḥ-dravya*); thus, the tail is a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*). Likewise, when there is a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), even though the tails constitute the substance and are subordinate, they would be combined (*samuccaya*).

Since the substance—the tail—is produced by the act of slaughter (*viśasana*), which is brought about by the ritual, it stands in need of a purpose once it has been produced; that purpose is its connection with the *patnīsaṃyāja*.

And since there is a distinction in the ritual action for each individual animal during the animal sacrifice (*paśupaṇa*), the tail (*jāghanī*) produced by the dismemberment of each respective animal would be for the purpose of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
This being the case, it will be performed according to the archetype (*prakṛti*), just as in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.
Therefore, even though they are purposeful actions (*arthakarman*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the tails; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
If it is argued that the same applies to the skull as well;
Someone objects to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"In the case of the potsherd (*kapāla*) as well, there should be a combination (*samuccaya*), just as with the tail (*jāghanī*). If it is argued that because they are produced during the act of slaughter, there is a combination of tails, then since the potsherd is employed for the ritual action in the statement 'he winnows the husks with the cake-potsherd,' the winnowing of husks must also be its purpose; consequently, it follows that for each cake in a group of cakes, the winnowing of husks must be performed with a separate potsherd."
Thus, there would also be a combination in that case.
If there is no combination in the case of the potsherds, then let there be none in the case of the tail-flesh either.
No, because the ritual action is for the sake of another.
The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) refutes both the objection and the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Because the act of using the potsherds is for the sake of another— that is, for the purpose of baking the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—
and because there is no production of potsherds for the purpose of winnowing the husks, there can be no combination (*samuccaya*) of them.

And thus, since the act of dismembering regarding the tail-ends (*jāghanī*) is for the sake of another, and since the covering and so forth have already achieved their purpose, there is no dismembering for the sake of the tail-ends; because they are not produced [in that context], there is no combination of the tail-ends.
However, their disposal (*pratipatti*) does take place because they are remnants (*śeṣa*).
The opponent says: The offering of the tail (jāghanī) to the Patnīsaṃyājas is not a primary act (arthakarma), but rather it is a disposal (pratipatti);
because it is a remnant, since the tail is a remnant of the animal already employed.
When the sacrifice with the animal has been completed, the tail—which is a remnant—is deposited in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Therefore, the act regarding the tail is a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Consequently, when the animal is purchased, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of tails in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Even though it is heard [in the text], it would be so because it is as before.
Someone objects by way of a counter-argument:
even though it is heard [in the texts] that "one should offer *caru* with *śr̥ta*" and "curd-*śr̥ta*," there would still be a disposal (*pratipatti*) even when curd is present,
because of the state of being preceded by the former, as both cases are preceded by something else.
The curd and the milk were presented to Indra on the new moon day;
on account of the rising of the moon, they both went toward Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
That going would be a *pratipatti* (disposal).
If that were undesirable, then even though the tail (*jāghanī*) occurs prior to the animal sacrifice, it would not have the status of a *pratipatti* (disposal) in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

Therefore, there is a combination (*samuccaya*). For if there were an option (*vikalpa*), the act would be a primary purposeful act (*arthakarman*) because its primary focus is on the restriction; furthermore, since the function of the ritual act inheres in the remnant, it would therefore be a purposeful act by virtue of that [remnant].

In this Sūtra there are two divisions; therein, by the passage beginning with "But in the case of option" (*vikalpe tu*), there is a refutation of [the view expressed in] "The performance, however, [is determined] because of being the remainder" (*pratipattistu śeṣatvāt*, Sūtra 14). [The phrase] "In the case of the remainder, when in proximity to a substance-injunction... (*śeṣe dravyavidhisannidhau*) [refers to] the collection of substances, numbers, causes, and aggregates.
The fifth position was stated that she might belong to some single caste;
regarding that, he states another argument.
Moreover, this is for the following reason:
the cognition of a word-meaning arises from a word-meaning only when it belongs to the same class, provided there is no sublation.

This is like common worldly usage; for example, when it is said in the world, "Let a hundred be given to these two," a hundred of the same kind is understood, not those of different kinds. It is just so in this case.
Therefore, the application of number belongs only to something of a single class. That [number] arises from the division of the produced animals.
It was understood from the two preceding sūtras that this number belongs to something of a single class.
Regarding the inquiry as to whether "of one kind" refers to animals or to grains, he states the sixth position from the beginning:
that number of one hundred and twelve should belong to animals such as cows and the like, and not to grains such as rice and other species;
for it arises from the context of distribution.
In worldly transactions, animals are counted by way of their natural division, as in "pleased with five horses" or "bought for five cows.
Such a usage does not apply to species such as rice and the like.
Therefore, that number should apply to the animals, not to the grains. Since there is no specific distinction, there is no fixed rule.
Now, regarding the inquiry as to which specific animal the number applies to among the animals, he states the seventh position from the beginning.
Because there is no distinction and because no specific [animal] has been mentioned, there would be no restriction, such as "of cows or of horses" and so forth.
Or, because of their commonality [as sacrificial animals], it might belong to cows.
Rejecting with the word "or" (*vā*) the seventh position reached by means of the Sūtra, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
That number would refer to cows,
because of their status as shares and because cows possess great value;
furthermore, the gifting, acceptance, and sale of horses are prohibited.
Among all animals, however, it is cows alone that possess great excellence;
therefore, the established conclusion is that the number one hundred and twelve must be understood as referring to cows alone,
because of the authoritative cognition [of this fact].
In the established conclusion (siddhānta), he states another reason:
in an enumerative sentence such as "the cow, the horse, and the mule," at the outset, there arises a cognition—namely, knowledge—of cows alone.
Since there is no reason to abandon that [initial cognition], the number must be understood as belonging to the cows alone.
"And because of the observation of an indicative mark.
Regarding the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he states another reason there:
"And because of the observation of an indicative mark, that number belongs to cows alone."

"Now, they indeed recite this *śabalī* [the brindled cow]: 'O *iḍā*, O delight, O invocation, O desirable one, O bright one, O light! O Sarasvatī, O great and far-famed one! These are your names, O blind one; for the sake of the gods, make me well-done. These are the names of cows.
And regarding the thousandth [cow] as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he speaks thus: 'These are your names.'"
If that [gift] were a cow, this would be possible;
therefore, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the number one hundred and twelve refers to cows alone—
this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Certain specific substances, when merged in duality, are designated as "male" or "neuter.
This is the section concerning the determination of the delimitors of the emergent state regarding substances.
Bhāṣya 3.1.5.11:
The section concerning the determination of the delimitors of the state of being the object (uddeśyatā) with respect to substance;
thus is the section on substance.
The section concerning the *sphyā* (wooden shovel).
In the *Bhāṣya*, the term for "substance" (*dravya-śabda*) is frequently employed by the followers of the *Chandoga* school.
Bhāṣya: [The action] pertains to the substance, the number, the cause, or the collection, due to its connection with the Vedic text.

Regarding the statement "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), does the sprinkling serve the purpose of the essential nature of the substance in the form of rice-grains, or is it intended to signify its status as a means for the *apūrva* (the transcendental result)?

Likewise, regarding the mantra "three enclosing-sticks, three fuel-sticks," does it serve the purpose of indicating the number of the enclosing-sticks alone, or rather the purpose of being a means for the *apūrva*?

Similarly, regarding the injunction "one offers with a winnowing-basket, for with it food is prepared," does the oblation serve the purpose of consecrating the instrument as a means of preparing food, or rather the purpose of the *apūrva*?

Likewise, regarding the touching [of the cakes] with the formulas "with the *Caturhotṛ*, one makes an offering over the full moon sacrifice; with the *Pañcahotṛ*, the new moon sacrifice," does this touching serve the purpose of the essential nature of the substances belonging to the full moon sacrifice and so forth, or rather the purpose of both of those?
Having thus reflected, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
