The substance, such as rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth; the number, such as the threefoldness residing in the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and so forth; the non-instrumentality residing in the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*); and the collection residing in the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) and so forth—the aggregate of these, namely the substance, number, non-instrumentality, and collection, would be the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites.
This is because of their connection with the Vedic text (*śruti*), that is, because of their connection with the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā-śruti*) and their connection with the particle *hi*.
The word "vā" (or) will be used here;

the sense is that modification (*ūha*) would not be established. Furthermore, if the substance were produced by the purpose (*arthakārita*), there would be no fixed determination by means of the substance.
The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position has been stated that substance, number, cause, and collection are the motivators for acts such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Here, he states the fault in the opposing view:
"artha" means that which is sought after (arthyate), and thus it is "arthakārita."
It would be unprecedented;

if it were accepted that the properties such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) are applied when [the substance] is brought about for the sake of the purpose, there would be no restriction by means of the substance.

The restriction by means of the substance (*dravya*) refers to such things as the mixing of the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup with milk alone, and the mixing of the *manthin* cup with groats alone, and so forth.
This restriction is established only if [the action] is prompted by the substance.

However, if it were prompted by the *apūrva*, there would be no restriction—such that the *manthin* cup might be mixed with either groats or milk, or the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup with either milk or groats—because the *apūrva* exists everywhere.
Therefore, it is the substance itself that is the motivator (*prayojaka*).

Furthermore, if the connection of acts such as sprinkling were with the substance *vrīhi* (rice) alone, there would be no fixed restriction; it would follow [unnecessarily] even in the case of *sruva* ladles and the like.
Therefore, since the form of the substance such as *vrīhi* is indeed the motivator for acts like sprinkling, there is no accomplishment [of these acts] when other substances are used.
Such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Alternatively, it should be the purpose (*artha*), that is, the motive for the others, because the purpose is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the injunction. The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), mantras, touching (*upamārśana*), and so forth are prompted respectively by the substance, the number, the cause, and the collection.
We state that "artha" (purpose) refers to the *apūrva* (the unseen potential).
It is so called because it is "sought after" (*arthyate*).
Substances and the like are not the purpose of acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), but rather the *artha* is.
The *apūrva* alone is the purpose;
acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) have the *apūrva* as their purpose;
the *apūrva* is the motivator for acts such as sprinkling.
Regarding the other factors, such as the substance and number, there is no injunction (*codanā*) in the sense of their being something to be performed;

that is, sprinkling and so forth are not an injunction for the sake of establishing the nature of the substance and its attributes. This is because the object is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), meaning it possesses subordination as determined by the *apūrva*.
These substances and other factors are subordinate with respect to the purpose and with respect to the *apūrva*;
therefore,
the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that sprinkling and the like are prompted by the *apūrva*.
"There would be a restriction because of its being a unique (unprecedented) factor.

Regarding what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that if the mixing with milk were accepted as being prompted by a unique factor (*apūrva*), then the mixing with milk [prescribed] for the Maitrāvaruṇa cup would apply to the Aindravāyava and other cups as well—the reply is given:

"Because of its being a unique factor"—that is, because it is preceded by the connection with the Maitrāvaruṇa; since the uniqueness of the Maitrāvaruṇa serves as the delimiting condition (*uddeśyatā-avacchedaka*) for that which is to be enjoined, there would be a restriction.
For there is no novelty (*apūrvatva*) in the *maitrāvaruṇa* [offering] distinct from other cups (*graha*), such that there would be a lack of restriction;
thus, if it were prompted by the novel element (*apūrvaprayuktatve*), there would be no fault whatsoever.
This sūtra has not been commented upon in the *Kutūhala*.
Regarding the point that the *dharma* is not restricted by the substance,

the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) states the flaw in accepting that *dharmas* such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are not restricted by the substance *vrīhi* rice. If it is accepted that the *dharma* of sprinkling and so forth is not restricted by the substance *vrīhi*, then it would apply to all objects, even for the sake of cooked rice (*odana*).
Sprinkling would also apply to those rice grains;
therefore, it is not prompted by the substance.
And if it were so prompted—

Regarding the objection raised by the Siddhāntin—that if the ritual duty (*dharma*) of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) were occasioned by substances such as rice (*vrīhi*), then sprinkling would also apply to rice intended for preparing *odana* (boiled rice)—the following is said in reply:

Since sprinkling is accepted as applying to the sacrificial rice substance (*yāgīya-vrīhi-dravya*) which is connected to the injunction and connected to the context (*prakaraṇa*), the fault of over-extension (*sarvaviṣayatā-doṣa*) does not arise.
There is no fault because, in the case of sacrificial rice, it is the factor that delimits the status of being the object (*uddeśyatā-avacchedakatvāt*).
If this is argued,
we say no, because it is not found in scripture.
That which was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view is not correct.
Because there is no scriptural injunction (*śruti*) stating that only those rice grains intended for the sacrifice must be offered,
nor because of the act of pressing;
rather, such rice grains are prepared as if already consecrated for the sake of the deity.

Furthermore, in this case, the delimitor of what is to be produced (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is not the rice used for the sacrifice, but rather rice in general. Thus, if the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) were occasioned by the substance itself, the defect of it applying to all [rice] would certainly follow.
If it is argued that this is not so "because of the qualification" (*adhikārāt*), [the reply is:

even if the sprinkling is occasioned by the substance, why does it not result in applying to all? Because of the qualification—that is, from the context (*prakaraṇa*), the Adhvaryu priest will know: "These rice grains are for the sake of the boiled rice (*odana*)," and "these are for the sake of the sacrifice."
If it is argued that "he shall sprinkle only those things intended for sacrifice," and thus there is no contingency of [the rule] applying to all objects, [we reply:
there would be no entitlement regarding equal [items], and the connection would not be enjoined.
The connection with the purpose of sacrifice belongs separately to those things that already exist; therefore, the sacrifice is the purpose.

As for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that "the Adhvaryu priest will understand the distinction of the rice grains intended for eating and for sacrifice from the context"—that is not correct.
The rice grains are identical;
they are the very same for the purpose of food and for the purpose of sacrifice.
Those intended for cooked rice are themselves intended for the ritual act.

At the time of offering, there are no distinct purposes for the ritual acts; likewise, at the time of offering, it indeed follows that [the rule] applies to all objects. Thus, while the rice grains (*vrīhi*) are equal [in status], there is no restrictive qualification (*adhikāra*) regarding the specific mode at the time of offering. Furthermore, such a connection is not enjoined by scripture.
Prior to the offering (nirvāpa), there is a connection of the rice grains with the ritual properties;
however, some [connection] is not enjoined.
Consequently, the offering would have a worldly basis.

The principle of the collection based on the cause of the number of substances applies here: the connection with the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) belongs specifically to the rice grains that exist separately as worldly objects and have been set aside individually for the sake of the sacrifice.
This is the principle of the collection based on the cause of the number of substances. 2172. The principle of the collection based on the cause of the number of substances:
there is a connection with the pouring out (*nirvāpa*).

Since there is no qualification among equal [acts], and no connection has been enjoined, but rather a connection with the sacrifice is made only for those [acts] performed separately, therefore the purpose of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is the unseen potency (*apūrva*) itself, and not the essential nature of the substance.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
[This is determined] by the principle of substance, number, cause, and collection (or by direct Vedic statement), due to their connection.

Having heard the injunction "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), one understands that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is connected with a substance; having [heard] "the three enclosing-sticks" (*trīn paridhīn*) from the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, it is connected with a number; having [heard] "He offers with a winnowing-basket, for by it food is prepared" (*śūrpeṇa juhoti tena hy annaṃ kriyate*) from the sentence (*vākya*), the oblation (*homa*) is connected with a reason; and having heard "He should touch the Full Moon sacrifice with the *Caturhotṛ* formula," one cites the mantra connected with the collection of [deities] such as Āgneya. When there arises a doubt as to whether these acts—sprinkling and the rest—are prompted by the form of the substance and so forth, or prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by means of the direct statement (*śruti*), the indicative power (*liṅga*) which characterizes them by that form, and the connection of the sentence (*vākya*), thus concluding they are prompted by the form of the substance and so forth. Then, by the sūtra "Or rather, the purpose would be the motive, because the others are subordinate to the purpose of the injunction" (*artho vā syāt prayojanam itareṣām acodanārthasya guṇabhūtatvāt*, 9.1.5.13), the author of the Bhāṣya establishes the final view (*siddhānta*): the *apūrva* being sought is the motive; since the substances and so forth are enjoined as things to be performed only as being subordinate to the *apūrva* being sought, they are not enjoined for their own sake. Anticipating the objection that there is no possibility of connection with the contextual *apūrva* because it would contradict the non-differentiation of the essential form (*svarūpa*) understood through direct statement and the other means of proof, [the author] will explain—out of fear of meaninglessness—that there is a desire to express the connection with the essential form by means of an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the means to the *apūrva*.

Su. Pṛ. 1469. By the principle of the "substance, number, cause, and aggregate" (*dravyasaṃkhyāhetusamudāyanyāya*), or by the principle of the "subject-matter" (*adhikaraṇanyāya*), [the term] is connected to its own form; for otherwise it would be meaningless. If, however, by the word *jajñyamāna* (being born), the status of being a means to the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is indicated—Vā. 3.4.5.9, p. 487. This is the principle of substance, number, cause, and aggregate (*dravyasaṃkhyāhetusamudāyanyāya*).
It is the principle of substance (*dravyanyāya*).
The Principle of Substance and Number:
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites, ritual duties such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) are prompted by the transcendental result (apūrva).
This is because they are connected by direct scriptural statement (śruti) with the substance, the number, the cause, or the aggregate.
The Commentary states: Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is enjoined: "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).

In that very context, the mantra "the rice-grains, the enclosing-sticks, the three fuel-sticks" (*vrīhīn paridhīn, tisraḥ samidhaḥ*) is enjoined (the phrase "it is enjoined" is to be supplied everywhere).
Furthermore, it is enjoined: "One should touch the Full Moon sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ* formula, and the New Moon sacrifice with the *pañcahotṛ* formula."
In the second festival of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, namely the Varuṇapraghāsas, it is prescribed in the sacred tradition: "One offers with a winnowing basket, for with it food is prepared.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: are ritual duties such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) prompted by the substance, the number, the cause, or the collection [of factors], or are they prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result)?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are prompted by the substance and so forth.

In this case, regarding the injunction "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would be prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), whereas by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is prompted by the substance (*dravya*).
For there is a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the sprinkling with the substance;
and even in that co-utterance, the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā vibhakti*) residing in the substance indicates that the sprinkling is prompted by the substance.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "three enclosing-sticks" (*trīn paridhīn*), it is understood that what is denoted by the word "thirty" (*triṃśat*) must be expressed here due to the power of the mantra's recitation;
and the number thirty is the meaning [of the term],
and its direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is the expressive word for it.
There would be an indication (lakṣaṇā) toward the unseen potency (apūrva) connected with that [winnowing basket].
"As many as are the familiarities, so many must be stated.
Likewise, by means of the reason, the property is conjoined with the sentence: "One offers with a winnowing basket" (*śūrpeṇa juhoti*).
What is the reason? Because by that [grain], food is produced;
thus it is connected with the oblation (*homa*).
The substance that produces food is prescribed for the oblation.

On account of the context (*prakaraṇa*), [the offering] would be prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result); because the *apūrva* is produced by this oblation, therefore it must be accomplished with a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*).
Since direct statement (*vākya*) is stronger than context, the context is thus set aside.

By whatever substance—whether a ladle (*darvī*), a cooking pot (*piṭhara*), or otherwise—food is prepared, by that very thing the oblation must be performed; in this way, the context of food becomes endowed with its specific quality.

But was it not stated in the first chapter (in the section concerning the consideration of the nature of a reason, 1.2.3) that the status of being a reason was refuted, and that this [passage regarding] the winnowing basket is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)?
True, this was said.

However, since the [use of the basket] is indeed prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), the injunction of the winnowing basket for the *homa* cannot be established within a single sentence; thus, it is construed as an *arthavāda*, and not otherwise.

"One should touch the full moon sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ* formula, and the new moon sacrifice with the *pañcahotṛ* formula. Because of this co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the two groups, the application [of the formulas] is established by the sentence (*vākya*). This overrides the application to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) understood through the power of the context (*prakaraṇa*), because that application to the *apūrva* is overridden by the sentence. Therefore, rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are prompted by the substances and other factors. As for the statement "by the two sprinkled ones," the sprinkling is indeed otherwise [prompted] by that sentence.

And that connection with the sentence is set aside by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)—namely, the connection of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with the sentence through the form of the verb *hanti* [is set aside].
Furthermore, the connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is indeed set aside by the direct Vedic statement—in the form of [the result] heaven and so forth.
In this section, connections with both indicative mark and sentence are not cited as examples, because they have already been refuted.
However, those whose purposefulness [toward another] is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) are the examples here.

Regarding those things whose purpose is established by *śruti*, there is the principle of substance, number, cause, and aggregate (dravya-saṃkhyā-hetu-samudāya-nyāya). 2173. The principle of substance, number, cause, and aggregate.
Considering the objects to be rice and so forth, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) argues as follows:

Having heard the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā vibhakti*) in the word "vrīhīn" (rice), it establishes that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) has rice as its purpose. Furthermore, the connection with the transcendental result (*apūrva*) would arise from the context (*prakaraṇa*). However, direct statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative than context.

In the case of "paurṇamāsīm" as well, the accusative case-ending itself, by means of direct scriptural statement (śruti), indicates that the touching refers to the collective object. Likewise, in "trīn paridhīn," the accusative case-ending also, by means of direct scriptural statement, expresses that the number is an attribute of the mantra.

(Regarding this, the *Tantraratna* states: "Now, one might object: how can this accusative case ending at the end of the word *mantra* establish that the mantra exists for the sake of that [the sacrifice], given the contradiction of an action directed toward itself?
True; what is cited as the *śruti* is one imagined (*kalpita*) from the mantra.

For, since it possesses the nature of a mantra capable of manifesting the thirty [deities], when it is being imagined, it would be imagined in such a way: 'One should manifest the three by means of this mantra.'"
Furthermore, this application by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) would not be possible, and that [application] has already been refuted.
True; however, another example must be given where such a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is perceived.
(This explains the marginal note found here in the Ānandāśrama edition.)
Therefore, even though the thirty mantras were previously employed, they are not employed for the first time [in this context].

In the case of the statement, "One offers with a winnowing basket, for by it food is prepared," the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is not an example [of an injunction], because it is indicated by an instrumental case-ending,
just as in the case of "One should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*).

The statement "one offers into the food-preparer" (*annakaraṇe juhoti*) is also not an example [of an injunction], precisely because of the mention of the instrumental case (*karaṇavibhakti*). If it were argued that it would indeed be an example because of its connection with the particle *hi*, [the author] refutes this: "That is not so; for it has been stated that this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) which is being enjoined."
It is said:
by the hearing of the word "hi" (for), the preparation of food is indicated as the reason;
because food is prepared by this [act], therefore the oblation must be performed with it (and not because it would result in the fault of being a mere figurative praise).
But surely, a reason must have a well-known relationship [with its probandum].

And no such relationship between the oblation (*homa*) and the syllables is apprehended through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as is the case with the two [terms] "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).
To this it is replied:

This is indeed true in the case of worldly matters (where a connection must be sought through another means of knowledge), but in the Veda, because of the hearing of the word *hi*, it is understood that the sentence establishes a connection between the act of making food and the oblation—namely, "whatever is an instrument for making food, that is connected with the oblation.
By means of that inferred sentence, the hearing of the reason (*hetu*) becomes intelligible.
And when there is the hearing of the reason, making food is the object to be prepared (*saṃskārya*), and the oblation is the agent of preparation (*saṃskāraka*).
Just as the act of giving is pervaded by the corresponding oblation (*homa*),
and just as wherever there is smoke, fire is pervaded therein;
(and the principal is pervaded by its subsidiary).
Therefore, hearing the word "hi" (for), one who considers that the oblation has the purpose of making food (*annakaraṇa*) formulates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

(Regarding what was stated in the first chapter—that its status as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) was established—he says: Since the oblation here is established as having an unprecedented purpose (*apūrvārtha*), [the question is: in the first chapter, is it the making of food that is enjoined with respect to the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) for the sake of the ritual substance (*padārtha*)?
Or is it the winnowing basket that is enjoined, and the making of food is a praise (*stuti*) of it? (This is a restatement of the position).
Such is this deliberation (thus concluded).
Furthermore, if the substance were produced for the sake of the purpose [of the sacrifice], there would be no fixed determination by means of the substance.
Bhāṣya: In the case of such a dharma being prompted by the apūrva, there would be no fixed determination of the dharma by means of the substance.
"He mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk, the mantha with barley meal, the haviryojana with parched grains, the śukra with gold, and the pātnīvata with clarified butter.
For whomsoever the Maitrāvaruṇa cup is the means of accomplishing an apūrva, for him that [apūrva] must also be resorted to;
and the Aindrāgna cup is likewise for an apūrva.
That too is to be mixed with milk;
it obtains [the result].
In this way, all [rites] beginning with the mixing of milk apply to all the cups.
In that case, the mention of Maitrāvaruṇa and others would be unintended; therefore, sprinkling and other such acts are connected with the substance and so forth.
Or rather, it must be for the sake of the purpose, because the others are not enjoined and that [purpose] is subordinate.
The Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
They would not be prompted by substances and the like.
What then? We say that their purpose is the *apūrva*; "purpose" means the *apūrva*.
They are for the sake of that.
For that [action] alone is heard as something to be performed; it is followed by its procedure (itikartavyatā).
As for the other factors, such as substance and so forth, there is no injunction regarding their being "to be performed. What then? They exist as subordinate elements (guṇabhūta) to the purpose.
Regarding the *apūrva*, these [subsidiary elements] are heard as being subordinate to it.
What follows from this? It means that for those things which are not themselves to be performed (*akartavya*), there can be no connection with a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
But surely, because of their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with rice and other materials, they must have a connection with them.
The second [view] is understood as being prompted by the collection of rice grains;
however, based on both indicative mark (liṅga) and syntactical connection (vākya), it is prompted by the substance and the cause.
To this, he says: "No."
If this were the case, a result would have to be postulated.
Therefore, [the action] is prompted by the *apūrva*.
But even so, in that case, a benefit must be postulated for the *apūrva*.
Truth must be established by bringing it into syntactic unity with the relevant context (*prakṛta*).
However, in the case of the suffix *-tva*, there would be syntactic unity with something not relevant to the context, namely, a statement of the result (*phala-vacana*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that context (*prakaraṇa*) sublates both sentence (*vākya*) and direct expression (*śruti*)? [Reply: True, but it does not sublate them.

Because there is no result, your position is abandoned; for when that [result] is not intended to be expressed, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is obstructed by the topical context (*prakaraṇatā*), and thus acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are enjoined. He says:
"It is a new [injunction] (*apūrva*)."
The principle of substance, number, cause, and collection (dravya-saṃkhyā-hetu-samudāya-nyāya) [2174]:
even by this principle, the ritual duty is applied only through those very grains such as *vrīhi* and so forth belonging to that [sacrifice].
What will happen in this way? For in this manner, the connection with the substance and so forth will indeed be established.
And one should not form conceptual constructions regarding the fruit.
It is said:
it is not possible in this way.

For in the statement "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), it is either the genus *vrīhi* that is indicated, or the substance *vrīhi* is indicated for the sake of characterization, or the specific means of accomplishing the *apūrva* is indicated for the sake of characterization. Since the purpose is served by the indication of one or the other, it cannot be for the sake of indicating both. Alternatively, it might be for the sake of characterizing the substance; however, in that case, the very act of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be a fault.
Considering that [the word] denotes a result (*phala*), the universal (*jāti*) is determined for the purpose of characterizing a specific means (*sādhana-viśeṣa*).
What is that means characterized by the rice-universal (*vrīhi-jāti*)? It is that from which rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are produced; that is what must be sprinkled (*prokṣitavya*).
For in this context, being a means consists in the capacity to bring about rice grains, not merely being a substance (*dravyatā*).
The same should be applied to number and other such factors as well.
Therefore, [the view is] that sprinkling and so forth are employed for the sake of the previously mentioned [grains].
*Ṭupṭīkā*: If the sprinkling were employed for the sake of the rice-grains themselves, then there would have to be an assumption of a result [for that act].

For it is not possible for the act of placing (*ādhāna*) to have the *apūrva* of the subject at hand as its purpose—even indirectly—through the act of pouring (*abhighāra*), since the purpose of placing has already been established [elsewhere].

(The Bhāṣya passage beginning with "This cannot be so" is logical. Furthermore, a single sentence cannot have two meanings: either that this is a property of the *apūrva* indicated by the preparation of rice-grains, or that it is a property of the substance characterized by the *vrīhi* species.
(But even the substance itself is not obtained [as the primary referent]).
For it is not possible for the word *vrīhi*, uttered only once, to convey both its own form and the specific means of accomplishment inherent in it.
In that case—since it would be purposeless if it were intended to convey its own form—it is understood that it indicates the specific means of accomplishment.

Regarding this, the text of the *Bhāṣya* states: "The means of accomplishment characterized by the genus *vrīhi*—what is that? That from which rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are produced—that is what is to be sprinkled; such is the meaning of the scripture."
Why? Because in that context, the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) consists in bringing about the removal of the rice-grains, not merely being a substance.

(Regarding this commentary: What is the intended meaning? (The answer: Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for the sake of that which is characterized as a means by way of being directed toward the removal of the rice-grains;
thus, even though the removal of the rice-grains is the same [in all cases], it is qualified [by its specific purpose].
Furthermore, no other substance can be characterized by its capacity to effect the removal of the rice grains.
Therefore, sprinkling does not apply to other substances.
Because it is a unique (apūrva) requirement, there must be a restriction.
Commentary: Now, as for what was said—"If [the word] were caused by the object, there would be no fixed determination by means of the substance"—[we reply:
since the genus (*jāti*) serves to characterize the specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there will indeed be such a fixed determination.
That which is performed in the case of a *maitrāyaṇī*...
In that case, there is the mixing with milk; it does not exist in the offering to Indra and Vāyu.

Therefore, the ritual properties (dharmas) of the offering to Indra and Vāyu do not follow from the offering to Mitra and Varuṇa, for the offering to Indra and Vāyu is indeed an independent (apūrva) rite.
Therefore, because it is something not previously established, there would be a restriction. And if the dharma were prompted by that [substance], then the dharma would have a universal scope.
The Bhāṣya states: "And for one who thinks that 'dharmas such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) are prompted by substances and the like,' it follows that the dharma would have a universal scope."
Even those rice grains intended for the deities would likewise have to be consecrated by sprinkling;
yet this is not desired.
Therefore, there is a fault in this position.
"If it is argued that it belongs to one connected with that"—the Bhāṣya says: if you think this, then the dharma will have all things as its object;
it will belong to one who is connected with that, namely, one who is connected with the context.
In this way, the context is upheld;
nor does dharma have everything as its object,
because it is not so stated in scripture.
Commentary: This is not so.
For it is not heard [in the scripture] that "the rice grains connected with the context are to be prepared and sprinkled.
Nor does this conclusion follow from the context.
He says: "No.
For a context (*prakaraṇa*) that has been sublated by a direct statement (*vākya*) does not abandon its capacity to restrict the ritual properties (*dharma*).
Even if it is not yet sublated, nevertheless, the context lacks the power to specify [the application].
For that [act] is enjoined as something to be performed; it is not [enjoined] as a qualifier, like a relationship already established.

Therefore, what is enjoined is the pouring out or the sprinkling of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) as qualified by the sacrifice under discussion. [Objection: The *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī* states: "The context (*prakaraṇa*) does not have the capacity to provide such a qualification."

"For that [action], being performed as something to be done, is enjoined, and not like a well-known relation as a subordinate qualifier of another" (Bhāṣya). What is the intention? (Answer: "One should bring about heaven.
By what means? By sacrifice.
Thus there arises an expectancy for the manner (*katham*).
And that mode [of procedure] must be performed because its own nature is differentiated.

That which is described as having a determinate nature serves as a qualification of another, as in the expression "a white cloth. In this context, when the requirement for "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) arises, the placement of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) and so forth presents itself; this constitutes the reason for its connection. (That *prakaraṇa*, consisting of the "how," becomes the cause for the connection of the placement of the fire and so forth with the "thusness" [*itthaṃbhāva*].)
And it cannot belong to anything else.

(The meaning is that the context by its own nature is not the cause for something else to have a connection [with it]. In the edition from Ānandāśrama, however, it reads here: "It does not belong to another, nor does it belong to another.")

The principle of substance, number, cause, and collection (dravyasaṃkhyāhetusamudāyanyāya), verse 2175; this is the reading. Furthermore, both sentences have been explained in the commentary (ṭippaṇī).
But that is not found in my own writing or in that treatise.
[Objection: "Because of the context.
[Response: The Commentary states: If you think this, [we reply] that the context is not a specifier for the *vrīhi* grains.
[The word] "bhāṭam" [is used].
From the context, the Adhvaryu will understand:
"These are for the sake of food; these are for the sake of work."

In that context, it is said: "One sprinkles them for the sake of the ritual purpose. There would be no qualification [of one over the others] among equals, since the relationship has already been declared; rather, there is a connection of those things existing separately with the purpose of the sacrifice. Therefore, that which serves the purpose [is what is intended]. Commentary: These rice grains (*vrīhi*) are equal.

Those very things that have the purpose of devotion (bhakti) are themselves the things that have the purpose of ritual action (karman); there are no separate things whatsoever called "having the purpose of ritual action.
[Objection: But surely those [entities] which were rejected are what have the purpose of ritual action. [Reply:
This may indeed be so.
In the case of sprinkling and similar acts, there would be no fault;
however, in the case of the offering (nirvāpa), there is a fault,
because no elements of the original archetype (prakṛti) are present there.
The pouring out of grains that exist separately for the purpose of the sacrifice is prescribed in the scripture.
How so? "To the west of the Gārhapatya fire, a cart stands facing east; having turned its right wheel toward it, one pours out [the grains] from the cart."
Therefore, it follows that the dharma indeed has all things as its object.
By the previous reason, it was established that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other such acts are prompted by the *apūrva*.
As for the Sūtra: "In that case, because of the superior force of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), [the act] is subordinate to the substance, such as rice."
The [rule] arrived at through the formal derivation also governs the state of being a supplement to what precedes.
If [the sprinkling] were subsidiary to the rice and other materials in their physical form, it would result in pointlessness;
for the nature of those materials is established even without this [sprinkling].
Therefore, the connection of sprinkling and other such acts with rice-grains, as enjoined by the scripture, is prescribed in their capacity as being instrumental to the sacrifice.

Therefore, all the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for the materials and other factors employed in the case of rice, such as threshing and so forth, are established on account of the production of the *apūrva*. These rites are to be extended (*ūhya*) to other materials used in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) when they serve the same purpose as the original ones.

As for the meaning of the Soma-sūtra: the material and other factors are the motivators (*prayojaka*), because of the hearing of the accusative case-ending; and the word "two" [is used] because of its connection [with the number].

The word *vā* (or) is intended to highlight the distinction of *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) from its association with syntactical connection (*vākya*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*). As it is said:
"In rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), practitioners [would otherwise] apply [the mantra] to the rice-grains and so forth by means of syntactical connection and direct statement;
however, the latter [application] does not occur through the requirement of what has been enjoined."

Bhaṭṭa: Here, in the root text, it is established that where substances, numbers, causes, or collections are the objects of reference (*uddeśyatā*) by direct statement (*śruti*), they are so by way of being means to the *apūrva*—just as in the case of *vrīhi* and other grains—and not merely by their own nature. This is because, according to the stated principle that "since contraction of the direct statement (*śruti*) through context (*prakaraṇa*) is improper," there would otherwise result in the fallacy of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) regarding their own form.
Thus, the conclusion is reached that [the qualification] is by way of being a means to the *apūrva*.

In this regard, although examples such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*)—which is a case of a visible result—and "with the Caturhotṛ [mantra], [he sacrifices] the full moon [day]" (*caturhotrā paurṇamāsīm*), which is a case of a collective [result], can somehow be possible, the Vārttikakāra has stated that the example of number, namely the mantra "the three enclosing-sticks" (*trīn parīdhīn*), cannot serve as an illustration because it is established that the mantra "O Agni, heaven" (*agnim suvaḥ*) has as its purpose the manifestation of the enclosing-sticks (*parīdhīn*) which are the means for the transcendental result (*apūrva*). The same applies to the inclusion of the reason (*hetu*).

Regarding the passage, "One offers with a winnowing basket, for by that food is prepared," one might suspect that because the winnowing basket is understood to be pervaded by its function as an instrument (the reason), and because logic shows predominance everywhere, the offering is enjoined as a purificatory act (saṃskāraka) with the preparation of food as its purpose. However, this has been set aside: since the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) reveals the winnowing basket's status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) toward the offering, and since the statement "for by that food is prepared" is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), it was determined that this offering is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) for the sake of the *apūrva*. That [previous argument] is disregarded here because even in the case of the *juhū* ladle and others—which are themselves pervaded [by their functions]—predominance toward the sacrifice is observed, and because the status of being an *arthavāda* has been established in the section on "Reason" (*hetvadhikaraṇa*), and because such an investigation would not be useful for the present *ūha* (adaptation).
Furthermore, it is described otherwise that the entire scope of this investigation has already been understood by the qualified student (*adhikārin*).

For although, by the sūtra *yajñakarma* (9.1.1), the definition of being a means to the *apūrva* was established for those things that provide direct assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), and by the sūtra *saṃskāre ca* (2), the causality of intermediate factors such as the nature of a sacrifice (*yāgatva*) was established; [the following is now addressed].

In such cases as "with those two, the mortar and pestle," or in other similar sentences, once the injunction has been made—wherein that which is qualified by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and that which is qualified by rice (*vrīhi*) serve as qualifiers of the enjoined action—then, subsequently, according to the principle of the black cow with a yearling (*aṇaikahāyanī*), there is no mutual exclusion. Consequently, even if that specific class [of substance] is absent in the modification (*vikṛti*), since sprinkling is obtained for another substance that occupies its place, the *ūha* (modification of the mantra) is established. Even if that class is lost in the modification, because sprinkling is obtained for another substance that takes its place, the *ūha* is accomplished.

At the time of the injunction of the qualification regarding the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), it is precisely the status of being a means to the *apūrva* that serves as the delimiting factor for the object of the injunction; there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) at all there, because the word *vrīhi* denotes the very nature of being rice-grain (*vrīhitva*).
This is because the status of being a means to the *apūrva* is denoted by its own term only within the context of an inferred injunction (*kalpitavidhi*).

Likewise, even in cases where, following a preparatory injunction (*saṃskāra-vidhi*), there is an application of the prepared substance by means of that [same] word— as in "when the milk has been heated" (*tate payasi*) and so forth— even there, within the preparatory sentence, the injunction for bringing curds (*dadhyānayana*) is made with reference to a subject delimited by a property co-extensive with the state of being milk (*payastva*), and not with reference to that which is merely delimited by the state of being milk, because that would be purposeless. And since that property is not specifically mentioned, it serves as a general restatement (*anuvāda*) of the collection [of parts] such as the heart and so forth, just as [the term] "desirable in general" (*iṣṭasāmānya*) [restates the specific desires].

In the *ālambha* injunction, there is a reference (*anuvāda*) to sacrifices performed with the heart and other organs by means of the root *yaj*, which is occasioned by the relationship between substance and deity.

Similarly, in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), there is a reference to the aggregate of sacrifices inferred from the relationship between substance and deity in the *aindravāyava* and other injunctions, for the purpose of enjoining the *soma* creeper as the material source (*prakṛti*) of the oblation.
Here too, as in the case of the *paurṇamāsī*, it is merely a reference to an aggregate.
Now, in sentences such as "He cuts from the heart first," a sacrifice (*yajati*) is neither explicitly heard nor even inferred; for the connection between a substance and a deity is not perceived,
and since the connection of the cutting with the heart and other parts— like the touching of the calf— is possible even without a sacrifice, it lacks the capacity to infer a sacrifice.

How so? Because the primary and subordinate terms are supported by the injunction of the sacrifice to the deities Paśu and Dravyāmīṣoma, the reference to the heart in the *dīkṣita* passage is made through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of its connection with the animal.
Therefore, in the case of the animal, a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not possible in any way.

Likewise, since there is a direct injunction of sacrifice in the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), how could there be an injunction of a sacrifice inferred from the connection between substance and deity in the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava cups and others? This would contradict the logical principle that "what is established by a direct injunction is obtained, whereas what is inferential is not."

Since the sentences concerning the *aindravāyava* and other offerings are already accounted for by the injunction regarding the drawing (*grahaṇa*) of the cups with the moon and wind as deities (*devatā*) as heard in the text, there arises no necessity to imply the injunction of an unmentioned sacrifice (*yajña*).

Or, even if we grant that five sacrifices such as the *aindravāyava* are enjoined through the connection between the substance and the deity, nevertheless, since the injunction of a sacrifice using the substance Soma is possible in the sentence "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), how can the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) function as a reference (*anuvāda*) to a sacrifice—even in the absence of the word *yat*—given that the injunction of the sacrifice with the substance Soma is already established? Therefore, how can there be a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the Soma sacrifice as well?

It is said: although the cutting (*avadāna*) of the animal is indeed prescribed in connection with the heart and other parts, nevertheless, by the very principle stated in *Sūtra* 8.1.40, "Or rather, the *sānnāyya*, because of its proximity," this act of cutting has the cutting of the *sānnāyya* as its archetype.
And since the cutting of the *sānnāyya* consists in the purification of the substance intended for sacrifice, this [cutting of the animal] also serves to purify a substance for sacrifice.
And that [purification] is possible only if the heart and other parts are the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.

Just as the status of *pūtīka* plants as a means of sacrifice is postulated through their connection with the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) that constitute the means of sacrifice, or just as the status of the *phalacamasa* as a means of sacrifice is postulated—even though it is not explicitly mentioned—through its connection with the [sacrificial] characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), so too here: by the word "animal" (*paśu*), the heart and other organs are referred to, and by the root *yaj* (sacrifice), which is connected to them, the sacrifice is referred to, and Indra and Agni are enjoined as the deity.

Nor is there the fault of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of the word "animal" being a reference (*anuvāda*) to the heart and other organs; for figurative indication brings about a fault only in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), not in the case of a reference.

Alternatively, since the injunction of the deity is already established by the sentence concerning the initiated (*yodīkṣita*), the sacrifice is inferred from the sentences concerning the heart and other parts.

Now, one might object: "In the sentence concerning the initiated, let there be an injunction for a sacrifice qualified by a deity; how can it be an injunction for the deity alone? This is not so. For it is thought as follows: even according to the Siddhāntin and others, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the cutting out of the heart and other parts must necessarily be accepted, and consequently, the word *paśu* (animal) must be taken as referring to the heart and other parts through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Thus, if the origin of the sacrifice (*yāgotpatti*) were [located] in the sentence concerning the initiated (*dīkṣita*), then there would be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the injunction (*vidhi*), and that is improper according to the maxim: "In an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [to be set aside]. However, if the sentences concerning the *avakāśa* grasses were the originators of the sacrifice, then the indication would occur in the restatement (*anuvāda*), which does not constitute a fault.
Furthermore, the establishment of an origin is observed even when referring to something yet to come, provided it is not overlooked.

Just as in the section concerning the number [of animals], the production of seventeen sacrifices is established after considering the future attainment of a group of portions (avadāna) by means of extended application (atideśa);

therefore, it is proven that by the word "animal" (paśu), the heart and other organs are inferred, and by the subsequent sacrifice (anuyājin), the sacrifices connected to them are inferred, and Indra and Agni are enjoined as the deity.

Similarly, in the Soma sacrifice as well, in the sentences concerning the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others, a sacrifice must necessarily be inferred by virtue of the connection between the substance and the deity.
For a statement that establishes the relationship between a substance and a deity does not reach its full meaning without a sacrifice.

As it has been said: "Just as the statements concerning the Āgneya and other offerings do not reach their own meaning prior to the inference of a sacrifice, so too should it be seen in the case of the Soma offering."
Thus [it is stated] (Vākyapadīya, p. 510).
Now, in this way, this sentence would result as being based solely on the Vedic revelation (śruti), namely: "One should sacrifice with that which has Indra and Vāyu as its deity."

If that were the case, then—just as in the *amīṣoma* sentence which restates a sacrifice enjoined by the *soma* sentence—one should simply enjoin the deity by restating the heart and other parts, as in the *hṛdaya* etc. sentences; what is the point of accepting a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) here? Not so.

If, by restating the sacrifice established in the *soma* sentence, one were to enjoin the deities through the *aindravāyava* sentences and so forth, then, due to the connection with a single sacrifice, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding those [deities] within that one sacrifice, just as in the case of the *palāśa* and other [wood] terms where they refer to a single object.
As it has been said: "Likewise, because of the meaning of the singular number, the word *palāśa* and others [refer to a single tree]."
In connection with that [offering], the deities are likewise conceptualized in relation to this sacrifice.
Thus [it is said] (Vārttika, p. 512). That being so, there is the observation of a sequence: "The Āśvina cup is drawn as the tenth; it is offered as the third."
Likewise, the observation of their combination—such as "these ten are taken" and "he takes the morning libation"—would not be possible [if they were not part of a single sacrifice].

However, if the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava and other cups were originative injunctions of sacrifices, then because they would relate to distinct sacrifices, the observation of both sequence and combination among the deities would be logical upon their combination.

This being the case, since there would be no injunction of a sacrifice due to the absence of a defining form (rūpa), even in the absence of words such as *yat*, the [cups] beginning with the Aindravāyava—
In the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), the word *yajati* is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the collection of sacrifices enjoined by other sentences;
the word *soma*, on the other hand, is for the purpose of enjoining the seven types of Soma plants known from the sentences concerning [the cups] dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others.
This being the position reached, it is replied as follows:
And this [repetition] would occur where there is a recognition of the sacrifice arising from another sentence, as in the case of the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).
Indeed, everywhere it is by the power of recognition that a restatement (*anuvāda*) occurs;
furthermore, recognition is postulated for the sake of establishing that restatement.

Furthermore, the sacrifice is not heard in the sentences concerning the house that has been dismantled (*avaghaṭita*), such that there could be recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) here. As it has been said: "Wherever recognition of the subject matter under discussion is perceived in a sentence, there there may be a restatement (*anuvāda*); but here it is not so perceived."
Thus [Vārttika, p.
Therefore, it is in the sentence concerning the initiated (*dīkṣita*) alone that there is the injunction of a sacrifice inferred from the connection between the material and the deity.
In the sentence concerning Soma, however, the injunction of a sacrifice qualified by a substance is established through direct perception itself.

Nor should it be argued that, since the heart and other organs as well as the secret [juice] are not yet enjoined at the time of the origination of the sacrifices characterized by the substances of the animal and Soma, the injunctions regarding the cutting off (*avadāna*) and the drawing out (*grahaṇa*) associated with them would be purposeless.

For there is no cognition of a mere animal-oblation; rather, because one observes the sentences concerning the cutting off and the drawing out, those two—remaining unmodified—are enjoined as sacrifices dedicated to specific deities.

What then? [The animal] extends from the heart and so forth up to the *rasa* (essence). Therefore, because the animal’s heart and the *soma*-juice contained within it are not used separately by that application of the *soma*, the injunction for the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) has as its scope only that which has already been applied.
Just as, since rice (*vrīhi*) extends up to the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*) and so forth, there is an injunction for a purificatory rite such as "he grinds the rice-grains.

Nor, in this injunction, do the words "animal" (*paśu*) and "*soma*" serve to indicate the purificatory rite; as it has been said: "When a substance is fundamentally distinct [from others], its relative strength or weakness is to be considered together with it."
The status of being a constant auxiliary belonging to the heart and other [limbs] belongs to the animal and the Soma sacrifice.
Thus [it is said] (Vākyapadīya, p. 516). Furthermore, specifically in the case of the example of an animal, a sacrifice involving slaughter cannot even be possible.

As for the argument that, since the cutting of the heart and other organs has the *sānnāyya* (curd-mixture) cutting as its archetype (*prakṛti*), it must possess those same properties because it is a refinement of the substance used in the sacrifice—and thus a sacrifice is inferred—this too is incorrect.
This is because, in the archetype itself, the *sānnāyya*-cutting has not been explicitly enjoined (*aghoṭita*), and therefore there is no connection with those ritual properties (*dharma*).
Furthermore, the cutting is not enjoined by the rule "he cuts twice from the oblation" (*dvir haviṣo 'vadyati*).
What then? It is merely a restatement of what is already established by the sense of the matter.
We shall explain this in detail in the section on "The Offering of All" (2.4.18, Bhāṣya 14.17).

Or, even if the cutting out of the heart and other parts were the primary material for that [offering], nevertheless, it does not possess the character of being a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the means of sacrifice.
Furthermore, it is the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) that is extended by analogy, not merely the generic property (*dharmamātra*).
Therefore, there is no inference of a sacrifice on its basis either.

However, in the case of the *pūtīka* plants and the drinking from the *phalacamasa* cup, they are taken up through their connection with the *pūtīka* and the *phalacamasa* respectively—by virtue of the context of the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the specific context (*prakaraṇa*)—as refinements of the very substances that serve as the means for the sacrifice; thus, there is a difference [between these cases and the previous one].

As for the argument that, because there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the injunction itself, one must first establish that the word "animal" (*paśu*) in the sentence concerning the consecrated person refers to the heart and other organs through figurative indication, and then infer a sacrifice from the very sentence containing the act of immolation by determining the relationship between the substance and the deity—that too is long refuted, since the primary sacrifice is already expressed by the word "animal" as extending to the heart and other parts within the injunction of the sacrifice. Thus, the example of the animal sacrifice is already set aside. Similarly, in the case of the explicit statement "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), it is impossible to even conceive of a sacrifice in the sentences concerning the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others.

Nor should it be argued that the sentences concerning the *āgneya* and other offerings do not achieve their own purpose without another sacrifice within the sentences concerning Indra-Vāyu and others;
for the sentences concerning Indra-Vāyu and others reach their completion simply by enjoining the taking up of the substance (*dravya*) with reference to Indra-Vāyu as the deity.

However, in the sentences concerning the *āgneya* and others, since the human activity (*puṃvyāpāra*) is the object of the injunction and the "thing-to-be-accomplished" (*bhāvya*) is not itself a human activity, a human activity must necessarily be postulated; and it has been stated that, given the connection between the substance and the deity, the sacrifice (*yāga*) alone is postulated as that activity.
In this case, since the human activity in the form of "taking" (grahaṇa) is heard [in the text], the sentence reaches its conclusion there.
Now, an objection may be raised: "The status of being the intended object (uddeśyatva) with respect to the oblation (havis) being taken is not connected to anything by way of a genus (jāti).
Therefore, how can there be a syntactic connection (anvaya) of the deity with the act of taking?"
It is said: this act of taking up (*grahaṇa*) is not a separate entity; rather, it is simply a constituent part of the sacrifice (*yāga*).
For [the substance] is not abandoned by merely designating a deity.
Nor does a sacrifice come into being when that which was taken up for one purpose is abandoned for another purpose.

Since a sacrifice (*yāga*) is simply the relinquishment of an oblation (*havis*) already taken for the sake of a deity, there is no contradiction in designating Agni as the deity when he is a constituent part of that sacrifice.

Thus, when a sacrifice is required, since this very sacrifice is directly heard in the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), there is no need here for the postulation of a sacrifice not otherwise obtained.
And this being the case, the deity connected with the grasping of the vessel that constitutes the place of sacrifice is connected with the deity required for the primary sacrifice.

Furthermore, this being so, there would not be an option (vikalpa) among the deities—even as there is no option between the *khadira* and *palāśa* wood for the purpose of binding—because the deities are intended for a single sacrifice.

For in this instance, the *khadira*, *palāśa*, and other woods are not prescribed by the sentence for the act of binding, nor are the deities prescribed for the sacrifice by the sentence, such that an option would result.
What then? Through the medium of the *grahaṇa* (drawings), there is a connection of the deities with the sacrifice.

Since the *grahaṇas* have distinct functions, they are grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) simultaneously; because they have distinct functions, they are to be combined, as [stated in] the injunction regarding the connection with the substance.
Because the injunctions pertain to substances,
it is logical that there is a combination of deities as well, by way of their being grasped [in the vessels].

However, there is this distinction: the deity for the taking (*grahaṇa*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*) is one and the same; therefore, that which was taken with a specific intention must be relinquished with that very same intention.
Consequently, each individual taking is a repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the Soma-sacrifice.
This being the case, for the three pressings (*trivarga*), the ten takings (*daśagraha*), and the ten cups (*daśacamasa*), the sacrifice is distinct with every repetition.
By the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma," it should be understood that [the sacrifice] is produced once.

This being the case, the observation of sequence—namely, "the Āśvina cup is drawn as the tenth, it is offered as the third"—as well as the observation of conjunction—namely, "the Adhvaryu draws these ten cups at the morning pressing"—become logically consistent; thus, the example of Soma is also faultless.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because the heart and other parts are distinct from the offerings to Indra-Agni and others, and because they serve their own specific purposes, when there is an extension of the ritual details (atideśa) for the sake of those [heart-offerings] based on the indicative mark of the specific injunction, there is no acquisition of all the ritual properties (dharma).
In the Siddhānta, however, because the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) and the Soma sacrifice (*somayāga*) are unitary, all the ritual properties (*dharma*) apply to the modified form (*vikṛti*).

As for the Sūtra: "Because of the connection with the substances of the animal and the Soma, there is an injunction of sacrifice—that is, a prescription of sacrifice—in the sentence concerning the animal and the sentence concerning the Soma; for in the case of the archetypal sacrifices (*prakṛtayāga*), the connection with the substance would otherwise be purposeless and devoid of utility.

Regarding the phrase "not for the sake of a subordinate quality" (*na hi tasya guṇārthena*), the author of the Bhāṣya, Śabarasvāmin, explains it by taking the Soma example: having raised the objection that the Soma plant might be for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) as the substance to be offered, he interprets the Sūtra as being intended to refute that by means of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

The author of the Bhāṣya has not grasped the true meaning of the sūtra, "Not for the sake of its quality" (*na hi tasya guṇārthena*). For it is not conceivable that Jaimini had in mind a doubt regarding a subordinate element (*guṇa*) being the substance to be offered (*pradeya*), as bound by the locus of a quality (*guṇādhikaraṇa*); rather, he considered [the grain] only as the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the substance to be offered, just like rice (*vrīhi*).
As it has been said: "Just as by the scriptural statement, 'In the case of the *akapāla* sacrifice and others,' rice and other grains are prescribed, so too shall Soma be prescribed."

(Vākyapadīya, p. 513) | On this point, some offer the following resolution: "In the case of the statement, 'There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni' (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālo bhavati*), there exists a supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) that establishes the connection between the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the deity Agni:
'They saw the sacrificial cake as a tortoise crawling; they said to it: "Be dear to Indra! Be dear to Bṛhaspati! Be dear to the Viśvedevas!"', and so forth."

Even though this [injunction] is primarily concerned with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), because it is restricted by the presentation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) intended for praise, its application culminates specifically in the *āgneya* (dedicated to Agni) cake within its own sentence.

That being the case, when there arises an expectation regarding the material source—namely, "Of what nature is the cake?"—the injunction of rice (*vrīhi*) as the material source is appropriate, as in the rule: "One should sacrifice with rice."

In this case, however, because no supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) such as "he takes the Aindravāyava cup" is perceived, and because the expectation of a material cause (prakṛti) for the Soma is understood through the observation of the context (prakaraṇa) in the phrase "he purifies the Soma," the taddhita suffix reaches its full meaning right there; thus, since there is no requirement for a material form, it is possible for the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" to enjoin the Soma plant itself as the material cause.

Furthermore, just as in the case of "one should sacrifice the *tvaṣṭṛ*-related [animal] dedicated to Pānīvat," where the nominal suffix (*taddhita*) culminates in the mere act of sacrificing as implied by the context, so too in the case of "one takes up the *aindravāyava*," the nominal suffix must culminate in the mere act of taking up as implied within its own sentence.

Moreover, because of the mention of something else in the sentence "he takes it with a thin stream"—where the word "thin" (*aṇvī*), being a figurative term, denotes a specific type of taking that does not deviate from others—it must be stated that the nominal suffix culminates in the substance itself which is presented by that which is not otherwise restricted.

This is because, according to the etymology, a "word whose primary purport is something else" (*anyapara-śabda*) denotes [an object] by the principle of implication (*arthākṣiptanyāya*), since it is not otherwise established. Furthermore, in the opponent's view, because there is a constant relationship between words and their meanings, even that which is implied by the sense would entail the assumption of a word expressive of it; thus, through syntactic connection (*anvaya*), the word *soma*—which is led by another word whose primary purport is something else in the context of the passage "he purifies the *soma*" (*somaṃ punāti*)—is understood to terminate its application precisely therein.
Nor should it be argued that because the word *soma* denotes a creeper, the word *soma* in the phrase "he purifies the *soma*" does not have the moon as its referent.

Since the word *punāti* (purifies), which primarily denotes the purification of a substance, cannot be logically applied to the Soma plant itself, one must necessarily admit that it functions as an indicator (*lākṣaṇika*) by virtue of its secondary application (*bhaktyarthatva*).
Nor should it be argued that, in deference to the word *soma* understood from the outset, the word *punāti* alone should be taken as figurative so as to mean "Soma plant";
for there is no evidence to determine (*vinigamanā*) which specific action appropriate to the connection with the Soma plant is intended by the figurative sense residing in the word *punāti*.

In the case of the word *soma*, however, because only that which originates from a lake (*sarasa*)—as is appropriate for the relationship already established—is fit [to be denoted], there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determination; thus, the definition applies to that alone.

This being so, since both [the *aindravāyava* and other cups] are primary actions (*pradhānakarma*), and because the word *soma* refers to the juice (*rasa*) in both instances, the juice of *soma* is connected [to each cup] by way of ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) in response to the expectation, "What [is to be taken] for Indra and Vāyu?

Nor is there an ellipsis obstructed by the intervention of the sentence regarding the stream (*dhārāvākya*), because even there, in response to the expectation, "What [is to be taken] with a stream?", there is a connection with the *soma*-juice.

Just as the word "body" (*tanūḥ*), which is connected with the phrase "that body of yours, O Agni, which lies in the goat" (*yā te agner ajāśayā*), is not separated from the term *irāśayā*, so too the connection of the Soma juice with Indra and Vāyu is not separated by the sentence concerning the stream [of the offering].

This being the case, since the application of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) finds its finality in the Soma juice itself, and because there is no requirement for a material substrate, the injunction of the creeper is possible as the material source (*prakṛti*) of that juice.

As it has been said: "In the case of the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) in the *Āgneya* and other offerings, since its constituent substance (*prakṛtidravya*) has not yet been specified, it is appropriate that there be a determination of that constituent substance;
for here the injunction arises from the connection with a substance."

"But because of the connection with a substance (*dravya*), the injunction is understood as referring specifically to the *soma* juice whose nature has already been determined; for there is no expectation [on the part of the injunction] such as 'what is the nature of the *soma* juice?

To this it is replied: Let the application of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) indeed terminate in the *soma* juice itself; nevertheless, the prescription of *soma* will be purposeful, insofar as it ensures—without any deficiency—the accomplishment of the sacrifice known as the *vi-hvaya*, which necessarily requires the juice produced from *soma* that has undergone the purificatory rites of purchase and pressing.

Otherwise, however, since there would be no necessary inclusion of the *anaṅga* (the non-essential part), the sacrifice could be performed even with Soma that has been received as a gift or purchased, and so forth. Nor can it be argued that—even if it is not an essential part—the juice extracted from the Soma that has been purchased, purified, and pressed in that manner is indeed the *aindravāyava* (the portion for Indra and Vāyu). This is because such an argument would result in a logical inconsistency (*vikalpa*).

Is this stated by relying on the status of the acts of purchasing and so forth as *saṃskārakarma* (preparatory rites), or as *pradhānakarma* (principal rites)? It cannot be the first alternative, because that [status] is impossible since it pertains to what has already been enjoined.

Nor can it be the second, for even in that case, if [the acts] were principal rites, then in the event of the loss of the purchased *soma*, or the loss of the pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*) during the pressing and so forth, the principal rite itself would necessarily be lost.
Furthermore, a general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*) depends upon a specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*) through the principle of *prasaṅga* (extension/application) due to the force of mutual requirement.

Just as the *padakarma* scripture is a specific rule concerning the subordinate term *ekahāyanī* when she is being led for the purpose of purchase, the rules regarding purchase, pressing, and so forth—since they are equal in their acquisition of the *soma* already established in common worldly practice—do not fall under the scope of *prasaṅga* (incidental application) according to the maxim "there is no further qualification among equals. Therefore, it is logical that the injunction of *soma* functions as the *prakṛti* (archetype).
As it has been said: "Even without a separate injunction, [the substance] is employed for the purificatory rites of purchase, pressing, and so forth, by the rule 'one should sacrifice with *soma*'."

Nor can the *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) status of Soma be denied on the grounds that it is not "employed" (*aviniyukta*), because it is not a non-member (*anaṅga*) of the sacrifice; for while Soma is understood as the material cause (*prakṛti*) in the statement "he purifies the Soma," it is subsequently employed in the sentences concerning the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others. Since that which possesses qualifications is useful for the ritual action, when such utility exists, a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) that serves only for cognition cannot be set aside. Furthermore, in the case of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), it is established everywhere that the qualifications possess a status as members of the ritual through their inclusion (*aupādānika-aṅgabhāva*).

Furthermore, it must be stated that the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice cannot be merely postulated for *soma*, because there is no room for postulation when the matter is directly perceived in scripture; and since the direct scriptural statement, "One should sacrifice with *soma*," establishes its status as an auxiliary, the injunction regarding *soma* must be understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that sacrifice which is already established.

Furthermore, the manifestation of the sacrifice for the *aindravāyava* cup is preceded by a connection with the *soma* mentioned in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), wherein there is a formal identity between the qualified object and its qualifier. However, because of the requirements of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and semantic competency (*yogyatā*), the absence of the deity as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the juice cannot occur without the juice being a subordinate element of the *soma*. Thus, once the status of the *soma* as a subordinate element is established through this "incidental" (*aupādānika*) necessity, the direct injunction of the *soma* itself becomes entirely redundant. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that the creeper (*latā*) itself must be the substance to be offered.

For it is not the case that in every instance of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there must be a uniformity between the qualifier and the qualified; rather, [the status of] being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) as a deity occurs solely by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and compatibility (*yogyatā*).
Even in that case, although the juice (*rasa*) is what is to be offered, its connection with the *soma* plant is established precisely through its being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of that juice.

Alternatively, even though the *soma* is not directly enjoined [in this context], it is an object of the sanctifying rite (*saṃskārya*) because it serves as an auxiliary through its role in the pressing and so forth; whereas the calf, being an auxiliary that is itself enjoined, is the object of the sanctifying rite in the injunction "one should touch the calf" (*vatsamālabheta*). Or, just as the *ṛc* verses are the objects of the sanctifying rite of the *sāman* because they serve as auxiliaries for the praise that is enjoined, or as the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is the object of the sanctifying rite of recitation according to the view of others, because it serves as an auxiliary for that which is enjoined.

[Objection: Since *soma* is not enjoined [in this context], it is not a constituent part (*aṅga*); and since that which is not a constituent part cannot be substituted, the statement "if they should not find *soma*, they should press *pūtīka* plants" would be an injunction for *pūtīka* as a substitute for the absence [of *soma*], not a restrictive rule for a substitute of *soma*.
If that were the case, then in the event of the failure of the *pūtīka*, one would incur a fault regarding that [substitute], and not the acquisition of a thousandfold *soma*.
Therefore, the acquisition of a thousandfold *soma* is logical; thus, there is a disparity between this and the injunction for *soma*.

Since the *somarasa* has already been assigned [as a primary substance], its inclusion within the *pūtīka* plant—which serves as its substitute—constitutes precisely a restriction regarding the substitute (*pratinidhi-niyama*).

Alternatively, even though *soma* is not a constituent part (*aṅga*), since that which is derived from *soma* as its material cause (*tatprakṛtika*) is what is prescribed, the juice alone constitutes the scriptural meaning (*śāstrārtha*) because *soma* is the material cause of the juice; and since the scriptural meaning can serve as a substitute, it is entirely appropriate to restrict the substitute to *soma*. What would the status of being a constituent part (*aṅgatā*) accomplish here? Nor can the status of being the substance to be offered (*pradeyatva*) or the character of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatva*) be established by the logic of the section on qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇanyāya*). For in that case, in the statement "the *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas," the *āmikṣā* is restricted by its own sentence; whereas in subsequent injunctive sentences such as "he draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu," the juice is not perceived [as the primary object], and thus there is a disparity.
Therefore, the Bhāṣyakāra’s argument that the creeper is the substance to be offered is logical.

To this it is replied: as for what was stated—that because the word "Soma" occurs in the *utpatti-vākya* (originative injunction), the derivative suffix (*taddhita*) must terminate in its meaning, and since that is so, it is impossible for the injunction of Soma to be merely indicated by that [word]—that is not correct;
for the juice of Soma is not heard in the *utpatti-vākya*.
Nor is it denoted by the word "soma" through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the impossibility of a connection with something already produced;
for if it were a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), then the juice—which is the substance to be prepared—would have to be indicated as existing within the plant that has already been produced.
Likewise, because it is so enjoined, the purpose would be the purification of the *soma* plant itself.
It could also be for the purpose of purification;
however, if one were to assume its application as a purification, it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya).
Therefore, by the principle of the mention of the past and the future (bhūtabhavyasamuccāraṇanyāya), it must be a primary action (pradhānakarma) itself.

And this being the case, since the primary substance, *soma* itself, constitutes the very form of the conceptualization of the material for the sacrifice, it is possible for it to be the means [of accomplishment];
this is not *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication).
Nor should it be said that because another substance must be conceptualized, the word *soma* itself undergoes *lakṣaṇā* to denote "the juice" (*rasa*).
In both cases, it is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Since it serves as the means for purifying (*utpavana*), one must indeed postulate another substance characterized by its juice (*rasa*) that is not earthen (*apārthiva*).

However, this is the distinction: in the former case, the primary meaning of the word "Soma" possesses the quality of being the means of purification through the act of making into a substance (*dravyīkaraṇa*), which is invariably concomitant with purification; whereas in the latter case, the word "Soma" is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) because it assumes the status of being the means invariably concomitant with purification.
It has been stated accordingly.

Alternatively, let it be that in the sentence concerning purification (*utpavana*), there is a verbal comprehension of the juice (*rasa*); yet, the derivative suffix (*taddhita*) does not terminate its application there.
Nor, that being the case, can it be said that the derivative suffix terminates its application only in the case of the sacrificial creeper (*homalatā*).
Because a continuous series of sentences (*dhārāvākya*) lacks connection due to the intervention [of other thoughts],

in the case of a continuous series of sentences, the principle regarding substances and purificatory acts (*dravyasaṃskāranyāya*) applies to the qualities, substances, and purificatory acts of that which is to be grasped.

"This armor is indeed made for him; it is the armor of the sacrificer for the sake of overcoming his enemies"—this is the declaration of the fruit (*phalaśruti*) in the ritual action consisting of [the production of] progeny and so forth.
*Parṇī* refers to the *palāśa* tree.
*Pāpaḥ ślokaḥ* means ill-repute or infamy.
He anoints his eyes;
he destroys the rival, the enemy.
He consumes; he causes destruction.
*Varma* means armor;
