Even though the form of the agent is one, the dual number is appropriate due to the difference in their substrates, just as in the case of the two deities [Agni and Soma]. Furthermore,
when linen cloth is worn over a garment that is not woolen, [the dual is used].

The two [sentences] beginning with "wearing" and "should put on" are merely restatements (*anuvādaka*). As for the objects of these restatements, they follow what is established by other means of proof; and that [established rule] applies to both the woman and the man.
Therefore, since linen cloth is already established as the material for clothing and so forth, those very two [the husband and wife] will be mentioned [as wearing it].
Therefore, a single man alone should establish the sacred fires together with his wife;
for in the original injunction, the singularity [of the agent] is intended as a qualifying factor.

As for the *Soma* passage—"The king and the domestic priest should sacrifice together"—the meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra is that the entitlement to the establishment of the fires belongs to two males.
Vi— "Either for one man alone there is the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*), or for two because of the mention of 'wearing';
the rule regarding the linen garment (*kṣauma*) applies to one, [but] the pair [is mentioned] for the husband and wife; therefore, their unity follows.
Bhāṭṭa—In the section on the laying of the fires (*ādhāna-prakaraṇa*), it is heard in scripture: "Wearing linen garments, the two should lay the fires (*āgnim ādadhyātām*)."

Therefore, because the injunction [regarding] the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) prescribes two agents, two males and two females are entitled to perform the *ādhāna*, as in the case of the statement: "The king and the domestic priest, desiring universal sovereignty, should sacrifice together.

Nor should it be argued that here—as in the example "Bring two roosters, I shall mate them"—the formation of a singular remainder of dissimilar forms (*virūpaikaśeṣa*) is possible by virtue of the grammatical rule "a male [is used] when a female is implied" (*pumān striyā*); for since the sentence can be explained as being concerned solely with the dual number and the *kṣauma* cloth, there is no impossibility of the singular number and the single location being taught at the time of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).

Since the retention of a single form (*sarūpaikaśeṣa*) is possible, it is improper to resort to the retention of dissimilar forms (*virūpaikaśeṣa*), which would necessitate figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nevertheless, because the vowel *au* intends both duality and masculinity, there is a mutual restriction such that when the state of having a single form is absent, masculinity is delimited by duality, and when masculinity is absent, duality is delimited; thus, the cognition of two males is easily obtained.

In the case of *virūpaikaśeṣa*, however, as in *pitarau* ("parents") and so forth, there is no exclusion of motherhood and the like, and as in *kukkuṭau* ("two roosters"), there is no exclusion of femaleness; therefore, figurative indication is necessary, and for this reason, *virūpaikaśeṣa* is weaker than the former.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that even in your own view, the term *kṣauma* (linen) is secondary (*gauṇī*) due to its similarity to "impurity" based on the proximity of the word in the opening statement; nor that there is recourse to a derivative etymology (*avayavayoga*) based on the grammatical rule "the word *kṣauma* [is used] in the sense of cloth"; nor that there is the fault of the redundancy of the subject (*anuvādyavaiyarthyam*); nor that the singular number in the originative sentence serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*). For these reasons, such a position is untenable due to its many defects. Rather, the sentence concerning linen itself enjoins the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) as qualified by both [the material and the season].
However, in the sentences concerning the garments and so forth, the injunction of seasons such as spring is contingent upon the status of the person as a Brāhmaṇa and so on.
For this very reason, in the word "brāhmaṇaḥ," both the singular number and the masculine gender are not intended to be significant (avivakṣita).
The same applies to the verb "ādadhīta.

If the injunction were connected with the word "brāhmaṇa" as "one who is a Brāhmaṇa should establish [the fires]," then the mention of "in spring" would merely be a contingent restatement (anuvāda) of a single instance, such as that of a Brāhmaṇa.

Therefore, two males who are friends are the qualified subjects. As for the other proof presented in the Bhāṣya and elsewhere to establish *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (the retention of one among identical forms), it concludes by stating that because *ekaśeṣa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *dvandva*, the meaning of *ekaśeṣa* is precisely the same as the meaning of *dvandva*.

And *dvandva* [is used] because of the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana: "A *dvandva* occurs when there is a simultaneous substratum (*ayugapad-adhikaraṇe*). Thus, it denotes simultaneous substratum. (Regarding this, the second *vārttika* on Pāṇini 2.2.29 states: "But it is established [that *dvandva* applies] when there is a statement of simultaneous substratum, because of the mention of *dvandva*. In that regard, the method of the *Mahābhāṣya* is: "'It should be stated that a *dvandva* occurs when there is a statement of simultaneous substratum.
A *substratum* (*adhikaraṇa*) is the object signified by a word; where multiple such objects are conveyed simultaneously by a single word, there a *dvandva* occurs.)
And likewise, in the expression "the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," the word *dhava* refers both to the *dhava* tree accompanied by the *khadira* and to the *dhava* tree accompanied by something else;
and here, from the word *khadira*, the word *dhava* refers to the *dhava* tree accompanied by the *khadira*.
Thus, there is simultaneous coreferentiality (*yugapadhikaraṇatā*).
This very same *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) is also [the meaning] here; in this very sense, the term *dvandva* [is used].
For the particle *ca* has four meanings: *samuccaya* (conjunction), *anvācaya* (subordinate addition), *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction), and *samāhāra* (aggregation).
Among these, *samuccaya* is the state of equality when there is mutual independence in relation to the meaning of the case-ending.

Consequently, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), nor to that of option (*vikalpa*), nor even to that of secondary addition (*anvācaya*).
For example: "Day after day, he brings a cow, a horse, and a man" (the reading *ca* here is incorrect); and so forth.

In the case of secondary addition (*anvācaya*), however, one element is the motivator (*prayojaka*) while the other is not; thus there is no equality between them, as in: "Bring wood and bring vegetables."

In the case of *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), however, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the case-ending through mutual association (*parasparasāhityena*), as in "Agni and Soma are the deities" (*agniś ca somaś ca devatā*).

In instances such as "the *dhava* tree and the *khadira* tree," when *itaretarayoga* is intended, simultaneous reference to the substratum (*yugapadhikaraṇavacanatā*) is necessary; otherwise, if the case-ending were connected to each [term] individually, it would result in the mutual conjunction being reduced to a mere disjunction (*samuccaya*).
For this very reason, the statement that "conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the connection of two independent [factors] with a single action" has been refuted by that same [author].
Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of this definition to the option (*vikalpa*) expressed in the sentence, "on the new moon day or on the full moon day.

As for mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) and collective aggregation (*samāhāra*), the distinction between them lies in whether the association (*sāhitya*) is subordinate or primary relative to the word-meanings; however, their status as mutual conjunction is equal.
In these meanings, the *dvandva* compound occurs only in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
For this very reason, even though the objects [denoted] are many, the *dvandva* consists precisely in the form of mutual conjunction.
Thus, the general rule "the *dvandva* is used in the sense of *ca*" has been explained by the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* and others as having a specific scope.

And for this reason, since even a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) compound conveys the meaning of a dual dvandva compound when there is simultaneous coreferentiality (*yugapad-adhikaraṇatā*), there is the cognition of two males in the word *vasānau*.
In that case,

even if one adopts the rule for the single-remainder of dissimilar forms (*virūpa-ekaśeṣa*), it is logically possible for both a woman accompanied by a man and a man accompanied by a woman to be expressed simultaneously.
Nor does this result in a fourfold combination consisting of two males and two females, because a pair of a female and a male is possible, just like a pair of two white *khadira* trees.
In reality, however, the notion of simultaneous expression of the substratum (*yugapad-adhikaraṇatā-vācitva*) stated by Kātyāyana was refuted by Patañjali himself. This is his intention:

Since there is no evidence for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the words *dhava* and *khadira*, and since the conjunction *ca* itself intends the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the triad [of meanings] is thus established.

For this very reason, in cases such as "the *dhava* and the *khadira*," one should also understand that when the expression "of the *dhava* and the *khadira*" is incapable [of expressing the intended meaning] due to the influence of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), metaphorical indication occurs. However, in a *dvandva* compound, because the case-ending is singular, the expression is faultless even without metaphorical indication in the case of mutual conjunction.
As for the occasional display of a compound analysis (*vigraha*) in the Veda such as *pra mitrayor varṇayoḥ*, that is merely a linguistic convention (*chāndasa*).

Therefore, it should also be understood that when a case-ending denotes a property (*dharma*) that functions distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), it is precisely the *dvandva* compound that serves as the indicator of such an intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*).

Furthermore, even from a *dvandva* word, the *ekaśeṣa* [formation] does not denote a property that functions distributively with respect to the case-ending following it, because the number [of the suffix] would otherwise fail to agree [with the referent].
Because the application of the rule for *ekaśeṣa* occurs subsequent to the connection with the meaning of the case endings, there is no evidence for the operation of *ekaśeṣa* prior to that.

In reality, however, even the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) regarding *ekaśeṣa* is merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), since the plurality required by the dual ending and so forth is established even without it, for the purpose of excluding *sarūpa-dvandva*.

As for *virūpa-ekaśeṣa*, the distinction is that there is a technical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the long vowel *au* based on the force of the grammatical instruction, in accordance with the intention (*tātparya*).
Since only a *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (retention of one form among identical items) is accepted here due to proximity (*sannidhi*), it follows that the entitlement belongs to males alone.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because in the sentence concerning the spring season (*vasantādivākya*)—“one should establish the fires” (*ādadhīta*)—the singular number would result in being a merely optional restatement (*pākṣikānuvāda*), and because there would be the contingency of the spring season applying to an establishment of the fires performed by two Brāhmaṇas, the injunction for the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) itself must be understood in the sentence concerning the spring season as well.

However, in the sentence concerning the garment (*vasana-vākya*), since the injunction prescribes a single agent, and because both the duality of agents and the linen cloth (*kṣauma*) would otherwise be enjoined [simultaneously], one must accept a grammatical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the rule of grammar (*ānuśāsanikī*) and admit a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (retention of one form among dissimilar items) through the indication of the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇā*).
In that case, it is appropriate to rely even on the dual number as being optional;
for this very reason, in that instance, merely the linen cloth (*kṣauma*) is enjoined with reference to the act of wearing.
And it is logical that there can be a relationship with a *kāraka* even for those things whose existence is otherwise established through implication.
The suffix that expresses the act of laying the fires (*ādadhāti*) alone is the enjoining agent.

Because it occurs in close proximity to the word at the beginning of the section and because of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), it is the enjoining agent even for a remote meaning. Everything else, however, is merely supplementary, as it is already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

And although, because the masculine gender is heard in the original injunction (*upatti*), mere gender does not result in duality [of the sacrificer], nevertheless—given that the author of the commentary has explained the Brāhmaṇas and others as being qualified for the ritual in order to avoid complexity in a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) and to avoid a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the sentence concerning the garment—it is logical that the masculine gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*) because it is a qualification of that [sacrificer] who is the object of the cutting. Thus, there is no obstruction to the attainment of duality by taking the action as the basis. Furthermore, the dual number here refers merely to the oneness of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction even in the case of many husbands. Consequently, only one man with a woman as his second is entitled to the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires).
Maṇḍana states: "The couple are declared to be those who wear [the sacrificial garments]."
Śaṅkara says: "In the case of the *pūrvādhāna* (the first laying of the fires), that [additional rite] does not apply to two males;
that is an additional performance.
In the mantras such as the *sugārhapatya*, which are recited in the *Adhvaryu-kāṇḍa* and the *Yajamāna-kāṇḍa* as examples, both are the performers."
The Adhvaryu [thinks], "I shall perform the rite as revealed by this [text]," and the sacrificer [thinks], "I shall not be negligent.
(Bhāṣya 3.8.3.17) [This is] because that which was previously recited is purposeful on account of the meaningfulness of the recitation.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantras for taking the clarified butter (ājyagrahaṇa), such as "For the restraint of the winds of cattle, I take thee," and the mantras for the Sūdgātṛ-priest, such as "By the impulse of strength (vāja)," are found in both the *Ādhvaryava* and the *Yājamāna* sections; thus they are recorded twice. Regarding these mantras recorded in two places, both—the Adhvaryu priest and the sacrificer—are entitled to their use.
Those mantras are to be recited by both.
In that regard, the Adhvaryu should say, intending, "I shall perform [the rite] as revealed by this," while the Sacrificer should say, intending, "I shall not be negligent.
Why? Because the dual tradition is purposeful and fruitful; for that reason, they are to be recited by both.
The meaning is that this is because the designation (*samākhyā*) and so forth possess equal force.

Regarding this, the *Sudhā* states: "A double recitation is improper; therefore, it is merely a double application. Since the scope is distinct, there is no possibility of sublation even by the general designation."
Section on the Dual Recitation:
The mantras recited twice in the sections pertaining to the Adhvaryu and the Yajamāna within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are to be employed by both.
The two [sets of] recitations [are distinct], because the dual recitation has a purpose.
Bhāṣya: The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices exist; therein, the mantras are recited twice—in the *Ādhvaryava-kāṇḍa* and in the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa*.
For example, those by which the clarified butter (*ājya*) is taken up, such as "I take thee for the restraint and support of the five winds," and so forth.

Likewise, there are the *sugandhi-ūhana* mantras: "He arranges [the fire] in the pure place, by the impulse of strength (*vāja*). A doubt arises: are these to be performed by both [the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ], or by the Adhvaryu alone? What is the prima facie view? That they belong to the Adhvaryu because of the name of the ritual manual (*samākhyāna*). To this, it is replied: The *sugandhi-ūhana* mantras are to be recited by both. Why? Because the action of arranging the fire is common to both priests. Furthermore, the mantra "by the impulse of strength" indicates a connection with the sacrifice; since the impulse of strength belongs to the sacrificer, the Hotṛ must recite that mantra. Therefore, the *sugandhi-ūhana* mantras are to be recited by both. Thus it is concluded.
"Both of them should perform [the ritual action].
Why? Because the dual mention is purposeful;
from the fact that it is designated for two, both are understood to be the performers."
Therefore, two should speak:
the Adhvaryu, "I shall perform what has been made manifest by this [formula]," and the sacrificer, "I shall not be negligent."

Or rather— regarding the mantras for taking the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth, which are recited both generally in the *Ādhvaryava* section and specifically in the *Yājamāna* section, are both performers the agents [of the action] through a disjunctive or a conjunctive combination, or is it one or the other? In that regard, since a choice (*vikalpa*) between the *Ādhvaryava* and the other might otherwise arise due to the presence of both, [the rule is established].
If it is argued that [this applies] to the *ṣṭoma*,
even in the absence of an explicit statement, two sacrificers will exist by implication:
he who is unable to perform it alone undertakes it with an assistant.
Therefore, when there is a sacrifice, just as one might say "having recited the sacrificial formula," the sacrificer will take up some assistant for the sake of what has been obtained;
in this way, the two [verses] will serve as the *pratipad* within the context.
Thus it is said: "and that which is proclaimed."
Or rather—due to the context, it finds its place in the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Nor is there, as in the case of the Ahīna sacrifice, an absence of a designation for a primary sacrifice (*aprakṛta-yajña*). Furthermore, the connection with the duality of sacrificers and so forth, being useful merely as a conditional factor (*nimitta*), is not capable of establishing a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgin*).
Nor can a connection with the seasons be established by means of that [number], as it would result in the necessity of resorting to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

For when items have already been employed according to the direct sense (śruti), it is not appropriate for them to be employed again through figurative indication. Even if the number two and so forth were of the same form [as the seasons], the injunction itself would become purposeless.
Furthermore, when postulating a result, it is more appropriate to postulate a connection with the context.
As for the objection that there is no basis for such a connection within the context, it is said in response: it follows from the sense of the passage.
For a basis is not restricted solely to that which is explicitly enjoined, since it can also be established through the force of the meaning (*artha*).
Furthermore, in the view that there is only one [principal] eye, there would follow the necessity of counting two eyes and two [yajamānas].
Moreover, we have not yet determined that the singularity of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is intended to be expressed.

Even if such an intention were present, by the rule "Or rather, it may apply even to a single part," just as something else is excluded due to incapacity, so too the singular sacrificer might occasionally be omitted, and two or many could perform the sacrifice; for there is a basis for this.
Alternatively, having observed this very injunction regarding the *pratipad*, we shall—by implication—infer a scriptural statement of the dual number for the agent who knows the two.
And that [inference] occurs only in this particular case, not in the cases of other *pratipads*; thus, the singular-numbered injunction will not be contradicted.
No, because of the connection with the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Commentary: For the Jyotiṣṭoma is the archetype (prakṛti). Its ritual details (dharmas) are directly enjoined therein; they are not obtained from anywhere by means of the extended application (codaka). What follows from this if it is so? Those [details] heard directly in the scripture cannot be sublated.
In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), however, those [elements] obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) being inferential would sublate [the modified elements].
For in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the singularity of the agent, which is directly heard in the scripture, is not sublated by implication.
Even where the agency of multiple performers is heard, there too only a single sacrificer is heard, as in: "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* every spring."
Therefore, these two *pratipad* verses are displaced from the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Now, why is this intended with reference to the wife?
When there is one wife and the sacrificer, [the verse] "For you two are... (*yuvaṃ hi sthaḥ*) is used; when there are two or many wives, [the verse] "These are united" (*ete asamr̥ddhvaḥ*) is used.

Just as the statement "wearing linen garments, the two should establish the sacred fires" is intended to refer to those wearing linen, so too here this [statement] is intended to refer to the installation [of the fires].
It is replied:
because the primary meaning is impossible there, the word denoting a man is used figuratively for a woman.
But here, since duality and plurality are both possible, the word cannot be a figurative term (*lakṣaṇāśabda*) such as "to many sacrificers" (*bahubhyo yajamānebhyaḥ*).

As for this dual number [in the phrase] "of two sacrificers," even there, the *ekaśeṣa* compound [formed by the rule] "the masculine remains when with a feminine" (*pumān striyā*, Pāṇini 1.2.67) is likewise a figurative term. Furthermore, [if it were not so], the *pratipadika* "upāsmāi gāyata naraḥ" would have no scope at all.
Therefore, it is established that these two are the *pratipad* of the *ṛtu*.
Alternatively—the mention of the *prakṛti* is for the sake of the *pratipad* under discussion;
or because, due to its being directly taught (*aupadeśikatva*), it is absolutely permanent (*atyantika*).
For that which is extended by analogy (*ātideśika*) may indeed be set aside by the force of the purpose;

however, this [rule] is prescribed for both optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites by the flow [of the text], since the singular number is heard in the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).
And there is no reason for this [singular number] not to be intended.
And how this intention [of the speaker] is established will be demonstrated in the sixth [chapter], at 6.3.12.
Furthermore, as for the indication made by one who is incapable, that too—because it is connected with the phrase "so that one might be able"—is understood to have no other scope;
for even a single person is indeed capable of performing the rite by setting aside the prescribed measure of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
In this context, it is only logical that the number [of sacrificers] should be included within the application of the rite at the time of its performance.
Therefore, since there is a cause for the archetype (prakṛti) when there is only one sacrificer, [the rule] is displaced [to the modified form].
As for the claim that this very statement is implied by the force of the context, that is not so, because it can be established in another way as well.
For if this cause were not implied [by the context] and were to become purposeless, then it would indeed be implied.

And how could it be purposeless? If duality and plurality were not present here and elsewhere in the original model (*prakṛti*). But they are not absent elsewhere, since they exist in the *kulāya* sacrifice and so forth.

Furthermore, here, because of the acceptance [of the view] by the learned, there is the consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*); therefore, the [plural] meanings do not deserve to be implied (*ākṣepa*). But if the intention were on the dual number, then because it is eternal (*nitya*), the mention of the cause (*nimitta*) would be purposeless. And as for the term "in the plural" (*bahutve*), it is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (a single remainder of dissimilar forms, i.e., *bahavaśca bahavaśca*). Since the plurality of males is understood by its own natural force (*svarasataḥ*), one might imagine that the injunction is being fashioned [for that].
Regarding the phrase "wearing linen" (*kṣaume vasānaḥ*), where it is understood as "he and she wearing" (*vasānaś ca vasānā ca*), the word in the dual number must necessarily refer to the wife here.
For nowhere is a great gift (*mahādāna*) prescribed for two men;
moreover, because it would contradict the ritual performance of a single couple, the mandatory *pratipad* verse would otherwise become meaningless.
Or else, an inconsistent alternative (viṣama-śiṣṭa-vikalpa) would have to be accepted;
therefore, [the rule] applies even to the superior case.

As for the objection that the connection with the seasons (ṛtu-sambandha) has not been stated, this is not a fault, because once the application to the seasons is understood from the word *prati* itself, the understanding of the specific [number], such as duality and so forth, is established.
Alternatively, the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) will bring to mind the sacrifice itself because it would otherwise be unintelligible.
Therefore, when there is a connection with something distinct [from the context], there is a contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa*);
and in that case, direct statement (*śruti*) possesses greater force.
Śā: "Since it will be stated that even a permanent rite may be performed by one who is deficient in a limb, therefore, setting aside the singular number, two or many [performers] are appropriate."
This is not so; for that which cannot be performed due to incapacity is indeed omitted.
However, the singularity of the sacrificer, like [the singularity of] time, is not something that can be omitted.
Therefore, there is an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the two *pratipad* verses.
Soma [says]: The connection is established by the removal of the previous inconsistency.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: that which is joined with duality or plurality—namely, this *pratipad*—should be displaced in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because that duality or plurality was not mentioned in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Regarding the two [verses] beginning with "yuvam hi" and the plural form "ete" in the verse beginning with "eta," one should employ them as the *pratipad* (introductory verses) in the Jyotiṣṭoma, whether it be a single-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) or a multi-day sacrificial session (*sāhargaṇa*). Alternatively, if one lacks the capacity for a single performance, one may perform it with two or even with many [priests].
That [procedure] should belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma by virtue of its being the archetype (prakṛti).
The plurality of the sacrificer is directly heard in the modified sacrifices;
therefore, let that *pratipad* be displaced and applied to the *kulāya* and other such rites.

Bhaṭṭa: In the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, having prescribed the *pratipad* "Upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ" as mandatory, the scripture states: "One should employ 'yuvaṃ hi sthaḥ svarvatī' as the *pratipad* for two sacrificers;
'ete aṣṭām indavaḥ' for many sacrificers.
In that context, if in the first sentence "dvayoryajamānayoḥ" (for two sacrificers) is in the locative case (*saptamī*), then it refers to [the condition] as a cause (*nimitta*).

And although there is a separate hearing of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), nevertheless, according to the principle of the section on the sacrificial oblation and so forth (*havirādyadhikaraṇa*, 6.4.22), because of the absence of optionality (*pākṣikatva*) and because the force of the sense requires each to be a cause, it is established that the causality belongs to the two [numbers]—duality and plurality—as delimited by the sacrificer's ownership, combined together, in accordance with their status as primary causes.

If, however, it is the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), then—as a restatement of the relationship termed "eligibility" (*adhikāritva*)—and for the sake of avoiding its own redundancy, it accepts figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even in the word *padya*. Thus, by parsimony, it establishes that both the state of being two (*dvitva*) and the state of being the measure (*mānatva*) constitute a single, co-inherent (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) ground [for the application of the term], since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) regarding their status as qualifier and qualified. Similarly, in the expression "many [wives] for the sacrificers" (*bahvayo yajamānebhyaḥ*), the dative of purpose (*tādarthya-caturthī*) also restates the relationship of eligibility, with figurative indication applied to the aforementioned ground. Consequently, there is no contingency of either one of the two [grounds] being unintended.

Even if the mantras are prescribed for the *pratipat* with reference to the *nimitta*, there is no plurality of objectives because they belong to different classes (*vijātīyatva*). Furthermore, through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the connection with the *pratipat* is obtained; thus, there is no dispute regarding these two positions. Now, in considering whether these two mantras are to be inserted into the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, or into sacrifices such as the Kulāya which have two or more sacrificers, it follows that they are inserted into the archetype (*prakṛta*) alone, because there is no conflict with the context.

Nor is there an absence of a basis (*nimitta*) in that case; for when the singularity expressed by the verb in such injunctions as "In every spring, one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" is intended as a qualification of the agent who is to be enjoined (*upādeya*), then—since it will be stated later that in the obligatory Jyotiṣṭoma one may perform it according to one's capacity even if unable [to fulfill all requirements]—if one person is unable [to perform it], then duality, plurality, or even the state of being alone (*anekatva*) would result, making it possible to establish a separate performance (*pratipadidhāna*).

Alternatively, since the word *yajamāna* denotes merely the performer of the sacrifice and this applies to the wife as well, there is no obstacle to its feminine gender in the first sentence; thus, that mantra pertains to the wife. In the second sentence as well, because it is impossible for the context (*prakaraṇa*) to override the grammatical gender (*liṅga*) according to the principle of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*, and because the grammatical instruction regarding the masculine gender is understood to include the feminine, the second mantra pertains to the wife.

[Objection: "But [the number] one is constant with respect to the individual substrate (*pratipatti*). This being the position reached, [we reply]: even though it is constant in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the state of having another object according to one's capacity does not apply to the singularity; for in the sentence regarding the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, because of the direct scriptural statement of co-referentiality (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*), that [singularity] is connected to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and is included within it. Thus, when there is incapacity, another measure of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is accepted merely by way of supplementing this very [requirement]. Furthermore, that which is subject to performance precisely because it is achievable through human effort (*kṛti-sādhyatva*) is likewise subject to performance according to capacity; however, this does not apply to non-performable things such as time and the like. Therefore, in the present sacrifice, duality and plurality [are also subject to capacity].

Furthermore, the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) does not refer to the wife (*patnī*), because its primary usage applies only to males, and there is no evidence for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the impossibility of such a shift. Moreover, since the masculine gender in the term *yajamāna* is prohibited in the context of "attainment" (*prāpta*)—just as in the case of the [prohibition regarding] sheep—it is illogical to accept the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) regarding eligibility (*adhikṛtatva*).

Consequently, since the syntactical statement (*vākya*) overrides the context (*prakaraṇa*), this [injunction] is to be transferred only to those cases where duality or plurality is prescribed, such as in the *kulāya* sacrifice and others, where it is stated: "The King and the domestic priest, desiring union, should sacrifice," or "One, or many, should sacrifice. It is in these instances that its displacement occurs.

Nor is there an absence of a means for bringing [the number] to mind (*upasthāpaka*) in that case; for once the general connection with the sacrifice is understood through its very relationship with the *pratipad*, there is no obstacle to the specific [number] being presented as the occasioning factor (*nimitta*). As Maṇḍana states: "The cognition [of the number] occurs in relation to duality. Thus, the linguistic usage of "two" and so forth is joined with duality and plurality.

14. Śaṅkara says: "Likewise, because there is the apprehension of two or many, it is the expressed [meaning] in the present context; for it is endowed with duality and plurality, since there is no injunction [to the contrary]."

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in the scripture: "For you two are the lords of wealth"—this one should be used as the introductory verse for two sacrificers; "these [many] are supporting this [sacrifice]"—this is for many sacrificers.

This collection of mantras, characterized by duality and plurality, is displaced from the Jyotiṣṭoma to the Kulāya sacrifice (where both a king and his domestic priest act together) and to the Ahīna sacrifices.
This is because in the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is no injunction (*codanā*) or placement (*adhidhāna*) for its being performed by two or many agents.
Therefore, there is a displacement from the Jyotiṣṭoma.
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of providing an illustration:
just as the twelve-fold *upasads* are displaced, so too is this [element] displaced.
Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
If it is argued that [the term] refers to what is performed for a purpose by means of a position (*pakṣa*),
the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says:

If the opponent (the *pūrvapakṣin*) should say: "In some cases, by way of an option (*vikalpa*), there is the possibility of two or more sacrificers (*yajamāna*)—which follows from the sense [of the text] and is thus obtained—even for the two *pratipad* verses occurring in the Jyotiṣṭoma; therefore, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*).

For even when a single sacrificer is unable to provide the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, it is possible for there to be two or more sacrificers by virtue of the mention of 'singularity' [as a mere formal attribute].
[This is the position of the opponent.]

"No, because the archetype is not connected [with multiple performers]," says the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin). Why? Because the archetype—the Jyotiṣṭoma, which is the archetype for all Soma sacrifices—is connected with only one performer, through its association with a single agent.
Because there can be no sublation of the singular number of the agent— which constitutes the very origin [of the injunction] "one should sacrifice with Soma"—

therefore, since the Jyotiṣṭoma has only a single performer, the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the two *pratipad* verses must indeed take place. However, in the section beginning with "that which is joined with duality or plurality" (3.1.17–19), it is stated that even the single [agent] belonging to the sacrificer himself is not something to be taken up [as a subordinate factor].

Vāla-pṛ. 97: Regarding the section [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.2.64], "And because there is no injunction for that which is joined with duality or plurality," the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated that the *ekaśeṣa* compound "pumān striyā" (the male [is used] with the female) is indeed a word based on secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Soma. 6.1.9: The "remnants" (*śeṣas*) beginning with duality, such as those for Indra-Vāyu and others. Vi. 3.2.13: These remnants of the Āgrayaṇa vessel are brought forward at the two [pressings]; thereafter, the Pātnīvata cup is drawn.
Bhāṣya 3.2.13:
The remnants of the [cups] beginning with the Aindravāyava, which are characterized by duality and so forth, are deposited in the Āditya vessel;
from there, they again come into the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
And from that follows the taking of the Pātnīvata cup.

Vārttika: In the case of the Āgrayaṇa and others, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the Agnīṣomīya sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), because of the commonality of having two deities.
Bhāṣya 8.1.1–2: The technical term "having two deities" (*dvivaitatva*) is used in Mīmāṃsā.

"Because this dual nature is accepted throughout the entire treatise (*śāstra*). For instance, in the discussions concerning the fourth *karana*, the *indrapīta* cup, and the portions for the *pūṣan-pratiṣṭhā*, [the author] will state that offerings dedicated to two deities—such as those for Indra-Agni or Agni-Soma—are not included by words like *āgneya* when those words denote deities who are exclusively [single] ones, due to a lack of semantic capacity. This is the *Vārtika* (p. 420). Regarding this, the *Sudhā* states: "The usage of the term 'dual nature' is not only among ritualists (*yājñika*), but also in Mīmāṃsā."

It will be stated in the sūtra "Or rather, there is a restriction" (3.1.27) that by the word *āgneya* ("belonging to Agni"), the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Indra-Agni and to Indra-Soma—which have dependent deities—are not included.

It will be stated in the concluding sūtra for the discussion on *indrapīta* ("drunk by Indra"), namely "Or rather, [it applies] to one [cake], because of the difference in deity" (3.2.41), that by the word *indra* occurring within the compound *indrapīta*, the Soma dedicated to Indra-Agni—which has a dependent deity—is not included.

In the discussion regarding the portion belonging to Pūṣan (*pūṣapratiṣṭhābhāgavicāra*), it will be stated under the rule *ekasminnekasaṃyogāt* (3.2.19) that offerings such as those dedicated to Indra-Pūṣan (*aindrāpauṣṇa*) are not included. Furthermore, in the rule *aikādhvaryavaṃ...* (8.1.28), it will be stated that the dual nature [of the *medhapati*] is based on the archetype of the two-fold abandonment in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dāśapaurṇamāsika*).

Thus, in the phrase "desiring the sacrificial animal for the two lords of the sacrifice" (*āśāsānā medhapatibhyāṃ medham*), the term *medhapati* occurring in the Agni-praiṣa mantra refers to two entities—the deities known as Agni-Soma—by relying on the dual-ended word *medhapati*.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the mantra known as *manotā*—beginning with "Thou indeed art the first *manotā*" (*tvaṃ hy eṣa prathamo manotā*)—is to be modified when used for an animal sacrifice dedicated to another deity or not, the author of the *Bhāṣya* will state (Bhā. pp. 1938–39) in the section on the *Iyāśaktika*: "Is it not the case that in the archetype (*prakṛti*), this recitation (*nigada*) has a different purpose? For in the archetype, Agni and Soma are the deities, whereas this [mantra] refers to Agni alone. Since it does not denote those [deities] who are present [in the modified sacrifice], it should be employed without modification. To this he replies: "True, Agni and Soma are the deities in the archetype, but they are there as a mixture, namely Soma and Agni."
Regarding this, it is stated in [Jaimini Sūtra] 10.4.2: "But in the case of the *manotā*, there should be no modification because of the specific scriptural injunction.
Furthermore, in the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the technical usage of *dvaitva* (duality) exists as well.

Under the heading of Pāṇini 6.1.26, "And the dual of deities," the rule 6.1.27 states: "In place of *idam* [the substitute *eta* occurs] when *soma* and *varuṇa* follow. Thus, when the words *soma* or *varuṇa* follow, the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of the word *agni*—occasioned by the dual of deities—is prescribed [as in *agnīṣomau* and *agnīvaruṇau*].

Furthermore, regarding the rule for the substitution of the cerebral (mūrdhanya), in the context of *Pāṇini* 8.3.82—"In *agni-dvi-vaitatva-vyavahāra*, *dvi-puroḍāśāyām*, and *stoma-tomāḥ*," since the word *soma* following the word *agni* is understood to undergo the cerebral substitution (*mūrdhanyādeśa*), the word *soma* is cognized as being preceded by the word *agni*; thus, by implication, there is the understanding of a *dvandva* compound.

Under the governing rule for the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member (*pūrvapada*), while the phrase "in *vanaspati* and so forth, both [members] simultaneously" (Pāṇini 6.1.140) is being carried over, the rule "and the *devatā-dvandva*" (Pāṇini 6.2.141) prescribes that in cases such as *indrāgnī* and *indrāvaruṇau*, the original accent applies to both members. Furthermore, under the governing rule for *vṛddhi*, while the phrase "in a *dvandva*, [the *vṛddhi*] is applied to the final vowel of the last member and of the first member" (Pāṇini 7.3.19) is being carried over, the rule "and the *devatā-dvandva*" (Pāṇini 7.3.21) prescribes the *vṛddhi* of both members in words such as *āśāvaiṣṇava*.

While the rule *ānaha krato dvaṃdva* (Pāṇini 6.3.25) is in force, the rule *devatādvaṃdvaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.26) prescribes the substitution of *ānaha* [for *ānaṅ*], as in the expression *mitrāvaruṇau*.
Thus, there is a sacrificer who has two wives and one who has many wives. (pp. 647–48).
Bhāṣya: In the modification involving two animals and so forth, the word *medhapati* must be uttered according to the deity (*medhapataye*, *medhapatibhyām*, *medhapatibhyaḥ*, as appropriate).
Bhāṣya 9.3.12.33–41. In the sacrifice of two animals, when there is a single offering, the word *ekadhā* is repeated: "Let these two be joined one by one."

VI. 9|3|12: In the sacrifice of two animals (dvipaśuyāga), there is a modification (*ūha*) of the word *pāśa* from its singular and plural forms to the dual form within the two mantras for the fetters (*pāśa*).
9|3|14: In the sacrifice of two sacrificial cakes (*dvipuroḍāśā*), [the modification] should occur because it serves an intermediate purpose.

Prior to the Soma sacrifice, the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) involves one sacrificial cake; after the Soma sacrifice, it involves two sacrificial cakes, because the *agnīṣomīya* sacrificial cake also exists [at that stage].
It is understood that the *upāṃśuyāja* occurs at the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).

Moreover, it occurs only when there are two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), namely the *āgneya* and the *āgnīṣomīya*, because its purpose is "between" (*antara*); the meaning expressed by the word "between"—namely, the state of being between two oblations—is possible only when there are two sacrificial cakes.
This is stated twice in the scripture: "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* between [the two]."
In the case of the *ekapuroḍāśā* (the sacrifice with a single cake), there is simply no intermediate stage (*antarāpadya*).
Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that before the Soma sacrifice, in the *ekapuroḍāśā*, the *upāṃśuyāja* (whispered offering) should not take place;
this is also because [the *upāṃśuyāja*] serves the purpose of preventing the state of being "unmixed" (*ajāmi*).

*Jāmi* is redundancy; the cause of *jāmi* is the production of redundancy. To avoid the production of redundancy—that is, to prevent the occurrence of redundancy—one acts in such a way. It has been stated in the scriptural passage: "Redundancy (*jāmi*) is indeed produced for the sacrifice when there are two final *puroḍāśa* cakes; one performs the *upāṃśuyāja* between them to avoid redundancy," that this [avoidance] is possible only when there are two *puroḍāśas*.
Therefore, the *upāṃśuyāja* occurs on the full-moon day when there are two *puroḍāśas*, but not before the Soma sacrifice when there is only one *puroḍāśa*.
This is another reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

If it is argued that it is "for that purpose," then for that purpose— that is, to establish that the *upāṃśuyāja* is for the sake of the interval between the two *puroḍāśa* cakes— the *upāṃśuyāja* would occur only on the full-moon day following the Soma sacrifice, when there are indeed two *puroḍāśas*.
If this is argued, [we reply]:
this is a restatement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of three sūtras.
For it is a well-known saying that the composition of the author of the Sūtras is indeed diverse.
No, because that is the primary factor.

The *upāṃśuyāja* is not performed only on the full-moon day when there are two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*); rather, it is performed even on the full-moon day when there is only one cake. This is because that is the primary factor—that is, because the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) itself is the primary context for the *upāṃśuyāja*.
But its quality is the intermediate space.
Therefore, even in the absence of an intermediate space, the *upāṃśuyāja* must be performed even in the case of a single *puroḍāśa*; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And because of the connection with what is not taught [otherwise].
If, however, an interval were required, then the prescribed *upāṃśuyāja* would have to be connected with an interval that is neither enjoined nor prescribed by authoritative tradition (*aśiṣṭa*).
And it is not proper to connect what is prescribed with something that is not prescribed.
Therefore, even in the case of a sacrifice with a single cake (*ekapuroḍāśā*), the *upāṃśuyāja* must be performed; this is another argument for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

But its placement should be at the point of origin, because the purpose exists without contradicting the subordinate quality, because the purpose is contingent upon another injunction, and because in its absence— such as in the case of the *dvipuroḍāśā* sacrifice or the *dvirātra* and other rites— it would lack authority. Therefore, by the very sentence of origin (*utpattivākya*), the placement of the *upāṃśuyāja* should be within the interval for the *dvipuroḍāśā* sacrifice.

"In the absence of that"—meaning in the absence of an interval, or rather, when it is impossible because no interval is mentioned; even in the case of a sacrifice with a single cake (*ekapuroḍāśā*), where an interval is not heard of, the *upāṃśu* offering would still take place.
However, there is no impossibility, since sacrifices with two cakes (*dvipuroḍāśā*) do exist.
Therefore, the opponent restates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The *upāṃśuyāja* does not occur in a sacrifice with a single cake."

Because both are enjoined. The proponent says: "We two shall sacrifice with clarified butter in a low voice on the full moon day"—since by the term *paurṇamāsī* (full moon day) the low-voiced sacrifice (*upāṃśuyāja*) is enjoined for both types of full moon days, namely the one with a single sacrificial cake (*ekapuroḍāśā*) and the one with two sacrificial cakes (*dvipuroḍāśā*), it must therefore take place even on the one with a single cake;
for both of them are indeed full moon days.
And because qualities (guṇas) exist for the sake of another, it would be "when [there are two cakes]," just as in the case of an instruction.

Since qualities exist for the sake of another—that is, for the sake of the principal—this quality of the interval, being for the sake of the Upāṃśuyāja, does not suffice to exclude the Upāṃśuyāja from the sacrifice with a single cake.
Therefore, the scriptural rule regarding the quality of the interval must be "when [there are two cakes]"; that is, when the Full Moon sacrifice has two cakes, then it occurs in the interval.

It is like the case of the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick); for instance, in the rule "He places the potsherds with the *upaveṣa*," when the *upaveṣa* exists at the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), it is understood that [the action] is performed with it.
However, at the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), even in the absence of the *upaveṣa*, the placing of the potsherds still takes place.
Similarly, even in the absence of two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the *upāṃśuyāja* should certainly occur.
"Therefore, that [procedure] applies even in the case of a single sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)," says the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin).
"And there is no loss [of the procedure], for the two cakes are merely the indicator (lakṣaṇa) of the time."

Even in the case of a sacrifice with a single *puroḍāśa*, there is no exclusion—that is, no absence—of the *upāṃśuyāja*. For the two *puroḍāśas* serve as the indicators of time; the interval between them is indicated by both: as being prior to the offering to Indra-Agni and subsequent to the offering to Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt.
In that case, even in the absence of the offering to Indra, the time for the *upāṃśuyāja* is indeed known as being characterized by its occurrence subsequent to the offering to Agni.
Just as when it is said, "One should arrive at the time of the conch-blast," one arrives at that specific time characterized by the blast even if no conch is present;
therefore, even in the sacrifice with a single cake (*ekapuroḍāśā*), the *upāṃśuyāja* must be performed after the offering to Agni.

The mention of "non-repetition" (*ajāmitva*) is for the purpose of praise, just as [the mention of] "being for that purpose" (*amutārthatva*) [is]. As for what was stated—that it is for the purpose of effecting non-repetition—it is replied here:
the non-repetition of the *upāṃśuyāja* is for the sake of praise, not for the sake of an injunction.

Just as in the passage, "The clarified butter is indeed nectar, while the oblation is mortal; when one spreads [the butter] beneath and pours [it] over, one makes this very offering nectar," the status of being nectar is for the purpose of praising the clarified butter, so it is here as well.

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the Upāṃśuyāja must be performed even at the Full Moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī) that has only a single cake (ekapuroḍāśā), prior to the Soma sacrifice.

In the case of employing two or more wives, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the mantra ending in the singular number (the first mantra, "patnīṃ saṃnahya"), because its application is appropriate as it stands. Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 9.1.16:
In the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, the portion for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest should be double.
One who has two shares in the consumption of the remnants is "dvibhāga.
The Adhvaryu’s duty is the *preṣa* (direction), and the Hotṛ’s duty is the *anuvacana* (recitation).
He who possesses these two duties is the Maitrāvaruṇa; thus, he is "dvikarmā" (one whose function is twofold).
The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that because it has two objects, it should consist of two parts;
however, because it is a single entity, it should consist of one part, since the division into parts is not explicitly stated in the scripture.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view.

In the case of the animal sacrifice, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest should not have two shares in the consumption of the remnants; rather, he should have one share—that is, he should possess only a single share. This is because the Maitrāvaruṇa is a single individual, and since his share—whether it be the share of the Adhvaryu or the share of the Hotṛ—is not explicitly mentioned as belonging to him (i.e., there is an absence of a scriptural statement to that effect), it follows that it is "unheard of" (*aśruta*). This is the meaning of the term *aśrutatvāt*.

The application [of the rule] occurs solely by means of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction); even in that case, because the Maitrāvaruṇa is singular, the *codaka* does not extend a second portion [to him].
Therefore, in the consumption of the remnants of the animal sacrifice, the Maitrāvaruṇa has only one share.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The two-night sacrifices (*dvirātra*) are:
Myuṣṭi, Āṅgirasa, Kāpivana, and Caitraratha; these are the two-night *ahīna* sacrifices.
It is established that in all of them, the final day is an *atirātra*.
On the second day of the *dvirātra* (two-night sacrifice), the *ṣoḍaśī* cup is drawn, based on the statement: "It is drawn on the later day of the *dvirātra*.
Vi. 20|9|19: In the *dvirātra*, it is restricted (*parisaṃkhyā*) to the *Aṅgirasām dvirātra* ritual alone, and not to other *dvirātras*.
This is the opinion of the Vṛttikāra.
[Agni] can be piled during a *dvirātra* sacrifice.
Sacrifices lasting from two nights up to eleven nights are *ahīna* sacrifices.

In that case, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) which has its form not deficient (*ahīnarūpa*). According to the rule of transfer (*codaka*), for the two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*) and others, the fire-altar (*agni*) is indeed optional.

Regarding the repetition [of the injunction] in the case of the *dvirātra* and other sacrifices: when there is a *dvirātra* sacrifice, then there is the engagement in those [rites] intended for specific qualities (*guṇakāma*).

In a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) such as the *dvirātra*, the throwing away of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā-prāsana*), which is prescribed by the general rule (*codaka*), is ordained to be performed on the very last day in order to prevent itching and other ailments.
In the case of the *dvirātra* and other such multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), the final day—being of the nature of a second day and so forth—is not designated as "the last" (*pānī-saṃjñā-jāntava*).

In a multi-day sacrifice beginning with the *dvirātra*, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the first two days of the middle ten days of the *ahīna* twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is to be adopted.
There is an extended application (atideśa) of the fire-piling (agnicayana) rite when it is joined with the two-night sacrifice (dvirātra) and others. This is the section concerning the Agnyatigrāha.

Bhāṣya 10.8.11.23–28: In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *dvirātra*, although the second and subsequent days differ from those belonging to the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) and the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), the opponent maintains that the performance should follow the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*) by using the designation "wife" (*patnī*) and the end of the day (*jānta*) exactly as they are. This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because the second day here is distinct [from the archetype], there must be a modification (*ūha*) in the entire performance, even for that which bears the designation "wife" and ends with the suffix *-jā*, due to the alteration in the ritual application (*prayogavikāra*).
Soma 9.1.8.

The Dviraatra, Triraatra, and others are long Soma sacrifices. Due to the repetition of the Soma sacrifice, in a long Soma sacrifice, the binding together of the two pressing-boards must be performed.
VI. 3.3.16: For the two-night, three-night, and other sacrifices, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) in its form as an *ahīna* is the archetype (*prakṛti*).

In the modifications (*vikṛti*) such as the two-night and three-night sacrifices, the days of the twelve-day sacrifice proceed in order from the beginning (the second day being the first day of the modified rite);
however, there is an omission (*lopa*) of the remaining [days].
VI. 10.1.12: The Principle of the Two-Night Sacrifice (Dvirātranyāya).

In a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) beginning with the two-night sacrifice, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the first two days of the middle ten days of the *ahīna* twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is to be adopted.

"But in the case of injunctions (*codanā*), there should be a restriction regarding *dharma* by means of the mark of being something previously unknown (*apūrvatva*). Commentary: There exist multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) such as the *dvirātra* (two-night rite), beginning with [the injunction]: "One should sacrifice with the *dvirātra*."

For in those [sacrifices], does the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the entire twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) apply, or rather that of the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), excluding the introductory (*prāyaṇīya*) and concluding (*udayanīya*) days? What is the prima facie view? That it applies to the entire [twelve-day sacrifice] because there is no specification.
This being the case, we reply:

In those injunctions, since it is impossible for the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* [days] to be preceded [by others], the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*) applies.
By what reason? The ritual procedure is determined by an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
What is the indicative mark? It says thus: "That which is the first, that is the second; that which is the second, that is the third; it enters into the *jagatī*."
Thus it makes known: that which is the first part of the *dvirātra* (two-night sacrifice), that is the second third-part (*traidha*).

It enters into the *jagatī*; by showing the *jāgata* day as the third of the *ṣaḍaha* (six-day period) among those to be included, it demonstrates the application (*pravṛtti*) of the *daśarātra* (ten-night sacrifice).
The phrase "that which is the first" is a reference to the *dvirātra*, because of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

"That third" refers to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), because there is no third day in a two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*). Furthermore, there is this other indicative mark (*liṅga*): "The *gāyatrī* enters the first day and the fourth; the *jagatī* enters the second. This shows that the third day of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) is *jagatī*. Therefore, the application is to the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*).
As for the attainment of results, it follows from the connection with the term "night" (*rātri*).
The commentary states: "One should sacrifice with a *dvirātra*"—here the word *rātra* [is used];
in the expression "ten-night rite" (*daśarātra*), it is that very same word.
Therefore, from this...

The principle of the *dvirātra* (two-night sacrifice): Regarding the subject matter of the second chapter, since there is no other purpose in the present case, and in order to avoid redundancy, it is understood that even though the ritual details (*dharmas*) are auxiliary to the mere day in the archetype (*prakṛti*), their extension (*pradeśa*) to the modification (*vikṛti*) occurs through the commonality of being a "group" (*gaṇatva*), specifically in the case of the *daśarātra* (ten-night sacrifice).

For this very reason, although there is an absence of connection with "primacy," there is no defect in the initiation of the ritual details by means of the designation of names for the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* [days].

Nor is it the case that there is an absence of evidence for extension (*atideśa*) everywhere simply because such an application would be purposeful only in the case of a modification of the form of the *daśarātra*—whether by means of extension through name (*nāmātideśa*) or extension through indicative marks (*liṅgātideśa*).

For in the *dvirātra*, based on the presence of the word "end of the night" (*rātrānta*), which is reinforced by the indicative mark—"What was the first, that becomes the second; what was the second, that becomes the third; it goes to the *jagatī*-mantra"—one understands its universal applicability precisely from the specific internal consistency [of the ritual].

Since the first day of the *dvirātra* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the second day of the *dvādaśāha*, according to this extended application (*atideśa*), there would be the omission of the second day of the *ṣaḍaha* in the *dvirātra*, but not of the second day of the *jāgata-ṣaḍaha*.
Therefore, this is another indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Likewise, in the *dvirātramadhyama*, the statement “the first is *gāyatra*, the second is *traiṣṭubha*” is also an indicative mark.
The second case ending is used in the *prāyaṇīya* [rite], as in: "Prepare the rice grains," and "Bring the rice grains; offer them."

When the accusative case is employed where "with rice" (*taṇḍulaiḥ*) or "with balvaja-grass" (*balvajaiḥ*) ought to have been used, it is understood that this [accusative] certainly has the same meaning as the instrumental.
To this, it is replied: "In all relations such as cooking and the like, rice and other such items possess two forms."
The second [case ending] is employed there by taking the predominant factor as the basis.

When rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are intended to be expressed as the means for producing a crest of cooked rice (*odanaśikhaṇḍa*) that is a distinct entity, then there is an absence of a word ending in the third case.

However, when rice grains are seen as the cause for the activity of producing rice fit for consumption, and *balvaja* grass is seen in the form of a crest as a mark of softness; [in such cases, the third case is used].

Likewise, because their status as subordinate factors (*guṇabhāva*) is understood from Vedic statements, in the case of the *Agnihotra* sacrifice where rice is the means (*dravyasādhanaka*), the analogy of gold and so forth is employed for the sake of elegance. For instance, a certain Brāhmaṇī woman, desiring to display the excellence of her own work, intends for the rice-grains to be connected with the oblation (*homa*). She thinks thus: "O you who desire a subordinate quality (*guṇakāma*), offer the rice-grains for me. In that case, the sense of the accusative case (*dvitīyārtha*) is absent.
Indeed, in common worldly usage, there are many such modes of intended expression (*vivakṣā*).

Even when something is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), a certain primary aspect may be intended to be expressed for some reason; likewise, even among things that are primary (*pradhānabhūta*), a subordinate aspect may be intended.
Sometimes both are intended, and sometimes neither.
Furthermore, there is no authoritative rule (*pramāṇa*) stating that whatever is intended to be expressed must necessarily be denoted by a word.

However, when there is a desire to express a secondary sense (lakṣaṇā), one merely resorts to another means; it is not an abandonment of the primary meaning itself. Therefore, predominance alone is the meaning of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*).
The second case ending occurs in relation to an action.
That [instrumental case] is not called a kāraka-case ending.
A kāraka is indeed an action (kriyā), not a substance (dravya).
Bhāṣya 10.2.28.65; the second case ending is characterized by the primary injunction.
As in the cases "he sings the Rathantara" and "he sings the Bṛhat.
Regarding the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā vibhakti*) occurring in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), the *Bhāṣya* states that the meaning of the nominal stem is the qualifier.

In the investigation of the subject matter of the eleventh chapter of the *Nyāya*, it is understood through the accusative case-ending, which is a kāraka-case ending, that there is predominance in the object (*karman*).

Pāṇini 2.1.3: In the example *dvitīyā* (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*, "he cleanses the cup"), the predominance of the *graha* is understood because it is the intended object (*uddeśya*) and because it possesses a purpose (*prayojanavat*). 3.1.17: The dative case (*dvitīyā*) [is used for] the injunction of a deity (*devatāvidhi*).

The injunction of a deity is fivefold, distinguished as: [1] by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), [2] by the dative case, [3] by the wording of a mantra (*mantravarṇa*), [4] by the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), and [5] by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

*Bālamanoramā*, p. 22: The accusative case (*dvitīyā*) establishes that which follows [the agent] in accomplishing the desired or undesired object (*īpsita-anīpsita-karman*), serving as the delimiter (*avacchedaka*) by virtue of its capacity. P. 75: The accusative case is common to the fourfold types of objects consisting of that which is to be attained through means (*upāya-āpya*), that which is to be modified (*vikārya*), and that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*).
*Siddhāntakaumudī*, p. 113.
The second case [accusative] occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*).
And that consists in being the locus of a result produced by an action.
In the example "he sees the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ paśyati*), the definition applies because the cognizedness (*jñātatā*) produced by the act of seeing resides in the pot.
If it is objected: "In that case, in examples such as 'Caitra goes to the village,' it would follow that Caitra is the object (*karman*), because he possesses the conjunction produced by the action;
furthermore, it would follow that the roots *tyajati* (to abandon) and *gacchati* (to go) are synonyms.
If this is argued:

On this point, the Naiyāyikas maintain that "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*) is a qualifier of the action, while "being the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthatāvacchedakatva*) is a qualifier of the result; furthermore,
"otherness" (*paratva*) is relative to the referent of the base of the second-case suffix.

Thus, in sentences such as "Caitra goes to the village," the village possesses the status of an object (*karmatā*) because it is characterized by a conjunction that is the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root, which is produced by an operation inherent in Caitra.

The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is likewise: "Caitra is the generator of an operation inherent in something other than the village, which is conducive to a conjunction that is the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root inherent in the village.
They say that since the root *tyaj* (to abandon) has its denotative power (*śakti*) in an operation whose result is disjunction (*vibhāga*), the aforementioned fault does not apply.

And that *karman* is of two kinds, according to grammar: "The object most desired by the agent is *karman*" (Pāṇini 1.4.49) and "likewise [that which is] connected [with the action] though not desired" (49). Of these, the former is expressed by the fourth case (*caturthī*).
This is due to the distinction in meaning between that which is to be attained through means (*upāya-prāpya*), that which is to be modified (*vikārya*), and that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*).
"Arising" (*utpatti*) is the bringing into being of something previously non-existent by means of an instrument such that the application of a verbal designation becomes possible.
Likewise, "attainment" (*prāpti*) is the reaching of something already existent that was previously unobtained.
In the same way, modification (*vikṛti*) is the production of a specific unperceived [potency] (*adṛṣṭātiśaya*);
refinement (*saṃskāra*) is the production of that very same specific unperceived [potency].
Thus [it is said].

For example: "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*), "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ kurute*), "he milks the milk" (*payo dogdhi*), "he threshes the rice-grains" (*brīhīnavahanti*), and "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*brīhīn prokṣati*). This has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "That which comes into being [as something new] and that which is manifested by its birth—these are the two types of objects established as the *vikārya* (transformable) object, once the [original] thing to be removed has been set aside."
Some things, such as wood and the like, arise from the destruction of their original nature;
others arise through the production of a different quality, such as the transformation of gold and similar substances.
That which is established through perception or inference, wherein a specific modification produced by action is obtained, is called real (tāttvika).
"Thus [it is said].
(This is not found in the Chaukhamba edition;
Ke. There are also four kinds of that which is undesired.
[The objects] are: the indifferent (*udāsīna*), the detested (*dveṣya*), that which is designated by another name, and that which has been previously possessed by another.

For example: *tṛṇaṃ spṛśati* (he touches grass), *viṣaṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats poison), *gāṃ dogdhi* (he milks the cow), *viṣamamanugacchati* (he follows after poison), and *agnimayujati* (he yokes the fire).
Regarding these, Someśvara maintains that there are two powers (*śakti*) corresponding to the states of being desired and undesired.

The states of being desired (*īpsita*) and not desired (*anīpsita*) arise from the mind; they are not two distinct meanings of the second case (*dvitīyā*), because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Nor is there any pointlessness in having two separate sūtras, as in the case of *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.27) in the example "he keeps the cow away from the barley" (*yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati*).
The second case ending (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*):

[The rule] *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51) exists for the purpose of ensuring that the second case ending applies to the cow— which, while being the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), is designated as the source (*apādāna*) by virtue of being desired in relation to the barley— and because the second [rule] is also meaningful in examples such as *viṣaṃ bhakṣayati* ("he eats poison").

In the case of transitive roots (*dvikarmaka-dhātu*) such as *duh* (to milk) and others, the second object is that which possesses the fruit delimited by the meaning of the root, being pervaded [by the action], and which lacks a possible syntactic connection with other *kārakas* such as the ablative (*apādāna*). Examples include:
*gāṃ payo dogdhi* (he milks the cow for milk), *rājānaṃ yācate vasudhām* (he begs the king for the earth), and *ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati* (he leads the goat to the village).
The cognition [arising from *gāṃ payo dogdhi*] is: "He brings about the production of milk by means of the milking whose object is the cow."
(One causes the cow to be milked for the sake of milk) — or conversely.
Here, there is one object (*karman*) which is directly pervaded by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and a second [object] which is pervaded by that which is itself being pervaded.
For this very reason, in the sentence "He pours curds into the milk that has been heated," the milk is construed as an object (*karman*) in relation to the second object.

According to the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇāṃ kartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), for roots meaning motion (*gati*), cognition (*buddhi*), consumption (*pratyavasāna*), those having sound as their object (*śabdakarman*), and those being intransitive (*akarmaka*)—such as roots meaning lying down (*śayana*) and the like—which are in their non-causative (*aṇyantā*) state, there is no result at all that serves to delimit the meaning of the root, such as *samabhivispandana* (vibration) and so forth; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) mentioned [in the objection]. Furthermore, the word "result" (*phala*) refers to a result produced by the action (*kriyājanyaphala*).

Therefore, because it is an operation delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the operation itself, nor to the lower region as a whole or to its parts.
Some maintain: "The result (*phala*) of the root *pat* is conjunction with a lower region; for this very reason, the usage 'he falls into hell' (*narakaṃ patati*) is also valid."

Now, one might object: in the sentence “Caitra causes Maitra to go to the village” (*grāmaṃ gamayati caitro maitram*), the definition of the *karman* (object) also applies to Maitra, because Maitra is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the meaning of the verbal root, which consists of the act of going. Nor can this be denied on the grounds that, according to the rule “those ending in *saN* and so forth are verbal roots” (*sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, Pāṇini 3.1.32), the form ending in *ṇic* is designated as a verbal root.

It should not be argued that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the meaning of the causative root *gam*—namely, the activity conducive to the act of going—is absent in Maitra; for [the definition] applies to him since the fruit called "going," which is the delimitor of that meaning, exists in Maitra as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
However, this cannot be maintained, because in that case, it would be impossible for the village to be the object (*karman*).
Nor can it be argued that even though the causative form is a verbal root, *gam* itself is also a verbal root, and thus the status of the village as its object is established.

If that were the case, then in the sentence "Caitra causes Maitra to cook" (*apācayati caitro maitreṇa*), Maitra would also incur the status of being the object (*karman*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would result in [Maitra] taking the second case ending (*dvitīyā*).

This is because, by the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmakākarmakāṇām kartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52)—which means that the agent of roots such as *gam* (to go) and others when they are not followed by *ṇic*, becomes the object when those same roots are followed by *ṇic*—the designation of "object" is prohibited in connection with verbal roots other than those beginning with *gam*. Therefore, even in that case, it is impossible for [Maitra] to be the agent [of the causative action].

Because the rule *hṛkroranyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.53) prescribes the optional designation of the object (*karman*) when used in conjunction with the roots *hṛ* and *kṛ*, there would result the two possible usages: *hārayati kārayati kartā bhṛtyam* and *hārayati kārayati kartā bhṛtyena*.

In that case, since the state of being the substratum of the fruit—which consists of the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojyavyāpāra*) and serves as the delimiter of the root-meaning—is always present in the *bhavya* (the one to be brought about), it is impossible to speak of both its status as an object and its absence [simultaneously].

By this, the view that "the state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in possessing a fruit—which is the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) produced by an action inherent in something distinct from the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)"—is refuted;
for there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *pācayati caitro maitram* ("Caitra causes Maitra to cook").
If this is argued, we say: no.
This is because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) differs according to the distinction between the manifestation of those respective actions;

otherwise, in a situation where both [the agent and the object] would possess the designation of "object," Caitra would incur the status of an object in the sentence "Caitra goes to Maitra" (caitro maitraṃ gacchati), since he is the locus of the conjunction that inheres in Maitra—who is distinct from himself—and which is the result of the action.
Otherwise, Maitra too would incur the status of an object, as he is likewise the locus of the result which is co-locative with the action.
Therefore, the definition must be stated precisely as "the state of being produced by that action" (*tat-kriyātvabhāva*).
In this way, since Caitra—who is devoid of action—lacks the property of being inherent in another (*parasamavetatva*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to him.

Consequently, the specific definition of the object (*karman*) is: that which possesses a result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) produced by a particular action, while itself not being the locus (*anadhikaraṇa*) of that action, is the object of that action.

Alternatively, the definition may be stated as follows: that which possesses a result (phala) which is the delimitor of the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvarthatā'vacchedaka) produced by an action (kriyā) inherent in another [entity] is the object (karman) of that action.
The application of this definition is clearly evident when taking actions such as "falling" (patana) and so forth.

In the cases of "Caitra goes to Maitra" and "Maitra goes to Caitra," the status of the village as the object must be explained by taking the action residing in its own agent, while the status of Maitra as the object must be explained by taking the action of going and the agent's own effort (nijavyāpāra) which is conducive to that action.

Expressions such as *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* (“he brings about a jar”) take only the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) [as the object], because the root *bhū* is transitive. Similarly, in *pācayati* (“he causes to cook”), the object is only the rice (*odana*), which is the object of the root *pac*, and not Maitra, who possesses the activity conducive to that cooking; this is in accordance with the aforementioned sūtra. For this very reason, in those cases, the meaning of the causative suffix is itself intransitive (*akarmaka*).
Alternatively, for that [agent] as well, the rice (*odana*) alone is the object (*karman*), because it conforms to the intended modification (*vikalpa*); thus there is no distinction.

And so, in the definition of the status of being an object as determined by the roots *hṛ* (to take away) and *kṛ* (to cause to do), the condition of being caused by a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) must also be included.
By this, the occasional status of being an object belonging to the agent of the taking away (*haraṇa*) and so forth is precluded.

And thus, the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*) must be provided as having the word ending in the accusative case (*sampratyanta-pada*) as its cause; that is to say, the definition of the intended meaning should be stated as: "that which is intended [to be expressed] as possessing a result produced by an action inherent in another is the object (*karman*) of the action of going.
