Alternatively, the definition of the word ending in the accusative case should be stated as: "the object of the action of going is that which, while possessing a result produced by an action inherent in another, is denoted by a word ending in the accusative case.
By this, the usage of expressions such as ‘*grāme gacchati*’ (he goes to the village) and ‘*narake patati*’ (he falls into hell) is also justified.

Nor does it follow that, because the nature of those objects of action differs, there would be the consequence of grasping distinct powers for the accusative case; rather, the accusative has its power (*śakti*) in both "occurring" (*vṛttitva*) and "absence" (*abhāva*), due to parsimony (*lāghava*).
This is because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a power for the accusative in respect to various other distinct categories of meaning.

To illustrate: in the expression "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the meaning of the accusative case—namely, subsistence (*vṛttitva*)—construes with the conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root.
The movement that produces that [conjunction] is indeed the meaning of the verbal root itself.

(Thus, even when the second case-meaning is the locus (*bhāva*), the meaning of the verbal root itself is [the object] through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*). This applies to both types of meanings expressed by the base (*prakṛti*) of words such as "village" (*grāma*) in the second case.

And thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: "the volition conducive to an action that produces a conjunction, which resides in the village and is the counter-correlative of the absence residing in the village," and so forth.

If, however, it were suspected that even the absolute non-existence of going (gamanātyantābhāva) resides in Caitra as a non-pervasive temporal property (kālikāvyāpyavṛtti), then difference (bheda)— defined by the inclusion of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) characterized by "residing in another" (parasamavetatva) and so forth— would be the meaning of the second case-ending.

And that [difference] would be construed with the act of going through the relation of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in which both [the locus and the counter-correlate] possess the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) and inherence (samavāya).

Consequently, the verbal cognition is as follows: "The one possessing the movement that produces a conjunction residing in the village, which is inherent in the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in the village," and so forth.

In reality, however, since the difference from Caitra—who possesses the movement—is equally present [in the village] according to the view that difference is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), the term denoting the village (the base-meaning) is construed with the difference through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*).

And this difference is construed with the movement through the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting of both the relation of the qualifier of absence (*abhāvīyaviśeṣaṇatā*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
Consequently, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: "inhering in a village which is qualified by a difference having the village as its counter-correlate," and so forth.

For this very reason, there is a distinction from the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) when it has the sense of "subsistence" (*vṛtti*), which is synonymous with "locatedness" (*ādheyatva*); for [in that case], the meaning is simply "difference" (*bheda*).
Furthermore, there is this other distinction.

The meaning of the second [genitive]—namely, *vṛttitva* (the state of occurring)—conjoins only with the fruit (*phala*) which delimits the meaning of the verbal root; whereas the meaning of the sixth [genitive]—namely, *vṛttitva*—conjoins with the meaning of the verbal root or the meaning of the nominal stem.
In this way, in expressions such as “the goer of the village” (*grāmasya gantā*), it should be understood that even though the object (*karman*) is not explicitly expressed, it is implied.
Similarly, in expressions such as “the village is being gone to by Caitra” (*caitreṇa grāmo gamyate*), both non-difference and difference of the fruit are admitted.
In this context, the village denoted by the first-case (nominative) word is construed with the difference (*bheda*) through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*).

That [difference] is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—namely, motion (*gamana*)—through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). That motion, in turn, is construed with the fruit (*phala*) expressed by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix through the relation of being produced (*janyatva*), and that fruit is construed with the village, which is the referent of the noun, through the relation of substratum (*āśrayatva*).

Consequently, the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: "The village is the locus of the conjunction produced by that motion which produces a conjunction inhering in something distinct from the village, and which has Caitra as its agent."
The same applies in cases such as "cooked rice" (*pakva odanaḥ*), where there is a *kṛt* suffix denoting the object.

However, in that case, the specific distinction is as follows: the referent of the *kṛt* suffix consists of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), the difference (*bheda*), the state of residing (*vṛttitva*), and the locus (*āśraya*).

The *odana* [rice] [is related] non-differently (*abheda*) to the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*); that [counter-correlative] is related to the difference (*bheda*) by means of the relation that is the locus of its own counter-correlativity; that [difference] is related to the action (*kriyā*) by way of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); that [action] is related to the occurrence (*vṛttitva*) by means of the fruit produced by itself (i.e., by the relation of residing in the fruit); that [occurrence] is related to the substratum (*āśraya*) by means of the relation of being the locus (*nirūpakatva*); and that [substratum] is related to the *odana* non-differently. Thus, the specific cognition (*viśeṣabodha*) is: "The *odana* is non-different from the substratum which is the locus of the property of being the substrate (*ādheyatā*) of the fruit produced by the occurrence of the difference whose counter-correlative is non-different from the *odana*. This is because, in accordance with actual experience (*anubhava*), the diversity of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) is not a fault.

Now, in this case, does the difference connect with the counter-correlate merely as a counter-correlate, or as having a counter-correlativity delimited by the delimitor of the property to be connected (*anvayitāvacchedaka*)? Not the first: because since a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a property that is both specific (*vaiśiṣṭya*) and pervasive (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) exists even in Caitra, the usage "Caitra goes to himself" would result [as an absurdity]. This is because it would entail the collapse of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that [the counter-correlate] must be delimited by the delimitor of the property to be connected. Nor the second.

In the expression "jalaṃ gacchati" (water goes), there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of "jala" because the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by water-ness (*jalatva*) resides in the third-case singular suffix; and in the case of "pācayati" (he causes to cook), there is over-extension in the act of cooking (*pāka*), which serves as the qualifier for the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Therefore, one must either postulate a delimitor-ship (*avacchedakatva*) consisting of a relation of identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), or postulate it as a distinct category (*padārthāntara*).

Furthermore, it must be stated that when a second case-ending is justified by the very means of knowledge (pramāṇa) that apprehends the substratum (dharmī), it is postulated only with respect to that [substratum] and not elsewhere.
And in this regard, there is no means of knowledge other than verbal usage (śābdavyavahāra).

Therefore, since it is possible to postulate that the objects of denotation for the second case and so forth are unanalyzed adventitious properties (akhaṇḍopādhi) in the form of "karmatva" (objecthood) and the like—according to the method to be explained—it is not appropriate to resort to a postulation of denotability that would necessitate the assumption of multiple linguistic conventions (vyutpatti) regarding "ādheyatva" (locatedness) and the rest.
To explain: first, regarding the second [view], there is the assumption of multiple powers (śakti), namely, that there is a power for each distinct occurrence and for each distinct difference.
Furthermore, there is one power in the root (dhātu) for the operation delimited by the result, and multiple powers for the result and the operation.
Thus it should be postulated.

However, regarding incapacity (*asamarthatā*), according to the method previously stated, the delimitors of the capacity to produce that [result] are simply the properties of *pācakatva* (cook-ness), *gamanatva* (going-ness), and so forth, which reside in the operation delimited by the result of that [action]. Therefore, there is no need to postulate multiple powers (*aneka-śakti*).
Furthermore, in your own view, if the result were understood as being identical with the action itself, then [the action would be co-extensive with] the separation from the previous location.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the existence of an adjunct (*upādhi*) denoting the object (*karman*) and so forth within the formation of the verbal base itself;
rather, it is the locus (*āśraya*) alone that constitutes the meaning of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*),
and its connection with the fruit (*phala*) occurs within the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*).

Thus, some have stated that the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is precisely the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; and in this way, grammatical injunctions such as "the third case is used for the agent and the instrument" (Pāṇini 2.3.18) and "the second case is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2) are also consistent. This is not correct.

For, while the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses a relation, it is accepted that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is construed with the meaning of the suffix through a specific relation. Here too, in order to avoid the cumbersome assumption of yet another relation, the expressive power (*śakti*) of the second case and others is postulated to reside in the very states of being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth, rather than in a distinct relation.

Nor is it the case that [the requirement for] the meaning of the locative case (*nyupayantyantara*) is likewise necessary in examples such as *aindraṃ dadhi* ("curds for Indra"), because we observe the coreferential (*abheda*) connection of the meaning of the nominal stem *indra*—namely, Indra—with the deity within the referent of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) which denotes a substance qualified by a deity; for even in that case, since the denotative power (*śakti*) of the secondary derivative can be accepted as residing solely in the substance qualified by deityhood, Indra’s status there is that of being the locus (*ādheyatā*).
(2236) (2237) The meaning of the accusative. The meaning of the accusative.
And the meaning of those verbal roots which have the same sense as the roots *daṇḍ*, *ruc*, *pracch*, *ci*, *brū*, *śās* (*ji*),
*math*, *artha*, *lokanirūpitopahitanatvaviśiṣṭadeśanirūpitopapari-muṣ*, *nīj*, *hṛ*, *kṛṣ*, and *vah*: [the suffix *ya* is applied after them].

The verbal cognition is: "an action whose agent is Hari, located in a place qualified by [the relation of] being in contact with that [action]. This occurs when there is no intention to express the status of the object as an *apādāna* (ablative) in relation to that [action].
In passages such as "The cognitions of the Lord move above the successive cognitions," since—
as in the expression "one should eat beans"— there is no intention to express a mere connection with the root-meaning,
[the meaning is]: "Above the successive cognitions, that is, the upward-moving cognitions, the cognitions of the Lord move."

Since the rule *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51) applies when a case-ending that expresses a relation of connection (*saṃbandha*) would otherwise be required, there is no second case-ending here because the status of being the locus of inherence (*ādheyatva*) is absent due to the performance of the action.
Thus.
Because the designation of "object" (*karman*) is applied figuratively by such grammatical rules as (Pāṇini 1.4.51),
the state of being "defined" (*nirūpitatva*) is also present in cases such as *grāmaṃ samayā* and *grāmaṃ nikaṣā*.
The use of the accusative case and others is seen, for example, in *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ("he milks milk from the cow").
And here,
the meaning is the accusative case;
and its proximity, which is denoted by words such as *samaya* and so forth—
The meaning of the accusative case is precisely the connection with the *godohana* (milk-pail); and that connection is established by way of the qualifier (*nirūpaka*).

In the expression ‘hā kṛṣṇābhaktam’ (Alas, the devotee of Kṛṣṇa!), the state of being the object [of compassion] relates specifically to the *bhāvanā* (the productive urge) through the relation of being conducive to milking,
and not to its meaning; for the purpose of verbal cognition is [to convey] the existence of distress, [specifically] the distress having that as its object.
Because it would result in the imposition of a different form through the addition of the prefix *ni* onto the meaning of the verbal root;
thus, the meaning is that which conveys what has gone there.
And in the case of the word *bubhukṣitam*, the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) expresses the state of being the locus (*ādheyatva*); furthermore,
the grammatical rule is intended to establish the relation [of the object],
while the intention to express the cow as the ablative (*apādānatva*) is not present.

The meaning [of the genitive] is objecthood (*viṣayatva*), and this is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) is the meaning of the nominative. However, in the case of the first [interpretation], there is the usage of the ablative ending in "goḥ payo dogdhi" (he milks the cow's milk).
And likewise, [the state of being] the object of a cognition whose manifestation is partially interrupted is [the definition of] hunger;
however, when there is a desire to express the syntactic relation (*kāraka-saṃsarga*) between the cow and the milk as the object of the action, the use of the genitive case occurs.
[This is] characterized by the objective state of the manifestation of the counter-positive of the absence [of that relation]. (This is "yat"...)
"Even here, through the general relation of connection, there is an integration with the meaning of the verbal root;
something appears, yet it does not satisfy the hunger"— this is what is suggested by the phrasing.

Since milk lacks the status of being an object (*karmatva*) when there is a desire to speak [of it as such], the cow related to it would also not have that status; this is to be understood in the case of the suffix *kāra*. Furthermore, in order to ensure that [the cow] is not the counter-positive of some delimited absence—that is, to ensure it does not lack the status of being an object—the qualification "restricted to the status of being an object" (*karmatvaniyata*) is employed.
Objecthood (*viṣayatva*) is defined by being the state of being an object of a manifestation that functions as the activity of one who is hungry;
for this very reason, the expression "he milks the cow of milk" (*gāṃ payaso dogdhi*) is not used.
Nor is it [the case that...].

Thus is the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). This second [view], however, holds that the meaning of the root *duh* is "causing to abandon" (*tyājana*), where "abandoning" (*tyajana*) is subordinate; and thus, it is subordinate to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
If one takes the sentence "nothing appears" (*pratibhāti tanna kiñcit*) as being suggested (*vyaṅgya*),
then because the basis [of the cognition] does not abandon its delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), the cow's status as the object (*karman*) remains primary.
Therefore, the meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is that [the cow] is the object of appearance in both cases.
How can it be said here that there is *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) in connection with the second case (*dvitīyā*)?
[It is because] the word "pratibhāna" refers to the verbal root-meaning of "pratibhā" as being qualified by the state of being the object of manifestation (*pratibhāniviṣayitā*).
Thus, even though [the object] is the primary object (*mukhyakarma*) when such a sense is intended, there is a general relation to the verbal root-meaning.
When it has the meaning of the verb as its object, the meaning is obtained through the condition of syntactic relation (*saṃsarga-maryādā*).

That too occurs here, because when there is a desire to speak [of the object], the definition of a relation is applicable to the accusative case prescribed by grammatical rule (*ānuśāsanika-dvitīyā*).
The second [alternative] is that the status of having the meaning of the verb as its object occurs by way of being a relation (*saṃsargatayā*) when the meaning of the verbal suffix is the object.
For this very reason, there is no pointlessness in grammatical rules such as *akathitaṃ ca*.
This is to be understood as "it appears."

Because the word *antarā* signifies "in the middle," for this very reason, in reality, the cow's connection here is precisely that of the ablative (*apādāna*). In the case of "you and me" (*tvāṃ māṃ*), the meaning of the accusative is the state of being related; [the phrase means] "between you and me."
It should be understood that the meaning of the second case is [the relation] in its form as a *saṃbandha* (relation). Others [hold this view];
such is the meaning.

In the phrase "antareṇa harim," the meaning is that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) denotes the state of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*). However, this would result in the rule "akathitaṃ ca" becoming redundant; thus, [the author] clarifies this very point.
It should be understood that [the objecthood] is delimited by the fitness for that [action] and by its connection with that [action].
Just as in these examples, even in the case of the root *duh* (to milk), "giving up" (*tyajana*) is not the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root.
Likewise, even when used in conjunction with words bearing the technical designation *karmapravacanīya*, the second case ending [is employed].

They say: "Since [the object] indeed exists, what possibility is there for it to be the primary object (*mukhya-karman*)? Therefore, [the designation 'object'] with respect to these things is figurative (*lākṣaṇikī*). For instance:"
Now, the *karmapravacanīyas* are as follows: *anu*, and likewise in connection with intransitive roots— *deśaḥ*, *kālaḥ*, *bhāvaḥ*, *gantavyaḥ*—
as well as *upa*, *prati*, *pari*, *abhi*, *adhi*, *su*, *ati*, *api*, and so forth.
According to the grammatical rule, "And [the word] denoting the cause is termed *karma*," as in "He sleeps in the Kurus" (*kurūn svapiti*),
the state of being a cause (*hetutva*) therein is the non-co-referential indicator (*lakṣaṇa*).

In expressions such as *māsam āste* (he sits for a month), *godohaṃ āste* (he sits while the cows are being milked), and *krośam āste* (he sits for the distance of a krośa), the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) has this meaning:
just as in *japam anu prāvarṣat* (it rained following the recitation), the raining is characterized by the cause and the fruit, which is the recitation.
In this context, the meaning of the second [case-ending] is delimitation (avacchedakatva),
and that belongs to the location;
such is the meaning.

Here, the meaning of the second case is "the state of being located" (ādheyatva); [this applies] when that [state] is the cause, as well as in the case of the path (adhvan), time (kāla), and state (bhāva). And the state of being located in time and state is temporal and direct.

And when [the verbal root] functions as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there is *anvaya* [of the accusative]; and when those two [the agent and the object] are related to the raining through the relation of being a qualifier (*nirūpakatā-saṃsarga*), the *bhāvanā* is connected [to them].
Thus, according to Pāṇini’s rule: "The object of the roots *adhi-śī*, *adhi-sthā*, and *adhi-ās*... (*adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma*).
And its connection [with the verb] is expressed as "in the sense of *kṛti*" (i.e., in the sense of action).
(In this regard, the rule Pāṇini 1.4.84, *anulakṣaṇe*, applies.)
Now, "in the sense of the third" (Pāṇini 2.3.46).
The sense of the second [case] is the sense of the second.
The maxim of "climbing onto a jar" (ghaṭārohaṇanyāya) is a case of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
Even in expressions such as "he sleeps happily," the meaning of the accusative case is the state of being a producer (janakatva).
The meaning is that "su" denotes easy birth, which is to say, sleep;
or alternatively, the word "sukha" refers to the absence of exertion. The second meaning [of the prefix] is as previously stated.
The meaning is that sleep and so forth are preceded by the absence of exertion.

Thus, it is established in every way that in all cases, the second meaning [the object] is connected with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). And this *bhāvanā* is established by the word associated with the optative suffix (*liṅ*).
And that [connection] occurs with both finite verbs (*tiṅ*) and nominal stems (*kṛt*, *uṇādi*, *taddhita*);
however, it does not occur with the nominative case alone as it does with finite verbs.

For this very reason, in examples such as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), "intending to make rice" (*odanaṃ kariṣyan*), and "he eats rice" (*odanaṃ bhuṅkte*), the connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) belongs to the accusative case in all instances; this is the summary.

*Rahasya*, pp. 67–91. The discussion regarding the second case ending (*dvitīyā*)—that its meaning is solely the object (*sādhya*) and not the instrument (*sādhana*)—is found in the *Saktvadhikaraṇa* (Kaustubha, 2.1.4, p. 1412). In the *Samārgādhikaraṇa*, it was determined (in the Kaustubha) that the second case endings and others in sentences such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) possess the intentionality of expressing a property that delimits their own expressive capacity (*svaśaktatāvacchedakadharma*). *Surāri*, p. 1168. This principle is as follows: just as heroes place the string upon a bow even when it is curved, so too do those within the Veda attribute excellence to a person who is by nature extremely crooked, provided that person enters into the sphere of their concern.

The reckless one. 896. Water-stalls established for an archer in Niṣadha bring harm to others.
Vākyapadīya 1.3.12, p. 166. "Even righteousness indeed covers a man wandering in *saṃsāra*;
for a man is not concealed by a body consisting of pure evil alone."
Or [as stated in] the Mīmāṃsākośa (281.29):
"Dharma is that which, being an object of human pursuit, is knowable through Vedic injunction."
The term "accessible through injunction" (*codanāgamya*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman, to objects of veneration such as *caityas*, and to things like jars.

The term "beneficial" (*artha*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension to ritual acts of sorcery (*abhicāra*) such as the *Śyena* sacrifice, which, though being the subject of an injunction, result in undesirable consequences and are thus of the nature of non-benefit. [Vi.
1.1.2] Dharma (in its form of sequence) is characterized solely by injunction; it is not established by means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Bhāṣya 5.1.1.1, Section: p. 1289. *Dharma*: the excellence of the desire to know (*jijñāsātiśaya*).
This person, proceeding toward an object without prior inquiry, might take up something [unfit] and be frustrated, and may even incur sin.
Therefore, *dharma* is the excellence of the desire to know.
Dharma is to be understood through the twelve chapters [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].
Introduction, p. 11: Dharma is called *apūrva* (the unprecedented), because only that which is *apūrva* possesses the nature of dharma.
2|1|1: We maintain that dharma connects the person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Bhāṣya 1|1|12, p. 11: Dharma is not an object of perception or inference.
VI. 1.1.2: Dharma is known only through injunction (*vidhi*), not through perception, inference, and so forth.
1.1.4: Dharma is an object enjoined by the Veda for the sake of a purpose, such as sacrifice and the like.
It has been stated that "Dharma is characterized by the Vedic word," namely, "Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by the injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*).

In this treatise (*Mīmāṃsā*), Dharma is introduced as the object of knowledge (*prameya*) in the form of an inquiry (*jijñāsā*). It is established that Dharma (the fire-sacrifice) has the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as its purpose;
thus, both the directly contributing (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) and the indirectly contributing (*ārādupakāraka*) factors function within the context of the primary rite.
*Ḍūpū* 9|1|1|1, Section 2: Dharmas (of the *agni*) have the *apūrva* as their cause and are prompted by the *apūrva*.
Bhāṣya 9|1|1|1, p. 1638: Dharmas (of the *agni*) are prompted by the *apūrva*.

Therefore, they are established according to their respective contexts (7|1|1|1, p. 1524). Dharmas are prompted by the purpose [of the sacrifice] (such as the dharmas of the sacrificial post, the dharmas of the enclosing sticks, etc.).
*Artha* means *phala* (result). 12|1|1|126. Those *dharmas* which are *saṃnipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing factors) are also *apūrva*s;
this is established in the *Nabha* [section] in two places.
9|1|1|1, p. 1638. Regarding *dharmas*: where there is concomitance (*sāhacarya*), there the *dharma* is obtained; in the absence of concomitance, there is no acquisition of *dharma*.
8|1|1|12 p. 1585. Some consider *dharma* to be a quality of the intellect (*buddhi-guṇa*), while others consider it a quality of the self (*ātma-guṇa*).
Bṛhatī p. 26. Regarding *dharma*, those of great learning are indeed divided; some declare one thing to be *dharma*, while others declare another.
Bhāṣya 1|1|1 p. 10. *Dharma* is the subject matter...
Having made *dharma* the object;
for from *dharma* [the suffix] *dhā* occurs,
and the kṛtya suffix is considered.

In this regard, is there no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all? Or is it only perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest that are the means of valid cognition? Or is it only the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)? Or is there an option (*vikalpa*) between them? Or is there a combination (*samuccaya*) of them?

Among these, since verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not itself a means of valid cognition because it does not provide what has not been obtained by other means of valid cognition, and since perception and the others lack the capacity [to know dharma], what is dharma if it is devoid of a means of valid cognition?
Another [view] holds that [dharma] is accessible through direct perception for yogins, but for those of the present age, it is accessible only through injunction (*codanā*).

Yet another position maintains that, since the diversity of the world implies the existence of some unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), dharma is established in a general sense; it is then understood through injunction in its specific forms such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice; therefore, there is a combination [of both means].
The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that only injunction is [the means], and that alone is the valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is here asserted for the sake of emphasis that *codanā* alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and that it is indeed a means of valid knowledge.
It is qualified by the word "artha" so that dharma should not be understood as consisting of anything characterized merely by *codanā*.
And by the word *codanā*, both an injunction that prompts action and a prohibition that restrains it are meant.

Furthermore, by means of prescriptive statements such as "one should not kill" (*na hiṃsyāt*), even acts like killing—which are indicated as being non-beneficial (*anartha*)—would have the status of *dharma*. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "beneficial" (*artha*) is intended to state that only that which is seen through prescriptive statements as having the form of a benefit possesses the status of *dharma*. And the mention of the *śyena* sacrifice and others in the *Bhāṣya* is for the purpose of indicating [such cases] as killing; this is because they will be explained later with the words, "For that is killing, and it is prohibited."
Regarding this, there is some discussion in the *Codanāsūtra* (pp.

18–26). This is because they accept that only that which is a direct means of accomplishing the fruit (*phala*) possesses the nature of *dharma*. Furthermore, they consider that which is connected with the word "fruit" to have *dharma* as its purpose and to be a means of accomplishing the *apūrva*.
Or:
[it] desires the dharmas being honored by means of the assistance of the instruments. (Vārttika 21|1|1, p. 303)
"Om. From Dharma, Prajāpati should be [the deity].
In the Upāṃśuyāja of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, Prajāpati should be the deity."
Because of the quality of being an *upāṃśuyāja* (whispered sacrifice).

Due to the nature of the *upāṃśuyāja*, it is whispered; and because of the scriptural statement, "Whatever is performed for Prajāpati, that is performed in a whisper," Prajāpati also possesses the quality of being whispered.
Therefore, Prajāpati should be [the deity].
This is one position.

The word "or" (*vā*) indicates a specific alternative position. However, there is no designation of a deity in that case; rather, it is the softness of the sound itself, and therefore this is the governing principle here.

The word "tu" (but) refutes the position that Prajāpati is the deity for the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice on the basis of logic. In that regard, in the sentence "One should sacrifice to Prajāpati with the mind," the non-specification of the deity Prajāpati would be the property of silence (*tūṣṇībhāva*), because it is distinct from the [other] properties.
The purpose of the *upāṃśuyāja* is for the sake of the *dharma* (the ritual merit). Therefore, there is no *upāṃśuyāja* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

Thus, another reason has been stated for the position of the Siddhānta. However, because of the injunction regarding Agni and Soma, the Upāṃśuyāja is prescribed on both occasions during the Paurṇamāsī; the word "tu" (but/however) refutes the position that it belongs to the Paurṇamāsī alone by means of logical reasoning.

By the sentence "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* immediately after," the *upāṃśuyāja* is enjoined without distinction in both cases, on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Since it is enjoined that Agni and Soma [are the deities] on the full moon—by the text "Those two, Agni and Soma, [should be worshipped] in a low voice on the full moon"—the *upāṃśuyāja* on the full moon has Agni and Soma as its deity; whereas, due to the recitation of a mantra [to Viṣṇu], the *upāṃśuyāja* on the new moon has Viṣṇu as its deity. Thus, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the deity. This is another prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Alternatively, Viṣṇu would occupy the same location because of the injunction following a prohibition.
The word "or" (vā) excludes the position that the Upāṃśuyāja occurs on both the full moon and the new moon days;
for, having prohibited [the sacrifice] on the new moon day, the Upāṃśuyāja is enjoined specifically on the full moon day.
Viṣṇu should occupy the same location as Prajāpati and Agni-Soma;
or rather, the location of those two—the full moon—is the very same location for Viṣṇu as well.
Therefore, the Upāṃśuyāja must take place on the full moon day itself, and there alone is the option of the deities—so says the proponent of the final conclusion (siddhāntavādī).

Having introduced the topic with the statement, "One should sacrifice for us with clarified butter alone in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) at the full moon," it is further recorded: "A redundancy (*jāmi*) is indeed created in the sacrifice when one sacrifices the two blameless *puroḍāśa* cakes consecutively without an intervening *upāṃśuyāja*.
The two blameless *puroḍāśas* occur only at the full moon, not at the new moon.

And in that very context, this injunction is given: "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice to avoid redundancy; Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in a low voice to avoid redundancy; Agni and Soma are to be sacrificed to in a low voice to avoid redundancy."
Therefore, the established conclusion is correct.
Likewise, there is the observation of another purpose;
that is, when the *upāṃśuyāja* is absent on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), there occurs the observation of another purpose.
"Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, and thirteen on the new moon day.
If the new moon day were non-existent, there would be fourteen oblations, not thirteen.
Therefore, there is no *upāṃśuyāja* on the new moon day.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

There are five *prayāja* offerings, two *ājyabhāga* offerings, two for Agni and Soma, one *upāṃśuyāja*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and three *anuyāja* offerings; thus, there are fourteen oblations at the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).

At the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), however, there are two specific differences—the offering to Agni and the *sānnāyya*—and the *upāṃśuyāja* is absent; thus, there are thirteen oblations. Furthermore, that which is not a subordinate part (*anaṅga*) cannot be enjoined for both occasions by a single scriptural statement, because of the requirement of a specific connection.
Thus, the *upāṃśuyāja* is indeed [performed] on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

Since the *upāṃśuyāja* is not a subordinate part (*anaṅga*) but a primary rite (*pradhāna*), and since it is heard of only once in the scripture (*śruti*) regarding the full moon, it would not be prescribed for both—the full moon and the new moon—if it were heard of only once;
for there would be no connection [to both], as the primary rite lacks a connection [to both occasions].
And because the qualities (guṇas) exist for the sake of another, he shows the indicative marks of an injunction regarding the activity of the primary principle (pradhāna).
Because the qualities exist for the sake of another, he shows the indicative marks of an injunction regarding the activity of the primary principle;
it is not [an injunction] for the primary principles themselves, because they are not dependent on anything else.
How so? [Because of the statements]: "He offers the two *ājyabhāga* oblations with the word *ap*," and "Offer eleven *prayāja*s, eleven *anuyāja*s.
The *upāṃśuyāja* is the primary [element].
If it were not present, there would be no indicative mark (*liṅga*) for its performance; thus, it does not apply in the *āmāvāsya* sacrifice.
And because there is no scriptural statement regarding the modification;

since there is no scriptural statement—that is, no mention—of the *upāṃśuyāja* in the modified form of the *sākaṃ-prasthāyīya* at the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), there is therefore no *upāṃśuyāja* even at the new moon sacrifice. This was stated in the sūtra "And in the case of immediate sequence" (5.2.1.56).
Therefore, the *upāṃśuyāja* occurs only at the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).

In that very context, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, and Agni-Soma are the deities as alternatives; however, in the *Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa*, the *upāṃśuyāja* is stated even for the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*). But the present investigation concerns another scripture, or perhaps it is not to be considered at all. Instruction (*upadeśa*) is the means of knowing—that is, the indicator—of Dharma characterized by the *agnihotra* and so forth, which is not apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge. "The instruction is the means of knowing it."

*Bhāṣya* 1.1.1, p. 23: Since dharma has purpose as its function, there is a connection with the injunction (*codanā*) when the sequence [of the investigation] regarding substance and quality is prohibited due to their inherent association. For example, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) prescribed for *vrīhi* rice applies to *nīvāra* rice in the Vājapeya sacrifice, according to the rule: "He offers seventeen *śarāva*-measures of *naivāra* [rice] sacred to Bṛhaspati. Or, as in the case of honey-eating:
"When the six-day period is completed, he should eat ghee or honey," where the prohibition "he should not speak much, nor ask another, nor speak to another" applies to the eating of honey.
Because dharma is produced by purpose (arthakṛtatva) and because dharma has sound as its source (śabdamūlatva), there arise many doubts: for instance,

in the Rājasūya sacrifice, when it is said, "Having offered the *caru* of *nairṛta*, one should enter the house of those who have not sown [grain]," does the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the mortar and pestle— which is archetypal (*prākṛta*)— apply to the nails, or not?

Regarding the question whether the ritual properties of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) should be performed on the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices— based on the injunction "one should bind the animal to the enclosing-stick"— and whether the property of the word *girā* (namely, the substitution of the vowel *āyī*) applies to the word *irā* based on the injunction "one should not say *girā-girā*, one should say *airaṃ kṛtvā*," the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) concerning this deliberation:
[The rule applies] in the case of the collection of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), modification (*vikāra*), transgression (*vyatikrama*), and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).

In this context, there is an "extension of the injunction" (*codanā-anubandha*) regarding substance, as in the case of *nīvāra* grain and the like; regarding quality, as in the case of wine, food, and so forth; regarding modification, as in the case of the nails; regarding transgression, as in the case of the *paridhi* wood—which, having transgressed the status of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), is prescribed as a means for tethering; and regarding prohibition, as in the case of the prohibited and then re-prescribed *irāpada*.
The term *codanā* is derived from the root *cud*, meaning that which is enjoined (*coyamāna*).
Such an extension (*anubandha*)—that is, an application by analogy (*atideśa*)—would belong to the enjoined act, such as the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites.
Because of the inherence [of the quality], there is a connection of the original (prakṛta) property even with the modified (vaikṛta) rite;
because the property, such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), has been performed for the sake of the transcendental result (apūrva);
and because the requirement for the producer of the transcendental result is identical.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that there is an extension (atideśa) of sprinkling and other such rites;
for dharma is produced by purposeful action.

Since there is an absence of *soma*-ness in the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*), how can the status of being an *anuṣṭhīcchatva* (a subordinate element of the ritual performance) be possible? This is not a fault, because the properties of *soma* are obtained through the transfer of characteristics (*snānāpatti*).
For it will be stated: "Because the property is produced by its purpose" (*dharmasyārthakṛtatvāt*).
[Vārttika 3.1.5–12, p. 1024]. It has been stated that the definition of a property (*dharma*) is that which is characterized by scriptural injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*).

Page 211, line 21; p. 370: First of all, perception is not a means [of knowing dharma]. Perception is that cognition which arises in a person when there is a connection between the sense organ and its object. Since the object [of dharma] is yet to come, it does not exist at the time of the cognition.
Therefore, perception is not a means [of knowing dharma].
And because inference, analogy, and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception, they too lack causal authority.
Even non-existence (abhāva) does not exist [as a separate means of knowledge]. Bhāṣya 1.1.4.
Even though *dharma* is an object of cognition (*prameya*), it is not suitable for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because direct perception has as its object only that which is present.
As for that *dharma* which is absolutely beyond the scope of direct perception, what need is there to mention inference (*anumāna*) and the other means of knowledge?
Therefore, *dharma* is understood solely through injunction (*vidhi*).
VI.1.4 | Since Dharma has the Veda as its source, [the Smṛti] would be invalid if it were independent of the Veda.
Regarding the inquiry as to whether Smṛtis such as "The Aṣṭakā rites should be performed" are authoritative regarding Dharma or not, he states the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view.

Since Dharma— defined as "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (1.1.2)— is rooted in verbal testimony and has the Vedic word as its sole authority, this Smṛti, being devoid of such Vedic verbal authority regarding Dharma,
would be independent [of the Veda] and thus not to be relied upon because it lacks a foundation.
However, the reading "anapekṣyam" (not to be relied upon) occurs in many different manuscripts.
The meaning, however, is not different.

The phrase "or rather" (*apivā*) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "the Smṛtis are not an authority regarding Dharma," by asserting that "inference may be an authority because of the identity of the agent."

Inference is a means of valid cognition; having reflected upon the fact that the Veda is a means of valid cognition, it follows that Smṛti should be a means of valid cognition regarding Dharma because it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition.
Due to the identity of the authors, the authors of the Smṛtis and the authoritative Vedas are common—that is, they are identical and non-different.
Because they share a common authorship, Smṛti is a means of valid cognition.
The specific meanings derived from the Vedas have been set forth by the authors of the Smṛtis;
therefore, it is inferred that the Smṛtis are rooted in the Śruti.
Therefore, the authority of the Smṛtis with respect to Dharma is established.
Consequently, the conclusion is that the Smṛtis are authoritative.
Who [says this]?
Since Dharma has its root in the Word (śabda), it must depend upon that [Word].
Thus far, the authority of the entire Veda has been stated.

Now, however, there arises an inquiry as to whether that which is not found in the Vedic word, yet is remembered by tradition as "this matter should be performed for this purpose," ought to be accepted as such or not.

For example: "The *aṣṭakā* rites must be performed," "The teacher must be honored," "A pond must be dug," "Water-stations must be established," and "The *śivā-karma* must be performed. Regarding these, the Prābhākara [school] has described this as a distinct category (*adhikaraṇa*) because of the absence of a connection [to a Vedic injunction]. Here, since all of these are of the nature of *smṛti*, they are understood as being, according to the circumstances, either injunctive (*vidhi*), prohibitive (*niṣedha*), or descriptive (*anuvāda*) statements. For instance: "Ritual action must be performed by one who has sipped water" (*ācāntena karma kartavyam*), "It must be performed with the right hand facing forward" (*dakṣiṇācāreṇa kartavyam*), "The sacrificial thread... [and so forth].

Furthermore, that being the case, since the unhesitating practical conduct of the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) would be established merely through the study of the Veda as it exists in its scattered state, the labor of composing the *smṛti* treatises would be rendered useless.

As it has been said: "For what reason was the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), which is the root of those [treatises], not presented by Manu and others themselves, along with their own words, through that very effort by which they caused their own compositions to be recited?"
Thus [it is said] (Vārttika, p.

Therefore, since Dharma has its root in only a portion of the Veda, and because the word "Veda" would otherwise imply a non-existent root, the eighteen [subsidiary sciences] would not be required as Dharma, and they would certainly not constitute Dharma. This being the position reached, it is replied: "But rather, on account of the commonality of the agents, inference should be a means of valid knowledge."
This is the intended meaning: in every respect, the Smṛtis of Manu and others, which possess authoritative wealth, must be preceded by prior cognition.

In that regard, it is first of all impossible for a Smṛti to be preceded by erroneous cognition (*bhrānti-vijñāna*). For if such an error were to be postulated, it would have to be explained as being based either on fallacious reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*) or on misheard words (*duḥśruta-śabda*).

Furthermore, such [an understanding] is not possible even in the slightest degree regarding the entire reality of logic (*nyāyatattva*), the pervasive knowledge of the six-limbed Vedas (*ṣaḍaṅga-vedavyāpti*), or the teachings of the various classes of sages;
nor is it possible regarding merit and demerit (*dharmādharma*).

Now, what indeed is this so-called *dharmatva* (the state of being dharma) or *adharmatva* (the state of being adharma)? It cannot be the state of being an enjoined action or the state of being a prohibited action, because that would fail to apply to enjoined or prohibited substances and the like.

For there is no absence of the conventional usage "this person is righteous" or "this person is unrighteous" regarding those who perform subsidiary elements for the sake of a result in a sacrifice, as well as those who employ silver and other such items [prohibited in sacrifices].
Furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of [such substances] falling under the scope of the scriptures in sections such as the *Indriyakāmādhikaraṇa*.

Furthermore, if it lacked the nature of *dharma*, that which is produced by it would also lack the nature of *dharma*, resulting in the undesirable consequence that it could not be proclaimed as such.

Nor is it devoid of the nature of action (*kriyātva*), for if it were, then in cases such as the injunctions of permission (*abhyanujñāvidhi*) regarding the recitation of the *Āryā* at weddings and so forth, it would result in those acts being *dharma*, and in the case of the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, it would result in it being *adharma*.
If this is argued, we say no.

The definition of *dharma* is the state of having the status of a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) as revealed by the Veda; the definition of *adharma* is the state of having the status of a means to the undesirable (*aniṣṭa*) as revealed by that same [Veda]. This is because such definitions are logically consistent.

For indeed, the status of being a means to the desirable or the undesirable regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, the prescribed consumption [of Soma], and so forth, is revealed by the Veda; thus, the definition applies there.
In this context, the latter part of the definition—“being revealed by the Veda”—is included to exclude [the application of the definition] to Brahman, heaven, hell, and the like.
Although acts such as the eating of forbidden food are means for achieving the desired or the undesired, they lack the status of *dharma* because they are not enjoined by the Veda.
In the case of the *śyena* sacrifice, however, since its status as a means to achieve the desired is indeed enjoined by the Veda, it possesses the nature of *dharma*.

Its production of the undesired occurs only when there exists the intention to perform violence—such as the killing of enemies or the destruction of hostile forces—which constitutes the result of the *śyena*.

In the same way, it is clearly explained in the fourth [book of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra] that the *śyena* sacrifice is not unrighteous (*adharma*) because it has been taught by the Veda as a means to an undesirable end;

however, even where there is an injunction such as "one who desires the death of an enemy should sacrifice," the sacrifice and so forth are indeed righteous (*dharma*), because the injunction makes known its status as a means to a desired end.

Nor does the sacrifice there fall under the scope of the prohibition "one shall not kill," since the sacrifice is a purposeful activity directed toward causing death; for the prohibition is satisfied by the avoidance of killing prompted by passion (*rāga*), and thus does not apply to what is enjoined.

Nor does such a scriptural fragment lead to the conclusion that the learned (śiṣṭas) would engage in it without hesitation—even through a traditional lineage—just as they do with the Śyena sacrifice, because even indirectly, a transgression (*pratyavāya*) would not arise [in the case of the latter]. This is because, upon examining the sequence of statements such as "That which is for the purpose of destroying another is declared to be *tāmasa*" (Bhagavad Gītā 17.19), the act of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is censured as being *tāmasa* due to its nature as a ritual act that produces malevolent magic. Consequently, by the force of the prohibition appropriate to it, even though that [Śyena] is enjoined for the sake of a specific fruit, it possesses the quality of unrighteousness (*adharma*) because it produces undesirable results; thus, there is a distinction between the righteousness and unrighteousness of those two acts.
For this very reason, since being *dharma* and being *adharma* are merely adventitious conditions (*upādhi*), there is no fault even if they overlap.

As for the objection that because the definition of *dharma* includes "not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence," and because that [condition] is absent in the *śyena* sacrifice and similar rites, they cannot be considered *dharma*— that is not so.

In that case, there is no purpose for causing [the enemy] to fall (vedha), because the intensity of undesirable defects such as disease depends upon prior karma; thus, the aforementioned method might occasionally occur even in the Śyena sacrifice.
Otherwise, if there were no dharma in the Śyena, there would be no inclination toward performing it due to the absence of merit.
Furthermore, if there were no dharma in the Śyena and similar rites, it would be untenable to describe them as having tamasic dharma.

Therefore, the application (*samanvaya*) of the previously stated definitions is appropriate even for that which is enjoined by way of permission (*abhyanujñā-vidhi*), because such a rule implies only the absence of fault and does not imply that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*). Consequently, even in the case of what is already desired due to natural passion (*rāga-prāpta*), since there is no status as a means to a desired end taught by the Veda other than what is [already] unenjoined, there is no resulting status as *dharma*.

Furthermore, in the case of the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, the prohibition does not imply that it is a means to an undesired end (*aniṣṭasādhanatā*), both because there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*) and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Moreover, even in the absence of this [prohibition], since the mere accomplishment of the excellence of the ritual through other means suffices for a person’s desistance, there is no need for a scriptural injunction to induce activity therein; for that very reason, the injunction does not imply a fruit in that case. Consequently, even there, the status of being unrighteous (adharma) does not arise.
And being "revealed by the Veda" means being known through the Veda while not being known independently by any means of knowledge other than the Veda.

Therefore, even though the knowledge of Brahman—which consists in the direct realization of reality and is established by other means of knowledge as the generator of liberation in the form of the cessation of the ignorance that is the creative play regarding Brahman—is revealed by the Upaniṣads, it does not follow that it possesses the nature of *dharma*.

Even if it is held that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not an effect of ignorance because it is real, and that liberation (*mokṣa*)—consisting of the destruction of the twenty-one types of suffering and so forth—is produced by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and this view is authoritative; nevertheless, since the fact that [knowledge] produces liberation cannot be known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one must, in order to exclude its being a *dharma* (religious duty) in that context, set aside "being taught by the Veda" and instead provide "being taught by an injunction" (*vidhi*). Since knowledge, by its very nature as a valid cognition of an existing object, lacks the capacity to be an object of incitement (*pravartanā*), it cannot be taught by an injunction.

In reality, however, there is no harm in [knowledge] being considered *dharma*, because the term *dharma* is applied even to knowledge in such passages as, "But this is the supreme *dharma*: the perception of the Self through *yoga*.

Nor is the word "perception" (*darśana*) in that context intended to mean meditation (*dhyāna*), for there is no evidence for such a figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*); moreover, it is impossible for meditation—which consists in the cessation of mental fluctuations—to be produced by *yoga*.

Furthermore, although knowledge (*jñāna*) is a form of dharma like ritual worship (*upāsanā*) and other such acts, it lacks the status of dharma in the context of Brahman because Brahman is not a means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*) as taught by the Veda. Consequently, the distinction between the *Dharma-mīmāṃsā* and the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* is logically established.

Alternatively, even if one were to maintain that the definition of dharma overextends to Brahman, one could add the qualification "being pervaded by human effort" (*puruṣakṛtivyāpyatva*) to the phrase "being a means for the highest good taught by the Veda.
Even in the case of a quality (*guṇa*), since it is pervaded by effort when qualified by its substratum (*āśraya*), there is no over-extension.

Furthermore, although knowledge itself is not directly pervaded by effort (*kṛti*) in its own nature, it is nonetheless established that it is indirectly pervaded by effort—just like the correct digestion of food and so forth—because the mental application (*manaḥ-praṇidhāna*) and other such factors conducive to it are themselves pervaded by effort. Therefore, there is no other [means].
For this very reason, [it is said]: "The Self, indeed, O Maitreyī, [is to be realized];
merit and demerit... [and] "the state of being dharma... [is not yet...].
Even the injunctive suffix in the expression "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) can be understood as having this very intention; this is easily stated in our system.

Alternatively, one may introduce "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*) into the definition of causality, such that this definition itself becomes the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for the terms *dharma* and *adharma*.

Since that [uniqueness] is common to both action and the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by it, the two words *dharma* and *adharma* can denote both the action and the unseen merit/demerit produced by it through a single [denotable property]. This is the summary.
*Rahasya*, pp. 1–3:
Dharma and adharma consist of a specific type of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force), not of the nature of action (*kriyā*).

For this very reason, in such passages as "Dharma perishes through [failure of] recitation," and in the Vaiśeṣika system, the terms dharma and adharma are applied to the *adṛṣṭa* produced by action; nevertheless, [it is said]: "Dharma, when performed by men... (as found in the *Viṣṇusahasranāma-kathās*).

"If there is no pleasure to be gained, then there is only mere exhaustion"—in such passages, the terms *dharma* and *adharma* are employed to denote those actions enjoined that produce [such results]. (Rahasya, p. 1) Dharma and adharma were investigated by Jaimini in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī* for their utility in ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).

one should then invoke the gods and the world-protectors (lokapālas) as before.

if I am impure, may sin come into my hand through the power of Dharma."

"Then, when the accused has been challenged by one of the two [ordeals], he should grasp [the object] without delay. If he grasps the *dharma* (the correct object), he shall be purified; but if he grasps the *adharma* (the incorrect object), he is defeated."

Regarding the statement "for the sake of dharma," a mean servant is not to be given away in the Viśvajit sacrifice (Bhāṣya 6.7.5–6). Regarding the phrase "inquiry into dharma" (*dharmajijñāsā*), the word *dharma* refers exclusively to the subject matter of the Veda (Ṛjuvimalā pṛ. 16). And what is its ultimate purpose?"—these four aspects are presented by the first sūtra (Sūtravṛtti p. 538). This is the inquiry into dharma.
The desire to know dharma is *dharmajijñāsā*.
Since the knowledge of dharma constitutes dharma, dharma itself holds primacy with respect to the desire; therefore, it is "the desire for dharma" (*dharmāya jijñāsā*).
And thus, because the sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) is perceived, this is indeed a case of the dative case [denoting purpose].

The general knowledge of dharma is the cause of the desire for a knowledge whose qualifier is a particular property of dharma (*viśeṣadharmaprakārakajñāna*). By the sentence "it attributes sin to dharma," there arises, through the general proximity (*asāmānyapratyāsatti*) of that [sentence] within the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) regarding the general knowledge of dharma, a knowledge of the knowledge of all dharmas; from that, there arises a desire directed toward that [knowledge]. Thus, in this sequence, the knowledge whose qualifier is a general property is the instigator of the desire whose qualifier is a particular property.

And that [desire] has the form "Let the knowledge of dharma (dharma-jñāna) arise along with its means of valid cognition," and so forth; it is produced by the knowledge of the instrumentality of such a desire.
And such knowledge [of instrumentality] arises through the universal-characterized mediation (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-pratyāsatti) of the property of being dharma (dharmitva).

[Page 2] Dharmitva is not, first of all, a genus residing in both the sacrifice and the apūrva, because the sacrifice, being of the nature of either an action or a desire, possesses the property of being an action (kriyātva).

The nature of dharma (*dharmatva*) does not reside merely in the action itself; for since one uses the expression "this person is righteous" (*dhārmika*) with respect to the performer of sacrifices and other acts, it consists in the state of being a means whose efficacy is established by the Veda.
Some maintain that the nature of dharma is simply an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) defined by both the sacrifice and its transcendental result (*apūrva*).
In reality, however, dharma is the state of being a prescribed action, or simply the state of being prescribed, by virtue of being a means to a transcendental good (*alaukika-śreyas*).
The term ending in the third case (instrumental) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to things like *soma* and so forth, which are prescribed as subsidiary parts (*aṅga*).

And "transcendental" (*alaukikatva*) consists in being an object of valid cognition (*pramiti-viṣayatva*), while being cognizable by a means of knowledge not exceeding the Veda and its dependent authorities.
The term *śreyaḥ* (the beneficial) is used to exclude [the definition] from undesirable things and so forth, which possess various characteristics.
The term *vihitā* (prescribed) is used to exclude the *apūrva* (unseen force).
Dharma consists of actions, substances, qualities, and so forth, which are prescribed as means for attaining that result (*phala*).

For even in the case of the Śyena sacrifice, because it lacks the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*), there is no possibility of its being considered Dharma. Furthermore, although false speech for the sake of marriage is something enjoined, it does not possess the status of Dharma; this is because it serves merely as a means to marriage and the like, and thus lacks the quality of being *alaukika* (transcendental).

Finally, the knowledge produced by the Upaniṣads—which generates liberation through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*)—does not constitute Dharma, as it is already established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Or let there be the nature of dharma (*dharmatva*) in that case. (Maṇi, pp. 7–9). *Dharmatva* has been stated as being the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
And it has been stated that [dharma] is characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*) by virtue of its being an object (*arthatva*).
*Ṛju*, p. 27. ✱ *Dharmatva* (the state of being dharma) consists in having the quality of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) as revealed by the Vedic injunctions that impel action.
For indeed, the very nature of *dharmatva* is the state of being a means to a non-worldly (*alaukika*) highest good.
