Having filled the mortar at the root of an *audumbara* tree with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadha*), when it is stated, "One threshes here; he places that [mortar] down," this refers merely to the ritual duty (*dharma*) which has only an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). Since no visible result, such as the production of rice grains, is observed in the act of threshing itself, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that completion (*apavarga*)—that is, the termination of the action—is achieved by performing the literal meaning of the word only once.
Therefore, because of the nature of the "all-medicinal-herb" [substance], there is a disparity from the threshing of rice, which must be repeated until the production [of grain] is complete.

In the section [sūtra] *dharmamātre taddarśanāt śabdārthenāpavargaḥ syāt* (JS 1.1.16–28), regarding the injunction "Having filled the wooden mortar with all kinds of herbs, one threshes; he places it on the path," it will be stated that because the threshing has no visible purpose such as the preparation of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) made from rice-grains, and thus serves an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose, it should be performed only once.
(Su. p. 626). By this same principle—*dharmamātre taddarśanāt śabdārthenāpavargaḥ syāt*—the conclusion is reached that the *prayāja* offerings should be performed only once.
This is the summary of the Bhāṣya.

But if it were merely an action upon a substance (*dharmamātra*), then it would be a primary act (*pradhānakarma*) because it does not cease [with the substance], like the *prayāja* offerings. Regarding the scriptural injunctions, "He cleanses the ladles" (*srucaḥ saṃmārṣṭi*), "He cleanses the fire" (*agniṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), and "He performs the sprinkling around the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśaṃ paryagni karoti*), there arises a deliberation as to whether this cleansing and sprinkling are primary acts or subordinate acts (*guṇakarma*). In this regard, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In all actions consisting merely of *dharma*—such as sweeping (*saṃmārga*), sprinkling (*paryakiraṇa*), and so forth—there would be "action" [in the technical sense], that is, it would have the status of a primary action (*pradhānakarma*).
This is because a visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*) is not produced.

Since having a visible benefit is the defining characteristic of a subsidiary action (*guṇakarma*), and since that is absent here, sweeping and the other such acts would consequently have the status of primary actions.

It is like the *prayāja* offerings. Just as the *prayāja* offerings [are subsidiary], because they lack a visible benefit to the principal rite (*pradhānakarman*), so it is here; for it should possess the same characteristics as these, owing to the identity of the scriptural injunction.
Refuting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of a counter-argument, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta):

"The collection of properties such as the sweeping (saṃmārga) would have the same property—that is, possess the same characteristic—as these subsidiary actions (guṇakarma), such as threshing (avaghāta). The meaning is that they share the nature of being subsidiary actions.

Because the scriptural expression is identical: just as in the injunction "He threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the accusative case-ending signifies that which is most desired to be attained (*īpsitatama*), so too is the accusative in "He cleanses the *sruva*-ladles" (*srucaḥ saṃmārṣṭi*) and "He prepares the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśaṃ paryagni karoti*).

And because they are what is most desired to be attained, the collection of properties such as cleansing and the like are subordinate actions (*guṇakarma*); whereas the substances, namely the rice and the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), are primary, because they are the objects to be refined.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In this context, the reading "sadharmāḥ sadharmāḥ" is found elsewhere;
nevertheless, the neuter reading ending in the suffix *an* (anivṛttyantaḥ), which follows the *ya-kuk* [rules], is indeed more appropriate.
If it is argued that this refers to the teaching of substance (*dravyopadeśa*), [we reply:]...
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) says:

Even when a substance is taught as a subordinate factor (guṇabhūta), the use of the accusative case is observed, as in "he offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*). Likewise, even though the accusative case is used in expressions such as "the sacrificial ladles [are for] the cake" (*sucaḥ puroḍāśam*), they would still be subordinate factors; consequently, acts such as the wiping (*saṃmārga*) would be principal actions (*pradhānakarman*).

Furthermore, [the use of] the accusative case is not restricted to denoting predominance (*prādhānya*), as it is observed even when a substance (*dravya*) is taught as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*). According to the *Vārttika*—"One offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*)"—the term "in the teaching of a substance" (*dravyopadeśe*) is a word ending in the locative case.

In the phrase "one offers the groats," there is an instruction in the accusative case for the substance of the groats, which is subordinate by virtue of being the means (*sādhana*) toward the oblation.
How so? Out of curiosity, one asks: "What is the teaching of a substance?"
Thus ends the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that, because the act of offering (*juhoti*) has ceased, [the result] is like the first self [of the agent], as if desiring musk?
[Response: No, because it is for the sake of that [offering], like a lamp, and because that [offering] is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*).

As for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that the accusative case is seen even in the instruction of a substance that has become a subordinate factor (guṇabhūta) in the injunction "He offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*)—that is not so.
It is true that the groats possess the status of a subordinate factor because they exist for the sake of that [offering], namely, for the sake of the oblation (*homa*).

However, the accusative case expresses their status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, the accusative does not denote something that is a subordinate factor.

Since the groats, the sacrificial cake, and so forth, are subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*), they possess an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭa-upakāra*) when they serve as the objects of acts such as wiping (*saṃmārga*) or scattering (*paryākaraṇa*). In that context, the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) indicates their primary status (*prādhānya*).
It is understood that even an invisible refinement (*saṃskāra*) exists;
this is just as in common worldly usage, where it is said that an invisible benefit is produced by the act of scattering for men who have arrived from another village.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that acts such as sweeping (*saṃmārjana*) and sprinkling (*paryakiraṇa*) are auxiliary rites (*guṇakarma*), not primary rites (*pradhānakarma*). [Objection: "But it would be a primary act with respect to the mere property (*dharmamātra*), because it does not cease [its purpose], like the *prayāja* offerings. It is heard in scripture: "He sweeps the ladles" (*srucaḥ saṃmārṣṭi*), "He sweeps around them" (*parīcīnaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), "He sweeps the fires" (*agnīn saṃmārṣṭi*), and "He performs the sprinkling of the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśaṃ paryagni karoti*). In this regard, there is a doubt: are the sprinkling and the sweeping primary acts, or are they auxiliary acts?

In the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), by the statement "those [acts] are of two kinds," the definition of primary acts (*pradhānakarma*) and subordinate acts (*guṇakarma*) was set forth in two sūtras.

Now, in certain specific cases such as the act of sprinkling (*saṃmārga*), a classification as a primary act is made; regarding this, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) is as follows:

"Those acts by which the substance is not intended to be produced (*na cikīrṣyate*) are primary acts, because the substance is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Thus, the definition of a primary act has been stated.

Furthermore, in the case of substances such as the *sug* ladle, no transformative effect (*rūpakāra*) produced by the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is observed that would be required for a desired result.

According to the principles: "When substances are connected with an action, they are related as subordinate factors (*guṇa*)," and likewise, "In the communication of what is already existent and what is yet to be, that which is already existent is taught for the sake of that which is yet to be," since substances such as the *sug* serve the purpose of the action consisting of cleansing, they constitute primary actions (*pradhānakarma*), just like the *prayāja* offerings.

Now, it might be argued: "Granted that, by setting aside the [direct] injunction, the intended action pertaining to the substance is understood through another means of knowledge; nevertheless, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) invariably denotes the object most desired (*īpsitatama*) everywhere. Therefore, even if its status as the *anīpsita* (unintended) object of the act of piercing is set aside, the accusative meaning remains uncontradicted."

Now, it may be argued that substances such as those denoted by the elision (*luk*) have their purpose established by another sentence, whereas actions such as *saṃmārga* (cleansing) have no established purpose.

Furthermore, there is a relationship between two things whose purposes are already established; it is logical that what lacks an established purpose is enjoined precisely for the sake of that which has one.

According to the maxim that "the injunction of what is required is weaker than the injunction of what is already required," even if there is no visible benefit, the fact that the accusative case denotes the most desired object (*īpsitatama*)—by virtue of the aforementioned logic—indicates that cleansing and other such acts are for the sake of substances like those denoted by the elision which have established purposes. Therefore, it is impossible for these to be subordinate actions (*guṇakarman*).
It is said: this would indeed be so if the injunction were accepted as having an unestablished locus (*aklptādhikaraṇa*).

For it, by its very nature, requires the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for that which is to be accomplished; it also requires the substance (*dravya*) and so forth that serve as the means to those, since without them, the accomplishment of the goal would not occur.

As for the purification (*saṃskāra*) and so forth pertaining to the substance, which are connected through the requirement for a substance with a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), these too are accepted by virtue of generating a further requirement.

Furthermore, in cases such as "he cleanses the ladles" (*srucaḥ saṃmārṣṭi*), there is no room for objection because the elision (*luk*) and other such operations serve a visible purpose, just like [the threshing of] rice grains. For this very reason, even in the case of "he initiates with six," since there is no possibility of [the original number] being set aside, the mantra derived by extension (*atideśika*) does not apply to the six vessels.

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), however, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of anything even regarding the *barhis* grass used for the purpose of placing the oblations of both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice;
therefore, there is no similarity with the *barhis*.

This being the case, since one observes in the archetype the various functions belonging to its own specific species, even if there were an injunction for the *śamyā* wood for the purposes of its own nature and for making it leaf-shaped (*parṇatā*), nevertheless, the quality of being made of *śamī* wood would belong only to the act of sweeping (*saṃmārjana*).

Because the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-wood), which is studied under the section on non-commencement (*anārambha*), is grasped by the *apūrva* of both the subsidiary and the principal through the door of heaven, it is conceived as having a distinct function by way of the connection with the auxiliary that assists the instrument of the non-principal *apūrva*; thus, it possesses the status of a function connected to the instrument that assists the principal *apūrva*. Furthermore, since the nature of the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is also the function of the *parṇatā*, and because there would otherwise result the fallacy of "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*)—whereby one would have to indicate the *parṇatā* first (as the object of the injunction) and then indicate its own nature as its function—the injunction is said to have its own function.

Although the injunction applies even to those things whose purpose is the state of being made of *parṇa* wood, nevertheless, since it pertains only to the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), there is no fault.
This is stated in the section on "mere properties" (dharmamātra).
Because [the application] of the *aupadeśika* (directly taught) and other [elements] is not observed.

As long as the instruction—which is a non-perception of what is otherwise possible—does not occur, there is doubt; and in that state, because it is sublated by a stronger, though doubtful, means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no spreading of the *barhis* grass within the sacrificial enclosure.

Furthermore, just as there is no application of an element being enjoined—even if it follows as common to both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*)—to a subsidiary that has no expectancy for a means obtainable from the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too, because of the doubt, in that state it is sublated by a stronger, though doubtful, means of knowledge.

Regarding the statements "those who are sacrificers are the officiating priests" (*ye yajamānāsta ṛtvijaḥ*) and "he who is the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryu*": if the archetypal (*prākṛta*) *ṛtvij*s and *adhvaryu* were already satisfied by their own functions as subsidiaries, there would be no connection between the sacrificer and the *hotṛ*.

This being the case, because the present [text] would lack purpose, the [injunction] itself would not exist; furthermore, this would contradict the logical principle: "In case of conflict, the instrument [prevails] due to a specific connection; the other is for the rest, since that from which the distinction arises."
Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

For this very reason, there is no restriction of the injunction even out of fear of sublation by what is extended by analogy (*atideśika*); for in that case as well, since the duties of the *ṛtvij* and *adhvaryu* are connected with the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cessation of the roles of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the *hotṛ* due precisely to the fear of sublation.
As for the rule regarding the great altar (*mahāvedī*) of the Soma sacrifice, it indeed sets aside the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites.

Regarding the statement "and [the displacement] from conjunction," the Vārttikakāra has stated that the entire Mahāvedi serves solely for the purpose of this Jyotiṣṭoma. Furthermore, even regarding the altar (vedi), the Bhāṣyakāra’s own view was stated here in order to refute the purpose mentioned by him through the principle of incidental application (prasaṅga).

Even in his view, the abandonment of the Mahāvedi rule for the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites is not due to a fear of sublation by extended application (atideśa); rather, it is solely out of concern for the diversity of rules—such as being sublated in some cases, being independent of sublation in others, and being merely the fulfillment of what is already obtained in yet others.

Similarly, in the case of the statement "one shall initiate with six [mantras]," there is no restriction of the original injunction (upadeśa) out of fear of superseding or displacing the archetypal rule (atideśa).

Rather, while the archetypal fivefold rites such as initiation and so forth are present, when they are connected with the modified (vaikṛta) five mantras, six modified recitations of the act of offering (*juhoti*) are heard in the text: "He offers twelve.

In this regard, when the doubt arises as to whether the repetition should be performed with the modified mantras alone or with the archetypal ones, the connection to the first repetition must be postulated due to the absence of a specific injunction.

In the case of favoring through extended application (*atideśa*), a restriction is postulated only for the eight mantras belonging to the original model (*prakṛti*) that are subject to such extension.

Here, however, the connection with the *rūṅ* [substitution] exists solely by way of direct instruction (*upadeśa*); therefore, it does not deserve to be restricted out of fear of subverting the extended application—this constitutes the difference.

As for the example cited by some regarding the modified rite (*vikṛti*)—"If both offerings of one who has been struck by misfortune should be lost, he should offer five *śarāva*-measures of rice to Indra"—where it is shown that the four-handful pouring (*caturmuṣṭi-nirvāpa*) obtained through extended application is reduced to the mere handful (*muṣṭi*) by subverting one of the two [requirements], that is incorrect.

For it is not the case that there is a contradiction regarding the instruction on the characteristic of the property (dharma-lakṣaṇa) in the mere property itself; rather, when both are not contradicted, because of the production of five śarāva-measures of cooked rice from [grain] lacking four handfuls.

In cases where the purpose cannot be achieved and one of two requirements must necessarily be set aside, it is indeed proper to favor the number (of the mantra) due to its priority, as in the case of reducing [the offerings] to a mere handful.
However, in this instance, because the setting aside is based on a direct injunction (*aupadeśika*), there is no inequality; thus, nothing is incorrect.

Now, if it is argued that the application of the rule is extended (*ātideśikī*) only to those [mantras] that are not explicitly known [in the model sacrifice], whereas for those that are not unknown, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is directly enjoined even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *patramāna* and others also being extended by analogy.

[Objection: Since the two instructions possess equal force, it is only the latter that is sublated, because its application is primarily based on a weaker status such as being *atideśika* (extended by analogy).
[Reply: Not so.

Is the status of being *aupadeśika* (directly enjoined) attributed to the cups simply because they are not among those extended by analogy (*atideśa*), or is there a direct injunction for those enjoined with reference to the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) that applies equally to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*)?

Thus, it is not the first [alternative], because it is the weakest even in terms of extended application (*atideśa*) due to its being dependent on an extension of the rule, and is therefore more easily sublated. Nor is it the second, for if that were the case, the *kṛṣṇala* oblation— though heard in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as intended for the *praśāja*— would undesirably apply to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), even when the *praśāja* has not been performed there.

Nor does there arise the contingency of the extension (*atideśa*) of the *patramāna* [quality], because in the archetype itself, by the injunction "one offers in the Āhavanīya," the Āhavanīya fire situated upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), and thus that very same status is obtained in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as well.

Now, it might be argued that even though it is based on extension, there is a difference regarding the time of application: since the assistance provided by the instrument is first connected with the subordinate element produced by the auxiliary (*aṅga*), and only afterwards with the primary act;
in that case, the oblation (*homa*), having been first obtained, would have its requirements fulfilled through the *suḍ* [suffix], and then the injunction regarding the *śamī* wood would apply.
It is not the case that [the subsidiary] does not depend on its own time, which occurs at the end of the main path;
for that would be incorrect.

If that were so, then even in the case of the *barhis* grass, since the first placement of the primary oblation (*pradhānīya-havis*) is already established by means of both direct statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), one would have to bypass the attainment of the subsidiary oblation-placement—which occurs later—merely by way of an auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*). Consequently, the *barhis* grass would be connected with the primary sacrifice alone.
And as it is there, so it is here; thus, even though there is a difference regarding the time of the *prātikas*, there is no laying down of the *barhis* grass.
Moreover, specifically in this case, even a difference regarding the time of the *prātikas* is not possible.

For, since the connection with the subsidiaries occurs by way of being subordinate to the assistance (*upakāra*), the extension of that connection applies only to those [subsidiaries] whose capacity for producing assistance was understood in the archetype (*prakṛti*) to be exactly as they are.
Because that which is accompanied by its own auxiliary parts produces a benefit for the primary rite (*prakṛti*), it attains its inherent nature along with them.
This too is merely something trivial.

And all of this has been stated on the assumption that the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is included within the *pūga* [of the cups], just as the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*) at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is included within the *pūga*.

From the perspective of ultimate truth, however, this is not tenable; for the treatise on the investigation of Dharma (*Dharmamīmāṃsā*), established through sixteen chapters and thirty-six sections (*pādas*)—namely, the six [chapters] and seven [sections]—is based upon the injunctions of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*) for those who lack knowledge.
[This is the *Saṃkarṣa*.]
That which pertains to liberation through dharma originates from that [Veda]; that which has pleasure as its object is preceded by worldly convention—thus it should be distinguished.
This is the definition of dharma.

The *Codanāsūtra*: "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction (*codanā*). The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "For we maintain that it (dharma) indeed unites a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)."
To this it is replied:
Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction (*codanā*).
They say that an injunction is a statement that impels one toward action.
That by which it is observed or characterized—namely, "I act because impelled by the Teacher"—is a *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic mark), as in the expression, "smoke is the *lakṣaṇa* of fire.
This is what they say.
We maintain that the object characterized by such [a mark] connects the person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

For an injunction (*codanā*) is capable of making known that which has been, that which is, that which will be, the subtle, the concealed, and the remote—that is, things beyond the reach of [other means]—and no other sense organ whatsoever [is so capable]. (Regarding this, the *Vaidyanāthī* commentary states: "The word division is *nānyat kiñca*; thus, only the Word (*śabda*) possesses the capacity to convey such a meaning, not the general category of means of knowledge other than that.
The reason for this is: 'not the sense organ' (*na indriya*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that nothing else is capable.")
"Furthermore, the meaning of 'what' is 'for the sake of wisdom'; as for the question 'from what,' the reason is the same as stated previously: 'it is not a sense organ.'"

Now, regarding the phrase "there is no other sense-organ whatsoever," what is stated here for the sake of demonstration is the sense-organ as intended by the author of the Sūtras; or alternatively, the word "nothing else" (*na-anyat-kiñca*) is employed with the sense of a general negation.
(Śloka 15, 1.1.2.2) Furthermore, once its incapacity has been established, the sense-organ is mentioned again.
In the case of a medial division [of the compound], the expression "something" (*kiñca*) is employed to indicate the reason.
Regarding this, it is explained in three ways in the Vārttika: "There is no other sense organ that is capable";
"There is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which the sense organ [is known]";
and "No other means of valid cognition is capable."
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "why"?

Because the sense organ is not capable [of knowing the dharma], and since the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is preceded by the sense organ, that [Vedic injunction] alone is capable—so say some.
But surely, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) might speak of something that is not as it actually is, just like any ordinary worldly statement such as, "There are fruits on the bank of this river."
It may be true, and it may also be false;
thus is the characteristic of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) described.
This which is said—that "it speaks" and yet "is false"—is contradictory.
By "it speaks," it is meant that "it causes one to understand; it becomes the cause for one who is understanding.
And when that which has become the cause exists, one understands; thus, it causes one to understand.
If it is understood from the Vedic injunction that "heaven results from the Agnihotra" when such an injunction exists, how can it be said that "it is not so"?
On the other hand, if it is not so, how is it understood?
To understand a non-existent object is a contradiction.
Furthermore, from the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," one does not perceive anything doubtful, such as "heaven either comes to be or does not come to be.
Nor can that which is perceived with certainty be false.
For a cognition is false only when, having arisen, it subsequently perishes with the realization, "this is not so."
And it does not undergo subversion at another time, in another person, or in another state; therefore, it is [considered] a valid cognition (*pratyaya*).
As for worldly speech, if it comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object of the senses, it is indeed non-false.

However, if it comes from an untrustworthy person or concerns something beyond the senses, it is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), as its extent depends on the power of that person's intellect.
For it is impossible for a person to know that;
one can only postulate that "something has been perceived," but there is no independence of the word [itself].
This is not so, for instruction may arise even from delusion.
In the absence of delusion, [knowledge] arises even from the Veda.
Since these two roots [of cognition] are possible here, it can be said that there is no other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) apart from those already established.
Therefore, because a contrary [result] from another means of valid knowledge is impossible, it cannot be asserted that the *codanā* possesses an intrinsic contact with its object.
Therefore, it is well-established that "Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo dharmaḥ*).

Furthermore, from a human statement, there arises the certainty that "this is the intended meaning," but no cognition produced by another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) occurs [regarding the truth of that meaning].
As it has been said: "Moreover, from a human statement, there arises the conviction that 'this person knows it to be so,' but not that 'this object is so.'"

Or rather, does there arise a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) upon the comprehension of a different object, as in the case of other means of knowledge? Certainly; for at that time, the means of knowledge is understood to follow the object [itself]. [Does one understand that verbal cognition is a distinct means of knowledge from the inference of the comprehension of an object? Certainly, it is so. By presenting the very cause [of the action], verbal cognition—in the case of an action such as a sacrifice—is understood as the *niyoga* (the mandate) which is the object of the action, and not merely as that which impels one toward the action itself. This we shall explain in the section on the *apūrva*.

Therefore, the injunction itself expresses the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*), whereas it takes [the object] as its domain (*viṣayatayā*). Why? Because the technical usage of the *Tantra* is that "whatever is taken up [as an object], that very thing [is the domain]," and not—as is the usage in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of Mīmāṃsā—that "whatever is made known as something to be done, that is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*)."

That which functions as the material cause (*upādāna-hetu*) is the "governing cause" (*adhikṛta-kāraṇa*), because it is the governing factor due to its being a qualification of the agent (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇatayā*). Since it is the cause for the undertaking (*upādāna*), it is not something to be discarded (*avapādeya*).
Therefore, it is established that in the case of an undertaking (*abhisāra*), the activity is not based on material appropriation (*an-aupādānikī pravṛttiḥ*).

Since there is no such sacrificial gift (*vaiśyapadāna*) that serves as the basis for qualification (*adhikāra*), it is precisely for this reason that the prohibition "one shall not kill" applies. Therefore, having accepted the non-deviation from the basis of qualification, it was said: "That [act] is indeed killing, and that is prohibited."

For a prohibition must pertain to the *kṛtya* (the action to be performed), because it depends upon the performance of that which is to be prohibited, and thus its purpose is already established; it does not pertain to the *adhikāra* (the qualification or context), because the activity therein is independent. Thus, the prohibition "One shall not harm living beings" is a prohibition pertaining to the *adhikāra*, serving the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, it is capable of establishing the harmfulness of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), whereas it cannot apply to the *iṣṭi* sacrifice for rain and so forth, because those have the *kṛtya* as their purpose.

Now, why is there this double negation in the rule "one should not harm living beings"? (The answer is: For a single injunction cannot simultaneously possess both the character of being an impeller and the character of not being an impeller. Furthermore, why does this [rule] not simply function as a prohibition (pratiṣedha) alone, for the sake of brevity in its application? (He states the answer: Between the status of being an impeller and the status of not being an impeller, the status of being an impeller is directly expressed by the Vedic word (śrauta), because it is understood without dependence on anything else. The status of not being an impeller, however, is understood through the consideration of other sentences.

Nor does there arise from the sentence "One should not harm living beings" a separate injunction, because it is an unattached prescription (*anārabhyavidhāna*). For initially, the optative suffixes and the like convey a duty (*kārya*), which is characterized by that suffix.

When a governing injunction (*adhikāravidhi*) is present nearby, the optative suffixes and so forth function merely as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that duty; thus, this prohibition is understood only through the governing injunction (it does not pertain to the material means). And [the application of the Śyena sacrifice] is indeed characterized by an injunction, because the injunction for the Śyena has that [harmful act] as its object.
Therefore, the commentary beginning with "Both are indicated here by the injunction" is appropriate.

[The objection] "But this Sūtra is incapable" is intended to demonstrate the distinction between worldly and Vedic sentences. Alternatively, it is intended to show that even according to the literal wording of the sentence, a single meaning is possible—[namely, that] "in the case of an injunction, there is no syntactical split (vākyabheda) characterized by the assumption of multiple meanings."
"But it certainly exists due to the difference in its positive concomitance (anvaya). [The commentary] states:
"A property that is the subject of investigation is considered to be either devoid of definition (lakṣaṇa) or endowed with means of valid cognition (māna), or indeed by both."
What indeed could be the characteristic of that which is devoid of worldly forms?
For here, the suspicion regarding its validity is difficult to dispel, since perception and the other means of knowledge do not apply to it.
For when an object exists, the form accessible through injunction (*codanā*) is its defining characteristic;
therefore, in this case, why should the injunction not be our means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

Then he states the opinion of the Guru: "When the very object to be known is [the meaning], is it that which is made known by the mantra? Or is it an established fact (*siddhārtha*) understood through an injunction (*vidheya*), or is it indeed a matter of action (*kāryārtha*)?"
Even when the birth of a son and the like are already established, there is justification for the application [of the term "siddha"];
there is no contradiction even if that which is established through mantras and so forth constitutes the meaning of the Veda.
The proficiency [of the Veda] arises from the abundance of causes for joy at the birth of a son;
however, that proficiency is difficult to attain in ritual action, whereas the meaning of the Veda is easily attained—therefore, it is that [meaning] alone which truly matters.
Therefore, the meaning of the Veda consists solely of what is to be done (*kārya*).

Since *dharma*, which is to be investigated, is *alaukika* (supra-mundane), it cannot be an object of perception; consequently, inference, which is rooted in that [perception], is all the more incapable of functioning with respect to it.
For this very reason, since even the definition [of *dharma*] is impossible [otherwise], the investigation of *dharma* is indeed appropriate.

This being the case, even though worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not apply, it is possible for the Vedic injunction—whether singular, triple, or accompanied by hundreds and thousands—to serve as the authority for that singularity; for while invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), validity (*prāmāṇya*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Therefore, *dharma* is indeed possessed of a means of valid cognition. For this very reason, the definition of *dharma* is either its being the means to a desired end known exclusively through the Veda, or, such being the case, its being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence [if it were otherwise].

Dharma is the property of being something that is in fact prohibited while being associated with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitva*); whereas being dharma [in the positive sense] consists merely in being enjoined (*vidhīyamānatvamātra*).

This latter is synonymous with "that which is to be undertaken" (*upādeyatā*) and is a specific kind of objective reference (*viṣayatā*) characterized by the form of an impulsion (*preraṇā*), pertaining to the primary action (*kṛti*), its subsidiaries (*aṅga*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and so forth.
And this [dharma] resides precisely in such things as the *Āgneya* sacrifice, the *Prayāja* offerings, the materials, the deities, the low-pitched tone (*nīcatva*), and the like.
And [this] does not apply to the notions of fruit, instrumental cause, agency, and so forth.

In the case of the statement, "In the fifth [year], for one desiring Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*)," there is no harm even if the time being enjoined for the sake of the fruit is not itself a *dharma*, because the initiation (*upanayana*) which is its substratum is indeed a *dharma*.

However, the status of being a *dharma* belongs precisely to the hawk-sacrifice (*śyena*) and the like when they are undertaken for the purpose of a hostile incantation (*abhisāra*), since they are described in the Purāṇas and other texts as *tāmasa* (dark) *dharmas*.

However, marriage and the like are not objects of injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, there is no prohibition regarding the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice. In those cases, because the optative suffix (*liṅ*) characterizes the *dharma* by way of indicating the absence of defects and the accomplishment of the ritual, it pertains to the instigation and non-instigation [of action] as having *dharma* as its object. (2263) *Dharmaviṣayaka*.

Because it is not [the object] of the Veda; or else, because dharma and adharma consist in being the objects of injunctions and prohibitions that project the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious.
The term "auspicious" (śubha) is common to both the wood used as an auxiliary to a sacrifice and that which produces the eight [supernatural powers].
An unwholesome state is common to the qualities of being a source of suffering, causing pain, and being base;
however, that which is the object of a permissive injunction is neither dharma nor adharma.
For this very reason, in the preceding sūtra, the term *dharma* indicates the scope of deliberation regarding characteristics such as non-affliction.

This is because the property of being connected to the meaning of a sentence that constitutes the intended purport of a non-human (apauruṣeya) utterance serves as the delimiting factor (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) for what is to be defined.
Furthermore, since it is subordinate to injunctions for the meditation on Brahman with attributes and without attributes,
etc., it is indeed accepted that Brahman, just like the ritual form itself, is an object of inquiry here within the context of specific ritual injunctions.

Alternatively, "being of the nature of a relation" (*saṃsargātmakatva*) should be specified as a qualifier for the meaning of the sentence included within the scope of the delimitor of the objecthood (*lakṣyatā’vacchedaka*).
Maṇḍana [says]—(at the beginning): "Now, by means of the second aphorism, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) has been instigated."

Distinguishing between the semblances of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) and the like through their intermixture, Śaṅkara states: "Dharma and the means of its knowledge are [defined by] *codanā*," and "Dharma and its purpose are accessible through *codanā*.
The definition of Dharma as that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*) is sublated [by the fact that it is known through scripture]."

*Bālapriyā*, p. 143: The treatise on the investigation of *dharma* (*dharmavicāraśāstra*), beginning with "Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ*) and ending with "And the *annāhārya* [sacrifice] because it is seen [in scripture]," consists of the collection of sūtras proclaimed by Jaimini.
Regarding this, the Bhāṭṭas maintain that the treatise on the investigation of *dharma* is directly enjoined by the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*).
The Prābhākaras, however, hold that study is prompted by the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*), and thus the treatise on the investigation of *dharma* is prompted by that [injunction].
1111. In the *Dharmavicāraśāstra*, the injunction "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ*) is the motivator.

1111. In case of a conflict between dharmas regarding subsidiary and principal elements: the favoring of dharma belongs to the principal alone. Bhāṣya 12.2.9.25. Declaration of the examination of the means of valid knowledge concerning dharma.
The Section on the Examination of Signs.
He is an examiner of the causes [of dharma].
The Commentary states: "The knowledge of dharma has the injunction as its cause.
That, however, was stated merely as a proposition.
"Now we shall examine its cause," thus [it is said] regarding the injunction (*codanā*); "and there is another [cause] as well.
Therefore, for the time being, it is not established that Dharma is an object characterized by injunction.
As the verses state: "Although the author of the Bhāṣya has [spoken] apart from the formal proposition (*pratijñā*..."
The reasoning for one's own position, which is about to be stated, has already been indicated.

This is stated to be the opinion of Jaimini: that it is merely a formal proposition (*pratijñāmātra*). However, the author of the *Vṛtti* has also stated that "the elements" (*bhūtādi*) and so forth serve as the means (*dvāra*).
Bṛhatī: "The examination of its cause"—by this statement, the occasion for discussing the reason (*hetu*) is being described.
But how can the injunction alone be the cause with respect to the effect? Because other means of knowledge, such as perception and so forth, have no connection [to it].
Why is there no possibility [of such other means]? (We shall explain this in the subsequent sūtra.)
In the *Sūtra* on the definition of injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*), the nature of the Vedic meaning was stated by means of two scriptural citations, and therein its authority was also proposed.

Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether the nature [of the Veda] should first be explained in terms of difference and non-difference, or whether the reason for its authority—proposed in the statement of the proof—should be explained. Since the nature of the subject is primary, it follows that it is that very nature which must be explained through difference and non-difference. To this, we reply: since the determination of difference and non-difference is not required for the sake of establishing authority, it is now the requirement for the reason for that authority which must be explained; thus it is stated in the following *Sūtra*.
And thus the Bhāṣya says: "Now we shall examine its cause.
Therefore, the Sūtra provides an occasion for stating the reason for validity, which consists in its independence (anapekṣatva).

Śā—By this Sūtra, the examination of the cause known as *codanā*, which will be discussed in this Pāda, is mentioned by way of reference to the Sūtra, just as in the cases of "Now, therefore, the definition of the subsidiary" (*atha ataḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*) and "Now, the definition of the particular" (*atha viśeṣalakṣaṇam*).

Candrikā: This is the meaning of the aphorism here: regarding that Dharma, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which is the cause for its cognition—that which is designated as *codanā*—its *parīkṣīḥ*, meaning its examination, must be performed.

From the root *iṣ* (meaning "to go"), by applying the suffix *yu* according to the rule "after *iṣ* when it has the sense of desiring," and because of the traditional rule allowing an option between the suffixes *kit* and *nu* in the form "paryeṣā," the form *paryaṣaṇā* is established when *yu* is applied; however, when *kit* and *nu* are applied, the form *parīkṣīḥ* is established.

Here, when there is doubt as to whether the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma* should be examined or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the object of cognition (*prameya*) is established by the mere instruction on the means of cognition, what is the use of examination? The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this is not merely a statement of definitions as if they were already proven; rather, because this is a treatise of inquiry (*vicāraśāstra*), the examination of the means of cognition must be carried out in every respect. As Viśvanātha states: "The means of cognition that makes *dharma* known has been stated to consist of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)."
Is this not to be examined, or rather, should it be thoroughly examined?
Since that which is to be accepted is established by the instruction on the means of valid cognition, what is the use of further investigation?
Do not speak thus; for why would even an examination be undertaken regarding this which is already refuted?
The teacher’s view is stated: "First, the meaning of the Veda should be examined by means of the authority of the injunction (*codanā*);
because the meaning of the Veda is primary, [the inquiry] first concerns the subject matter of *dharma*."

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not indicated by another *bhāvanā* through [the mediation of] an action (*kriyā*) and so forth, as in examples such as "one threshes rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) or "one cooks rice-gruel" (*odanaṃ pacati*); in those cases, the meaning of the verbal root itself serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

However, in instances where there exists no other unobtained instrument, the meaning of the verbal root—being already established by the context—is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that root-meaning.
The verbal root (*dhātu*) is for the purpose of establishing correctness;

however, its meaning does not connect as an instrument (*karaṇa*), nor as a substratum (*āśraya*). This is because a substratum distinct from the status of being an object (*karman*) cannot be defined, and since the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is already established as having the form of an object (*karman*), if the *homa* were also connected as an object, it would result in the undesirable consequence of there being only a single object.

For this very reason, the *Kaustubha* and other works state that the basis for the defectiveness [of a sentence] is the presence of a single object, even when there is a distinction based on multiple intended objects (*uddeśya*) or conditions (*nimitta*).

Furthermore, "having a single object" (*ekakarmakatva*) does not mean having exactly one object, nor does it mean having objects that reside in a single substratum; for otherwise, [the rules] such as "the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices [are performed] for all [desires]" (*sarvebhyaḥ darśapūrṇamāsau*) and "bring the pot" (*ghaṭam ānaya*) would fail to apply, because in those cases there is a multiplicity of objects—such as sons and so forth—qualified by [the desire for] a son and so on. Nor does it mean "that which excludes having multiple objects," for otherwise [the rules] such as "the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices [are performed] for all [desires]" and "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) would fail to apply.

In that regard, although there is a difference between the objects— such as the son and others— and the qualifiers of the objecthood (*karmatā*) such as their being the means to an unprecedented result (*apūrva*),

it has been stated in the *Kaustubha* that [the unity of the object] consists in the property of being a substratum wherein the objecthood is fully resident (*paryāpti*) and which is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the scope of a single cognition.

Furthermore, since all the properties that delimit the scope of the substratum where objecthood is fully resident among the various relata (*nirūpakatva*) are produced by a single word in a single cognition consisting of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), the status of having a single object is established.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "The Adhvaryu and the sacrificer restrain their speech" (*adhvaryuyajamānau vācaṃ yacchataḥ*), there would be the undesirable consequence of it being a "two-object verb" (*dvikarmaka*), because the two properties of being the object (*karmatva*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*)—namely, those belonging to the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer—would not be the objects of a single cognition. Therefore, [the relation] is "paryāpti" (pervasion/totality). In that case, since the property of being an object (*karmatva*) does not reside in each member of the compound by virtue of the dual suffix—as is the case with the deityhood (*devatātva*) and so forth—the pervasion of that [objecthood] resides in the property that delimits the locus, namely the "duality of both Adhvaryu and sacrificer. Consequently, because this [duality] is the object of a single cognition of the *dvandva* compound, its status as having a single object is established.
This has been established in the *Kaustubha* and other works.

Similarly, in cases such as "Bring the white pot" (*śuklaṃ ghaṭam ānaya*), since there is a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) between the quality "white" and the pot, the status of having a single object of action is justified either through the denotation of both words or through the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "pot" alone for the pot qualified by the quality of whiteness.

Likewise, in cases such as "Bring the pot and the cloth" (*ghaṭaṃ paṭaṃ ca ānaya*), that status is justified through the secondary signification of the two words ending in the accusative case, in accordance with the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) expressed by the suffix *-ka*.

And just as, in the case of a locus consisting of multiple causes (*nimitta-dravya*), the reason for the defectiveness of a sentence split by multiple intended causes is the resulting loss of the status of having a single action (*ekakarmakatva-bhaṅgāpatti*), so it is made clear in the *Kaustubha*.

Thus it is established that where another object (*bhāvyāntara*) capable of syntactic connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is presented by means of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) and so forth, there the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) does not possess the status of being the object (*karmatva*).

However, where that [instrument] is the cause and the fact that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is a means to the desired end (*ihasādhana*) is established by another means of knowledge, then, provided there exists another quality (*guṇa*) to be enjoined which has its own substratum, the meaning of the verbal root itself functions as the object (*karman*), as in "He offers oblation with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) having two objects (*dvikarmakatva*)—since the root *juhoteḥ* is already transitive and there is no other substratum for an object—in the case of "He offers oblation with a ladle" (*juhvā juhoti*), because even for a transitive verb, the object can be understood as being delimited by the action itself, just as in the case of a verb expressing a state (*bhāvākhyāta*).

Even in such a case, if there is the hearing of a name ending in the third case, then there is indeed instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), as in "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground" or "One should recite loudly with the Pravargya," and so forth.

However, where there is no hearing of such a quality, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the verbal root's meaning itself as the object (*karman*) for another purpose, as in the two sentences concerning the learned (*vidvat-vākya*).
But in the absence of that [other purpose], as in "He sacrifices with the *tanūnapāt* offering," and so forth, it is clearly established that this is indeed a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

However, where the status of being a means to the desired (*iṣṭāsādhanatva*) is not cognized, or where—as in the case of *uddiṣṭa* and others—there is no hearing of a name ending in the third case within its own sentence (such as in "one should sacrifice with Soma" or "one should offer the Agnihotra"), then even if the status of being a qualification of the desired is understood in its own sentence, because the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) exists as an injunction, one must accept that only the desired in general is the objective (*bhāvya*). Consequently, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) possesses only the status of the instrument (*karaṇatva*).
Regarding the word "Agnihotram," the traditional authorities (*sāṃpradāyikāḥ*) hold that even the accusative case there is intended solely for the purpose of indicating the status of the instrument.

In such a case, by virtue of the direct hearing of the same word (*samāna-pada-śruti*), the object required by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the verbal root itself; this is all the more so when one hears the accusative ending in "agnihotram.

Nor is it impossible for that which is not known as a means to a desired end to function as an object, since its connection can be established as an unintended object (*anīpsita-karma*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the instigatory nature of the injunction (*vidhi*); for although the cognition of non-sublation derived from the injunction is a cause for activity, it is not a cause for the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) itself. Thus, even in its absence, the delimitation of the productive urge by the oblation as its object remains logically possible.

Furthermore, since that [action] which is connected as something to be brought about (*bhāvya*) has no requirement for another *bhāvanā*, it would follow that it does not appear even in the sentence stating the result (*phala-vākya*) as a means to heaven; however, this is not the case. For just as there is a cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛti-sādhyatva*) when [an action] is connected as a means, so too, even though it is already understood as achievable through effort, its status as a means to a specific desired object is established by another sentence—either through the requirement of an injunction (*vidhi*) or by the maxim of the Viśvajit sacrifice (*viśvajin-nyāya*). Therefore, the view that "in the originative sentence (*utpatti-vākya*), the meaning of the verbal root alone is construed as the object (*karman*)" is untenable, because the meaning of the verbal root is not delimited by the *bhāvanā* [in that way].
The *Tarkadīpikā* maintains that even what was stated by the Prābhākara is reasonable;

thus, it is established in every respect that the objective character (*karmatva*) of the root-meaning, through its internal relation, functions as a qualifier (*prakāratā*) in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).
However, the traditionalists (*sāṃpradāyika*) hold that the root indicates, by means of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), either the objecthood or the instrumentality residing in its own meaning.

Its connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) occurs through either the relation of being its own qualifier (*svanirūpakatva*) or the relation of being the property of being the object of its own qualifier (*svanirūpakoddeśyatvatva*).
However, [relations] such as *karmatva* (objecthood) do not function as relations [in this context].

If they did, it would result in the redundancy of the grammatical rule which teaches that "the base and the suffix express their meanings together" (*prakṛtipratyayau pratyayārthe saha brūtaḥ*), since that rule pertains to a connection characterized by simultaneity (*sāhitya*).
For those [grammarians] who are engaged in the instruction of word-meanings (padārtha), it is not appropriate for them to provide an instruction regarding syntactic relation (anvaya).
Therefore, even the introduction of [the meanings of] the object, the instrument, and so forth, appears precisely as a word-meaning through the operation of the *vṛtti* itself.
For this very reason, it is consistent that the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) in "jyotiṣṭomena" also restates the instrumentality appearing as a word-meaning.
They say that it is a general rule that the quality of being a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) for both the qualifier and the qualified.

Thus, it is established that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is everywhere a qualifier of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). It will be explained later that this [meaning of the root], whether conveyed by a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) or by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*), is what connects with gender (*liṅga*).
Therefore, in the cultivation (bhāvanā) denoted by the term "entity" (vastu), there is nothing else;
even though it is secret, it is that which is to be accomplished.

An investigation into the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*): Even such usages as "merely by virtue of being denoted by the verbal root" (*dhātvācyatvamātrāt*) are consistent when there is an intention to speak [in that way]. Therefore, every operation (*vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the verbal root.
In the case of verbal roots with transitive meanings, the object is expressed when there is a *vikaraṇa* such as *yaṅ*, while the agent is expressed when there is a *vikaraṇa* such as *śap*.

In the case of intransitive roots, where there is no *vikaraṇa* such as *caraṇa*, the meaning of the root itself takes the form of the "state" (*bhāva*). This is according to the grammatical rule: "The suffixes *la* [denote] the object... (Pāṇini 3.4.69). Furthermore, all these factors are subordinate (*guṇa*) with respect to the meaning of the root through their respective appropriate relations.

According to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) cited from the *Nirukta*, "The verb denotes the primary action" (*bhāvapradhānam ākhyātam*), it is stated that the meaning of the verbal root—which is expressed by the word "action" (*bhāva*)—is primary with respect to the meaning of the finite suffix. Grammarians, however, maintain that the traditional rule regarding the primacy of the suffix-meaning refers specifically to the domain of nominal suffixes (*suvādi*).
But even that is not correct.

Regarding the theory that blowing [into the fire] is the meaning of the root: this is because "blowing" is not understood from the word *pacati*; because that which is not being measured cannot be the delimitor of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*);
and because even in the absence of blowing, one uses the expression "Caitra cooks" when rice is produced through a fire ignited by some other action residing in Caitra.

Furthermore, if the operation were experienced as such-and-such a specific entity, then there would be no possibility of the disputants' divergent views regarding whether it is "sacrifice," "desire," or "cognition."

Therefore, that which is accepted as the object of the verb *pac* (cooking) and so forth—namely, the cooking, the sacrifice, and the like—is indeed the producer of the result; thus, a universal in the form of a partial adjunct (*khaṇḍopādhi*) consisting of the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the delimitor of the word-potency (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) for words such as *pac*.
The evidence for its existence is the uniform cognition "cooking, cooking" and so on.
Its establishment occurs either as the delimitor of the state of being the producer of the result, or simply as the delimitor of the word-potency itself.
The cognition of [the meaning] such as "being an operation that brings about a result" arises from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not through verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).
For this very reason, even the result itself is not cognized by the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*).
This is because it will be established that the meaning of [the accusative] is "objecthood" (*karmatva*) in the form of an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).

And the delimitor of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is the nature of each respective verbal root (*dhātutva*). Furthermore, the result such as "cooking-ness" (*pākatva*) consists only in an activity that produces softening (*viklitti*), and not even by way of such [auxiliary] actions as effort (*yatna*). This is because, in expressions such as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), effort and the like are perceived as distinct from the act of cooking itself.

Nor does it follow that there is a separate analysis [of the root] because one assumes the capacity (śakti) of the verbal root—when co-uttered with words such as "pot"—to reside solely in the result (phala), for this would involve the fault of postulating multiple capacities or assuming a capacity directed toward an operation (vyāpāra). Furthermore, the cognition of the operation is necessary, lest there arise the undesirable consequence of the cognition that "the village possesses the act of going" (*grāmo gamanavān*).

For this very reason, the meaning of the word *pāka* (cooking) is simply the collection of operations that produce softening (*viklitti*), and not also the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) and so forth that produce it; for since those are analyzed separately, they lack the status of being the primary referent (*paryāptatva*).

For this very reason, the claim that "the meaning of *pacati* is merely conjunction with fire (*tejaḥsaṃyoga*), and not a general operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*)" is also refuted. This is because the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*) is used even when there is no softening of the food, provided there exists a state conducive to conjunction with fire. Therefore, since qualities such as being cooked—which appear as distinct from the act of cooking itself—are observed, when one seeks the cause for their manifestation, it follows by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that they must indeed have the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as their denotative cause.

And in that case, the status of "cooking" and so forth as the qualifier (*prakāratva*) follows precisely from their being the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). Thus, the traditional rule (smṛti) regarding the predominance of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthaprādhānya*) is not restricted [or contradicted]. (Rahasya, pp. 47–49). Furthermore, the prescription of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthavidhāna*) by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is scriptural (*śrauta*), because it is directly expressed by its own word (*svapadopātta*).

Vārttika 2.3.14, p. 593: "The efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is unable to grasp the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) by means of the specific meaning of the verbal root. Vārttika 3.6.16.3, p. 1069: "Even though this [efficient force] is not perceived as distinct from the meaning of the verbal root, nevertheless it is understood in its entirely general form."
For in all cases, such as the act of placing [the pot] on the fire, even the general aspect of activity (*vyāpāra*) is understood through the term "he does" (*karoti*).
(Vārttika 2.3.1.1, p. 382). By the establishment of the existence of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), the establishment of the existence of the prefix-meaning (*upasargārtha*) is sublated.

For the root-meaning is expressed as existence by the suffix through direct audition (*śruti*); whereas the existence of the prefix-meaning is remote and, due to that remoteness of meaning, becomes weaker.

Bhāṣya 10.4.6.1: "The generality of the root-meaning is *bhāvanā*"; this is not incorrect. It is true that there is a generality consisting in the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*), but not in the form of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.

Vārttika 2.3.1.1, p. 382: The view that words such as roots—which are distinct from suffixes—denote only their own essential forms is the theory of "connection of what has been denoted" (*abhihitānvayavāda*). In the suffix, there is the "denotation of what is connected" (*anvitābhidhāna*).

In reality, however, there is no such thing as "expression of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) anywhere. [This is because] the distinction between sentences (*vākyabheda*) is not characterized by [the presence of] verbal roots and so forth. (Vāla., p. 181). The meaning of a verbal root and a prefix is not contradictory, since it is obtainable through the power of expression (*abhidhānasāmarthya*).

*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 7.3.4.136: Even though there is a rule regarding the simultaneous employment of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and its suffix (*pratyaya*), the distinction between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) is established due to the difference in their meanings. *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 776: One view holds that "the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and so forth, as indicated by the verbal root, functions as a qualifier (*prakāratā*) within the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Another view maintains that "only the meaning of the verbal root, when connected with instrumentality and so forth, functions as a qualifier within the productive urge."
Murāri (Bhāṣya, p.):
The status of being an action (*kriyā*) is not established merely by being denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*).

This is because roots such as *gaḍi* (in the sense of "speaking"), *śaki* (in the sense of "capacity"), and *viśi* (in the sense of "a part") are recognized as verbal roots even though they do not denote an action; furthermore, words such as *gandha* and others [denote things] without denoting an action.
The coreferentiality with the verbal root (dhātu-sāmānādhikaraṇya) [is established] because the action resides in the substratum of the grain;
nevertheless, for the most part, verbal roots denote action.

Bhāṣya 3.8.22.44. Section on Grain.
In the Śakvānāmayana sacrifice, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the word "grain" (*dhānya*) found in the original mantra for the scattering of grain, by substituting the word "meat" (*māṃsa*).
[Objection: It might be argued that this is merely a word expressing a quality (*guṇaśabda*).
9|1|1|38 Commentary on the Section:
Or rather thus.
Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), they prescribe: "Thou art grain; satisfy the gods"—with these words, one pours the rice grains into the mortar.

In this regard, there is a doubt concerning the word *dhānya*: does it denote that which is inherent [in the action], or not? What is the prima facie view? This word *dhānya*, which appears like a word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*), should not be one that denotes something inherent.
For the word *dhānya* denotes grain (*dhānya*), but grain itself is not sown.
For the word "grain" (dhānya) indeed applies to that [rice];
when rice grains alone are being sown,
the depositing of grain is performed so that there may be no deficiency in its manifestation.
"Therefore, it need not be modified in the modified sacrifices (vikṛtis).
No, because of the inherent connection (samavāya).
The Commentary states: "This is not so."
For the meaning of the word "grain" (dhānya) is inherently inclusive.
It applies to rice grains through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), because rice is a derivative of grain.

Just as in the cases of the expressions "Śāli rice is eaten at Kāśī" or "Cows are being drunk," since the literal sense (śruti) cannot be maintained, a figurative sense must be postulated; thus, a term based on secondary indication is employed.

Therefore, it expresses that which is inherent; [the rule] "that which is enjoined in the modification" applies. There is a purpose: by way of the commonality of capability, regarding the thirty-six-year sacrifice, this is recited: "On each completed day, he goes hunting for deer; the *tarasa* (flesh) of those deer which he kills there become the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes.
In that case, according to the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), the formula "Thou art grain, prosper the gods" should be employed without modification.
According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), a modification (*ūha*) must be made: "Thou art meat; prosper the gods. [The *Ṭupṭīkā* says: Here an objection is raised regarding the purpose.

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the modified form (*vikāra*)—the rice—is indicated by the word for the archetype (*dhānya*, "grain") through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); here too, in the *Śākyāyanas’ sacrifice*, the extended application (*codaka*) brings forth the meat in the same way (by means of the word for the archetype through secondary indication).

Therefore, it is not the case that meat is indicated by the word "mṛga" through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Rather, in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the purpose is extended by means of the general rule (codaka).
We shall explain in this very [third] section (*pāda*) that sound is not expressive.
And if it is asked why that [meaning] is manifested through an inexpressive word when it is being employed, [the answer is:
in the case of the base form (*prakṛti*), the manifestation of the modification (*vikāra*) was accomplished by some inexpressive word [such as *āman*] associated with the word for grain (*dhānya*).
And that [term for grain] is excluded here by implication; it is not brought forward by the rule of extension (*codaka*).
Nor is there any statement that the modification (*vikāra*) is to be understood through the original model (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, only the word "meat" (*māṃsa*) is to be used [in its place]. (In reality, however, there is no mixing of meat at all.)
Regarding *soma*: it was stated that this should be considered as being for the purpose of seasoning the meat (*māṃsa*).

However, in reality, since the seasoning is for the purpose of grinding (*peṣaṇa*), and the meat is also for the purpose of grinding, it should be understood that both the seasoning and its mantra are excluded. Vi— "There is no modification (*ūha*), or rather, the word for grain (*dhānya*) is not inapplicable."
Inference (*ūha*) arises from the connection of this [word] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In the case of "The cows are being drunk," although there is an absence of primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*), people describe the word as having a meaning that is indeed inherent; however, by indicating milk through the word "cow" (*gośabda*), they understand the very meaning that is inherent [in the context]. Thus it is.
Bhāṭṭa: Or rather, it is thus.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra "dhānyam asi dhinuhi devān" is revealed. And therein, the word *dhānya* refers to the receptacle of grain [in the phrase] "dhānyam asi."
By the statement, "The lord of the rice-grains is in the mortar," [the mantra] is enjoined with respect to the sin related to the rice-grains.

In that context, the word *dhānya* (grain) denotes a substance possessing husks; when it is employed in the state of being rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), it serves for the purpose of praise through the superimposition (*āropa*) of "grain-ness. Just like words such as *Savitṛ*, its meaning is not literally inherent (*asamavetārtha*). Therefore, it should be employed even in the case of the month by means of that same superimposition.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: because in the sentence "rice is eaten" (*śālayo bhujyante*), there is the use of a word denoting the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the effect, the application of the definition [of *samaveta*] is appropriate; and because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the agenthood implied by the word "itself" (*asi*)—which refers to rice—the word "grain" (*dhānya*) refers to rice through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and thus its meaning is indeed inherent (*samaveta*).

Now, even if the meaning is thus inherent, since the use of the word "grain" can be justified through metaphorical indication even in the case of a month (*māsa*), there would be no necessity [for the rule].

Because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the word "grain" (*dhānya*) has rice as its essence, whereas in the ectype (*vikṛti*), it somehow serves as a basis for inference (*ūha*)—as in the case of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth—with meat as its essence; or because, even if that were not the case, the word "meat" (*māṃsa*) functions as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) by virtue of being a "grain-word" (*dhānyapada*).

For just as in the archetype, since the mantra is applied by the indicative power (*liṅga*) and the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) such that the word "Agni" must manifest the deity who is the recipient of the *apūrva* through its primary denotative power (*śakti*), in the ectype there is no introduction of another word, because the word "Agni" itself would necessarily manifest the aforementioned deity through its primary denotative power in relation to the Agni-deity.
Since there is a possible course [of action], it would result in the adoption of the original mode of operation; furthermore, there is no evidence for such a sublation.
Rather, that [application] pertains only to another deity.

For in that case, it is impossible to manifest that [deity] through the word "Agni" by means of its primary power, because in the archetype (prakṛti), there exists the intention to employ the term in its original sense.

Furthermore, since in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) the status of being the referent of the word "Agni" is understood through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) itself—due to its being an unaccomplished act and because it serves as the primary means [of the rite]—the word "Agni" cannot manifest that meaning without recourse to secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, in that case, when the original power [of the word] is to be set aside, the only resort is the introduction of another word, such as "Sūrya.
This does not apply, however, to the deity Agni in the modified sacrifice.

If it is argued: "In the same way, by means of the word 'grain' (*dhānya*), through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), one should manifest the original substance to be offered; thus, because the application of the mantra occurs even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) via a figurative capacity (*gauṇa-sāmarthya*) based on a direct statement (*śruti*), and because the word 'grain' is extended (*atideśa*) to the meat by way of its functional role (*upakāra-pṛṣṭha-bhāva*) and its generic nature (*tajjātīyatva*), it is logical for the meat to be manifested by the word 'grain' itself without contradiction, so there is no need to insert another word. [This is the opponent's position.]

It is true that, following upon the assistance consisting in the manifestation of the archetypal form (*prākṛta*), there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the archetypal mode of functioning; and following upon that, there is an extension of the word-meaning, such as the status of being the referent of the words "Agni" and so forth. However, in this case of the extension of the function, since the manifestation follows upon that [extension], it would be possible for the word to manifest [the meaning] even through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*); consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that no other word need be introduced. Nevertheless, it is the archetypal status residing in the archetypal word that is extended to the modification, and not merely the mode of functioning, because there is a lack of evidence [for the latter].

Therefore, even though there is a sublation (*bādha*) of both the original word and its original function in the *saurya* sacrifice, this occurs precisely through the restriction to the word "Sūrya" in accordance with the other words of the mantra. Consequently, since the original [word] is characterized by a relationship consisting of the natural connection between the material (*prakṛti*) and the form (*rūpa*), and because there is no evidence for assuming a different type of relationship when that original one is sublated, the word "meat" (*māṃsa*) is introduced in place of the word "grain" (*dhānya*)— which would otherwise necessarily be sublated— solely in accordance with the other words of the mantra and the requirement of the function of manifesting meat.

For this very reason, even when there is no expectancy for a word denoting the archetype (prakṛti), another word cannot be introduced through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) when it is possible to introduce a word that is directly expressive (śakta). This is because such an introduction would be improper. Therefore, in the case of the statement, "The Savanīya cakes are made of other substances," when the addition of meat is being performed during the month, the formula "Thou art meat" (māṃsam asi) must be modified accordingly.
And this is established by the *kṛtvācintā* [hypothetical consideration]:

because in the third [section] (3.8.23, Mādhava), it has been settled that the injunction regarding *tarasa* is made solely on the basis of its being the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) with reference to the *savanīya* [animal];
or even if it were the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the *puroḍāśa*, the act of pouring (*adhivāpa*) would be set aside there due to the sublation by the purpose, just as in the case of the *caru*.

This has been established in detail in the *Kaustubha* on the second [section], under the sūtra "But in the case of the measure of dharma, there would be ritual action" (2.1.9), following the refutation of the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*.

And [the fire] must be maintained because it is for the sake of another.
