Vārttika 2.1.31, p. 476. There would be a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) across different recensional branches (*śākhā*) due to the following reasons: difference in name, form, specific qualities, repetition, censure, incapacity, mention of completion, expiation, and the observation of logical principles.
In this context, examples from other recensions include the Kāṭhaka, the Kāṇvaka, the Paippalādaka, and so forth.
Regarding these, there is a doubt: when any rite such as the Agnihotra is heard of in one recension, is it rendered redundant (mriyate) when it is heard again in another recension, or is it not?
Having previously established the difference in performance (*prayoga-bheda*), the present section provides an exception to that difference.
In this matter, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows:
by the principle that "in a single context, a repeated mention must serve to qualify [the action]," it has already been established that there is a difference between ritual acts due to repetition;
and that repetition, moreover, is indeed indistinguishable [in both cases].

Furthermore, a repetition in another recension (śākhā) cannot be for the sake of a different object, such as a subordinate element (guṇa) or a fruit (phala). Therefore, it must be the action itself that is enjoined; and since there is no injunction of what has already been enjoined, it is indeed a distinct action (karmāntara).

Nor should it be said that even if the ritual action (*karman*) is one and the same, the repetition of its mention in different recensional branches (*śākhā*) is purposeful only by way of specifying details such as the alms-begging (*mikṣā*) and so forth, and thus [the action] is not distinct on account of the name;
for there is no evidence for a rule that restricts [the application of a rite] to each individual branch.

Although the singular number attached to "one's own Veda" (*svādhyāya*) is heard in the injunction "one should study one's own Veda," and the word *svādhyāya* denotes one's own specific recensional branch (*śākhā*), nevertheless, since the Veda—already established as being for the purpose of knowing the meaning—is the object (*uddeśya*) of the injunction regarding its refinement through study, and because a qualification of the object (such as "he cleanses the cup") is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), it is not contradictory for a single person to study multiple recensional branches.

Furthermore, if the study of only one branch (*śākhā*) were mandatory for a single individual, then the study of branches belonging to other Vedas would not be attained. And that being the case, [the injunction] would be contradicted: "One should enter the householder stage of life having studied a Veda or a branch of another Veda, according to the sequence, provided the method of transmission (*tantra*) has not been impaired."
This is according to the principle stated in *Manu* 3.2.
Therefore, because the repetition (*punaḥśruti*) serves a different purpose, the action must indeed be distinct due to repetition.

Furthermore, where even within a single recensional branch (*śākhā*), there is a distinction between actions due to their being enjoined toward a non-optional result—since they are not to be adopted [as part of a prior context]—then, all the more so in other branches, there is a difference of action based on "separation of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*), because the actions are enjoined toward a result that is not to be adopted due to the complete interruption of the mental impression (*buddhiviccheda*).

Likewise, there is a distinction based on the difference in the names of the rituals, such as the *Kāṭhaka* and others, because it is illogical for multiple words to apply to one and the same object. Similarly, there is a distinction based on the qualities [of the ritual]. In one school (*śālā*), they prescribe the *Āgnīṣomīya* cake as having eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla*), while in another, they prescribe it as having twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*).
As it has been said: "Because of the form.
Likewise, among those studying the *Kārīrī* passage, the followers of the Taittirīya school practice eating from the ground, while others do not.
As it has been said: "Because of the distinction in dharma."
Likewise, in one [text] there is a censure of the *udita* oblation, while in another there is a censure of the *anudita* oblation.
This has been stated: "Because of the words of censure."

Likewise, having resolved upon various duties for each individual hall (*pratiśālam*), no one is able to perform them all due to their mutual contradiction; however, when there is a distinction of actions (*karmabheda*), one is able to do so.
Thus it has been said: "And because of incapacity.

Similarly, some authorities prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the omission of the pre-dawn oblation (*anudita-homa*), while others prescribe it for the omission of the post-dawn oblation (*udita-homa*).
Thus it has been said: "Because of the specific nature of the expiation.
Therefore, in all these cases, because of mutual contradiction, there is a distinction [of rites] where the injunctions are otherwise impossible.

Consequently, even due to repetition, a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), connection with other qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth, as well as other indicative marks (*liṅga*) and the like, there is indeed a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*) in other scriptural traditions.
This being the case, we reply:
"Or rather, it is one [action], because there is no difference in its connection, form, injunction, and name.
This is the intended meaning.
This would indeed be so, were it not for the identity of the ritual action (*karman*) established here through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

For instance, even in another scriptural text (*śāstra*), there is the same name, the same substance and deity, the same qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, the same result, and the same injunction regarding the object of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) delimited by the meaning of the verbal root.

Thus, since the identity of the ritual action is established on the basis of recognition—even if some slight difference or deficiency is perceived—the unity established by recognition is not discarded, just as when a cow’s testicles have grown back or its tail has been cut off, its identity as the same animal is not revoked.

As it has been said: "Because of recognition everywhere through name, form, quality, and so forth, the cognition that [the Veda] is a single action does not depart from the scripture" (Vākya-kāṇḍa, p. 635).
And there is no other cause for differentiation.
But has it not been said that practice itself is the means of valid cognition for differentiation?
Not so.
For each individual scripture, denoted by the term *svādhyāya*, is established for every person and validated by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*).

Since [the ritual action] is understood as being part of a single syntactical unit with that which has become authoritative, the action differs according to the repetition [of the specific recension].
Furthermore, the textual passage belonging to both branches (*śākhā*) is not authoritative for a single person, such that [the action] would have to differ [merely] to avoid redundancy.
As it has been said: "By the term *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic study), one's own branch [of the Veda] is understood;
and since the actions have the same purpose, there will be an option (*vikalpa*) among them when the ritual action is one and the same" (Vārttika, p. 635).

But surely it has been stated that, by implication—since the purpose [of the Veda] is the knowledge of its meaning—the injunction regarding the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of study, directed toward the *svādhyāya* (one's own recitation) which is already established for that purpose, intends the single [Vedic] self.
Therefore, how can it be said that another branch (*śākhā*) lacks authority with respect to a single person?

This would indeed be so if the determination of the *svādhyāya*'s purpose were made prior to the injunction of study; however, according to worldly usage, there is merely the ascertainment of its capacity.

Furthermore, that the dependence of the study injunction (*adhyayanavidhi*) on the intent toward recitation determines its orientation toward the meaning has already been explained in detail in the section concerning the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Thus, although it is possible to determine [the meaning] by following worldly convention, there is an injunction for the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of study directed toward the Vedic text (*svādhyāya*), which is functionally assigned to ensure that the study has the purpose of conveying meaning—this being necessary because the intention of the utterance would otherwise be absent. However, since the knowledge of meaning is employed as a result of the study precisely through the single status of the Vedic text as the object of action, the Vedic text itself is also something to be taken up (*upādeya*). Therefore, the unity inherent in that [text] is indeed intended; consequently, only a single branch (*śākhā*) is authoritative for a single student, and thus there is no difference in ritual acts (*karma*) due to repetition.
The study of the branches (*śākhā*) belonging to other Vedas, however, occurs solely by virtue of scriptural injunction.

Nor does it follow from this that there would be a plurality of Vedas due to the repeated performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*—which are like the branches of other Vedas—because the distinction [between them] is all the more clearly understood through injunctions that establish their combination (*samuccaya*). For instance, when they are taken up for the sake of understanding the ritual, they are combined; thus, there is a single performance of the rite.

The distinction of the three Vedas here is for the purpose of their coexistence; for there is no possibility of their being combined within a single ritual action due to the difference between the Vedas.
By this, it is established that even differences in context and subordinate qualities (guṇas) function as differentiators.
As for names such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth, they do not pertain to the ritual action itself, but rather originate from the act of recitation, meaning "that which was proclaimed by Kaṭha."

And it is not action that is being denoted; what then? It is the *grantha* (the text) itself. Or, even if it were the name of an action, nevertheless, a name is indicative [of its referent] only when it is connected with its origin.
As it has been said: "A name [is determined] by connection with its origin."
And this [difference] is not such as to cause a division of the ritual action (*karma*).

As for the indications [of difference], they will be explained through the sequence of the Sūtras, Bhāṣyas, and Vārtikas in a manner that does not contradict the unity of the ritual action. Thus it has been said: "Therefore, according to the view that 'it is that very same [action],' the ritual action is not in any way considered different across the various Śākhās."
"There is no seventh cause other than these; rather, the establishment of the distinction [of the self] is through those [means] already mentioned. (Vākya-pada, p. 646).
The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is the performance of rituals based on knowledge established in accordance with the scriptures;
however, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is the performance of all that is enjoined by the scriptures.

As for the Sūtra, its meaning is: "It is indeed one [rite], because of the connection with the fruit of the action, and because there is no distinction among the injunctions, names, and so forth, due to the absence of difference in substance and deity, and because the recognition is clear."

*Tautā*. Because of repetition, censure, incapacity, statements of completion, expiation, and the observation of another purpose, there would be a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*) in other recensional branches (*śākhā*).

By means of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the six means of proof that differentiate ritual actions—namely, difference of word, repetition, number, connection, and difference of context—have been stated. However, in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*), having raised certain other grounds for differentiation, he refutes them.
In this regard, the following is the sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), which investigates other reasons for differentiation:
"There, due to the difference in names, there is a difference in ritual acts;
the *Kāṭhaka* is one, and the *Kālāpaka* is another."

Therefore, the *kāṭhaka* Agnihotra—that which is declared in the Kaṭha recension—must be distinct from the Agnihotra of the Kālāpaka school. If they were one and the same, why would there be an injunction for both? Because of the difference in form, there is a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*).
In one recension they prescribe the cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Soma (Agnīṣomīya), while in another they prescribe it on twelve potsherds.
Thus, there is a difference of ritual action due to its different forms;
there is a difference of ritual action due to a specific characteristic of the property.

The Taittirīyas, reciting such Kārīrīṣṭi mantras as "O great darkness, [this is] your great vigor," and following the Bodhāyana-sūtra, practice eating on the ground; however, other Taittirīyas, though reciting the same Kārīrīṣṭi mantras, do not practice eating on the ground.
Therefore, due to such specific differences in dharma—that is, due to a difference in dharma—the ritual action (*karman*) also differs.
There is a distinction of rituals due to repetition.
The Agnihotra and other rituals are prescribed for every house;
however, if there were only one ritual, this repetition in every house would not be justified.

Therefore, the distinction between ritual acts is established through repetition and through reiteration; it is also established through censure. For instance, when the injunction "the oblation should be offered at sunrise" has been introduced, the offering at non-sunrise [is mentioned as a distinct act].

The meaning is that falsehood is incurred when one says, "Sūrya is the light, the light is Sūrya, svāhā," before the sun has risen, as stated in the passage: "Those who offer the Agnihotra before sunrise speak untruth every morning; they proclaim what is to be proclaimed by day while not yet being day; for them, Sūrya is the light. Thus, the recitation performed while the sun has not yet risen results in falsehood.

However, in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), in the context of introducing the offering after sunrise, the offering before sunrise is censured: "If one were to offer the morning oblation when the sun has risen, it would be as if they were to bring [the food] for their own consumption after having already served a guest. This is what is meant here.
This is its meaning: "Verily, the sun enters into fire at evening;
verily, fire does not ascend the rising sun"—this was stated previously.
Therefore, the sun has entered into the fire and dwells in the house of the sacrificer during the night.

But when [the sun] has risen, one goes away leaving the fire behind. Consequently, it becomes like this: as if food were offered to a guest who has turned his face away and gone far from the house; or as if food were to be given to an empty dwelling, that is, to an empty guest-house—where the fourth case endings are used for the sake of the conventional expression—or rather, as if the guest were to give to a mere empty, inanimate house; such is the nature of that offering made after sunrise.
Thus, because both are censured, the offerings made at sunrise and those made before sunrise are distinct.
In this way, the difference between the rites is established through censure.
Due to incapacity, there is a division of rituals.
A person lacks the capacity to combine, within a single ritual, the various distinct mantras prescribed in the different Vedic branches (*vedaśākhā*);
however, such a combination is possible to some extent when the rituals are separate.
There is a distinction of ritual acts based on the difference in the statements of completion.
In the Maitrāyaṇī Śākhā, within the collection of mantras for the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), certain specific mantras for ascending the sacrificial mound called *anyārohas* are recited;
however, those mantras do not exist in some other Śākhās.
In this regard, the students and ritualists explain as follows: "Among the Maitrāyaṇīyas, the fire-altar is completed in the *anyāroha* rites, whereas for others, it is completed elsewhere.
For this reason also, there is a difference in the rituals (*karmabheda*). Furthermore, there is a difference in the rituals due to the difference in expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).

Some authorities prescribe an expiation for the transgression of offering after sunrise, based on such passages as, "If the sun should rise while one's Agnihotra has not yet been offered," and so forth;
and this expiation is indeed accepted even in the case of offering before sunrise.
Moreover, when the action is one and the same, an increase in both ways is not possible;
therefore, there is a difference in the actions.
Now, [we shall consider] how the perception of another purpose serves as a differentiator of actions.

For example, it is heard in a certain branch of the *dvādaśāha-sattra*: "If they should approach this very [sacrifice] characterized by the *bṛhat-sāman* before the initiations, for their *rathaṃtara* has already been approached; but if they should approach one characterized by the *rathaṃtara-sāman* before the initiations...
Thus it is said.

If they were previously initiated— that is, if they have already undergone initiation and performed their first *soma* sacrifice— they should resort to this very *Atirātra* with the *Bṛhat* *sāman*, because in their first *soma* sacrifice, the *Rathaṃtara* was employed. But if they are uninitiated— that is, if they have not yet performed their first *soma* sacrifice— then they should resort to the one with the *Rathaṃtara* *sāman*.

Because of the restrictive rule: "One should not perform the *bṛhatsāman* sacrifice after having prescribed the *rathaṃtarasāman*," this very statement regarding the twelve-day sacrificial session (*dvādaśāhasatra*)—even for those who have not performed the first *soma* sacrifice—indicates a difference in ritual action across the various recensions (*śākhā*).
Now follows the second [point], the observation of another purpose.

In the *Taittirīyaka*, regarding the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), it is heard: "If one were to erect [the posts] level with the wings [of the altar], he would attain a lesser sacrificial power (*yaśakratu*), and his offspring would become more wretched. He erects them level with the altar (*vedisaṃmitāṃ*); thus he attains a greater sacrificial power, and his offspring does not become more wretched."

The wing of the altar for the piling of the fire—having divided that wing into ten parts, if one were to arrange a row of eleven sacrificial posts with the *agniṣṭha* post in the middle and five posts on each side—that would result in a smaller and more insignificant sacrifice; moreover, the offspring of this sacrificer becomes more wretched and poorer than himself.

Therefore, having divided the space measured from the altar (vedisaṃmita) up to the front part of the Agnīdhra’s shed into ten equal parts, one should set up the eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī) as before; by this, the superiority of the sacrifice and so forth is established.

This censure of the [measurement] corresponding to the wing (pakṣasaṃmitā) and the praise of the measurement corresponding to the altar (vedisaṃmitā) indicates a difference in ritual action (karmabheda) according to other recensions (śākhāntara).
Now, the third [point], the observation of another purpose: the Jyoti-...

Regarding the *ṣṭomātirātra*, it is stated in one scripture, "Two *virāj*s of the *saṃstuta* [verses] remain over," whereas in another scripture it is heard, "Three *virāj*s of the *saṃstuta* [verses] remain over.
The term *saṃstuta* refers to the hymns (*stotra*).
As for the term *virāj*, each individual group of ten [syllables] is taken as a unit.
Thus, this excess of two or three [sacrificers] occurs as a single instance of a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) in other treatises.

Now follows the fourth [reason], the observation of another purpose (*anyārthadarśana*): it is heard in the *Sārasvata Satra*, "Those who offer the *puroḍāśa* fast; those who offer the *sānnāyya* keep the calves.

Those sacrificers who are *puroḍāśins* are those who, having not yet performed the first *Soma* sacrifice, have designated the *Darśa* sacrifice as having only the *aindrāmna-puroḍāśa* as its substance.
However, those who perform the *sānnāyya* sacrifice and have already performed their first *soma* sacrifice keep the calves near their mothers and do not let them go for milking.
This very observation of the *Sārasvata-sattra* even among those who have not performed their first *soma* sacrifice leads one to understand a distinction between ritual acts.

Now, regarding the fifth [point]: in one recensional school (*śālā*), it is heard in the *Upahavya* Soma sacrifice that "it is an *agniṣṭoma* with the *rathantara* melody, and a dark-brown horse is the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*); however, in another scriptural tradition (*śāstrāntara*), it is heard that "the *Upahavya* is an *ukthya* with the *bṛhat* melody, and a white horse is the sacrificial fee.
This distinction is only logical if there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karma*) due to the difference in recensional schools, not if there is no difference in the acts.
Thus, by means of reasons such as the name and so forth, there would be a difference between the rituals taught in various distinct recensional schools.
Or rather, [the action is] one, because there is no difference in its conjunction, form, injunction, and name.
This refutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is a distinction among rituals such as the *agnihotra* due to differences in name, form, and specific properties;
for despite differences in name and so forth, there is no distinction of the ritual action across different recensions (*śākhā*).

However, the ritual action (*karman*) is one and the same, being confirmed by all Vedic branches (*sarvaśākhāpratyaya*) and confirmed by all Brahmins (*sarvabrāhmaṇapratyaya*), because there is no difference—and thus no distinction—in its connection (*saṃyoga*), its form (*rūpa*), its injunction (*codanā*), and its name (*ākhyā*).
Among these, "connection" refers to the purpose (*prayojana*):
whatever fruit, namely heaven (*svarga*), is prescribed for the Agnihotra rite in one branch, that very same fruit is indicated in another branch as well.
Thus, because they possess a single result, it is understood that the Agnihotra rite is one and the same across all recensional branches (*śākhā*).
Likewise, despite the difference in recensional branches, there is no distinction in the ritual form consisting of the Soma sacrifice dedicated to Indra as its deity.

Similarly, the injunction (*codanā*)—which consists of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) whose nature is the meaning of the verbal root in the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—is identical across all recensional branches.

Furthermore, there is no distinction in the designation "Jyotiṣṭoma" and so forth, even when there is a difference between Vedic schools (śākhā). Therefore, since there is no difference in the connection, the form, the injunction, or the name, there is no difference in the rite of Agnihotra despite the difference between Vedic schools.
In this way, the non-difference of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites is also to be understood.
Thus, the ritual action is one and the same as recognized across all recensional branches (śākhās).
It cannot be differentiated by name, because a name serves merely as a designation for the injunction.

Regarding what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that there is a difference in ritual acts due to differences in names such as *Kāṭhaka*, *Kālāpaka*, and so forth—the proponent of the established conclusion says:

even with such a different name, there would be no difference in the ritual act, because it is not a designation of an injunction (*codanā*). An injunction is the sentence that originates the ritual act.
The designation pertaining to that [action] is the name, which is a designation of an injunction;
because names such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth do not exist in that manner [as inherent properties of the action].
A name occurring within the originative injunction differentiates the ritual act.

However, the designation "Kāṭhaka" and so forth does not occur within the original injunction (utpattivākya); therefore, it is unable to differentiate the ritual action. Thus, there is no differentiation of the ritual action by means of names such as "Kāṭhaka."
And there would be a single ritual action for all [the schools].
He states another reason why there is no difference in ritual action based on names such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth:
if difference were to arise from a difference in words, then identity of ritual action would follow from the identity of the word.
Furthermore, there would result a single ritual unity for all the rites—Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and Jyotiṣṭoma—located within the Kāṭhaka section;
and that is undesirable.
Moreover, the designation [of the name] is something produced.

Regarding the point that there is no difference in the ritual action (*karma*) due to differences in names such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) states another reason:
the designation "Kāṭhaka" and others is artificial and modern;
for the name "Kāṭhaka" has been in use only from the time onward when the speech of a particular person was first composed.
Furthermore, it is not possible to effect a distinction among beginningless actions by means of something artificial;
therefore, there is no distinction based on name.
Moreover, they are identical.
Regarding the statement that "there is a difference in ritual action due to a difference in form," the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) offers this reply:

even if there is unity [of the deity], and even though it exists at the time of the ritual, the subsequent argument stated by the opponent as a cause for the difference in action is possible. For although it is a single ritual action, according to the scriptural injunction, just as in the case of rice and barley, the eleven and twelve potsherds for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are established as alternatives.

Therefore, there is no difference in the ritual action (*karma*) due to a difference in form. Regarding the statement made by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) that "there is a difference in the ritual action because of specific differences in the rules (*dharma*), such as the [use of] ground and food in the case of knowledge (*vidyā*)," the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) states the following reply.

The *Dharmaśāstra* that prescribes eating on the ground and other such rules during the study of the *Kārīrī* passages pertains to the discipline of learning (*vidyā*), not to ritual action (*karman*).
This is a rule of study, not a rule of ritual performance.

Therefore, a distinction between ritual acts cannot be established on that basis. Regarding the statement that "repetition constitutes a distinction between ritual acts," as in the case of the *āgneya* [offering], the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) offers this reply.

The repetition—meaning the re-statement in another recensional branch (śākhā) of a rite such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which has already been prescribed with its constituent parts in one branch—is not a cause for the differentiation of the rite, even though it exists, just like the case of the Āgneya. Just as the repetition "That which is the Āgneya on eight potsherds at the new moon" is not a cause for the differentiation of the rite because it is equal to the Aindrāgna, so it is here.
Or rather, there is no difference in the statement because there is no distinction in the connection with the Vedic revelation (śruti).

Regarding what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that there is a division of ritual acts due to repetition—the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) offers a reply by means of another argument.
The word "vā" signifies an alternative sense. "Not a dual expression" means that it is certainly not a dual number.
That is not a tautology at all.
Tautology would occur if one were to speak repeatedly to the same person;
however, when speaking again to a different person, it is certainly not what is called a tautology.

Because there is no distinction in the connection with the revealed texts (*śruti-saṃyoga*), that is, because each respective branch of the Veda is connected with different persons; and because this connection with the revealed texts— namely, the connection of each specific branch with different persons— is not a case of distinction [in the sense of redundancy], therefore, the teaching of rites such as the *agnihotra* in those various branches is addressed to different persons, and thus it is neither a dual expression (*dvivacana*), nor a double statement (*dvirukti*), nor a tautology (*punarukti*).
Therefore, there is no differentiation of the ritual action (*karmabheda*) due to such a repetition, because it does not belong to the sentence (*vākyāsamavāyāt*).
Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "In this interval, the eighth sūtra of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) is: 'Because it does not belong to the sentence.'"
It should be explained in this way: "The sentence of another hall does not coincide within a single person.
And thus, because the sentence and the sentence of another hall do not coincide within a single person, there is an absence of connection; consequently, there is no tautology.
Therefore, since there is indeed an absence of tautology, that which was asserted by the proponent—that there is a distinction between rituals due to tautology—is refuted from its very foundation.

And [the ritual action is one] because of the non-proximity of the constituent parts (*artha*). That which is sought after by the principal [action] is the "constituent part" (*artha*), namely the section on subsidiaries (*aṅgakāṇḍa*).

Since there is no proximity—that is, an absence of proximity—of that entire section on subsidiaries within a single recensional branch (*śākhā*), and because only certain subsidiaries are prescribed in each individual branch, it is said that a single ritual action is expressed when all the branches are combined; thus, the ritual action is one, as it is recognized through all the branches (*sarvaśākhāpratyaya*).
Thus, in the established doctrine (siddhānta), this sūtra provides another reason;
or rather, the sūtra is intended solely for the purpose of avoiding tautology.

"In that case, indeed, there would be a redundancy where the previously stated meaning is already present for that very same person; however, since there is no such presence here for one who belongs to another recension (śākhā), it is not redundant," so says the Vārttika. Furthermore, it is not taught with reference to a single individual.
The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) has stated that because even a single ritual action is repeated across different recensional branches (*śākhā-bheda*), there must be a difference in the ritual; the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) refutes this by means of another argument:
the ritual actions such as the *agnihotra* are not enjoined or prescribed for only a single person.

However, with respect to the mere object [of the injunction], that which is prescribed in all recensional branches (*śākhā*) applies to a single person. In that case, since one person hears [the same injunction] in multiple recensions, there would be a repetition; and because the purpose is identical when the action is distinct, a combination (*samuccaya*) is impossible, so there would have to be an option (*vikalpa*). Therefore, it is better to maintain the identity of the action through recognition, and to hold that the restriction to specific persons belongs to the recensions themselves. Since it is impossible for a single person to study multiple recensions, there is no redundancy.
And the inquiry [regarding the ritual] is like that regarding completion;
this sūtra is intended precisely to refute the statement of completion as a reason for the differentiation of rituals.
For indeed, a single ritual, complete with its limbs and sub-limbs, is not recited in each individual śākhā.
In some places certain limbs [of the ritual] are recited, while in others they are fewer or more;
wherever a rite is recited in its entirety, the performance of that rite is completed within that very branch.
Furthermore, the formal inquiries and instructions take the form: "Our ritual is completed here."
In this regard, it occurs as follows:
one should not conclude that the ritual action is exactly of that extent merely because of that much [text].
For in the *Aitareyaka*, the *hotṛ* and *devasū* recitations belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) are mentioned, but not those of the *maitrāvaruṇa* and the others.
Nor is it proper to say that on that account the *śākhās* (branches) of Maitrāvaruṇa and others do not exist at all.
Thus, just as the completion [of a rite] is indefinite, so too the inquiry (*saṃpraśna*) is likewise indefinite; this follows from the sequence [of the argument].
In every respect, it can be determined that, like the completion, the inquiry also does not cause a division of the ritual action (*karma*).
Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: the word division is *asamāpitaḥ*.
(And it is not taught for the sake of a single [person], as in the case of "completion" (*samāptivat*); thus, even by eliding the vowel *a* in the *susaṃhitā*, a word division is possible.
Thus says the *Sudhā*.

Even though there is oneness [of the sacrifice], the subsequent statements regarding censure (*nindā*), incapacity (*aśakti*), and completion (*samāpti*) are not proofs for a difference in action, as the Siddhāntin states.

Regarding those factors cited by the Pūrvapakṣin as indicators of a difference in action, the Siddhāntin argues that among them— censure, incapacity, and the triad [of completion]— the first two are common to both [types of action] and thus do not establish a difference.

Furthermore, the three factors—censure (*nindā*), incapacity (*aśakti*), and a statement of completion (*samāptivacana*)—which are recited later with reference to subsequent [rites], are applicable even when the ritual action (*karman*) is one and the same; thus, they do not establish a difference [between rites].
To explain: censure is not employed for the sake of censuring that which is censured; rather, it is for the purpose of praising something other than the censured.
In that case, the prohibition of the censured is not understood, but rather the injunction for the other.
In that regard, for a single morning *agnihotra* oblation, two times are prescribed: before sunrise and after [sunrise].
These two are treated as alternatives (*vikalpyete*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Likewise, even within a single Veda, those who are incapable lack the power to collect all the prescribed injunctions that they do not know;
however, those who are capable possess the power to collect even additional injunctions brought from all the various recensions (*śākhās*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction even when the ritual action is one and the same.
Likewise, in a single ritual action, the word "completion" (*samāpti*) is employed with reference to the completion of a certain portion of the matter;
for example, in the context of the *ācārya-veda* or the *hautra*, one says, "the *agnihotra* is completed.
Yet, by that much alone, the entire *agnihotra* does not become completed.
Regarding the statement that "by means of the occasion for expiation"—

that is, by means of the transgression of the prescribed times for the *udita* (sunrise) and *anudita* (pre-dawn) offerings— the distinction between separate acts (*karmabheda*) is established— and as to what the rebuttal to that is:
this is the end of the introductory discussion (*ābhāṣānta*) of the Sūtra.
Alternatively, there will be an expiation based on the cause or a specific characteristic of that cause;
yet by that much, the distinction of separate acts is not established, since it is possible even when there is unity of the act.
Thus, this is a sūtra providing a general rebuttal.
Alternatively, by way of a formal application (*niyoga*),

the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) states a specific refutation of the reason for expiation (*prāyaścitta-hetu*)— which was cited in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) as a proof for the difference between ritual acts (*karma-bheda*).
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to distinguish this specific rebuttal from the general one previously mentioned.

When there is a mandatory rule (*niyoga*) regarding the performance of optional items, the performance must proceed by determining one or the other. Thus, if one has determined "I shall offer the oblation when the sun has risen" and has commenced the morning *Agnihotra* before sunrise, a fault occurs. Likewise, if one has commenced with the intention "I shall offer when the sun has not yet risen" but then performs the oblation after sunrise, a fault likewise occurs. In both these cases, the prescription of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is justified even though the ritual action (*karman*) remains the same.
Therefore, because of the prescription of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), there is no division of the ritual action (*karmabheda*).
Its completion is understood as being as before, just as it was known [in the case of a single performance].
In the sūtra (21), “Even though there is oneness, the subsequent [acts]...,” the term "subsequent" (*parāṇi*) was introduced generally as things to be avoided.
By means of the method of "looking back" (*vihāvalokita*), he further establishes the conclusion.

The conclusion consists of the statement regarding the attainment of the *anvārohaṇa* rites of the Maitrāyaṇīyas; it is understood as referring to that entire collection of ritual items which, as far as they are known, are traditionally taught (*āmnāta*) in that particular school (*śālā*). This is because the employment of words is preceded by intention (*tātparya*), just as in previous cases.
And the intended meaning (*tātparya*) here is the purpose of completing the entire collection of ritual items prescribed for that particular hall.
Thus, there is no contradiction even though the action is one and the same.

In the rule "And the completion [is indicated] by the *saṃpraiṣa*" (20), the evidence for the oneness of the action was established; here, however, the contradiction regarding the oneness of the action is resolved—therefore, there is no tautology.

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) itself is non-distinctive because it applies as a remainder to all [cases]; for there is no injunction of ritual action (*karmacodanā*) therein. Therefore, the designation of "eating" (*āhāra*) should apply to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
He refutes the first observation of the indicative mark stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*):

as for the indicative mark stated—that even one who has not performed the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice [may do so] just like the twelve-day sacrificial session (*sattra*)—that too is non-distinctive; nevertheless, it remains untenable.

Why? Because it is supplementary to all [Jyotiṣṭomas]; for in the Tāṇḍaka, the *prāyaścitti* (expiatory rite) is prescribed by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of all Jyotiṣṭomas found in every recensional branch (*śākhā*).
Indeed, there is no other injunction (*codanā*) for a Jyotiṣṭoma present in that Tāṇḍaka which would cause the *prāyaścitti* to apply specifically to only that particular Jyotiṣṭoma.

Therefore, even under the view that there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*), because it would contradict the observation of the first undesirable [periods] in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, one must supply the words "if they have not previously sacrificed with the *dvādaśāha*" and "if they have not previously sacrificed with the *dvādaśāha*" in order to avoid that contradiction. Thus, in both alternatives, there would be a designation of the *āhāra* (the preparatory rite) as an adjunct (*anubandha*) of the *dvādaśāha*. Furthermore, since the substances are not specifically enjoined, there would be a lack of restriction among the injunctions; however, [the restriction] would be established by the specific direction. Therefore, it must be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*). [The author] now refutes the second [argument regarding] the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).

Since the measurement equal to the altar (*vedisammitatva*) is not enjoined when the substance is the object of the statement, and because there is an absence of an injunction [for it], while the measurement equal to the sacrificial post (*pakṣasammitatva*) is established as an implied injunction (*ārthika*), the injunction of being equal to the altar would be merely traditional (*smṛtika*); thus, there would be a lack of fixed determination among the injunctions—this is the potential indicative power (*liṅ*).

[Objection: But then, what scope remains for the sentence concerning the space between the two protective cords (*rakṣāttarāla*)? [Reply: To this he says: "On account of the specific direction (*nirdeśa*), since it is not inclusive (*anabhividhya*), it should be restricted to that which is produced by the *sarvastoma* and other [rites], because of the direction regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth.
In that case, that sentence possesses completeness (*sākalya*).

Therefore, since the measurements equal to the altar and equal to the rear interval have been prescribed, the measurement equal to the wing would be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*), like the statement "not in the intermediate space, not in heaven.
Because of the prohibition of what has been prescribed, there would be an excess in one alternative case.
[The author] now refutes the third indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the excess of two or three *stotriya* verses.

Because of the prohibition of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—which had been prescribed for the *atirātra* sacrifice—there would be an excess of three cups in the case of its optional inclusion, and an excess of two cups in the case of its non-inclusion.
Thus, even though there is no difference in the *atirātra* ritual itself, a difference in terms of excess is possible.

To explain: in the case of the inclusion of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, there are nine *stotriya* verses in the *bahiṣpavamāna*; in the four *ājya* stotras, the *mādhyandina-pavamāna*, and the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*, because they possess the fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*) *stoma*, there are seventy-five verses in total; in the four *pṛṣṭha* stotras and the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, because they possess the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) *stoma*, there are eighty-five; in the three *uktha* rounds and the *ṣoḍaśin*, because they possess the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) *stoma*, there are one hundred and five; in the twelve *atirātra* stotras, because they possess the fifteen-fold *stoma*, there are one hundred and eighty; and in the *rathaṃtara*, there are nine.

In that case, when all [the days] are combined—(9 + 75 + 85 + 105 + 180 + 9 = 463)—since there are four hundred and sixty-three *yojanas*, dividing by ten leaves a remainder of three. However, in the view where the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is not taken, since one *ṣoḍaśin* cup is missing from the twenty-one, there are one hundred and forty-two *yojanas*; thus, dividing by ten leaves a remainder of two.
Due to the contradiction regarding the *Sārasvata* [session], it should be "when" (*yadā*).

Regarding the statement, "The *sārasvata* sacrifice, which has the *agnīṣomīya* as its first [animal], is not seen," this fourth [point] is a perception of another purpose; it is discarded because there is a contradiction regarding the sequence of Mitrāvaruṇa in the *sārasvata* sacrifice. Even if a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) were established due to the unavoidable contradiction with the observation of the *puroḍāśa* cakes in the rule "those who have *puroḍāśas*," since all seasonal sacrifices that are modifications of the *jyotiṣṭoma* must be preceded by the *agniṣṭoma*, the phrase "when" (*yadā*) would indeed be required for the sake of the word "that" (*yat*) in order to prevent that difference in ritual action.
The meaning must be stated as follows: "When [the sacrifice is] on the full moon day, it involves the *puroḍāśa* cakes; when on the new moon day, it involves the *sāṃnāyya* offerings.
And thus, this observation of the text does not serve as a proof for the distinction between separate rituals.
In the case of the *upahavya*, it is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
The author of the Sūtras restates the fifth [point], the observation of another purpose, as being free from flaw (*nirāmāya*).
The disjunction (*cheda*) occurs in two ways: *pratiprasavaḥ* and *apratiprasavaḥ*.
The *Sudhā* commentary notes that the reading including the negative particle (*na*) is indicated by the Vārttika.
"Reinstatement" (*pratiprasava*) means a re-enactment (*punarvidhāna*).

Since the *rathantara* and *bṛhat* sāmans, as well as the *śālā* and *ādyavyavitaya*, are already obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*) in the *upahavya* sacrifice, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says that because there is a difference in the ritual acts, there must be a fixed application of those respective *śālā* and other elements in the *upahavya* for the sake of establishing them; thus, it is a reinstatement, a re-enactment.
The proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) says that there is no reinstatement—that is, an absence of reinstatement—because a re-enactment would be purposeless.
Or rather, the repetition is for the sake of a specific quality (guṇa).
Having stated this, he provides the answer.
The word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of removing doubt.
The repetition [of the injunction] must be for the purpose of specifying a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

When it is said, "When the *rathantara* is the *sāman*, then a dark-brown horse is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); when the *bṛhat* is the *sāman*, then a white horse with a mark on its forehead is [the fee]," this repetition is for the purpose of enjoining a specific subordinate quality in the form of a particular sacrificial fee. Furthermore, the text itself demonstrates this understanding.
He states the authority for the position that ritual action is one and the same across all recensional branches (*śākhā*).
The particle combination *cāpi* (and also) serves to aggregate the previously mentioned authorities.
The Veda demonstrates that in all branches there is the cognition—that is, the injunction—of one and the same ritual action.

Among the Maitrāyaṇīyas, the *samidh* and other offerings are not recited for the sake of progeny (*prajā*), yet their qualities are heard: "The seasons indeed are progeny; they should be offered together.

Likewise, for those followers of a branch for whom the address "Thou art *kuṭaru*" is not recited, it is said: "He takes the fire-stirring stick with the formula 'Thou art a cock,' or 'Thou art *kuṭaru*.
Therefore, we understand that it is a single ritual act.
Furthermore, due to the connection with the sequence of injunctions, the distinctness of the injunction would be established even for a single [rite].
The word "non-injunction" (avidhā) refers to direct perception as a means of knowledge.
Thus, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) demonstrates that there is indeed a difference in the ritual acts across different recensional branches (śākhā).
It is not the case that there is only one and the same ritual act for each branch.
The term "viśiṣṭaṣṭaḥ" refers to the specific state of the ritual act intended for performance; and in the word "ekasyām," the distributive repetition (vīpsā) is intended.
The meaning is: in every single one of all the branches.

Through the sequential conjunction—that is, the connection—of ritual acts, there would be established a distinction between injunctions, a distinction between the things enjoined, and a distinction between the rituals themselves. However, if all [acts] were to be combined together, there would result a confusion of sequence, time, and measure. But in the case of such distinction, the recitation of the constituent parts (aṅgas) prescribed in one's own Vedic branch remains uncontradicted, whereas the sequence [prescribed elsewhere] would be unenjoined.
The time of the forenoon and the measure of the constituent parts are performed and thus come into being.

However, because there is no connection with contradictory elements when there is a single action, there would be a connection with those [contradictions], resulting in all the injunctions being subject to the entire number.
The word "tu" (but/however) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

When there is a single action (*ekakarmatva*), because of the connection with that one action— namely, the connection of the injunctions located in all recensions (*sarvaśākhā*) with the enjoined subsidiaries (*vidheya-aṅga*) stated in those injunctions— the various opposing prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding sequence, time, measure, and name are refuted; for since there is no connection with the name (*nāmadheya*), due to its absence of connection, there is a total dissolution (*sarvapralaya*) of [those arguments] situated in all recensions.
"One desiring cattle" (paśukāmaḥ). Vi. 1412:
The name [of the sacrifice] would lead, through the force of the injunction (codaka), to the cognition that the various rites constitute parts of a single action.
Therefore, it is established that [the latter] is stronger. Why? Because it is directly perceived.
The name is directly perceived, whereas in another recensional branch there is even a difference in the originative injunction and the performance injunction;
however, the extended application (codaka) is inferential.
Bhāṣya 7.4.12.5.

And therefore, the established conclusion is that the ritual action (*karman*) is one and the same across all recensional branches (*śākhā*). Why? Because the name (*nāmadheya*), being heard [in the text], is capable—through indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—of conveying the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). The name, which is applied to those [actions] in its own usage, [establishes their identity].

In order to cause [the application] of these [names]—for which words the *codaka* (the impelling factor) provides the acquisition through the attainment of what is indicated by comparison—the sūtra states: "The names of those [words].
For which words?
It causes [the word] to go [to its primary meaning].

The name *darvihoma* belongs to the ritual action; it is not a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) for those words being employed in their own sense at the time of origination—that is, at the time of their initial utterance.

In Bhāṣya 1.4.1.2 (p. 126), it is stated that "the name [of a sacrifice] is meaningful through the statement of its qualities and results," because the form of names such as *darvī-homa* and others is perceived within the designation itself. This is established by the fact that the status of being a name is determined by the very nature of the designation.

However, it should be understood that the Sūtra—*ekādaśadhye nāmadheye guṇaśruteḥ syād vidhānam iti cet*—formulates precisely two sets of three attributes (*ciddhatrika*) based on the status of being a name (*nāmadheya*). Just as there is the state of being for another’s sake (*parārthatva*), being a number of others (*parasaṃkhyātva*), and being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), so too there is the state of being subordinate (*avamānatva*), being primary (*pradhānatva*), and being for one’s own sake (*svārthatva*); likewise, there is the state of being what is to be adopted (*upādeyatva*), being what is enjoined (*vidheyatva*), and being a quality (*guṇatva*). Thus, the occurrence of these two triads of attributes is indeed what is enunciated in the Sūtra. *Taulā. oṃ nāmadheye guṇaśruteḥ syād vidhānam iti cet*. (If it be argued that because a quality is heard in the name, there must be an injunction.)

Regarding the inquiry—“One desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya”—as to whether the word *vājapeya* is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or a name of a rite (*karmanāmadheya*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: In the case of a name, a word such as *vājapeya* is considered to be a name because of the mention of an accessory, namely the grain-offering (*vāja*) which is a constituent part; thus, it would be the injunction of that very [accessory].
This is because the two actions are equal.

As for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that the word *vājapeya* is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)—that is not correct. This is because there would be the undesirable consequence of equality between this *vājapeya* rite—which has substances such as grain (*vāja*) as its objective—and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rites; that is, they would become equal. Consequently, the mention of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the attendant days (*upasad*) in the formula "the *vājapeya* consists of seventeen *upasads*" would be redundant. This defect would follow if the word were taken as an injunction of a subordinate quality.
Therefore, it is not an injunction of an accessory.
Or rather, it is not an injunction of an accessory.

Why? Because the two actions—the action of the Vājapeya and the action of the Jyotiṣṭoma—are equal, the observation of the consecrations (dīkṣās) and the Upasads in the Vājapeya is logically consistent.
Therefore, it is the name of an action (*karmanāmadheya*).
Just as in the eleventh [chapter], it is for the sake of another;
by means of another reason, he rejects the position that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
The word "not" (na) is carried over from the preceding sūtra.

Its meaning is that, since the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) occurs in the eleventh [section], it is not proper for its utterance to be for the sake of another; that is, for the sake of enjoining a subordinate quality.

The point is that it is not proper to designate the sacrifice—which has been expressed as something to be undertaken (*upādeya*), as a subordinate element (*guṇa*), and as a new injunction (*apūrvavidhi*)—as being for the sake of another, by means of an unaccented [vowel] indicating it as the subject (*uddeśya*) and as the primary element (*pradhāna*), because this would result in the fallacy of two sets of three contradictory characteristics (*viruddha-trika-dvaya*).
Therefore, the word *vājapeya* is not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*),
but rather it is the name of the ritual (*karmanāmadheya*). Why?

Oṃ. In all ritual names, the word "name" functions as a descriptive term following the actual meaning through its connection to that meaning, and not by disregarding the worldly sense in favor of a mere technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), as is the case with qualities of the intellect.
For example: *agnihotra*, *śyena*, and *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Likewise, *dvādaśāha* is a name through connection with the meaning, not by virtue of being the thing itself.
Bhāṣya 1.4.1.31:
Om. In the section concerning names (nāmadheyādhikaraṇa), it is considered whether a name, like a ritual injunction or a traditional recollection (smṛti), serves as a means of valid authority or not.
The section concerning the *udbhid* sacrifice (*udbhidādhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.
Su. Pṛ. 115:

Oṃ. Since for the authors of the Vārttika the presentation of the meaning of a word is accomplished through the word's own power, even though they accept the supplementation (*adhyāhāra*) of words everywhere for that purpose, there is indeed the recourse to another justification in the case of the connection with a name (*nāmadheya*). And this has been established by them themselves in the section on Names (*Nāmadheyādhikaraṇa*).
Advaita 2.4.60–61:

*Oṃ, the section on names (nāmadheyādhikaraṇa).* Even though the sūtra [2.4.59] has the sense of asserting the established conclusion (*siddhāntābhimāna*), because it is the first [of the group], the word "also" (*api*) is explained as being for the purpose of refuting the view that even in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of this section, an application [of the previous logic] is possible—by way of citing examples such as "and therefore, since otherwise the status of being for the sake of action is impossible, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 402).

Because of the refutation—in the *Vaiśvānara* section (*Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa* 1.4.12–17)—of the nature of the agent (*kāraka*) which [was established as] a name in the *Ādyādhikaraṇa* (the *Nāmadheya* section), where it was argued that there is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) based on the originative statement (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).
[The conclusion is: "In well-established cases, the status of being a name is set aside by its being an injunction of a quality."
Vāla-pṛ. 145:
And the status of being a name arises from its functioning as a cause [of cognition].
Since there is no presence of a possessive indication (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*), the word *udbhid* is a name [in the sentence]: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*."
2. Due to the fear of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the word *citrā* is a name (*nāmadheya*): "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrā*. 3.
From the force of the scripture’s purport (*tātparya*), the word *agnihotra* is a name: "He offers the *agnihotra*" and "He sacrifices the *samidh*s. 4.
From its designation (*tadvyapadeśa*), the word *śyena* is a name: "One should sacrifice for victory with the *śyena*."

Some maintain that because it possesses the strength of qualities prescribed by originative injunctions (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇabalīyastvāt*), the word *vaiśvadeva* in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*" is a name (*nāmadheya*).
As for its status as a name, it is due to the scriptural teaching regarding it (*tatprasthaśāstrāt*);
for in that context, a quality enjoined [by the name]—namely, Agni as the deity—is already obtained from another source.

The *Miśra* [commentators], however, state: When a word conveys a connection with a quality in a particular ritual action, and if that connection is established by another scriptural authority (*śāstrāntara*), then that word is a name (*nāmadheya*) for that action because of that [other] authority. And that other authority may be either an injunction (*vidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
In the case of the word *agnihotra*, it is an injunction.
In the word *vaiśvadeva*, it is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*);
likewise, in the word *jyotiṣṭoma*, it is also merely an explanatory eulogy. *Mīmāṃsā*.

By virtue of being names, the status of the *Nāriṣṭha-homa* and others as injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) is set aside; [this applies] in cases of etymological derivation (*yaugika*), logical inconsistency (*prasajya*), syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), synonymy (*tanmatya*), and indirect designation (*tadanyapadeśa*).
Bāla. pṛ. 145.
Without co-referentiality with the generic term (*dhātu*), the application of the principle of a name (*nāmadheya*) is impossible. (Sūtra-pṛ. 396) || *Nāmadheya-nyāya* ||
This is the fourth quarter of the first chapter.

In the Quarter on Names (1.4), the subject of investigation here is whether names serve as a means of knowing dharma or not. Furthermore, in determining that [the status of names], it must be considered whether these [names] are recited with the effort of being connected to injunctions and so forth, or not.
Su. Pṛ. 393:

In the first section (the section on the authority of names), within the sub-section concerning whether [certain terms] are injunctions of qualities or names, the authority of all words [in the Veda] has been established.

Oṃ. The superiority of the name [as a means of differentiation] was established in the seventh book (*Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra* 2.2.22) regarding the conflict between the injunctive statement (*codaka*) and the name.
*Sūtraprakāśikā*, p. 481.
Oṃ. Due to the difference in names, there is a difference in rituals.
Ke. 2|1|1|1 | Oṃ. Connection with a new name is a cause of difference.
Su. pṛ. 945.
Oṃ. The visual power (*nayanaśakti*), though unitary and undivided, perceives [objects such as] the moon as if they were divided;
this is the *bṛhatī*. Page 228.
Oṃ. The analogy of coconut water (*nārikelajalanyāya*).
Just as it is not known how water came to be inside a coconut, so too is the summary:
*Oṃ*, the maxim of the coconut fruit (*nārikelaphalanyāya*).

Just as it does not fall within the scope of reasoning to ask how water came to be inside a coconut fruit which possesses firm internal parts, so too, once Fortune has arrived, she is not perceived at all.
And it has been said: "Once arrived, she is not perceived at all, like the water within a coconut fruit";
the word "Fortune" (lakṣmī) is to be supplied [as the subject].
The rash one.
268 | Oṃ: The principle to be established in the section on *nāriṣṭha* is "the insertion of newcomers at the end.
Oṃ. The principle of the *nāriṣṭha* [offering];
the principle of the *upahoma* [subsidiary offering]—these are to be understood from the *Vindī*, at Ke.

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) view is that, according to the *nāriṣṭha* principle, since the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is obtained through the water at the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*), the offering to the gods (*videvanā*) and other rites should be performed first, and only afterwards [the *nāriṣṭha* offerings].

The *nāriṣṭha* oblation is prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the purpose of the principal oblations and so forth, because it is stated: "He offers the *nāriṣṭha* oblations. The mantras used therein begin with: "O sacrifice, you have ten bodies worthy of sacrifice," and so on.
VI. 10|4|1: "Oṃ. It is observed that the *nāriṣṭha* oblations are performed in all [sacrifices] where all *pṛṣṭha* chants are employed.

(Bhāṣya 8|4|1|18). "In the *nakṣatreṣṭis*, the *upahoma* oblations follow after the *nāriṣṭha* oblations" (1|2|19|19). For even in the *nāriṣṭha* oblation, there is an injunction using the verb *juhoti*: "He offers the *nāriṣṭhas*."

8|4|1|19: In the *nāriṣṭha* oblations, the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance would apply by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), because [the mantra] forms a single syntactical unit (*aikavākyatva*) with those mantra words; however, the *svāhā*-utterance applies, for syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context.

Om: In the case of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations and others that are extended by analogy (*atideśika*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) with the oblations and other rites taught in the *nakṣatreṣṭi* and similar sacrifices.
Due to the connection with the characteristic marks of the archetype, there should be an addition of ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*) in the modified form (*vikṛti*).
Commentary: There is the fire-altar (*agni*) [prescribed] by the text, "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar.

In that context, there is the Nakṣatreṣṭi sacrifice: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṛttikā; he offers here: 'To Agni, Svāhā! To the Kṛttikās, Svāhā! To the cloud, Svāhā! To the continuous [rain], Svāhā! To the cloud-producing, Svāhā! To the rain-making, Svāhā! To the raining, Svāhā! To the dew, Svāhā!'"
However, the *nāriṣṭha* oblations exist in the archetype, as it is stated: "He offers the *nāriṣṭha* oblations.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is there an exclusion of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations, or rather, their non-exclusion, that is, their combination?
Likewise, in the *Śyena* sacrifice, it is heard: "The priests proceed wearing red turbans, red garments, and with the sacred cord suspended around the neck."

In the original ritual context (prakṛti), it is stated: "The *anīvīta* is for men, the *prācīnāvīta* for the ancestors, and the *upavīta* for the gods; he wears it over the shoulder (*upavyayate*), thereby performing the very state of being a deity.
This [rule] is extended here by the general injunction (*codaka*).
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is there an exclusion of the *upavīta*, or is there no exclusion, but rather a combination?
Likewise, it is heard in the context of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*: "One should consume either milk or ghee.
However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the rule: "Milk is the fast-food for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel for a Rājanya, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for a Vaiśya.
This [rule] is thus obtained here by means of the extended application (*codaka*).
In this regard, there is a doubt: is there the cessation of that [doubt], or its non-cessation, or their combination? What is the prima facie view? That there is its cessation.

The *upahoma*s and other such elements directly heard in the scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruta*) are the sublaters of those [elements] obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) which are inferential (*ānumānika*).

Furthermore, there is a connection with the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*), as in the cases of "he offers" (*juhoti*), "they proceed wearing the *nivīta* garment," and "he should cause to eat.
For example:

Regarding the statement, “The Bārhaspatya [offering] consists of *śara* grass,” the *śara* grasses set aside the *kuśa* grasses; they do not exclude them. In the same way, they would not exclude the *nāriṣṭa* oblations either.
This being the case, we reply as follows.
"Non-cessation means combination.
Why? Because of the connection with the archetypal characteristic (*prakṛtiliṅga*).
There is no connection of these [elements], such as the secondary oblations (*upahoma*), with the archetypal characteristic.
For that [prohibition] occurs either through direct observation, as in the case of "the sacrifice of wild rice" (*naivāraścaruḥ*);

or it occurs by way of a prescriptive injunction regarding absence, as in: "The voice indeed becomes exhausted when the Puṣya-day ritual concludes; one should not speak much, nor ask another, nor answer another, but should cause him to eat honey or ghee."
It occurs either through modification, as in “the *nairṛta* oblation for the *nairṛta-pūtanā*”;
or by means of the word *kha*, as in “one should bind the animal to the *paridhi*”;
or by means of prohibition, as in “One should not say ‘girā-girā’; if one were to say ‘girā-girā’, he would swallow his own self; therefore, one should say this [other] verse.”

Or rather, by whatever means the primary rite is understood to be completed—since the *nāriṣṭha-homas* and so forth belong to that same time—the force of the word establishes that these rites, which occur after the principal sacrifice, share the same location and thus produce a single effect; consequently, the *nāriṣṭha-homas*, being of an enjoined form, supersede those that are extended by analogy (*atideśa*), just as the *śara* grass supersedes [the *kuśa*]. This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

For while it is appropriate that the *śara* grass—being enjoined as the substitute for the *barhis* grass indicated by the word "barhis" through its functional effects (*kārya*)—should receive the properties of the *barhis* by virtue of following after those effects; there is no evidence whatsoever regarding the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*), since they do not share the functional effects of the *nāriṣṭha-homa*, because perception and other means of knowledge do not apply to matters of transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Nor [can it be argued that] because they occupy the same position and have the same effect, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the function of the *nāriṣṭha* offerings—which is obtained through the injunction of the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*)—into the context of those offerings; for, since there is no word present to indicate them, they cannot be the objects of reference (*uddeśya*), and thus the injunction of the subsidiary offerings cannot be understood as being for their sake. Consequently, even though the name "nāriṣṭha" is obtained through extension by virtue of the presence of the function and the substance, it does not apply here. This is because, unlike the principle of the *śara* grass, the mere fact of occupying the same position is not a determining factor.

Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for the injunction of a separate ritual action in the *upahoma* passage, since it could be explained as an injunction of mantras by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the *nāriṣṭha* offerings.

For, apart from the established sequence, it is precisely a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) that causes division when multiple mantras are enjoined, as this would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Indeed, this is a single sentence; for, according to the Taittirīya scripture known through the particle *iti*, the connection of the mantras is understood to be with the act of offering (*juhoti*) itself.

For this very reason, since the application of mantras ending in *svāhā* to the *nāriṣṭha-homa* would follow from their indicative power (*liṅga*) alone, a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is established to avoid the contingency of rendering other applications redundant. Furthermore, whether that [distinct act] is considered one or many is another matter, based on the force of the collection of mantras ending in *svāhā* understood through their inclusion in a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyopādāna*).

Nor can it be argued that, even so, the *nāriṣṭha-homa* would not apply because the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) would have no further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) once satisfied by the enjoined homas, and thus there would be no basis for the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule.

Since the *upahomas* (subsidiary offerings) do not have their utility established [in the archetype], the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) first grasps only those elements transferred from the archetype by virtue of its requirement for assistance; thus, even though the *nāriṣṭha* offerings are obtained [from the archetype], they are not included.

For this very reason, modified elements such as the *upahomas* are grasped solely through one of the two mutual requirements (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*), because it is cumbersome to postulate another unestablished result.

Therefore, where there is a restatement (*punar-śravaṇa*) of archetypal elements whose utility is already established within the context of the modification—as in the case of the *yājyā* verses of the *Āgneyī* sacrifice—the transfer (*atideśa*) is set aside by satisfying the modification's requirement for assistance right there.
Or rather, it is where there is a deficiency in the collection of auxiliary factors required for immediate assistance;
however, in this case, even the substance itself is not present.
Therefore, there is no sublation of the *nāriṣṭha* offerings by the *upahoma* offerings.

Regarding this, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having raised the objection that the rule "the priests proceed without the *nīvī* [sacred thread] in the Śyena sacrifice" might—by way of purifying the performers who are auxiliary to the performance—sublate the *upavīta* (worn over the left shoulder) which is prescribed for the purpose of all rites through extended application (*atideśa*), establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) because both serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Therefore, since this [wearing of the sacred thread] has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there arises the possibility of its conjunction with the *prācīnāvīta* even in rites such as the *śrāddha*; thus, this point was set aside. For, just as in the case of the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*), there is the possibility of conjunction between the specific modes of wearing—such as the *upavīta*, *nivīta*, and so forth—which depend upon the wearing of the thread and are prescribed according to the knowledge of each respective rite, and which constitute a lifelong vow. Even though it might be suspected that on that particular day [of the *śrāddha*], the [usual] wearing would cease—just as the original performance ceases when the eating from the middle (*madhyāśana*) is prescribed by the rule "when [the rite] is concluded, he should eat from the middle"—it was stated that because it serves an invisible purpose, there is indeed conjunction.
That [example] is set aside because consuming wine—which causes the decay of both bodies—is incapable of performing the function of the milk-vow (*payovrata*);
furthermore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is disregarded due to the absence of meditation and the absence of the milk-vow on the day of the sacrifice.
Or, let that too be cited here as an example.
Maṇḍana: "The subsidiary offerings (upahoma) do not sublate the nāriṣṭha offerings.
Śaṅkara: "The nāriṣṭha offerings are not to be sublated by the subsidiary offerings."
The *darvihomas* are preceded by the *nāriṣṭha-homa*. (Bhāṣya 8.4.1) Clarified butter (*ājya*) is fresh butter (*nāvanīta*).

The term *nīta* is not used for both the old and the new clarified butter (*ghṛta*). (Ci. 1|4|120). According to the principle that "destruction is dissolution into the cause," it is taught that even at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) persists by virtue of having existence as its essence.
(Śrīkara. 2|2).
The Topic on Destruction (*nāśādhikaraṇam*).

This topic is to be seen under the section stating: "In the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, there is no omission of the subsequent ritual acts (*śeṣakārya*) regarding the substance that has been consumed for the sake of those acts" (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2073).

Regarding the rule "for whom the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are burnt," if only a portion is burnt, then according to the principle of the aforementioned Topic on Destruction (6.4.12), the performance is merely completed with clarified butter (*ājya*) or with what remains after being burnt.
Bhāṭṭa 6.4.15: "The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple staff, and smearing oneself with ashes—these, says Bṛhaspati, are the livelihood of those who lack the manliness of a Buddha."
Thus, it has been stated that the Agnihotra and other such rites have a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatva). [Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 135].
*Nikāntaḥ* means "extremely desired" (*nitarāṃ kāntaḥ*) or "exceedingly dear.
As in the phrase: "For cattle are indeed *vāstunikāntāḥ*."
Ke. 2.3.16–17: *Nikāya* means a collection (*saṃghāta*) situated one above the other;
those who possess such a [collection] are called *nikāyins*, just as, for example, [the gods] consisting of thousands (*sāhasrāḥ*).
*Nikāya*: 2331. *Nigada* or *sādhyasrkāḥ*.
Bhāṣya 8.1.12.19. *Nikāya* is a collection (*saṃgha*) characterized by the simultaneous production [of members] by means of a single word.

Su. Pṛ. 860: "And for those belonging to a class (*nikāyin*), there should be the application of the preceding to the subsequent" (8.1.12.19). According to this principle, the purpose of the final position (*siddhānta*) is that the previously extended (*atidiṣṭa*) properties of the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice are to be performed here for the sake of the animal sacrifice.
Kaṣṭūri. 2.1.12.16: "And for those belonging to a class, there should be the application of the preceding to the subsequent."

A *nikāya* is said to be a collection (*saṃghāta*). Those which belong to such collections are called *nikāyins*; [in this context, they refer to] those consisting of thousands or those consisting of six thousand.

Because the permanent [obligation] (*nitya*)—consisting of the desire for intercourse during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*)—is set aside by the undertaking of the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-vrata*) out of devotion to the ancestors, and by occasional (*naimittika*) vows, there is no fault even if one approaches a married woman under the stipulation: "I shall marry this wife solely for the sake of fulfilling my religious duty (*dharma-mātra*).
(Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya). Su. p. 192. The rule is that for a permanent [obligation], which is inherently capable [of being performed], there is an absence of [any specific] fruit and so forth.

*Maṇi*, p. 45: "For there is likewise a sublation of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite by the optional (*kāmya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*). *Vārttika* 3.6.10, p. 1033: "Obligatory duties cannot be [performed] in conjunction with a desire for a specific result. *Bhāṣya* 6.1.16: The author of the *Bhāṣya* accepts a fruit in the case of an obligatory rite, stating: "The fruit belongs to the principal [rite] from beginning to end; the fruit will arise from the principal rite even when it is joined with only a portion of its subsidiaries."

The author of the Sūtras maintains that in obligatory rites (*nitya*) there is a prescribed procedure (*itikartavyatā*), as indicated by the citation of the *prayāja* sacrifice in the rule: "In the case of an obligatory rite, the *ārambhaṇīyā* is to be repeated like the *prayāja*s" (9.1.34). By employing this example, he shows it to be an established fact. Vārttika 6.3.12 states: "In an obligatory rite, even one who performs it according to his capacity has the entitlement (*adhikāra*). This is the section concerning performance according to capacity (*yathāśakyatva-adhikaraṇa*).

Bhāṣya 6.3.11–7: In the case of a compulsory (*nitya*) rite, there is no injunction based on its being a means to a fruit; rather, it is connected to the occasion consisting of one's life. Vi. 6.12: It is established in the sixth book (in the first and second sections of the third pāda) that for a compulsory performance, one is qualified even by performing only a single part; whereas for a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), only one who is able to perform the entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is qualified.

*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 11.1.3.11: Even when the cognition of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*)—which relies on a cause accompanied by an injunction—is produced regarding an obligatory (*nitya*) rite, the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are not [required] therein, because they are not required. Rather, subsequently, when the primary productive urge (*bhāvanā*) requires a means, it is understood that the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for previously committed sins is the means (*bhāvyatve avagate*).
