*Bhāṣya* 6.3.1, p. 250: Even though the omission of auxiliaries is possible in the case of obligatory rites, the omission of auxiliaries cannot be tolerated in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites.

VI. 6|12. Because the obligatory (*nitya*) rites cannot be abandoned by one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), he retains the entitlement to perform the obligatory rites even while enduring the loss of what is desired or the occurrence of what is disliked. 6|1|10. The desire to perform an occasional (*naimittika*) rite supersedes the desire to perform an obligatory (*nitya*) rite. Bhāṣya 12|2|13|33. In the non-performance of an obligatory rite, there is both sin (*pratyavāya*) and the necessity for expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

VI. 6|3|2: The accomplishment of the *prasaṅga* (incidental application) occurs when the obligatory (*nitya*) *agnihotra* is performed by means of the optional (*kāmya*) *agnihotra*. Bāla. p. 132: The details of the first [performance] of the obligatory *agnihotra* are extended (*atidiśyante*) to the monthly *agnihotra*. Ke. 7|3|1|1: There is the maxim that "the rule for the obligatory is stronger than the rule for the optional" (*nityānityayor nityavidhir balavān iti nyāyaḥ*).
That which applies regardless of whether [the condition] has been performed or not is *nitya* (eternal/obligatory);
that which is the opposite of this is *anitya* (non-eternal/optional).
For this very reason, in forms such as *vardhati*, the suffix *śap* and so forth occur before the augment (*guṇa*), because they are *nitya*.
Thus, too, is the worldly convention: "The reckless one. Bhāṣya 10.8.14.39: "Because there is no conjunction between the eternal and the non-eternal."

Vārttika 2.3.21, p. 583: "A prohibition where there is no possibility [of occurrence] is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), as in: 'One should not sacrifice on the earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in the sky. Bhāṣya 12.2.18: "This is a constant restatement: 'Not in the intermediate space... [This is a constant restatement.]
The distinction between the obligatory and the optional [rites] must be established in heaven;
for when [the goal] is already attained, it is not a restatement of the obligatory.

A prohibition that does not depend on prior attainment (*prāpti*), but rather whose nature as a negation is understood by the word itself as being inherently established, is a *nityānuvāda* (eternal restatement). For example: "It is not to be sprinkled in the intermediate space nor in the sky," or "One does not sprinkle with clarified butter in the Soma sacrifice.
Where a prohibition functions as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), there it constitutes a *nityānuvāda*.

*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 7.3.8.22, p. 1559: Regarding the Soma sacrifice, although there is the general rule that a hundred cows, horses, and so forth are to be given, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that when it is stated, "In this case, no cow is given, nor cloth, nor gold," this is a prohibition of only certain items and thus implies the giving of other things. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) replies: "It is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), not an implicative injunction (*kalpaka*). *Kevala-vyākhyā* 10.2.11.
From the censure of that which is censurable, there is the understanding that the prohibition is a *nityānuvāda* (a restatement of what is already established).

Su. pṛ. 998. Having rejected the view that obligatory (*nitya*) ritual action serves the purpose of maintaining the prior absence of the cognition produced by the enjoined cause, it was established in the *Sarvaśakti-adhikaraṇa* (6.3.2) in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* and the *Tantrarahasya* that, because it is an injunction (*vidhi*), the result is indeed the destruction of sin (*pāpakṣaya*).

However, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* states that the destruction of sin is not the fruit of obligatory ritual action; rather, he asserts that its fruit is solely the maintenance of the prior absence of the cognition produced by the enjoined cause.

Soma 2.4.1: Regarding the injunction for obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), it is established that lifelong performance is not possible without a fixed result; thus, even though they are desireless (*akāmya*), a result is inferred. Bāla. p. 144: In the case of obligatory rites, the impossibility of abandoning them has been established in the sixth [chapter]. p. 157: In obligatory rites, there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*).
Ke. 12|3|7|18-19. Regarding the sequence between the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) follows the principle of the occasional (*naimittika*);
as in the case of the fifteen-fold hymn (*pāñcadaśya*) and the recitation of the *viśvajit*. (Ṭup.)

Since it is impossible to prevent the general requirement [of materials] when the Vedic substances such as *vrīhi* rice are unavailable for both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites, that general requirement must terminate in some particular substitute; thus, because there is a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its existence, a substitute (*pratinidhi*) exists. (Vi. 6.3.4). Obligatory, optional, and occasional rites are to be performed whenever the opportunity arises. (Bhā. 11.3.12–14). The distinction between obligatory and optional rites.

According to the view of the author of the Vārttika, the distinction between optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya) rites is established as being characterized by the completeness or incompleteness of their constituent parts (aṅga).
Some indeed maintain that there is no difference whatsoever between obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites, because in both cases all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) must be combined.
Furthermore, because certain partial theorists (Ekadeśins) have set forth weak arguments with little effort, their view has been accepted as prevalent.
[Now] the correct logic is demonstrated by refuting both positions.
By which a clear distinction between the two types of action—the optional (kāmya) and the obligatory (nitya)—might be established.
In this regard, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows:
"For eligibility everywhere depends upon application;
otherwise, there would be an undesirable consequence, such as the eligibility of Śūdras and others."
"Everywhere"—meaning not only in optional rites (*kāmya*) but also in obligatory ones (*nitya*).

It has been established in the *Tiryagadhikaraṇa* (6.1.2) that eligibility for a particular rite belongs only to one who possesses the capacity to perform all its constituent parts, provided those parts are not already known through scripture (*śruti*) and so forth, but are obtained through Smṛti, custom (*ācāra*), verbal designation, injunction, indicative mark (*liṅga*), cause (*nimitta*), or direction (*adeśa*).

Because the accomplishment of the fruit depends upon the commonality [of the constituent parts], and because the status of being a cause (i.e., the status of being an instrument) belongs only to that which is joined with the distinctness of the agent, there must be a combination of all the required subsidiaries; otherwise, the contingency of eightfold deficiencies in the underlying causes would arise. Furthermore, since that which is deficient cannot be performed, how could there be the accomplishment of the application according to one's capacity?

Moreover, if the accomplishment of the fruit were possible even through the combination of only a few subsidiaries, then it would also apply to optional rites (*kāmya*), as there would be no distinction between them.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in injunctions such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), because there is a scriptural statement regarding the occasion (*nimitta-śruti*), the rite must necessarily be performed when that occasion occurs; and because its non-performance would contradict that [scripture], the principal act (*aṅgin*)—along with its subsidiaries (*aṅga*)—is a means to the fruit, and thus it is performed in that very manner?
Whereas in the case of a rite for a specific desire (*kāmya*), since there is no such contradiction, it is performed with the inclusion of all its subsidiaries. [Response: This is not so.
The necessity of performing [the rite] even due to the presence of a causal occasion (*nimitta*) resides precisely in the qualification (*adhikāra*).
Furthermore, the qualified person is one endowed with all capacities, and no other.
Since the qualification of all [persons] is understood from the statement regarding the causal occasion, the collection of subsidiaries (*aṅga-upasaṃhāra*) follows accordingly.

If it is argued that "the attainment of the fruit for each person is exactly as much as they are capable of performing," then it would follow that even in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), those desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) would have the right to perform them in that same manner [even if they lack some subsidiaries].

Furthermore, if the inclusion of subsidiaries were determined by the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), then there would be eligibility for one who is pure but has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), as well as for those who have maintained the fires but lack Vedic knowledge, and even for those who possess other subsidiaries but lack this one.
Therefore, the capacity to perform all subsidiaries is a qualification for eligibility (*adhikāraviśeṣaṇa*).

For this very reason, the determination of eligibility (*adhikāra*) follows after the fifth chapter, because eligibility depends upon capacity, and capacity is determined by means of the definition of what is possible (*śakya*), which is ascertained through the five chapters. As it has been said: "The distinction between obligatory and optional duties..."
"The distinction between the obligatory and the optional would constitute the qualification for the Śāstra.
By this, they reject the relationship of the signified and the signifier and declare that the qualification is characterized by the [proper] occasion.
They should be understood as rejected.
Thus, in both cases (whether it be a compulsory or a desire-driven rite), there is a requirement for the inclusion of all constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*).
Some [hold that] "the state of being the object [of the ritual] is preceded by the state of being the instrument."
Therefore, they say that in rites performed for specific desires the constituent parts must be complete, whereas in obligatory rites the opposite is the case.

It is established that, first of all, the primary meaning of the sentence regarding the *apūrva* is the form of the action (*kāryarūpa*). And since that [action] cannot be attained except through human effort, and human effort is directed toward such things as these,
it requires a conscious agent.
And his status as an agent depends upon qualification (*adhikāra*).
For he who understands, "This action is for my sake; I am the master here," performs it and no other.
And he is called "qualified" (*adhikṛta*).
Furthermore, entitlement (*adhikāra*) in such cases depends upon the person to be enjoined.
For that indeed becomes an action which accomplishes the purpose of someone.
Therefore, the understanding of a person's entitlement to an action that accomplishes that [purpose] arises from the thought, "This is my task," regarding the specific task to be accomplished.
And he who perceives the task as his own is the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled).
Furthermore, in the case of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as the task, the state of being either pleasure or the avoidance of pain is not an object of anyone's desire;

for if that were so, one who seeks that [pleasure or avoidance] would have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the action simply through the scriptural injunction of the task, even without any other means of knowledge.
Therefore, it must be established by the verbal expression itself that "this is the task for this [person].
Thus, the task is dependent upon the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and that person is characterized by qualifications that are not themselves objects of attainment (*anupādeya-viśeṣaṇa*).
And those non-attainable qualifications are of two kinds, distinguished as the fruit (*phala*) and the cause (*nimitta*).

In this context, since the fruit cannot serve as a qualifier by its own nature because it has not yet been established, it qualifies the person to be enjoined (niyojya) through the medium of its own desire.
One who desires the fruit is said to be "one who wishes to accomplish the fruit for himself.
And such a person understands that very action to be the task to be performed which is conducive to his own desire.

[Objection: "But if the *apūrva* is connected as the producer of the fruit, then since it has attained the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the injunction (*niyoga*) itself would be the primary meaning of the sentence; thus, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) fails. To this he says: "But the injunction... The meaning is that even for the injunction, which is the primary element, there must be accepted—that is, admitted—a conformity to the fruit, for the sake of its own establishment, namely, its connection with the injunction qualified by the desire for the fruit.
This is the commentary on the subsequent section:

Even for the principal [action], which is the object of the mandate (*niyoga*), its conformity to the fruit must be accepted as being for the sake of the specific mandate itself, which is required for its own accomplishment.
And that task, which is to be accomplished by the principal [action], requires a delimiting factor, because an uninterrupted effort cannot be defined [otherwise].

And the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) is generally the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), precisely because it is related to that [action] by its very nature. Indeed, in the world, an effort is not observed whose object is a mere thing such as cooking and the like; rather, in some cases, by virtue of the word, the relationship between substance and deity and so forth becomes the delimiting factor for the effort that serves as the cause for accomplishing the meaning of the verbal root.

Thus, since the task (*kārya*) is delimited by the effort (*kṛti*), and since effort is not perceived without being delimited by the meaning of the verbal root, the meaning of the verbal root becomes the delimiting factor of the task through the mediation of effort.
And the object is said to be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).
For an object is that which is invariably concomitant with cognition;
and since an effect cannot be pursued when it is undelimited, that which delimits it becomes the object by virtue of being invariably concomitant with that [cognition].

Furthermore, since that objective (bhāvārtha) lacks an object for an action that conforms to a desire, it becomes an object in the form of a means, because it is possible to attain it as a means to the desired end. And its status as a means consists in the assistance provided by all its constituent parts (aṅgas); thus, if there is a transgression involving the omission of some parts, the assistance from the entirety of the parts will not be achieved. In the absence of being a means, there is an absence of being an object; and since even a deviant action would not be perceived as an "action" (kārya), one could not perform it with deficient parts by virtue of that [status].
However, this mode of operation is not possible in the case of obligatory rites (nitya).

For in that case, the person to be impelled (niyojya) is not one who desires a fruit, such that he would not understand what is not already established as something to be accomplished (kārya). Rather, being characterized by a predicate that is already established, he first understands the verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha) itself as the task to be accomplished. Since a task that has an understood object cannot exist without an effort (kṛti), and since an effort is impossible without an instrument (karaṇa), the agent—requiring an instrument—provides the instrument for the verbal root-meaning which has become the object of the task and is conjoined with it.

If it is asked: "How then can the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), which is accomplished solely by the agent's effort (*kṛti*), be an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to that [effort]? [The answer is: Because that [root-meaning], as delimited by that [effort], is the very effort (*kṛti*) that produces a specific *apūrva*; and because such a thing is well-known in the world as having the nature of an instrument.

For instance, just as the axe is the action characterized by raising and lowering, yet even while being so, it is an instrument with respect to that very [action], since that kind of action has the result of splitting [the wood];
for in the case of iron, raising and lowering do not result in splitting.
[It bears fruit, it causes fruition.

Thus, although the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is pervaded by the act of doing (*kṛti*), nevertheless, since its status as the object of that act depends upon the production of a specific *apūrva*, it is indeed correct for the meaning of the verbal root to have the character of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
As for the *apūrva*, however, because it is the goal (*uddeśya*), it possesses the character of the task to be accomplished (*kāryatva*).

Thus, when an action that has already come into being is enjoined as permanent (*nitya*), its status as a means (*karaṇatva*) and its association with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are subsequently understood; therefore, there is no lack of a subject matter even in the case of missing subsidiaries. Consequently, since the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is perceived in the action as a means, the mandate (*niyoga*)—by the force of that entitlement—compels the performance of the permanent rite even if it lacks some subsidiaries, just as a modified (*vaikṛta*) mandate compels the performance of subsidiaries other than those that are either substituted or prohibited. Thus, the distinction between optional (*kāmya*) and permanent rites is established.
This very [teaching], which appears auspicious at first glance, acts like brass when examined skillfully from the perspective of subtle reasoning.
How so? "Because the fruit is remote, because it is mentioned first, and because its status as the object [of meditation] is established by the abandonment of its primary [status]."
Because its own nature is not lost through the state of being equally primary;
and because there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence of [the universal] *jāti* and [the quality] *gauḥ* (cowness) being non-causal.

For the result of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is remote, being dependent on other words, whereas that which is proximate is previously presented by its own word. In that case, having first been construed as the means through the remote [result], and then connected with those [auxiliaries] presented in other sentences, it subsequently delimits the *apūrva*—which is to be conveyed by its own word—in a form already so construed. Thus, who could claim a preference for direct statement (*śruti*) over syntactical connection (*vākya*)?

Although the status of being a means to the desired end (kāma) necessarily belongs to the verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha)—which constitutes the object of the action and is the intended referent—nevertheless, that [status] should not be determined first.

For one should not understand a thing solely by focusing on the determination of that without which it would not be possible; rather, even when the thing itself has been understood, the thing that establishes its possibility is indeed understood afterwards, just as fire is understood after smoke.
Therefore, by the initial hearing of the word, only the verbal root-meaning [is grasped].
The distinction between the obligatory and the optional is as follows: "One should procure rice grains according to one's capacity, or one should thresh them according to one's capacity.
However, the form of the Āhavanīya fire and so forth is not enjoined by this rule.

Although the nature of the *homa* (oblation) is presented as something to be attained and its specific form is not prescribed, if it were enjoined there that "one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should offer in the *āhavanīya* fire, while the other [who has not] may offer anywhere," then a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) would result.

Nor is it possible to enjoin this as a common rule for both by saying, "one should offer after procuring an *āhavanīya* fire according to one's capacity," because the procurement of the *āhavanīya* and so forth is already established here by implication, just like the procurement of *vrīhi* rice and other materials.

Therefore, either the mere performance of the oblation would be enjoined without taking the *āhavanīya* fire into account, or the oblation would be performed in the *āhavanīya* with reference to its status as such.
In that case, if disregard were shown, there would be the consequence of an absolute annulment of the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya*.

Since the word "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) achieves its purpose even within the lifetime of that [person], there is no total affliction; thus, what is intended is simply: "One who possesses the fire and is living should offer the oblation."
By this, the rules regarding time and so forth have been explained.
Now, one might ask: why is it that even in the interval between [the two rites], living is not considered a constant requirement?
This is because of the principle of pouring out [the remainder].

Whether [the fire] has been extinguished or not—if it were to go out suddenly, that is, without cause, one should not rekindle it; for having heard the scriptural injunction, "If he rekindles it, he creates an enemy for himself," a prohibition was established. Thus, it would not be the case that there is no rekindling at all.
From this prohibition, it is understood that rekindling does indeed exist.

Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that there should be an option (*vikalpa*) between the obligatory holding (*nitya-dhāraṇā*) and the optional holding (*kāmya-dhāraṇā*). Or rather, the prohibition applies to one whose prosperity has departed (*gata-śrī*), because of the obligatory holding. For one whose prosperity has departed, having heard the scriptural text, "One should hold [the staff] or not," the holding of it is established by virtue of the injunction for obligatory holding.
This being the case, having heard the scriptural statement "one should not reassemble it," the prohibition becomes logical.
Therefore, there is no permanent maintenance as a separate entity.
Consequently, there is no optionality; rather, there is simply non-maintenance due to its obligatory nature.
Such is the established conclusion (siddhānta):
the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites do not share the same injunction (samānavidhitva).
The section concerning the similarity of rules regarding the *soma* sacrifice and the *dharma* [of the sacrificer] should be consulted (*bhā.* 3.6.126).
Between the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*) rites, the former takes precedence according to the principle of priority for the occasional over the obligatory.

[The substances such as] curd and so forth serve both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) purposes, as in: "One offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and "One desiring sensory power should offer with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*); and "One binds the animal to a post made of *khadira* wood" (*khādire paśuṃ badhnāti*) and "One desiring vigor should make the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *khadira* wood" (*khādiraṃ vīryakāmasya yūpaṃ kuryāt*).
There is no constant application (*nityaprayuktatva*) for occasional rites (*naimittika*),
because the constant performance is not included within the optional (*kāmya*) rite. (Bhāṣya 4.3)
Or [it may be so]. Bhāṣya 6.3.1212, p. 1407.
Regarding the inevitability of the destruction of sin, its nature as a matter of destiny (bhāgyatva) is understood from such scriptural statements as "One dispels sin through dharma" (Bhā.
The cause of dropsy is [the consumption of] water.
Furthermore, in no medical treatise (vaidyakasaṃhitā) is non-receiving [of gifts] heard of as the cause of any [disease], nor is it apprehended through perception, inference, and so forth.
Sleep occurs due to the weakness of the mind when it is accompanied by *nidrā* (the faculty of sleep). For one is said to be in deep sleep as if through a state of unconsciousness.
Bhāṣya 1.1.5, p. 30.
The Nidhana:
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Brahmasāman (the Sāman of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin) is prescribed for the Gomat, Aśvavat, and Marutvat Ukthas.
... (In that regard,) one should perform the Nidhana "hīp" for one desiring prosperity, "ūrk" for one desiring food, and "ū" for one desiring heaven.
Furthermore, another division of the *sāman* is designated as the *nidhana*.
(Vārttika 2.1.3.28, p. 563). The *nidhana* is the final constituent part of the *sāman* to be chanted by all—the *udgātṛ*, the *stotṛ*, and the *pratihartṛ*.
(Keśava): The *nidhana* is the last portion of a *sāman* that is endowed with five or seven [syllables] according to the path.
VI. 2.1.3. The purpose of the cake-crust and other items is for the *nidhana* (concluding offering).
"In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, one places the cake-crust in the vessel for Indra and Vāyu, the parched grains in the vessel for the Aśvins, and the curd-mixture in the vessel for Mitra and Varuṇa.
In this context, only those cakes and other items that are part of the primary sacrifice (*prakṛta*) are to be understood.
Bhāṣya 3.8.28.134: The pouring out (*ninayana*) of the *praṇītā* waters within the altar is not the motive for their fetching, but rather a disposal (*pratipatti*).
However, the kneading (*saṃyavana*) is the motive for the fetching.

Ke. 4.2.16.14–15: Since the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) serves solely as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial offering (*havis*), even though it does not motivate the taking up of the remnant—according to the principle of the "portioning of the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśakalpanā*) at 4.1.12.26—it is nonetheless logical that it motivates the holding [of the vessel] (this is precisely the *puroḍāśakapāla* logic; the timing of the pouring out is not intended to be significant).

Bhāṭṭa 4.2.14. The Principle of the Disposal of Water (Ninayana-nyāya): In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the pouring out of the *praṇītā* water is a rite of disposal (*pratipatti-dharma*). Because it is not connected with the production [of the substance], there should be a division of the *praṇītā* waters, just as there is for the clarified butter (*ājya*).

Commentary: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recorded in the scripture: "He pours forth the waters; the waters, indeed, are faith (*śraddhā*); having grasped faith itself, he performs the sacrifice."

In both cases, the operation of the *praṇītā* waters is heard [in the scriptures]: "He mixes the sacrificial offerings with the *praṇītā* waters," and likewise, "He pours out the *praṇītā* waters within the altar.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: are both mixing and pouring out the motivators for these waters, or is the pouring out a disposal (*pratipatti*) for those waters intended for mixing?
What is the prima facie position? There is no connection with their production to any specific purpose.
For those things that have been provided for both, there is a conjunction.
Therefore, a distinction is understood.
When no distinction is perceived, this is the division of the purposes of both: one portion is for mixing, and another portion is for pouring out.

Like the clarified butter (*ājya*). As it is said: "The clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel is indeed taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice. [Objection: The *praṇītā* waters, having arisen without being connected to any specific purpose, desire ritual action (*karmya*). [This is established] by two sentences: "He sprinkles the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) with the *praṇītā* waters" and "He pours the *praṇītā* waters within the altar (*antarvedi*)."
Regarding the statement "he leads," they are led toward the purposes of restraint and leading.
Therefore, by virtue of serving both purposes, they are employed for both.

[Objection: But surely, because of the use of the instrumental case in the context of mixing (*saṃyavana*), it has the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*); therefore, that [mixing] alone is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the *praṇītā* waters. However, because of the use of the accusative case in the context of pouring out (*ninayana*), it has the status of a primary factor (*prādhānya*); thus, the pouring out is not a motivator. [Reply: It is said:

Since the status of being a remnant (*śeṣabhāva*) is already understood through another scriptural statement (in another context), when there is subsequently a connection with something else, it becomes a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Just as in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

Furthermore, [if it were otherwise], only that much [of the flour] would be taken which is for the purpose of kneading alone—namely, as much as is required to complete the kneading; how then could there be an application [of the same material] elsewhere?
Since the firewood is connected with both purposes, both must be accomplished by it; therefore, [the materials] are employed for both.

[Objection: Surely, like the clarified butter (*ājya*), its being for all purposes (*sarvārthatva*) is understood; so how can it be said that it serves both purposes? [The author] says this in response: the position that it is "for all" (*sarvārthā*) has not been adopted, because it is already established [as such].

When a specific relationship—namely, the relation of primary and subsidiary (*aṅgāṅgitva*)—is understood through the direct scriptural statement (*śruta-vākya*), then its being for all purposes would have to be inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*).
That, however, is improper.

Even if it were assumed [to apply to all], since they are obtained there and elsewhere due to the connection with the context, they are restricted by the specific statement regarding the kneading and the pouring out from others;
therefore, the view that it applies to all purposes is poorly taught.
Alternatively, the disposal of those intended for kneading is established because of their being for that purpose.
Commentary: The *praṇītā* waters are for the purpose of mixing.
Why? Because of the indication by the instrumental case.

In the act of mixing, water has a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*), whereas in the act of pouring out (*ninayana*), it has a primary status (*prādhānya*) because of the indication by the accusative case.

The purpose of the reflection is that in the absence of the *puroḍāśa*, there is an absence of the *praṇītā* waters, as in the case of the *payasyā*. [Objection: On account of the force of the instrumental case, the pouring out (*ninayana*) is solely for the purpose of mixing (*saṃyavana*).
As for what was said—that only that much [of the water] would be taken—[that is not so].
To this he says: it is not possible to perceive merely that much;
this substance is necessarily something in excess.
Therefore, there is the apprehension of what is in excess, but there is no scriptural authority for the state of being in excess itself.

Furthermore, an excess [of water] is inevitable. (Why? Because) if only a small amount were taken, since the kneading (*saṃyavana*) would remain unaccomplished (because the kneading of all the flour would not have been performed), the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *praṇītā* waters would have to be performed again; thus there would be the burden of complexity. Moreover, due to the disruption of the sequence, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would [unavoidably] follow.
"Because there is no connection at the time of their production, both [the *mantras*] belonging to one who stands in the state of *karman* (ritual action) would be accepted as longing for it;
therefore, it is said that they serve both purposes.
In the mixing of the oblation (*havis*), their status as subordinate factors (*guṇabhāva*) is indicated by the instrumental case."

The pouring out (*ninayana*) of the second [set of *praṇītā* waters] is prescribed as a disposal (*pratipatti*). Since the *soma*-branch has already been used, its casting away (*praharaṇa*) is indeed a disposal; however, because there is no other use for the waters being poured out, their pouring out is not a disposal. This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) due to such an objection. The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Since at the time of their origin (*utpatti*) the *praṇītā* waters are not connected with any specific purpose, they should be employed by distributing them across multiple functions, just like the clarified butter (*ājya*) used for the *śrī* sacrifice.

Regarding the statement, "He pours out the *praṇītā* waters mixed with the sacrificial offering (*iṣṭa*)": what is intended? Are two purposes for the water obtained, or is it likewise for the mixing of the oblation (*haviḥ-saṃyavana*)?

Now, since it is said "he brings forth" (*praṇayati*), there is a commonality of purpose for both; however, having heard that its purpose is for the mixing, the pouring out (*ninayati*) is a disposal (*pratipatti*).

The Bhaṭṭas maintain that in this very context, the water consecrated by the *praṇayana* (carrying forward) enjoined by the injunction "He carries forward the water" (*apaḥ praṇayati*) has a dual application: just as its purpose for kneading the sacrificial offerings is established by the statement "He mixes the oblations with the *praṇītā* waters," so too at the end, its purpose for disposal (*ninayana*) is established by the injunction "He pours out the *praṇītā* waters within the altar" (*antarvedi praṇītā ninayati*).

Nor can it be argued that because the accusative case is used in the disposal injunction as well, it must be a mere *pratipatti* (disposal rite); for a skillful teacher [would point out] that since these waters have no remaining function after their *praṇayana*, they cannot be considered a *pratipatti* based on the two separate injunctions.
Therefore: since the pouring out (ninayana) has a purposeful meaning according to the principle of that which possesses qualities (saguṇanyāya), it does not function as a motivator (prayojaka).
This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), [we reply]: because of its connection with the accusative case, it is a disposal (pratipatti) for the sake of clearing away the scattered remains;
nor is there an absence of a remnant, because it must be discarded.
Furthermore, because the cognition of being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) alone serves as the determinant for the causal efficiency (*prayojaka*),
therefore, kneading (*saṃyavana*) itself is the determinant.
And in this context, the cooking of the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) such as the *Āgneya* is likewise [determined] by that very kneading.
Therefore, substances such as *caru* and the like certainly become *praṇītā*.
For this very reason, curd and milk will also be mentioned as *praṇītā* when they are poured out.

In reality, however, the *kapāla* (potsherd) is intended [as the object] only for the kneading of the dough (*piṇḍa-saṃyavana*) by means of the cooking (*pāka*) produced by the cleansing (*śodhana*), because there is no evidence for accepting it [as the object] through the property of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Having performed the ritual treatment of the *praṇītā* waters for curd and milk by way of a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*),
the ritualists, however, perform the *praṇītā* pouring even at the very beginning.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, since the mixing [of the flour] occurs after the pouring, there would otherwise be no production of those *praṇītā* waters for the purpose of pouring them out.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The pouring out of the waters is indeed a disposal (pratipatti). Śaṅkara [states]: "Likewise in the case of the carrying away of the praṇītā waters.
[In both cases], they possess the status of being the objects to be disposed of, just like a branch.

The *ninayana*-nyāya (the principle of pouring out): 2348. Regarding the threshing of the *nimitta* (the cause), the *ninayana*-nyāya is impossible precisely because there is no desire for disposal (*pratipatti*).
Kau. 2119. Censure (*nindā*).
That [eulogy] which culminates in that alone results in negation;
however, that which is directed toward an injunction arises for the purpose of praise, because the justification of that [injunction] serves a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha).

Vārttika 12.2.121. Some forms of censure culminate in the praise of something other than that [which is censured]; some forms of non-censure—even while preceded by the function of an injunction—culminate simultaneously with those functions of injunction in the praise of something else.

For example, after stating, "Devadatta is indeed exceedingly learned," and praising him by saying, "Even Bṛhaspati is not his equal," one then says, "He too is unlearned compared to such-and-such a person. Thus, every instance of praise ultimately results in [the praise of] everything.
*Parākrama*, folio 4912. A deprecatory explanatory passage (*nindārthavāda*) is so called because it consists of a sentence that enjoins a prohibition.

*Sūtra-pṛṣṭha*, page 171. That which is denoted by the word "deprecation" (*nindā*) is "non-excellence" (*aprāśastya*), which is characterized by being fit for connection with an undesirable result, like a quarrelsome wife.
In the explanatory passages (arthavādas), the particle (nipāta) serves as an indicator of meaning. (Bhāṭṭa, 1.2.22).
Regarding prefixes (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*):
they possess no function whatsoever in the actual denotation of meaning;
rather, that which illuminates their meaning is considered to be the expressive word (*vācaka*).

Vārttika 1.3.133, p. 306: One view is that a particle (*nipāta*) is denotative (*vācaka*); another is that it is indicative (*dyotaka*). Even under the view that it is indicative, [the first case ending applies] because it is a scriptural injunction for application (*viniyojaka-śruti*). Bālamanoramā, p. 41: When the agenthood or objecthood expressed by a finite verb (*tiṅ*) or a particle (*nipāta*) is present, the first case ending (*prathamā*) is used.
*Rahasya*, p. 64–66: It is established that a particle (nipāta) can have a syntactic connection with the meaning of a co-occurring word (*upapada*).

*Bhāṭṭa*, 7.3.4: A difference relation (*bhedānvaya*) is impossible between the meanings of nouns other than particles and the act of abandoning [the primary meaning]. *Maṇi*, p. 112: [Concerning] particles (*nipāta*) and prefixes (*upasarga*).

"The determination of meaning is made [by this]; doubt does not arise regarding prepositions (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*). For it is precisely in the expression of their meanings that they are investigated" (see under the entry for *nipāta*).
Vārttika 1.3.131, p. 306: Because particles (*nipāta*) and prefixes (*upasarga*) lack the capacity to denote independent meanings.
Sūtra, p. 311: Particles and prefixes are devoid of gender and number, and they function as grammatical operations (*kāryatva*).

p. 1442: An invitation (*nimantraṇa*) is an instigating desire that leads one to infer a cognition regarding the non-performance of an action that would otherwise result in an undesirable consequence.
Just as, for example, there is the instigation of a daughter’s son and others to perform ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and so forth;

and that [instigation] occurs because the conviction regarding the meal is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). *Rahasya*, p. 10. Invitation (*nimantraṇa*) is the act of commanding, which is the instigation of one who is inferior.
*Bāla*, p.
75: *Nimantraṇa* is the act of assigning a duty in the case of obligatory *śrāddha* ceremonies and the like.
(*According to the Saṃskārakaumudī, it is the instigation of the daughter’s son and others toward the eating at the obligatory *śrāddha* and other such rites.*)

[In the sense of the *liṅ* suffix: Maṇi, p. 117. A cause (*nimitta*) that is not something to be undertaken (*anupādeya*) functions as a differentiator of ritual acts (*karmabheda*). Examples include: "Having resolved to perform a sacrificial session (*satra*), one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," and "The Viśvajit [performed] at the Sāmudhyāna," and so forth.
Vārttika 2.3.12–25, p. 617. A cause is expressed either by the locative case (*saptamī*) or by the word *yadi* joined with another term.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 4.4.121: That which is called a *nimitta* (occasioning condition) is that, when present, the *naimittika* (the rite occasioned by it) necessarily occurs.
*Kaṇikā*, p. 333: A *nimitta* consists of place, time, fruit, or the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*), and is characterized by being non-prescriptive (*anupādeya-dharmaka*).
*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 88: A *nimitta* is expressed by a word ending in the locative case, as in "he offers [an oblation] when [the vessel] has been broken" (*minne juhoti*).

Or as it is stated in the *Tup-ṭīkā* (1.1.1.12, p. 2098): "Regarding [the passage] 'If both sacrificial offerings (*havirāti*) should perish'—that which is not being enjoined is called the occasion (*nimitta*). For if it were itself enjoined, it would simply be an injunction."
And if that which is the cause [of the cognition] were also intended [as the primary object], then there would be no doubt at all regarding the two things being cognized simultaneously.
Bhāṣya 6.4.4.13. Furthermore, that which is the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is the cause for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as it functions toward its qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
And that which is the cause, because it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), is the primary denotation (*mukhyam abhidheya*); the qualificand is secondary (*lākṣaṇika*).
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.6.12, page 674: "It is not an absolute rule that the cause must exist prior to the effect, which is caused by it;
for even a future thing can be a cause, just as the performance of agricultural labor is undertaken with the thought, 'It will rain.'"

Bhāṣya 2.3.12, p. 577. Since a *nimitta* (occasion) is that which impels performance, even though it is the objective (*uddeśya*), it lacks the status of being something desired to be attained (*īpsitatva*) or something to be avoided; therefore, [the occasion] is established by the *nimitta*.

2350. The injunction regarding the qualification of the person (*puruṣādhikāravidhi*) associated with the destruction of defects produced by specific occasions and the attainment of subsequent results is the *jāteṣṭividhi* (the injunction for the sacrifice on the birth of a son), beginning with "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born" and ending with "When one offers this sacrifice upon the birth of a son, he becomes purified and radiant," and so forth.

p. 15. *Nimittataḥ* (based on a specific occasion): An expressly stated restricted option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*), such as: "For one whose teeth have emerged, [impurity lasts] for one day; for an offspring born after [the mother's delivery], for eight days; for one whose tonsure has been performed, for four days; for one who has been initiated (*upanīta*), for ten days"—as stated by the author of the Vārttika in the section on resolving contradictions (*virodhādhikaraṇa*). *Bālambhaṭṭī*, p. 160. *Nimittataḥ*: An expressly stated restricted option, such as: "Impurity (*aśauca*) due to death (*śāva*) is ordained for ten days among *sapiṇḍa* relatives; prior to the collection of the bones (*saṃcayana*), it shall be three days, or even one day."

Page 160, *nimittataḥ* (by reason of a cause): A formal rule based on scriptural statement (*vācanikī vyavasthā*), such as: "If the Soma sacrifice has the *rathaṃtara-sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*; if it has the *bṛhat-sāman*, the cups beginning with the *śukra*. Also, according to the traditional law (*sārte*): "For men whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, impurity is declared to last for a night; but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is held to occur after three nights."
Thus says Manu (p. 19).

Regarding "by reason of a cause" (*nimittataḥ*): the mention of a specific [occasion] serves to establish by implication that the obligatory five-day impurity (*nityapañcadasya*) is superseded by the eight-day impurity caused by a Vaiśya. (p. 147). Regarding "by reason of a cause": a restriction is a prohibition, such as "the abandonment of Smārta rites occurs only during an eclipse, not during birth-impurity" (*sutaka*).

Page 35: It is determined that when something arises in dependence upon another, the latter is the *nimitta* (condition) for the former. Vārttika 2.2.15, page 392: Even though the status of being a *nimitta* and the status of being a *kāraka* (efficient cause) are distinct, there is still a connection with the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) because [the *nimitta*] possesses the quality of being an instigator (*anuṣṭhāpaka*).
Maṇi, page 193: Between being a *nimitta* and being a motivator (*prayojaka*), there is a distinction between the nature of the accomplished (*siddha*) and the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*).

The state of being a cause (*nimittatva*) is established, while the state of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) is to be proven. That which exists when something is performed is the cause; that for the sake of whose accomplishment something is performed is the motivator.
VI. 2.1.1, Section 3: Because there can be no status as a *nimitta* (condition) without prior establishment.
Su. p. 966. Regarding the non-recurrence of the *nimitta* and the *naimittika* (the conditioned):

In the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*), the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) expresses totality; thus, it falls under the category of a *nimitta*. By the principle of the "condition" (*nimitta-nyāya*), since the totality pertaining to life is already established through its connection with the *naimittika*, [the word *yāvat*] becomes a restatement of its own meaning.
The convergence of causes (nimittasaṃpāta) [is established] by the rule "niyamastu" in the section concerning the sacrificial oblation and so forth (havirādyadhikaraṇa, 6|4|128–29).
Page 6, Section 5.13:

Where there is a concurrence of causal conditions (*nimitta*), the inquiry is whether another rite occasioned by those conditions is to be combined (*samuccīyate*), or whether it is an option (*vikalpyate*), or whether it is set aside (*bādhyate*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they are to be combined.
Or [it is said]: "The connection with a specific cause is the particular (viśeṣa), while the context is the general (sāmānya).
And a general rule is set aside by a particular rule.
This is the *nimitta-sūtra* from Bhāṣya 3.6.130.

The establishment of the meaning of the first word and so forth [is achieved] by the sūtra *tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ* (1.1.2.13). However, according to the author of the treatise (*śā.*), the sūtra concerning the cause (*nimittasūtra*) does not have much utility. (Soma., 1.2.1, p. 2). That alone is included within the essential nature of the cause without which the cognition of the cause would not be complete; other factors, however, even if understood first, are not intended because they are unnecessary.
*Soma*, 6.4.16, p. 485. *The maxim of the flow of a river* (*nimnagāpravāhanyāya*).

There is excessive effort involved in diverting elsewhere—by means of the maxim of the flow of a river—the stream of wealth and other accumulations gathered since beginningless time that has already set out toward another destination.
*Saṃgraha*.
The analogy of the flow of a river:

Just as insects and other creatures carried by the current of a river do not find rest as they quickly move from one whirlpool to another, so too living beings, wandering through birth after birth and deluded by their own karma, never attain happiness.
As it is said in the *Pañcadaśī*: "They perform actions for the sake of experiencing [their fruits], and they experience [the fruits] in order to perform further actions."
In the Nairṛtī river, those insects quickly move from whirlpool to whirlpool;
passing from birth to birth, they never attain liberation.
Only at the end of the ripening of their wholesome karma, when they are uplifted by the impulse of compassion, do they escape.
"Having reached the shade of the bank, they rest at their ease. [Sāhasī 151] The bark is exceedingly fragrant like sandalwood, yet it does not possess the scent of other perfumes.

Ku. 1|1|6|13: *Naimittika* Vedic action is that which has a fixed occasion (*niyatanimittaka*), such as "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives" and "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring. Bāla. p. 85: The injunction regarding the qualification of a person for occasional rites (*naimittika-puruṣādhikāravidhi*) based on a fixed occasion is "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives. p. 14: For mantras have a fixed sequence of words.
Bhāṣya 1.4.4:

Even the restrictive rule (*niyama*), consisting of lifelong repetition, is not a property of the action (*karmadharma*); rather, it is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*), as stated in [Sūtra] 2.4.12: "Or [it belongs] to the agent, because of its connection with the scriptural injunction.
Bhāṣya 8.1.3.21: The restrictive rule is taught as something that ought to be performed.
That which ought to be performed results in merit;
that which ought not to be performed results in evil.
This is the principle based on the rule: "But the restriction [of the fee] is by means of the sacrificial gifts, because of their connection with the Vedic revelation" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.3.7.17).

By the statement regarding the *ṛtvij* (priest), the injunction for the pure selection (*varaṇa*) [of the priests] is established; otherwise, there would be the contingency of the *ṛtvij*s being subordinate to the act of giving. Furthermore, because the requirement is satisfied by the single word "one should choose" (*varayet*), the sentences concerning the *adhvaryu* and others would result in being incapable of supporting the choice through an alternative (*vikalpa*) with respect to the *ṛtvij*s. However, if these are injunctions for specific types of *ṛtvij*s, then by the principle "but it is a restriction" (*niyamastu*), since the status of being an *ṛtvij* is determined specifically for the *adhvaryu* and others, the knowledge of the specific individuals to be chosen is accomplished. (Sūtra 3.7.18, p. 23). But the restriction is by means of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), because of the connection with the Vedic text.
It was previously established that in the Jyotiṣṭoma there are seventeen *ṛtvij*s.
Now, it is considered: which are those seventeen?

The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view that any seventeen out of the twenty-seven [factors] may be intended. It is not a lack of restriction; rather, there is indeed a restriction.

That [the distribution of the sacrificial fee] is to be understood as being connected with the *dakṣiṇās* (sacrificial fees) through the conjunction of the words "Agnīdh" and so forth with the word "Śrutīnām" (of the scriptures), by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is because in the sentence concerning the sacrificial fee—"One hundred and twelve is the fee"—which begins with "He gives the fee to the priests," "first he gives to the Agnīdh," "then to the Brahman," "then to the Hotṛ," and so on, up to "an endless [fee] to the Pratihartṛ," the coreferentiality of the terms "to the Agnīdh," "to the Brahman," and so forth, with the phrase "to the priests" (*ṛtvigbhyaḥ*) is heard in the scriptural text.
Therefore, it is heard that only seventeen priests— excluding the *camasādhvaryus*— are connected with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Consequently, they alone are designated as the "seventeen officiating priests" (*ṛtvij*),
because their status as sacrificers (*yajamāna*) is established by the injunction for their initiation (*dīkṣā*).

In the Siddhānta (the final conclusion), this Sūtra is presented to establish another reason: in the Satra sacrifice, having stated that "those who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are themselves the sacrificers (*yajamāna*"), it describes their initiation (*dīkṣā*) as follows: "Having initiated the Adhvaryu and the Gṛhapati, he initiates the Brahman; then the Udgātṛ; then the Hotṛ. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated them, initiates the Ardhins: the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin for the Brahman, the Prastotṛ for the Udgātṛ, and the Maitrāvaruṇa for the Hotṛ."
Then, having initiated him, the *tṛtīyins* initiate [the others]: the *agnīdh* for the *brahman*, the *pratihartṛ* for the *udgātṛ*, and the *acchāvāka* for the *hotṛ*.
Then, having initiated him, the *unnetṛ* [initiates];
this is the rule for the purpose of the restriction.
"He initiates the *pādin* [cup-bearer], the *potṛ* for the *brahman*, the *subrahmaṇya* for the *udgātṛ*, and the *prāvastṛt* for the *hotṛ*.

A Brāhmaṇa initiates them, or a religious student (*brahmacārī*) sent by his teacher"—since initiation is enjoined by this sentence, it is understood that only these possess the status of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, there are exactly seven priests, excluding the *camasādhvaryus*.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include another reason.
What [is that]? A restrictive rule (*niyama*): namely, that in the *upāṃśuyāja*, which belongs to the framework of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is a restriction regarding the deity.
Bhāṣya 10.8.16.49–50. This is either a restrictive rule (*niyama*) or an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), and it is not set aside by a logical argument (*nyāya*).
"But why is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) not accepted as one that effects mere permanence?
(Vārttika 1.3.8.27, p. 282). "The restrictive rule applies to those with multiple deities; there would be a modification. [Examples include:
"He offers these animals to the Ādityas for the sake of desire," and "One should offer the *dhūma* animal to the Viśvedevas"; such are the animals with multiple deities.

In the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, which follows the model of the archetype (prakṛti), the term *medhapati* appears in both the singular and dual forms: "to the two lords of the sacrifice" (*medhapatibhyām medham*) and "to the lord of the sacrifice" (*medhapataye medham*). These two forms are extended by the rule of transfer (*codaka*) even when there are many deities.
In that case, the dual form ("to the two lords of the sacrifice") must be modified into the plural form (*medhapatibhyaḥ medham*).
In the deliberation as to whether the singular ending is set aside, or whether both [the dual and singular] are applied optionally, he states the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view:
there is a rule that even in the case of a deity that is plural, only the dual ending is extended (atideśa);
and in that case, there would be a modification (vikāra) consisting of the dropping (jaha) by means of the plural ending.
Or it is an option, as in the case of the original form (*prakṛti*).
By the word "or," he sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
It is true that the term *medhapati*, which ends in the dual number, must be modified [to the plural].
However, even for that which ends in the singular number, there would be an option as in the case of the base (*prakṛti*); that too would function by way of an option.
The singular number is not contradictory when intended to refer to a group (*gaṇa*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that both [the singular and the plural] function by way of an option.

The rule (niyama) is that for a Vedic [act], only a Vedic cause is the occasion. There is an exception (vyabhicāra) to this in the case of the *kṣāmavatī* offerings and others. Parākrama [states]: "And the rule is a mental act."

Bhāṣya 10.2.18.49: When there is the possibility of an application occurring elsewhere as well, a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is one that restricts the application to a specific subject. Bālakrīḍā, p. 17. A preclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*) occurs when there is the possibility of application both there and elsewhere, as in: "He takes hold of the horse with [the mantra] *imāmagṛbhṇan raśanāmṛtasya*. p. 26.
An example of a restrictive injunction where something dependent on another serves a different purpose is: "One desiring vigor should make the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *khadira* wood."
Su. P. 321: If there were an abandonment of the intended application of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), it would result in a contradiction with established practice (*ācāra*).
Bhāṣya 11.3.16.14: There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the lifelong nature of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* restrictive rule to the *saurya* sacrifice and others.
[This refers to] the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule.

"Even when something is already seen [to be established] everywhere, an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), whether for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), due to the distinctness of their connection. (Vārttika 1.3.8.27, p. 283). By means of the purpose of a restrictive rule, that which has an entirely unseen purpose is set aside; this is an "annulment of what was not previously established" (*aprāptabādha*).
Vārttika 1.3.17.48, p. 860: The *apūrva* produced by a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is not brought about by the action itself. Vārttika 2.4.11, p.
371: Regarding the *apūrva* of a restriction—since a restrictive rule lacks a perceptible fruit, one must postulate an *apūrva* generated by it.
An example of that which is produced by the rule of threshing is as follows:

Ke. 2.13. This statement, "He offers in the Āhavanīya fire," has the purpose of restriction. For even without this verbal injunction, the offering in the Āhavanīya and elsewhere would have been established [as options].

This is an injunction of restriction (*niyama*). Bhāṣya 12.2.13 states: "An injunction is sometimes for the purpose of restriction" (6.3.4.16). [The meaning is: "One should apply all the ritual properties of the *homa* to that very [substance], and the deficient properties of the *soma* residing in the *pūtīka* plants."
For he will say: "For the purpose of restriction" (Vārttika 3.6.15.40). The purpose of restriction in the third sūtra is that the initial rule [applies] only when there is exclusion.
3.2.8: A purpose not previously established, when being enjoined, does not serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Vārttika 6.3.4.16: Restrictive rules concern the injunctions regarding the agent, place, and time.
Bhāṣya 4.2.12.23–24: An auditory mention of a quality serves as a restrictive rule.
In the Agniṣṭoma, it is directly heard in scripture that "if one should not find Soma, one should press Pūtīkas"; thus, the substitute for Soma is indeed explicitly stated as being called Pūtīka.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether that Pūtīka is subject to the same injunctions (*samānavidhāna*) as Soma or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which, in the absence of a specific rule, is initially reached—is that it is not. This is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):
the scriptural mention (*śruti*) of the quality—the Pūtīka, which is a quality of the sacrifice—is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

"In the absence of *soma*, something similar to *soma* is to be taken, and nothing else"—this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). An analysis of restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) shows that restriction (*niyama*) arises from the rule: "Only the *pūtīka* plant, which is similar to *soma*, is to be taken, and not anything else."
And that *pūtīka* plant is substituted for *soma* as its representative, not merely as a substance for the sacrifice.
Therefore, the *pūtīka* is subject to the same injunctions as *soma*.

The meaning is that all the properties of *soma*, such as its purchase and so forth, are enjoined for the *pūtīka* from the very beginning by the extended application (*codaka*), even without [the explicit mention of] the original injunction.

Regarding the phrase "guṇaśrutiḥ," the reading in the *Kutūhala* is "punaḥśrutiḥ," but the meaning remains the same. If it is argued that this scriptural statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthā*), we say no; for it is impossible to exclude by means of a restriction those things already established by scripture.

In the first place, every restrictive rule (*niyama*) is improper because its result is merely the exclusion of others. Nevertheless, in cases where other entities are implied by the sense of the matter, the hearing of one [term] excludes the other. (Vārttika 2.1.2–16–18, p. 564). The Vedic revelation exists for the purpose of restriction.

What is this restriction (*niyama*)? It is the necessity of that which was previously unrestricted. Bhāṣya 4.2.12.24: That which would apply even in the absence of an injunction, yet is heard [in the text], is called a restriction when it enters into the scope of what was previously unrestricted.
Ṭup: Regarding restrictive injunction (niyama) and exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā).

Even though there is no difference in the exclusion of the other alternative, in a case where—in a ritual application such as "one should sacrifice on level ground" (*same yajeta*)—the level ground is not otherwise obtained, the injunction implies a mandate (*vidhyākṣepa*) to bring about that which has not been established by scripture. Since the exclusion of the uneven ground and so forth—which would otherwise obtain—is attained through the exclusion of the other, it is the first to present itself. Because it is specifically associated with the level ground and thus proximate, and because its nature is positive (*bhāvarūpa*), it possesses a lighter form; therefore, the fulfillment of the unobtained portion is its result. The avoidance of the uneven day, however, is not a result in itself, but follows by implication from the performance of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) consisting in the fulfillment of the unobtained portion. In the case of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), since both alternatives are already established, the fulfillment of an unobtained portion is impossible as a result; thus, the result is solely the exclusion of the other. Consequently, in the statement "one should sacrifice only on level ground," the use of the particle *eva* expresses the exclusion of non-application (*ayogavyavaccheda*) as the realized meaning, and not the exclusion of other applications (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) as in the case of *parisaṃkhyā*. This distinction between *niyama* and *parisaṃkhyā* constitutes the third type of injunction (*vidhiprakāra*), which cannot be avoided.

*Soma*, 4.2.9: Rules of restriction (*niyamavidhi*) and exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*) generally concern only the application (*viniyoga*). *Maṇi*, p. 99: "In the case of a substance, the mention of a quality is for the purpose of enjoining a restrictive rule:
'One should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu.'"
"One should offer a caru oblation moistened with Soma made of white rice";
"One should offer a caru oblation to Indra made of black rice," and so forth.
Bhāṣya 4.2.10.25: A restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) has only an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).

For example, when in the archetype (*prakṛti*) there is an option between the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans], both serving an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding one of them is heard in a certain modified rite (*vikṛti*). (Vāla. p. 24). A restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is an injunction for purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the *anvāhārya*. (Bhā. 4.2.1.126). A restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is an injunction concerning the agent, place, or time.
"For the sacrificial rite of the *abhīhotra*, there is one officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); for the sacrificial rites of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, there are four officiating priests;
for the sacrificial rites of the *cāturmāsya*, there are five officiating priests;
for the sacrificial rite of the animal sacrifice (*paśuyajña*), there are six officiating priests; and for the sacrificial rite of the *saumya-adhvara*, there are seventeen officiating priests."
"One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]" and "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on ground sloping toward the east.

"One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day. (Bhāṣya 4.2.12.23–24). Regarding the futility of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), there is the statement: "One should sacrifice with Soma."
VI. 4.2.9. Restrictive Injunction (*niyamavidhi*).

"A restriction (*niyama*) occurs when there is a possibility [of an option]. When, because something has been previously mentioned, a partial application is possible, the injunction that operates by fulfilling the unobtained alternative is called a *niyama* because it restricts; for example, "One threshes the rice grains.

Since its purpose is simply the preparation of the rice grains, it is established that the result of an injunction is not merely the attainment of what was unobtained, but rather the fulfillment of the unobtained portion.
And on the view that those [grains] are not obtained, they would be drawn in because of the nourishment provided by the rice grains;
however, since the old [grains] already exist, their cessation occurs by implication (*arthāt*), not from the sentence itself, nor is there a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for that purpose.

Vārttika 2.2.3.4, p. 152: A restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is sublated by a counter-injunction (*pratiprasavavidhi*). Bālamanoramā, p. 144: [The restrictive injunction] is subject to option (*vikalpa*). Parākrama 40.2: A restrictive injunction is, for example, in the Vājapeya sacrifice: "He gives the chariot used in the sacrifice to the *adhvaryu*"; here, it is restricted to the *adhvaryu* alone.

Ci. 10.3.20. Restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*): In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) such as the *Vājapeya*, when one of several optional archetypal elements is restated. Bhā. 10.1.6.51–57. Restrictive injunction: Regarding the quality of whiteness in the *Vāyavya* animal sacrifice, "One should sacrifice a white [animal] to Vāyu" (*vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta*). Vi. 4.2.10. By means of a restrictive injunction, an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) is established.

Just as in the Bālamanoramā (p. 182), where a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) establishes an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*), such as "one should approach one's wife during her season" (p.
143); all varieties of restrictive injunctions are thus explained.
Furthermore, it should be observed in the Vindī [commentary] on the Mīmāṃsāprakāśa that "injunction (*vidhi*) is also of two kinds."
The analysis of restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) by the author of the *Maṇi* (Pārthasārathi Miśra) is to be found in the *Vidhinirṇaya* section of the *Tantravārttika*.
Regarding the possibility of a restrictive injunction, [there is] the *niyoga* at 2354.
Because when a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is possible, it cannot be a novel injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).
*Soma* 6.7.9. A teaching of restriction (*niyamaśāsana*) is understood to have as its object a case where there would otherwise be the contingency of non-restriction (*aniyamaprasaṅga*).
*Bhāṣya* 1.2.13.
If a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is possible, an absence of restriction (*aniyama*) is untenable. *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 525. Proximity (*ānantarya*) is not the restrictive factor.

*Bhāṣya* 3.1.14.24–25. The enjoined sentence—“One should touch this very [wind] while it is being employed in speech”—has the purpose of enjoining another ritual act involving two fields, wherein the deity is Vāyu characterized by the quality of being employed (*niyuktatva*).
*Soma*, 1.2.1, p. 5: *Niyoga* is that which denotes what is to be done (*kārya*), such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others.

When Devadatta is being prompted by the words of a teacher or similar authority—such as "Devadatta, fetch the fuel"—an observer standing nearby determines this: "This activity of his is preceded by cognition; for just as I have acted after having understood [the meaning], so too does he act now, since he is not different from me. And I did not act merely because of the action itself, nor merely from the understanding of a result, nor even from the understanding of the action being a means to a result, but rather from the understanding of its being something to be accomplished (*kāryatā*)."
As long as even an action such as suckling at the breast was not understood by me as something to be done (*kārya*), I did not engage in it.

Nor is that very status of being a means to the good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatā*) the same as the status of being something to be done. The quality of being a means toward the good is one thing, whereas the status of being something to be done—characterized as the primary object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with respect to human effort or exertion (*kṛti*)—is another. Thus, the dull-witted do not perceive the difference between the two: that the "to-be-done-ness" of an action follows from its being a means to a result, while the "to-be-done-ness" of pleasure follows from its being a result itself.

Thus, since there is an understanding of the task (kārya) even without its being easily accessible as a means to a result, Devadatta infers: "My activity arises from a cognition of a task distinct from being a means to a result; therefore, he too must be prompted by the very same cognition.
And since this cognition of his arises from something other than [perception], it must be a verbal one; thus, he concludes that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others denote the task (*kārya*).

Since it is established that the denotable object is that which is connected to the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished), in sentences such as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," it is settled that the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) must be presented as the *niyojya* (the person to be directed) by means of the word "desiring heaven" in accordance with the genitive case-ending.

And he who understands the *kārya* is the *niyojya*. Furthermore, for the one desiring heaven, there is a connection (*anvaya*) with that very *kārya* equivalent to [the agent's] understanding, insofar as it alone is capable of being experienced as the means to that which is desired by him.
Furthermore, an action that perishes in a single moment cannot be the cause of a result that occurs at a later time.

Therefore, it is connected by implication with the person to be impelled (niyojya) as something to be accomplished; for only that which is to be accomplished even at a later time enters into a logical concomitance (anvaya) with that person.

Thus, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote an object to be accomplished (*kārya*) that is distinct from the action and is known solely through another means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*).
And because it is not previously known through any other means of knowledge (*māna*), it is called "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*).

Now, one might ask: from what is that effect established? If you say "from the sacrifice and so forth," then it follows that the fruit must occur immediately after [the action], since that which occurs immediately after an action is the cause of the fruit. To this, it is replied:
Even if that [cause] has been produced immediately [before], its fruit will not arise immediately, because a delay is possible due to the dependence upon auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).
Nor does the dependence upon auxiliary factors entail a loss of causal capacity.
If it is asked, "What is that auxiliary factor?", we reply: "Space, time, and so forth."
Nor does that [apūrva] have any manifestation apart from its specific excellence (viśeṣa).

Nor is there a loss of the status of the apūrva as the meaning of the sentence because it is subordinate to the production of the fruit; for it assumes a state of being favorable toward the fruit in order to obtain its own subordinate qualities and the person to be enjoined (niyojya).
Just as a master, while bestowing consciousness upon himself alone, benefits his slave born in the house, so too is this case.

Consequently, since the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of meanings as already connected) is established, it is understood that in common worldly usage, the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and others denote an *niyoga* (an injunction). [Ṛjuvimalā, pp.
287–88] An *niyoga* is that by which one is enjoined (*niyujyate*); thus, the injunctive suffix and so forth, which are denoted by the word *niyoga*, are the means of enjoining (*niyukti*).
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 16: "Niyoga," "vidhi," "preraṇā," and "śabdabhāvanā" have one and the same meaning.
*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 75: "The single niyoga is differentiated according to the distinction of its adjuncts (*anubandha*).

*Bṛhatī*, p. 19: "Furthermore, in the context of optional rites (*kāmādhikāra*), the niyoga does not state that the sacrifice is something to be performed (*kartavyatā*), because the status of being something to be performed is established solely by way of the result."
*Ṛjuvimalā*, page 29: "That toward which a person is enjoined is the *viṣaya* (object/domain). Thus, the status of being a *viṣaya* does not arise from being a motivator (*preraka*) for the action.
What then? It is that wherein the person is enjoined by the action, meaning the task (*kārya*) is made known.
For the enjoining of a person consists precisely in making the task known.

This is what is meant: through the ritual action, such as a sacrifice, the *niyoga* (the mandate) is understood as the effect to be accomplished; it does not, however, impel one toward the action itself.
(Page 30). Even the *niyoga* for a widow is improper for a celibate student.
(Sūtrārthasamgraha, Page 185).

Having raised doubts regarding many modes of verbal expression (*vacanavyakti*) according to the principle stated in [Vākyapadīya 1.3.130, p. 293]: "By way of necessity (*niyoga*), by way of option (*vikalpa*), or both together as a conjunction (*samuccita*); or as a collection (*saṃcaya*), or as a composite whole (*samudāya*), or as a qualified unity (*viśiṣṭaikya*)."
Su. pṛ. 742.
Regarding the *niyoga*:

even in the case of a worldly matter that is cognizable through other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is determined that the *niyoga* does not depend on the establishment of a relationship between a goal and its means.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 148.

[The term] *niyoga* is a synonym for [the injunctive force]; [it is called so] because one attains a human activity that constitutes the object of the injunction (*vidhi*), which is itself a synonym for *niyoga*. This is the meaning of the sentence expressing the *niyoga*.
Su. Pṛ. 756.
The presentation [of the view] that the meaning of a sentence is *niyoga* (an injunction), and its refutation (*Kaṇikā*).
First, it is understood from the words of teachers—such as "Boy, fetch the fuel"—that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote something to be accomplished (*kārya*).

For instance, having observed the student proceeding to fetch fuel immediately after hearing this sentence, an onlooker who has attained linguistic proficiency determines as follows: "His activity is preceded by cognition, because it is an independent activity, like my own activity.
And just as I act upon having cognized something, so too does he, because he is no different from me.

Furthermore, I do not act merely from the cognition of an action, nor merely from the cognition of a result, nor even from the cognition of a result's means; rather, I act from the cognition of it as a *kārya* (something to be accomplished)."
Indeed, there is no activity—such as the desire to suckle at the breast and so forth—that occurs even for a frog unless it has first been understood by me through the Blessed One [the Veda].

Nor is the state of being a means to the good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*) identical to the state of being an end to be accomplished (*kāryatā*), because they are based on a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion. For it is impossible that the very same thing which is a means toward what is desired could simultaneously be the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with respect to human effort (*kṛti*).

Some, however, perceiving no difference, have held that for an action, being an object to be accomplished (*kāryatā*) is necessarily concomitant with its being a means to a result (*phalasādhanatā*), which they consider to be the internal organ of affliction (*kleśamanas*).
Yet, there is an understanding of being an object to be accomplished even without the ease of [knowing] it as a means to a result.

Therefore, because activity arises from the cognition of an "object to be accomplished" (*kārya*) distinct from being a means to a result, even a child determines that his own activity proceeds precisely from the cognition of that [distinct object].
And the comprehension of that [meaning] arises for him immediately following the teacher’s words;
thus, those who maintain that the word denotes an action (kārya) postulate that this comprehension is based solely upon that [action].

And since that action is established as the denoted meaning in its state of being related [to other factors], it is settled that in sentences such as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," the person desiring heaven is presented as the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) by means of the term "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), in accordance with the use of the genitive case-ending.

And he who understands what is to be done (*kārya*) is the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*). For one who desires heaven, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with that very thing to be done, provided it is capable of being experienced as the means to that which is desired.
Furthermore, an action (*kriyā*), being momentary, cannot be the cause of a result that occurs at a later time.
It does not connect with the person to be enjoined as something to be accomplished (*kārya*).

Since that which is a task (*kārya*) even for another time must connect with that [person], the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. denote a "task" (*kārya*) that is distinct from action and is known only through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). Because it is not known through other means of knowledge, it is called "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*); because it is necessarily perceived as a task, it is designated as "enjoinment" (*niyoga*) since it enjoins the person toward the self.
