Nor does the action, even though it occurs immediately [after its performance], produce heaven and so forth only immediately by depending on auxiliary factors such as place and time.

Furthermore, there is no loss of the *apūrva*’s status as the meaning of the sentence due to its being subordinate to the production of the fruit, because it adopts a state of being conducive to the fruit in order to obtain the status of an object for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), who is itself subordinate to that fruit.
It is just as a master, while providing benefit to himself, assists his slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*). Thus it is said.

Nor is it the case that linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) arises solely from the Veda; for proficiency derived from common worldly usage itself extends, in accordance with Vedic sentences, as far as the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).
Furthermore, it is not the case that the capacity of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such words to denote multiple meanings is not perceived.
For if the young student, being impelled by the teacher— that is to say, being directed toward a task—
is not indeed capable of acting unless he possesses a corresponding cognition, then,

since such commands and the like are recognized in common worldly usage and since activity is impossible without the cognition of a task, the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] occurs therein; and it is precisely this [cognition of the task] that constitutes the final goal in the case of the Veda as well.

But surely, in common usage, [meanings] such as *praiṣa* (command) and so forth are also understood; how then can it be said that the optative (*liṅ*) and other suffixes denote only the "thing to be done" (*kārya*)? These are merely adventitious conditions (*upādhi*), not the actual word-meanings. And those alone are adventitious conditions which, by the mere observation of their usage, establish a specific distinction for the word-meaning, just as "being a beast" is an adventitious condition for that which is denoted by the word *hari*. To illustrate:

Just as the words "hare's foot" (*haripada*)—because they do not enter into the denotation [of the hare's foot itself]—are restricted to the animal [called the hare], so too the injunctions (*praiṣa*) and the like, because they do not enter into the denotation [of the specific action], establish themselves in a particular function; they are not, however, the denotata [themselves]. Since the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] is thus possible, it is logical that the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. denote an injunction (*niyoga*).

The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*); however, that which is to be done is the action (*kriyā*) itself, not the *apūrva*, because the capacity of words is determined by worldly usage.
Furthermore, it is precisely that [action] which, as a task to be accomplished, serves as the cause for engagement, since it is known through another means of knowledge within one's own experience.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that this *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge, yet in the world, for those who understand the existence of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth merely as expressing 'what ought to be done' (*kartavyatā*), there arises in the Veda the apprehension of a specific *apūrva* through their connection with the word 'one desiring heaven' (*svargakāma*)? To this we reply: Let it be granted for now that this very "what ought to be done" is the meaning of the optative suffix; however, on what basis can it be said that this does not also apply to worldly actions? For it is an improper principle (*anyāyya*) to assume multiple meanings [for a single word].

Furthermore, since the use of worldly optative suffixes and the like in reference to an action is possible through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and because the "what ought to be done" pertaining to an *apūrva* is invariably concomitant (*āntarīyakatva*) with the "what ought to be done" of the action itself.
Because it is impossible for an action whose status as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) is not established to serve as the means to that [apūrva],
since this does not contradict worldly usage;

whereas, in the case of the status of the *apūrva* as something to be performed, one never observes its being invariably concomitant with the status of worldly actions as things to be performed, and thus the reverse is impossible.

If it is argued that because of the practice of extreme usage, even a word with a secondary (lakṣaṇika) meaning may be taken as having a primary denotative power (vācakatva), and thus the injunction (*niyoga*) expressing the *apūrva* is established—[we reply: But from what source is this principle that a word may have multiple meanings? If you say it is because of the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating multiple potencies (*śakti*), [we ask: But since the *apūrva* also occurs in various forms as the primary or subsidiary parts of a sacrifice, how can the optative suffix (*liṅ*) have a single meaning? If you argue that because the "state of being to-be-done" (*kṛtisādhyatā*), which is the cause for engagement (*pravṛttinimitta*), is common to all instances, the optative suffix has a single potency for the *apūrvas* despite their formal differences—just as it does in the case of "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*) and so on—then alas! What wrong has the action (*kriyā*) committed here, which consists of the state of being to-be-done, such that the optative suffix and others, after denoting it, do not prefer to narrow down their other potencies like a husband?

If it is argued that there is no fault because, despite the identity of the word "to be performed" (*kartavyatā*), there is a difference in what is to be performed—[we reply: No, because there is no difference.

If one should think: "Even though there is an identity of the word 'to be performed,' nevertheless, in the case of the *apūrva*, 'to be performed' means the state of being the most desired object (*īpsitatamatā*) for the sake of which human effort (*kṛti*) proceeds; for human effort proceeds toward the *apūrva* with that as its objective."
And that very [apūrva] is also the cause for the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth.
Nor is the "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā) of such a nature as the action itself, because since that [action] is suffering, it cannot be the primary object; rather, it is the apūrva.

The "to-be-done-ness" of that [apūrva] consists in its being the object of an effort directed toward the attainment of rice and the like, which are characterized by being pervaded by that effort; and that [to-be-done-ness] is the domain of the optative suffix and so forth, since it cannot otherwise be established without some other means.
That is not so; for there is no distinction regarding the necessity of performing the action. Indeed, an effort (*kṛti*) cannot be set in motion unless the *apūrva* has been established.
For that [desire] is indeed human effort;
and that [effort] follows upon desire, so it would be cut off precisely there.
Whatever is the action of desire, that alone is its object, namely pleasure, because desire is well-disposed toward what is pleasant.

And [if you argue] that the *apūrva* is not happiness, how can this be so? If it is undesirable (*aniṣṭa*), how can there be an engagement in action for its sake? If it is argued that because it is understood as such from the word, even though it is not happiness and even though it is undesirable, the *apūrva* is the primary object with respect to the action—do we then say that the word makes something known that one does not desire to obtain? Or is consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), according to the Vedic scripture, "Consciousness is bliss"?
If it is argued that this is not so because of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no;
for here too, that [contradiction] is equal.

This is because it is accepted that the *apūrva*—which has the fuel (*samid*) and other materials as its object and is itself to be performed—is to be carried out as something subsequent to the [primary] qualification for performance;

and since the *apūrva* is conducive to heaven, even though it is not pleasure itself, it remains an object of desire. If it is asked, "In that case, how could there be a contradiction with another means of knowledge? we say: no, for even in the case of an action, its status as a means to what is desired is likewise established.
Because there is no possibility of those two [the apūrva and the fruit] being devoid of a result in the case of a prohibition regarding a contingent rite (*naimittika*),
the *apūrva* of the prohibitions regarding contingent rites is not established by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth.

This is because there is no contradiction in understanding the necessity of performing the action for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), who is characterized by the possession of the contingency and is delimited by the specific qualification of being the agent of the prohibited action.

Furthermore, because it coexists with the primary constituent parts of the ritual complex, its validity is established even through the mediation of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), which is not directly denoted by the words and is postulated based on what has been experienced.

Moreover, why would the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), who is characterized by the attainment of heaven, not consider the action itself as the "how-to" (*itikartavyatā*)? It is because that action, being subject to extremely rapid destruction, lacks the capacity to be conducive to that result; for something is conducive to the attainment of a goal only when it exists at the time the goal is realized, not when it has ceased. And a result such as heaven, which belongs to the next world, does not come to pass upon the performance of the act if that act has long since perished.

If it is argued that [the *apūrva*] exists because it arises in relation to that [sacrifice], then does the *adhikārāpūrva* (the apūrva of entitlement) not also possess the status of being a means (*sādhana*) in the case of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices? Or do you merely figuratively accept its possession of a means? For if it were merely figurative, its connection with the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure) would not be possible.
A boy who possesses only a figurative fire is never employed for the purposes of burning or cooking.
Furthermore, you admit that these [sacrifices] have a single objective (*viṣaya*), yet you maintain that the duty (*kartavya*) to be performed is manifold.
This is because those two consist of different modes of metaphorical application (*upacāra*) regarding the primary element (*pradhāna*).
For the object, which is connected to the understanding, ceases to exist as it actually stands [in its differentiated state].

In that regard, the *Āgneya* and other rites, though uttered [separately], are understood only once by the statement: "One should sacrifice for the sake of prosperity with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*).

In the same way, they experience the object; thus, their status as objects pertains to the *apūrva* (the unseen potential) of the entitlement (*adhikāra*). However, their status as instruments (*karaṇatva*) pertains to the subsequent realization (*pratipatti*). And that [instrumentality] depends on the essential nature [of the act], not on the realization.

And the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of these [rites], such as the *āgneya* and others, is understood from such injunctions as "The *āgneya* [cake] on eight potsherds," and so forth; the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*) that follows from that [nature] is likewise established. Nor is it the case that there is a state of being a means for those [rites] while they are mutually independent.
This is because the supreme *apūrva* is established in dependence upon conceptualization based on what has been heard (*śruta*).
Furthermore, many instruments (*karaṇa*) for this [apūrva] are heard in scripture; thus, it cannot be the case that it is unachievable through a single means.
Indeed, even in the world, it is observed that a single action can be accomplished by multiple instruments.
Just as it is said that "the king moves about with a lamp," even though he moves by means of the axle, the sword in hand, and the horses;

if you argue that there is a distinction between the instruments (sādhana) such as the eye and so forth due to their intermediate operations (avāntaravyāpāra), then here too, the [mental] states preceded by the [sensory] contacts are themselves the intermediate operations, and they differ according to the respective objects of cognition (prameya) and so on— thus the two cases are the same.
And thus, even when [the sacrifices] are being performed together, there is no confusion of their respective properties (*dharma*).

This is because, although they are all prompted by the ultimate *apūrva*, the means of accomplishment (*sādhanabhāva*) differs due to the distinction between the intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*) and the production-*apūrvas* (*utpattyapūrva*), and because those properties are restricted to their specific means of accomplishing the *apūrva*.
Otherwise, if there were no such distinction, it would follow that there is a confusion of properties.

Therefore, just as at the time of the originality (*apūrvatva*) of the qualification (*adhikāra*), the intermediate operations— the *apūrvas*— are capable of being understood as the subordinate functions of the *niyoga* (the meaning of the sentence of injunction), even though the Āgneya and other rites have not yet [directly] attained the status of means according to the verbal expression; so too, they are understood as having the status of means with respect to the fruit.
The intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) or the potency (*śakti*) of the ritual action will reside in the *apūrva*.
[Objection: How can there be a potency of one thing that does not inhere in it, or how can it possess an operation if it does not exist?

[Reply: If you say it is an "intermediate operation," then the same applies to the intermediate operations of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices which are the means to the ultimate *apūrva*; for they are equal in their status as being *apūrva*, since their connection with the final result is identical.

If it is argued that, since the *āgneya* and other sacrifices have their status as means (*sādhanabhāva*) understood from words independent [of other injunctions], and because they cannot coexist [simultaneously], the intermediate operations (*vyāpāra*) or capacities (*sāmarthya*)—even if residing in other things and even if not occurring at the same time—are what constitute the *apūrva*, then why is it not understood, in accordance with worldly usage, that "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*" implies an action qualified by the heaven to be accomplished? Or rather, why would the suffix not indicate its own specific object in the form of the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*), such that, failing that, an intermediate operation or capacity—not the *apūrva*—would be attributed to the action? It is false to say that an action which is the means to the means of the fruit is not the means to the fruit itself, for it becomes a means to that fruit precisely through the activity directed toward the fruit.

Just as the *āgneya* and other rites, which are engaged in as means to the ultimate *apūrva*, possess the status of being means to the intermediate *apūrvas*; and just as the act of plowing, though engaged in for the purpose of reaching the harvest, possesses the status of being a means to breaking the soil and so forth;
it is not correct to say that the *āgneya* and other rites are the means to the ultimate *apūrva* only through their being means to the intermediate *apūrvas*.

For in the expressions "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "one should sacrifice," there is no denotation of the intermediate *apūrvas*; rather, there is the denotation of the collective groups of the six rites—the *āgneya* and others—which are enjoined and mentioned in connection with specific times.

Nor can they, by means of their own operation, establish that the *apūrvas* preceded by those [ritual acts] possess causality toward the result as it truly is; for the *apūrva* of the qualification (*adhikāra*)— which is conveyed by the power of denotation (*abhidhāśakti*) in the immediate proximity of the qualifying statement— is apprehended instantaneously, whereas the [apūrvas] belonging to the subordinate acts (*upatti*) cannot be so determined, because that would lead to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Because it is only that whose power is fixed which makes [the meaning] known, and because it is precisely by virtue of making [the meaning] known that it is equivalent to the *śakya* (the denotable).

It might be thought: "This is the greatness of words such as the optative (*liṅ*), that they cause one to understand their own meaning even though their power is not fixed. This, however, is without authority.

If it is granted that the suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) can be derived from common worldly usage by signifying merely an action to be performed (*kārya*), then it is untenable to postulate that they possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) for something whose relationship [to the word] has not been grasped, on the grounds of their being distinct from other words.
If it is argued that this is postulated because the cognition of an unprecedented task (*apūrva-kārya*) arises from Vedic sentences, we say no;
for that very [cognition] is unestablished.

It is established by the force of linguistic usage (*nyutpatti*) that it is action alone (*kriyā*) that is understood from Vedic sentences as the task to be accomplished (*kārya*), whereas the notion that an unprecedented task (*apūrva-kārya*) is perceived is merely a mental fabrication. Therefore, how could an optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like, whose relationship [to its meaning] has not been grasped, denote an unprecedented task?
Thus, the task (*kārya*) is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

For it is only that which is already denoted [by one word] that another word denotes. Thus, how could other words ever express their own meanings as related [to that first object], when such a relation lies far beyond the path of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*)? Since that [first object] is not perceived, there is no perception of anything related to it; consequently, the determination of the connection with the *sūtra* (the primary term) is impossible. Therefore, the idea that other words convey their own meanings as related to that [first object] is utterly discarded.
He begins the final conclusion: "To this it is replied:

When indeed Caitra is told by a single person, 'Caitra, bring water,' and Caitra brings it, then another who possesses a similar understanding of the relationship between word and meaning understands it in that very same way."
"This activity is preceded by cognition.

Having observed the activity directed toward a specific object in one who has understood [the meaning] solely upon hearing the sentence containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, the child learning [the language] reflects thus: "This voluntary activity of his is preceded by my own cognition."

Furthermore, this reflection arises in him: "That which I have undertaken after having understood it, this [other person] has also done; and that cognition which was the cause of my undertaking, being directed toward a certain object, is the cause of his undertaking as well, being directed toward that very same object. From this, an inference based on analogy (*nyutpatti*) arises. Thus, there are these two inferences: "The undertaking of one who has already awakened [to the truth] is itself the subject (*dharmin*); it is preceded by a cognition, such is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*);
because it is an independent undertaking, like my own independent undertaking."

Likewise, the cognition that serves as the cause for the Buddha's activity is the subject (*dharmin*). That which is its object—and which, being such, is the cause of my own activity—is precisely the property (*dharma*) to be proven regarding him as well:
"Because he possesses a cognition that is the cause of activity, just like my own cognition that is the cause of activity.
Furthermore, this reflection arises concerning him:

However, that object which is made known to me by this word—namely, the object of that cognition which serves as the cause for my activity—is made known by the word in its own proper place, because [the word] is understood when that object exists. But in my case, that object is made known by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*); this is the distinction between us. Since my activity arises from a cognition of a certain thing, one determines that the word makes known that very object which is the cause of activity, by means of the word in its own proper place.

Furthermore, in order to determine what that object which serves as the cause of activity is—that which is denoted by the word—he reflects upon the cause of activity already apprehended within himself: "In that case, having engaged through my intellect, did I act on my own accord?
He desires to know: "Acting here independently of words, having understood what, have I engaged in this activity?"
By this, it is stated that the state prior to linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is [the same].

The very cognition that an unlearned child produces within themselves by way of causing a representation is what is postulated for the proficient person as well, and nothing else; this is the meaning.
By this, the view that "it is the word itself, or the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*), which serves as the cause for activity" is refuted.
Because their names are seen to be derived from the cause of their activity;
and these two positions have not been refuted directly due to their extreme weakness.
To explain:

If the very nature of words such as the optative (*liṅ*) were the instigator of action, then all who hear them would necessarily act; however, this is not observed, as action occurs only for some at some time.
As for the claim that the operation of the optative and other suffixes is heard to be the cause of action—let the gods accept that!
We humans, with our fleshly eyes, are not capable of penetrating the realm of valid cognition to prove it.

The verbal *bhāvanā* (word-efficient-force), which consists in the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, is postulated as being of the nature of an instigation (*preraṇā*). It is conducive to the production of human activity, has its own denoted meaning as its instrument (*karaṇa*), possesses as its *itikartavyatā* (procedure) the excellence proclaimed by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and is characterized by the form of an impulsion.

For, by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*), all injunctive texts—which are denotable by the term "one's own Veda"—as well as the [verbal] self itself, are enjoined with the words "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*).
In that context, when the expectation arises as to "what [is to be brought about]," human activity is resorted to [as the object].
When there arises the expectancy as to "by what [means]," the injunction alone is accepted as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of its suitability.

For once the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) is known, it impels activity; and by virtue of that same suitability, the knowledge of excellence arising from the collection of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is assigned the status of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

For the *arthabhāvanā*— which consists of the operation of a person (*puruṣavyāpāra*), is delimited by the states such as pregnancy and so forth, has the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) as its instrument (*karaṇa*), possesses the assistance of the instruments consisting of the ritual acts obtained through Vedic, Smṛti, and customary practice, and is expressed by the same suffix [that expresses the *śabdabhāvanā*]— is supported by the knowledge of excellence (*prāśastya*) when the *śabdabhāvanā* (the operation of the injunction) is sinking.
In this regard, there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that a similar operation exists in the optative suffix (*liṅādi*) itself.

If it is argued that the very activity occurring subsequent to words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no; for activity is not observed elsewhere to be caused by that [suffix] alone.
Indeed, activity is based upon that [cognition];
having perceived that very [cognition], it is possible to infer [the suffix].
Furthermore, it is not the case that the specific operation of the word "śabda" has a causal nature that was never previously established. (pp.

25–27) And it is sheer audacity to claim that words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) alone constitute a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because a word whose relationship [to its meaning] has not been grasped is not expressive.
For when the correlate is not determined, there is an absence of the cognition of the relationship [between them].

Furthermore, in that context, by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), all prescriptive elements and the Self are enjoined. Indeed, an injunction impels a person; it is not logical that those which are impelled and that by which they are impelled should be insentient, nor is it possible for insentient things to be objects of an injunction.
If they are not objects of an injunction, what is it that is enjoined therein?
That too is untenable;
for verbal *bhāvanā* (the productive energy of words) belongs to all words by their very nature as agents, and thus they do not depend upon an application (*viniyoga*).
If it is argued that they are not employed for the purpose of impelling a person, but rather for the purpose of awakening the meaning; [we reply: so be it.
That too is not tenable,
because even in that case, the requirement for an injunction is equal. Furthermore,
the interruption of study would imply a non-acceptance of those injunctions that enjoin study in the form of the refinement of syllables (*akṣara-saṃskāra*).

And so they have said: "In which category among substances and the rest would the private recitation (svādhyāya) be included? It is rightly placed within the category of things to be consecrated (saṃskārya), for it is clearly an action, and it is that [recitation] which is directly consecrated."

Thus, the injunction for a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) is not enjoined upon the object to be purified (*saṃskārya*), because its utility has already been established by another means of knowledge. Furthermore, an injunction for a purificatory rite, which culminates in the purification itself, is not conceived as having the effect of the object to be purified as its purpose.

And since both alternatives—either that the Self is enjoined by the injunction to study or that it is employed [as an instrument]—are impossible, [the claim that the Self is the object of the injunction] is untenable.
And how does the activity of a person [proceed]? It must be its future state; for it cannot be [the result] immediately following [the activity], because it has not yet been accomplished.
For there would be no occasion for the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) for that which is produced by the injunction.
For in that case, the person's engagement would have the action itself as its fruit.
Furthermore, an action does not require an instrument for the manifestation of its own fruit; nor does the act of going require an instrument for the commencement of conjunction and disjunction.
It might be thought:

"The word, having generated the cognition of an injunction, being assisted by its instruments, initiates its own operation in the form of an impulsion; thus it possesses the status of an instrument, because the status of an instrument exists only in the accomplishment of an action. But this is unworldly.
For it is not established that anything whatsoever is the cause for the production of its own cognition;
and thus, even the commendation (prāśastya) expressed in an explanatory passage (arthavāda) possesses the status of a procedural requirement (itikartavyatā),
because its being such is due to its inherent suitability (yogyatā).
Nor can it be understood that the capacity to assist the cognition— which serves as the instrument for the verbal act of instigation— is the function of the word itself;
rather, its capacity is understood in relation to the activity performed by a person,
because such activity is observed toward what is commendable.
It might be thought: "If there is the possibility of a person engaging in what is not praiseworthy, then instigation itself is not possible.
That is incorrect; for the accomplishment of the action does not consist merely in the possibility of the result.

In the world, it is well known that the accomplishment of the fruit follows from the completion of the action; therefore, even in the case of that [action] which is fruitless, activity would occur because the impulsion is established. If it is argued that the fruit itself is included within the category of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), like the commendation (*prāśastya*), and thus in its absence the impulsion is not accomplished—then let the fruit alone be what fulfills the requirements of the procedure; what is the use of a commendation?
This is true; since that [injunction] also exists, it is not abandoned.
If this is so, then let there be no dependence on that [injunction] regarding the praise which has not been heard.

Consequently, even that construction of place and so forth—which would otherwise be untenable—is possible through the assumption of an instrument and a procedure for the injunction of the *kalpa*, just as in the case of the *darvihoma*.
It is merely a mental construction (*kalpanā-mātra*), and the example of the *darvihoma* is established;

for in that case, it is accepted that assistance is obtained merely through the performance of the required acts, such as the pouring of the substance and the invocation of the deity as prescribed by scripture, along with the customary rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*).
Indeed, it is not possible for a single entity to simultaneously possess both the status of being the benefactor (*anugrāhaka*) and the beneficiary (*anugrāhya*).

Now, it may be argued that the word indeed effects an instigation (*preraṇā*), but activity (*pravṛtti*) does not arise from the mere [existence of] that instigation; rather, it occurs when there is knowledge of it.
If this is so, then activity is simply the fruit of knowledge and not the fruit of instigation, because it exists when that [knowledge] exists and is absent when it is absent.
And this being the case, it is not established that the injunction (*vidhi*) is the verbal instigation (*śabdabhāvanā*).

Furthermore, sound must be accepted as a quality of space (*ākāśa*) by one who maintains that the sense organs function through contact; otherwise, since the ear—which is of the nature of space—and sound would lack the possibility of contact, and because contact consists in either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), and since conjunction—whether produced by the action of one of the two, by the action of both, or by another conjunction—is restricted to being a property of substances, and since sound has no such connection with space [as a substance], it follows by elimination that it is an inherence.
Thus, sound is a quality of space.
Furthermore, no such operation is possible for that [word],
because operations reside in substances.
How, then, can an operation characterized by denotation (abhidhāna) be attributed to a word?
Listen to how that is:

when that cognition of objects and cognition of words which arises immediately after [the initial perception] within the self becomes an object itself by virtue of being the action of the word, it is then called "denotation" (*abhidhāna*).
For even in a transitive operation, agency indeed belongs to the self, just as in the case of physical movement.
Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

And how is this operation of the word (*śabdavyāpāra*) the object of the objective-efficient-force (*arthabhāvanā*)? If it is argued that it is because [the two] have the same object of explanation (*ekaviṣayavyākhyeyatvāt*), [we reply: no.
As it has been said:
"How can injunction (vidhi) and the verbal root meaning (śabdārtha) be grasped by a single suffix? First of all, a connection [of the suffix] with the meaning of the root is determined."
In that regard,
on this view, it is difficult to establish that the suffix denotes *bhāvanā*.
But surely, it is determined through its grammatical coreferentiality with the verb *karoti* (to do) that all verbal suffixes denote *bhāvanā* (the efficient force).
For instance, *bhāvanā* is the activity of the instigator directed toward the agent of the action expressed by the root; and that very [activity] is *kṛti* (volitional effort).
Because that which is being honored is being performed, it constitutes the object of the action (*kṛtikarman*).
This is understood from the observation of questions and answers such as: "What did he do? He cooked (*apākṣīt*); what does he do? He cooks (*pacati*); what will he do? He will cook (*pakṣyati*).
Thus, it is understood that the meaning of "to do" (*karoti*) is expressed by all verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*).
Otherwise, if one were to ask about the object of the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do), that answer would be untenable.

For even when the verbal base (*prakṛti*) is present, the meaning of "doing" is not understood in forms such as those ending in the suffix *ghañ* (e.g., *pāka*), whereas it is understood when there is the proximity of a verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*). Thus, it is determined that this meaning belongs to the verbal suffixes alone.
That is incorrect.

If the meaning of the question "What does it do? is "What is that which it does," and if the answer were "It cooks" (*pacati*), then [the analysis] would be "it performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*); in that sense, the term *pacati* would apply.
And thus, the fact that finite verbs have "doing" (*karoti*) as their meaning would be established.
But this is not the case.
For when the specific operation denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is not yet understood, it is precisely that specific [operation] which is thus questioned;

and in that case, "he cooks" (*pacati*) is the answer. Consequently, it is not established that finite verbs (*ākhyāta*) express an object consisting of the act of "doing" (*karoti*) as something distinct from the verbal root.

Furthermore, all verbal roots (*dhātu*) signify an action that, when conducive to the coming into being of something previously non-existent, attain the sense of "doing" (*karoti*) and can thus be designated by the verb *karoti* to indicate the agent. Therefore, these very [roots] are the basis for such questions regarding their meaning.

Moreover, since both the question and the answer are logically consistent on the grounds that they express specific operations denoted by the verbal root itself, it cannot be asserted that finite verbs (*ākhyāta*) denote an "act of doing" (*karoti*) distinct from that.

Moreover, in the case of Devadatta and others who act with effort, since a distinction of operations is possible regarding an object distinct from the meaning of the root *kṛ*, the question and answer would be consistent; for when asked "What does he do?", the answer "He goes" would be appropriate only if there were an operation distinct from going. However, if the scope of the question were restricted to the specific meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then even in that case it would be inconsistent.

Now, if conjunction and disjunction are the meaning of the root, while motion (*parispanda*) is the meaning of the suffix, then too there is no inconsistency, because an operation distinct from the meaning of the root is still possible.

In this regard, since the meaning of the verbal root *gam* (to go) is exclusively motion (*parispanda*), the word *grāmaḥ* (village) would apply only to conjunction or disjunction; for it is not used with respect to a post (*sthāṇau*) when [the action] is either disjoined from or conjoined with it.
Nor does it apply to both together, because that would entail the use of *grāmaḥ* even with respect to a post when one has "jumped up and landed" (*utpatya nipatite*).

If it were argued that conjunction and disjunction produced by a single moment of action are what is denoted by the term "go," then let action alone be the denotation; why is it included within the category of adventitious attributes (upādhi)?

For in this way, determination occurs through the weight of relying upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Moreover, the determination of word-meaning arises from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
And there is no inconsistency in the linguistic usage of elders unless verbal roots denote productive activity (*bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, the relationship between question and answer occurs at a subsequent time;
therefore, the determination of that relationship cannot be made on the basis of that [subsequent] part.
Since the use of a verb is justified by its denoting merely the number of the agent and so forth, it is not possible to postulate any further denotation.

Moreover, in the expression "Devadatta performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti devadattaḥ*), the word *pāka* (cooking) expresses the act of being cooked, while the verb *karoti* (performs) denotes the effort corresponding to that [act]. However, since the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) expresses only the number of the agent, it is established that its denotation consists of that alone.

Therefore, it is logical that even elsewhere [in the analysis], it refers to that very same thing; and thus, the analysis of "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadattaḥ*) as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) is also untenable.

In the expression “he cooks” (*pacati*), the exertion of the person—which, through its connection, renders the meaning of the root *pac* something to be accomplished—is taken up by the verb *karoti*, which serves as the base form, and thus the analysis is justified.

Even in cases where there is no other effort [than the action itself], such as in the usage “he performs going” (*gamanaṃ karoti*), the use of *karoti* must be understood as figurative in order to show that the act of going is something to be accomplished; for this is the same in both positions.

As for the one who claims that in expressions such as "Devadatta cooks rice," the verbal suffixes (ākhyāta) denote effort—since they are used in the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha*) to signify effort beyond the meaning of the verbal root—he should be instructed thus: "Do you not know the principle: 'The meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained from any other source'?"

And here, since the cognition of effort (*prayatna*) is established even by implication from the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it is not possible for those who explain [the matter] to rely upon [effort] as the denotation of finite verbs (*ākhyāta*).
But how do the Prābhākaras also maintain that the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) expresses *bhāvanā*?
It is said in reply:
It is not accepted that all verbal suffixes denote *bhāvanā*; rather, it is the optative (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes that express the task (*kārya*).

For it is only when there is a connection with a task that the task would be expressed through the non-expression of effort (*kṛti*). Indeed, it is impossible for effort not to be expressed while the task is also not expressed.
Now, it might be thought: "Just as in the case of 'daṇḍī' (the staff-bearer), the staff is not denoted by the suffix, yet there is nevertheless the cognition of a person qualified by that [staff];
so it would be here as well."
In that case,
as long as the staff is not perceived, that cognition does not occur;
yet the word "staff," which constitutes the base form (*prakṛti*), exists there, and it is the cause of that cognition.

But this is not possible here, because there is a rule that the *prakṛtis* denote the operation of the person (*puruṣa*). For the conscious person is made aware of the task by means of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth;
however, he is not himself capable of understanding a task related to the *prakṛtis*. Therefore, this denotation has as its object the family [or nature] belonging to that [person].

And since that [action] is an effort (*prayatna*) by nature, and there is no experience of the denotation of that [effort] upon the experience of the relation, this is not a case for the "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) maxim.
It might be argued:

just as the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) denote only the number of the agent and so forth, while the cognition of the agent and so forth occurs through the implication (*ākṣepa*) of the action, so too here the action implies the effort, lest it be expressed by the optative suffix itself.
That is incorrect;

for although effort (*prayatna*) is implied by the action which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root, how can the *apūrva* be understood through that [effort], given that its establishment depends on being implied by that [action]?
When effort (*prayatna*) is denoted, that which is expressed as being delimited by it is understood to have its establishment dependent upon it, and not otherwise.
Nor is the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) of anything previously denoted ever capable of implying an action (*kṛti*).
For it is only an object whose relation [to the action] is already known that can imply it.
Moreover, there is no other means for understanding the connection of the *apūrva* with human effort apart from the word;
therefore, how could it imply that effort?
Consequently, it has been demonstrated with great precision that the denotation of effort by a term expressing the *apūrva* as its object is necessarily impossible; enough of this digression.
In this regard, I have not begun to act merely upon perceiving the action alone, nor merely the result, nor merely the relationship between the action and the result.
Even when the relationship of the action and the result as the means and the end is understood, activity is not justified.

For instance, with respect to eating, there is no engagement whether the cause [of hunger] has passed or is present, because there is an absence of performance so long as those two [the action and the result] are not perceived as if they were present together.

Furthermore, the cognition of a person (the agent) is not the cause of activity even in the case of destruction, because independent activity is brought about by the weakness of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).
Rather, having understood [an action] as something to be accomplished, one engages in it; having realized "this is my task," I engage in everything.
For instance: "Let alone actions in the world such as going and coming..."
Ultimately, even with regard to an action such as suckling at the breast,
as long as it is not definitively determined that "this is my duty," there has never been any inclination toward it on my part.
1. [The section on] setting in motion.
For in the world, the understanding regarding that which is a means to what is desired by the agent is "this is to be done" (kartavya);
conversely, regarding its opposite, the understanding is "this is not to be done" (akartavya). Therefore, [the Veda] has that as its subject matter.
To this, first of all, this must be said:

the state of being a means to a desired end exists for both the past and the present, yet it is not determined by the capacity to produce an effect; therefore, the state of being an effect is one thing, and the state of being a means is another.
And likewise, even the engagement [of an agent] does not occur by merely understanding that [the action is a means];
therefore, setting aside for the moment that distinction between being a means to a result (*phalasādhanatā*) and being something to be done (*kāryatā*), he points it out:
that which is called "being a means to a result" is certainly not itself something to be done.

"Being an effect consists in being achievable through volitional effort (kṛti), whereas being a means to a result consists in being an instrument (karaṇa) for the production of that result; these two are distinct from one another."
Even though both [the means and the end] reside in a single entity, there is nevertheless a difference in their essential natures (*svarūpa*).

For that very same entity is called a "means to the result" (*phalasādhana*) because it serves as the instrument toward the result, and it is called an "effect" (*kārya*) because its own acquisition depends upon an action (*kṛti*). Why is it that the cognition of "what ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*) occurs only with respect to the means to the desired object and not elsewhere? To this he says: "But the action itself, being of the nature of suffering, declares its own 'ought-to-be-done' status."
In that context, being the means to the fruit is the "task" (kārya); by that, it possesses the nature of a task (kāryatā).
That which exists whenever something else exists is always perceived as being of the very nature of that [other thing].
For actions, by their own nature, result in the production of suffering;
the understanding of them as effects is fueled by the understanding of them as means to a [specific] fruit.

For "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) consists merely in having its establishment dependent upon an effort (*kṛti*); however, that which is the primary object (*pradhāna*) with respect to an effort and whose existence is dependent upon that [effort] is called an "effect. And that is the primary object of the effort, directed toward which the effort proceeds.
Now, it is not at all possible for an effort to be directed toward suffering or toward that which has suffering as its cause.
Nor is it suffering or the cause of suffering;
rather, it is happiness or the cause of happiness. In that regard, karma is not, first of all, happiness in its own nature.

Furthermore, if even the means to happiness were not [an object of desire], then it would not be tenable to accept its primacy with respect to purposeful action (*kṛti*). Therefore, the understanding of ritual acts (*karman*) as things to be done (*kārya*) is based upon the understanding of them as means to a result. Thus, while the status of being a means to a result and the status of being a thing to be done are entered into the category of that which makes known (*jñāpaka*), they are not identical in essence. Consequently, even happiness, though not itself a means, possesses the status of being a thing to be done.

For pleasure, indeed, is understood by all as something to be accomplished (*kārya*); it does not depend upon being a means to a result. Therefore, activity proceeds from the comprehension that pleasure possesses the nature of a task (*kāryatā*) transcending the status of a mere means. Thus, a clever and learned person, having observed Caitra engaging in activity, infers: "Caitra also engages in activity because he has the cognition of a task. In this inference, the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is: "Caitra’s activity is preceded by the cognition of a task."
Because it is an activity preceded by cognition, like my own activity;

and because the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, which denote that which serves as the cause of activity, express only the "task" (*kārya*), since it is precisely that [task], once understood, which is the cause of the subsequent cognition.

Although desire (*icchā*) is the cause of activity, it is nevertheless not denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like, because its cognition is not required for activity. For it is [desire] as it arises that is the cause of activity, not [desire] as it is cognized. Now, even so, how is there an understanding (*vyutpatti*) of the optative suffixes and the like in the sense of what is to be done (*kārya*)? To this he says: "Just as other words are indeed understood in their own respective meanings..."
Likewise, through the method of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), one understands that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote the "task" (*kārya*).

Upon hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix, one infers the comprehension of a specific meaning based on the resulting activity (*pravṛtti*) which occurs when that [sentence] is present; thus, one first understands the sentence's status as a cause [of that activity].

Even there, when distinguishing which part of the meaning is expressed by which word, one observes that the cognition of the task arises upon the insertion of the optative suffix and the like. Consequently, since it is through those [suffixes] that the cognition of the task is produced—just as with other words—it is established that the optative suffixes and the like possess the capacity to convey the task.

Now, it may be argued that since verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) are learned through worldly usage as denoters specifically of commands (*praiṣa*) and the like, their expressive power (*śakti*) regarding things past has also ceased; this is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and thus it cannot be postulated as something enduring.
Furthermore, once the substratum has ceased to exist, upon what could the power subsist?

If it is argued that this very [efficacy] is what is resorted to as the means for attaining heaven, we say no; for the power belonging to one thing does not reside in another, precisely because that would contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the term "efficacy" (*śakti*), it is not logical for there to be a result when the efficacy itself is absent.
For the means of accomplishment is that which possesses power (*śaktimat*), not the power itself; otherwise, it would not be a possessor of power.

Now, it may be argued that ritual action such as sacrifice, being a means for propitiating a deity, may indeed be described as something to be accomplished (*kārya*); yet that [action] and its exertion are capable of producing a fruit even at a later time through the persistence of the mental impression (*cittadhāra*).
The deity, who is capable of bestowing the fruit, is propitiated by rituals.
Once propitiated, she becomes pleased; and being pleased, she certainly unites the agent with the fruit even at a later time.
This is not so;
for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that sacrifices and the like are causes for propitiating a deity.
Indeed, there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that sacrifice is a cause that serves as a means for propitiating a deity.

But is it not the case that sacrifice (*yajati*) is traditionally taught as being solely for the purpose of worshipping a deity, and that all worship is said to be for the sake of the one being worshipped? To this, it is replied:
Memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), precisely because it is memory.
Furthermore, the description of the objects of memories depends upon other means of valid cognition, for they follow after those.
And it has already been stated that, according to another means of valid cognition, sacrifice is not the means for propitiating a deity.

Therefore, the statement that "sacrifice (yāga) is the renunciation of a substance for the sake of a deity" should be understood as figuratively signifying the nature of worshiping a deity; for even worship proceeds only by means of designating an object of worship. Furthermore, [the deity] is propitiated by rituals—that is, it becomes the recipient of propitiation.

Moreover, the notion that a deity is perceived through worship performed by a person traveling to various locations is indeed contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, the beginninglessness [of such a deity] is untenable.
Furthermore, since the argument will be refuted in the section concerning the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*), one need not exert oneself too much here; the text has already disposed of it.
Nevertheless, it might be argued that the action, which serves as the cause for the refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), is expressed by the word as something to be performed.
Consequently, because of its connection with the person desiring heaven and so forth, the fruit will arise at a later time precisely from that refinement of the person.
In this regard, there is a lack of evidence for the view that [the Vedic injunction] effects a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person.

For neither through other means of valid cognition nor through verbal testimony is it established that sacrifices and the like are causes for the refinement of the person; thus it has been stated [in the *Śābarabhāṣya*]: "Because the action is something to be commenced" (*karmaṇyārambha-bhāvāt*, 1.1.2.4). Now, one might argue: let the action itself be declared as the object to be accomplished (*kārya*), and let its status as the means to the fruit be accepted as belonging to that very action. However, since this would otherwise be inexplicable, let some other entity be postulated—produced by that action, subordinate to the emergence of the fruit, persisting until another time, and residing in the self—and let it be the thing denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, rather than the action itself.
It is said:
for that indeed is postulated through its logical consistency which is the establishing factor of that [other].
Nor is the status of an action as a means established by another, imagined factor that produces the result;
for the means to a means does not become the means of that [primary action].
Rather, it is either an intermediate operation or a capacity that brings about its status as a means.
It is precisely through the connection with an operation (*vyāpāra*) that things possessing potency attain the status of being means (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, since there is no distinct entity (*arthāntara*) inherent in the self (*ātmasamavāya*), nor is there potency in the immediate operation of actions, it is not logical for that [self] to be cognizable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Rather, given that the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is established, it is more appropriate that [the self] is simply denotable by words due to its compatibility with the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); thus, it is well said.

"It is the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished), which exists through time and is connected with the person to be impelled (*niyojya*), that is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers as something distinct [from the mere action].

Now, this very procedure was established in the *Codanāsūtra* as having the *kārya* as its object. In the same way, by means of the genitive case, heaven and those desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) are presented as being related to that *kārya* as the person to be impelled (*niyojya*).

And regarding that effect, its status as a cause conditioned by a desired object—which serves as a qualification for the person to be enjoined—is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning deities).

Furthermore, such [an action] does not take the form of a ritual act (*kriyā*), because a ritual act is incapable of being a means to a fruit; this was demonstrated in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* by showing that there is no fruit through the mediation of propitiating a deity, nor through the mediation of merit or spiritual impression (*saṃskāra*).
Thus it has been stated.
Furthermore, it was established in the *Apūrvādhikaraṇa* that neither the action nor its potency possesses permanence.

Moreover, it is a matter to be proven through numerous logical arguments (*nyāya*) that the *apūrva*—as an effect inherent in the self—is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, based on other means of knowledge (*māna*) through the mediation of another person who is to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
And this effect is that which is to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛti*).

Action (*kṛti*) is nothing other than human effort (*prayatna*). And since this [effort] does not exist without an objective that is to be brought into being (*bhāvārtha*), it is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the [first] *adhikaraṇa* that it is precisely the injunction (*niyoga*) related to that [objective] which is expressed.
Furthermore, it is determined in the *Śabdāntara-adhikaraṇa* that this objective to be brought into being is delimited by its state of being connected [to the injunction].
And it has been stated in the *Bādarāyaṇikaraṇa* that the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), when it becomes the object [of an injunction], becomes something to be accomplished (*karaṇīya*).
It is also stated in that very same work that the person possesses sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) over the verbal action (*bhāvārtha*) for the sake of accomplishing its own effect.

Regarding the unsuitability of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) for an effect that persists until another time, he says: "For that [effect] would have to endure until another time for the sake of the attainment of heaven and so forth."
Furthermore, its connection with the person to be enjoined who possesses desire is also logically established.
But surely the author of the Bhāṣya stated that the *apūrva* is the meaning of the suffix, saying: "That effect which is distinct from action and so forth is known through other means of knowledge;
therefore, even when preceded by another means of knowledge, it is designated as *apūrva*."
[Objection: Even so, in this case, the sentence-meaning would be the *apūrva* (the unprecedented), not the *niyoga* (the mandate);

yet the Prābhākaras declare that the *niyoga* is the sentence-meaning. To this, he says: "By [presenting] itself as something to be accomplished (*kārya*), it impels the person to be directed (*niyojya*) toward its own self."
"One who is to be enjoined" (niyojya) is the term used by those proficient in Mīmāṃsā.
Even so, he explains how it can be the meaning of a sentence: "Because the task (*kārya*) alone is primary, its status as the meaning of the sentence is appropriate;
for it is that [task] which the sentence expresses, conjoined with the object and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)."

For it has been stated that whatever is presented as the primary element is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and since the "task" (*kārya*) is said to be the primary element, it alone constitutes the meaning of the sentence here.

Furthermore, the denotation of [the task] as connected with the person to be prompted (*niyojya*) is the fundamental position, because the origination of primary injunctions—such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and Vedic study—is accepted as being denoted when the injunctions are unknown to the person to be prompted.
Indeed, the authors of the *Vivaraṇa* maintain that even the subject matter of the fire-establishment (*ādhāna*) is a distinct injunction.
Because there is no recognition of a connection to a specific sacrifice (*kratu*), for such recognition of a connection to a sacrifice is not possible in the absence of that context.

Nor can recognition be established through the medium of the sacrifice—as is the case with the injunctions regarding the *varṇana* and so forth—because prior to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), words such as *āhavanīya* are understood through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) without any knowledge of their connection to a sacrifice.
In the case of the *juhū* and other implements, however, since they denote a generic form (*ākṛti*), recognition is possible even before their specific application (*viniyoga*).
Objection: Since the fires (*agni*) are also objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*), how can two things to be accomplished be connected within a single sentence?
Response: It is said that even here, the injunction (*niyoga*) alone is the primary object to be accomplished.

As for the status of the fires (*agni*) as an unintended object of action (*anīpsita-karma*): even though the fires are unintended objects, because the word *āhvanīya* and others are applied to that which is connected with the fruit produced by the respective *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) rites, and because the *āhvanīya* and others are connected with the sacrifice (*kratu*), it is logical that a person’s activity is directed toward them solely for the sake of accomplishing those [sacrifices]. Since the performance [of the rite] is thus obtained, there is no need to explicitly state the person to be prompted (*prayojya*). Similarly, it is established that even for the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), since its performance is obtained through the prompting of the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*), there is no need to state the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

The injunctions for the production of primary acts achieve their fulfillment only through the performance of their respective objects; therefore, there is no need to seek the mention of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) therein.

Even the injunctions for the production of subordinate acts (*ajñotpatti-niyoga*), because they have as their object the *praiṣa* (direction) and so forth already employed in the ritual procedure, are established as being nothing other than injunctions of qualification (*adhikāra-niyoga*); thus, what purpose would there be in mentioning a person to be enjoined in connection with them?
But how is it that the injunctions for the *praiṣa* and so forth have as their object that which is already employed? It is said:

In the proximity of the injunctions possessing a qualification (*sādhikāra-niyoga*), sentences such as those concerning the *praṇītā* water are heard; they are not, however, capable of conveying a separate injunction (*niyoga*) whose object is the *svaga* (self-benefit).

Since it is possible for them to be restatements (*anuvāda*) of acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*), they merely establish the essential nature of the injunction as qualified by its own constituent elements.

And because that [nature] requires a purpose, it is supplied by the very injunction possessing a qualification which serves as the purpose; thus, through the sentence of qualification alone, the injunctive suffix (*liṅ-śabda*) denotes its own meaning as connected with that [qualification].
And that *anvaya* (logical connection) is fit for the grasping of the *prayāja*s and other rites by means of their mere capacity for such a purpose (*idamarthya*).

Furthermore, the conceptualization of the *apūrva*—which stands in need of assistance from the instrument—as being the assistance to the instrument is the function of *prakaraṇa* (context). In this regard, the conceptualization of those [rites] as producing assistance to the instrument is derived from that [contextual function].
There is no separate *niyoga* (injunction) externally in the *prayāja*s and so forth.

Nor is it the case that there is no possibility of those momentary [cognitions] acting together as a collective performance (*itikartavyatā*), because another mandate (*niyoga*) must otherwise be resorted to.
That very [word] such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which was previously suspected of being for the purpose of inference, now expresses a different mandate.

For this very reason, in the Veda, the sense of ownership associated with the mandate of qualification (*adhikāra-niyoga*) is not admitted for those [subsidiary acts] such as threshing (*avaghāta*), even though they are included in the subsidiary injunctions (*aṅga-vākya*).

For if that were the case, at the very moment of its origination, because it would not be distinct from the nature of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) due to ignorance, it could not be the object of another injunction (*niyoga*). However, when it has been taught, since there is the conceit that it does not terminate in anything else, its status as the object of another injunction is logical.
Why, then, would that which is not distinct [from the subsidiary] be the object of another injunction? Because it is impossible to comprehend its connection with two separate effects (*kārya*).
For it is not possible for a single [injunctive force] to be understood as being simultaneously connected with two distinct effects.

Furthermore, that other injunctive force (*niyoga*) which exists in the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, is expressed by the very same word as the injunctive force of the qualification (*adhikāra-niyoga*),
because otherwise there would be a contradiction between the object (*viṣaya*), the substance (*dravya*), and the injunctive force.
Enough of this excessive digression.

Now, one might object: since it is accepted that the *niyoga* (the mandate) is the means for attaining the desired fruit, and since the fruit is the primary element, the fruit alone must be the meaning of the sentence. To this he replies: “For the sake of establishing the *niyoga* which is conducive to its own realization, even heaven and the like, though [usually] primary, are for us merely the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished).”

Regarding that duty which has not been previously accomplished, its realization is impossible without a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), because it cannot occur without performance; nor can it occur without an action (*karman*), since there would be no agent (*kartṛ*) without an eligible person (*adhikārin*), and eligibility is untenable without being subject to an injunction (*niyojyatva*). Furthermore, since an injunction is understood even in the case of what does not accomplish a desired object, the injunction is established solely for the sake of the self’s own attainment, and it is thus obtained as the means for accomplishing the desired fruit through the state of ownership.

Just as a master, being conscious of his own self-interest, benefits his slave born in the house, so too does the injunction (niyoga) benefit the injunction itself; thus, its lack of independent application does not detract from its primacy.

Now, since the injunction is the means to the fruit, and that [means] is accomplished only through the performance of the constituent acts along with their subsidiary details, the accomplishment of the fruit should follow immediately upon the accomplishment of the injunction. If the injunction is established immediately thereafter, one might ask: "How can that [fruit] be established for one who has merely performed the action? To this he says: "When the ritual procedure has been performed, the injunction is indeed established, but the fruit is not."
At that very moment, it acts by depending upon auxiliary causes.

This is the established position here: the primary origination-apūrva (*pradhānotpattyapūrva*) and the subsidiary origination-apūrvas (*aṅgotpattyapūrva*) are accomplished solely through the performance of their own respective spheres of application, joined by subsidiaries that provide immediate assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).
Among these, those which are subsidiary apūrvas (*aṅgāpūrva*) assist the primary origination-apūrva collectively, and from that, the supreme apūrva (*paramāpūrva*) is produced.

Furthermore, even regarding those subsidiaries such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others—which possess specific subsidiaries providing remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) and so forth—it should be understood that they have a single subsidiary apūrva, just like the primary [sacrifice].
Everything is to be understood by this method.

Thus, although the accomplishment of the application (*viniyoga*) depends solely upon the performance of the ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*), nevertheless, that which follows immediately after the fruit is postulated through logical reasoning (*upapatti*): there exists another requisite factor, the absence of which [renders] the injunction (*niyoga*) baseless, as expressed by the term "the doctrine of the lack of support" (*nirālambanavāda*).
This is the interpretation of Śālikanātha himself.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Examination of Niyoga," in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā* composed by the venerable Śālikanātha Miśra (*Prakaraṇapañjikā*, pp. 25–27). [According to the *Ṛjuvimalā*: by the word *niyoga* is meant that which, being distinct from action, enjoins the person toward their own duty.]

Page 288, 12|7|25: *Niyojana* (the act of tying) is indeed another form of assistance; therefore, it is to be performed according to the original model (*prakṛti*) in the case of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati.
*Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 5|2|1: Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*), in its modified form (*vikṛti*), the tying is prescribed as being done on a post made of *udumbara* wood.
In the original model (*prakṛti*), however, it is simply a post made of *khadira* wood, as stated in the injunction: "He ties [the animal] to a post made of *khadira*."
Bhāṣya | 10|1|18|63: The tethering of the animal occurs upon the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) situated on the *uttaravedi* during the Soma sacrifices and the Cāturmāsya offerings.
[The injunction is: "One should tether the animal to the enclosing-stick."
This is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi), not a separate rite.

[Citrādhikaraṇa-sūtra 10.1.3] Having restated the original act of binding, there is a sublation of the original sacrificial post (yūpa) by the prescribed paridhi in the Soma-related Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Ke. 10|1|3|18–22. Tying to the sacrificial post (*niyojana*) is a property of the animal.

This is according to the maxim: "In a place where trees have been cleared away, even the castor-oil plant acts like a tree."

Where the wise and virtuous are difficult to find, even one of little knowledge acts with great boldness. As it is said: "In a place where there is no learned person worthy of praise, even a mere prattler is esteemed; in a land devoid of trees, even the castor-oil plant passes for a tree."
Thus [it is said]. *Sāhasrī*, 645. Refutation (*nirākaraṇa*) is sublation by means of reasoning (*yukti*).
