The Doctrine of Non-Objectivity (Nirālambanavāda).
Commentary: Now, is it not the case that every cognition is indeed without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), like a dream?
For the absence of an objective basis is observed to be the very nature of cognition in dreams.
Even for one who is awake, there arises the very same cognition as "a pillar" or "a wall"; therefore, that too is without a real objective basis (*nirālambana*).

It is replied: the cognition "pillar" arises with firm certainty; how could it be a state of error? Even in a dream, such a cognition was likewise firmly certain prior to awakening; thus, there is no difference between the two cases.
No;
because in dreams there is the perception of error,
whereas in the other state there is no error.
If it is argued that [the falsity] will occur elsewhere as well due to that commonality:
if the falsity of a dream-cognition is because it is a cognition (*pratyayatvāt*), then the waking cognition ought to be likewise.

If, on the other hand, the reason is the fact of being perceived and its being of such a nature, then it cannot be said that "this one is different" simply because it is a cognition. (The reading *vaditum* is found in the *Bṛhatī*.)
On the other hand, the dream-cognition is false because it is erroneous.

If one asks why, it is because of the weakness of the mind when under the influence of sleep; sleep is the cause of falsity, as in the case of dreams and so forth, and at the end of a dream, there is simply the absence of deep sleep (*suptasupta*).
One who is not conscious at all is said to be in deep sleep.
Therefore, the cognition of one who is awake is not false.
[Objection: But might there not be a defect of the instruments even for one who is awake? [Response: If there were such a defect, it would be perceived.
If it is argued that [the object] is not apprehended even at the time of the manifestation of the form, [we reply]: upon waking, one indeed understands, "My mind was overcome by sleep. (Bṛhatī, pp.
28–30): "But surely every cognition is without an external basis, like a dream-cognition?"

Why? Because there is no specific characteristic—whether it be its being "associated with that" (*tatsamprayuktatva*) or its "not being associated with that"—by which a specific nature of perceptual cognition could be apprehended.
(Page 53). *Ṛjuvimalā*: If an object existed in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), then one could say that perception is "produced by association with that.

However, since all cognitions are without an objective support (*nirālambana*) and thus lack ultimate reality, this [definition] is not established. Therefore, the connection [of this section] is through the critique of the definition of perception; such is the meaning.
The *Bṛhatī*: How, then, is it that "every cognition is indeed without an objective basis (*nirālambana*)"? For the nature of a cognition as being without an objective basis is observed in dreams.
[Objection: But surely the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is said to be a memory-cognition due to the loss of the [perceptual] experience (*pramoṣāt*).
[Response: This is appropriate in the case of silver and the like.
For in that case, it is logical that the bright form of the mother-of-pearl, which is determined by the eye, serves as the substrate for the recollection of silver.
In dreams and similar states, however, because nothing is perceived at all, the avoidance of the arising of a recollection directed toward some other object seems possible.
Therefore, we conclude that this entire collection of cognitions has its fuel solely in latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The arising of a memory regarding a similar object occurs upon the perception of something similar;
however, in the case of a dream, it is logical that there is no apprehension of anything [external].
Therefore, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) alone is the cause—this is the parsimonious hypothesis—and there is no recourse to another object, because such a thing is not perceived.
Therefore, even in the case of walls and the like, cognition is caused solely by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and not caused by objects such as walls; this is the established position.
It is replied: for a cause is postulated for the sake of accomplishing an effect, not for the sake of destroying it.
In dreams and similar states, consciousness appears as something external; yet that [appearance] is not possible without an external object.
That without which something cannot occur is the cause of that thing.
Therefore, it is logical to postulate that the object itself is the cause.
However, that which is without an objective basis (nirālambana) is not at all perceived by direct sensory cognition (pratyakṣabodha).
Therefore, it has been stated that knowledge arising from the senses is not caused by latent impressions (vāsanā).
[Objection: But surely, for one who has awakened, the cognition regarding what was perceived in a dream is understood to be false.
Nor is it logical for that which is false to have a collection of causes;
yet, it is not the case that the arising of a false cognition devoid of a cause is impossible.
It is true that it is not possible, but it is not inconsistent with the nature of non-comprehension.
For in that case, there would not even be false cognition itself.

(Even though a cause for the arising of cognition must be postulated, nevertheless, it is not the object that is to be postulated; rather, it is merely latent impressions. Therefore, false cognitions have delusion as their cause, and the cause of delusion consists of the latent impressions of transmigratory existence.
Therefore, those who know reality have declared that this web of cognition has nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its fuel (Jñānamīmāṃsā, p.
297). [In this context,] delusion (*vyāmoha*)—which is the emptiness of objective referents—is the cause of false cognition.
Delusion arises from latent impressions, and latent impressions arise from delusion; because they are beginningless, like the relationship between a seed and a sprout, there is no logical fault.

(He begins the presentation of his own established conclusion: Now, it was indeed replied that "the cognitions of memory are themselves devoid of the cognition 'I remember'. But was it not stated that this is impossible because there is no cause for the awakening [of memory]?
That remains unproven.
For even in the case of one's own [body] at the beginning [of life], there is the possibility of the arising of thought and so forth;
for even in a dream, pleasure and pain are experienced,
and the cause of that pleasure and pain is unseen merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).

Therefore, dream-cognition and the like are likewise unperceived, being caused by some reflection or other; thus, it is established that dream-consciousness is equivalent to the cognition of mother-of-pearl and similar objects.

This has been stated [in the following words, which the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) describes as "an error consisting of non-apprehension is the cause of falsity"]: "How can the well-established cognition of a pillar for one who is awake be a state of error?
How is this said? [It is not improper; "ascertained" means "delimited."

How does it become delimited? (One might ask: "If non-apprehension were not the cause, would all cognitions not be false, since no cognition apprehends an object in its entirety? Thus he asks: "Then how does one who has awakened know [the dream] to be false? (The answer is: It was said: "Because of the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*), [one thinks] 'I remember'; that [dream-cognition] is then regarded as equal to perception. But for one who has awakened, the conceit of perception (*pratyakṣābhimāna*) disappears. When the weakness of the sense organs is determined, perception is untenable, and thus there is the certainty that it was memory."

He clarifies that the object of inference is an error consisting in the non-apprehension [of the thing]: "Now, because there is an absence of cognition, one cannot say that it is not apprehended from the cognition," and also, "If [it were] because of being a cognition.
He does not think that this is a false understanding.
"For the falsity of dream-cognition arises from something else";
thus he shows that [dream-cognition] has the cause of deception (*pramoṣa*). Why? Because of the mention of the weakness of the sense organs, such as "my mind is overcome by sleep," and so forth.

And weakness is the state of being incapable of performing its function, not the capacity to produce another effect; this has been stated. (On page [number], verse [number]—[he states the purpose of the subsequent section]: "Validity and invalidity, merit and demerit and so forth, as well as their results."
The postulation of the meaning of explanatory passages (arthavāda), mantras, names (nāmadheya), and so forth, for the sake of knowledge.
In all these characteristics, the state of being like a dream remains constant;
yet, through differences in the expression of words, they fall into the categories of prior established doctrines.
Through etymological derivation, there is a connection between actions and their fruits across both the next world and this world; thus is the doctrine of non-referentiality [established].
It would be improper to say "all" regarding the existence of dharma within these cognitions;

therefore, prior to [these], one should exert effort toward the action based on the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) accepted by the world, in order to determine whether an object exists or does not exist.

Ratnākara: If all cognitions were to terminate solely within their own parts and have no external objects as their referents, then this entire worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) would be untenable—namely, the practice that "injunction (*codanā*) is the means of valid knowledge regarding Dharma, while anything else is not a means of valid knowledge"; that "perception arises from contact with that [object]," and "inference arises from contact with that [sign]"; that "the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites are merit," and "the killing of a Brahmin is sin"; that "their fruit consists of both, being of the nature of prosperity and calamity, yet distinct from those two"; that "the meaning of an injunction is the instigation to act (*pravartana*)," and "the purpose of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is its intended meaning"; that "mantras have the function of illuminating what is to be performed," and "the investigation into whether the names of rites are for the purpose of enjoining qualities or results"; and, as included by the word "etc.," the investigation into the validity or invalidity of Smṛti and custom; likewise, the distinctions between rituals based on different words, direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth; the determination of the meaning of a sentence through various modes of expression; the fact that some rituals have results to be experienced in subsequent lives, some have indefinite results, and some have results such as livelihood in this very life—and all such practices would be improper due to the absence of injunctions.

Therefore, those persons who are devoted to the Dharma must certainly exert effort to refute—by means of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) accepted by the world—the existence of external objects as conceived objects, which are [merely] measured by the blessings of the Sugata.
This means that the accomplishment of practice regarding ritual action is the goal. (pp.
217–218). Śrotra: "And just like the enjoyment in dreams and so forth, there is the conceptualization of being an object of enjoyment."
It is precisely for the sake of being intent upon that [ultimate reality] that one is made to understand the ultimate truth here;
for no one engages in dharma for the sake of their own dreams or pleasures. Since a dream is merely accidental, the wise would simply remain silent regarding it.

One who desires the fruit of the ultimate truth should, with effort and according to what is desired, apply themselves through reasoned arguments to the objects of meditation. In this regard, the Yogācāras have relied upon consciousness that is empty of [external] objects.
Even those who are proponents of the Madhyamaka doctrine assert the non-existence of that [cognition] as well.

In that regard, the emptiness of external objects is common to both [positions] for the time being. Through the cessation of this [external object], there follows, in relation to cognition, a corresponding conceptualization of its connection [with an object].

Therefore, because it is common to all [schools] and because it is the very foundation [of their systems], the author of the Bhāṣya has exerted effort regarding the existence or non-existence of external objects. Even for one who denies the existence of cognition, cognition must first be established, since cognition without an object is impossible; thus, even he must accept the existence of cognition.

Therefore, the denial of objects [is refuted] because it is common to both [theories], and since the denial of cognition—which is rooted in that [denial of objects]—is established by the very rejection of the latter, it is that [denial of objects] which is being rejected here. *Ratnākara*, *Nirālambanavāda*, pp. 217–221. In the *Nirālambanavāda*, it is held that there is no external object, nor do the forms such as blue existing within consciousness exist. *Bālabodhinī*, p. 6. The existence of external objects through the refutation of the *Nirālambanavāda* was stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Aupaniṣada-sūtra* itself.

Vāla-pṛ. 6: For the proponents of non-apprehension (*nirālambanavādin*), all conceptual cognitions (*savikalpakajñāna*) having external objects such as jars as their domain have false objects as their content, because they are cognitions having external objects as their domain, like dream-cognition.

Indeed, for dream-cognitions, the object is cognition itself transformed into the form of an external jar and so forth, not the jar itself, because [the jar] does not exist at that time, because there is no mental proximity (*manaḥpratyāsatti*), and because [actions] such as cutting off one's own head do not exist.
Therefore, in those cases, the object is of the nature of cognition alone.
Thus, by means of this illustration, they claim that not even a single cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*).
In that regard, their example is unestablished because [their own] cognitions are proven to have the self as their object.
Furthermore, if determinate cognitions such as "this is blue" had the self as their object, they would result in having the form "I am blue."
Therefore, this [cognition] has an external object as its content;
and in the absence of a sublater, it is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*). Maṇi, pp. 23–24. Thus it is explained.
In this context, "nirihāḥ" means those who have gone beyond activity; "nirihākāḥ" means those whose activity is contemptible.
This refers to the repetition of the application [of the term]. (Vi. 1131312)
The term *vitarām* means "more exceedingly"; thus, *niriham* means "without effort" (*nirihameva*), which signifies being employed in a single ritual act.
Even for officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are without personal effort, and for the location, the learned (*śiṣṭāḥ*) do not prohibit its repeated employment.
According to the *Nirukta*, the learned do not practice performing an action again once it has been completed.
Those who are disciplined do not perform a sacrifice without a purpose; there is instruction even regarding what is etymologically explained. (Bhāṣya: Nirukta 1.20)
That from which the desire for application— the longing for what is desired and sought— has departed is "nirihaka," meaning that which has been employed.
The instruction regarding the employment elsewhere of that which has already been employed in one place is the "nirihakopadeśa" (instruction on the employed).

Ku. 4|1214129: Nirukta is an auxiliary of the Veda (vedāṅga). Although it is of human origin, it is authoritative because its tradition has continued without interruption and because it is rooted in the Veda.

[Commentary on Bhāṣya 12.4.4.14]:
It should take place when the [offering] has been set aside; because of its connection with that.

The *candrābhyuditeṣṭi* (the sacrifice performed when the moon rises) should take place when the oblation has been set aside—that is, it should take place when the moon rises after the oblation has already been poured out.
"Because of its connection with that.

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that, because the sacrifice is described as being connected with the pouring out [of the oblation] in the statement, "For whom the oblation has been poured out beforehand and the moon rises," [the rite applies].
Or rather, it applies when [the moonrise] has occurred, because the cause [of the rite] has been reached.
Having refuted the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached through the sūtra by means of the word "annulment" (*bādha*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
When one has already commenced the rite at an improper time and the moonrise occurs, this *iṣṭi* should take place;
for the occasion, namely the moonrise, has been reached and is thus present.
For the rising of the moon is indeed the occasion (*nimitta*).
If that occurs prior to the extinguishing [of the fire], then because the occasion exists, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) must certainly be performed;
the other [details] are merely secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

If the *abhyudayeṣṭi* were to take place upon the rising of the moon even when the *darśa* rite has merely commenced prior to the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), then one might ask: for what purpose is the connection with the pouring out expressed in the words "whose sacrificial offering has been poured out"? To this, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) replies:
the word "poured out" (*nistam*) is merely an indicative mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the commencement of the rite;
the word "poured out" indicates the commencement of the rite.
Furthermore, the commencement of the ritual action occurs even before the pouring out [of the oblation].
Likewise, there is an observation of another purpose.

Thus, regarding the view that the *abhyudayeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for the rising of the moon) should take place when the moon rises while the Darśa sacrifice has merely begun—even prior to the pouring out—there is an observation of another purpose: "If the oblation should rise [with the moon] while it has not yet been taken up, then the procedure for the vow remains exactly as it was."

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *abhyuditeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one by whom the moon has risen) applies when the moon rises while the ritual action has merely commenced.

The meaning of the Vedic text (*śruti*) is this: if the moon should rise while the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) has not yet been taken up, then the procedure following the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), or the observance of the vows (*vratacaryā*), must be performed exactly as prescribed.

[Question: What are "etymological words" (*niruktāni*)? They are said to be words accompanied by their derivations; the investigation into them belongs to the section concerning their instruction (*tadupadeśādhikaraṇa*).
The *ke* [animal sacrifice], the *nirūḍha-paśubandha*, and others should be performed even before the Soma sacrifice. (Ratna. 5.4.8.25).
In the case of the *nirūḍha* and other such sacrifices, the *śālāmukhīya* fire is present.

Since the carrying forward of the fire from the *prājahita* occurs in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, it would likewise be possible in the *nirūḍha-paśubandha*; therefore, the *śālāmukhīya* fire should be present there as well.

This being the case, since there is no function of any Soma-related rite at the Śālāmukhīya fire in the archetype (prakṛti), the Śālāmukhīya fire— having been taken up solely for the sake of the functions pertaining to the animal sacrifice (pāśuka)— must indeed be present even in the Nirūḍha-paśubandha, due to the extension of the injunction by the rule of transfer (codaka). The Nirūḍha-paśu is a modification (vikāra) of the Agniṣomīya.
In the *Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra*, however, the opposite view is accepted. Ke.
[states]: "In the case of an animal sacrifice (*nirūḍapaśu*), even though there is no initiate (*dīkṣita*), the handing over of the staff (*daṇḍadāna*) is the motive for the procurement of the staff.
Therefore, the handing over of the staff is for the sake of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the Maitrāvaruṇa."
Wearing a garment made of hair from a washed donkey is improper conduct (*anācāra*) for both those of the North and those of the South.
They perform this [act] like the washing of a woolen blanket (*kambala*).
For the demonstrative pronoun performs both functions: it effects the purification of the blanket and the cleanliness of the feet.
For a pronoun is the substitute for that which has been previously specified.
A nominal stem (prātipadika) possesses the power to indicate what has been previously specified.

*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 1.2.1.2.1: Specification (*nirdeśa*) is performed in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by means of [the formulas] such as "This for Brahman," regarding the cake (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni which has been divided into four parts.
But in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* beans, since everything is offered to the Brahman priest alone, no specific assignment need be made;
for even a distribution does not exist there at all.

The general rule that the Adhvaryu is the performer [of the *japa*] is set aside by the specific instruction "he mutters while seated," according to the maxim "that which is indicated by a specific mention [is stronger]. Since there is no such specific word [indicating the Adhvaryu] in the case of "he causes Garga to perform the *vila*," that [general rule] continues to apply.
Vaijayantī 1.3.25.
And because of the specific mention, that which has been initiated in the case of an option [prevails].
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, the sacrificial post (yūpa) is prescribed as an option among the Khadira, Pālāśa, and Rohitaka.
Furthermore, the performance has been commenced with the specific quality of the Khadira;
however, in that instance, the Khadira is absent.
This being the case, a substitute for the *khadira* wood must be taken;
and that substitute must be sought as something resembling the *khadira* itself.

When there is an option (*vikalpa*), the substitute to be accepted must resemble that which was undertaken—that very substance with reference to which the performance began—and not simply any optional substance that serves as a substitute.

Because of the explicit mention—since a word denoting the primary substance also denotes that which resembles it due to the persistence of some constituent parts, and thus its mention is possible—it is not possible to mention an optional substitute in such a manner. Therefore, in the absence of *khadira* wood, the *kadara* (the white *khadira*) is to be taken; and in the absence of *vrīhi* rice, *nīvāra* grains are to be taken.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

If [the opponent] says "it is like a horse" (*aśvavat*), then in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) he might say: "That which is like a horse, namely *khadira* wood, should be accepted as merely optional because it possesses the same sound."
If it is argued that "aśvadam" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has no word to express [it]," this is not so,
because it lacks the required suffix.
That which was stated by the opponent is not correct.
Because of the lack of knowledge [of the specific tree], since the optional *palāśa* wood is absent in a performance characterized by the resolve for *khadira*, it is not to be taken;
rather, only a *kadara* tree, which resembles the *khadira*, is to be taken.

Although a substitute (sahaśa) is not directly denotable by the primary term (*mukhya-śabda*), it is indeed understood by that primary term through secondary figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) as being similar to the primary.
Therefore, a substitute is necessarily similar to the primary, and is not merely an optional alternative substance (*vaikalpikaṃ dravyam*).
And because of the specific instruction, there is an extension of the previous context.

Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, it is heard in the scripture: "The sacrificial post has the quality of being surrounded by the *barhis* grass," and "He anoints the sacrificial post with clarified butter.
In that case, the properties of the *barhis* grass apply to the *barhis* used for surrounding the sacrificial post.

Regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the clarified butter (*ājya*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which is not explicitly stated as a sūtra—is that the properties (*dharmas*) of the clarified butter must be performed [therein]. The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the word *tu* ("but"), which serves to exclude the prima facie view.

Because of the specific mention [of the term], the transfer (*atideśa*) of properties in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) occurs only through the medium of the original function; therefore, in the case of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*), there is no qualification, no application, no recurrence, and no transfer of the properties belonging to the sacrificial post—such as its being made of palāśa wood, the selection of the site, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the purpose of making it known as a post—which are new (*apūrva*) and not part of the original model (*aprākṛta*).

Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) here is that only worldly (*laukika*) *barhis* grass and clarified butter (*ājya*) are to be taken. Regarding this, the nature of the principle of the section [Mīmāṃsā Sūtra] 3.8.16–32, "And because of the specific instruction in the modified sacrifice" (*nirdeśācca vikṛtau*), is as follows: "When there is no possibility of employing those [elements] whose assistance is already established (*klṛptopakāraka*), there is no requirement for those whose assistance is not so established (*aklṛptopakāraka*), because that would entail the fault of conceptualizing [an unnecessary] complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*)."

Su. Pṛ. 634: Furthermore, the purpose of the section concerning *barhis* and *ājya* (1.4.7) will be clarified under the heading "And because of the specific instruction in the modification" (*nirdeśācca vikṛtau*).

On page 469, regarding the statement "And because of the specific instruction in the modification (*vikṛti*)," there arises an inquiry as to whether or not the non-original (*aprākṛta*) encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—expressed by the phrase "there is the state of being like the sacrificial post with the *barhis* grass"—is for the sake of a property that is not a primary duty (*akāryadharma*), namely, whether the original (*prākṛta*) properties of the *barhis* apply. This inquiry concerns the sequence of the application of original and modified auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). Since the act of churning (*mardana*) does not exist in the fire-pan (*abhri*) which serves as the instrument for cooking, and since being produced by churning exists even in butter (*navanīta*) and other such things used in cooking, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
