VI. 5.1.3. Thus, the ritual properties such as the pouring out of the oblation have their application restricted to specific objects.
And that [distinction] is established by direct perception regarding perceptible objects; however, in the case of the Adhvaryu priest, it is established through scriptural audition (*śruti*).

Thus, the rites beginning with the *upanayana* (pouring) are the properties (*dharma*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) alone, not the properties of the rice (*vrīhi*); whereas the rites beginning with threshing (*avaghāta*) are the properties of the rice alone, not of the clarified butter.
The principle of the offering-mantra (*nirvāpamantranyāya*).

In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, regarding the offering (*nirvāpa*), the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhirlavana*), the strewing of the altar (*vedistaraṇa*), and the taking of the clarified butter (*ājyagrahaṇa*), there is a repetition of each respective mantra for every individual act of offering and so forth.
Regarding the substance:

if it is intended as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), then by the principle of the offering and the touching (*nirvāpa-ālambha*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is a property of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the statement regarding its performance.
For that [property] belongs to the *dāśata* mantras which do not constitute parts of the ritual action.
It has ceased; for this very reason, it is a qualification (as in "He worships the Āgnīdhra with an *āgneyī* verse," etc., Vārttika 3.8.1.21, p.

775). After the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), the Adhvaryu must not first perform the Soma-related ritual items belonging to the Adhvaryu’s portion, such as the *pracaraṇī-homa* and others which belong to the archetypal rite; rather, first the present-worldly items such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, up to the decoration (*alaṃkāra*), which belong to the archetypal rite, should be performed, and after that, the Soma-related items.
Ke. 5.1.13.25–26. Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 298.

At the time of the *nirvāpa* (offering of the oblation), the sacrificer’s recitation of the mantra “For Agni, [I shall give] to Dāsa” is for the purpose of relinquishing ownership—characterized by the absence of the power to dispose of the object as one pleases—which consists in the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to abandon it for the sake of the deity. This is the purport of the *Sudhā* commentary, p. 1634. Furthermore, in the acts of *nirvāpa*, *plavana* (sprinkling), *staraṇa* (spreading), and *ājyagrahaṇa* (taking the clarified butter), there is a single purpose because they involve a single substance.
Commentary: In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is said, "He pours out four handfuls.
Its mantra is: "Thee, belonging to the god...
And in that very same context, the mantra for the cutting of the *darbha* grass is: "I cut the *barhis*, the seat of the gods."

Likewise, there is the mantra for spreading [the grass]: "I spread you, who provide wool. There is also the mantra for taking the clarified butter: "Thou art the nourisher. Regarding these, a doubt arises: should the mantra be used once, or should there be repetition with each handful, each offering, each strike, and each taking? What is the prima facie view? That in the acts of pouring out, sprinkling, spreading, and taking the clarified butter, there is a single application of the mantra, because they involve a single substance and have a single purpose.
In rites such as the *nirvāpaṇa* (offering), there should be a single substance; that is to say, there is a single performance.
Why? Because the purpose is one.
In each instance, there is a single purpose.
In the act of offering (nirvāpaṇa), there is the pouring out of the sacrificial oblations;
in the cutting (lavana), the placing near of the sacrificial grass (barhis) suitable for strewing upon the altar; in the strewing (staraṇa), the covering of the altar;
and in the taking of clarified butter (ājyagrahaṇa), the procuring of the clarified butter fit for sacrifice.
To whatever extent there is a purpose, that much has been stated; thus it is said, "that which is the mantra.
It should be like other substances, because of its refinement (*saṃskāra*).
Commentary: Or rather, it should be like other substances, not like a single substance.
The meaning is that there would be fat.
Why? Because of its refinement (*saṃskāra*).
Those rice grains which are husked by a single handful are refined.
Because the act of pouring out (nirvāpa) provides assistance through direct contact,
the second handful indeed consecrates other grains of rice.
In that case, if the mantra were not employed, those grains would be excluded from the consecration performed by the mantra.
Thus it is in all cases.
Therefore, in each respective instance, there is a repetition of the mantra.
The case of that which is preceded by *soma* is a counter-example; because it is a remnant of what precedes it, it is connected with that [preceding rule].

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: in the acts of pouring out (nirvāpa) and threshing (plavana), there should be a single performance [of the mantra] for each substance, because the four handfuls of the pouring out and so forth are intended to be performed simultaneously due to having a single purpose. This is the *nirvāpa* principle (2378). Regarding the meaning of the *nirvāpa* mantra: "In the acts of pouring out and so forth, are those mantras used once or separately? [The answer is: "Once. *agnimaḥ*.

[The opponent argues: "It is not so, because of the unity of the substance. [The Bhāṭṭa replies: No, because of the distinctness of the preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*). In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is the mantra beginning with "devasya tvā" for the prescribed pouring out (*nirvāpa*) measured by four handfuls;
likewise, there is the mantra "barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi" for the prescribed cutting (*lunana*) enjoined by the rule "he cuts odd numbers of handfuls."
Similarly, regarding the act of strewing prescribed by the injunction "He strews the altar with three layers or five layers," there is the mantra "I strew thee, the unaging and immortal";
and regarding the taking of clarified butter prescribed by the injunction "He takes [the butter] four times," the mantra "Thee, the bright, in the bright [ladle]" is recited.

When considering whether these [mantras] apply to each individual handful (muṣṭi) and so forth during the repetition of the pouring (nirvāpa) and other acts, or not—the conclusion is that the number does not pertain to a distinction in the pouring and so forth, because the number is perceived as residing in the handfuls and such; rather, it is merely a repetition of the pouring and other acts.
Therefore, as in the case of the mantra for threshing, there should be no repetition.

This being the prima facie view, we reply: it is appropriate that in the case of threshing, because the two purificatory acts constitute a single unit, those very same rice grains are threshed at every stroke; therefore, in that instance, the mantra is rightly used only once.

In the present case, however, due to the distinction between the two purificatory acts, even though the action—such as the pouring out (nirvāpa) and so forth—is the same, there is a difference of mantra with each repetition.

Furthermore, even though there is a difference in the preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) such as the pouring out [of grain], the cutting, and the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*), why would there be a difference in the preparatory act regarding the spreading (*staraṇa*)? For the second altar (*vedi*) is for the purpose of being prepared by the spreading, and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) therein. However, in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, in the injunction "he spreads the sacrificial grass" (*barhiḥ stṛṇāti*), it is understood that the sacrificial grass itself is the object of the preparatory act of spreading.
Moreover, because of the statement "he places the oblation on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi havīṃṣy āsādayati*), the sacrificial grass is already employed for the placing of the oblations.

As for the statement, "He places the oblations on the altar" (*vedyām havīṃṣy āsādayati*), it is not untenable because the altar (*vedi*) is also, by way of a traditional sequence, a substratum for the oblation. Nor is the altar [identical to] the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), because the wording of the mantra, "Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass, svāhā! (*vedir asi barhiṣe tvā svāhā*), cannot be taken as enjoining direct substratum-ship—which would result in an option with the sacrificial grass—since the altar is already established as the substratum for the grass. For this very reason, in the passage "three-layered or five-layered," it is the sacrificial grass itself that undergoes the consecration (*saṃskāra*).
One should rub [the altar] with the thought, "I am the altar.

Alternatively, by virtue of the principle of "separateness despite connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), just as the act of spreading serves to purify the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), it may also serve to purify the altar; for when the altar and the grass mutually purify one another, there exists a mutual relationship between them. Since a logical alternative (*vikalpa*) is impossible, the statement "he places the oblations on the altar" merely restates an indirect relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*).
Furthermore, because the altar is subordinate (*guṇatva*), the wording of the mantra "Thou art the altar" is justified.
Furthermore, because it is considered refuse—as in the statement, "The altar is indeed a woman; he makes her fleshless"—its purpose is for the act of strewing, which is thus justified.
In every respect, since the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is also something to be consecrated, there exists a distinction in the consecration even during the act of strewing.

Nor does a distinction in consecration arise with each repetition, because the memory produced by the mantra recited once remains uninterrupted, and thus no such contingency occurs as in the case of the mantra for threshing (*avaghāta*).

In all cases regarding the *uttama* (second person) mantras, because one hears the second-person pronoun (*yuṣmat*) and its derivatives (*saṃbuddhi*, etc.), it is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that these mantras serve the purpose of manifesting the offering (*nirvāpa*) and other acts whose objects are the meanings of the second-person pronoun—acts which have not yet been performed (*apūrva*). This is understood from the injunctions concerning the mantras. Since such a recollection (*smṛti*) does not produce a refinement (*saṃskāra*) directed toward the offering and other acts that constitute the object of the second-person meaning, there must necessarily be a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the mantra in those instances. Likewise, in the case of the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), since the mantra is employed for the purpose of manifesting the second-person meaning and other qualifiers, it can be said that there too there is a repetition of the mantra.
Maṇḍana: "The acts of offering (nirvāpa) and so forth are distinct rituals.
Śaṅkara:
"In each individual handful of the offering, that same mantra is used."

15. [The self] is not to be designated as the object of the act of offering (*nirvāpa*), because it is that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*) through the removal of mental distraction caused by itching, and because, since it is one, the logic of the act of offering (*nirvāpa*) does not apply to it.

*Bhāṭṭa* 11.4.16. When the spreading of the altar (*vedi-staraṇa*) and so forth are not included under the act of offering and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), there is a repetition of the offering and so on, and the beginning [of the mantra] is included because of its being that mantra in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

*Ke.* 11.4.144. In the mantra for the offering, "to Agni, what is pleasing" (*agnaye juṣṭam*), in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) such as the Saurya, one must perform the modification (*ūha*) to say "to Sūrya, what is pleasing" (*sūryāya juṣṭam*) or "to Indra and Agni, what is pleasing" (*indrāgnibhyām juṣṭam*), and so on; because [the mantra] expresses the deity associated with the ritual action.
VI. 9.1.13: In the *nirvāpa* mantra, the word "Aindrāgni" [is used] in the case of the *Citreṣṭi*; this is the defect regarding the word "Aindrāgni.
KE. 9.1.1–8: In the *nirvāpa* mantra beginning with "devasya tvā," there is no modification (*ūha*) for the modified forms involving Savitṛ, Aśvin, Pūṣan, and Indra;
rather, in those cases, the mantra remains unmodified.
9|1|12|13–37: Summary of the *nirvāpa* mantras; substitution of the term *viśvedeva*. 9|1|12–8: The meaning of the *nirvāpa* mantras.
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ"—that is, impelled by the god Savitṛ, or when the sun has risen;
"by the arms of the Aśvins," as if being purchased by the arms of the two divine sacrificers.

For those two [sacrificers] have resorted to the Aśvins at the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) through the gift of a horse, or because they have resorted to them by giving the fruit of their labor.
He designates the two arms with the words, "Thus he spoke.
The portions of cooked rice for the deities belong to the Aśvins;
these two are the arms.
"But he considers Pūṣan to be the sacrificer himself; [the mantra says] 'by means of Pūṣan, for you.
Bhāṣya 9.1.11.137. The meaning of the *nirvāpa* mantra is:
'By means of this offering (*nirvāpa*), I perform those [acts] so that they may be serviceable to Agni.'"
The principle of the offering-mantra (nirvāpamantranyāya): 2379. The principle of the offering-mantra [applies] even in the interval during the arrival of the *nivid*.
The principle of the *nirvāpa* (offering) mantra should be observed (*Ke.

11.4.144*). However, when the scratching—which is the object of both the singular and plural [forms of the] command—occurs at the very same time, there is no repetition of the mantra due to the interruption of the recollection (*smṛti*).

Nor, even in that case, does repetition occur according to the principle of the *nirvāpa* mantra (*11.4.144–48*) based on the distinction between each individual limb, because since the limbs have already been employed, they do not constitute a countable number, and thus it is impossible to refer to them by means of the word "you" (*tvā*).

Bhāṭṭa 11.4.16. Oṃ. In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the word "Agni" in the *nirvāpa* mantra—which denotes that which is present—must be modified (*ūhya*). This section is to be consulted under the heading: "Modification of the word 'Agni' in the *nirvāpa* mantra in the modified sacrifice" (Mīmāṃsākośa, Part 3, pp. 1225–26). At the time of the *nirvāpa*, only the mere act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) is performed in the form of the resolve, "I shall give this," and not the actual sacrifice (*yāga*).
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.4.24, page 983:
"The author of the Bhāṣya has presented this argument; it should be understood as being made according to the principle of *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical deliberation).
For the status of being a rule (*vidhitva*) is not applicable to the position that [the mantra] pertains to human qualities and so forth, given that it concerns humans."

Considering it to be an injunction (*vidhi*), the author first introduces the subject, then examines it in accordance with its defining characteristics, and finally concludes by restoring its status as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). This same method should be applied, as far as possible, to other sections (*adhikaraṇas*) as well. In this regard, it is an injunction precisely because of the principle: "It must be an injunction, on account of its being something not previously known; otherwise, it would be merely commendatory."

And by the principle of "that which is neither deficient nor redundant," it becomes a genitive [relationship], such that it is considered a human attribute (*manuṣyadharma*) because of their ownership; humans are not [considered] as its constituent parts,
due to the absence of an indication of a subordinate quality (*guṇavibhakti*).
Furthermore, since that [status of being a deity] exists as a matter of fact, the term "human" would not have been employed;
yet it has indeed been employed.
For this reason also, we conclude that it is a human duty.

Or it is a reference (apadeśa), because the object already exists. The Commentary states: "Apadeśa" is a statement of a general principle; this is not an injunction (vidhi), but rather a restatement (anuvāda).
Why? Because the meaning is already established. That which is worn by humans is indeed the *nivīta* (worn around the neck). For humans generally wear it in that manner for their own purposes.

Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda). Or rather— some remember *nivīta* as the knot at the front of the neck (*galaveṇikāgrantha*), while others [remember it as] the binding of the waist-cloth (*parikarabandha*).
In that regard, the binding of the neck-turban (galaveṇikābandha) is not applicable except in battle;

however, the binding of the girdle (parikarabandha) is applicable in all activities because it is not restricted [to a specific occasion]. Therefore, he states a restatement based upon that [girdle-binding]. As for its purpose, it will be explained later.
It would be so because of its being an injunction and possessing a prior [result].
The Commentary states: It must indeed be an injunction, for in that way it possesses a purpose;
otherwise, it would be a mere discussion and thus useless.
The rest is a reiteration as before; however, this is something new, namely that it should be performed continuously (*nitya*). Or rather—this is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*).
Why? Because it would be a restatement (*anuvāda*) due to being "as before" (*pūrvavat*), meaning [only] when there is absolute necessity (*atyantaprāpti*).
But this is not absolutely necessary, because it is possible even without it, as it is capable of being repeated (*abhyasta*).

Furthermore, since the tying of the neck (*kaṇṭhabandha*) has not yet been reached at the time of departure (*prāyaṇa*), there is scope for a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). That [injunction] would be a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).
The Commentary states: "If it was said that it is an injunction (*vidhi*), this is accepted."
As for the claim that this is a duty for human beings, that is not accepted;
rather, this is a duty pertaining to the ritual act (*kṛtudharma*), because of the context.
For this is stated while duties are being set forth primarily in relation to ritual acts by their very nature.
Therefore, it is a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).

Or rather—given that it is an injunction (*vidhi*)—because its location is primarily among those [passages] concerning the properties of ritual actions, and because it touches upon the mere [act of] measuring, it is a property of the ritual action;
for it is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*).
Commentary: The name *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) is the supplementary statement for the rule "the *nivīta* [mode of wearing the sacred thread] is for humans.
If this is a subsidiary element of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then it must be performed by the Adhvaryu priest;
in that case, the name will be upheld.
Or rather—when two possibilities exist, one must resort to that course of reasoning for the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which does not contradict another means of knowledge.
And because of the knowledge from the Yajurveda, the sentence [prescribing] the *nivīta* and so forth sets aside the designation (*samākhyā*) of "pertaining to the Adhvaryu.

In that case, if this were a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), then, since there would be a requirement for a specific agent, the designation would become meaningful through its restriction to the Adhvaryu priest.
However, we shall explain that among human qualities, designation is not the restrictive factor;
in that case, the former is sublated,
whereas otherwise it will be favored.
Therefore, it is also a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).
In that regard, whatever is performed during the performance [of the rite] is connected to it, because there is no contradiction.
The Commentary says: It is stated.
From the context and the name, it is understood to be a property of the ritual action;
from the syntactical connection, it is a property of man.
Therefore, it deserves to be transferred [to another context].
We say: no.
For one who adheres strictly to the context, it will be appropriate that the human being is the primary factor.
How so? That which has the human being as the primary factor in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is to be applied there, namely, in the Anvāhārya rite.
In this way, both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the sentence (*vākya*) will be properly supported.
First, [the word] "human" (*manuṣya*) refutes the status of [the practice] as a duty of ritual action (*karmadharma*).
For thus has the position been indicated by the term "intoxicating liquor" (*sura*).
It is accepted.
For, having heard [the text], the context and the name being set aside, it follows that this is indeed a human duty (*manuṣyadharma*).
To this, it is said:
Let this position be accepted for the sake of favoring all.
As for the phrase "of men," the genitive case is produced by way of distinction from the primary action; it does not refer to the *nivīta* [wearing of the sacred thread].
Furthermore, that [genitive] is understood from the context to refer to the giving of food and so forth, and nothing else.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence: "If it is the ritual action of humans, then it must be performed there [in that context].
Or rather, because it is mentioned as being equal [to other actions] when that [human agency] is the primary factor, the other [the ritual action] exists for its sake.
The Commentary states: This is not so; it is included within the context [of the sacrifice].
Thus, in a rite where humans are the primary agents, the *nivīta* mode [of wearing the sacred thread] should apply. Why? Because they are enumerated as being equal;
that is, these [modes] are presented as being on an equal footing.

As for the statement, "The upavīta is for the gods; one wears it over the left shoulder," that prescribes the upavīta mode for the two rites under discussion, the New and Full Moon sacrifices. As for the statement, "The prācīnāvīta is for the ancestors," that prescribes the prācīnāvīta mode for the ritual dedicated to the ancestors.
Furthermore, as for this statement, "The nivīta is for humans," that also prescribes it independently for the rite of hospitality (ātithya).

How is it understood that [the rule] prescribes [the suffix] when a human is the principal? Because of the connection with the word "manuṣyāṇām" (of humans) ending in the genitive case, it would apply only to humans, not when a human is the principal. It is said in reply:
Or rather—when [the suffix] is prescribed for humans, a separate fruit [for the principal] must be postulated.

Furthermore, the genitive case will apply to that which is the principal among humans, and the relationship will thus be logically established; nor will it be necessary to postulate a separate result.
Having attained syntactic unity with [the word] "together" (saha), it will then enter into syntactic unity with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices under discussion.
For two relationships are not enjoined within a single sentence.
For the sentence is indeed completed in that manner;
since the other mention of "man" is connected with the *nivīta*, it will form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that very word through the suffix.
When that single syntactical unit is meaningful, a connection with the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*) is not to be assumed.
Therefore, setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*), it should be applied to the *Ātithya* [offering].
Or rather—[the word] would be devoid of context and have man as its primary referent.
Why? Because in this [Vedic] hymn, an enumeration is observed that is equal [to the number of the fingers].
In that case, it would be primarily concerned with the intermediate state, just as [the rites] are primarily concerned with the ancestors and the gods.

Just as the injunctions "the *upavīta* for the gods" and "the *prācīnāvīta* for the ancestors" are rules pertaining respectively to rites primarily concerned with the gods and the ancestors—each being independent of the other—so too, because it follows that same understanding, the rite primarily concerned with humans is likewise for each [individual] alone. When asked, "How is this known?", the answer given is "because of the connection with the word 'of humans' (*manuṣyāṇām*) in the genitive case. To the objection that [if this were so], it would follow that [the rite] applies only to humans, he replies again: [it is not so].
Alternatively, the entire question is indeed one;
it is true that [the result] follows,
but it is set aside due to the excessive complexity resulting from the assumption of a fruit.
Therefore, the genitive case is used solely because of the distinction from his [the sacrificer's] own action;
thus, there will be no assumption of an unsuitable relationship regarding the *nivīta* as being connected to that [sacrifice].
Furthermore, the mention of "human beings" (*manuṣya*) is for the purpose of indicating the primary action; hence, there is no occurrence of an untenable relationship.
And while that [mantra] exists, syntactic unity with the primary injunction is not possible;
rather, it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because of the context.
The Commentary states: "This is not so; it is an injunction, and that [injunction] pertains to a ritual action where humans are the primary agents."

The phrase "of men" (manuṣyāṇām) indicates here a connection with human beings, not a connection with a rite where humans are the primary element. If humans were the primary element, a fruit would have to be supplied.
However, it is connected instead with the act of hospitality (ātithya-karman), which is not explicitly mentioned, is not the subject under discussion, and must be inferred.
What is the fault in that? There is the possibility of a conflict with the context (*prakaraṇa*). If it is asked, "How is there a conflict?"—this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
It connects the nominal stem (*subanta*) under discussion to the context; being an injunction (*vidhi*), it is displaced [from its original position].
Therefore, the injunction pertains to a rite where human agency is primary. Or rather—strictly speaking, not even a single one of these positions is entirely faultless;

for if there were a connection with the context, it would be a matter of syntactical connection, and as for a connection with food, wealth, and so forth, even that dual connection is utterly baseless.

Even by means of the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, non-contact with humans is inferred through its connection [with them]; however, that is not correct, because even that sixth case-ending is perceived as being produced solely from the exclusion of its connection with the word *nivīta*.

Indeed, case-endings do not arise from an exclusion of a connection when the correlates (*saṃbandhin*) of those exclusions have not been mentioned (the analysis of the compound is: "those whose explanations of the connections of the exclusions consist of unmentioned correlates").
Therefore, it follows that [the passage] must have human benefit as its purpose.

Furthermore, even in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to assume a result that contradicts the context. And when another alternative is available, it is not proper to resort to such an assumption.
And there is the possibility [of this being an explanatory statement], since its status as an *arthavāda* is established in the section concerning the Udumbara wood;
furthermore, because it forms a single syntactical unit with an injunction.
The Bhāṣya states: "In this way, it is not an injunction."
Why? Because it forms a single syntactical unit with an injunction; "He leads him up like one possessing divine marks; he thereby makes him such" is that injunction.
It constitutes a single syntactical unit with this [other passage].
If the other were also an injunction, the sentence would be split.
Indeed, there can be no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between an injunction and that which is enjoined, because of the difference in their modes of expression (*vacanavyakti*).
In that case, the form of syntactic unity is sublated.
What is this form of syntactic unity? "Nivīta is for men" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established.
What is the purpose of this repetition regarding the *prācīnāvīta*? It is for the sake of the *upavīta*.
How is it a praise of the *upavīta*? Because the *nivīta* is prescribed for divine rites known as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, whereas that [the *nivīta*] belongs to humans;
likewise, the *prācīnāvīta* belongs to the ancestors and not to divine rites.
The sacred thread (upavīta), however, is appropriate in that context;
therefore, [the phrase] "because you possess the nature of the sacred thread" is used.

Just as when praising Devadatta, one mentions the dress of others—such as saying, "The dress of those who bow is like that of this [person]," or "The dress of the Brahmins is like that of Devadatta"—so too is this an instance of praising Devadatta by mentioning the attire of others.
In the same way here as well, the mention of the *nivīta* occurs alongside the *upavīta* as its counterpart;
there is no injunctive word here stating that "the *nivīta* should be performed by men.
If it is argued that the statement regarding the performance of the *ātithya* rite is what enjoins its performance, this is not so.
Since it possesses purposefulness by way of being a praise, it is not possible to assume [anything else];
for that [assumption] would have to be postulated out of a desire to avoid its meaninglessness, which is an indirect [consequence].
But since there would be pointlessness in a mere description, nothing further need be imagined here;
therefore, it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
And thus, the context (prakaraṇa) speaks meaningfully without contradicting the sentence (vākya).
Or rather—by this injunction "he invests" (*upanayate*), a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is observed between the *nīvīta* and *prācīnāvīta* modes;
and that is possible through the medium of a restatement (*anuvāda*) when there is a direct Vedic text (*śruti*), but not in the case of inference (*liṅga*).

For there can be no syntactic unity between two independent things that are being enjoined as mutually connected, provided they lack the mark of being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of a ritual action, because their modes of verbal expression (*vacanavyakti*) differ.
For the mode of expression of a primary injunction is one that restricts itself to that [specific] element alone, whereas that of a scriptural mention (śruti) is different;
its form conforms to being a subordinate auxiliary (parāṅga).
And here, no injunctive [word] is observed.
Whether it be the *adhyātavya* [offering] itself, or even one occurring within the *ātithyā* and other rites, it might be imagined to be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) [of the *iṣṭi*].

However, such an imagination is not tenable; for that which is not prescribed cannot be a subsidiary, and that which is not a subsidiary is not included by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).
For he will state later: "And that which is not prescribed does not become a subsidiary."

In that case, since the injunction would not be known [prior to the context], the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) would have to be inferred from the injunction; thus, a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*) results.

Furthermore, when a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with a perceptible injunction is possible in some way, a mediated syntactic unity is not appropriate. If that were the case, there would be the assumption of multiple unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, praise is offered according to propriety (*aucitya*).
Just as the *nīvīta* and *prācīnāvīta* modes of wearing the sacred thread are prescribed for humans and the ancestors respectively, so too is the *upavīta* mode for the gods.
This is also observed in the world: just as Vasiṣṭha has Arundhatī, the Moon has Rohiṇī, Nala has Damayantī, so Devadatta has Yajñadattā.
Or rather, it is a praise by way of contrast.

Since those two [the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder and under the left arm] pertain to the ancestors and humans respectively, they are unsuitable for the gods; therefore, the *upavīta* alone is praised for the gods.
Consequently, in rites for the gods known as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), that very mode must be performed.
Śālikanātha: This is a matter for further deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*).

Soma: Although here too the investigation is indeed conducted regarding whether there is a contradiction with the Vedic texts (*śruti*) and so forth within the context (*prakaraṇa*), nevertheless, they say this is a separate section (*pādāntara*) because, in this instance, it is primarily established that [the practice] has the purpose of a ritual action (*kṛtyarthatva*) by means of the context.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: in the statement "The *nīvīta* is for humans," the *nīvīta* is enjoined as a duty (*dharma*) of humans, because the word "human" ending in the genitive case conveys its predominance (*prādhānya*) therein.

"But the *nīvīta* is for human beings; this is an injunction, not an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), because it conveys something previously unknown (*apūrvatva*). Or rather, it is enjoined as part of the sacrifice due to the context. Since the *nīvīta* is already established in the *Mānava* [texts]—as it is generally seen there—it would otherwise be an explanatory statement subordinate to the injunction of the *upavīta*, because it forms a single syntactical unit with it."

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the Śruti: "The *nīvīta* is for humans, the *prācīnāvīta* for the ancestors, and the *upavīta* for the gods; when one is invested with the sacred thread (*upanīyate*), he makes himself a likeness of the gods.

In this context, it has been established by the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa* itself that all of this is a supplementary part (*śeṣa*) of the injunction regarding the *upavīta* (contained in the word *upanīyate*), and not an independent injunction.
When it is an injunction, then the discussion regarding the sentence on the *nīvīta* is undertaken as a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvā-cintā*).

In this regard, the first position is as follows: based on the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is a duty for pure humans (*śuddha-kṛta-dharma*); however, the mention of "human" (*manuṣya*) is not contradictory because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the relationship denoted by the genitive case—specifically the relationship called "agency" (*kartṛtva*) which is delimited by a general connection.

The second position holds that, since the mention of "human" would otherwise be rendered purposeless (*vaiyarthyāpatti*), the genitive case directly expresses a relationship of "limb and principal" (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*). Consequently, one must accept that the *nīvīta* produces a result desired by humans; therefore, it is a duty for pure humans, whether by virtue of the genitive case or the context.

In this case, since there is no sublation when [the injunction] can be established through a non-futile application, and because it would entail the assumption of a separate result (*phala-kalpanā*), and because it lacks the quality of being an auxiliary that directly assists (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), another [teacher] maintains that—like the *yajñāyajñīya* mantra which is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*)—this is a duty pertaining to the person engaged in the sacrifice (*ṛtuyukta-puruṣadharma*).

Although the sequence of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been arranged differently in the root text, it is required here as well due to its consistency with the performance. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that [it is not so], because it would result in an inconsistency with the *prācīnāvīta* [wearing of the sacred thread].

In accordance with the syntactical connection (*vākya*) consisting of the bringing together (*abhihāra*) of those [elements], the genitive case directly expresses a relationship characterized by being an auxiliary to the giving of the *anyāhya* wealth and so forth—which is contextually relevant and has humans as its recipients. By means of this aforementioned relationship, it serves the purpose of humans. For indeed, since the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) is known from the context of the *prokṣaṇī* water-residue-pouring rite dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛdevatya*), it possesses the status of being an auxiliary to that ritual action within the ancestral context.
Therefore, due to this bringing together, this [genitive] also possesses that [status].

In this way, the designation *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) is also upheld. Otherwise, as will be explained later, that designation would function as a restrictive rule only for the attainment of a subordinate agent; however, if [the act] were a duty of the person associated with the sacrifice (*ṛtuyuktapuruṣadharma*), such [a restriction] would be untenable.

Nor can it be argued that even in your view, since the giving is performed by the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), how could the designation be justified; for since the *nīvīta* mode is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), the benefit to the act of giving is accomplished even by it being performed by the Adhvaryu.
Alternatively, there is no fault if it is accepted that [the injunction] is for the purpose of cooking and so forth.

Therefore, since there is an absence of all [other] means of proof (*pramāṇa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is simply that the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) are intended for human beings mentioned in the context.

As for the other alternative presented as the established conclusion in the root-text—namely, "On account of the sentence (*vākya*), this is an injunction [stating] that the *Atithyā* and other rites, which have pure humans as their primary object, are auxiliaries (*aṅga*) [to the sacrifice]."
Nor is there an absence of that which brings it [the meaning] to mind; for, by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the word "man" can refer to Sanaka and others, since—

as in the section on the *nīvī* (Nīvītādhikaraṇa) and the principle of the *niśīthinī*— there is the possibility of bringing to mind the primary elements such as the *hantakāra* offering and hospitality.
Therefore,
there is the principle of the *niśīṣṭi* sacrifice;
[it is performed] on the *amāvāsyā* (new moon) night.
Thus, even the conceptualization of a fruit [is not required]— this is because of the sublation [of that view] by the scriptural statement.
The establishment of this [point] follows by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), since it has already been demonstrated in our own system that [the text] refers to Sanaka and others.

In the *niśīṣṭa* sacrifice, there would be the application of the archetypal [rules], because it is directly perceived; and because, since the *ātithyā* and other rites have already occurred, there is no lack of performance, it cannot be said that they are not taught.
Because it is possible [to interpret it otherwise], and because there is no evidence for either the context (*prakaraṇa*) or the association (*sāhacarya*), [the opponent argues].
The Commentary states: This is heard [in scripture]: "To Agni Rakṣohan, an eight-potherd [cake]...
Furthermore, since the restriction of the final conclusion (*siddhānta-niyama*) is established merely as a matter of deliberation (*cintātvena*), it is not necessary.
"One who fears the *rakṣas*es should offer [this sacrifice]"—
thus it is stated. Furthermore, in that very same place, this view was disregarded by the author of the Vārttika because he described that position as being forced (*kliṣṭa*).
Therefore:
"One should sacrifice at night on the new moon day. In that regard, what [is the case]?
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that [the rite] is indeed a subsidiary part of the primary human action related to the context.
Regarding the inquiry as to whether the *amāvāsyā* sacrifice would consequently be [included] or not, this is the prima facie position (pakṣa).

But this is not an injunction, because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); rather, the *upavīta* is adopted as the rule, while in the *niśīṣṭa* sacrifice there is the non-application (*apravṛtti*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rule.
Thus, the *upavīta* alone is the subsidiary (*śeṣa*), just like the *prācīnāvīta*.
And just as in this *niśīṣṭa* sacrifice,
the *nivīta* [mode] pertains to the ordinary *amāvāsyā* ritual procedure (*tantra*),
whereas in the *prācīnāvīta* mode, there is a connection with humans and ancestors through the relation of being primary to that [ritual].
The application [of the rule] does not follow.

Why? Because it is directly enjoined; it is appropriate for the direct perception, and likewise the *upavīta* (sacred thread) as well, by virtue of its connection with the gods; therefore, that alone [is to be used].
The learned authorities maintain that it is desired [as follows]: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rakṣohan;
it is praised in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," so says the Śruti.
Or rather, those [details] are to be applied there and there.
"One who is afraid of those who protect [me]," it is said.

What follows from this? From that very point, as will be stated later, it is prescribed for the auspicious occasion; however, in this case, by divine necessity, it is indeed the *upavīta* (sacred thread) itself.
It is understood that this praise of the *karmastana* is an independent discovery (*upajñā*) belonging to no one else;
it stands in the middle.

Just as with the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for Agni-Soma: "Having performed the offering with the omentum (vapā) of the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma, one should offer the animal-cake for Agni-Soma on eleven potsherds. — Maṇḍana: "The praise [is given] while wearing the sacred thread around the neck (nīvīta), after having performed the prescribed rite of wearing it over the left shoulder (upavīta)."
Śaṅkara: "The *nīvīta* should not be prescribed.
[This refers to] the injunction (*vidhi*).
Thus.

And just as it is said regarding the Vaiśvadeva offering for a Vaiṣṇava: "Whatever might be spilled below and whatever might be smeared upon the wooden sword (sphya), that one should offer to Viṣṇu Urukrama."
The combination of the *nīvī* and the *upavīta* [is prescribed] according to this [rule].
(Karka 10).
[At the time of cutting the portions, that which remains uncrumbled and adhered to the lower part of the *sruk*...]
4 | 1–2 Varṇaka 1:
Whatever may be the most excellent [portion] on the *sphya* should belong to Viṣṇu.
This concludes the fourth quarter of the third chapter, beginning with the section on the *nīvīta*.

Such is the meaning of the passage beginning with "ityādi. Now, an objection is raised: [the word] "amāvāsyāyām" is heard in the middle of the ritual action known as the *Amāvāsya*, yet the word *amāvāsyā* itself does not denote the ritual action. [Pāṇini 2.4.3: *tatra ca dīyate kāryaṃ bhavavat*].
The mention of *nīvīta* in the *nīvīta*-statement has the same meaning as *upavīta*;
it is not a statement regarding the mode [of wearing the garment], but rather a statement regarding time.
The scriptural injunction (*śruti*) pertains to time, not to the ritual action (*karman*).
Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and direct statement (*śruti*); direct statement is more authoritative than indication, unless [the latter] pertains to something else.
Cessation is established by negation (Su. p.
4). Or rather, cessation is heard of in the middle of the ritual action; whose procedure (tantra) will be adopted?
Therefore,
because of the difference in ritual action (karmabheda), as in the case of a modified sacrifice (vikṛti). (8.1.14.24) Just as in the modification...
It will be independent; it will be the *camasa* cup itself (and not the *godohana* vessel), as in the eighth [chapter].
Furthermore, there would be a difference in the ritual procedure (*tantra*) due to the difference in time and sentence.
He will say: "Or rather, it is cessation" (Vākyapadīya 3.6.1.10, p. 1037). The Bhāṣya states: "Because of the difference in time and because of the difference in sentences."
There is a rule that the activity of a prohibitory injunction must be preceded by an activity [of its opposite];
therefore, the *niśīṣṭi* sacrifice takes place on the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), while [the other] takes place on the day of the first lunar day (*pratipad*).
And these two sentences, "One should sacrifice on the new moon day" and "One should sacrifice at night on the new moon day," refer to the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsya*).

One [instance] occurs in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and one in the optional (kāmyā) iṣṭis. What follows from this? If these two were in the same location, then it would be understood that the time prescribed for the Amāvāsyā rite—namely, "one should sacrifice on the new moon day"—would be the very same time enjoined for the midnight offering (niśītha).
In that case, the status of being an Amāvāsyā rite would also have to be accepted as prescribed for that [midnight offering].

Furthermore, when there is a difference in location, just as the time prescribed in the injunction "one should sacrifice on the new moon day" is enjoined as something to be adopted, so it is here as well.

Nor does the contingency of having the same time arise; for example, although the modified sacrifices (*vaikṛtīṣṭi*) have the same time as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), they do not depend upon the ritual framework (*tantra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Therefore, there is indeed a single framework.
The digging up of the altar-ground (*vedyudvanana*) would be the same as that [of the *darśī*], because it is a prohibition of the consciousness [of difference].
Commentary: Is this the general rule—that every ritual system (*tantra*) is distinct? Certainly not.

It may be that the digging up of the altar-ground is considered to be the very same as that which was performed for the *darśī* altar; by that, it is said: there is no purpose whatsoever in digging it up again, for it would merely result in the refutation of what has already been done.
Furthermore, once a vow has been undertaken and performed, it is impossible to undertake it again;
and if it were undertaken [again], it would be as ineffective as grinding what has already been ground.
Therefore, both of these [consequences] would result in that very same [absurdity].

Or, because it is prescribed within the *tantra* of that [deity], it belongs to that *tantra*, since it must be performed together with it. The commentary states: "Or, the *Niśīthī* may belong to that *tantra*;
this is a *tantra* of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), not an independent one."
Why? Because it is prescribed within the context of the *tantra*.
This [offering] is prescribed in the midst of the *amāvāsyā-tantra* by the injunction: "One should offer [the oblation] at night on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
But has it not been stated that this word *amāvāsyā*, being a designation of time, does not denote the ritual action?

It is true that it is a statement regarding time, but that time is within the context of the ritual procedure (*tantra*). Since it is being enjoined there, it becomes enjoined within the ritual procedure because it is connected to it. Likewise, the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) to be prepared are not enjoined with reference to the animal sacrifice (*paśukarman*), yet they become enjoined within the animal ritual procedure.

The place where [the rites] are prescribed is within the *paśutantra* (animal sacrifice ritual system). If this too falls within the *tantra*, it cannot be independent (*svatantra*), as it would merely be a subordinate part. Furthermore, because of the presence of defects and other factors, the external [rites], such as the kindling of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) and so forth, are performed if they are for the sake of the deity.

The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Here it is asked: Is this the general rule that the *niśītha* accomplishes the entire *samāvāsyā-tantra*, or is it not so? Indeed, it should accomplish the fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Why? Because of its deficiency.

The *idhma* (sacrificial fuel) is for the purpose of kindling the fire; if it is offered on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), it would not accomplish the objective of facing the midnight (*niśītha*) occurring at night during the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).
As for the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), it is for the purpose of spreading over the altar (*vedi*) and so forth.
If those two were performed together, the night-rite would be deficient;
therefore, they should be performed separately.
And the adding of fuel to the fires should be done if it is for the sake of the deities.
If the *agnyanvādhāna* is for the purpose of encompassing the deities (*devatāparigraha*), then that too must be performed separately;

for by the original (*prākṛta*) *agnyanvādhāna*, the deities of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*) are encompassed, and not the *rakṣo’gni*. Furthermore, since it is also for the purpose of encompassing that [fire]—that is, for the purpose of maintaining the fire—and because the fire has already been maintained by the original rite, it need not be performed.

The fact that [the animal sacrifice] is for the purpose of being taken over by the deities is heard in the supplementary portion of the text: "May splendor be mine; may it not depart. Thus, even previously, one takes it over; indeed, the deities themselves have been taken over by the preceding [sacrifice]. [This is indicated by the statement: "When it has become auspicious, one should sacrifice. Regarding Soma: since the Savanīya animal and the Savanīya cakes are both encompassed by the single injunction for the Soma sacrifice (*saumika-prayoga-vacana*), although there is the possibility of *prasaṅga* (extension of benefit) of the animal-related [rites] into the cakes, because of the authority of the distinct injunctions (*bhinna-prayoga-vacana*), there is no extension of the New Moon (*dārśika*) rites. This is stated as the connection (*saṅgati*).

But surely, when the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs immediately after the *āghāna* sacrifice and even before the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), then the *darśa* ritual procedure (*tantra*) does not apply to that [new moon]; for since the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices begin with the *pūrṇamāsa*, the performance of the *darśa* rite would not be prompted at that time. Consequently, because its performance is possible during the midnight [of that day], the rule that the midnight time is restricted to the procedure of the new moon (*amāvāsyā-tantra*) is untenable.

Furthermore, there is no evidence that the performance of a modification (vikṛti) which arises due to the influence of a cause (nimitta) and so forth must necessarily occur even when the archetype (prakṛti) has not been commenced; for if that were the case, the performance of the *niśītha* [offering] would be impossible prior to the commencement of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Such being the case, since there would be no performance of the archetypes in the form of the *sānnāyya* and *agnīṣomīya* prior to the *soma*, those [offerings] would not be performed; thus, at the *niśītha* [of the *soma* sacrifice], the *nipādasthapati* [receives] the cooked meat (*śṛta*).
In this *niśītha* [rite], there is no application of the ordinary *amāvāsyā* ritual;
rather, its application should occur independently, because the *niśītha* is taught directly and is prescribed as an autonomous rite.
Therefore, the *niśītha* is independent.
Thus is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Alternatively, there is the reading *apavṛttiḥ*.
In that case, since *apavṛttiḥ* means "cessation" (*nivṛttiḥ*), its intended meaning is precisely "non-engagement" (*apravṛttiḥ*).
In the Bhāṣya manuscript, however, "na prasajyate" is printed in the root text (*mūla*).
In that case, having stated "na prasajyate," the reading "apravṛttiḥ" alone becomes clear [as the intended meaning].
Furthermore, there would be a division of the *tantra* due to the difference in time and sentence structure.

Due to the difference in time and the difference in the statements, there would be a distinction between the *tantra* (ritual procedure) of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the *tantra* of the night (*niśi*). There is a difference in time because the sacrifice is performed at night on the new moon day, whereas [the other] is performed during the day on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*).
There is also a difference in the statements, as these two statements—"one should sacrifice on the new moon day" and "one should sacrifice at night on the new moon day"—refer to different locations.
Therefore, there would be a difference of ritual procedure (*tantrabheda*).
Because of the triple prohibition regarding the *vaiyuddhananna* [offering], it must be that very same procedure.
Even though the ritual procedure for the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā-yāga*) and the ritual procedure for the *niśitha* [offering] are distinct, [the former applies here].

The statement in the Bhāṣya, "by virtue of the force of the injunction," is incorrect. [The author] refutes this: The isolated injunction (anārabhyavāda), "that which is in the Āhavanīya fire," pertains to the archetype (prakṛti), just like the rule regarding the *khadira* wood; it does not apply to all [rites].
For the quality of being made of *khadira* is enjoined for the *sruva* ladle (which is taught in the archetype itself).

Since the *āhavanīya* fire is also prescribed for the *homa* only in the context of the archetype (*prakṛti*), it would rightly follow by extension (*codaka*) in the *khapateṣṭi* sacrifice; thus, the commentary is indeed correct. Regarding those rites in which the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) have the right to participate, there is no application of the injunctions concerning the *āhavanīya* and other fires. Why? Because they already possess the fire. Their possession of the fire follows from their capability (*sāmarthya*).

The scriptural texts concerning desires (*kāmaśruti*) imply the injunction for the formal establishment of the fires (*ādhānaśruti*) for them, as it would otherwise be impossible [to fulfill those desires].

For their scriptural injunctions regarding the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) are indeed intended for that purpose, and by them, the logical necessity (*anyathānupapatti*) [of the fire] is satisfied.
Furthermore, that establishment of the fires is prompted by the fires themselves, not prompted by the ritual season (*ṛtu*).

This being the case, since the *Svapa-tīṣṭi* sacrifice is performed by one who possesses the fires—because the *Niṣāda-sthapati* has not been provided with fires by another injunction, and because he himself possesses the fires—it is prompted by the fires; and since the fires also have the capacity for the establishment (*ādhāna*), they too are prompted [by it]. Therefore, this establishment of the fires is prompted by the *Svapa-tīṣṭi* sacrifice.
Therefore, for that purpose:

by means of that [specific] establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), one who has fallen away from the *khapatīṣṭi* [is restored]; by means of the other [general] establishment of the sacred fires, the Brāhmaṇas and others are permanently possessed of the sacred fire (*agnimant*).

(Thus, since the *Khapa* sacrifice cannot otherwise be logically accounted for, it necessitates another performance of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*)—one distinct from that enjoined by the sentences concerning spring and so forth—which serves its own purpose.

Therefore, its completion (*apavarga*) is mentioned. (What is this mention of "completion"? To explain: If [the *Khapa* sacrifice] were not performed because it is for the sake of that [other consecration], then, because it has been performed, one might think—"The *Khapa* sacrifice is capable [of conferring qualification]," and thus there would be eligibility for other rites as well. (It is to dispel such a misconception on the part of those of dull intellect that the mention of "completion" is made.)
Or rather, it should take place in the worldly fire, because the *ādhāna* (consecration) is not subsidiary to all [fires].
Commentary: There is a repetition of the fifth case ending in the word *agniciti*.
It should take place in worldly fires, not in consecrated ones.
Why? Because the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) is not subsidiary to all [rites].
The sacred fires are subsidiary to all rites;
their establishment is a subsidiary to them, not a subsidiary to the rites themselves.

Because there is an absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth, the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not prompted by ritual action (*karman*); rather, by the force of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is prompted by the fire itself.

And that which is prompted by the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is obtained through the extended injunction (*codaka*), not that which is prompted by the material substance (*dravya*).
Therefore, the *Khapa* sacrifice is performed in worldly fires.

The laying of the fires (*dup-ādhāna*) is not obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of extension) because it is not an integral part [of the sacrifice] (due to its being a feature of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*), nor is it recited in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *khapatīṣṭi*.
Therefore, it is neither based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*) nor based on extension (*atideśika*).
Rather, the fire is that which is common in worldly practice (*laukika*).

And that [rite] is obtained through traditional practice (*ācāra*), because of the traditional rule of Gautama: "In that [fire], one should perform the *gṛhya* rites" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 5.8). The meaning is "those connected with the household" (*gṛha-yā-hitāni*). Furthermore, the word *gṛha* refers to the husband and wife;

In those cases where there is no *āhavanīya* fire, in all such instances, the fire is worldly (*laukika*).
Regarding that, the text beginning with "In that [fire] one should take [the portions]" and so forth is the *Tantraratna*, according to the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*.

Even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that [since the *upanayana* ceremony lacks the possibility of *ādhāna*], here the *ādhāna* is possible—the present objection constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*).
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Just as the *khapatīṣṭi* necessitates the *prayāja* offerings, so too would it necessitate the *agnyādheya* (the laying of the fires).

This being the case, someone might argue that because one possesses the fires (*agnimat*), there would be eligibility (*adhikāra*) for other rites as well; however, the author of the Sūtras says: "And because it is for that purpose, it would follow [otherwise].

Therefore, since the *ādhāna* is a stage of purification (*saṃskāra*), one does not possess the fires [in the required sense] until after it, and thus there is no eligibility for other rites prior to it.

The *Vi-khapatīṣṭi* should take place either in the Vedic fire or in the worldly (secular) fire; it would necessitate [the fire], for the *Ādhāna* (fire-consecration) would be the final [requirement] because there is no Vedic consecration of the fires [in the case of the Niṣādas]. According to the Bhaṭṭa school: Since the *Niṣādeṣṭi* is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *Āhavanīya* and other fires are obtained by extension (*deśena*). Because those fires depend upon the *Ādhāna*, even though there is no independent injunction for the *Ādhāna*, the *Niṣādeṣṭi* itself would necessitate the performance of the *Ādhāna*.

This being the position reached: although that [fire] has the capacity to produce fire, since the *ādhāna* (consecration) is established as being performed by Brāhmaṇas and others, there is no authority for it being performed by a Niṣāda. Furthermore, because in the archetype (*prakṛti*) one subsists on what is provided by another, there is no acquisition of the *āhavanīya* and other fires here; thus, the [consecration] does not apply to them. However, there is a difference: since the sacrifice of the Niṣādas is impossible without knowledge (*vidyā*), and since the requirement [for knowledge] is fulfilled through worldly means, the implication [of its necessity] is justified. Thus, there is a disparity [between the two cases].

Therefore, although [the fire] implies the Āhavanīya and other sacrificial fires, there is a Smṛti injunction stating: "In whatever place one might offer an oblation, having performed the five purificatory rites of the earth, one should establish the common (laukika) fire. Since this prescribes the common fire for the purpose of any mere oblation in the absence of other fires, the sacrifice should be performed after establishing that very fire in that location. As for the statement of Gautama, "In that [fire], he performs the Gṛhya rites," which was cited in the *Tantraratna* as a source for the common fire, it is disregarded here because the word "that" (tat) refers back to [the context] in Gautama’s Smṛti, and because the Niṣāda-sacrifice does not fall under the category of Gṛhya rites.

It cannot be argued that this [wife] also possesses the status of being denoted by the word "house" (gṛha) on the grounds that she is beneficial to the husband and wife who are themselves denoted by that term; for the word "house" is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) through the usage of experts to denote the duties of a householder, and thus its etymological derivation (*yoga*) is not determinative.
Otherwise, the other [wife] would also incur the status of being the "house. As Maṇḍana says: "A Niṣāda should perform the sacrifice in a worldly fire."
The sacrifice for the Niṣāda chieftain (*niṣādasthapati*) should likewise be performed;
that is, just like the initiated student (*upanīta*), it is to be performed in the worldly fire (*laukikāgni*).
There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the status of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) to the Niṣāda chieftain.

However, since kingship and the like are qualifiers of the agent, and since that [agent] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), its extension (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*) is indeed desired.
This includes the case of the *niṣādasthapati*.
In the *raudra* oblation (*caru*), the office of the *khapati* belongs to one of the Niṣāda caste;

The Bhāṣya states: "Having introduced this sacrifice—'One should offer a *raudra* oblation in the middle of the dwelling, where Rudra might afflict the subjects'—it is said: 'With this [oblation], one should cause the *niṣādasthapati* to sacrifice.'"
Regarding the term "Niṣādasthapati," there is a doubt: is he one among those already entitled [to perform sacrifices], or is he someone else entirely?
We say it is one among them, for he is capable due to his learning and his possession of the sacred fires (agnimat).
Another [person] is incapable because of his lack of knowledge and lack of fire.
But surely the term *niṣādasthapati* would not be applicable there? It will be a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), meaning "the chief among the Niṣādas."
Therefore, it follows from the word itself that this refers to one who is already authorized [to perform the sacrifice].
This being the position reached, we reply: only a Niṣāda ought to be the lord of the hut.
Why? Because of the force of the words.
For the word "Niṣāda" is able to denote the Niṣāda caste through direct audition alone;
however, it would have to express the Niṣādas' lord only through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
And when there is a conflict between direct audition and secondary indication, direct audition is the proper course, not secondary indication.
From this it is understood: this is not a fault.
The word *niṣāda* denotes the *niṣāda* caste itself;
the genitive case expresses a relationship.
In that case, because the genitive is not heard;
for here the genitive is not explicitly mentioned. He says: the genitive is understood for the purpose of establishing elision, since the genitive is not heard.
But not by way of elision (lopa).
By what, then? By the indication (lakṣaṇā) of the word *niṣāda*.
And its weakness has already been stated.
However, the *samānādhikaraṇa* compound is stronger;
for in that case, the word retains its own primary meaning,
and the second case ending is connected to both [members] by means of *tantra*.

By that, Niṣāda, who is designated as the second [member of the compound], is understood. In that case, by assuming the sense of the genitive case, one would be grasping what is not explicitly stated. Therefore, Niṣāda himself must be the *khaṣpati*.

(He states the established conclusion: This is a *karmadhāraya* compound, not a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. (Why? Because (if this were the case), both words would be functioning in their own primary sense (*svārtha-vṛtta*); otherwise (in the case of a genitive compound), the word *niṣāda* would have to be superimposed upon the "husband of a Niṣāda woman" through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). (To the question "Why resort to figurative indication? he replies: It is for the purpose of establishing that the compound is one of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

(Also in the case of the *nīlotpala* compound,) the referent (*adhikaraṇa*) is the same for the word *utpala*, and it is likewise the same for the word *nīla*. Therefore, the capacity (*sāmarthya*)—characterized by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—which constitutes grammatical coreferentiality (*aikādhikaraṇya*), is established; and from that capacity, the compound is formed. In the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), however, one must resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in order to establish grammatical coreferentiality.

Otherwise (if by the word *niṣāda* only a *niṣāda* were meant, and by the word *khapati* only a *khapati* who is a different entity were meant), there would be an absence of semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) due to their having different substrata; and from the absence of semantic connection, there would be an absence of compound formation (*samāsa*). Therefore, for the sake of establishing the compound, the word *niṣāda* must extend its meaning as far as the *khapati*; this is what constitutes figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, no genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) exists here, because none is perceived.
If it is argued that [the genitive case] is elided, it is replied:

if the elision of the genitive is postulated here on the grounds of its non-hearing, then why is it not postulated that words such as *syāt* are elided? For there is no difference in their non-hearing. Therefore, there is no evidence for elision.
Regarding the phrase "rājapuruṣa" and so forth, the analysis (*vigraha*) should be made as "he who is both a king and a man.
Even there, because the genitive case is not explicitly heard, it does not exist;

however, based on the relationship between owner and owned, one superimposes the sense of the genitive onto the word "king" (in the pair *rājapuruṣayoḥ*), and at that time—namely, at the moment of forming the compound—the compound is established.
The analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) "the king's man" is for the purpose of illustrating the meaning—that is, for the sake of clarification.

Therefore, whatever case-ending (*vibhakti*) is present in the word *rājñaḥ* (the genitive), that is attached (*anuṣajyate*) to the other word (*niṣāda*), resulting in "the Niṣāda king" (*niṣādarājñaḥ*).
This is because no other [case-ending], such as the genitive, is heard.

Alternatively, because [the case-ending] arises from the whole (i.e., from the compound word *niṣādasthapati*), it should be understood as applying to both [members of the compound] even without *anuṣaṅga* (supplying the case-ending to each part).
Therefore, there is no other [meaning] than a Niṣāda, because the status of being a *sthapati* is absent [in any other].
By the power of the word itself, this *sthapati* must be a Niṣāda;
and because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Commentary: An indicative mark is observed: "The sacrificial fee is a spear-throw" (*kūṭa dakṣiṇā*), which shows that the material belongs to the Niṣāda.
For the *kūṭa* (the wooden post) is indeed beneficial only to the Niṣādas, not to other purposes;
thus, it belongs to the Niṣādas alone.

Regarding this, having established [the context] with the injunction, "One should offer a *caru* oblation made of *vāstu* wood to Indra," it is heard [in scripture]: "With this [offering], one should cause the *sthapati* (chief) of the Niṣādas to sacrifice."
In that regard, in both cases, this word functions solely by virtue of its etymological derivation (*yoga*).

Therein, if it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the qualification would belong to the learned person (*vidvas*) and to one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); however, if it is intended as a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*), [the qualification belongs to the former].
It would follow that even a common person who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) would possess the qualification [for the office];
therefore, when it is argued that this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it is replied:
"In this way, however, the word *niṣāda* itself would function as an indication (*lakṣaṇa*) for the carpenter (*sthapati*)."

For no genitive case-ending is heard [in the text], by virtue of which there could be an injunction related to that [Niṣāda]. Therefore, the word "Niṣāda" itself must indicate this meaning of the genitive.
However, in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound, there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) whatsoever.
It is understood from the Vedic text that the *niṣāda* alone is the *sthapati*.
Therefore, by the force of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), he is one who is ignorant [of the Vedas] and has not maintained the sacred fires;
indeed, the *niṣāda* alone is the *sthapati* entitled to participate in this ritual act.
Soma—The connection [of this section] arises from the refutation based on the aforementioned inconsistency.
One named Niṣāda is born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother;
however, he is endowed with the duties of a Śūdra.
For this very reason, the teacher Āpastamba stated, "The call 'O preparer of the oblation' is for the Śūdra," thereby referring to the Niṣāda specifically by the term "Śūdra.

Thus, since the Śūdra caste is prohibited [from officiating], it should be understood that only those who have transgressed such prohibitions may act as priests. As Viśvarūpa states: "Either a twice-born person, a Sthapati, or a Vaiśya; the 'twice-born' is so called because of the *ṣaṣṭhī* compound."
Because it functions as a *karmadhāraya* compound, the *niṣāda* is the performer of the *raudra* sacrifice.

The *Bhāṭṭa* school explains: Having established the injunction, "One should offer a *caru* oblation consisting of the materials of a dwelling for Rudra," the scripture states, "With this [offering], one should cause the *niṣādasthapati* to sacrifice.

In that context, although a *bahuvrīhi* interpretation—where both words would require *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) toward a referent external to the words themselves—is not accepted, [the term is instead understood as a *karmadhāraya*: a Niṣāda who is a chief].

Nevertheless, because that [implied knowledge] would be absent in a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound such as "the chief (sthapati) of the Niṣādas," one must accept a *karmadhāraya* compound—assuming the capacity to imply [the requisite] learning—and thus that very [compound] is resorted to.
Nor is there even in that case a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the status of being a Niṣāda in the first member of the compound, for there is no reason [for such a shift].

For indeed, when the meaning is established through the connection of the already-established meanings of the constituent parts, it is not authoritative to assume a distinct power for the whole compound to convey a specific meaning.

Nevertheless, in a *karmadhāraya* compound, since it is logically possible for non-difference itself to appear through the very cognition of the relation (*saṃsarga*)—such as the relation of owner and owned—which exists even in a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, there is no ground for the charge of "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) regarding the need for secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
Nor do we have any evidence, as the Naiyāyikas do, that for us there is only the relation of difference (*bheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of two nouns.

This is because in all instances such as "The king is a man" (*rājā puruṣo 'sti*), we accept the connection of the meaning of one noun with the meaning of the case-ending, and that [case-meaning] in turn with the meaning of the verb; for there is nowhere except in compounds that the mutual connection [of nominal stems] is not strictly maintained.
Therefore, since it is logically possible for that [meaning], which is applicable only in a compound, to appear by way of being a relation (saṃsarga), there is no secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).

This being the case, since in instances of co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) words—such as "the king, the man, exists"—after the connection with the verb, the subsequent lateral connection is experienced only through the relation of identity (abheda), whereas in instances of non-co-referential (vyadhikaraṇa) words—such as "the king’s man exists"—it is experienced only through the relation of difference (bheda), one must, for the sake of parsimony, postulate a rule that the verbal cognition of the connection between a word-meaning induced by a noun has identity as its sole object. Consequently, since relations such as owner-and-owned can be established as appearing as the relational mode (saṃsarga) in compounds like *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, one must necessarily accept that there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the relation to its own meaning in the first member of the compound, and that this [meaning] connects with the second member through identity.

For this very reason, it should also be understood that with respect to a cognition characterized by non-difference as its relational mode (*saṃsarga*), whose qualificandum is the meaning of one name and whose qualifier is the meaning of another name—both of which are not prompted by a [prior] name—the necessary condition (*tantratva*) consists in either the co-occurrence of two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) whose referents reside in a single substratum, or the co-occurrence of two names other than a *dvandva* compound.
By this, it is also understood that in cases such as *dhavakhadirau* ("the dhava and khadira trees") and *nīlaghaṭau* ("the blue pot"), the cognition arises from the names themselves.

It should not be argued that, because in a compound (*samāsa*) the relata are construed as non-different (*abhedena*), whereas in the analytical statement (*vigraha*)—such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*)—the relationship denoted by the genitive case is construed as different (*bhedenānvayāt*), the two (the compound and the sentence) would result in having different meanings; for if this were so, the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.11] allowing for an option (*vibhāṣā*) would become redundant, since the application of one form would not necessarily preclude the other.
This is because, given the existence of one, the existence of the other is necessarily implied, and thus the meaning is intended [to be the same].

Therefore, since a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) would otherwise result in a genitive *tatpuruṣa*, the term *niṣādasthapati* is indeed a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), consisting of "the *sthapati* who is a *niṣāda*."

Therefore, since the Vedic knowledge (vidyā) is already implied for that specific subject matter, the eligibility belongs to the Niṣāda alone, even though he has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni).
For this very reason, the indicative mark (liṅga) in the statement, "The fee is a counterfeit coin, for that indeed belongs to the Niṣādas," is also consistent.

And in that case, although the Āhavanīya fire is not implied because [the rite] is prompted by another, there is the Smṛti injunction: "Wherever one might offer oblations, having performed the five-fold purification of the elements, one should establish the worldly fires. Thus, in the absence of other fires, it refers to the mere act of offering oblations.
