For example, in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*, regarding the injunction for the Hotṛ priest to recite the *Ṛtavyā* hymns while seated upon a golden cushion—expressed as "He recites while seated on a golden cushion"—and regarding the injunction for the Śunaḥśepa narrative intended for human benefit—expressed as "Those desiring sons should also have it narrated"—the prohibition of these is inferred through censure. This occurs because, in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) of these injunctions, it is said: "They did not find anyone to appoint [as slaughterer]," and "They did not find anyone to expand [the narrative]. Furthermore, since the act of slaughter (*śāmitra-karma*) is understood to be defective due to greed—as seen in the thought, "Give me a hundred cows more; I shall distinguish myself"—it is prohibited by means of such censure.

Although here there is a general prohibition, "He shall not [act] as a priest" (*na hiṃkṣāt*), which—by means of the general authority of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) over their own specific duties—is indeed established even for those who are not formally appointed as priests through the mere status of being an agent; and for this very reason, the author of the Vārttika stated in the section on the *Śamitṛ* (the slaughterer), at *Tarkapāda* 3.7.13.28–29, "Therefore, he censures the non-priesthood"; nevertheless, the specific prohibition is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to indicate a particular defect. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 57). This is the maxim: "The double negation results in a single negation."

The meaning is that there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the negation of the knowledge of negation, and not otherwise; thus it is said in the *Śaṅkaravijaya*: "It operates within the scope of the object.
*Sāhasī*, 893. *Niṣkāsa* means a certain portion of the food smeared on the vessel, as well as a portion of the boiled rice smeared on the cooking pot (in the vernacular, *kharapuḍī*).

The *niṣkāsa* (scrapings) is the remnant remaining upon the taking up of the vessel. Jyotiṣṭoma 7.3.4: The *niṣkāsa* of the *prāyaṇīya* [offering] is for the purpose of the *nirvāpa* (pouring out) of the *udayanīya*.
Jyotiṣṭoma.

VI. 7.3.4: "The *niṣkāsa* [remnant] is used in the *avabhṛtha* of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices; for its connection is understood as being with a subordinate act. Bhāṣya 11.2.15.56: "In the *avabhṛtha* involving the *niṣkāsa*, there should be a separation of the offering (*pradāna-viprakarṣa*), because it is a part of that [sacrifice], just like the animal sacrifice.
Regarding the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "With the *vāruṇī* [offering] and the *niṣkāsa*, they descend to the *avabhṛtha* bath."
The *vāruṇī* is the meat offering dedicated to the deity Varuṇa; its *niṣkāsa* (residue) is the portion smeared upon the vessel.
For one whose sacrificial ground is of this origin, there would be a delay in the offering of the residue at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).
At the place of insertion (*āvāpasthāna*), one portion of the *āmiṣā* is offered together with a ram made of barley flour.
However, because of the distance between the place of the scrapings and the place of the fuel-sticks, the offering must be made only in the high-altar (vihāra) area.
The term "avabhṛtha" (concluding bath), moreover, is merely a figurative reference;
for the scrapings are indeed only a portion of the *āmiṣā* offering.

"Like the animal sacrifice. Just as there is a temporal separation of the portions of the animal—namely, "they proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing, with the sacrificial cake at midday, and with the limbs at the third pressing"—so it is here.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Or [it is] a removal, because of its connection with what is well-known. The Siddhāntin says: the word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of setting aside the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
The removal of the *niṣkāsa* (remnant) must be performed from the preceding rite;
its application (*viniyoga*) should be in a distinct rite called the *avabhṛtha*.
This is because of the connection of the *niṣkāsa* with the well-known term *avabhṛtha*, and because it is so stated by the expression bearing that designation.
And thus, there is no temporal separation from the act of giving in the case of the dismissal and so forth; rather, this is an instruction for a different ritual action (*karmāntara*).
If it is argued that this is a disposal (*pratipatti*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) objects.

If it is argued that because the *niṣkāsa* (the scrapings) consists entirely of *āmiṣa* (impure remnants) and is a remnant of what has been consumed, its disposal through the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) would be a mere act of ritual purification (*pratipatti*) and not a purposeful ritual act (*arthakarma*), [the author] says:
No, because of its connection with a specific ritual action (*karmasaṃyoga*).
The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) gives the reply: it is not a mere act of disposal.

Why? Because of the connection with an action; for there is a connection of this *niṣkāsa* (the scrapings), which functions as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), with a purposeful action (*arthakarman*). This is understood from the connection [indicated] by the instrumental case-ending in the word *niṣkāsenā*.
Therefore, it is established as the final position (*siddhānta*) that this is an instruction for a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Ke.
The section concerning the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the discharge [of the Soma].
The purchase;
the section concerning the final purificatory bath with the discharge.
This refers to another rite characterized by the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath);
see *Mīmāṃsākośa*, Part 2, pp.
703–705 (*Ke.* 11.2.15.63–66). This is known as the *niṣkāsāvabhṛtha-nyāya*.
The *avabhṛtha* belonging to the *Varuṇapraghāsa* has as its substance the scrapings (*tūṣanikā*) [of the sacrificial cakes].

In the case of a substance-instruction, that which pertains to the substance [is applied] because of its connection with the Vedic text; in the case of an instruction for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), [the properties of the model sacrifice apply] because it is the material cause thereof.
Commentary: It has been stated that the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) belonging to the *Vāruṇapraghāsas* is the receiver of the ritual details (*dharma*) from the *avabhṛtha* of the Soma sacrifice.
With regard to this, the following is now considered.

Is this [sacrifice] one whose substance is the *puroḍāśa* cake, or is it one whose substance is the husks (*tuṣanikāsa*)? What is the prima facie view? That its substance is the *puroḍāśa*. Why? Because the *puroḍāśa* is obtained through the name.
[Objection: But surely it is directly heard [in the text] as being like husks.
[Reply: True, it is directly heard, but it cannot be enjoined.
Here, in the context of the *avabhṛtha*, it is enjoined: "They go to the *avabhṛtha*."

If, however, another threshing were to be prescribed, then there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), as in: "They go to the final bath (*avabhṛtha*)," and "that [they go] by means of threshing. Why is there no mention of threshing now? It would be purposeless, because of the absence of a connection.
This being the position reached, we reply:
In the case of a substitute for a substance, it should consist of that substance.

When there is this substitute for a substance—as in the statement, "They go to the final bath with the chaff and the scrapings"—it should consist of that substance; that is, it should consist of the substance of the chaff and the scrapings.
Why? Because of the connection with the direct Vedic statement (śruti).
The *tuṣanikāsa* is directly heard in the scripture (*pratyakṣaśruta*), whereas the *puroḍāśa* is inferential (*ānumānika*),
being obtained through extension (*atideśa*).
But is it not the case that the *puroḍāśa* is also directly heard by name?
Although it is directly heard [in the scripture], it is obtained only in a general sense;
however, the *tupanikāsa* is obtained specifically.
And the general is set aside by the specific.
Moreover, by indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) would be understood, whereas by direct statement (*śruti*), it is the *tuṣanikā* (husks).
Between direct statement and indication, direct statement is more powerful.
Therefore, the substance is the *tuṣanikā*.
Now, as for what was said— that it is not enjoined by the *avabhṛtha* rite because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)—
to that we reply: if, setting aside the *avabhṛtha*, it were enjoined by means of the *tuṣanikāsa* (the husks), then indeed there would be a syntactical split.
An unprecedented *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is heard in which the substance is husks;
likewise, it would contradict the injunction of a qualified action.
Furthermore, if the husks were not being enjoined, that substance would be merely for the sake of a purpose [other than the sacrifice].
Therefore, it has *tuṣapinākī* as its substance.
However, in the absence of a specific injunction, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) [is used], because that is its natural material.
If no substance were explicitly heard in the text here, then the sacrificial cake would be used as the substance by virtue of being its natural material.
But here, the *tuṣanikāsa* (husk-scattering) is directly heard in the text; therefore, it is not the *puroḍāśa*.
For Śabara says: "By the injunction of a new ritual act, even many [subsidiaries] are enjoined;
otherwise, there would be the fault of the word *tuṣanikāsa* being meaningless."
The *puroḍāśa* is set aside by that which is prescribed as qualified by it;
for, having heard the husks, it is enjoined specifically.

However, the *puroḍāśa* cake is obtained through the word "avabhṛtha" used in a secondary (figurative) sense, which also encompasses all the characteristics (*dharma*) of the *avabhṛtha*. Therefore, it is set aside (*bādha*).
This [discussion] follows from the context of the previously mentioned ritual preceded by the Soma sacrifice.

Because the words "husks" (*tuṣa*) and "scum" (*niṣkāsa*) are primary and thus restricted to a specific scope, they leave no room for other applications; consequently, the *puroḍāśa* cake—though obtained through the word "avabhṛtha" in its secondary sense which applies to other characteristics—is set aside, and thus it does not serve as the substance (*dravya*) for that [rite].

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: when there is an injunction for a *tuṣanikāsa* (husk-scraping) substance, that very substance must be taken because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

For, in the absence of an explicit injunction regarding the substance, since the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) belongs to the Soma sacrifice as its archetype (*prakṛti*), the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) would be obtained from that [archetype].
Thus: "In that case, the substance is the *puroḍāśa*, joined with the husk-scraping."
When [the Avabhṛtha] is reached, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is [established] by extension (atideśataḥ) through the word "Avabhṛtha."
In this case, because of the direct scriptural instruction regarding the *tuṣopavāpa* and the *kapālāni*,
there is a sublation of the *puroḍāśa* which would have been obtained through extended application (*atideśa*).
Furthermore, even according to the Bhaṭṭa school's theory of extended application (*atideśa*), there is no extended application of its own substance—the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*).

This is because the substance specifically prescribed by the direct injunction (*aupadeśika*)—namely, the husks (*tuṣanikāsa*)—sublates the substance obtained through extended application, which is indicated only figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) and generally prescribed.
(This point is established in *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 7.3.4.12–16).
Maṇḍana: "The substance explicitly mentioned here is what is to be offered.
Śaṅkara: "That substance is not the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake).

My view is that for the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* sacrifice, there is a disposal (*pratipatti*). Furthermore, when there is an expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), its extension (*atideśa*) is established through association with the sacrifice produced by *soma*, according to the principle of the *niṣkāsa*, *avabhṛtha*, and *vājina* sacrifices."

Kau. 3|2|16|38, p. 297: The word *niṣkāsa* signifies only that which remains; by this, that which is attached to the *ulā* is expressed. Bhā. 11|2|16|67: "He recites the *niṣkava*" refers to the act of offering the *śastra*, not a subordinate act (*guṇa-karma*).
Bhā. 2|1|5|13–29: *Niṣkraya* is the making of one's own [something] belonging to another by the payment of its price.
In the case of the *niṣṭhā* (perfective) suffix, there is again the cultivation [of the result] at the conclusion; this is the "maxim of the king and the barber's son."

Vārttika 9|1|2|2: *niṣpakvam* refers to butter that is slightly melted so as to be poured upon the head. For example, in the case of the *nigadas*, the requirement for low tone (*upāṃśutva*)—which would otherwise apply because they are *yajus* formulas—is set aside by the rule for loud recitation (*ujjaistvena*). VI. 6|3|2. Om. The Maxim of Water and Milk (*nīrakṣīranyāya*). This maxim applies where there is a need for the discrimination between the real and the unreal. Just as when water and milk are mixed, they are not perceived [as distinct], so too the real Brahman and the unreal, false things such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, when perfectly blended and attained to identity, are not perceived.

Just as when milk and water are mixed together, no birds except for the swan are able to separate them, saying "this is the milk" and "this is the water," so too, no one—not even a scholar—is able to know what is true and what is thus, except for the Paramahaṃsa who possesses discernment; this is the intended meaning. As for the occasional [observance], it follows from the subsequent [text].
Regarding the term *uttarayogāyatāni*, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that the word *uttara* denotes a number;
however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the two verses recited in the *Uttaragrantha* which follow the *yoni* are to be understood by the word *uttara*.
And because of the unity of purpose, there is the repetition of that [sāman].
In the Agnihotra, by the words "with the two following [verses] in the Gāyatrī meter," only those two *ṛc*s recited in the *Uttarā* collection are to be taken.
And it is upon such a triplet (*tuc*) that the repetition of that *rathantara* and other *sāmans* would constitute "the repetition of that."
Because the word *tuca* signifies a single unitary meaning, its status as having a single referent is established;
thus, the word *tat* (it) is appropriate when applied to a triad of verses recited within a single textual section,
but not when applied to three verses recited elsewhere in different places.

Therefore, the established conclusion is that by the word "uttarā" (the latter), only those two [verses] recited in the *Uttara-grantha* are to be understood. According to the principle stated in *Jaimini Sūtra* 6.3.1.10, "But the occasional [rite] is a modification of the archetypal [rite], because of a specific connection," the optional fire-altar (*kāmya-agni*) will be a modification of the obligatory one (*nitya*).
Bhāṣya 12.4:
"But the occasional [rite] belongs to the archetype; its modification [belongs] to the ectype because of a specific connection.
This is a counter-exception to the exception stated previously.

In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard [in scripture]: "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a *godohana*," and regarding the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma (*āgneyīya paśu*), it is stated: "A *vailva* [wooden vessel] for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Here, a *godohana* is the vessel from which the cow is milked for the purpose of the obligatory *agnihotra* or the *sānnāyya* offering at the *darśa*. Since that *godohana* and the *vailva* [vessel] have their requirements satisfied by the cup known as *camasa* and by [vessels made of] *khadira* wood and so forth, they would—by the principle of being already provided with a connection—be relegated to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) which stands outside the rule (*utsūtra*). To this, the author of the Sūtras provides the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "tu" (but) indicates a counter-exception to an exception.

That which is occasional (*naimittika*), produced by means of a specific occasion (*nimitta*) according to the fivefold sequence, should take the place of the *namasya* in the modification of the *camasa* cup within each respective primary rite (*prakṛti*), namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). This is due to a distinction in conjunction, specifically because of the difference between the conjunction of the permanent and the occasional, and the difference between the conjunction of the general and the particular.
The *camasa* (wooden cup) is permanent (*nitya*), while the *godohana* (milk-pail) is occasional (*naimittika*).
The context (*prakaraṇa*) is general, whereas the occasion (*nimitta*) is specific. The permanent is set aside by the occasional, and the general is set aside by the specific.
Similarly, regarding the sacrificial animal, *dāridrya*, *pālaśa*, and *rohitaka* are mentioned as general options for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*),
while the *vilva* is specifically prescribed for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
Therefore, both the *godohana* vessel and the *vilva* tree find their application only in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), not in the modified rite (*vikṛti*).
An occasional rite (naimittika) does not have the same injunction as a constant rite (nitya).
Bhāṣya 3.6.12.136: An occasional rite is more extensive than a constant rite.
"For indeed, everything is prescribed as permanent when no contradiction has arisen;

however, that which is occasional (naimittika) is characterized by being the object of repeated practice and so forth. Furthermore, "In the general performance [of rituals], everything is prescribed as permanent."
But the conditional [injunction] applies to a specific case; therefore, it is more powerful than that.
"Or [it is] occasional; it is inserted into the archetype. (Bhāṣya on PMS 3.6.1.10, p.
"Or the occasional [element], because of its connection with the agent, since the indicative mark has that as its cause. (PMS 3.6.1.10).
The word "vā" (or) serves to exclude the reason and the proposition stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The term "naimittika" (occasioned) expresses the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the word [denotes] its primary application as the occasion.
The phrase "due to connection with the agent" means that the connection with the agent is possible only at the very moment of the first application of the word.

"Of the indicative mark" (*liṅgasya*) means of that indicative mark which is explained as being in grammatical apposition with the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*). "Because it is caused by that" means because it is caused by the first performance.
(This is the summary of the *Sudhā*.)
This is contained in the present Sūtra.
For an occasional (naimittika) rite does not apply to the mere essential form of the action, but rather only to that specific performance in which the occasion has arisen.
Consequently, when it is performed in another performance, there is no perfection of the rite.
Occasional rites are not performed as part of the regular daily practice.
Because it is a modification (*vikāra*), that which is occasional (*naimittika*) should be subordinate to the seasonal (*ṛtu*) primary.

Commentary: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there is an occasional rule: "One should perform the *Bārhadgira* as the *Brahmasāman* for a Brāhmaṇa, the *Pārṣadya* for a Rājanya, and the *Rāthautrājīya* for a Vaiśya.

Likewise, regarding the fire-altars (*agni*), there is an occasional rule: "One who has built the first [altar] consisting of a thousand [bricks] should build; one who has built the second should build with two thousand; one who has built the third should build with three thousand."

Likewise, regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a cow-milking vessel; one desiring spiritual luster with a bronze vessel; one desiring stability with an earthen vessel. These are occasional (naimittika) injunctions. Regarding them, there is a doubt: are these very same vessels intended for the obligatory (nitya) purpose, or is there something else for that purpose? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? That these very same vessels are intended.
Why? Because in this context, the *brahmasāman* and so forth must necessarily exist;
for they have been enjoined and require proximate means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), yet these [means] do not exist [for them here].
Various specific means have been prescribed for various specific purposes.
The occasional (naimittika) rites are situated nearby.
By these, being present and relevant, these [other requirements] are rendered free from expectancy; such is the principle.
How so? For the occasional rite is understood from the sentence as being proximate, and nothing else is heard.

Whatever fault there is in [assuming] what has been heard, that very same fault exists in the postulation of what has not been heard. He says: "But surely those [passages] mentioned in the context are for the purpose of providing a cause.
It is replied: [True].
This is not a fault;
for even that which is undertaken for one purpose may be connected with another purpose.
Just as jars are brought forth for the sake of grain, yet water is drunk from them and used for ritual rinsing as well.
The same should be understood here as well;
or rather, this very [statement] constitutes an intermediate sentence here, such as: "One should pour out [the water] by means of a milking vessel."
Therefore, it brings about the performance [of the sacrifice] for one who desires cattle by means of the *godohana* vessel;
and it is not possible to override what is directly stated in the scripture (*śruta*).
Furthermore, this expression "for one desiring cattle" is intended to apply to one who desires cattle because it is possible [to do so], and not to preclude the meaning of the intermediate sentence.
Nor can it be said that the "presently being traversed" (gamyamāna) is not intended [to be expressed] without a reason;
for there are indeed sentences that reside in two [meanings], such as "the dog runs away from here" (*daveṭo dhāvati*) and "go to Alambuṣā" (*alambuśānāṃ yāta*).
Therefore, it follows that only occasional rites (naimittika) can serve the purpose of the obligatory (nitya).
This being the position reached, we reply:
the occasional rite, as it is heard in scripture, must be something distinct for the sake of the seasonal sacrifice (ṛtu).
Why? Because it is a modification (*vikāra*).
The meaning is that it is heard in the specific [text].
For in that specific instance, an occasional (*naimittika*) rule is heard.
Therefore, in the absence of that specific distinction, it cannot be as stated—
that they must necessarily be performed.
This is not a fault.
They will certainly be performed because they are mandatory.
As for the objection that a means prescribed for one [rite] cannot be used for others, there will be no fault, as it will be prescribed generally.
What is that? The *abhīvarta* is the *brahmasāman*; the fire mentioned in the eighteenth mantra; and the vessel for the *praṇayana* rite dedicated to Varuṇa.
Now, as for what was said—that the *Brahmasāman* and other such elements will be connected with the occasional (*naimittika*) rites that are proximate and under discussion—we say: no.
For the *Bṛhadrathantara* and others do not constitute the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Now, it might be argued that these are connected with the *stotras* and so forth belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
This too is untenable.

For although the *stotras* and so forth belong to the archetype and are permanent, nevertheless, they are heard in the scriptural statement (*vākya*) as being connected with specific conditions (*nimitta*), and thus they apply only to those [sacrifices] such as the Bārhadratha.
Therefore, in each such case, [the injunction] is eternal as opposed to that which depends on other causes.

Now, as for what was said— that even the *godohana* vessel, being obtained through a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākya*), cannot be bypassed, and it is impossible to assume it unintended without a specific reason—
this is because it belongs to both [contexts].
It is said:
[the term] is not intended [to be taken] as a cause.
What is the reason? For this does not occur simultaneously—namely, the expression of the meaning by the complete [sentence] and by the intermediate sentence.

How so? The verb "he brings forth" (*praṇayati*), being preceded by the prefix *pra* and containing an injunctive suffix, enjoins by direct audition (*śruti*) the meaning residing within its own word. It also enjoins by direct audition the connection between the *godohana* vessel and the act of bringing forth, and by syntactical connection (*vākya*) the connection between the *godohana* and other factors. However, as for the connection between the fruit and the *godohana* vessel, that occurs by syntactical connection alone, setting aside the force of direct audition.

Now, it would be appropriate for the injunction to establish a connection between the *praṇayana* (the act of carrying forward) and the *godohana* (the milking vessel), etc., on the one hand, and the result, on the other. For in that case, the sentence would not be split by the expression [of two distinct acts]. However, [in the present case], the sentence would be split even more severely.
This is not indeed that same principle.
As for such cases as "the dog runs," there might be an understanding of a secondary meaning based on the comprehension of a qualifier;
but here, a specific distinction is understood.
The utterance of the word expressing desire (*kāmapada*) would be considered here as being directly stated (*śrauta*).
If the connection of the milking of cows (*godohana*) and so forth with the action were intended to be expressed, the word expressing desire would be a mere error.
Nor is this a case of negligence;
nor is the connection with the word *kam* appropriate when the meaning of the intermediate sentence is intended to be expressed. Therefore, the sentence has two referents.
In this case, only the connection with the milking of cows and so forth is stated; it cannot be intended for the sake of an obligatory (nitya) rite.
This applies everywhere. [The opponent says:
The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is formed by not seeing that the cups (camasa) and other vessels serve a visible purpose.
However, some say: having disregarded the cup of fruit-juice (*phalacamasa*), this is a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) [made by way of a hypothetical inquiry].

He states the prima facie view: although the *godohana* vessel and others are heard to be for the sake of a result, nevertheless, because they are present [in the mind] and thus recur [to the context], they are connected with the performance as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) as well.
Alternatively, they are grasped by the context even without [actual] performance.

The meaning is that what is called the "modified" (*vaikṛta*) sublates the "natural" (*prākṛta*).

For the modified (*vaikṛta*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the archetypal (*prākṛta*) is based on inference (*ānumānika*); therefore, the archetypal is sublated by the modified.

Here too, because it is impossible to enjoin multiple things by means of a restatement of the morning sacrificial fee (*prātardakṣiṇā*), a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is indeed accepted in this case.
"Spun again" (*punarakhyūtam*) means that which was torn and then mended by sewing; "yoked again" (*punarakhyūtaḥ*) means that which had broken and then been repaired.

The *nyūṅkha* are specific types of mantras used in the *śastras*. Bhaṭṭa [in his commentary on Jaimini] 9.2.27, section 3, states that the form of the *nyūṅkha* is as follows; the Atharvaṇa says: "The second vowel, the syllable *o*, three morae long, acute-accented, repeated thrice."
And above each of those, there are immeasurable or five half-morae (*ardhakāra*) that are unaccented (*anudātta*);
however, for an accented (*udātta*) syllable, there are three.
The meaning of this is: one should perform the vowel *o* as the second accent of the first and subsequent quarters of a verse (*ṛkpāda*) three times.
One should pronounce each *o*-kāra with three morae (*trimātra*) and as acute (*udātta*).

Then, above that *o*-kāra, one should pronounce an unlimited number of *o*-kāras—specifically five according to the ritual manual (*yājñikapaddhati*)—each with half a mora (*ardhamātrika*) and as grave (*anudātta*).
However, in that case, one should utter only three such grave half-mora *o*-kāras above the final third *o*-kāra.
Thus, this much—the form of a collection consisting of sixteen syllables—is one *nyūṅkha*.
And the example for that is found in the very same place: the first quarter-verse of the *prātaranuvāka*, namely, "O wealthy waters, you indeed abide in wealth."
